en: The Śāradātilaka, First Chapter: Salutation to Him whose body is eternal bliss, by whom— through the fifty phonemes flowing forth incessantly in succession— this entire universe, consisting of moving and unmoving beings, is pervaded in the form of both word and meaning.
May that splendor of the Lord of Speech—the abode of the moon—which the virtuous call the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) and which is the inner consciousness—protect you perpetually.

May the auspicious side-glance of Bhavānī bring prosperity to you—she who, out of a fondness for the wonder of curiosity, repeatedly gazes at Śrīkaṇṭha as he is intensely absorbed in his *tāṇḍava* dance; a glance that is languidly playful like a wave of the milk-ocean gently swaying, and in which an emotion has arisen through her repeated observation.

May that Śaiva splendor—which is served by sages headed by Sanaka and others, which is accessible through yoga, imperishable, and the primordial source; which destroys transmigratory existence and is the essence of the investigation into the core of the Vedas—bestow joy upon my mind.
May the speech of Bhartṛhari, which is permeated by devotion and whose playful expression of words is exceedingly rare, flourish within your memory for your welfare.
In accordance with the instructions of my gurus, this commentary on the *Padārthadarśa* is composed by Rāghava within the *Śāradātilaka Tantra*.
Whatever has been stated here that has come down through tradition and is consistent with the scriptures of mathematics, the virtuous should examine it.
If a slanderer should become a corrupter, that corruption does not constitute a fault;
for it is the transformation that brings about the defect, whereas one's inherent nature is indeed difficult to abandon.
The Lord of Wealth (Kubera) taught all the Śrutis for the sake of heaven and liberation to those beings bound by the fetters of worldly existence;
furthermore, it is well known that other Smṛti scriptures and the like possess authority because they are rooted in them and expound their meaning.
But how can this Āgama-smṛti have such a root?
The Śāradātilaka states:
Furthermore, when it is argued that heaven or even liberation will result specifically from those very [means] when they are properly contemplated—so what is the use of this [knowledge]?—we reply:
"He (the Self) thought: 'May I become many; may I procreate.'"

And likewise, beginning with "Seek to know that from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at death," and concluding with "All this is indeed this Self; bliss, verily, these beings are born from, by bliss, once born, they live, and into bliss they enter at death," and so forth—this entire section is summarized as such. Now, [the marks of a scripture's unity are]: the opening (upakrama), the conclusion (upasaṃhāra), repetition (abhyāsa), novelty (apūrvatā), fruit (phala),...
Exegetical praise (arthavāda) and logical consistency (upapatti) are the indicators for determining the intended meaning (tātparya).

Because this has been stated, the meaning established by the scriptural passages through both the opening and the conclusion is as follows: the Supreme Brahman itself—whose nature is supreme bliss, whose essence is eternally pure, conscious, and free from attributes, and which possesses as its auxiliary the beginningless and indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by its own illusory power (*māyā*)—creates the entire universe as a manifestation (*vivarta*) of its own self. Now, one might ask: "Granted that Brahman is the creator of the universe, for what purpose is the acceptance of beginningless *avidyā*? If this is asked, the answer is no;
for without that [ignorance], causality itself would be impossible for that Being who is devoid of attachment (*asaṅga*).
Likewise, both Śruti and Āgama also declare this meaning:
"Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā)," and "For Śiva, being devoid of power (śakti), is not able to do anything."

Thus, when the world had come into being, sentient beings—bound by the snares of their own karma, lacking self-knowledge, and fallen into the stream of birth and death—were unable to cross the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
Observing them in such a state, out of supreme compassion, [the Lord], assuming certain limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), taught all the Vedas (*śrutis*).
Within those Vedas, there is a threefold division according to the distinction between ritual action (*karma*), meditative worship (*upāsana*), and Brahman (*brahma*).
Among these, the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) has been correctly expounded by Jaimini and others;

this section on meditation (*upāsanākāṇḍa*) by Nārada and others; and the section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*) by the venerable Vyāsa and others. Furthermore, its basis in the Vedas consists of both that which is based on directly perceived Vedic texts and that which is based on Vedic texts not directly perceived.
Indeed, the *Rāma-pūrvottaratāpanīya*, the *Nṛsiṃha-pūrvottaratāpanīya*, the eight-syllabled *Saura-mantra*, and the five-syllabled *Śaiva-mantra* are directly perceived as Śruti;

for in that section concerning ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), every qualified person— even one seeking liberation— is entitled to perform rites for the sake of purifying their own mind and for the removal of transgressions until the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Similarly, in the section on meditation (upāsanā-kāṇḍa) as well,
since from meditation upon the Formed (sākāra-upāsanā) there arise many fruits such as heaven and, gradually, liberation,
whereas from the section on ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa) heaven and so forth are obtained only through much greater expenditure and effort.

Even liberation from the Brahmakāṇḍa is accomplished through practice performed with diligence, continuity, and over a long period of time; it occurs only after such many births have passed, as stated in the words: "One who has attained perfection through many births then goes to the supreme goal.
Therefore, it is established that this Upāsanākāṇḍa alone, consisting of the scriptures of the Āgamas, is the more important.

In this regard, Śrī Lakṣmaṇācārya, the disciple of the venerable master Utpalācārya, [composed] the first chapter for the sake of those of small intellect and short lifespan in the present age, concerning the many ancient tantras which are extremely extensive, profound, and devoted to describing the ritual procedures for individual mantras.

Observing that this [vast] system of all mantras is difficult to fathom due to the lack of capacity among men who desire its practice, the exceedingly compassionate author, wishing to compose the *Śāradātilaka Tantra*, first composes a benediction for the sake of completing his intended work without obstacles and for its widespread propagation. Thinking that at the commencement of any desired undertaking, one desiring its completion should perform a benediction in accordance with the consensus of all cultured scholars (*śiṣṭas*), he—establishing for the instruction of his disciples a benediction characterized by the remembrance of the Supreme Deity as enjoined by the Vedic revelation inferred from the conduct of the virtuous—says, "May His splendor protect you eternally," the syntactical connection being: "May that splendor [of Him] protect you incessantly."

Since the accomplishment of the recollection of the Supreme Deity (paradevatā) is achieved by this much alone, the fact that this word [“tanmah”] requires some action indicates the presence of the Deity’s face-to-face manifestation (*sāmmukhya*) through the performance of the act of protection, which consists of bestowing the desired fruit by means of the pacification of obstacles.

In that regard, although a connection with a general action would have been expected, the specification of the object as “vo” (you) is intended to indicate the author’s compassion toward his disciples—the students who desire the faultless recitation of the work being composed.
“Vo” means “you,” that is, the disciples.
Since these [students] alone are worthy of being addressed here, and because the word *yuṣmad* (you) primarily functions as a vocative,

the Teacher— who has already known all that is to be known through his disciples— proceeded to compose this work. Once their protection for a certain period was established, it was stated [in the verse beginning with] "constantly" (*aniśam*) that, due to the impossibility of achieving uninterrupted mastery of the recitation even among the disciples of those [original students], the propagation of the work would not otherwise occur.

Furthermore, once their long-term residence [in the forest] is established, the intention is that the propagation of the text will occur through the unimpeded mastery of recitation by their disciples and even the disciples of those disciples.
In response to the inquiry, "What is that festival? he says, "The embodiment of eternal bliss" (*nityānandavapuḥ*).
That which is this eternal bliss is his body; by this, the nature of Paraśiva as non-different from Śakti is stated.

One might object: "Since it has been stated that 'in the subtle Śiva, apart from Śakti, neither name nor abode exists,' how can He—who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), unattached (asaṅga), and formless (nirākāra)—be the agent of the act of protecting? To this he says, "Lord of speech" (vācāmadhīśam). By this, His form as Sadāśiva, which is endowed with Śakti, is indicated as the teacher of speech. However, the status of being a teacher of speech also belongs to the one endowed with the adjunct (upādhi) of the four-faced Brahmā; therefore, to exclude that [possibility], he says, "whose abode is the moon" (śaśāṅkasadanam).
The "abode of the moon" (śaśāṅkasya sadanam) means the place of the moon, which is adorned by the digit of the moon;
because the primary meaning here is the creation of sound, it indicates that essential nature consisting of mantra.

From these two [letters], Viṣṇu arises, and from him Saṅkarṣaṇa; with him and the vowel *au*, the night (*niśā*)—that is, the letter *ha*—is joined. By the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in the expression "effort" (*yatna*), the form *hau* is established.
By the verse beginning with "śaśāṅka" (the moon), the *bindu* is described.

Therein, strengthening the mastery over speech and indicating the creation of sound and meaning about to be described, he declares its pervasiveness: by which this world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving, comprising both the stationary and the animate, and taking the form of sound and meaning—is pervaded in succession; by what? By the fifty letters flowing without interval—that is, by those fifty phonemes (*varṇa*) that flow incessantly and continuously, becoming manifest.

In this compound, it must be stated that there is an optional elision (*vā-lopa*) of the word *varṇa*; thus, just as in the word *svarṇa*, when *valopa* occurs, the word *arṇa* denotes "color" (*varṇa*).
Some, however, say that from "always" (*nitya*) up to "of *aṇ*" (*aṇām*) constitutes a single word.
Here, although there are fifty-one letters (*varṇa*), the number fifty is mentioned by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the relationship of proximity (*sāmīpya*).
Since the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*)— just like the impossibility of the logical connection (*anvayānupapatti*)— is accepted as a ground for *lakṣaṇā* (indication),
or else, because of the statement "The letter *ma* is the Puruṣa" and because that [Puruṣa] is its own essential nature, there is the expression "fifty" in the *Śāradātilaka*.

Alternatively, because the letter *c* consists of the conjunction of *k* and *ṣ*, its instruction is effectively included within the instruction of those two; thus, the mention of "fifty" is not redundant. Or rather, since the *visarga* is purely a power (*śakti*) and lacks the nature of the five elements, yet is the cause for the arising of all phonemes, it is excluded [from the count], and thus that statement was made.
As it has been said: "The *amāya* is either the last one or indeed the final one."
In some cases, the expression "burning" (*dāha*) is used because even within the object to be burned (*dāhya*), there is the utility of exactly that many [letters].
Alternatively, since the fifty phonemes reside precisely within the six cakras from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *ājñā*, the expression "fifty" is used.
It should be understood that between these two explanations, the distinction is established by way of the external and internal [levels].
Furthermore, because that which is internal is primary, it should be understood that the scripture everywhere employs the primary [designation].
By this, the *antarmātṛkānyāsa* is also indicated; that will become clear in the final chapter (*antyapaṭala*) during the discussion of Kuṇḍalinī.
Therefore, it is also indicated that everything elaborated from the second chapter up to the twenty-fourth chapter is a modification (*vikāra*) of Mātṛkā.

Now, one might object: since it will be stated that "Sadāśiva is all-pervading," and since he is all-pervading by his very nature, why should there be a dependence on causes such as "by whom" or "from what"? This is true;
he is indeed [all-pervading] by his very nature.

However, regarding its all-pervasiveness, the statement here that it is the "cause consisting of fifty letters flowing without interruption" is intended to highlight the primacy of the creation of sound (*śabda*) according to this scripture.

Furthermore, although it was previously stated that [the Lord] is characterized by some limiting adjunct of power (*śakti*), the expression "the sovereign of speech" (*vācām adhīśam*) implies that even the statement here regarding the letters pervading the form of meaning does so only after first pervading the nature of the sound itself; thus, there is a mention of sequence.
The pervasion of those [words] over sound-forms is indeed possible;
however, the pervasion over object-forms must be understood as applying to every object whatsoever, because of the rule that all objects are manifested by words.
As it was said by the venerable Bhartṛhari:
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all this knowledge is perceived as permeated by speech.
Thus;
or rather, this was stated by relying on the view of those for whom there is no difference between word and meaning, as he himself has said:
"The distinction of the single self alone is such that word and meaning do not exist separately."
Thus,
for this very reason, the identity of the mantra and its deity is established in the Mantraśāstra;
for this same reason, the extraction of the Sadāśiva-mantra was presented previously.

Alternatively, because it is permeated by *śakti*, its pervasion of the form of the word (*śabda*) should be understood as its aspect of *śakya* (the signified), and its pervasion of the form of the object (*artha*) as its aspect of Śiva;

as it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "The beloved of Śaṅkara sustains the entirety of the collection of words, while the one whose crest is the charming moon sustains the entire nature of objects."
Thus,
in this view, the instrumental case is to be understood as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa);
its status as an indicator, moreover, is due to those [elements] arising from that.

Reinforcing the very primacy of the creation of sound, he says: "The consciousness residing within those of meritorious deeds is called *śabdabrahman*"; the meaning is that the wise ones call it such. "The consciousness of all beings is *śabdabrahman*"—thus ends the first chapter.

Because it is stated [in scripture], "This is my thought," and because that [Bindu] is all-pervasive, and because a portion of it alone constitutes the consciousness of all living beings, it is indeed possible for the Pure Brahman to possess the nature of Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman).
Furthermore, since Sadāśiva also arises from that very Bindu from which Śabdabrahman originates, this too is possible.

In this regard, the expression "Śabdabrahman" refers to the creation of sound, while "Sadāśiva" refers to the creation of objects; this is the specific distinction. From the supreme, differentiated moon-like source, there arose an unmanifest sound;
those proficient in all the Agamas call that "Śabdabrahman."
Then, from Śambhu, who is of the nature of the Bindu and the bond of time, and who is of the nature of Kalā, there was born Sadāśiva, the witness of the world, the all-pervading one.
This is because it will be stated [later];
or else, the connection should be made by way of the relationship between cause and effect:

since those of virtuous deeds have declared that the consciousness contained within [the heart] is the *Śabdabrahman*, therefore the world is pervaded by that [consciousness] through the fifty letters flowing without interruption.
Having attained that form of Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings,
it manifests through the nature of phonemes, distinguished by prose, verse, and other such forms.
Since this will be stated [later],
others, however, interpret it differently:
that which is the nature of Paramaśiva, the Vedāntins who have performed meritorious deeds call "Brahman" by that very word.
This is the meaning:
that which we call Paramaśiva is called Brahman by them; thus, there is only a difference in terminology.
In reality, however, we also accept exactly as they do that its essential nature consists of eternal bliss and other such qualities.

What is that Lord of Speech like? Since the Lordship of Speech is well-established by such scriptural passages as, "The Vedas are His very breath," it should be applied there [to Him] as far as possible: that this world is pervaded by the fifty meanings flowing incessantly from Him, who is the Lord of Speech, preceded by His thought. This is because the Veda consists of phonemes (*varṇa*).

Alternatively, since in this scripture both the creation of sound and the creation of meaning arise from Kuṇḍalinī alone, and since she is declared to be the Supreme Deity (paradevatā) in the statement "Kuṇḍalī is the Supreme Deity," it is appropriate to remember her alone; thus, by the word *mahaḥ*, Kuṇḍalinī is expressed as being of the nature of light (*tejas*), according to the statement:
"The all-pervasive Lord consists of that which is composed of the light of the sun, moon, and fire.
Of what nature is she? She is one whose body is eternal bliss (*nityānandavapuḥ*).

He himself will describe the nature of Kuṇḍalī in the final chapter with the words, "Consisting of eternal bliss, raining down a shower of supreme nectar," and so forth. By means of this Kuṇḍalī, the world—which consists of both sound and meaning—is pervaded by the perishable body (*jagat-vinaśvara-śarīra*). This is because she generates sound through the forms of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī; thus, by the metaphorical application of cause to effect, she is of the nature of sound. Furthermore, because she is the object of experience, she possesses the nature of meaning (*artharūpa-svabhāva*); and because she proceeds toward the non-transient (*acara*)—the earth element being predominant—by the metaphorical application of cause to effect, she is the non-transient. Thus, she pervades the perishable world-body.

Alternatively, by her the entire universe—the world consisting of the moving and the non-moving, whose nature is both word and meaning—is pervaded, as will be stated later: "She who possesses all limbs, whose form is the universe, and who is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. (Śāradātilaka).
By whom? By those from whom fifty phonemes flow without interruption; for it will be stated that "the garland of fifty phonemes, multiplied by fifty wives, produces [this]";

the meaning is that the virtuous ones, the meritorious souls, the *tattvavits* (knowers of reality), call her the one consisting of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahmamayī*). She gives birth [to Kuṇḍalinī], for it will be stated: "The all-pervasive Kuṇḍalinī consists of the Word-Brahman."
Consciousness is of the nature of the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
this very point will be stated [later] with the words, "And therefore she is of the nature of consciousness.
The term "internal" means situated within the *suṣumnā*.

Because it is said to be "situated within the hollow space between the head and the staff," it is the abode of the moon; because it moves through the thousand-spoked [wheel] and resides within the lunar orb,
it is the sovereign of speech, being the source of all sounds and the originator of all mantras.
Likewise, this very [author] will state: "Awakened as the soul of the universe, she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra.
Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the sovereign of speech, having the form of the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatā), according to the statement:
"She who is called Kuṇḍalinī is declared to be the power (Śakti) known as Āī."

Alternatively, since Sarasvatī is the presiding deity (devatā) for the present work at its commencement, by recollecting her alone, the manifestation of the work will occur; furthermore, because the mantras of Sarasvatī themselves are to be stated at the very beginning of this book,
it is therefore most appropriate to recollect the deity Sarasvatī.
May that splendor, the sovereign of speech—the radiant energy of Sarasvatī—protect you.

Alternatively, by the phrase "the sovereign of speech," it is stated that the *vāgbhava* syllable alone constitutes the mantra of Sarasvatī. Chanting this, the best of men on earth obtains the perfection of the nectar-like essence of sublime speech known as *vāgbhava*.
Since it has been said thus, what kind of abode of the moon is that? By this [epithet], meditation on her as having the digit of the moon as her crest-ornament is expressed;
as they say: "May she whose crest-jewel is radiant with a fragment of the moon held therein grant you immediate success in speech."
Furthermore, it is called *Ānanda* because it constantly and at all times gladdens; thus, "Ānanda" means that whose body generates bliss.
The meaning is that it produces delight for practitioners through the radiance of its eloquent sayings (*sūkti*), which are as flavorful as the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*).
And so, in the *Sarasvatī-stava*, the Teacher says: "In the dwelling of joy, clothed in silken garments, adorned with pearl ornaments..."

Thus, what kind of consciousness is contained within? By this, the subtle [power] called Parāpathyā, also known as Parā, has been described; as they say: "The subtle speech, which never departs, is said to be the light of one's own essential nature."
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "The subtle Kuṇḍalinī in the center is considered the supreme, consisting of pure light."
By that Great Sound (*mahāsā*), which consists of the fifty letters (*varṇa*) flowing without interruption, the world—whose nature is both word and meaning—is pervaded.
Here, by the phrase "by the fifty letters," *paśyantī* in the form of letters is expressed; by the phrase "whose nature is word and meaning," *madhyamā* in the form of words is expressed.
That greatness of Sarasvatī which the virtuous call the *Śabdabrahman*—
here, by the term *Śabdabrahman*, the Vedas are meant;
thus, the meaning is "consisting of the Vedas."

This has been stated by the venerable author of the Vārttika in the section on the "Grahas": "That which is called Śabdabrahman, the scripture of the Vedas, is what is referred to by the name 'Veda'";
thus ends the first chapter.

By this, *vaikharī* in the form of sentences has been described, as they say: "We worship the Mistress of Speech, whose fourfold substrates— sound (*dhvani*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*)— exist through her subtle and other distinctions."

Thus it is said elsewhere: "Because she is intensely eager for the playful manifestation of the letters from A to Kṣa, that Fourth (Turīyā), consisting of the Vedas and other sciences, triumphs after having embraced the three worlds."
Others, however, the authors of the *Tvac*, say that the extraction of the *Bhairavī* mantra has been performed;
it is as follows:
"May that great glory of the Puruṣa protect you."

Furthermore, what is its nature? It is indestructible and imperishable. It has an eternal body of bliss; it is the eternal Puruṣa, and thus the letter *ha*. Because it consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) or because it generates bliss, it is *ānanda*, which is Śakti. By this, he [the Puruṣa] is meant. These two constitute his *vapuḥ* (body).
By this, it is stated that these two exist even within the three seed-syllables (*bīja*).
"Antaḥ" means the middle, specifically the central seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*).

What is that like? It is "krama," which, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), means that which devours (*atti*) the letters *ka*, *ra*, and *ma*—namely, the letter *ka*. Below that is the letter *la*.
"By that, there is grasping"—for this very reason, O Maheśānī, there is an equality between *ra* and *la* even in *saṃhitā*.
Thus, below that is the letter *ma*, which is Puruṣa; by that, [there is] *ha*.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that in which the letter *ra* (repha) has gone to the end—that is, joined at the end.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "attained by *vi*" (*vyāptavi*), where *vi* signifies the number four—the fourth vowel (*ī*)—and by that it is attained or grasped;
here, the intended convention of the author of this work, Vāraruca, is meant.
This will become clear in the second chapter:
"And [the term] 'nañ' should be understood as 'void' (śūnya); this is the convention of Vāraruca.
Therefore, it is void because its nature is that of a bindu, and thus it has emerged from the bindu."
By this, the six-peaked middle seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*) has been extracted;
for this very reason it will be stated: "The mantra of Tripurā consists of six peaks.
Having thus described the middle seed-syllable, since the letters *ha* and *sa* have already been mentioned in the first seed-syllable, the letter *ai* should likewise be joined [to form the second].
"What is the first lunar mansion?"— by this, the first seed-syllable situated in the *bindu* has been extracted.

What is the nature of the other [term] consisting of "word" (*śabda*) and "object" (*artha*)? Here, by the word "word" (*śabda*), sound and the rest are understood; the word "object" (*artha*) denotes a sense-field (*viṣaya*).
Thus, "sound and the rest as sense-fields" refers to the ten [objects], and by that number ten, the vowel *au* is indicated. That which has that form is thus described.
Furthermore, according to the convention stated by Vāraruci—"the movement of the limbs is from left to right"—the letter *ta* represents the number six.
Regarding the statement, "The limbs [are formed] by the letters ending with the *piṇḍa*," since the letter *ya* ends in *nya*, it constitutes one limb;
thus there are sixteen [limbs],
and in this way the third seed-syllable is extracted, including the *visarga*.

This has been stated in the *Siddheśvarīmatatantra*: "There are three *haṃsa* [syllables] joined with the dental *sa*; they are differentiated by the vowels of the Vasus (8), the oceans (4), and the Paṅkti (5).
The last one is accompanied by the *visarga*, the other two are with the *bindu*, and the middle one is joined with Brahmā (1), Indra (1), Hara (3), and Agni (3)."
Thus, the meaning of this is:
*vasu* refers to the number eight.
The ocean is the number four;
likewise, according to Amara, "paṅkti" refers to the meter of ten syllables and also to the number ten— thus,
*paṅkti* is the number ten.
The three *haṃsa*s are the three *ha* syllables; according to the *Śāradātilaka*, what are they like? They are joined with the dental *sa*.
Likewise, in sequence, by means of the vowels *vasu* (8), *abdhī* (4), and *paṅkti* (5)—excluding the neuter vowels—the eighth is *ai*, the fourth is *ī*, and the tenth is *au*.
These are joined with the four vowels beginning with *ṛ*; for it has been stated that "the quartet which is in the middle of the vowels is neuter.
Thus, setting aside the neuter vowels, one should understand that the eighth vowel among those accompanied by the bindu and visarga is *aikāra*, and the tenth is *aukāra*.
He states the distinction: the third [syllable] is joined with *visarga*, while the first and second are accompanied by *anusvāra*.

Furthermore, the middle [syllable] is joined with *viriñci* and so forth—*viriñci* being *ka*, *indra* being *la*, *hara* being *ha*, and *agni* being *ra*—joined with these, this is the six-peak (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) middle seed-syllable.

This is *Cibojā Bhairavī*, and it is also designated as *Ai* due to its independent instruction; it is "pervaded" (*vyāptam*) because of the inclusion of the word "attained" (*āpta*); and it is "of the nature of sound and meaning" (*śabdārtharūpam*) because of the employment of the word "form" (*rūpa*). It is indicated that the three vowels alone constitute the conscious mantra of this [deity], as they say: "The first seed-syllable is the eighth [vowel] of Śiva alone, and the other seed-syllable of Bhaga is the eighth [vowel] preceding [it]."
The threefold collection [of sciences] is said to extend up to the supreme head; this science of conventions is to be attained from the mouth of the Guru.
Thus, "Śiva" is the letter *u*; its eighth is *ai*.
"Bhaga" is the letter *e*; its eighth preceding [letter] is the fourth vowel (*i*).
The "head" (*śiras*) is the *bindu*; that which has this at its end is the *au* vowel.
Regarding the aforementioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), he states their nature as Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śākta respectively;
by the phrase "Lord of Speech" (*vācām adhīśam*), the first [seed-syllable] is declared to be Vāgbhava.

Sexual union (*maithuna*) consists of the moving and the unmoving (*carācarātmaka*), because the world arises from desire (*kāma*). Since the middle seed-syllable (*madhyamabīja*) is said to be the King of Desire (*kāmarāja*), and since they say that the final seed-syllable (*antyabīja*) is the *Śabdabrahman*, by this it is stated that the final [seed-syllable] is of the nature of Śakti;
for it will be stated later: "The Goddess, the mother of the three abodes, has the nature of the *Śabdabrahman*."
As it is stated in the *Siddheśvarīmata*: "The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmarāja, and the third is Śaktibīja; these bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life."
Thus, as it is said:
"The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: Om, Tat, and Sat"—this refers to the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), which is the Praṇava.
It is that by which the world, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, [is pervaded]; and because it arises from desire through sexual procreation, it is the seed of desire (Kāmabīja).
The letter *na* belongs to speech;
because it is placed together with the letter *na* during the placement of the Great Principle (*vṛhattattva*), it is the Mañca due to the placement of the principle of sound (*śabdatattva*).

"Intellect (dhīḥ) is the Lord (īśa) whose nature is power (śakti); by this [intellect], the emission (visarga)—known as the power of Māyā—is the creation consisting of all beings; [he is] the Lord," so it is said.
Thus, the word "namaḥ" is the mantra of this [deity];
it is said to be the mantra of the speaker.
As they say: "The lotus [syllable] has its middle and final vowels elided, joined with the letter 'o' and so forth, together with the bindu and nāda."
This is declared to be the Heart of the Goddess (Devīhṛdaya), shining upon the earth within the [text] beginning with *nigama* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Thus ends the first chapter.
He states the general qualification of the three seed-syllables with the word "constantly" (aniśam).
"Night does not exist where there is no 'ha' at the beginning"—this is the remainder [of the statement].
In the *Keśavādi* system of assignment, "night" is the letter *ha*, which is Śakti;
therefore, by the absence of *ha* at the beginning, it is stated that the letter *sa* occupies the initial position.

Therefore, there is the letter *sa* first and the letter *ha* afterwards; or rather, since the *bindu* of the initial seed-syllable has already been extracted by the word "nir," [the phrase] "the abode of the moon, constantly devoid of *ha*"— where "moon" (*śaśāṅka*) is the letter *sa* and "abode" (*sadana*) is its place—
indicates that the letter *sa* occupies the place of *ha*, from which the letter *ha* follows below by implication.

And it has been said: "If the Bhairavīya [mantra], preceded by Akula and Uditā, should be preceded by Kula when employed by teachers, that very same [mantra] bestows swift results on earth; it is called a Vidyā, and it must be kept strictly secret from those who are bound as cattle (paśus)."

By this, its status as both a *mantra* and a *vidyā* is stated; for it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That which begins with Śakti is a *vidyā*, while that which begins with Śiva is called a *mantra*;
initiation, consecration, and worship [performed with these] bestow enjoyment and liberation upon living beings."
Thus,
he states another general qualification for the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), meaning they are "characterized by fifty [letters].
By this, the recitation (*japa*) of the entire mantra through its interspersion with the *mātṛkā* is taught.
As they say: "One should recite this king of mantras, which is the cause of enchanting the entire world, interspersed with the Mātṛkā letters, both in direct and reverse order."

Thus, or alternatively, by this qualification, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *anta-moṭaka* mantras—such as *haha seṃ sahasaiṃ*, *hasakalahī sahakalatī*, *ahasauḥ āhasauḥ*, and so forth—is also indicated. As they have said:
"One should sequentially place the letters of the six cakras within their respective petals."
The knower of mantras should likewise bind the goddesses and the obstructors by means of the sequence beginning with the wheel.

Thus, in other instances as well, in the context of describing the *mūlādhāra*, one should place the deities Water, Fire, and Wind— either individually or with the nasal bindu (*sabindu*), possessing great power and well-known— upon the four petals of the lotus.

Alternatively, by using the word "fifty" (*pañcāśat*) through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of proximity to signify fifty-one, the phrase "indicated by them" suggests the extraction of the *dopinī* of all three seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Among these, the *dopinī* of the first seed-syllable consists of seventeen phonemes, formed by separating the consonants from the vowels.
The second seed-illuminator consists of twenty-five syllables, just as before;
the third seed-illuminator consists of nine syllables, likewise as before; thus, it comprises fifty-one letters in total.

In that regard, since the letter *kṣa* exists in both the second and third [syllables], and since only one consonant (*vyañjana*) is taken for it— because it is taught separately in the *mātṛkā*— if this were composed of two consonants, then like the letter *kṣa*, it too would not have been taught separately.
There are indeed two *bindus* belonging to those very [vowels], yet they are not counted separately,
because such a [combination] is itself considered one of the fifteen vowels; likewise, the *bindu* within the *praṇava* is included within the *praṇava*— thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
With a smile shining from within, adorned with the crescent moon as an ornament, and beautified by eyes resembling the interior of a blue lotus—
since this [description] was not counted separately as being thus [included], everything is faultless; and here,
the author has indicated the removal of this defect.
However, I shall clarify this in the Bhairavī-paṭala;
or rather, it is intended that the extraction of the Bālā-mantra has already been performed,
since that very [extraction] is the fundamental basis for the mantras of Bhairavī and the others as well.
As they say: "This origin of the Vidyā-bhūta, released from the child [state], has been taught by me; this should be understood by teachers who desire accomplishment.
It is as follows:
"Vācāmadhīśam" refers to the Vāgbhava [bīja].
"Antarmadhyam" means situated in the middle.
According to the sequence, *ka* and *ra* together with *mā*, which is Lakṣmī, form the vowel *ī*.
By means of the letter *ra*, there is the grasping of the preceding vowel;
the nasal drop (*bindu*) is thus the middle seed-syllable.

The letter *śa* is the moon (*śaśāṅka*), the letter *sa*, the vowel *au*, the letter *a*, and the letter *na* constitute the two voids (*śūnyadvaya*); by these, the visarga [is formed], because it is said:
"In the case of *neje*, the void is to be known; likewise when a solitary vowel is uttered."
If it is asked how the syllable *om* is included by the word *sat*, the answer is as follows:

since both are remembered as designations of Brahman in the statement, "The threefold designation of Brahman is remembered as *om*, *tat*, and *sat*," and because of the saying, "*sat* is declared to be *om*," the word *sat* denotes *om*.
Here, however, only the simple form of *sat*—with the subsequent vowel elided—is intended.
And that [vowel *a*] indicates the subsequent [vowel *au*] through the relation of proximity;

or rather, as the Teacher has stated: "Or it may be that the syllable *au* [arises] from the conjunction of *u* with that very [vowel *a*]," thus the vowel *o* itself indicates its own product, the vowel *au*.

Alternatively, when the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*)—as in "that which has the form of a hare (*śaśa*) in it"—then *śaśa* means the moon; by that, *śaśin* means "one who moves like a hare," i.e., the swan (*haṃsa*); or by that [suffix], it is he [the Supreme Self].
By the word *aṅga*, according to the logic of the *piṇḍa* (the whole representing its parts), the letter *a* is meant;
as in the example, "That hand of Vāmaṭṭaka is endowed with the qualities of wind," where by the word *kara* (hand) the letter *ka* is intended.
Similarly, as in the example, "The forest has six horses of Hari," where by the word *vana* (forest) the letter *va* is intended.
By the word "sat," there is only the vowel *o*;
when that is joined with the preceding [vowel], it becomes *au*, and from these two, the *visarga* arises.
[Objection: "But since the *praṇava* possesses the *bindu*, the author of the treatise mentions only the *visarga* as the final seed-syllable of *Bālā*;
and here [in the present case], both the *bindu* and the *visarga* have been extracted—thus there is a contradiction. [Reply:
No, for among the various forms of the *Bālā* mantra, in some cases the *bindu* is extracted, in some cases the *visarga*, and in some cases both the *bindu* and the *visarga* are extracted.
To indicate that as well, such an extraction has been made,
as they say in the Sanatkumāra: "The third of the eighth, joined with the fourteenth—
this indeed is declared to be the Daṇḍakuṇḍala, the Sārasvata."
Thus,
elsewhere it is said: "The entire Kula known as Sammohana is joined with that which ends in 'da' and 'ṇḍi'."
The rest is as before; this is the summary.
And since these two explanations have been composed by me under the guidance of my teacher’s words, they should be forgiven by the lords among spiritual preceptors. || 1 ||
May the inner apartments of the one who wears the crescent moon on his crest— the cause of the splendor of the three worlds— bestow blessings upon you with devotion.
I bear upon my head the gurus, whose very nature is Śiva, for they are the sole means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
The dust from whose lotus-feet brings forth the splendor of ablutions at sacred fords;

[he] praises the creative agency of Śiva, who is established therein: "May the inner apartment of the one whose crest is the new moon grant you auspiciousness with reverence"—this is the construction of the verse.
By the phrase "May he grant you prosperity even here," his compassion for the disciples is indicated;

for although in reality, according to the Śaiva philosophy, there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti, and in truth there is no difference between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.

Thus, although there is indeed the identity of Śakti and Śiva, nevertheless, because creation is impossible without a second, His form assumed for sport—the nature of a woman—is described. By this, the creation through sexual union is indicated;
likewise, His expansion is His manifestation as the cause of the world, consisting of all that is moving and unmoving.

He said to her, "In what way is she the cause of the prosperity of the three worlds? [She replied: "This world shines forth as something imagined, with an internal smile radiating from within"—this is the cause of his laughter;
or rather, it is laughter arising from a longing for the Lord.
By this, her power to agitate the Lord is indicated;

furthermore, according to the Smṛti which states, "In that harmony between husband and wife, the three goals of life flourish," the creation of the diverse world is indicated through the mutual concord of the couple. Again, of what nature is she? She who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Here, by the word *avataṃsa*, the ornament of a crown is meant;
thus it is stated in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*: "The two words *uttaṃsa* and *avataṃsa* are masculine when referring to an ear-ornament as well as a crest. Furthermore, [it is asked]: "What kind?"
By the phrase "shining with eyes like the interior of a blue lotus," a beauty that surpasses all else is described; alternatively,
by the phrase "of the one whose crest is the new moon," the mantra of Bhuvaneśī is stated.
Its extraction by means of qualifiers is the cause of the splendor of the three worlds; therefore, it is Śiva, represented by the letter *ha*.
The fire within is that which has a smile (*smita*) within—that is, the letter *ra*—and by that it is "blazing," meaning endowed with it.
In the term *indukalāvataṃsam*, the *bindu* (dot) represents the long vowel *ī*. She whose eyes are like siblings to the interior of a blue lotus (*indīvara*) is Lakṣmī; thus, there is the long *ī*.

Alternatively, her eye which is a sibling—that is, a friend—to the interior of the blue lotus is in the form of the moon, and that is on the left; hence the long *ī*. By that [long *ī*], she is "adorned" (*śobhi*), meaning endowed with it.
Thus, when combined, it is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī. || 2 ||
For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the teacher as he does the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly.
I shall speak the essence of the tantras, the auspicious Śāradātilaka,
which is the primary cause for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (4)

From such scriptural authority (*āgama*), since devotion to the Guru is understood to be an internal means for the attainment of knowledge—just like devotion to the Supreme Deity—he states the salutation to the Guru immediately after the recollection of the Supreme Deity with the words "saṃsāra...
(verse 10). The grammatical construction is: "I place upon my head the Gurus whose nature is Śiva.
"Whose nature is Śiva" (*śivasvabhāvān*) means those whose very essence is Śiva (*śivasvarūpān*).
By this it is stated that the meditation on the Guru should be performed as being the very form of each respective deity;
as it has been said: "One should not perceive the Guru as a mere mortal; for if one perceives him as such, then never at any time will there be success through mantras or the worship of deities."

Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "Therefore, having understood this, one should worship the Guru and the God in no other way than by prostrating at the three times of day and through the yoga of meditation."
Thus,
even in this state of blindness— having placed an eye upon my forehead and a digit of the moon within my two arms— I shall speak; for the Guru is honored in the mortal world.
By the phrase "I place [him] upon my head," it is stated that the meditation on the Guru should be performed upon the head;
as it has been said: "In the morning, one should meditate on the white Guru, who has two eyes and two arms, upon the head."
One should remember him with a serene face and peaceful countenance, preceded by his name.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "He who, with sattvic dispositions, always remembers the lotus feet of the glorious Guru as being situated right upon his own head, shall before long become a Khecarī."
The plural form "gurun" (to the gurus) is used for the sake of honor, or with reference to the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru;
thus is the lineage of gurus according to the author of the treatise.
“Śrīkaṇṭha, Vasumān, Śrīsomānanda, and Utpalācārya”—thus [Abhinavagupta] salutes Lakṣmaṇa; and “I revere Śrīkṣemarāja,” say his disciples.
Of what sort are they? They are the sole cause for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
It has also been stated that without this instruction from a guru, it is impossible to cross the ocean of saṃsāra;
thus says the Śruti: "A person who possesses a teacher knows," and "He should approach a guru alone.
And the Āgama also states: "For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the probe of the ointment of knowledge..."
Salutation to that glorious Guru by whom the eye was opened.
Thus he has stated the greatness of bowing to the guru with the verse beginning "rajāṃsi.
By this, it is implied that one should perform obeisance to the guru preceded by the clasping of his feet. ||3||

A listener proceeds to listen to a treatise only when its purpose and the relationship between that purpose and the treatise have been established; therefore, at the beginning of a work, the relationship must be stated along with its purpose.

Having spoken thus, in order to conform to the understanding of his disciples and while manifesting the majesty of the treatise, he states the first chapter, which serves as the cause for the engagement of the listeners:
"In this body [of the work], the creation of words and meanings, along with the sages, meters, and deities, as well as the ritual procedure for the Yantras and Mantras, is here set forth. (1.5)

He demonstrates the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*sambandha*), and the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) by means of the two verses beginning with "The essence" (*sāram*).
By the phrase "the essence of the tantras, the most excellent, and in the form of a compendium," both its worthiness of adoption and its extreme brevity are stated.
Therein, "of the tantras" refers to those of the Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, Śāktas, Gāṇapatyas, and Sauras; because it is the essence of these, it is therefore auspicious (*śubha*).
Even in its brevity of words, auspiciousness consists precisely in its capacity to convey all intended meanings;
as it will be stated [later], "Dharma, Artha, Kama," and so forth,
the name *Śāradātilaka* is indicative of that which is conducive to those ends.
*Śāra* means that which is coarse (*sthūla*), namely the fruit of karma; she who bestows that is *Śāradā*.

Alternatively, having ascended as the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), she who cuts (*dyati*) or shatters (*khaṇḍayati*) various things by being their cause is the conscious power (*cicchakti*), *Śāradā*.

Or, when *śara* is independent (*svatantra*), its state is *śāra*, which is independence; she who bestows that is the giver of supreme sovereignty by cutting through beginningless ignorance and eliminating the sense of being a limited individual soul (*jīvabhāva*).

As it has been stated by Gautama in the *Tantravyākaraṇa*: "The arrow (*śara*), the independent one (*svatantra*), the heart (*hṛdaya*), the throbbing (*sphurattā*), the supreme ruler (*parameśitṛ*), and the arrow-maker (*śāra-kṛt*)—these are the words declared to be synonyms denoting their own respective meanings."
Thus,
by stating that the tilaka is her ornament, its excellence is demonstrated.
Even there, it is not another ornament, but rather takes the form of a *tilaka* (forehead mark).
The intention is that just as a *tilaka* located on the face is the first thing seen from all sides, so too is this [the first cause].
"First" means the primary cause.
How this [work] possesses primacy has already been explained by us previously during the discussion on the connection of the text;
its subject matter is the creation of words and meanings, and so forth,
and its fruit is the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
The relationship between these two is that of the subject to be explained and the explainer;
the qualified person is one who seeks that [subject], and the relationship between this treatise and that [person] is that of the explainer and the object to be explained.
The relationship between the subject matter of the treatise and its result is that of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*);
other [relationships] such as these should also be inferred accordingly,
as they are connected with the word "together" (*saha*) by means of the three [factors].
By the sages (*munis*), who were the first worshippers and who received the *mantras* through the power of austerity and yoga,
it was stated by Gautama: "That pure-souled teacher who, having learned the *mantra* from the mouth of Maheśvara, accomplishes it through austerity, is first called a *ṛṣi*."

Thus it is said elsewhere: "That mantra by which a particular seer perceived [the truth] and by which he indeed attained accomplishment—that is declared to belong to that seer; such is the nature of the *ārṣaka* (seer-originated) [mantra]."
Thus, the etymology of the word *chanda* has been stated elsewhere: "Because it covers (*chādanāt*), it is designated as *chanda*, like two garments for a form;
in ancient times, it was indeed covered by the gods who were afraid of death."
The Śāradātilaka states: "By the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras, those meters were indeed established."
Thus it is elsewhere as well: "In former times, the gods, fearing death, recollected the *chandāṃsi* for their own concealment; they were concealed by them, and thereby became immortal."
Because it conceals, it is designated as *chandas*; everything is enveloped by the *chandases*.
Thus,
that deity which is well-known as Gāyatrī and so forth is the one specifically indicated by its respective mantra.
As it is said: "Whichever deity is specified for whichever mantra, that mantra should take on the form of that deity; its divinity is thus called 'deityhood'."
The phrase "by the deities" is also an indicator for the application (viniyoga);
its nature has been stated elsewhere: "In a former aeon, the mantras arose specifically for the sake of ritual action."
"By this, this must be performed; that is called *viniyoga*.

Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "The application (*viniyoga*) of a perfected mantra within the realms of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation according to the path of the scriptures is thus proclaimed by the wise."

The fault arising from the absence of that knowledge is stated elsewhere: "The mantra of one who does not know its application (viniyoga) becomes weak. Thus, knowledge of the meter (chandas), the seer (ṛṣi), and the deity (devatā) is absolutely required for the efficacy of the mantra.

Thus it is said in the *Māṣeya Brāhmaṇa* of the Chandogas: "Whoever, indeed, performs a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose *ṛṣi*, meter (*chandas*), deity, and *brāhmaṇa* [application] are unknown, he either strikes a stump, falls into a pit, perishes, or dies; he becomes worse off, for his meters become exhausted (*yātayāman*). But he who knows [these] for every single mantra reaches a full lifespan, becomes superior, and his meters do not become exhausted. Therefore, one should know these for every mantra. He becomes established among the *ṛṣis*, he becomes established in Brahman, and he is magnified in the heavenly world; remembering [this], he is not born again."

Kātyāyana also states: "He who studies, recites, mutters, offers oblations, sacrifices, or officiates at a sacrifice without knowing these [details], his Vedic knowledge becomes exhausted. But he who studies after having understood these—being one who knows the meaning as it truly is—his Vedic knowledge becomes most powerful; by muttering, offering oblations, and sacrificing, he attains the fruit. Thus it is said in the Āgama. Yājñavalkya also says: "The seer, the metre, the deity, and likewise the application (viniyoga)..."

This should be understood with effort, especially by a Brahmin. However, for one who performs sacrifice, study, recitation, fire-offerings, or anything else whatsoever without knowing this, the fruit thereof shall be meager. Thus is the injunction.

The eternal Śiva is to be known as both Nirguṇa (devoid of attributes) and Saguṇa (possessing attributes), characterized by the performance of nyāsa, japa, pūjā, homa, tarpaṇa, abhiṣeka, sampāta, pāta, and so forth; the word "and" (ca) indicates that these are the first [topics] of the chapter.

The one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti), while the one endowed with qualities (saguṇa) is remembered as the manifest whole (sakala). Regarding the combination of primary and secondary rites such as creation and so forth, even when expressed by a single term like "mantras and yantras," they are connected to the sages and others as appropriate;
therein, for the sage and the meter, the mantra alone is used for the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa).
The other [entities], such as deities and so forth, apply to both cases;

however, the "falling of the impact" (*sampātapāta*) applies specifically to the yantra and to those things characterized by it—namely, images, jars, stones, statues, pills, oil, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so on.
These are described as the gross forms for the worshiper of the deity.
Regarding those for whom the form is subtle, as they have said: "The deity is declared to be one's own self, delightful and possessing a universal body;

the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is the conceptualization of one's own body as being the nature of the deity; and recitation (*japa*) is rightly described as the contemplation of the form of identity with that [deity]."

Pūjā, even in the state of restlessness, is the state of non-negligence through absorption in That (Tanmayatva). Homa is considered the setting of all dualistic conceptualizations (vikalpas) within the Self. The contemplation of the mutual merging of these is known as Tarpaṇa. Abhiṣeka, however, is Vidyā; it is the Great Self itself, which is its own support. The ritual applications (prayogas) consist of the self-reflection upon the Self for the sake of the limiting adjuncts (upādhis). Worship during the junctions (sandhyās) is the abandonment of their beginning, middle, and end.
"The cessation of delusion, ignorance, and other sufferings within the Self is firm. Thus [it is said]. To introduce the account of creation, he says "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities):
Śiva, who is eternal and constant, should be known as both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities.
Regarding the nature of the former, he says "niḥ" (without).
"Other than primordial nature" means free from its connection,
because here the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is primarily intended to denote that [freedom];
thus, the meaning is "subtle."
For this very reason, because there is no referent for another word, this is not a fifth [category]; were it so, it would result in a mere restatement (anuvāda).
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "He is eternal, omnipresent, subtle, ever-blissful, and free from affliction."
"Free from modification, truthful, auspicious, and eternal—thus is Śiva to be known.

Thus it is also stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Actionless, devoid of qualities, peaceful, blissful, unborn, undecaying, ageless, immortal, unmanifest, incomprehensible, immovable, and constant; consisting of knowledge, the supreme Brahman, self-realizable, and abiding in the heart."
"Truth is known to be beyond the intellect, eternal, stainless, and partless.
Thus he describes the nature of the second [state]; "He" refers to the one with qualities (*saguṇa*), who is "with parts" (*sakala*), for "part" (*kalā*) is *prakṛti*, and he is accompanied by that.

In the Sāṃkhya system, *prakṛti*—also known by its synonym *pradhāna*—is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; therefore, it is endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*). [This is stated] in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"From the Supreme Lord, who is the entirety and whose glory is existence, consciousness, and bliss..."
"From Śakti arose Nāda, and from Nāda the emergence of Bindu"— this is the statement; however,
in the Vedānta system, this is *avidyā*, whereas in the Śiva-tantra, it is *śakti*.
And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya* and the *Prayogasāra*: "The Lord of all, who is the power of that [Brahman], is distinct from the forms of Brahmā and the others;
he is the creator, the enjoyer, and the destroyer, the possessor of all attributes, and identical with the universe.
He describes creation with the word "Being" (*sat*).

He dispels the doubt—namely, how there can be agency in creation if [the Self] is insentient due to being variegated by ignorance—by the phrase "from the glory of Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānandavibhavāt*).
By this, the meaning is that even when conditioned by ignorance, there is no loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The construction is: "All power (*śakti*) was present."
If it is asked, "How could there be power (śakti) again from that which is already endowed with power?"—the answer is true.

That power which exists in a subtle state during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) through the superimposition of consciousness (caitanya) in its beginningless form, its very state of swelling (*ucchūnāvasthā*) for the purpose of accomplishing the effects of the phenomenal world to be created—whether characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), passion (*rājasa*), or darkness (*tāmasa*) in accordance with the imbalance of the qualities (*guṇavaiṣamya*)—is metaphorically called "origination.
This statement by the author of the treatise is made by relying upon the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the origination of the existent (*sadutpatti-vāda*), and thus it should not be taken [literally].
Thus it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "Therefore, she has emerged as the eternal, all-pervading source of the universe.
And in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* as well: "By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva)."
"Then, at the beginning of creation, [the world] manifests, like oil from sesame seeds.

Thus it is said in the *Pañcarātra*: "Having thus perceived, at the beginning of creation, [Her] whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, who is the form of the substrate for the manifestation of the entire aggregate of principles (*tattva*)."
"The Supreme Person makes that eternal Prakṛti manifest.

Thus, for that very [Prakṛti], Nāda and Bindu are the forms of her state during the process of emanation. As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "Awakened by means of Nāda, she [Prakṛti] is directed toward the stainless state."

"When [Śakti] is oriented toward Śiva, she is then remembered as having the form of the Puruṣa; for that very reason, she alone is capable of creation. Thus say the teachers: "At that time, by virtue of the proximity of the light of pure consciousness, she is designated as 'Tattva' (the Principle)."
"Desiring to act, having become dense, she in some cases attains the state of a drop (*bindu*).

Thus it is said elsewhere: "The supreme power (*parā śakti*), characterized by inseparable concomitance, is the undivided power of pure consciousness; it is all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, and omnipresent. [End of] the First Chapter.
Consisting of supreme power (*para-śakti*), she is manifest; yet she is further divided into three forms.

Her divisions are proclaimed as *bindu*, *nāda*, and *bīja*. *Bindu* is of the nature of Śiva, *bīja* is Śakti, and *nāda* is declared by those learned in all the scriptures to be the union of these two. From *bindu* arose Raudrī, and from *nāda* arose Jyeṣṭhā; [and] from *bīja* [arose Vāmā].

From them arose Vāmā, the sovereign of Rudra, Brahmā, and Rāma. Possessing the nature of all the *tattvas* and endowed with the unfolding of the teachings (*śāsa*), she proceeds as the state of the *bindu*, characterized by the predominance of action (*kriyā*). Thus it was done.
The state of *nāda* was indeed indicated by the teachers who introduced the topic of *kāla*, as they said:

"Then, within the Self... (3). [The text] states that the *bindu* has a threefold nature through its form as the power of will (*icchāśakti*) and so forth, saying "the supreme" (*para*), which is directly composed of the supreme power (*paraśakti*), and thus possesses a dual nature.
Because it will be stated that "the *bindu* has the nature of Śiva," it is divided into three types;
these two, *nāda* and *bindu*, are to be understood as distinct from the previously mentioned *nāda* and *bindu*, being of the nature of their effects.
Thus it has been said: "That [state] becomes the *bindu* which is threefold. (8) Regarding the nature of the succession of the triad beginning with *bindu*, he says: "The *bindu*...

The sequence here is inverted because the *dharmins* (the subjects) have already been stated, and the intention is to state their relationship (*sambandha*), following the order of the emergence of power (*śakti*). In the previous case, the order was as follows:
*samavāya* (inherence) is the relationship, characterized by the states of the agitated and the agitator, and is the cause of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the point stated, he provides the authoritative source [pramāṇa] with the words: "by those proficient in all scriptures" (savīgamaviśāradaiḥ). || 8 ||
*Raudrī* [arises] from that; because she originates from that *bindu*, she consists of Śiva, and thus her name is etymologically appropriate (*anvarthatā*).
From *nāda* comes *Jyeṣṭhā*; since she is uttered in the middle [position], her etymological appropriateness should be understood through that very principle.
The connection is that from the seed (bīja) Vāmā was born;
it possesses its etymological significance because it consists of Śakti.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "There, the Bindu is of the nature of Śiva, and the Seed is remembered as being of the nature of Śakti."

From the union of those two arises *nāda* (sound), and from them are born the three powers (*triśakti*). [Śāradātilaka 1.18] They consist of consciousness, will, and action, and have the nature of the three trees (*vanīndu-arka*). From the supreme *bindu* being differentiated, the unmanifest self (*avyaktātman*) arose. [Śāradātilaka 1.11] *Raudrī* was produced from the *bindu*, and *Jyeṣṭhā* was born from *nāda*.
From the seed-syllable (bīja), Vāmā arose as Śakti; from those two, the three gods were born. Thus [ends verse 10].
Regarding the term *saṃjñāne*:

in the sphere of cognition (*saṃjñāna*), there are the powers of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*), whose essence is that [cognition]. Therefore, Rudra, Brahmā, and Īśvara are, respectively, the embodiments of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the power of will (*icchāśakti*), and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Although in some places the reading *jñānecchā* (knowledge and will) occurs, that is simply not according to the traditional lineage (*asāmpradāyika*).

These—the lords Rudra, Brahmā, and Rāma, who possess the nature of the moon, the forest (vanī), and the sun—are to be understood as specific states of Śakti alone, existing within the creation of sound (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*) and having the form of the *nirodhikā*, the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the *bindu*.
Their essence consists of will (*icchā*), action (*kriyā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), because they have arisen from Śakti.
And it will be said: "She is this [Śakti], whose nature is will, knowledge, and action."

Even in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it is stated: "Since they desire to know or to perform actions by their own will, there subsequently arises the power of knowledge and vision regarding those effects; for that exertion which is directed toward that [knowledge] is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); from that, the entire universe arises as supreme. Furthermore, because they [the powers] will be discussed later, it follows that Rudra emerges from that, then Viṣṇu, and then Brahmā.

Otherwise, there would also be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows; for the author will later state regarding that [line], "by the three syllables of the *praṇava*," namely the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
In that context, the components of the *praṇava*—the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*—are identical with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
This is because it will be stated later that [Brahmā] was born from the syllable *a* (*akāra*),
and because another scripture states: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are established within their respective maṇḍalas."
Therefore, in that context, the letter *A* is Brahmā in the form of the sun, while here Viṣṇu is in the form of the sun;

thus, the sequence to be described should be understood in accordance with the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*). And the author of the work will say: "She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the world consisting of words and their meanings, sustains it again by her own power in the form of the Sun."
"Carrying that entire [universe] as its very essence, it withdraws it at the end of the age; I never forget that Śāradā within my mind.

Also, in the *Gorakṣasaṃhitā*: "Will, action, and likewise knowledge—Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī—the triple power (śakti) which resides therein is that supreme light, Om. The Teachers also say: "That which, through the first three divisions ending with 'tapa'..."
With the words "from that which is being divided" (*bhidyamānāt*), he describes the origin of the Śabda-Brahman.

By the phrase "from the supreme *bindu*," it is meant that from that first *bindu*, which is the state of Śakti, there arose the unmanifest self—the indivisible, mere resonance (*nāda*) devoid of specific distinctions such as phonemes (*varṇa*). || 11 ||
The First Chapter.
18. Those proficient in all the scriptures declare that [the Absolute] is the Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman).

Others have sung that "Śabdabrahman" refers to the meaning of the word, while others say it refers to the sound itself. For neither of these two [positions] is established for them, since both are insentient.

"Consciousness is the Śabdabrahman of all beings; this is my conviction. He states its true nature with the words "sound," etc. Those who are experts in all scriptures and knowers of the meaning of all the Vedas have said: "That sound, as perfected by the Vedas, is called Śabdabrahman. (13)
Thus:

the meaning of "Śabdabrahman" is that it is the all-pervasive, Brahman-natured sound, which consists of *nāda* and *bindu*, being unfragmented (*akhaṇḍa*), unmanifest (*avyakta*), and merely the first unfolding of the Supreme Śiva from his face at the time of emanation.
And it has been said: "Sound is the cause of both word and meaning for [the Power] in whom the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) predominates."

From Prakṛti, who is of the nature of the *bindu*, the supreme Śabdabrahman arose. Now, [the author] begins to refute the internal *sphoṭa* theory—whether it be the view that the *sphoṭa* consists of both genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*)—as well as the external *sphoṭa* theory, by stating "Śabda... and so forth.
Certain teachers declare that the word-meaning, which is the internal *sphoṭa*, is Śabdabrahman.
As it has been said: "The internal *sphoṭa* is indeed partless, undivided, eternal, of the nature of consciousness, and composed of both word and meaning."

Other grammarians, however, maintain that the word—characterized as the *sphoṭa* of the sentence—is the *Śabdabrahman*, which reveals a single, indivisible meaning. This word is manifested by the utterance of each preceding phoneme and is perceived through the apprehension of the final word, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of those respective words. As it has been said: "The external form is indeed one, eternal, indivisible, and manifested as a sentence; it is either the individual *sphoṭa* (*vyaktisphoṭa*) or the generic *sphoṭa* (*jātisphoṭa*). (12)
Refuting both of those views, he states his own position with the words "Not so" (*na hi*).
In the opinion of those disputants, the establishment of those two— namely, the word and its object— is not the establishment of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*),
because both of them are insentient (*jaḍa*).
If either the word or its meaning is called *śabdabrahman*, then it would not be tenable for it to be the referent of the term "Brahman.
For the referent of the term "Brahman" consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), whereas those two [the word and its meaning] are insentient (*jaḍa*).
As it has been said: "Brahman is without beginning or end, the essence of sound, the imperishable syllable."
"From which the process of the world evolves in the form of objects.
Also elsewhere: "The wise know that the object understood through sound is Śabdabrahman;
because it does not inherently cognize objects, such a [material] sound is not so described. But that [Śabdabrahman] is interwoven everywhere, even when the mine of elements has come into being."

"It manifests within the bodies of living beings, expanded for their benefit. Thus, this [statement] forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "those who are experts in all the Agamas," because it will be stated that the *bindu* of that [Supreme Reality] manifests within all bodies.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*—the *Śāradātilaka*:

"Having attained that form of Kuṇḍalin which has entered the bodies of living beings, she manifests as the nature of the phonemes (varṇas) through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth. Now, from Śambhu, who is of the nature of the Bindu, bound by time, and whose essence is Kalā..."

The all-pervading Sadāśiva, the witness of the universe, was born. From Sadāśiva arose Īśa, from whom Rudra was produced; from him came Viṣṇu, and from him Brahmā—such is their origin. That Lord is the inner self (antarātman), and as the essence of sound (nādātman), he resounds by himself.
Through the differentiation of positions (saṃsthāna-bheda), he again attained the state of phonemes (varṇatā).

Driven by the vital air (vāyu), this [individual] shall emerge from the *piṇḍa* as a distinct manifestation (*vyakti*). However, some—having formulated the interpretation that "the Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*) refers to the meaning of the word as being the word itself—claim that those skilled in the *saṃhitā-pāṭha* represent one position, while others hold that the *bindu* represents the second; they then proceed to offer a refutation of these two. That is not correct.

The reason "due to insentience" (*jar̤atvāt*) is not possible in the first position, and it would result in a contradiction with the Teacher’s (*Ācārya*) doctrine; therefore, this very position—that [the Lord] is "proficient in all the scriptures"—is the one intended by the author of the work. Having thus described that supreme creation of sound in general, he concludes it with the words "having attained that": "That consciousness, residing within the bodies of living beings in the form of Kuṇḍalī—the essential nature of Kuṇḍalinī—manifests itself as the essence of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth. This is the connection. Having done what? Having performed the *nyāsa* (ritual placement) of the letters of the alphabet, which are the source of all mantras, upon the body. How? By means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To purify the body. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having purified the body by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To awaken the power. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having awakened the power by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To unite with the Self. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having united with the Self by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To attain liberation. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having attained liberation by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To become one with the Supreme. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having become one with the Supreme by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To destroy all obstacles. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having destroyed all obstacles by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To enjoy all objects of desire. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having enjoyed all objects of desire by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To protect the world. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having protected the world by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To attain the state of Śiva. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having attained the state of Śiva by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To fulfill all desires. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having fulfilled all desires by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To be free from all bonds. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having been freed from all bonds by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To attain the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*). How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having attained the state of the Absolute by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To be established in the Self. How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having been established in the Self by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How? By means of the six limbs. Where? Upon the six parts of the body, beginning with the heart. Whose? Of the practitioner. What is the purpose? To be liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). How? By means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet. Whose? Of the mantra. Whom? Of the deity. For the mantra is the body of the deity, and the deity is the body of the mantra. Thus, having become liberated while living by means of the *nyāsa* of the letters of the alphabet, he should perform the *nyāsa* of the mantra. How
"Having reached the organs such as the throat"—this is the ellipsis.

Therefore, it should be understood that the creation about to be described proceeds from Kuṇḍalinī.
