Thus, having first described that supreme creation of sound (*parā śabda-sṛṣṭi*) which was mentioned at the outset to highlight its primacy, [the author] now begins the description of the creation of meaning (*artha-sṛṣṭi*), because the creations beginning with *paśyantī* cannot be explained apart from the creation of the body. Now, "Kalā" refers to Māyā; [the Supreme is called] "of that nature" because it has arisen from that. The Bindu (*bindu*) is also merely another state of that very same [Supreme].
The phrase "of that self" (*tadātmanaḥ*) is applied in both cases through the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect.

As it has been said: "That which is always non-different from the Self, endowed with qualities such as omniscience," or else, "the *kalās*—namely *nivṛtti* and the others—which produce, in reverse order, the presiding deities beginning with Sadāśiva; [this is] 'of that self,' meaning of the Self who is bound by time. The meaning is: "of the Self, together with Time in the form of creation, throughout beginningless and endless time."

From Śambhu, who is Paramaśiva, [Sadāśiva] was born as the performer of the fivefold cosmic functions—creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace—and thus as the seed-form of the world's manifestation and the witness of the universe. Furthermore, he is "the binder of time" (kālabandhu), for which reason he is "of the nature of time" (kālātman); this is the connection established through the relationship of cause and effect. As it is said by the Teacher: "That [power], however, is always fully known by me alone through my own nature as the soul of time. Thus ends the first chapter.
By these two qualifications, it is stated that both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and time (*kāla*) persist even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*);
for this very reason,
these two possess relative eternity.

The reasoning should be understood as follows: the eternity of the *puruṣa* is intrinsic, because the destruction of everything has the *puruṣa* as its ultimate limit; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, in the phrase "of the kinsman of time" (*kālabandhoḥ*), the word "kinsman" (*bandhu*) indicates that time is the instrumental cause.

As they say: "This time, which begins with a lava and ends with the dissolution [of the universe], is the manifestation of the power of darkness (tamas); it is the instrumental cause for the birth and destruction of all entities."

Thus it is said elsewhere: "O twice-born one, the Blessed Time is beginningless and its end does not exist; therefore, these processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution proceed without interruption."
By the phrase "of Kālabandhu," another time— beginning from a lava and ending with the dissolution (pralaya)— is also indicated,
since by that very [phrase] the supreme time (parakāla) has been stated.
Furthermore, the time required to pierce each leaf in a cluster of lotus petals with a fine needle is designated as a *lava*.

The sequence of the text beginning with “*lavaistuṭiḥ syād viṃśaṅgiḥ*” and ending with “*asmāyurmama nivāsaḥ kālenaiva pracodyate*,” has been analyzed by the teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*). However, we have not stated it here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Others, however, explain it thus: in the term *kālabandhoḥ*, which means “of the one whose nature is time,” the consonants are grasped through the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) *ka-ś-ca-la*.
By the word "aśva," the vowels are also included.
Regarding the phrase "tadātmanaḥ," others explain it differently: *ka* and *la* are the "ātman" (the self), which is the long vowel *ā*.
Because it is said that he is the fourth among the four selves, the word *kāla* refers to the Sun; by that [Sun], *maḥ* [is formed].
Alternatively, by the word *kāla*, Mahākāla—the form of Rudra—is understood through the letter *ma*.
Just as in the case of "Bhīma" and "Bhīmasena," by joining [the letters] in that manner, the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) is extracted.
Therefore, it is said:

"Because He is the root of the universe, one should meditate upon Kāma—whose radiance is like that of a throbbing, dark-red *bandhūka* flower—revolving within the womb [of Śambhu] and possessing a crest like ten million moons in His belly," and so forth;
for it has been stated that in the body, at the *mūlādhāra*, He alone exists in the form of the threefold light, and because He is of the nature of *Śakti*, He is of the essence of the *bindu*.

As it has been said: "Having led the entire universe—which consists of the elements, the senses, and the internal organ, and takes the form of the moon, the sun, and fire—along with all the phonemes, into the Pradhāna, which is composed of the power of manifestation and exists as the seed-form; having led that [Pradhāna] into the Puruṣa, whose nature is the Bindu; then that [Puruṣa] into the Sun-self (the individual soul); then that into the principle of Time; and finally, one should lead that [Time] into Śakti, whose nature is consciousness, and her into the solitary, peaceful Abode."
Thus others [explain]: from the letter *ha* of Śambhu arises the *kalā*; the *ātman* is the letter *ī*, and the *bindu* is the *bindu* itself; Kālāgni is Śāradātilaka.
From that unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the root and yet transformed (*vikṛta*), [proceeds] the supreme reality.
It is said that there was the Great Principle (mahattattva), which consists of the qualities (guṇas) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Because it causes the destruction of everything at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*),
the seed-syllable of *māyā* is thus extracted;
therefore, it is said "from that" (*tasmāt*), for its status as the fundamental seed of this world is indeed well-known.
And this explanation is approved by the venerable teachers;
as it was said by them: "O Lord, be gracious, O Ruler of the Universe! Who are we, by whom have we been brought forth, what is our source, and what are our duties? You ought to tell us all of this."
Thus questioned, the Supreme Light spoke in measured words.
In the commentary on this verse, Padmapādācārya explained as follows: "The Lord of All has stated the material cause and so forth in brief. He says:

"That which is measured (pramitā) is *prakṛti*, because it is thoroughly measured (*pra-mīyate*) or known; that which measures (*praminoti*) or knows is the *puruṣa*, termed 'the measurer' (*pramita*); that which measures or delimits is *kāla*, termed 'the measurer' (*pramita*).

The syllable (*akṣara*) that denotes these 'measurers' (*pramitānām*) is non-different from them; thus, the supreme speech (*parā vāk*), the reality (*satattva*), is the letter *Ha*. This is the meaning."
Its capacity to denote primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth should be understood through its form as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the point (*bindu*), and the sound (*nāda*);
the meaning is that he spoke the subsequent [verse] by means of this.

Having observed a lack of comprehension regarding what was stated in brief, he explains that very same [point] in detail: "You are born from the syllables, the causes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution."
Thus,

by the etymological derivation "it does not move" (*na carati*) or "it is unheard" (*aśrute*), [the term *akṣara* refers to that from which this entire universe originates, as stated in the passage beginning with] "from the Imperishable (*akṣara*) all this comes into being," and so forth;
[this refers] to them.
The emergence of those [categories] through the creation of sound has already been stated;

"their emergence in this manner" means [their emergence] during the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*). Thus, regarding the creation of objects under discussion, he begins to describe the creation of the principles (*tattvasṛṣṭi*) starting with the word "from the Root":
from the Root, which is the source of all creation and therefore the Supreme Reality, from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) in the form of the Bindu.
Alternatively, from the mouth created as a modification of Śabdabrahman, the Great Principle (mahattattva)—the entity named "Great" (mahan)—came into being;
in the Śaiva system, this is designated as the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).
What is its nature? It consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, and has the form of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta).

The nature of the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇacatuṣṭaya*), however, is due to the metaphorical application of cause to effect, since it is the cause thereof. Thus say the followers of the Śaivasiddhānta;
as it has been stated by Īśānaśiva in the *Vāmakeśvara*: "That very Prakṛti, which is the manifestation of Power (*śakti*), is characterized by that which is to be known."
The manifest principle that arises, resting upon the quality of sattva, is that very intellect (buddhi); in Sāṃkhya, it is called by the name "the Great" (mahat).
Thus,

from the unmanifest Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), whose form is unmanifest, the manifest principle of intellect (buddhitattva) was born— manifest and characterized by the quality of sattva— and it is the cause of all.
Thus ends the first chapter.
From that [Mahat] arose the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra), according to the distinctions in creation.
From the *vaikārika* ego arise the ten deities who are themselves *vaikārika*.

From the principle of egoity (taijasa), the sense organs arose through the sequential application of the subtle elements (tanmātra): those of direction, wind, sun, rain-god, horse-headed god, fire, moon, and Viṣṇu.

In the Sāṃkhya system, however, *prakṛti*—also known by the synonym *pradhāna* and referred to by the term *avyakta*—is that state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. That is the supreme reality, the root of all things. From it, when there is an inequality of the *guṇas*, the *mahat* is produced through transformation.
What is its nature?
It has the qualities and the internal organ as its essence;
the qualities are the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
For those [schools], the causal form of even the fourfold internal organ is, by way of metaphorical designation, of both natures;
likewise, the sequence of its creation is: from primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat), and from the Great One comes the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
Thus, from that Great One (mahat), the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) was born through the distinction of its creative functions:
namely, the modified (vaikārika), the radiant (taijasa), and the elemental (bhūtādi).

As it has been said: "The unmanifest itself becomes manifest as that which is characterized by the Great Principle (mahat); from that arises the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra), which is differentiated by the qualities of sattva and the rest."
That ego (ahaṅkāra) is threefold, distinguished by the separate qualities of sattva and the others:
the vaikārika is named sāttvika, the taijasa is remembered as rājasa, and the bhūtādi is tāmasa; these too separately brought forth the principles (tattvas).
Thus,

while describing those various effects, he reveals this manifoldness by means of the passage beginning with "the vaikārika," because its nature as *vaikārika* arises from its production from the Supreme Lord, who is transformed through the equilibrium of the powers (*śaktisāmarasya*).
Because they are produced from that, the gods also possess that same nature;
likewise, even in the Sāṃkhya system, because the Pradhāna produces its effects through the predominance of the Guṇas, it possesses that same nature. || 18 ||
He states those very [deities] with the words "the directions," and so forth.
Although these two, Aśva and Aśvinīkumāra, are distinct, they are mentioned as one because of their constant association and simultaneous birth.
Upendra is a single form of Viṣṇu.
Mitra is the third sun;
as it is said, "Mitra is the third light," he is one form of Brahmā.
Candra (the Moon) is also to be known [as one of them];

it should be understood that these are the presiding deities of the sense organs, as they say: "The eleven [deities] beginning with Dig (Space), who are products of the *vaikārika* [sattva], are traditionally recorded as being under the Moon."
The presiding deities of the sense organs are proclaimed to be those very ones.
Thus, from the taijasa ego— specifically from the taijasa ego— the sense organs arise, namely the organs of action, the organs of cognition, and the mind.
As it has been said: "And that other principle, the mind, which possesses conceptualization and discursive thought, is born from Taijasa alone."
From the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), beginning with the element of being (bhūta), the five elements were born:
from sound first arose space (viyat); from touch, air; from form, fire; from taste, water; and from smell, earth—such is their origin. (20)
The sky is clear, the wind is black, fire is red, and water is pure white. (21) Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "From the *taijasa* [ego] arise there the mind and the senses;
from the *bhūtādi* [ego] arise the subtle elements (*tanmātras*); from these comes this creation."
Thus,

according to the Sāṃkhya system, the sense organs (akṣāṇi) and their presiding deities (akṣādhiṣṭhātṛ-devatāḥ) arose from the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), combined with the *taijasa* ego; thus the sense faculties were produced.
In this way, from the *bhūtādi* [ego] as well, when accompanied by the *taijasa* ego, there arises the production of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

As it has been said: "The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the *vaikārika* ego; the subtle elements proceed from the *bhūtādi* [ego], which is characterized by *tamas*; and from the *taijasa* [ego], both [proceed]. (Verse 18)
Regarding the word *bhūta*:
the connection is that the five elements (*pañcabhūtāni*) were born from the *ahaṅkāra*—beginning with the *bhūtādi*—through the sequential application of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The suffix *ka* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*).
In that regard, first, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arise as the causes of space and the other gross elements:
the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
From these, the five gross elements—space, air, fire, water, and earth—are produced.
And it is said: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these subtle elements (tanmātras) alone became the objects [of the senses] in succession from the source of the elements (bhūtādi)."
From that, the ether arose, having the nature of the subtle element of sound;
from that, the wind, whose essence is touch; and from that, the fire, whose essence is form.
From that [the unmanifest], water, whose essence is taste, arose; from those [waters], earth, whose essence is smell;
from those, the five gross elements; and from them, the Virāj as well.

Thus it is said. Regarding that, he states the manner of the origination of the elements: "From sound," and so forth. From the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra) comes ether (ākāśa); from the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra) comes air (vāyu); from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) comes fire (agni); from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) comes water (jala); and from the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra) comes earth (pṛthivī).
Some, by the force of the word "prior" (pūrva), assert that each preceding member among these is the cause of the subsequent ones.
As it has been said: "From sound, ether; from touch, air; from those two and form, fire; from these and taste, water; and from these and smell, earth."
He teaches the colors of the five elements, beginning with "translucent.
"Translucent" means white.

Here, the mention of the color of certain formless substances is for the purpose of meditation, in accordance with one's own scripture; their true nature is stated elsewhere—this concludes the first chapter.
The wise know that the earth consists of the five elements, each supported by the others;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are recorded as the qualities of the elements.
The circle of the sky is marked with six dots;
that of the wind is triangular and endowed with a svastika; that of fire is joined with a half-moon.
The wise know that the mandalas are like a lotus for water, square for earth,
and circular for fire, each possessing the luster of its respective element.
"Even the earth possesses the signs of porosity, movement, capacity for transformation, and ripening; likewise, water possesses flavor, and the clouds are solid earth.
This means that those [elements] are known by these [characteristics].
"Each having its own basis" means that they each have their own respective causes as their basis. As it has been said: "By the fourfold great elements which have mutually entered into one another..."
Pervading all space, it brings forth the entire visible universe in its totality.
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "In space is the wind; there is fire; there is water; and upon that water is established the earth.
Thus.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that the qualities of the elements are their respective specific qualities (*tattad-viśeṣa-guṇa*). Alternatively, sound is the quality of space; sound and touch are the qualities of air.
According to the Sāṃkhyas, those two [sound and touch] belong to fire;
taste along with them belongs to water;
and smell along with [the other four] belongs to earth.
This very point is clarified by the statement "each having its own substratum.
And it has been said by Īśānaśiva: "Space has sound as its sole quality; wind possesses the qualities of sound and touch;
fire is held to possess the three qualities of sound, touch, and form."
Water possesses four qualities through sound, touch, form, and taste;
earth possesses five qualities through sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Thus [it is said].
He describes the circles of the elements, beginning with "the circle":
the circle of the sky (divaḥ) is the atmosphere;
that very same circle, marked with six dots at equal intervals along the central line of its circular perimeter, belongs to Mātariśvan, the wind.
The triangle is the upper [triangle].
This is because it has been stated that "the fire is the energy (ūrjā) below, and the power (śakti) is below.
It is also said elsewhere: "The solar mandala is located in the corners of Indra, Rākṣasa, and Vāyu."
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that one should extend the lines from the junctions of the triangle until they form the shape of a svastika there.
As it has been stated: "In the heart is a triangle; from it issues a svastika of red radiance."
Thus [it is said].
A *svastika* is a pair of lines extending toward the intermediate directions, mutually connected and possessing four faces.
The word "of the arms" (*vaṅgeḥ*) connects with what precedes it.
The connection is that the lotus is joined with the moon of Indra (the syllable *aiṃ*).
This is the *Śāradātilaka*.
They say that [these] are adorned by their own respective letters, and they are also multiplied by eight according to their own names.
The five elements, beginning with earth, are traditionally taught to correspond to the five kalās, beginning with nivṛtti.
Regarding the phrase "joined with a half-moon":
the compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of a grammatical rule) for the locative case (*saptamī*).

Alternatively, it means that the half-moon is joined with the lotus; both being combined, one should form a circle of water and, having made the half-moon therein, create two lotuses on both sides of it.
As it was said by the Teachers: "The lunar orb, free from waning, is made of water.
And elsewhere: "The half-moon is liquid, gentle, white, and joined with a lotus."
Thus it is said;
and in the *Prayogasāra* as well: "The half-moon is without limbs, [arising] from the water."

Elsewhere also: "In their sequence, the lunar disc, the six-pointed [figure], the triangle joined with fire and weapons, the pair of lotuses, the crescent moon, and the four-cornered [figure] together with the ten [spokes]—these are the mandalas here."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Or else, there is a white lunar disc (candrārdhamaṇḍala) joined with a pair of lotuses."
In the *Svāyambhuva-nārasiṃha* it is also stated: "It should be marked with water, the letter *ja*, the moon, and the lotus.
He who says that one should first draw an eight-petaled lotus and then fashion crescent-moon shapes at the tips of its petals is indeed mistaken.
Others, however, say that one should draw a half-moon and write a lotus in its center;
since that will be explained in the section on the *bhūtalipi* (earth-syllables), it need not be discussed here.
The connection is that the square [mandala] of the earth is together with the vajra-mark.
Some say that one should draw lines for the intersection of the squares and fashion eight lotuses (*aṣṭavajrāṇi*) by expanding [the grid].
However, those who know the tradition state that the eight lotuses should be fashioned directly upon the lines of the square itself.
As it is said in the *Śaunakakalpa*: "The ground-enclosure (*bhūgraha*) should be square and adorned with eight lotuses."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Hiraṇyagarbha-saṃhitā*: "Then, [there should be] an auspicious square adorned externally with eight vajras."
The teachers, however, say: "the eight [spokes] joined with the vajra. The author of the text also says: "among the eight vajras.
A vajra consists of two lines joined to one another, facing each other, with three faces.
Some maintain that there are two lines with their middles mutually connected.
He describes the meditation on the mandala with the words "tattat" (that and that).
By this, it is also stated that when drawing the mandala on the ground and so forth, it should be filled with the respective colored powders corresponding to those syllables.
"By colors" means by the elemental letters (bhūtavarṇa) that will be described in the second [chapter].
The meaning of "eightfold with their respective names" is this:
it refers to the mantra written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) within the diagrams (*yantra*) of the elemental scripts (*lipi*) that are to be described.
The traditionalists think as follows:

"Because it was previously stated that [the elements] consist of *kalās*, he says 'the Earth' (*dhara*) and so forth for the purpose of the ritual application (*prayoga*) and others, referring to the powers (*śaktis*) which have emerged from the principle of *bindu* (*bindutattva*) and constitute the causes of the gross elements, according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*)."
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "the producer of the five elements, beginning with earth.
This is stated in the first chapter of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Nivṛtti shall be accompanied by Pratiṣṭhā; after that come Vidya and Śānti."
It should be known as "Beyond Peace" (śāntyatītā), arising from the body of sound (nādadeha).
26. Śakti is first produced, followed by the state beyond peace (śāntyatīta-pada);
from Śakti comes the state beyond peace, and then, in sequence, the state of peace (śānti-pada).
From that, the stage of knowledge (vidyā-pada) arises; from that, the stage of establishment (pratiṣṭhā-pada) is comprised.
The stage of cessation (nivṛtti-pada) arises after the stage of establishment.
Thus has emanation, impelled by the Lord, been described in brief; now follows their dissolution in reverse order.
No other creation is intended beyond these five stages taught;
for this entire world is pervaded by these five digits (kalās).
Thus [it is said]:
"from the nāda.
That whose body is from the nāda is the *nādadeha* bindu; [the phrase means] "arising from that."

Alternatively, he states the gross denotative aspect of those [vowels] with the words *nādadehasamudbhavāḥ*. *Nāda* is the letter *ha*; that from which the body (*deha*)—the origin (*utpatti*)—of *nāda*, which is sound (*dhvani*), arises is *nādadeha*, namely the wind (*vāyu*). Because of the non-difference between a property and its possessor (*dharmadharmiṇorabhedāt*), the word "body" is used here to signify "origin," as it is said: "The wind moving in the chest produces a deep sound. Thus, its nature is to be the cause of the origin of *nāda*.
*Samuddīpyamānā* means whose radiance (*bhā*) or light (*dīpti*) is fully kindled; thus, *samudga* is fire, and by that, the letter *ra*.
Or [it refers to] their own essential form (*svarūpa*).

In that context, although the horses (*ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, *la*) ought to be mentioned in their sequential order, the fact that he has mentioned only four of them implies that the letter *la* is also present.
Furthermore, because *nāda* (the nasal sound) is mentioned first, one should understand that the union with the *bindu* (the nasal dot) also applies to these.
These are the seed-syllables of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) in reverse order.
Alternatively, *nāda* is the letter *ha*; its "body" is its essential form. Those whose origin and abiding are therein are the vowels *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ai*, and *au*.
It should be understood that these possess the bindu (*m*).
As it is said in the *Trikonottara*: "That which is called Nāda is the supreme seed-syllable (bīja) residing within all beings;
it bestows form, is supremely divine, and grants all accomplishments (siddhi).
It is peaceful, all-pervading, void, and established within the five measures (mātrā)."
Thus it is said.
Some maintain that these should be joined with *lava*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* in sequence.
For example: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hya hoṃ*.
These are the seeds of the unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūtabīja*).
Alternatively, *nāda* is the letter *ha*.

Because the body has a predominance of the earth element, it is designated by the word "body" (*deha*), which refers to the letter *la*; that in which its origin and persistence reside is "the origin of the body of *nāda*" (*nādadehasamudbhava*).
In those [syllables] beginning with *ā*, they emerge from the body of *nāda*.
Here, they state the conjunction of *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* in sequence.
For example: *vāṃ*, *havīṃ*, *haiṃ*, *haiṃ*.
Hraum! These are the seed-syllables of the fivefold-composed elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta).
It should be understood that these very seed-syllables of the elements serve as the seeds for the cessation and so forth of the presiding deities of those elements.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "They consist of the *nāda*, the *kalā*s, and so forth. (25 || 26 ||)
The Śāradātilaka states:
This entire world, consisting of moving and non-moving beings, is composed of the five elements.
The non-moving [beings] are divided in many ways according to the distinctions of mountains, stones, trees, and so forth. (27)
Having thus described the elements, he states that the world consists of them by saying "five" (*pañca*).
By this, both the theory of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the theory of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) are indicated.
In that regard, for those gods who are composed of light (*taijasa*), half of their body is luminous, a fourth part is earth, and a fourth part is water; such is the theory of triplication.
In the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), however, four parts belong to earth, and one-eighth part each belongs to the others;
the same applies elsewhere as well.
As it has been said: "Having divided each [element] twofold, and then having again divided the first [half] into four..."
"By being joined with their own and other second parts, they become fivefold each.
Alternatively, fire consists of six parts, while earth, water, air, and ether each contribute a tenth part.
Thus, even in our own earthly bodies, there are six parts of earth and a tenth part each of the others.

In this same manner, it should be understood for those dwelling in the worlds of Varuṇa and others, whose bodies consist of water and the other elements. As it has been said: "One should divide each of the elements, beginning with earth, into two parts; then, taking one part from each, one should further divide them into five."
One should cause each single part to enter into each single element in due order;
thus, for the element of space, there are indeed six parts belonging to itself.
"One should assign the four parts, such as wind and the rest, to wind and the others;
this is the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), so say those who know reality.
Elsewhere, there is a specific detail: "Bone, flesh, skin, sinew, and hair as the fifth."
Thus, earth, which is characterized by solidity, is said to be of five kinds.
Saliva, urine, semen, blood, and marrow as the fifth—
these five qualities of water are proclaimed to be liquid in form.
Hunger, thirst, fear, sleep, laziness, and impatience— these qualities,
characterized by heat, are proclaimed to belong to fire (tejas).
Flowing, supporting, ingestion, contraction, and expansion—
these five qualities of wind are established in the form of its functions.
"Passion and hatred, as well as shame, fear, and likewise delusion—these are the five qualities of space, which is called 'void' and whose nature is hollow. Thus [it is said].
"Moving" means that which is locomotive.
The immobile is stationary.

Since there is much to be said regarding mobile beings, setting aside that which was first observed—the immobile—the mobile are declared to be of various kinds: those born from sweat, from eggs, and from the womb.
Worms, insects, and the like are born of moisture; snakes and the like are born of eggs.
[Verse 28] "I say they are not immobile.
In that regard, he will state that those mobile beings are born of moisture, eggs, and the womb.
Because they have been refined by that [process], their status as *oṃgi* (possessing the *oṃ*) has been stated.
As they say: "The body of a living being is to be known as fourfold, according to the difference in its mode of birth:
born from a sprout (*udbhijja*), born from moisture (*khedaja*), born from an egg (*aṇḍaja*), and fourthly, born from a womb (*jarāyuja*)."

"Breaking through the earth and emerging, that which is stationary is called *audbhida* (earth-born). The manner of their origin is stated elsewhere: "The *sthāvara* (stationary) are to be known as *udbhida*, taking the form of grass, shrubs, and so forth.
Therein, the earth, sprinkled with waters and ripened by internal heat, [produces them]."
Being dispersed by the wind, it attains the state of a seed;
likewise, the seeds thus sown are again moistened by water.
"Swelling and softness attain the state of roots;

from that root arises the production of limbs, and from that the emergence of leaves. From the leafy nature comes the stalk, and from the stalk, further reproduction. (27) Having first presented this division, he points out the moving beings with the words "the moving beings," etc.
Demonstrating the individual connection of each [term] with the genus *jani* (birth), he states its specific varieties beginning with "born from sweat" (*khedaja*).
The distinction between "flies, insects, and so forth" (*klamikoṭādyāḥ*) is based on both [categories] being either stingers or non-stingers.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), moths and other such creatures are included.

As they say: "Worms, insects, moths, and the like are embodied beings known as sweat-born (*khedaja*). The manner of their birth is shown elsewhere: "The sweat-born are produced from existing moisture and bodily parts."
Therefore, their non-origination from a womb (ayonija) has been stated.
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "However, those among these who are born of sweat (svedaja) are also to be understood as non-womb-born;
they are stable, wind-like, and divided into forty thousand varieties."
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "serpents and so forth," birds, tortoises, and the like are included.
As they say: "All birds are born from eggs; crocodiles, fish, and tortoises are born from moisture.
The manner of their birth is also described: "The egg-born arises from the union of semen and blood that has become rounded."
"Emerging from the [lotus] that has opened in due time, the Full Self (Pūrṇātmā) will proceed forth. Thus [ends] the *Śāradātilaka*.
Among those born from a womb, such as humans and others, the [process] for men is now described.

The birth of male and female arises from the union of semen and blood. A single drop, possessing the nature of both, enters the womb; according to the sequence, if *rajas* (ovum) is predominant, she becomes a woman, and if semen is predominant, he becomes a man.
The established rule is that when there is equality between both [factors], the result is neuter (napuṃsaka).
The *jarāyu* is the womb (*garbhāśaya*) in the form of a membrane.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "humans and so forth," animals and others are included.
"Among these, womb-born living beings are divided into sixty-four thousand kinds.
Thus it is said;
the connection [of the sentence] is that "the origin of humans is described among them."
Since all treatises have human beings as their qualified subjects,
the phrase "joined with blood" indicates that [the mother] is secondary;
therefore, the son is endowed with the caste and other attributes of the father.
And so it is said in the Mahābhārata: "The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very same as the one by whom he was begotten.
A *bhastrā* is a bellows, a leather vessel for holding air.
Consisting of both—that is, consisting of semen and blood—it is therefore of the nature of Agni and Soma; thus, the single *bindu* enters the womb.
This "it" is connected with what follows in sequence:
this *bindu*, when exceeding the *rajas*, gradually becomes a woman.
The construction is: "If the semen is superior, a male shall be born in due order.
Here, superiority is to be understood according to the stated measure.
It should also be understood that when there is equality of the stated measures, the birth of a neuter occurs.
As they say: "Twenty-two parts of the male seed and fourteen parts of the female seed arise at the time of conception for both males and females."
"A woman occurs when the female seed (rajas) is in excess in the [male] portion; a man occurs when the male seed (śukra) is in excess in the [female] portion;
when the count of both is equal, the birth of a neuter occurs.
By the word "successively" (kramāt), this is what is meant: that very drop, when divided separately by the vital air (vāyu), produces many offspring.

As it is said in Vāgbhaṭa’s Śārīrasthāna: "Furthermore, when the semen and menstrual blood are repeatedly divided by the wind (vāyu) according to their respective natures, there is a lack of progeny."
Those of deformed appearance are born from the womb through deformed impurities;
a woman who has reached sixteen years of age, when united with a man who has reached twenty.
When the womb, the channels, the blood, the semen, the vital air, and the heart are pure, one gives birth to a powerful son;
however, when these are deficient, the child is born weak.
He becomes sickly, short-lived, or unfortunate, or he does not even conceive at all. Thus [ends the section]. 28||30||
First Chapter:
Constrained by the noose of delusion in accordance with its prior karma, a certain self then attains the state of a living being (jīva) therein. 31.
Then, nourished by the food, drink, and other provisions brought by me, he who possesses a body of reality (*tattvadehavān*) gradually grows over a day, a fortnight, and then a month.
Regarding that drop (*bindu*), he describes the movement of the living soul (*jīva*) with the words "previously," etc.

Among the karmas accumulated over hundreds of previous births, there is one powerful karma—consisting of merit or demerit, resulting in both pleasure and pain, and fit to be experienced in a human body—that is ready to yield its fruit. Bound and fettered by the noose of delusion (*moha-pāśa*), which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), [the Self] is born.
By this, the non-arising of the eternally existing Self is stated;
the meaning is that the Self has entered the body as if it were a house.
The phrase "some [are]" refers to the fact that selves are manifold due to their distinct dispositions, in accordance with the *Kaṇāda-sūtra*,
and because of the Sāṃkhya statement: "The plurality of puruṣas is established."

In the Vedānta system, however, a distinction fabricated by ignorance (*avidyā*) must be accepted; otherwise, if ignorance were destroyed by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), then— according to the statement, "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes"— previously accumulated actions would lack the capacity to yield their fruits, and consequently, there could be no possibility of being untainted by future actions.

Because of the scriptural statement, "He is not stained by these [actions], just as a lotus leaf is not by water," and because of his oneness and state of liberation, there could be no descent at all; therefore, it is said that the cause for his descent is the snare of delusion (*moha-pāśa*).

As it has been said in the *Adhyātmaviveka*: "Brahman exists—consciousness, bliss, self-luminous, stainless, omnipotent, and all-pervading. Its parts are known as individual souls (*jīvas*). Overspread by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), like sparks from a fire, they are divided by limiting adjuncts (*upādhis*) such as length and so forth, and are constrained by these beginningless adjuncts which bestow pleasure and pain in the form of merit and demerit."

"Endowed with their respective species, they undergo in each birth a body, a lifespan, and enjoyments born of karma. (31) Now, regarding this, the method is stated in the *Yogārṇava*: "Having entered the food that has been eaten, that wind divides it into two parts."

Having entered and being situated within the intestines, [the *prāṇa*] separates the waste (*kiṭṭa*) from the water. Having placed the water above the fire and that food upon the water, the *prāṇa* itself, remaining below the water, gently fans the fire. As the fire is fanned by the wind, it makes the water exceedingly hot. (From the *Śāradātilaka*)

That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water; once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter separately and the nutrient juice separately. By means of that juice, the vital breath (prāṇa) fills those channels again. Being fully filled, they nourish the body from all sides. The mother’s channel carrying the nutrient juice is pierced [into the fetus] and is called "the other" (parā). This channel, situated at the navel of the embryo, carries the nutrient juice received from the mother. Thus.
Regarding this, it has been said: "A living being increases by two *trasareṇus* in a mere instant; in the time of a *nāḍikā*, it becomes a louse; and in a *muhūrta*, it becomes a pair [of lice]."
"And for lice, [the growth] lasts for a period of days equal to the number of Vedas (fourteen), up to the size of a barley grain.

And in the *Yogārṇava*: "In one night it becomes *kalala*; in five nights, a bubble (*buḍuda*); blood in ten nights; and in fourteen nights, a mass of flesh (*māṃsapeśī*); in twenty days, solid flesh characterized by the formation of a lump (*piṇḍa*)."

On the twenty-fifth full day, it becomes a *pala* in size with all its limbs complete. When one month is fully completed, it sustains the five elements. Upon reaching the second month, the marrow and fat are produced. The bones and marrow [are formed] in three months; the hair and nails in the fourth;
and the cavities of the ears, eyes, and nose in the fifth month. The mouth, anus, and belly are formed in the sixth, and the anal opening in the seventh.
"It is held that all the limbs and joints are fully formed in eight months.
However, there is a specific detail in the *Adhyātmaviveka*: "In the first month, the state called *kalala* arises;
in the second, a solid mass (*ghana-piṇḍa*); [in the third], a *peśī*; and in the sixth, a *arbudam* (tumor-like mass). These stages generally occur in this sequence for males, females, and neuters."

In the third [month], the five limbs—hands, feet, and head—are considered to be formed; at that time, the parts of the major and minor limbs become subtle simultaneously, excluding the beard, teeth, and so forth, which arise after birth. This is the natural state (prakṛti), while anything else is regarded by the wise as a modification (vikṛti).
In the fourth [month], the manifestation of those constituent elements also occurs. The First Chapter.
When the embryo has reached its state of well-being through the visible humors (*doṣas*), it attains manifestation by means of its own sense organs.

They know these [constituents] to be skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. Its heart is born from the mother and longs for sensory objects; therefore, one should fulfill the mother’s desires for the sake of the well-being of the fetus. The wise call such a woman—one whose heart is shared with the fetus—a *dohadinī* (one experiencing pregnancy longings).

From the non-granting of longings (*dohada*), deformities and other defects may arise in the fetus. Whatever object the mother fails to obtain during her longing, the son will be born with a deficiency in that regard. If the longing is for the sight of a king, the fetus will be wealthy and enjoyer of pleasures; if for ornaments, he will be very graceful; if for a hermitage, he will be most righteous;
if for the sight of a deity, he will be devoted; if for the sight of a serpent, he will be violent; if for eating a monitor lizard, he will be sleepy; and if for eating beef, he will be powerful.
By means of the buffalo [essence], one gives birth to a son with red eyes and hairy body. On the fifth day, the fifth *piṇḍa* is offered; there is nourishment by flesh and blood.
On the sixth, there is the distinct formation of bones, sinews, nails, hair, and body hair. On the seventh, strength and complexion increase, and the limbs reach fullness.
On the eighth, the skin and ears are formed, as well as the vital energy (*ojas*) and consciousness (*cetas*) arising from the heart. It is held that the pure water and blood are the signs of life.

"Again it runs toward the mother and again toward the womb; that [vital energy] is fickle. Therefore, born in the eighth month, he does not live, being abandoned by his vital strength (*ojas*). Thus also says Yājñavalkya: "Again toward the nurse and again toward the womb his *ojas* runs away; therefore, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life."

Thus, when the *ojas* (vital essence) resides in the child, it should be understood that the mother does not live; and when it resides in both [the father and the mother], then the *ojas* is not present in either, so it should be known that neither lives. One who possesses the body of the principles (*tattva*) is one whose body consists of the twenty-four principles.

He will explain the principles immediately thereafter. "By the defects" means that it reaches manifestation through the defects—that is, the objects of the senses—in such a way that pleasure may arise;
by this, growth up until the eighth month is described.
He states the humors and so forth with the words "vāta" etc.,
and "tān" refers to the elements (dhātus);
it should be understood that among these, each preceding one is the cause for each succeeding one.

This has been stated in the *Suśruta*: "The wise know the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) to be the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; the objects of the organs of cognition are traditionally held to be sound and the rest. They also call the organs of action (*karmendriya*) those known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. *Śāradātilaka* states: The organs of cognition are known to be the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; the objects of the organs of cognition are traditionally held to be sound and the rest. The wise have also declared the organs of action to be those named speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation—these are declared to be the objects of the organs of action.

The internal organ of the self is proclaimed to consist of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). Chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents (*dhātavaḥ*);
all of these, when accumulated, arise from one another through the heat of the bile (*pitta-tejas*). Thus it is said.
If it is asked, "How then can the skin be the cause of blood?", the answer is: it is true that both the skin and the blood are produced from the nutrient essence (*rasa*).
As it has been said: "That nutrient essence, situated within the channels, is intensely nourished by the bodily *oṣman* (heat)."

From that which is being cooked, two kinds of cooking (transformation) occur again; having been enveloped on all sides by the skin, blood is produced. Thus it is said elsewhere: "Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the seven constituents (*dhātavaḥ*). Among them, it is stated that the skin and blood arise from the food-essence (*annarasa*) through the digestive fire (*jāṭharavahni*); likewise, [the subsequent constituents] arise from blood and so forth."
"The elements are produced in succession by being cooked by the fire of their respective sheaths.
Thus, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, after reciting "skin" and so forth, it is stated that "some read 'rasa' [nutrient fluid] and 'blood'";
and it is further stated that "[the self] becomes manifest through its own senses."
Having mentioned those sense-faculties, he also mentions their objects due to that same context, beginning with the word "jñāna.
The word *artha* denotes "object" in both instances; in both cases, these are sound and so forth—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
It should be understood that whereas [the qualities of the elements] were previously mentioned [in the plural], here they are mentioned starting with "and so forth" (ādi).
The remainder of the sentence is: "The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the means of apprehending the self."
By this, it is stated that the self (ātman) is the object of the mind; furthermore, he describes the fourfold nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) starting with the word "mind" (manaḥ),
wherein the mind consists of resolve (saṅkalpa) and doubt (vikalpa).
The intellect (*buddhi*) determines all objects;
the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is characterized by the conceit of being a knower;
and the mind (*citta*) is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
Such is the distinction between these;

as it has been said: "This supreme power (śakti), whose nature is that of the individual soul (jīva) and which possesses the aforementioned characteristics, becomes the mind (manas) when it performs both volition (saṅkalpa) and conceptualization (vikalpa)."
Likewise, that which takes the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), which effects the determination of all states of being,
and which arises from the conceit "I am" and so forth, is known by the name *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-maker).
The first chapter:
The ten sense organs, the elements, and the mind constitute the sixteen transformations; the five elements, ego-consciousness, and the [other] principles are the eight primal natures.

The knowers of reality understand that the seven— the unmanifest, the great principle (mahat), and the eight subtle elements (tanmātras), along with the great principle itself— constitute the seven transformations (vikṛti).
That very [reality], which is non-conceptual in nature and indeed the true essence of the mind, appears as one yet manifold, like a dancer.
Thus,
having previously mentioned the elements and the sense organs, he states their collective designations as "the ten" in two verses;
or else, since it was said that [the body] possesses the principles (*tattva*), he states those principles as "the ten."
It should be understood that the designations such as "modification" (*vikāra*) were stated by way of connection with their respective contexts;

or else, according to the maxim of the needle and the kettle (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*), after stating the defects, he states the principles (*tattva*) indicated by the phrase "possessing the body of reality" (*tattvadehavān*),
and in response to the inquiry "What are those?", he says "knowledge," and so forth.
The meaning is that the objects of the organs of action are said to be earth and the other [elements].
Thus, there are the five elements, the ten organs, and the ten objects of the organs; in this way, there are twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
As they say: "The twenty-five principles are seen through the elements, the organs, and the objects of the organs."

Furthermore, by treating the phrase as "endowed with the bliss of emission" (*visargānanda-saṃyutā*), and because emission alone is the function of the anus and the genitals, it follows that these two are devoid of bliss; thus, the number of principles (*tattva*) remains twenty-four.
As they have said: "With those [principles] including bliss, the twenty-four principles are likewise proclaimed."

By the statement "the intellect (*manobuddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*citta*)," and by the exclusion of speech and so forth, it is implied that there are twenty-four principles (*tattva*) when these four are added; as they say: "The principles have been stated together with these [faculties] provided with their instruments, but excluding speech and the rest. While stating the twenty-four principles mentioned in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, he also mentions some of their well-known designations, saying "ten."

By this, it is stated that there are twenty-four principles (*tattvas*): the ten faculties, the five gross elements (*bhūta*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or nature (*prakṛti*).

The author himself will state this in the fifth chapter: "The wise know the five gross elements, the subtle elements, the sense-faculties, as well as the mind, the embryo [of the ego], the intellect, and primordial matter as the 'friends' (*maitrāṇi*)."
Thus,
these would be modifications; the connection is that their status as modifications arises from their nature as eternal effects, [referring to] "the eight prakṛtis."
Because they serve as causes for each subsequent element, they possess the nature of *prakṛti*; here, the word "elements" (*bhūta*) refers to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*),
since the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause.

Because the elements (*bhūta*) are mentioned among the evolutes (*vikāra*) solely as effects, and because of the subsequent reference to them as "the subtle elements" (*tanmātra*), they say: "The seven that are not primordial materiality (*aprākṛtika*) are designated as both primordial materiality and its evolutes."
Thus, in the Śāradātilaka: "The body consists of fire and moon; the bindu is that which possesses the nature of both."
The sun is known as the right portion, and the moon is the left part.
The "unmanifest" (avyakta) means primordial matter (prakṛti), which has "pradhāna" as its synonym;
the inversion [of the order] to "the unmanifest, the Great" (avyaktaṃ mahat) is either for the sake of metrical convenience or for the purpose of concealment.
The reading "sāvyaktam" or "mahat" is [preferred], since the sequence of dissolution is intended here; as they say: "The twenty-four principles, ending with Prakṛti, have been enumerated."
Thus, elsewhere, with reference to the order of emanation, it is said: "the unmanifest, the great [intellect], ego, the elements,
and the subtle elements."

The term "with ego" (*sāhaṅkāra*) is a qualifier for that alone; by it, there is a transposition [of the case ending], and by the word "and" (*ca*), there is a conjunction with the word "evolvents" (*prakṛtayaḥ*).
Thus, the meaning is that these seven are denoted by the terms "evolvent" (*prakṛti*) and "evolute" (*vikṛti*).

Because each preceding element serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for each succeeding one, and each succeeding element serves as the modification (*vikṛti*) for each preceding one, these possess the nature of both material cause and modification.

As they say: "The root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), are both natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only a modification; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor modification."
Thus he concludes: "The knowers of reality know this"—
this is the meaning.

From "the organs of knowledge" (*jñānendriyāṇi*) up to this point, the exposition of the principles (*tattva-nirūpaṇa*) which has been composed by me is approved even by those who know the principles; or rather, by the phrase "those who know the principles know," it is indicated that the principles stated in the three previous modes are not what we accept,
but rather these twenty-four principles ending with *prakṛti*.
It has been stated that there are twenty-five principles ending with the Puruṣa, and twenty-six ending with the Supreme (Parā); this is our accepted view,
and such is the traditional interpretation.
This is stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "Beyond the twenty-three principles, Prakṛti is said to be supreme; they declare that beyond Prakṛti is the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth."
For that primordial nature (prakṛti), which is characterized by concealment, he who is the other is Maheśvara;
for both nature and the person (puruṣa) proceed under his control.

Thus, having described the creation of the ego (ahaṃkāra) from the elements and so forth, and having indicated that "the senses arose from the taijasa [ego]," the author— following that context— also states their objects with the passage beginning with "jñāna" and ending with "parikīrtitam. Furthermore, as a supplement to the subsequent discourse, and as a supplement to the assignment of the *varṇas*, *tattvas*, and *nyāsa* for certain mantras, he demonstrates the modifications and so forth with the passage beginning with "daśa."
Those who know reality (tattvavidaḥ) know this, because these [categories] are included therein; the meaning is that these designations were made by those who know reality.
Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, he states the subject at hand, beginning with "In the fire," etc.

In response to the inquiry as to why the body consists of the nature of Agni and Soma, he states the reason: because the *bindu* (vital drop) is of a dual nature—the semen being of the form of Agni and the blood being of the form of Soma; [the body] is composed of these.
The first chapter:
There are ten channels (nāḍīs) in the body, among which three are proclaimed as the principal ones:
the Iḍā on the left side of the body, the Suṣumṇā in the middle, and the Piṅgalā on the other [the right].
As they say: "The moon consists of sixteen digits (kalās), the sun has twelve digits, fire is endowed with ten digits, and [the wind] consumes thirty-eight parts of the digits."

There are thirty-seven [or thirty-eight] [deities] here for the purpose of the conception; by them, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is proclaimed to consist of the nature of Agni and Soma.
Through the conjunction of a portion of the digits, the formation of the embryo shall come to pass.
Thus,
even in this way, the meaning is that [the body] consists of the nature of Agni and Soma;
it has been stated that the body consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
He states their established position for the sake of conventional usage regarding specific locations based on the distinction of their application and so forth: "The southern portion.

In this treatise, the southern part is sometimes referred to by the term *agni* (fire) and sometimes by the term *sūrya* (sun), as indicated by the statement: "That which is the southern portion of Agni."
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā as well: "The function of the fiery [element] is indeed twofold: that which has the nature of the sun and that which has the nature of fire.
To establish the position of the previously mentioned sun and moon, he speaks of the channels (nāḍīs) within the body;
the syntactical connection is that among those infinite channels, they know ten channels to be the principal ones.
It cannot be said that "the first ones are infinite," because it will be stated [later] that "among those ten, three are proclaimed as primary";
thus, the word *mukhyāḥ* ("primary") is to be construed by repetition with each of them.
The inclusion of the word "prakīrtitāḥ" (are proclaimed) is for this reason: otherwise, its meaning would already be conveyed by the word "viduḥ" (they know).

And it has been said therein: "Of these, the first three are traditionally held to be the most important instruments for the performance [of the sacrifice]. He states their specific status with the words beginning with "ir̤ā."
The term "of the body" (*tanoh*) is connected to three locations:
*Iḍā* is on the left, arising from the left testicle; being curved like a bow, it extends as far as the left nostril—this is the meaning.
In the middle of the body is the *Suṣumṇā*, situated within the spinal column, as it has been said: "That which has entered the cavity between the staff [of the spine] and the support of the head."
The other [nāḍī] is on the right; it originates from the right testicle and, curving like a bow, extends as far as the right nostril—this is the meaning.
As they say: "That which is connected to the left testicle, embracing the *suṣumṇā*, takes recourse in the right eye, remains curved like a bow, and is situated in the heart."
That which arises from the left shoulder and passes through the middle should go to the right nostril; likewise, that which arises from the right hip should go to the left opening of the nose.

Thus it is said in another Tantra: "The Suṣumṇā, having been fashioned, descends and takes recourse in the right testicle; then, being drawn upward, it takes recourse in the middle of the collarbone on the left side."
O Daughter of the Mountain, one reaches the right nostril;
likewise, the other, arising from the left groin, reaches the left nostril.
Thus [ends] the Śāradātilaka:
"Among those [channels], the central channel should be the embodiment of Agni and Soma."
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Supūṣā, Alambuṣā,
Yaśasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kuhu— these are considered the seven nāḍīs.
The essential nature of these two is described in the *Yogārṇava*: "The *iḍā* has the luster of a conch or a jasmine flower and is situated on its left side;
the *piṅgalā* has the luster of white and red and rests upon the right side."
Thus, by this, the abiding of the sun and the moon in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* respectively is stated;
for it is said: "The moon moves in the *iḍā*, and the sun in the *piṅgalā*."

Stating that the *suṣumṇā* is the principal [channel], he describes its nature with the words "in the middle.
Because of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "among those also," the word "principal" (*mukhyā*) is understood to carry over.
Among those three, the *suṣumṇā* in the middle is the principal one.
And because it is stated that "among those [channels],
the *suṣumnā* alone is the channel," its nature as consisting of fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*) should be applied as the reason for its primacy.
For it is because of the dissolution right here of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, which have the previously mentioned forms of Soma and Agni;
as it is said: "having entered the mouth of Rāhu.
By this, it is also stated that her location extends as far as the *brahmarandhra*.
As they say: "Between those two, the suṣumṇā is situated, leaning against the spinal column as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)."

He states the names of the remaining seven as "Gāndhārī," etc. Their location and essential nature are described in the *Yogārṇava*: "On the back of the *iḍā* is Gāndhārī, resembling the throat of a peacock; extending from the left foot to the eye, she is proclaimed as Gāndhārī."
The channel resembling an elephant’s tongue (hastijihvā) is situated in front of that [channel];
it rests upon the left side, extending from the head down to the big toe of the foot.
Pūṣan, however, is on the back of Piṅgalā; resembling a dark blue cloud, she extends from the corner of the eye of the southern side down to the soles of the feet.
Alambuṣā, the color of a new cloth, is situated in the middle of the throat;
Yaśasvinī, the color of a conch shell, goes to the eastern region of Piṅgalā.
The Śaṅkhinī is considered to be situated between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī;
she is golden-colored, extending from the feet to the ears on the left side.
"Extending from the big toe up to the head, it is hollowed on the right side.

Others, however, state that Vāraṇā, Sarasvatī, Viśvodarā, and Payasvinī are also mentioned as primary; as they say: "There are many more [channels], but among them, fourteen are declared to be the principal ones."
Suṣumṇā, Piṅgalā, Kuhū, and Sarasvatī.
First Chapter:
Innumerable channels (nāḍīs) have arisen from the five joints of the Suṣumṇā;
the vital breath (prāṇa), having ascended from the Mūlādhāra, pervades that body by means of them.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, the illustrious Vāraṇā,
Viśvodarā, Śaṅkhinī, and then Pūṣā and Payasvinī.
Alambuṣā—thus [ends the list]. Their meditations and physical forms have not been described here for fear of making the text too voluminous; they are indicated by the very term "principal" (mukhyāḥ).
