Thus the principal channels have been described; now he speaks of the general channels with the words "the channels.
From the five joints of the Suṣumṇā, infinite channels have arisen. The five joints are those ending with Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā.
In this context, the completion of a *parvan* (joint) extends from the lower joint upwards until the upper joint.

Although the lexicon states that "a *granthi* (knot) is not rough like a cane-joint" (*ikṣu-parva-avadhiḥ smṛtaḥ*), and there is common usage to that effect, nevertheless, because all six joints are present here, it is explained in this manner.
This is because the commentator on the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra explains the word *parvan* in the rule "one should recite at the *parvan*" (*parvaṇy añjapet*) in exactly this way.
It is with this very intention that he will say [later], "at the middle joint of the finger of the Madhu-mantra.
It should not be understood that there is a union of the Iḍā and Piṅgalā within these joints of the Suṣumṇā;
rather, some vessels (śirā) are endless and downward-facing, while others are upward-facing.
And its circumference is three hundred and ten thousand [yojanas].
The primary channels, numbering seventy-two thousand, have been described;
within all of them, the powerful vital breath (prāṇa) pervades everywhere.
It is eternally established and all-pervading;
within this body, its count would be three hundred and sixty. Dhanvantari has declared that there are exactly three hundred bones here.
There would be one hundred and ten joints of the bones here;
two thousand joints of the flesh, sinews, and vessels are considered [to exist].
There would be nine hundred sinews and five hundred pieces of flesh as well.
In women, there are more than twenty [veins] in the breasts, and ten in the generative organ.
The *Śāradātilaka* states:
"Ten winds (vāyus) are proclaimed here, and ten fires (vahnayas) are likewise remembered.
The five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa are the Maruts; [the others are] Nāga, Kūrma, and Dhanañjaya."
Known by the names Kṛkala and Devadatta,
these ten embodied beings are fires that have become latent within the six defects.
There are twenty-nine lakhs of vessels (śirā-dhamanikā),
and likewise nine hundred and fifty-six of their branches (sājāni).

Thus [it is said]. "Prāṇa" refers to the vital air (vāyu). As they say: "That which is characterized by passion (rājasa) is known as prāṇa; it is primary and the sustainer of the body. Its ten well-known divisions are those by which the entire body is pervaded."
Thus; and that aforementioned body is the "tanu" (body).
While speaking of these [organs], he mentions the fires as well in passing, saying "and the winds.
He states their very names as "prāṇa and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna are included; they are mentioned first because they are well-known.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Yogārṇava*: "The form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is proclaimed to resemble a sapphire;
it resides in the middle of the mouth and nose, in the center of the heart, and in the middle of the navel."
Some say that the *prāṇa* resides even in the big toe;
this *apāna*, however, carries away food and waste products.
The downward wind (apāna) carries out semen, urine, and excrement;
it resembles the indragopa insect and is like a twilight cloud.
And it resides in the penis and the anus, in the thighs, the groin, and the knees; in the shanks, the belly, the hips, and at the root of the navel.
Vyāna circulates the food and provokes all diseases;
it resembles great silver and is the agent of rejection and acquisition.
And it remains constantly here between the eyes and ears, at the ankles and also the heels, as well as in the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks.
The vital air named Udāna causes the lower lip to quiver, agitates the body and the eyes,
and excites the internal organs.
Having the color of lightning or fire, it causes one to rise from bed or leave one's seat;
it resides in the joints of the feet, the hands, and elsewhere.
The first chapter.
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa); sorrow and delusion are recorded as belonging to the mind; and old age and death belong to the body—these are the six fruits [of karma].
The wind named Samāna, having consumed and smelled the food, brings the blood, bile, phlegm, and wind into equilibrium throughout the limbs of the body.
Resembling a cow's horn in shape, it is situated throughout the entire body;
in the upward breath (udvāra), it is called Nāga, resembling a dark blue cloud.
The tortoise is situated in Unmīlana, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium;
while Kakara is in Cūta, resembling the hibiscus flower.
In yawning, Devadatta is like pure crystal;
likewise, Dhanañjaya is the color of great gold in his roar.
In the forehead, the chest, the shoulders, the heart, the navel, and in the skin and bones,
the five winds beginning with Nāga are firmly established together.
Thus [it is said].
But the teachers maintain: "The one named Dhanañjaya produces various kinds of sounds within this body;
yet, because he is the worldly wind, he does not leave the dead man. Thus.

Vairambhaṇa is the chief of the stations, as are Pradyota and Prakṛta; Vairambhaṇa and the others there are all subject to the power of the winds. Thus, with the words "the fires," he describes the abiding state of the fires.
Their names are stated elsewhere: "They are all Jātavedas, Kalmāṣa, Kusuma, Dahana, Śoṣaṇa, and the mighty Tapana; also Piṭhara, Pataga, Svarṇa, Agādha, and Bhrāja. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere, however, other names are mentioned: "The Jṛmbhaka, the Dīpaka, the Vibhrama, the Bhrama, the Śobhana, the Āvasathya, the Āhavanīya, and likewise the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Anvāhāryapacana, and the Gārhapatya—these are the ten fires. Thus it is said.

And other [substances] have been described differently: "The illuminator (bhrājaka), the colorer (rañjaka), the moistener (kledaka), the unctuous (snehaka), the supporter (dhāraka), the digester (randhaka), and the seventh called the liquefier (drāvaka); the pervader (vyāpaka), the purifier (pāvaka), and the tenth is remembered as the adhesive (śleṣmaka).
Thus [it is said].
The humors (doṣas) are vāta, pitta, and kapha;
the constituents to be afflicted (dūṣyas) are the seven bodily tissues (dhātus); this has already been stated previously in the Śāradātilaka.
Tendons, bones, and marrow arise from semen; skin, flesh, and blood from blood.

This is declared to be the sixfold sheath (*ṣāṭkauśika*) within the bodies of all embodied beings. Being thus situated in the womb, remembering the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of his previous birth, he remains there, miserable in nature, his body covered by the fetal membrane (*jarāyu*). In the course of time, that infant, even while causing distress to his mother...

Then, with its body congealed, it is born facing downwards. Having thus described the specific states of the soul once released from the vital breath (prāṇa), [the author], in this context, also speaks of the mind and the body. "Bubhukṣā" refers to a particular state called a wave (ūrmi) that produces hunger; in connection with the six waves, he describes the sixfold sheath (ṣāṭkauśika). Distinguishing the products of semen and blood, he explains them as sinews (snāyu) and so forth.
From the father’s semen, [the body] arises as semen and so forth;
from the mother’s blood, it arises as skin and so forth.
As it has been said: "Three parts from the mother, three parts from the father."

Thus, elsewhere it is said: "The soft parts—blood, fat, flesh, spleen, liver, rectum, heart, navel, and so forth—are considered to be derived from the mother. The beard, body hair, head hair, sinews, veins, arteries, and nails [are derived from the father]."
"The teeth, semen," and so forth; "firm, they arise from *pitta*.
Thus he describes the manner of its stay within the womb.
"In such a state" means: with his hands bound behind his back and his ears covered, leaning against the mother's back, he meditates upon the means of liberation.

As they say: "Covering his ears with hands placed between his armpits, he remains agitated within the womb, filled with fear; remembering the various torments of different wombs previously experienced, he dwells intent on practice while contemplating the means of liberation. Thus it is said.

There is a distinction in other cases: with palms joined at his forehead, he rests against the mother’s back; with limbs well-proportioned, he dwells in the womb on the right side. A female is known to rest on the left side, and one who is neuter is considered to rest in the middle. || 48 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the course of time," Yājñavalkya states the sequence of time as "in the ninth or even the tenth [month]";
likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "The time for birth is then in the ninth month and so forth."
Thus, with his body contracted, his limbs cramped, and his face turned downwards, he is born— that is, he comes into existence—
by means of the winds of labor; "the fetus" is the understood subject.

As they say: "The first stage [of the embryo] remains motionless for a moment; out of fear, it wishes to weep. (50) Then that [consciousness], whose nature is sentience, all-pervading, and possessing the form of the universe, having attained proximity to Śiva, becomes the source of the qualities of eternal bliss. (51) In the ninth or tenth month, by means of powerful winds of birth...
"The living being, afflicted with fever, is drawn out through the opening like an arrow.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "Then, with its head downward, by the powerful winds of labor, the infant is drawn out from the womb through the vaginal opening, crying out in pain."
"He remains motionless for a moment on the ground"—this is the remainder of the sense [of verse 48].

Having analyzed the creation of sound, [the author] states that one desires to weep out of fear; since even weeping consists of indistinct phonemes (*varṇa*), he describes the manner in which phonemes arise and declares the general origin of all mantras from Kuṇḍalinī, beginning with the words "Then," and so forth.

As it has been said: "The state called *Parā* which first arises from the *Mūlādhāra*, and subsequently that called *Paśyantī*; then, reaching the heart and joined with the intellect, it is called *Madhyamā*."

When this living being desires to speak, the *vaikharī* [speech] arises; from that, impelled by the vital air (*pavana*), the collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṅgha*) emerges. Because the channel-path is not yet differentiated at that stage, there is no manifestation of the phonemes.

Thus, after the production of the body, that Goddess Kuṇḍalinī—the Supreme Deity who consists of the *Śabdabrahman* and is of the nature of consciousness—being coiled with all her limbs, and therefore awakened as the soul of the universe and the soul of the *saḷi*, having attained full awareness, gives birth to the world consisting of mantra; such is the connection [of the passage].

There, in the *mūlādhāra*, a channel exists like a coiled serpent; its movement therein by the power of the vital air (*vāyu*) is itself called "recitation" (*japa*). In that context, the phrase "having the nature of consciousness" is a description of its essential character.
That well-known pervasion common to all states has been shown;
by the phrase "possessing universal form," the pervasion of objects is indicated.
The ellipsis "she remains" is to be supplied after "having attained proximity to Śiva.
By this, it is stated that she is denoted by the word *śakti* according to the Śaiva Siddhānta;
the term "proximity" (*sannidhi*) is used figuratively.
In that system, because Śiva and Śakti are non-different, it has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta: "And Śakti does not desire separation from the nature of the Possessor of Śakti;
there is eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its power to burn."
Alternatively, the meaning is that having attained the true nature, which is the perfect treasure—the very nature of Śiva—as it will be stated: "The body becomes Kuṇḍalinī, whose essence is Śiva.
She is she in whom there is the arising of the qualities (guṇas), namely sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The *Śāradātilaka* states:

Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, auspicious, and pervading all bodies, this Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) is remembered as being divided into the higher and the lower; she dances eternally and spontaneously within the lotus-heart of the yogis. (52)
In the support (ādhāra) of all beings, she flashes forth with the form of lightning. By the term "Nityānandā" (Eternal Bliss), the nature of Kuṇḍalinī is stated;
by the term "Guṇodayā" (Source of the Guṇas), it is stated that she is what is designated as *prakṛti* in the Sāṃkhya system.
As they say: "That which they call *pradhāna* is what is described as *śakti*. 51.
Space and time.
"Pervading the entire body" means the pervasion of the body;
it is a certain supreme power (*paraśakti*) that constitutes the division between the higher and the lower. Even through that division, this remains the supreme power alone.

As they say: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus my material nature (prakṛti) is divided eightfold. But know that there is another, higher nature of Mine, O mighty-armed one, which is the life-force (jīvabhūtā), by which this world is sustained. Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, "para" refers to the gross [state], while "apara" refers to the very gross, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth; by their division, there is the supreme power (paraśakti) and the gross power (sthūlaśakti),
as it is said, "from the gross, the grosser," whereby the pervasion of the Great Principle and so forth is indicated.
Alternatively, by the phrase "pervading all bodies," the pervasion of the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders is shown both through the word and its meaning.

As for the word, she is called Śiva, she is called Kuṇḍalinī, and she is called Pradhāna; yet, even though she is of such a nature, she is indicated specifically as feminine. Thus he says: "She is both supreme and non-supreme" (parāparā).
The supreme *prakṛti* is the other [aspect], the neuter-masculine *prakṛti*; through its differentiation and its relinquishment, this is remembered as the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*).
This is the meaning:

although she is denoted by the three genders, nevertheless, for those devotees who are utterly exhausted by the burden of their unwavering devotion, she is designated by the term "Supreme Power," being like a wish-fulfilling creeper for all their desires.
For this very reason, it is auspicious and delightful,
as the teachers have said: "Though equal in the case of males and neuters, it is distinguished [as superior] in the case of women."
Also in the *Nityātantra*: "For she resides everywhere, yet she shines forth especially within passionate women; therefore, one should not cause them to turn away from their desires.

This means that by the very truth of her nature, she is known by the yogis themselves through the instruction of their guru, as indicated by the phrase "dancing eternally in the lotus-heart of the yogis."
Because it is said that "she is visible through those taught by the Teacher," the Goddess stands pervading all beings as the first chapter, according to the sequence of the Śaṅkāvarta.
She has attained the beauty of the limbs of coiled serpents;
she is the Goddess consisting of all deities, consisting of all mantras, and auspicious; she consists of all principles (tattvas), is manifest, subtler than the subtle, and all-pervading.
The Goddess, the mother of the abode of consciousness, whose nature is the Śabdabrahman,
consists of forty-two syllables and takes the form of fifty syllables;
multiplied throughout all her limbs, she is the Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity.
Awakened as the soul of the universe, she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra.
By the phrase "throbbing in the mūlādhāra-cakra, the support of all living beings," the location is specified;
by the phrase "having the form of lightning," meditation (dhyāna) is described.
As they say: "Resembling the flash of a lightning bolt, with a natural luster that has surpassed the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Alternatively, by this [description], it is stated that she possesses manifold splendors because she is the cause for the production of many sounds.
The meaning is that just as the whorl within a conch shell remains by supporting the conch itself, so too does this Goddess.
This intermediate sentence is indeed distinct;
it connects the two terms "śaṅkha" (conch) and "kuṇḍalī" (coiled) by way of the relationship between cause and effect:
"of those serpents which have become coiled, having attained the form of a coil."
Some describe *kuṇḍalī* as a separate word, meaning that just as these elements and serpents have a coiled (*kuṭila*) movement, so too does this [power]; however,
that is not correct.
Because of the repetition [of the idea] in the phrase "Kuṇḍalinī is the supreme deity," the term "consisting of all deities" refers to the pervasion by the gods;
and "Devi" means she who shines, that is to say, she whose form is splendor.
By this, the pervasion of fire is that which consists of all mantras; thus, the pervasion of mantras is Śiva, meaning it has the form of Śiva.
Or, "Śivā" means she whose nature is auspicious;
by this, there is the pervasion of auspiciousness.
Furthermore, because she is directly composed of all the *tattvas*, there is the pervasion of the *tattvas*.
Regarding the resolution of the contradiction in the statement "the omnipresent one is subtler than the subtle": she is subtler than the difficult-to-perceive;
or else, she is subtler even than the subtle *trasareṇu* (sunbeam-dust) because she resides within it; being subtler means more minute.
By this, her pervasion of the atom and other [subtle elements] is demonstrated.
As it has been said: "The Mother of the three worlds is similar [in size] to a single part of a hair-tip split a thousandfold;
because of her subtlety, she cannot be known by her dimensions. (52–55)
"Tridhāma" means having the form of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni; alternatively, "tridhāma" refers to the three locations consisting of Pātāla, Bhūḥ, and Svarga.

By this, the pervasion of the locations is shown: [the mantra] consists of the nature of forty-two phonemes, being composed of the *bhūtalipi* mantra; it has the form of fifty phonemes, being composed of the *mātṛkā*. || 56 || 57 ||
The Śāradātilaka states:

Power (Śakti), when multiplied by one, is the impeller of the entire universe; she is the seed-syllable of the Vedas, the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, and the seed-syllable of Manobhava (the god of love).
Prāsāda, Tumburu, Piṇḍa, Cintāratna, Gaṇeśvara, Mārttaṇḍabhairava, Dorga, and Nārasiṃha-Varāhaja.
He certainly produces Vāsudeva, Hayagrīva, the seed-syllable of Śrī Puruṣottama, and other seed-syllables as well at that time.
When that consciousness becomes doubled in form, it consists of the two—
the *haṃsa* and its color (*varṇa*), or the Supreme Self (*parātman*) and the Word (*śabda*)— as day and night.

Having thus described the general process of origination, the author now speaks of the creation of sound (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*) through specific forms such as "once" (*ekadā*) and so forth. In this context, he begins to explain the creation of meaning (*artha-sṛṣṭi*) indicated by the word *jagacchandas* (the meter of the world). The connection is as follows: the entire universe, consisting of both word and meaning, is set in motion; the power that impels and produces it, when multiplied "once," generates the seed of the Vedas and other scriptures.
In this manner, it should be understood for what follows as well;
the seed-syllable of the Vedas and so forth is the *praṇava*, while the seed-syllable of *Śrī* will be stated at the end of the eighth [chapter].
The seed-syllable of Śakti is in the ninth [chapter], the seed-syllable of Manobhava in the seventeenth,
and the Prāsāda [mantra] in the eighteenth.
Tumburu is in the nineteenth;
the Piṇḍa is in the penultimate [eighteenth];
Cintāratna is in the nineteenth.
Gaṇeśvara in the thirteenth, Mārtaṇḍabhairava in the fourteenth,
and Daurga in the eleventh.
Nārasiṃha in the sixteenth,
Vārāha in the fifteenth, and Vāsudeva with the seed-syllable *glauṃ*.
This has been extracted as the seed-syllable (bīja) of Gopāla;
it is expressed by the word Vāsudeva in the seventeenth [chapter].

The *Nāradapañcarātra* states that the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva is merely the letter *vi*; or it refers to Hayagrīva, because it is said that in the fifteenth [chapter] there is "Śrīpuruṣottama," which means the Puruṣottama conjoined with Śrī. Due to the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), the seed-syllable of the power of Puruṣottama is expressed by the term "the seed-syllable of Śrīpuruṣottama."
In this seventeenth [verse], the seed-syllable of Kāma itself is stated to be the seed-syllable of Puruṣottama, as they say:
"Brahmā, embraced by Dharā and adorned with Māyā and the Bindu."
"The deity here is the embodiment of Manmatha, resembling Puruṣottama. Thus,
there are other [syllables] as well, such as *candra*, *bīja*, *bimba*, and *bīja*, along with the fourteen *haṃsa* syllables.
The two letters *parā* and *ātman* are connected [to the preceding];
the meaning is that they denote the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
At the end, they take the forms *to* and *soham*.
Regarding the phrase "Prakṛti and Puruṣa":
although Puruṣa is beginningless, his manifestation here is figurative due to his being intermingled with Māyā;
the connection is that another pair was born from her in this world.
And that [is] the pair of mantras pertaining to Tripura, beginning with the Jyotir-mantra, in the twelfth [chapter],
and Śaktivināyaka in the thirteenth.
Although at first it consisted of twelve syllables due to the addition of nine syllables, nevertheless, this supreme Goddess creates the first chapter; then she brings forth both Prakṛti and Puruṣa,
and whatever other pair exists in this world, all that was born from her.
The consort of Śiva, whose form is consciousness and whose every limb has been rendered perfect,
gives birth to the Vaipura Mantra, the Lord of Power (Mantraśaktivināyaka).
The one-syllable mantra of Pāśa, the Tripuṭa, Caṇḍanāyaka, Saura, Mṛtyuñjaya, Śaktisambhava, Vinatāsuta,
the one-syllable mantra of Vāgīśī, Nīlakaṇṭha, and the poison-destroying [mantra].
The Yantra is multiplied by the Goddess; it is the three worlds, the three qualities, the three abodes, the three Vedas, and the auspicious triad of letters.
The Goddess [expounded] the *vipuṣkara*, the three groups of *kharas*, the triad beginning with Brahmā,

the triad of *vana*, the triad of time (*kāla*), the triad of power (*śakti*), the great triad of conduct (*vṛtti*), the triad of channels (*nār̤ī*), the triad of the three aims (*trivarga*), and whatever else is considered to be threefold.
Then the fourfold-folded Śāmbhavī of the Lotus-Born Lord, bestowing bliss, performs the *caturacara* [meter] in the *Śāradātilaka*.
The fourfold reality of the goddesses belongs to the Great Goddess;
the four oceans are the fourfold internal organs.
The four subtle elements and so forth, the fourfold forms of Viṣṇu,
the fourfold Gaṇeśas, and the fourfold [principles] beginning with the Self.
The Ojāpūka and other sacred seats (pīṭhas), the fourfold set beginning with Dharma, the elephants beginning with Damaka, the Goddess, and whatever other fourfold sets there may be.
The consort of Śambhu, who bestows all goals, is fivefold;
she is the five peaks of the Puruṣa, and her two sets of five syllables are likewise.

Or rather, the three modes of livelihood in the form of mantras— namely sacrificing, teaching, and receiving gifts— as it is remembered in the tradition: "Three activities constitute one's livelihood."
In the reading "the three modes of livelihood— agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade—
are great," the word "great" (*mahat*) should be construed as an adjective qualifying the triad of channels (*nāḍītraya*).
This triad of channels consists of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā*, which are present from the beginning.
The *trivarga* consists of *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*,
according to the statement, "The *trivarga* consists of *dharma*, *kāma*, and *artha*";
the word "other" (*anyat*) refers to the "friend of the lotus" (*padminībandhu*).
As stated in another tantra,

the fourfold divine reality (devatattva) of the Great Goddess Mahālakṣmī consists of the eight syllables comprising the *praṇava*, *māyā*, and *ahaṃsa*; these are the self-reality (*ātmatattva*), the knowledge-reality (*vidyātattva*), the Śiva-reality (*śivatattva*), and the universal reality (*sarvatattva*).
"The four oceans" refers to the four directions beginning with the east; however, in reality, that [ocean] is one.
The "internal organs" consist of the forms of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta).

Regarding the phrase "the subtle and so forth" (*sūkṣmādīn*): in the first [interpretation], the subtle (*sūkṣmā*) is the supreme (*parā*), while by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī* are meant.
As it has been said: "Vaikharī, Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Sūkṣmā—these arise in reverse order from Kuṇḍalinī onwards in succession.
Thus [one should understand] the states (bhāvas), which are the specific conditions of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya).
Or else, there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified;
Viṣṇu’s form is in the eighth [chapter],
and that of the Gaṇeśas in the thirteenth.
"Of the self and so forth" refers to the fourth *pīṭha*; "Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa" refers to the fourth [set] of the *dharma*s and so forth.
This is also an elliptical expression for unrighteousness and so forth,
or for righteousness, wealth, and so forth; thus, in the eighth [chapter], [the phrase] "elephants at the beginning" [is used].
"Other" refers to the initiation into the mandalas of Siddha and the others, as well as the Heramba-mantra, the Devī-dūta, the Bīja-mantras, and so forth. This is the first chapter:
the Five Jewels of the Great Goddess, which bestows the fruit of all desires;
the five-syllabled mantra of Maheśa; and the five-colored [mantra] of Garuḍa.
The five objects of desire that cause delusion, the five arrows of the gods' trees,
the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, and the five colors of the Great Lord.
The *Śāradātilaka* [mentions] the six-syllabled mantra of Himaruci (the Moon), the six-syllabled *Nārasiṃha*,
the six seasons beginning with spring, and the lords of the Gaṇas beginning with Āmoda.

The Supreme Goddess has produced the seventy-six sheaths (*kośa*), the waves, the tastes, the powers (*śakti*), the Śākinīs and others, the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), the sixfold machine (*yantra*) of power, the six supports (*ādhāra*), and whatever else exists in this world in its sixfold variety. She is all that.
The eternal Goddess, who shares half the body with Śaṅkara, is multiplied sevenfold;
she is the seven-syllabled mantra of Tripurā and the seven-syllabled Vināyaka.
The Gāṇapatya mantra mentioned in another Tantra ends in the fourth [case]; the six-syllabled Śaiva mantra "Vakratuṇḍa" ends in "vam";
and the six-syllabled Kṛṣṇa mantra is in the seventeenth [chapter].
Or there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified;
the six-syllable [mantra] belongs to the Moon (Himaruci), the Narasimha [mantra] to the fourteenth, and the sixteen-syllable [mantra] to the sixteenth.
The Pāśupata weapon [is described] in the twenty-sixth [chapter],
the relationship between qualifier and qualified in the twentieth, and the seasons in the twenty-third.
In the thirteenth [chapter], "Āmodādi," [he describes] the thirteen types of fragrances and, in the first [chapter], "Kośānu," the six flavors beginning with sweet (*madhura*).
In the thirteenth [chapter], it says "the powers of Āmoda and so forth," while in the twentieth,
it says "the powers such as Śākinī and so forth"; thus, there is either a relationship of qualifier and qualified between these two.
One should contemplate the six paths in the fifth [tattva],
and the nine supports in the fifth.
Whatever exists in the world, all that which is sixfold—the six limbs, the Sītā-mantra, the Anuṣaṭ-karma, the postures, and so forth—[is contained herein].

"Saptārṇam" means a mantra of seven syllables; "Padmāvatī-mantra" refers to [the mantra of Padmāvatī]; and in the tenth [chapter], "Atripurā-mantra" refers to the Bhairavī-mantra consisting of the Māyā-bīja in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order.
The mantra of the seven-syllabled conch (*śaṅkha*) is in the seventeenth [chapter],

and Subrahmaṇya with seventeen syllables is in the thirteenth; or alternatively, the seven-syllabled *tripurā* mantra is the "seven-syllabled Vināyaka," which constitutes a relationship of qualifier and qualified.
Regarding the *vyāhṛtis*: in the twenty-first [chapter] is the seven-syllable mantra; in the seventeenth is the *aṅkuśa* mantra;
and in the sixteenth is the *sudarśana*.
Or [he perceives] the relationship between qualifier and qualified,

The six notes—*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *niṣāda*;

And so it has been stated by the teacher Varāhamihira: "Because of the extraordinary taste of nectar, this head of the Asura, even though severed, was not deprived of its vital breaths; thus, it does not attain the state of a planet."
By these and other [verses],
the first chapter [is concluded]; that [mantra] consisting of the seven *vyāhṛtis* is the seven-syllabled *sudarśana*.
The worlds, the mountains, the vowels, the elements, the sages, the islands, and even the planets.
The fuel-sticks are reckoned as seven, and there are seven tongues that consume the oblation;
whatever else is of a sevenfold nature, that has been produced from her.

The eight-syllable mantra of Hari, the pair of eight-syllable mantras of Śakti, the eight-syllable mantra of Bhānu, the eight-syllable mantra of Durgā, and the eight-syllable mantra of the Supreme Self.

That asura Rāhu, to whom a boon was formerly granted by Brahmā, saying: "At the time of an eclipse, you shall receive nourishment from the portion of the oblation offered."

The auspicious eightfold incense is heart-pleasing to the goddesses and gods;
it [satisfies] Brahmā and the others, the Bhairavas, the serpents, the Mūrtis, the Directions, and the Vasus as well.
The great goddess has eight seats, accompanied by the eight groups of eight;
she [bestows] the eight primordial natures (prakṛtis) and [the deities] beginning with Vighna and Vakratuṇḍa in due order.

One should write the syllable *vyom* (the void) in the pericarp, together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the beloved woman, preceded by the *ativindu*; and one should write [the mantra] upon the eight petals like Brahmā, Indra, and the lords of the worlds.

One should write the root mantra, differentiated by vowels, upon the leaves of the month and the digits; and upon the leaves of the teeth, it should be written with the consonants beginning with 'ka' ending in 'sa', differentiated by their respective colors.

One should encircle this with a temple (mandira), and outside that with a power (śakti) and a goad (aṅkuśa); they know this same [arrangement] with a jar-bolt (ghaṭārgala) to be the "bolt of desire" (kāmārgala).
Thus Dharma, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are remembered as the eight Vasus.

Thus, the sixty-fourfold [pīṭhas] consisting of eight groups of eight, arranged upon eight pedestals, are as follows: Māyā, Maṅgala, Nāga, Vāmana, Mahālakṣmī, Caritra, Bhṛgu, Chāyā, Chatra, Hiraṇyahastina, Mahendra, Uḍḍauśa, Campāpura, Ṣaṣṭhacīraka, Mañjñjaneśvarapura, Ilā, Candrapūḥ, Śrīgiri, Kolā, Kullaka, Pūrṇaparvata, Kurukṣetra, Kaliṅga, and Arbuda.
Kāśmīra, Ekāmra, Kāñcī, Malaya, Giri-vara, Eka-randhra, Tāmravarṇī, Koṭṭa, Amrātiśa, Jālandhara, Surabhi, Manīṣā-dri, Kāśī, and Prayāga; [these are the seats].
The first chapter [describes] the powers such as *aṇimā*, the serpents, the forms of the guardians of the directions beginning with Yama, and so forth.
When it expands everything eightfold in this world.
The eternal [power] multiplied ninefold gives birth to the ninefold mantra;

She possesses the ninefold seat-powers (*pīṭhaśakti*), the nine aesthetic sentiments beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*),
the nine gems beginning with ruby (*māṇikya*), and she is endowed with the nine classes [of letters].
The auspicious mandala of the nine life-breath messengers consists of nine groups; as it moves through the world, everything within it rises up from her.

86. Trisrotas, Kāmakoṭṭha, Jayinī, Samathura, Kośalā, Kānyakubja, Udyāna, Aṅga, Rāṣṭra, Hāsa, Aviraja, and hereafter Kuṇḍina, Rājagṛha, Nepāla, Puṇḍravardhana, Mālava, Parasora, Kāmarūpa, Kedāra, Vindhya, Mahāmaṭha, Gośruti, Kāmpilya, Śrīpīṭha, and Marudośā.

Regarding "aṇimā and so forth": aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva as the eighth.
In the fifth [chapter], "vanti" and so forth; at the end, "yamādikān";
and "anyat" refers to the mantra of Śrīvāṇaratipriyadhūmāvatī and others. (81–86)

The preceding verse ends with "setyantam" (up to that), and it is connected to the subsequent verse by the subsequent action.

Regarding "of the powers of the seats" (poṭhaśaktīnām), this refers to [the rasas] such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and so forth, in their respective mantras here and there. [The rasas are:
the erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, and the terrifying.
"The loathsome, the fierce, and the peaceful are remembered as the nine aesthetic sentiments (rasas) in poetry.
Thus [it is said]. "The nine jewels and the six classes" is in the sixth [chapter];

In the third [chapter], the mandala with nine centers is described.
Regarding the phrase "whatever...":
this refers to the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), the nine planets (graha), the tortoise-wheel (kūrma-cakra), the nine squares (navakoṣṭha), and so forth. (87–88)
The *Śāradātilaka*:
The consort of Śambhu, who destroys the suffering of existence, is tenfold in her transformations.
The mantra of Gaṇapati consists of ten syllables, and that of Tvaritā likewise consists of ten syllables. (60)
The ten-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī is that of Yajñikī; the ten-syllable mantra whose essence is Vāsudeva belongs to Aśvārūḍhā. Tripurā’s ten-peaked mantra is the ten-syllable mantra of Tripurā.

By name, there are the Padmāvatī-mantra, the Ramā-mantra, and the ten-syllabled mantra (62). These are the ten principles of Śakti; Maheśvarī is the embodiment of these principles. O Viṣṇu, there are ten channels (nāḍīs) and ten stars in their respective order.
The ten [verses] concerning the world-protectors (lokapālas), and whatever else he creates; thus [ends the section on] Gaṇapati. [Now begins] the thirteenth [chapter], concerning Kṣipraprasādana.
Regarding the mantra of Tvaritā, in the tenth [chapter] it is devoid of *māyā*.
As it has been said: "VA-ME-KHE, its final letter joined with Śiva (SA), the last one (PHA) joined with the Lady (Ā), then DYĀ with a half-mora (LAVAM);
the final one (KṢA) with the womb (I), followed by ASTRĀNTIKA (PHREṂ), and SATĀRA (OṂ)—this is the ten-syllable mantra. Thus it is stated.
Varbheti | Varmā hūṃ | Khe svarūpam |
And its own form [is *cha*].
That which is the last [of the consonants] is *ka*; joined with the letter *i* and the syllable *śiva* (the *yuga*), it becomes *che*.
That which is the final [vowel] is *sa*.

The word *aṅganā* is *strīṃ*. The letter *ha* (*h*) with the nasal dot (*bindu*), joined with the vowel *u* and the anusvāra, becomes *hūṃ*. The final letter is *kṣa*, joined with the letter *e* and the nasal dot (*bindu*). Thus: *strīṃ hūṃ kheṃ*.
"Astra Phaṭ" at the end;
"with the Tāra," meaning joined with the Praṇava at the beginning. Thus is the extraction of the ten syllables of Tvaritā.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśa*), the Punisher of Beings (*bhūtadaṇḍin*), the end of the Kalās (*kalānta*), the final one with its source (*sayonika*);

that fifth [syllable] ending with that, together with Rudra (*sarudra*), ending with the limit of the Sāman (*sāmantāntālaya*); the one called Vāmā, the first long [vowel], and the Principle of Wrath (*kopatattva*) joined with the end of Hara (*harānta*).
One should know this ten-syllabled mantra, beginning with Om (*tārādi*) and ending with Phaṭ. Thus it is said.

Regarding "bhuvana": *bhūvaneśa* is *ha*; *bhūta* is *u*; the staff (*daṇḍa*) is the anusvāra; thus, *hūṃ*. The *kalās* are the vowels; that which is at their end is *ka*; the one after that is *kha*; together with its source (*sayonika*), it is joined with *e*; thus, *khe*.
The fifth letter of that [group] ending with *ta* is *cha*. Together with *rudra* (*ra*) and joined with *ekāra* (*e*), it becomes *ke*.
That which ends with *sāmanta* (*sa*) and ends with *visarga* (*ḥ*).
The syllable *ā* is the *ālaya*.
The one called *vāmā* is *svauṃ*.
The first is *hūṃ*, and its long form is *hūṃ*.
The *tattva* of anger is *kṣaḥ*.
When joined with the letter *e* at the end by Hara (*ha*),

The zodiac signs, the suns, and the forms of Hari—she is the twelvefold one;

the Gāyatrī of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the Gāyatrī of the Consort of Śambhu.
"Hara, Bahurūpa, Trāgvaka, Aparājita, Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardī, Raivata, Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kāpālin— these are considered the forms of Śiva.

The *Dakṣiṇāmūrtti*, the *Śāradātilaka*,

One does not perform [it].

"Namo bhagavate aghorarūpāya hana hana daha daha paca paca bhrāmaya bhrāmaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the thirty-four-syllable Aghora mantra; it is an Aghora-anuṣṭubh, and its deities are Aghora and the others.
The six-limbed [mantra]. The mantra of Bhadrakālī is in the twenty-fourth [chapter]: "She consists of will, knowledge, and action; she is of the nature of light and of the nature of the qualities."
In this sequence, Kuṇḍalinī creates the garland of phonemes, consisting of forty-two elements, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'sa'.

That very [power], having entered into *sattva* and being permeated by *rajas*, is denoted by the term *dhvani*; it is the state of the *akṣara*. That same [power], when permeated by *tamas*, is denoted by the term *māda*; it is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) state. That same [power], due to the predominance of *tamas*, is denoted by the term *nirodhikā*. That same [power], due to the predominance of *sattva*, is denoted by the term *aḍeṃdu*. Due to the conjunction of both, it is denoted by the term *bindu*. As they say: "Excelling through the power of the will (*icchāśakti*), illuminating the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and possessing the form of the Person (*puṃrūpiṇī*), that Power, called Action (*kriyākhyā*), creates as the Lord."
Thus, this very *bindu*, when situated in another location, becomes known by names such as *parā* and so forth. "From that" means from the *bindu*.
One perceives *parā* at the root (*mūla*), *paśyantī* in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *madhyamā* in the heart, and *vaikharī* in the mouth.
As it has been said: "The subtle *kuṇḍalinī*, whose nature consists of pure light, is beyond the range of the ears; from there she rises upward, moving upwards."
Self-luminous, she becomes perceived when one resorts to the Suṣumṇā; reaching the heart-lotus, she is the Madhyamā in the form of sound.

Then, from that mere internal discourse, she becomes undifferentiated and moves through the *uṅkha*; she herself resides in the chest, throat, and palate, and is situated in the head, nose, and teeth.
Vaikharī speech, which is grasped by the ear, originates from the root of the tongue and the lips, encompasses all phonemes, and gives rise to the manifold expansion of sound.
Thus it is said.
Also in the Kādima-tantra: "By the activation of the power of one's own will, the supreme sound called Parā arises in the Mūlādhāra from the nature of the vital breath."
That very *oṃ* is led by that [power] and, having blossomed within the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, it attains the name "Paśyantī"; by that same power, the *oṃ* gradually [attains the state of] *Madhyamā*.

In the *anāhata* [cakra], conjoined with the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), it is called the "Middle" (*madhyamā*). Likewise, being impelled upward from there, it reaches the region of the throat for purification.
Then, that which is called Vaikhari resides successively in the throat, head, palate, lips, and teeth; likewise in the root, tip, and back of the tongue, and finally at the tip of the nose.
The first chapter:
Multiplied by fifty gates, she gives birth to the garland of fifty phonemes; non-different from those phonemes, she produces the Kalās and the Rudras and so forth in sequence.
The phonemes, from the beginning up to the letter *kṣa*, arise in sequence from the throat, palate, lips, and throat-lips, as well as from the teeth and lips.
It is declared that these [letters], beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', possess the nature of vowels.

Thus it is said. And so the Śruti declares: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave of the heart, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what human beings speak."
Thus it is said.

Alternatively, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) itself, when designated as "Supreme" (*parā*), is the illuminator characterized by the manifestation of consciousness; it is *māyā* in its state of quiescence, meaning it is the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*).
Its states of vibration are *paśyantī* and the others.

In this context, he speaks of *paśyantī* as that which consists of the essence of the *bindu*-principle, whose nature is universal vibration and luminosity, and whose locus of manifestation is within the region from the *mūlādhāra* up to the navel;
"paśyantī" means she is so called because her essence is knowledge (*jñāna*).

He speaks of *madhyamā* as that which consists of the external and internal organs, whose form is Hiraṇyagarbha, which is composed of *nāda* and *bindu*, whose locus of manifestation extends from the navel to the heart, and whose true nature consists of specific volitions (*saṅkalpa*) and the like; "madhyamā" refers to her intermediate position.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose intellect (*buddhi*) is in the middle.

Referring to speech as *vaikharī*—which has the form of *virāj*, consists of seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), is manifested in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the mouth, and is of the nature of general sound—the meaning is that it is called *vaikharī* because of its specific clarity (*viśeṣeṇa kharatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "tadvarṇa" (those phonemes): she gives birth to those digits (kalās) which are non-different from those phonemes;
she gives birth to Rudra and the others.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there are their powers (śaktis); the Viṣṇus and the powers of Viṣṇu; fifty medicinal herbs and fifty desires (kāmās) along with their powers; fifty lords of the Gaṇas (gaṇeśas) and their powers; and fifty guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) and their powers.

In this regard, the fifty medicinal herbs are as follows: sandalwood, red sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, uśīra, roga, water, and ghusṛṇā; kakkola, jasmine, māṃsī, murā, coraka, granthi, rocanā, and pattra; pippalī, bark, guhā, aruṇa, ṭaṇaka, lavaṅga, avakumbhī, and vandinī; audumbara, kāśmarī, sthirā, darapuṣpikā, and mayūraśikhā; prakṣa, agnimanthā, siṃhī, kuśā, darbha, and black darapuṣpī; rohiṇī, ṭuṇḍuka, kaṣṭahatī, pāṭali, citrā, tulasī, and apāmārga; śatamakhaltā, dvirephā, viṣṇukrāntā, musalī, and añjalinī; dūrvā, śrīdevī, sahā, and likewise lakṣmī and sadābhadra. These medicinal herbs have been enumerated according to the sequence of the letters; through their various forms—as pills, decoctions, or ashes—they bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, another application of these medicinal herbs is stated in the Kādimata: "Whichever mantra there may be, [the beads] for that very mantra are fashioned from the medicinal herbs corresponding to its syllables."
The number of pills produced from each respective syllable grants the accomplishment of the mantra.

Through that [practice], there shall be consecration, the warding off of obstacles, the attainment of reality, its anointing, and likewise worship; this leads to the attainment of siddhi, and not otherwise.
Thus are the fifty Kāmas and their Śaktis as follows: Kāma, Kāmada, Kānta, Kāntimān,
Kāmagas, Kāmācāra, Kāma, Kāmuka, and Kāmavarjana.
Rāma, Rama, Ramaṇa, Lord of Rati, Beloved of Rati, Lord of Night, Consort of Ramā, the one who delights, and the wanderer of the night.
Nandaka, Nandana, Nandī, and again Nandayitā; Pañcabāṇa, Ratimukha, Puṣpadhanvan, and Mahādhanus.
Bhrāmaṇa, Bhramaṇa, Bhramamāṇa, and another, Bhrama;
Bhrānta, Bhrāmaka, Bhrāntācāra, and Bhramāvaha.
Delusion is the deluder, and delusion is indeed the increaser of delusion; it is Madana, Manmatha, Mātaṅga, and the leader of the bees.
Gāyana, Gotija, Narttaka, Khelaka, Unmatta, Mattaka, Vilāsa, and Lobhavardhana.
And those on the left side, possessing the luster of pomegranate flowers, are gentle, endowed with Śaktis, all clad in red garments, and holding flower-arrows and bows.
Wearing all ornaments, the fifty Kāmas are proclaimed:
Rati, Prīti, Kāminī, Mohinī, and Kamalapriyā.
Vilāsinī, Kalpalatā, Kāśyāmalā, Śucismitā, Vismitācī, Viśālākṣī, Lelihānā, and Digambarā.
Vāmā, Kunā, Dharā, Nityā, Kalyāṇī, Mohinī, Madanā— the best of goddesses— and likewise Lāpinī and Mardinī.
Kalahapriyā, Ekācī, Sumukhī, Nalinī, Japinī, Pālinī, Śivā, Mugdhā, Rasā, and Bhramā.
Cārulolā, Cañcalā, Dīrghajihvā, Ratipriyā, Lolākṣī, Bhṛṅgiṇī, Pāṭalā, and likewise Mādanī.
The first chapter:
Mālā, Haṃsinī, Viśvatomukhī, Nandinī, as well as Ramaṇī, Kānti, Kalakaṇṭhī, and Vṛkodarī.
These fifty Śaktis described are dark as clouds, intoxicated with passion, resembling saffron in hue, adorned with all ornaments,
holding blue lotuses in their hands, and capable of attracting the three worlds; they are to be meditated upon thus.
Thus,
the fifty Gaṇeśas and their Śaktis are as follows: Vighneśa, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, and Gaṇanāyaka.
Gajendra, Sūrpakarṇa, and he known as Trilocana; Lambodara, Mahānanda, Caturmūrti, and Sadāśiva.
Āmoda, Durmukhī, Sumukha, Pramodaka,
Ekarada, Dvijihva, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha.
Varada, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍaka, Senānī, Grāmaṇī, Matta, Vimatta, and Mattavāhana.
Jaṭī, Muṇḍī, Khaḍga, Gokhara, Vareṇya, Vṛṣaketana,
Bhakṣapriya, Gaṇeśa, and the one known as Meghanādaka.
The pervasive Lord of the Gaṇas has declared these fifty leaders of the Gaṇas to be like the rising sun in hue, with elephant faces and three eyes.
Holding nooses, goads, boons, and gestures of fearlessness in their hands, they are endowed with power: Śrī, Puṣṭi, Śānti, Svasti, and Sarasvatī.
Svāhā, Medhā, Kānti, Kāminī, Mohinī, Naṭī, Pārvatī, Jvālinī, Nandā, Supāśā, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
Umā, Tejovatī, Satyā, Vighneśā, Vighnarūpiṇī, Kāmadā, Madajihvā, Bhūti, Syāṅgītikā, and Sitā.
Ramā is said to be Mahiṣī, as well as Bhañjinī and Vikarṇapā; Bhṛkuṭi, Lañjā, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Dhanurdharā are likewise [her forms].

She is known as Yāminī and Rātri; she is blinded by passion (Kāmāndhā) and possesses the luster of the moon (Śaśiprabhā); she has tremulous eyes (Lolācī) and flickering radiance (Cañcalā Dīpti); she is both auspicious (Subhagā) and inauspicious (Durbhagā), yet she is the bringer of welfare (Śivā).
In the *Śāradātilaka*, the fire [triangle] becomes the *nirodhikā*; the half-moon is the moon;
and the sun is formed by the union of both, being the essence of the point (*bindu*), a treasury of splendors.

Since the castes (varṇas) were born from the Bindu, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, they must be of the nature of Agni and Soma; for they have come into existence from that Sun which consists of Śiva and Śakti, and thus they possess the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
Bhargā, Bhaginī, Bhoginī, Subhagā,
Kālarātri, and Kālikā are considered to be the fifty Śaktis.

Blazing with all ornaments, stationed on the limbs of their beloveds, and possessing beautiful eyes; holding red lotuses in their hands and wearing red garlands, garments, and being reddish in hue—thus they are to be meditated upon.

Thus, the fact that the phonemes consist of Agni and Soma, as well as their nature as Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, will be useful later on; therefore, having analyzed that, he says "the obstructive" (*nirodhikā*),
because the obstructive, being of the nature of Agni, is the very essence of Śiva.
Ai~īṃ: because the Moon (Indu) is of the nature of Soma, it possesses the essential nature of Śakti;
for this reason, [the vowels] have arisen from the Sun which consists of both Śiva and Śakti, and the Sun itself consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Since it is said that "the conjunction of both is the *arka*," they thus possess the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire,
because of the non-difference between cause and effect.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, the commentary on the *Śrīśāradātilaka* composed according to the authentic tradition.
Oṃ.
The second chapter:
Next, I shall explain the manifestation of the phonemes in the mouths of men,
which are constantly impelled by the vital air and emerge from the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*.
The phonemes (varṇas) manifest sequentially through the organs of articulation, such as the throat;
among these, the vowels (svaras) are said to belong to the Moon, while the consonants (sparśas), which bring about auspicious results, belong to the Sun.
All these are pervasive and belong to the fire element; they have the moon, sun, and fire as their deities.
The sixteen vowels are well-known, and the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five.
He promises to speak [on this] with the words "tataḥ" (then),
meaning that they were impelled by the wind (*marut*); that is to say, having been successively impelled by the wind, they were brought to the station of *paśyantī* and made ready for emergence.
Therefore, the connection is that the phonemes, having emerged from the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*, manifest sequentially through the articulatory organs such as the throat;
the word "sequentially" (*kramāt*) is used because there is no simultaneous utterance of the *anāhata* and *viśuddhi* centers within the apertures of the *suṣumṇā*.
This was stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari: "The self, having come together with the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the bodily fire, which impels the vital air;
that air, moving within the chest, produces the deep-toned voice."
Thus, by the word "beginning with the throat" (*kaṇṭhādi*), the palate (*tālu*) and other locations are included;
as it has been said: "There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head."
The root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.

Thus, regarding that which was stated—that all phonemes (varṇas) possess the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—it is now said that they are manifold through a systematic arrangement for the sake of their subsequent application and for the conventional usage of the thirty-eight digits (kalās). Among these phonemes, the vowels (svaras) range from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*); the consonants (sparśas) range from *ka* to *ma*; and the pervasive letters (vyāpakas) range from *ya* to *kṣa*.
Thus, all these auspicious deities— Soma, Sūrya, and Agni— arise; among them,
the arising of the vowels will be explained immediately hereafter,
while the arising of the others should be understood as occurring through the "arising of the elements" (bhūtodaya) which will be described in the final chapter.

Regarding the statement by the Teacher, "Its emergence is through the elemental parts (bhūtakalā)," he will indicate this very point here by describing the number of elements, saying, "without vowels. In response to the inquiry as to how many vowels and so forth there are, according to the method about to be described, he says: "The vowels..."
“Especially renowned” means they are independent;
as they say: “Among those, the vowels are independent.”
The consonants are known to be of the nature of the principles (tattvas), since the letter *ma* is the Puruṣa;
those ten pervaders bestow desire, wealth, and dharma.
The letter *k* among the vowels has been mentioned previously; the subsequent ones are long, and these, in their sequence, consist of Śiva and Śakti, ending with the Bindu and the Sarga (visarga).
The bindu is declared to be the male, the sun; emission is the female, the moon. That which is the middle of the vowels is the neuter quartet.

"Consisting of the principles (tattva-ātmānaḥ)" means that their essential nature consists of the twenty-four principles beginning with *prakṛti*; this is a statement regarding their true form (*svarūpa*).
Now, since they are numbered as twenty-five, how can it be said that they consist of twenty-four principles? To this he says: "Because the syllable *ma* is the *puruṣa*."
For this reason, the letter *ma* signifies the Person (*puruṣa*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*).

The letters beginning with *bha* represent primordial nature (*prakṛti*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as hearing, speech, space, and so forth; while the other letters are the remaining phonemes.

It has been stated that these are employed in the ritual installations (*nyāsa*) of the principles of power (*śakti-tattva*) and others, and it is also indicated therein that among the twelve solar digits (*kalā*) mentioned in the sequence of the twelve letters, there is the abandonment of the final one.
Thus, these [elements] consist of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
As the Teacher has stated: "The final [element] is the Self (*ātman*), remembered as the Sun.
For this very reason, because of the connection with the letter *a* in the form of the *bindu* within all seed-syllables (*bīja*), it should be understood that the Puruṣa is one with them.

Because the letter *ma* has the nature of a *bindu*, and because it will be stated later that "the *bindu* is said to be the male [principle] and the sun," and because it is pervasive throughout its own constituent parts beginning with *ka*, and because it is touched by the letter *ma* in the form of the *bindu* which is the sun, they are called "contacts" (*sparśas*). For this very reason, they are solar. Alternatively, the construction is as follows:

The letter *ma* is the *puruṣa*; the other consonants (*sparśas*) have the *tattvas* as their essence— this connects with what follows, namely "because," from which [the letter] *ya*, ten pervasive [elements arise].
Because they reside within the *doṣas* (humors) and *dūṣyas* (tissues), they possess pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).

Furthermore, since the fires (*agnis*) also exist therein, they are called "fiery" (*āgneya*); alternatively, they may be regarded as "fiery" because they terminate in the syllable *kṣa*, which represents the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) known as Nṛsiṃha.
Their fruits for the three [classes] are, respectively: the granting of desire, wealth, and dharma.
For this very reason, he will state later: "The mules are granters of desires," and so forth.

Demonstrating the distinct individuality of the vowels themselves, he states two modes for the sake of expressing their nature as the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtti) and their powers (śakti), and for subsequent practical usage: "The short [vowels]," etc.
Although *e* and *ai* are technically long, they are here designated as short by technical convention (*pāribhāṣika*).
These short and long vowels are, respectively, composed of Śiva and Śakti.

The short vowels *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o* are composed of Śiva and have masculine forms; this is the meaning. The long vowels *ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ, ai, au* are composed of Śakti and have feminine forms; this is the meaning.

Desiring to express that these two—the Bindu and the Sarga—are distinct from one another as the forms of Puruṣa and Prakṛti within the recitation of the *Bindusargāvajapa*, he says: "They should be those ending with the Bindu and the Sarga."

The short vowels are joined with the nasal drop (bindu) at their end, and the long vowels are joined with the visarga at their end; the meaning is that among the short vowels, the bindu is the eighth, and among the long vowels, the visarga is the eighth.
The second chapter:
Krakhā is situated in Piṅgalā and joined with Iḍā;
she should be known as being in the midst of Suṣumṇā, along with the four who are neuter.

For this very reason, he says: "The Bindu is the male," and "the Moon" is the designation for the other vowels because they consist of lunar days (*tithi*) which are the digits (*kalā*) of that [Bindu]; thus, the Visarga, in the form of the Moon, serves as the cause for completing its own number sixteen.
They are called *svaras* because they sound (*svarante*) or speak; for this very reason, they are gentle (*saumya*).

This is precisely the position favored by the author of the treatise, since we observe such usage as "by the six groups [of consonants] included within the non-neuter short and long vowels, in their respective order," at the occasion of describing the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Māṭṛkā.

However, some maintain that among vowels, *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ* are short (*hrasva*) with one measure (*mātrā*), while *ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au*, as well as those followed by the nasal dot (*bindu*), the visarga (*sarga*), those at the end of a word (*avasānika*), and those followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), are long (*dīrgha*). This person is merely worthy of salutation;
for [the term] "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) denotes the property of being neuter, and since these possess that property, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśa-ādi* group.
6. Regarding the emergence (*udaya*) of the vowels, [the text] says "in the Piṅgalā": the short vowels are *a, i, u, e, o*;
the long vowels are *ā, ī, ū, ai, au*; and [the vowels] before the bindu and visarga are *ra* (the sun) and *niśākara* (the moon), since their emergence has already been stated by that very [rule].

This purpose has been stated by Gautama: "The rites such as killing, which are proclaimed to arise from the *Ṣaṭsvarodaya*, yield fruit when performed during the rising of the cruel breaths (*hastaiḥ*); otherwise, they do so during the long rising (*dīrghodaye*). Thus [ends the section on] Suṣumṇā.
In that regard, the method is as follows: at the time when the body-wind begins its entry from the northern part into the southern part, it flows through both for a certain period;
that is the time of the commencement of the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
At that time, the short pair consisting of the phonemes *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *ṭ* arises.
Thus, at the time of beginning the entry into the northern part from the southern, for a certain period the bodily wind flows in both directions;
that is the time of the transit of the summer solstice (*uttarāyaṇa-saṃkrānti*),
and then a long pair of breaths arises.

As stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Starting from the seventh vowel, those four which are neuter arise when the vital breath (*prāṇa*), resting in the *suṣumṇā*, moves during the transition of the solstices (*ayanasaṃkrama*).
Others, however, hold a different view: that the short vowels are *ai, u, ṛ, lṛ*, while the long ones are *āi, ū, ṝ, lṝ*.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "When the vital breath moves toward the south, then there is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*);
therein, five short vowels consisting of the nature of the five elements arise."
When the vital breath (prāṇa) rests in the left [nostril], then it is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
at that time, the five elements become elongated and they arise individually and separately. Thus says the Śāradātilaka.
Without the sibilants (kharas), the manifestation of other [consonants] does not occur directly;
therefore, the wise declare that the phonemes consist of Śiva and Śakti.
When the vital breath is situated in the right channel, there are, in their respective order, the winds Parā, Recikā, the one called Indhikā, the one called Vidyā, and Nivṛtti.
"Pratiṣṭhā, Śānti, Dīpikā, Mocikā, and likewise Sūkṣmā—these are the vowels arising in the vital breath (prāṇa), O Dear One, resting upon the Uḍḍiyāna.

According to this view, although the emergence of the diphthongs (ekāra, etc. is not explicitly mentioned, nevertheless, because they are *sandhyakṣaras* (conjunct vowels), their emergence should be understood as occurring simultaneously with that [of the constituent vowels].

Padmapādācārya, however, states: "Since even the delay resulting from the aforementioned procedure is untenable for an internal *ayana* [solar transit] occurring over five external *ghaṭikās*, one should understand that the measurement of time through inhalations and exhalations (*khāsocchvāsa*) is to be applied there;
and whether it consists of a day and night, a fortnight, or an *ayana*, it is to be known according to one's desire."

7. Demonstrating the etymological derivation of the term *vyañjana* (consonant), he states that they too consist of Śiva and Śakti: "Without" (*vinā*) vowels (*svaraiḥ*), the manifestation (*vyaktiḥ*) of others—the consonants beginning with *ka*—does not occur directly (*añjasā*) or easily (*prākaryeṇa*).
Therefore, all phonemes (*varṇāḥ*) consist of Śiva and Śakti.

The etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of *vyañjana* as "that which manifests" (*vyakti-rañjanāt*) has been shown; as they say: "From being manifested by them (*taiḥ vyaṅgyāt*), it becomes *vyañjana*. This is what is meant.
It has been stated previously that vowels consist of Śiva and Śakti;
since it is impossible to pronounce consonants without vowels, they possess the nature of Śiva and Śakti when pronounced together with vowels.
Thus, because the emergence of consonants is subordinate to the emergence of vowels, the arising of the consonants is to be understood through the emergence of the vowels alone.
And it is said in the Mantramuktāvalī: "And the mantras have that as their primary object."

8. Regarding the phrase "in these": because the drop (bindu) in the form of the Sun is all-pervasive everywhere, the term "auspicious arising" is stated as a qualification of the solar [element]. Now, one might object: "If this is the division, then the previously mentioned reason, 'by which,' which was stated as common to all the letters, would not be applicable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "All [the letters] have the Moon, Sun, and Fire as their deities."
If it is argued that even so, the contradiction remains as it was, we say no;
for this [unity] is ultimate, whereas the distinction is to be understood as being for the sake of practical application and the like.
Regarding the statement that "vowels, consonants, and semi-vowels" [constitute the phonemes], in response to the inquiry as to what these are and how many there are, he says "vowels," and so forth.

Śānti, Kriyā, Dayā, Medhā, Harṣā, Śraddhā, Lajjā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
These are declared to be the powers of the vowels (svara-śaktis), in order, [residing] in joy and delight:
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī, Vilāsinī, Vijayā, Virajā, Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunadā, and Smṛti. || 52–53 ||
She is supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), prosperity (*samṛddhi*), purity (*śuddhi*); she is devotion (*bhakti*), intelligence (*buddhi*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and forbearance (*kṣamā*).
She is Rāmā, Umā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudā, and the other Vasudhā.
She is the Supreme (*parā*), the Ultimate Goal (*parāyaṇā*), the Subtle (*sūkṣmā*), the Twilight (*sandhyā*), Wisdom (*prajñā*), Radiance (*prabhā*), and Night (*niśā*).
Amoghā, Vidyutā, and others such as Koṭī grant all desires.
Seated upon the limbs of their beloveds, with smiling faces,
their bodies resemble streaks of lightning, and their hands hold lotuses and the gesture of fearlessness.
From the various divisions of the letters of the Mātṛkā, all mantras were born;
through the classification of mantras and vidyās, the diverse lineages of mantras arose.
All mantras are declared to consist of male, female, and neuter natures.

Mantras are to be known as male deities, and Vidyās are remembered as female deities. (From the *Śāradātilaka*, verse 58): Male mantras should end in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, while those of females are considered to end in *svāhā*.
It is said that there are three kinds of *mantras*: those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter.
These various *mantras* are praised for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*).
One should understand that *mantras* consist of the nature of both fire and moon, corresponding to the cruel and the gentle.
The Manavas are said to consist mostly of fire, wind, earth, water, and space; those belonging to Agni are fiery, while those belonging to Soma consist for the most part of the nectar of the moon.
[This is so] of that which is composed of consciousness, non-dual, partless, and bodiless.
The conceptualization of Brahmā's form is for the sake of the ritual duties of the lay followers.
Thus, there is the conceptualization of male and female organs and so forth among the deities residing in the realm of form. || 58 ||
The endings of those [mantras] are both separate and combined;
"ending in *diṭha*" means ending in *svāhā*. The *bindu* is now described.
According to the lexicon [Amara-kośa], which states, "Ṭhaḥ is in the void, and lahaḍūnau," its doubling results in *visarga*. And that [visarga] is of the nature of Śakti.
By that word "seen" (dṛṣṭa), the power of fire is indicated: mantras ending in *vaṣaṭ* or *phaṭ* are masculine; those ending in *vauṣaṭ* or *svāhā* are feminine;
and those ending in *huṃ* or *namaḥ* are neuter—thus mantras are remembered as being of three kinds.
"Even by means of the *tāra*, the mantras are inferred from their beginning, end, and middle;
just as males, females, and neuters are distinguished by their proximity to their own nature, so too are they proclaimed to end with the *bindu*, the *visarga*, and the crescent moon. (58)
He states the purpose for the three types in sequence with the words "are recommended" (*śastāḥ*).

It is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The remaining males are recommended, especially for subjugation (*vaśya*) and eradication (*uccāṭa*); women are for the destruction of minor rites and diseases; and eunuchs are for other [purposes]."
Thus ends the second chapter.
Those belonging to Agni become fully awakened when the vital breath moves through the right [nostril].
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is situated in another portion, the gentle [deities] attain awakening.
When the vital breath has entered both channels, they all attain awakening;
once awakened, they always bestow their fruit upon the practitioners (mantrins).
He demonstrates that even for those [names], as in "agnau" and so forth; the word "karmaṇoḥ" connects back to the previous [rule];
and "vanaḥ" becomes "ra".
*Tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*;
the final [letter] is *kṣa*;
*viyat* is the letter *ha*.
The word *prāyaḥ* expresses abundance; as Amarasimha states: "The word *prāyaḥ* [is used] in the sense of 'mostly,' 'wonderful,' and 'gradually'. It is connected with the preceding term *āgneyāḥ*.
That is the moon (indu);
for in the *tattvanyāsa*, the lunar orb is assigned as beginning with the letter *sa*.
It is nectar (*amṛta*) for you.

In this regard, for a single [mantra], the final and initial letters, as well as the first and last letters, of the stars and the sky [constellations] should be fiery (āgneya); the others are lunar (saumya). A mantra ending in *namaḥ*, even if fiery, is lunar; a mantra ending in *phaṭ*, even if lunar, is a fiery mantra.
Through fiery [mantras], the accomplishment of cruel rites occurs; through lunar [mantras], one should duly perform gentle rites.
Thus it is said;
and in the *Nārāyaṇīya* as well: "A mantra whose final syllable is *tāra* (om), *agni* (ra), or *viyat* (ha), is generally considered to be fiery (*āgneya*).
The remainder is praised as being watery (*taumya*), according to the sequence of the cruel and the gentle."
Generally, a mantra belonging to Agni (the fire element) should be of a gentle (saumya) nature and endowed with "namaḥ" at the end;
likewise, a mantra belonging to Soma (the moon/water element) should be of a fierce (āgneya) nature and endowed with the syllable "phaṭ" at the end.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Even a mantra of the wrathful class attains a state of tranquility when endowed with a peaceful seed-syllable;
even a peaceful mantra attains a state of wrathfulness if it is sprouted with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*."
Thus it is said.
Regarding this, the specific detail is found in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should recite the two mantras called Āgneya and Saumya, with the *Tāra* at the beginning and end of both."
One constellation consists of four degrees.
Among those constellations belonging to Agni, the two eastern degrees are the head and the other two are the tail;
among those belonging to Soma, the two northern degrees are the head and the other two are the tail.
Gārgya maintains that no ritual application should be performed during the time of the tail.
The lunar mansions belonging to Agni and Soma will be mentioned in the "Snake-Wheel" (*ahicakra*).
Among those, the solar and fiery (*agni*) lunar mansions are as stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "A mantra, whether asleep or just awakened, does not grant success."
The time of sleep is when [the breath] flows through the left [nostril], and the state of waking is when it flows through the right.
This is the reversal of the Saumya-mantra belonging to the Āgneya-manu. From the *Śāradātilaka*:
Those mantras which are defective—such as being "cut" (*chinna*) and so forth—do not protect the practitioner;
they are described as being cut, obstructed (*ruddha*), devoid of power (*śaktihīna*), or turned away (*parāṅmukha*).
Deaf, devoid of sight, paralyzed, as well as stunned, burnt, exhausted, bewildered, soiled, insulted,
pierced, fast asleep, intoxicated with passion, and fainted.
Furthermore, there are those whose vitality is stolen, the deficient, the ruined, the childish,
the boy, the youth, the mature, the bound, the merciless, the seedless, the one devoid of accomplishment, the dull-witted, and the fraudulent.
"One should know the time of awakening for both [the breaths] as they flow in both directions.
As it is said elsewhere: "But at the time of sleep, the recitation of the mantra does not bestow its intended fruit."
Thus,
elsewhere the time of sleep is described differently,
as they say: "From the union with breath-control (prāṇāyāma), there is the merging of the individual power (śakti) and the universal power (Śvīśakti)."
"The time of awakening is to be known, and the time of sleep follows thereafter.
However, elsewhere another method for the purpose of awakening has been stated: "Having carefully encapsulated the letters beginning with *la* along with the nasal bindu..."
Furthermore, one should recite the letters ending with the visarga followed by the letter *ta* alone;
if taught in this manner, it is said that the awakened [mantra] bestows swift accomplishment.
By describing the essential nature of male, female, and other [categories], their mutual opposition is also indicated, as they say:

"Those with female deities are generally enemies of those with male deities; among those with female deities, there is mutual enmity between the gentle and the cruel, and the same applies to those with male deities."

Thus, by way of reversing the previous [argument], there is a connection with what follows. Since it has been stated that mantras arise from the *mātṛkā* which consists of Śakti and Śiva, the defects such as *āṇava* and so forth serve as the cause for their arising; consequently, mantras associated with defects such as *chidra* contained within those [defects] produce contrary results. To this he says: "Is it not so? (*kiṃ na*)?
The general result for all [planets] is that, when they are afflicted by defects such as being "chinnā" (cut), they do not protect the practitioner;
however, it should be understood that in some cases there are specific results for each, as will be stated.
He explains the meaning of the word "ādi" (and so forth) with the term "chinna" (cut).
Furthermore, by the phrase "likewise again," he states that the *kūṭa* itself indicates the partless;

"that which is excessively increased" (*ativṛddha*) is a qualification of "devoid of moisture" (*niḥsneha*). Therefore, immediately after being devoid of moisture, it becomes excessively increased, and from that, it is afflicted;
this is the second layer (*paṭala*).
One who is without parts, devoid of essence, squint-eyed, and lacking seed; one who is enveloped by smoke and deluded, afflicted by hunger,
emaciated, deficient in limbs, and exceedingly enraged— these are thus described.
One who is excessively cruel, yet also modest and tranquil-minded;
one who has fallen from his position, is incapacitated, and is very old—he is proclaimed as such.
I shall now describe the characteristics of those who are devoid of affection and those who are afflicted.
That mantra whose beginning, middle, and end are said to contain the seed-syllable of Anila (the letter *ya*),
whether conjoined or unjoined, and further pervaded by vowels—
whether in four or five ways— is known as the *Samanvaśchinna*.
"Of *manas*" means [the seed-syllable] *yaṃ*;
"at the beginning, middle, and end" indicates a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The construction is as follows: whether conjoined with another syllable, disjoined, or solitary—each of these is connected twice;
that which possesses either a distinguished *anila* (wind) or a distinguished *bīja* (seed) is designated "cut" (*chinna*). Here, "seed" (*bīja*) refers to the seed of power (*śaktibīja*).
Those who know the tradition say that it is "conquered by vowels" when it is overlaid by long vowels—namely *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ai*, and *au*.
If one asks how the word "seed" (*bīja*) refers to the "seed of Māyā," it is stated in the Śaiva scriptures: "The names of the seed of Māyā are Mālinī and Śivavallarī."
Vātāvartī, Kalā, Vāṇī, Bīja, Śakti, and Kuṇḍalī—
thus it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "That mantra in which [these] are seen at the beginning, middle, and end..."
"Divided fourfold, fivefold, twofold, and as the solitary hero, endowed with vowels—
this is proclaimed and celebrated as the Vāyu-bīja mantra."
In that very [work], beginning with "Now, the explanation of the seed-syllables of the mantra-parts," it is explained:
the seed-syllable of wind is the letter *ya*;
the solitary hero is *kra*.
Overpowered by its own vowel and joined with long vowels, they are, in due order: *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hūṃ*, *haiṃ*, *krīṃ*. An illustration of this has been shown in that very same place:

"To those who are not terrible, *hāṃ*; to those who are terrible, *krīṃ*; to those more terrible than the terrible, *krū*; to all those who are everywhere, *hai*; salutations be to you who possess the forms of Rudra, *krauṃ*."
And in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Or [the mantra] as a single hero (*ekavīra*), especially when pervaded by the vowels.
However, in another text it is said: "The half-seizure (*ardhagraha*) is a broken mantra (*manuśchinna*)," meaning that the seizure is interrupted in the middle of a verse (*ṛc*) or a *śloka*.
But elsewhere, the *Śāradātilaka* states: "By the omissions of the seed-syllables at the beginning, middle, and end, [the mantras] are pierced.
[This means] marked by the earth-seed syllable (*laṃ*) and the hand-symbol (*hastalāñchita*) at the beginning, middle, and conclusion.
That mantra should be known as "obstructed" (ruddha), which is devoid of enjoyment and liberation; furthermore,
that mantra is said to be "powerless" (śaktihīna) in whose middle there is neither the *māyāvitattva*, the *śrībīja*, nor the *rāva*.
The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) has *māyā* at its mouth and an *aṅkuśa* at its head;
this is declared to be *parāṅmukha*. The letter *ha* conjoined with the *bindu* is known as *badhira* if there is no *indu* (the nasal drop) at the beginning, end, or middle.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) indicates their conjunction;
"bhū-bījaṃ," "laṃ," and "indra" refer to each [of them] individually.
Experience is the fruit pertaining to this world;

as it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "If it is twofold at the beginning, twofold in the middle, and again twofold at the end, this mantra, which is the seed of Indra, is called 'obstructed' (*ruddha*)."

And elsewhere it is said: "O Dear One, a mantra that is joined with the *vaṃ* syllable in two ways at the beginning, three ways in the middle, and again in two ways at the end, is proclaimed as 'obstructed' (*niruddha*)."
Thus,
the *vañca* suffixes are of three types in both cases; this is the remainder [of the statement].
By the letter *ca*, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) in both cases is also indicated;
by this, the claim made by some that the word *bhūboja* is *glom* is refuted.
However, in another text, there is a different method: "The *ruḍa* is remembered as being without a sandhi."

That in which there is no euphonic combination (*svarasandhi*) or consonantal junction (*vyañjanasandhi*) as prescribed by grammar is "without junction" (*niḥsandhika*). In another tantra it is said: "Obstructed, accompanied by a retinue"—this refers to *māyā*.
Māyā is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī; the three principles are the syllable HŪṂ, or the Praṇava,
or the sound PHŪṂ.
There is no combination of these [factors],
as it has been said: "Wherever the seed-syllable of Māyā is absent, or the three principles (tritattva), or the sound RĀVA, or even the Śrīgṛha— such a mantra is proclaimed to be devoid of power."

Thus it is also stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "If the seed-syllable of Māyā or the syllable *vit* is not present where the *śrī-gṛha* (the House of Śrī) should be, he is known as 'devoid of power' (*śaktihīna*); [such a mantra] destroys the efficacy of the practitioner."
Thus,

having begun with "Now follows the explanation of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) which are portions of the mantra," it is explained in that very same place: "of whom" refers to *tritattva*, *hūṃ*, *śrīgrahaṃ*, and *oṃ*.
The syllable *kroṃ* is at the beginning in the mouth, and at the end on the head, pervading the limbs.
The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction; some read it as *ca*.
As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "If the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is not in the middle, and the final letter [of the mantra] is at the beginning of *māyā*."
"He is called 'turned away'";
thus ends the second chapter.

A mantra that possesses five vowels but is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (the letter *r̥*), and the moon (the letter *l̥*), and is lacking in the two eyes (the letters *e* and *o*), should be known as one that bestows suffering, grief, and disease.
