(76) [Furthermore, those mantras] in which the syllables *haṃsa*, *prāsāda*, *vāk*, and *amava* appear at the beginning, middle, and end [are auspicious].
The letter *ha* with the bindu is the living soul (*jīva*), or it is the sound consisting of four *kalās*.
I bow to the word *māyā*; that in which [the letter] *na* does not exist is "pinned" (*kīlita*).
For one in whose central place the seed-syllable of the *kāmakalā* is not found— 77.
"At the beginning is Māyā and at the end is Aṅkuśa; this one, turned away, is to be understood"— this refers to the letter *Ha*.
The phrase "that *indu* joined with a *bindu*" is also connected here [to the preceding rule];
it is not a cumulative conjunction [of all three positions], as indicated by the expression "at the beginning, end, and middle."
As it has been said: "One for whom the seed-syllable of the individual soul (jīvabīja) does not exist— whether joined with the *bindu* at the beginning, the end, or in the middle— is known as deaf."
By this, the claim made by some that the word *indu* denotes the letter *ṭha* is also refuted. 73–75.
"Five" refers to the letter *ha*.
It is solar (*arka*) because, in the Vaiṣṇava *aṣṭhatattva-nyāsa*, it is installed as the first [letter] of the solar orb.
Or, because the syllable *haṃ* has the form of a male (*puṃs*), it is the sun (*arka*);
the moon (*indu*) is the syllable *sa*.
The phrase "both" and so forth refers to both being seeds of defects (*doṣabīja*).
The results are, respectively, the bestowal of suffering, grief, and disease.
Since the three eyes consist of fire, sun, and moon, one should understand that there is also partial blindness due to the absence of one, two, or all three.
As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "A mantra that lacks the fire, moon, and sun [syllables] is deficient."
"He should be known as one deprived of sight, bringing forth suffering, grief, and disease"—thus [it is said].
Now, beginning with the "Explanation of the Seed-syllables of the Mantra-portions," it is explained in that very same place: "Candra is *sa*, Arka is *ha*. || 76 ||
"Ādi" (and so forth) refers to a collective group of these, such as the *haṃsa* and others; it does not refer to a collective group beginning with *haṃsa*,
because it has been stated that "or the sound (*rāvaṃ*)."
In another text as well: "Or even the *haṃsa* consisting of *māyā*.
*Haṃsa* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The seed-syllable of the *Prāsāda* is *hauṃ*.
The speech-born is Aiṃ; the letter Ha with the bindu;
the life-force is Saḥ.
The sound *phreṃ* consists of four *kalās*; *hūṃ* likewise consists of four *kalās*.
That in which the syllable *māyā*, the seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*), and the word "I bow" (*namāmi*) are absent is called *kolita*.
In this context, "hakārovindumān" is one word, and "jīvaḥ" is another. Therein, what is the *jīva*? It is that which possesses the letter *ha*, the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the *bindu*.
By that, "śoṃ" is established.
Here, by the [expression] "the vowel *a*, the vowel *u*, and the bindu," the syllable *oṃ* is meant, as in the example: "let there be *aumāḥ*."
And so it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata—[the *Śāradātilaka*]:
"That mantra in which there is one 'Bhūḥ' (earth) in the middle, and both the weapon (*astra*) and Indra (*purandara*) are present, shall be paralyzed and an obstructer of success. (78)

If the fire and wind [syllables] are joined at the head of a mantra and it is seen seven times, the knower of mantras should consider that mantra as burnt. If it is conjoined with the ninth vowel, mounted upon the letter *jīva* (ya), and accompanied by the bindu; 76.
For whom the self is not seen at all, or rather, what is the fourfold sound?
"Wherever the *prāsāda*, the *vāgbhava*, the *haṃsa*, or the *māyā* are seen—at the beginning, middle, or end—it is called 'staked' (*kīlita*). Thus it is said.
Then, having begun with "Now, the explanation of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) which are portions of the mantra," it is explained in that very same place: "The ninth vowel is the syllable *o*."
The self is *haḥ*.
The sound is *phreṃ*.
The four-part [syllable] is *hūṃ*.
In another tantra, however, having read "or that which consists of *haṃsa* and *māyā*," it is explained as *kroṃ*.
Others say that even in the statement of Piṅgalā, "the *haṃsa* is *māyā*," this is the very same meaning.
Elsewhere, however, it is said: "That which is pervaded by another seed-syllable within is called *kolita*."
In another text: "Kolita is devoid of seed. || 33 ||
"One" refers to the end of the head; "astra" is the syllable *phaṭ*.
*Puraṃdara* consists of *laḥ*.
In the middle, there is one *phaṭ* or a *la*.
At the end, there are two *phaṭ*s or two *la*s.
Some explain that there is the syllable *phaṭ* in the middle and the syllable *la* twice at the end;
that is incorrect, because it contradicts other texts.
And likewise in the Piṅgalāmata: "If the seed-syllable of Śakra (LŪM) occurs twice in the middle and at both ends of a mantra, the wise who know mantras call that mantra 'paralyzed' (stambhita).
And in another text: "Where [the seed-syllable] is seen at the end of the mantra divided into two, three, eight, or sixteen parts..."
"That great weapon, the mantra, was paralyzed by the Lord of Śrī"—thus it is proclaimed. Because this contradicts two other texts, the reading "that mantra does not exist" is a careless one;
rather, the traditional reading is "that mantra indeed exists."
But elsewhere it is said: "He who is appointed to an action but does not perform it is paralyzed. (78)
Regarding the word "vadbhiḥ": *van* becomes *ra*; *vāyu* is the letter *ya*. It is conjoined with that, or [conjoined] with *ūrjā* below; [the syllable *va*] is at the beginning, on the head.
Thus it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "When a mantra is ignited by the seven seed-syllables beginning with 'A' and the syllable of fire (*ra*)—that is declared to be 'burnt' by Āryā.
In another text, it is stated in a different manner: "That which has been overheard by six ears is burnt."
But in other cases, they are burned by the predominance of the fire-seed. || 78 ||
The second chapter.
A *vasta* is said to be that [mantra] which is seen with two, three, six, or eight syllables,
and in whose mouth the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) does not reside.

Whether it be Śiva or Śakti, that is proclaimed as the one called Bhīta. That mantra which possesses the four *m* sounds at its beginning, middle, and end is impure; the knower of mantras should avoid it.
Regarding the term "astra":
it is that in which the *astra-phaṭkāra* (the weapon-syllable *phaṭ*) is seen with either two syllables, three, six, or eight syllables.
This is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* by the name *Bhauta*.
"If a mantra is joined with the weapon-mantra (astra) at its beginning, middle, and end, it is called *bhauta* in the Tantra.
Others, however, read the text as: "That mantra is designated as *vasta*."
In another tantra it says: "Terrified and made fearful of the siddhis.
Regarding the word "yasya" (of whom):
at the beginning, in the mouth.
The traditional teachers maintain that "Śiva" is *ha* and "Śakti" is *sa*.
Some, however, claim that by the word "Śiva" they mean the *bindu* and by the word "Śakti" they mean the *visarga*; that is incorrect.
Because neither the solitary *bindu* nor the solitary *visarga* exists at the beginning of a mantra and so forth;
if it is argued that [the bindu] must be understood as joined with another syllable,
then it is better simply to follow the traditional meaning.
At the end of the treatise, the author will state: "Those two are called *puṃ* and *prakṛti*; *haṃ* is the male (*pumān*), and *saḥ* is *prakṛti*.
This very same fault has been stated under another name in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That mantra at the beginning of which there is neither Śiva, nor Śakti, nor the syllable *oṃ*, [is defective]."
"They say that what is devoid of the *mātṛkā* bestows inferior accomplishments.
Thus, having begun with "Now, the explanation of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) which are portions of the mantra," it is explained in that very same place: "I am Śiva; she is Śakti. (80)
"Ādi" (and so forth) indicates a conjunction of these. "The four groups ending in *m*" is likewise a conjunction.

Therefore, by combining these three positions, four instances of the letter *ma* are required. As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Where the letter *ma* is seen in four ways at the beginning, middle, and end [of the mantra], one who knows the mantras should know that mantra to be *malina* (defiled) and should abandon it."

However, in another [text] it is said: "That mantra which is seen by the Lord to be of three kinds—namely, with the letter *ma* at the beginning, in the middle, and in the heart—is declared to be impure (*malina*). This is not a contradiction, as it represents a different school of thought (*matāntara*).
The word *hṛdaya* signifies "the end.

However, elsewhere it is said: "That mantra in whose middle there is the letter *da*, or in whose head there is *krodha* in two ways, and in which the *astra* remains, is declared to be 'obstructed' (*tiraskṛta*). (82)

If a mantra has two *bhyos* at the heart and the head, and *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā* in the middle, it is pierced; such a mantra should be abandoned by the wise in the pursuit of accomplishments (*siddhis*).
That which is colorless and devoid of the *haṃsa* is declared to be "asleep" (*suṣupta*).

The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is the Wrathful One (*krodha*) in the center; there is an option regarding the two *da* syllables of the Wrathful One. "At the head" and "at the end"—this is the connection with the phrase "the weapon (*astra*) in two ways."
There is a conjunction of the middle and the end.

As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That seed-syllable whose middle is established with the letter *da*—the seed of wrath (*krodha*)—and which has *phaṭ* at its end, that *aṇu* (individual soul) is disregarded."

Elsewhere also, in another tantra it is said: "He in whose [mantra] the seed-syllable of wrath (*krodhabīja*) stands in the middle, with the syllable *ṛ* situated in the heart, and at both ends there is the sound *phaṭ*—he is one who is humiliated. Thus, [the phrase] "defeated" means "humiliated. (82)
"Śirṣa at the beginning, vaṣaṭ and the weapon (astra) in the middle"—
meaning *śirṣa* at the end and *vaṣaṭ*;
the weapon *krauṃ* is in the middle.

In the Yamalārjunamuktāvalī: "That mantra in which the two syllables of the weapon (astra) appear in the middle and likewise at the end of 'vaṣaṭ' is known as 'divided' (bhinna), and it is devoid of success. Likewise, in the Piṅgalāmata: "The two syllables of the weapon appear in the middle, at the end of 'vaṣaṭ', and likewise at the beginning."
"Oṃ āḥ—this mantra is proclaimed as 'divided' (bhedita).
Thus it is stated; and having begun with "Now follows the explanation of the seed-syllables of the portions of the mantra," it is explained in that very same place:
"Akhaṃ: Kraḥ."
*Oṃ*: *Oṃ* is the *oṃkāra*.
Some read: "The *bhyaḥ* at the heart, the *svāhā* at the head, and the *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* in the middle.
Others read: "*Vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* in the middle."
"Elsewhere"—meaning they have been brought to a state of difference, that is, differentiated. || 83 ||
Regarding the term "three-colored" (*trivarṇa*):
the state of being three-colored refers to the single [syllable] being devoid of the *haṃsa*.
As it is stated in the *Piklāmata*: "Where there are three phonemes (*varṇa*) devoid of the *haṃsa*, that [is taught] by Śambhu."
"In the established doctrine, that which is called 'deep sleep' (suṣupta) is said to deprive one of the desired fruit.

Thus it is also stated in the *Mantramuktāvatī*: "That mantra which consists of three syllables but is devoid of the *haṃsa* [syllable] should be known as 'asleep' (prasupta); it deprives one of the fruit of all accomplishments."
The second chapter: A mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables, beginning with five *phaṭ* syllables, is declared to be "Madonmatta" (Intoxicated with Pride). || 85 ||

Likewise, that mantra whose weapon (astra) is situated in the middle is said to be "fainted" (mūrchita); that which resides in the place of rest (virāma) is called "deprived of its potency" (hṛtavīrya). A mantra endowed with four weapons at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the head [is fully empowered].
It should be known as "inferior" (hīna) if it consists of eighteen syllables. That which has eight, seven, and ten syllables [respectively] is thus one of eighteen syllables.
The term "pañcaphaṭkārādi" is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which there is a pentad of *phaṭ* syllables at the beginning.
As it has been said: "Whether it be a *vidyā* or a *mantra*, if it consists of eighteen syllables and is preceded by five *phaṭ*s, it is called 'Madonmatta' (Intoxicated with Pride)."

In the *Piṅgalāmata* it is also stated: "Whether it be a Vidyā or a King of Mantras, if it consists of seventeen syllables plus [the others], and if there are five *phaṭ*-kāras at the beginning, it is proclaimed as 'Unmatta'.
Thus, here too, there is a fault in being characterized by these two qualifiers.
"Thus it is five times.
In another text, there is a different method: "Furthermore, those who are coagulated are devoid of consciousness"—thus ends the section.
The phrase "yasyāstram" is connected [to the preceding];
the meaning is "at the end of which there is a weapon-mantra.
In some recensions, the reading is: "the mantra that has a weapon at its point of cessation."

Thus it is said in the Piṅgalāmata: "That mantra whose Astra-mantra is placed both in the middle and at the end by Śambhu is known as 'one whose power has been taken away' (hṛtavīrya); such a mantra is never a bestower of success.
It is also stated elsewhere: "That [mantra] which occupies the position of the pause (virāma) is called 'one whose power has been taken away'."
Thus they say [it is] "deficient in potency" (hīnavīrya); elsewhere, however, it is said that [a mantra] is "seedless" (nirbīja) and has "excessive syllables" (adhikākṣara). || 85 || 86 ||
"At the beginning" implies a conjunction;
"the four weapons" refers to the four weapons combined across the three locations.

But in another tantra, this is stated by the name Bhīta: "Bhairava spoke that mantra of eighteen syllables, which is joined with the letter *ṭra* in four ways—at the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific case of having eighteen syllables, it is said here:
"That which may have eighteen syllables" refers to the *caraṇa* (foot). Or, as stated in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Or that mantra which has nineteen syllables, joined with the *tāra* (the syllable Om)."
They declare that [the mantra] beginning with *halle khāṅga-śabījā* is *avyasta* (uninverted) and *pradhvasta* (destroyed).
A mantra of seven syllables is a child; one of eight syllables is a youth; one of sixteen syllables is a young man; and a mantra of forty syllables is an adult. (88–89)
A mantra of twenty syllables, one consisting of sixty-four groups, a hundred-syllable mantra, and even one of four hundred syllables is designated as "Vṛddha" (the aged).
Any mantra of nineteen syllables that is endowed with the Praṇava is likewise [so called].

"Endowed with the qualities of Mahāmāyā, he is proclaimed as 'Pradhvasta' (the Destroyed). Thus, this mantra consisting of nineteen syllables, or twenty when joined with the limbs of Māyā and Aṅgāra, is celebrated by the god Śambhu as "Pradhvasta. Thus [it is said].
"This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Māyā, the imperishable [syllable] of the three worlds;
it is Hṛllekhā, the Lord of Yoga, and the Yoginī Bhuvaneśī. Thus [ends verses 87 and 88].
Bāla consists of seven syllables, while Kumāra has eight syllables.

"A mature [hero] has forty syllables, while a youth has sixteen. Thus it is stated in another work; however, elsewhere it says, "youths are exceedingly arrogant," and in yet another place, "the mature are those who are fierce toward their master. (88)
The second chapter:
The mantra consisting of nine syllables joined with the *dhruva* is declared to be the sword (*nistriṃśa*), at the end of which is the heart-mantra and in the middle the head-mantra.
If the *śikhā* and *varma* mantras are absent, as well as the syllables *vauṣaṭ* and *phaṭ*,
or if it is devoid of the phonemes of Śiva and Śakti, that is remembered as being "seedless" (*nirbīja*).
In these positions, the syllable *phaṭ* is seen in six ways.
That mantra would be devoid of success; a mantra of five syllables is dull.
[A mantra] of twenty, four hundred, or one hundred and four syllables is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyapadalopa*).
Some explain the term *catuḥśatākṣara* as "that which has four hundred syllables," but that is incorrect because it contradicts other texts.
"Twenty, thirty, forty, sixty, or likewise one hundred and four;
even one hundred and four more is designated as 'old' (vṛddha).
Thus also in the Piṅgalāmata: "Where there are thirty, fifty, sixty-four, or one hundred and four..."
"There are hundreds of syllables; that mantra is designated as 'Vṛddha'.
Thus, he himself will state this later in the definition of the *ativṛt* [meter]: "Starting from four hundred [syllables] up to a thousand syllables."
And there would be a contradiction with that,
as it is stated in another text: "The elders perform only minor actions."
"Navā" is indeed the syllable Oṃ.
The meaning is that having nine syllables, being joined with the *dhruvaka*, and being singular constitutes "Nikhiṃśa," which signifies "the slayer.
In the *Piṅgalāmata* it is said: "That which has nine syllables, is joined with the *dhruvaka*, and is Nikhiṃśa brings about untimely death (*apamṛtyu*)."
Thus,
"of whomsoever" is the heart-mantra; [it is] *namaḥ*.
The head-mantra is "svāhā";
Śiva is "haṃ," and the syllable of power is "sa."
Right in the midst of the two conceptualizations is the crest-lock: *vaṣaṭ*, *vamme*, *huṃ*.

If the seed-syllables consisting of Śiva and Śakti are not present at the end of the heart and head, or in the middle of the crest (śikhā), armor (varma), eyes, and weapon (astra)— that king of mantras is declared to be "seedless" (nirbīja) and is censured for all ritual acts. Thus it is said.
In that interval, however, it is said: "The seedless [mantra] is declared to be devoid of the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning.
(81–82) The word "in these" (*eṣu*) is used to indicate the inclusion of other characteristics mentioned in other tantras, such as those defining the seedless mantra.
Thus he says:
"In these," meaning at the beginning, middle, and end;
the combination of these in those three places amounts to six, which is why it is called "slow" (manda).
The *paṅkti* consists of ten syllables;
as it is said: "The *manda* shall consist of ten syllables.
And in another tantra: "Those lacking radiance are *manda*s. (83)

In the Śāradātilaka, a mantra consisting of a single syllable formed by the combination [of letters] is said to be "without parts" (niraṃśaka); one of two syllables is "devoid of essence" (sattvahīna), while one of four syllables is "squint-eyed" (kekara). || 64 ||
A six-syllabled mantra that is devoid of a seed-syllable (bīja), or one of seven and a half syllables, is considered "smoky" (dhūmita) if it is twelve and a half years old; such a mantra is censured.
A mantra of twenty-one syllables containing three seed-syllables is likewise [censured].
That mantra which consists of twenty syllables or thirty syllables is called "Embraced" (āliṅgita).
A mantra of twenty-two syllables is proclaimed as "Deluded" (mohita),
while one of twenty-seven syllables belongs to a twenty-four-year-old.
But that mantra, afflicted by hunger, is to be understood as having twenty-four syllables, or eleven syllables, or twenty-five syllables;
or the mantra is declared to have twenty-three syllables when it is arrogant (dṛpta). || 68-69 ||
Regarding the term *kūṭa*, it has been stated: "A *kūṭa* is either a single syllable or a mantra that is partless"; thus, it refers to a two-syllabled [mantra].
As it has been said: "The two-syllabled [mantra] is devoid of *sattva*";
whereas elsewhere it is said: "Devoid of *sattva*, they are intensified by *tamas*. Thus, the four-fold [mantra] consists of four seed-syllables.
In the Piṅgalāmata, there is this distinction: "That which lacks the *dhruva* [refrain] and consists of four or six seed-syllables (*bīja*) is considered *kekara*.
Thus ends the section on the six-syllable [mantra].
"Except otherwise— that is, excluding the seed-syllable and devoid of the syllable *oṃ*"— thus they say;
this refers to the state of having six and a half or seven syllables and the state of having eleven and a half phonemes, which is to be understood because there is a consonant at the end.
"Similarly, the three seeds are sāība; 'seed' means a phoneme (varṇa),
and the meaning is that it is marked by those."

As it has been said: "A mantra of six and a half syllables, or one of twelve and a half syllables, is declared to be 'smoky' (dhūmita); or likewise, one of three and a half syllables. Thus, for a thirty-syllable mantra, there is likewise the state of being 'grown' (vṛddha) and 'embraced' (āliṅgita).

One should not think: "Since 'the arrogant' (dṛpta) was already observed during the occasion of the enumeration (uddeśa), how can its definition (lakṣaṇa) be formulated during the occasion of the definition?
For even though there is a prefix (upasarga), there is no difference in meaning.
As it has been said: "One [prefix] subverts the meaning of the verbal root; another follows it;
yet another qualifies that very same [meaning]; and another is employed as being devoid of meaning."
The second chapter: A mantra of twenty-six syllables, or likewise one of thirty-six syllables, or one of nineteen syllables, is said to be "devoid of limbs" (aṅgahīna). || 100 ||
One with twenty-eight syllables, or even thirty-one,
is said to be extremely wrathful and is censured in all ritual activities.
A mantra with twenty syllables, or even thirty-three, [is likewise censured].
He is said to be extremely cruel and is censured in all ritual acts.
From forty up to sixty-six, the number of mantras falling within that range is declared to be designated as "bashful" (brīḍa). 102–103.
Those mantras which consist of sixty-five syllables are said by the wise to be "those whose minds are peaceful" (śāntamānasa);
from sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine syllables,
those mantras are declared by the learned to be "fallen from their place" (sthānabhraṣṭa).
Those mantras which consist of thirteen syllables or fifteen syllables are designated as "vikalā" (deficient). They number one hundred and fifty, or one hundred,
or two hundred, or ninety-two, or even ninety-one.

It is stated thus in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "A mantra of twenty-four syllables, or one of eleven syllables, or one of twenty-three syllables—know that such a mantra is exceedingly proud (*matidṛpta*). (85–88)
Those [mantras] which consist of one hundred syllables or more are declared to be "without oil" (niḥsneha),
starting from four hundred syllables up to one thousand syllables. || 107 ||
Mantras that are excessively long in their applications should always be abandoned by the wise; those consisting of more than a thousand syllables are called *daṇḍaka* or *pauḍita*.
Mantras of two thousand syllables are divided into a hundred parts.
These mantras, existing in the form of hymns, must be understood exactly as they are;
likewise, the vidyās must be comprehended by practitioners in rites for specific desires.
That dull-witted person who resorts to a mantra without recognizing these defects [will fail].
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Thus, there are ninety-one, three hundred, and five times five varieties.

In the Piṅgalāmata, however, it is said: "Those consisting of one, two, or three hundred syllables are devoid of oily essence. Thus, the sixth [category] is indeed stated in the Mantramuktāvatī as being of three types: "But three hundred minus one."
Some say one method is one hundred and ten,
another is ninety-two,
and yet another method is ninety minus one or ninety plus one; thus they spoke.
If it is argued that since it has been stated that those numbering from sixty-six up to ninety-nine are designated as "fallen from their position," then—
just like the thirty phonemes— a single entity will possess both defects, we reply: no.
In this context, since it has been stated that [the number] must be greater than one hundred up to a maximum of three hundred, the phrase "whose number" (*yatsaṃkhyā*) is connected everywhere; thus,
the connection is that those mantras whose number exceeds one hundred are "without oil" (*niḥsneha*).

The connection is as follows: those *daṇḍakas* which exist within the *yogas* and *prayogas* are of the nature of hymns (*stotra*); they are to be understood as being non-dual (*advaya*) when afflicted [by the senses]. || 106-108 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "Are these defects stated to belong only to the *mantras*, while the *vidyās* are faultless? To this he says: "These are the *mantras*.
Just as these *mantras* exist as being possessed of defects, so too should the *vidyās* be understood by the practitioners of mantra (*mantrin*s).
As it has been said: "Just as the *mantras* are, so are the *vidyās*; they are distinguished from one another by their differences."
"These [defects] have been described in various tantras and should be known by the preeminent teacher.

By the phrase "in rites for specific desires," it is implied that since these defects do not exist when reciting mantras for the sake of liberation (*mukti*), even the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) need not be performed;
this is merely an illustrative indication.
Therefore, the purification and other rites characterized by what will be stated later should not be performed for the sake of liberation. || 110 ||

One should join those mantras, which are corrupted by defects such as being "second" or "chapter," with oneself; one should purify them while the upward breath is held by means of the *yonimudrā*. 111.

By the phrase "and so forth," one should understand defects such as *mīlita* (closed), *vipakṣastha* (standing on the enemy's side), *dārita* (split), *mūka* (mute), *namra* (bowed), *bhujaga* (serpent-like), *śūnya* (empty), and *hata* (struck). Their definitions are as follows: "Mantras that are *mīlita* are excessively inert, even when employed by a practitioner. And *vipakṣastha* means those which have taken refuge in the faction of the enemy.
“He for whom stability is not found in the beginning, middle, and end is known as ‘the torn one’ (dārita) in this tantra by the One Clad in Skin (Kṛttivāsas). Thus,
“without the ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes mute.”
"A mantra without its *pallava* is proclaimed to be naked;
it is like a serpent deprived of its seer (*ṛṣi*), deity (*devatā*), and meter (*chandas*)."
"Whose recitation another hears, that mantra is called 'void';
it is declared to be 'struck' when its head is missing.
Thus he describes the method of purification, [saying] "he places the mantras within himself."
The cultivation of the idea that the effect is indeed non-different from the cause is "application to the self" (*ātmani yojanā*).
There is a reading, "one should apply the mantras to one's own self," which states purification by means of another method: "one should purify."

Having bound the *yonimudrā*, which has the characteristics to be described, and having meditated upon the syllables of the mantra arising from the *mūlādhāra* as they move up and down as far as the *brahmarandhra*, one should perform breath-retention (*vāyudhāraṇa*) and recite [the mantra] a thousand times; thus they describe the method of purification. As it is said: "Having bound the *yonimudrā*, having reached the *unmanī* state by means of the path of the seed-syllable, the drop (*bindu*), and so forth, one should recite the mantra a thousand times there; that mantra will then become awakened. The definition of *yonimudrā* is as follows: "Having firmly pressed together the perineum and the anus with the palms of the hands..."
Drawing the downward breath upward is called the mūlabandha.
One should contract and bind that vagina (yoni) which is situated between the anus and the navel; even an old man becomes young through constant practice of this root-binding (mūlabandha).
Thus, because it seals the location of the yoni, it is called Yonimudrā.
Regarding this, they say: "This very Yonimudrā has indeed been described by me; its binding is difficult even for the gods to attain.
By means of this binding, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for the preeminent practitioner."

Those who are bitten by snakes, those who are distressed, those bound with ropes, those who are paralyzed; those who are asleep, intoxicated, or unconscious; those who are weak, burnt, terrified, or standing on the side of the enemy; and those who are children, the elderly, or arrogant in their youth.

Those mantras which are seedless, those which are deficient in essence, those that are fragmented, and those deprived of their limbs—all these become effective through the binding of the mudrā of the womb (yoni). Thus it is said.
In the Śāradātilaka, the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of mantras, which bestow accomplishment,
are described: first birth (janana), then life-giving (jīvana), followed by striking (tāḍana), and likewise awakening (bodhana).

Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana), satiation (tarpaṇa), kindling (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)— these ten are the purificatory rites for the mantra.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth."
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (OM) interspersed between them; those proficient in the Mantra-tantras call this "the living" (*jīvana*).

Thus, for those practitioners who have not mastered the *yonimudrā* and are unable to perform the retention of the vital breath (*pavanadhāraṇā*), he describes their purification through the ten sacraments (*daśasaṃskāra*) with the words "of the mantras. Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the practitioners are joined with such defects as these;
therefore, a certain sequence is proclaimed for the destruction of those defects."
Birth, life, awakening, striking, purification, nourishment, and consecration— by these seven acts, the ground becomes a fit locus for ritual action.

"Indeed, all mantras become granters of desires once they have been purified. Thus it is stated in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa*: "Then, at an auspicious moment, one should impart the consecrated mantra to him; these seven purificatory rites for mantras are difficult for human beings on earth to obtain."

It should be understood that by the words "birth," "life," and so forth, the three purificatory rites (saṃskāras) characterized as *tarpaṇa* (satisfying), *dīpana* (kindling), and *gopana* (concealing) are generally well-known; therefore, it should be known that the statement "seven" is made excluding those [three].
Regarding the phrase "of the mantras":
by the expression "from the midst of the *mātṛkā*s," this is what is meant:

having written the *mātṛkā* alphabet with saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), or other substances upon an auspicious seat or similar surface, one should extract each individual syllable of the mantra from the sequence of the *mātṛkā*s.
As it has been said: "Having written down the letters, one should extract this which is born of mantra."
Regarding the term *praṇava*:
therein, the state of being interspersed with the *praṇava* is as follows: *a~rāṃ oṃrā ū~mā oṃya oṃna oṃmaḥ*.
By the word *sudhīḥ*, it is meant that [this is repeated] one hundred and eight times.
As it has been said: "One should recite the syllables of the mantra together with the *praṇava* according to the prescribed method; this is called 'liberation while living' (*jīvanmukta*).
By the phrase "those expert in the system of Manu," it is stated that others call this state by the name "seeding" (*bījana*).
As stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "The *praṇava* is said to be the seed (*bīja*); one should place it at the end of the seed.
Having interspersed it with other syllables, this mantra is considered to be 'seeded' (*bījita*)."
Thus [it is said].

The Second Chapter: Having written out the syllables of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should strike each one with sandalwood water using the Vāyu [seed-syllable]; that is declared to be "striking" (tāḍana).
Having written that mantra, the practitioner, using *karavīra* flowers equal in number to the syllables of that mantra,
should perform the awakening with the mantra ending in *yā*.

Following the ritual procedure prescribed in his own tantra, the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the mantra with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, for the sake of purification.
Having reflected with the mind upon the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should burn away mental impurities by means of the mantra;
this is indeed the purification within the mantra.
He recites the mantra.
By the word "mantra," it is stated that one should inscribe the letters of the mantra upon birch bark using saffron, yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and so forth.
[The syllable] *yam* is by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vāyu.
One should strike each [letter] one hundred times.

As it has been said: "Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra upon birch bark, one should strike each one a hundred times with sandalwood water using the *vāyubīja* (the seed-syllable of air); this is declared to be the 'striking' (*tār̤ana*)."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "having written": by the word "mantra," it is stated that the writing is to be done on a birch-bark leaf with saffron, gorocana, and so forth.
By the phrase "born of *karavīra*," it means with the flowers of the red *karavīra*.
It is moved by means of the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
As it has been said: "In this [mandala], one should draw [the design] with red oleander flowers (*karavīra*) equal in number to the syllables of the mantra;
this is declared to be its awakening by means of the seed-syllable *raṃ*."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding "independently" (*svatantra*): it means according to the procedures taught in the independent [tantras].

This should be understood as follows: in the case of a Śaiva mantra, in accordance with the Śiva-tantras; in the case of a Śākta mantra, in accordance with the Śakti-tantras; and in the case of a Vaiṣṇava mantra, in accordance with the Vaiṣṇava-tantras.
As before, having written the syllables of the mantra upon birch bark, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣiñcet*).
By the word "mantra," the practical application is stated as: "I consecrate such-and-such a syllable of such-and-such a mantra; *namaḥ*.
Thus it has been said: "One should consecrate [the disciple] with a sprout of the *pippala* tree according to the path prescribed in one's own tantra."
This is the consecration [performed] with the mantra written on birch bark one hundred and eight times.
Thus it is said.
In the *Piṅgalāmata*, there is this distinction: "One should place the syllable of the mantra upon the pericarp using jasmine buds;

then, one should perform the consecration with pure leaves of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own tantra."
Thus,
having written the syllables of the mantra with *mālatī* buds, one should perform the consecration.
"Having reflected thus": by means of the *jyotirmantra* which is about to be described. By the word "mantrin," [it is implied] from the *Mūlādhāra*; according to the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The *Tāra*, followed by the sky (0), fire (3), and the moon (1), joined with the staff (daṇḍin)—this is considered the *jyotirmantra*."
One should sprinkle water consecrated with kuśa grass over each syllable of the mantra while reciting it.
This nourishment is considered to be performed according to the rule with that mantra;
the satiation with water while reciting the mantra is traditionally known as *tarpaṇa*.
The conjunction of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is said to be the illumination of the mantra;
the concealment of the mantra being recited is its non-disclosure.
It has been stated that by raising Kuṇḍalinī, the burning away of defects occurs through her.

The three impurities are the innate (*sahaja*), the adventitious (*āgantuka*), and that which belongs to Māyā (*māyīya*). It is also said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The practitioner of mantra should burn away the three impurities—known as the innate, the adventitious, and that called Māyā—in the form of light; thereby he becomes stainless."
Thus [it is said].
He states the mantra of light as "tāra":
*tāra* is the *praṇava*;
*vyoma* is the letter *ha*.
The syllable *agni* is *repha* (the letter *r*).
*Manuḥ* is *au*.
"This pair is the staff joined with the *anusvāra*" is an epithet of the mantra.
In the reading "daṇḍi," it is a qualifier of the sky (*vyoman*).
As it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭumāṭakā*: "Amakrūreśaka, Daṇḍa, Binduka, Kāmaguhyaka, Kacnu, Prācīnayoni, and Saukhyaduḥkhaprabandhaka."
Thus [it is said].
Likewise, even further on, the state of being denotable by the word "staff" (daṇḍa) must be understood for the *bindu*.
Regarding the word "kuśa":
"Recited one hundred and eight times"—
the drawing is exactly as before.
The word "by that" (tena) is connected to both instances.
As it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "If the mantra is sprinkled with water from kuśa grass at every syllable after being purified by one hundred and eight applications, it becomes nourished."
This is incorrect,
because it contradicts other texts.
As it has been said: "The nourishment [of the mantra] should be performed with water and kuśa grass, recited syllable by syllable with one's own [mantra].
By this, the meaning is "with that root-mantra."
The procedure for this is as follows: having uttered the mantra to be given, one should perform the libation with water, saying, "I satisfy this mantra, *namaḥ*.
This is precisely what is meant by "mantra-libation" (*mantratarpaṇa*).

As it has been said: "The word 'I satiate' (tarpayāmi) should be joined at the end of the mantra when the desired names are in the nominative case; however, when they are in the accusative case, [the name itself should be used]. This same method is to be observed everywhere else in all acts of satiation (tarpaṇa).
This also consists of one hundred and eight [verses].
*Tāreti*: *Tāra* is the *praṇava*, *oṃ*; *māyā* is *śakti*.
Ramā Śrī.
Second Paṭala. Ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been proclaimed, which are hidden from all other traditions.
Having performed these according to the tradition, the practitioner of mantra attains his desired object.
One should employ a mantra that is favorable to one's own nakṣatra, rāśi, and koṣṭha;
for through greed for wealth, even a clever man may lose his abundant fortune, just as Ruru lost his hand to Rudra on the mountain.
The wicked one, clever in local matters, reached the heavens;
the letters, divided among the *bha* [nakṣatras], follow in sequence, while the two final consonants always reside in a portion of Revatī.
"At the end of the mantra, there should be the application of the name; this is considered [the method] for eradication (*proccāṭana*).
Since the definition of the *yoga* has been stated thus, here the mantra itself takes the place of the name.
Therefore, the teachers maintain that one should recite the mantra seven times, preceded by these seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Regarding the phrase "according to the tradition":
the tradition concerning each refinement has been stated by me and should be investigated accordingly.

Now, he shows a secondary deliberation regarding the worship of the qualified (saguṇa) form, which serves as an auxiliary to the worship of the unqualified (nirguṇa), by means of the verse beginning with *svatārā*.
"Sva" refers to one's own name; its *tārā* is the corresponding lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Similarly, in what follows: [one should employ] a mantra abounding in syllables that are enemies to the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and the evil planets (*duṣṭa*).
A wise person, having examined it thoroughly with effort, should avoid it.
Because of this statement, in order to understand the *tārā* (star) and the *maitrī* (friendship/position) therein, he states the asterisms (*nakṣatras*) among the syllables, beginning with "prāpa.
Here, the system of Vāraruca is intended by the author of the work.

As it is said: "In this system, the digits are to be known from the final letters of the groups *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya*; likewise, when a vowel alone is uttered, it should be understood as zero (*śūnya*)."
Thus [it is said].
Here, in the hip, there are nine syllables; the foot consists of five syllables; that which has eight meanings ends with the letter *ha*;
and the *piṇḍa* is a conjunct consonant.
In that regard, another [method] is by means of the limbs (*aṅga*):
*prā 2 pa 1 lo 3 bhā 4 tpa 1 ṭu 1 prā 2 jyaṃ 1 ru 2 dra 2 syā 1 dri 2 ru 2 ruḥ 2 ka 1 naṃ 2 lo 3 ka 1 lo 3 pa 1 pa 18 1 prā 2 pa 1 kha 2 lau 3 yo 1*.
One should give [the results] in this manner as stated for the others; the constellations beginning with Aśvinī are to be inferred accordingly.

The meaning is that, among the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the phonemes (varṇas) are distinguished and shown according to their respective divisions. This is connected with what follows, namely "then" (tadā).
Here, because the letters *gha* and *ya* are identical in the Nāgarī script, the reading *ghakāra* is due to a scribal error.
By that [syllable], the single limb *dya* is comprised.
The vowels *aṃ* and *aḥ* are situated in the portion of Revatī.
Therefore, in Revatī, there are three syllables: *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and *la*.
Because it is stated by the very phrase "gone to the portion of Revatī," it is not included among the [other] limbs (aṅga),
just as in the description of another zodiac sign to be mentioned later, such as "the young, fair, and hoofed" [referring to Aries]. By the letter *ra*, only two syllables are expressed for Virgo.

Since it is stated for others by the very word "śādaya" regarding the daughter, it should be noted that this applies even without giving her away. In the nakṣatra Uttarabhādrapadā, the number three is taken by means of the letter *la*.
The *Śāradātilaka* states:
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, benefactor, death, friend, and supreme friend— these [houses] beginning with birth recur again and again.
Therefore, there are six syllables;
since the letter *ṣa* is a constituent part of *kṣa*, the letter *kṣa* is also included by that very [count].
Therefore, there is a group of four syllables here.
As stated by the Teachers: "Then the letter *ca* arose; Nṛsiṃha is its deity. That [letter], together with *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, went to the latter Proṣṭhapadā.

Also, in the *Īśānaśiva*: "The beloved, small, harsh, and charming Śrī is the mistress; another is the night; [the others are] the female of the bird-family, the mountain, the woman, the vessel, and the child—such is the numbering."

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, however, regarding the passage beginning with "rājya" and so forth, the letters are not mentioned among the twenty-six asterisms; rather, they are stated in the asterism of Aśleṣā.
On this point, some read the letters as "lvau" and explain that the letter *la* represents three digits and the letter *va* represents four digits.
That is incorrect.
Because it contradicts the established convention (*saṅketa*).
For in that convention, it is stated that "the limbs (*aṅga*) consist of the final syllables of the *piṇḍas*.
It is precisely with this intention that the assumption of the dual number is made.
That too is merely an error;
for, regarding the letters of the convention (*saṅketa*), the singular number alone is appropriate for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*),
and not the dual number formed by joining them together.
This is because it is not seen anywhere else [in the sources].
For this very reason, this reading has been disregarded by commentators such as those of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.

Others, however, read "ba-vau" and say: "By the letter *ba* belonging to the *pavarga*, there are three limbs; by the following letter *va* belonging to the semivowels (*antasthīya*), there are four limbs."
That too contradicts the *Prapañcasāra*, the *Īśāna*, and other texts;
therefore, this very reading is also found in the *Nārāyaṇīya*. However, there is an error on the part of the commentator in that regard.

The first semi-vowel (*antastha*) is *va*, which signifies the number four; the second is the *pavarga* [consonant], which signifies the number three. Thus, everything is consistent. However, in order to avoid contradiction with the *Prapañcasāra* and other texts, some read "phullā" instead of "devadeveśī"; they explain that there, by the first *la*-sound, three limbs are taken, and by the subsequent *la*-sound, another three limbs are taken.
That too contradicts the established convention (*saṅketa*).
Because the limbs of the body are not grasped by means of a collective symbol (piṇḍa) even in conventional usage;
by this [principle], one should understand: *a ā* is Aśvinī, *i* is Bharaṇī, *ī u ū* is Kṛttikā, and so forth. || 124 || 125 ||
The phrase "beginning from the first letter of one's own name" (*svanāmādyakṣarāditaḥ*), which is to be mentioned later, should also be applied here.

Therefore, the syntactical connection is as follows: "Then, when there is a difference in the asterisms (*varṇabheda*), one should repeatedly count the [states] beginning with birth (*janma*) and so forth, in clockwise order (*prādakṣiṇyena*), up to the asterism of the first letter of the mantra"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Consequently, the meaning is that one should determine the result by performing a clockwise count starting from the asterism of the first letter of the practitioner’s name and continuing until the asterism of the first letter of the mantra.

As it has been said: "The wise practitioner should count [the syllables] in a clockwise direction starting from the letter known as the name of the seeker. Elsewhere also: "Starting with the first letter of one's own name and continuing up to the ninth, one should consider the fruit corresponding to the number of syllables in the mantra up to that point. And elsewhere: "Having thus assigned the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) to the divided letters, beginning from the birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*) and ending with the star of the mantra... [End of Second Chapter].
This, however, should be understood as the unification of two names that are well-known by their collective name (*rāśi*).
Having divided [the letters] into groups of nine, O Rāma, those [groups] consisting of five, five, and seven [letters] are to be excluded;
the remaining ones grant the accomplishment of desired goals through recitation (*japa*) and other such practices. Thus it is said.

Excluding the first, the fourth, the fifth, and the seventh, the remainder is auspicious. As it has been said: "The stars beginning with the third, excluding the fifth and the seventh, [are auspicious]. Furthermore, elsewhere: "The sixth, eighth, ninth, and those occurring in pairs (the second and fourth) are auspicious; the others are not auspicious—this should be known by those skilled in the Tantras."
Some even desire the first [year] to be auspicious;
as it has been said: "The *vipat*, *badha*, and *pratyari* [years] should be avoided by the wise.
This refers to the first birth-year (*idavādi*).

In this investigation of the friendliness of the stars (tārāmaitrī), the friendliness of the birth-signs (yonimaitrī) and the friendliness of the lunar mansions (gaṇamaitrī) must necessarily be examined as well, because they too consist of constellations; likewise, the examination of one's own family and other families must also be considered.

In the *Piṅgalāmata*, it is stated: "Likewise, that which belongs to a single lunar mansion is one's own family (*svakula*), while the other is indeed the supreme non-family (*akula*). Since this is said, and likewise in the *Mantramuktāvalī* in the description of the division between one's own family and the non-family, it is also stated that "that which belongs to a single lunar mansion is one's own family."

In that regard, the matrix-friendliness (*yonimaitrī*) is as follows: the horse, donkey, goat, snake, dog, cat, bull, ram, and mouse; then the rat, monkey, cow, and buffalo; then the tiger, buffalo, tiger, deer, monkey, elephant, monkey, lion, horse, king of beasts (lion), and the beast (elephant) and the crow—this is the matrix of the signs (*bhānām*). Thus it is said.

Here, since Abhijit is also included, there are twenty-eight [asterisms]: 1. Aśvinī, 2. Bharaṇī, 3. Kṛttikā, 4. Rohiṇī, 5. Mṛgaśiras, 6. Ārdrā, 7. Punarvasu, 8. Puṣya, 9. Āśleṣā, 10. Maghā, 11. Pūrvaphalgunī, 12. Uttaraphalgunī, 13. Hastā, 14. Citrā, 15. Svātī, 16. Viśākhā, 17. Anurādhā, 18. Jyeṣṭhā, 19. Mūlā, 20. Pūrvāṣāḍhā, 21. Uttarāṣāḍhā, 22. Śravaṇā, 23. Dhaniṣṭhā, 24. Śatabhiṣā, 25. Pūrvabhādrapadā, 26. Uttarabhādrapadā, 27. Revatī, 28. Aśvinī (again). As for the natural enmities (*virodha*), they are as follows: "The cow and the tiger, the elephant and the lion, the horse and the buffalo, the snake and the mongoose, the monkey and the ram—these are great natural enmities; likewise, the owl and the rat. [The list of animals corresponding to the asterisms: 1. Horse, 2. Elephant, 3. Ram, 4. Snake, 5. or 6. Cat, 7. Ram, 8. Cat, 9. Rat, 10. or 11. Cow, 12. Buffalo, 13. Tiger, 14. Buffalo, 15. Tiger, 16. Deer, 17. or 18. [Deer], 19. or 20. Monkey, 21. Mongoose, 22. [Mongoose], 23. Monkey, 24. Lion, 25. Horse, 26. Lion, 27. Cow, 28. Elephant. The conflict is thus: Cow-Tiger, Elephant-Lion, Horse-Buffalo, Snake-Mongoose, and the very great enmity between Monkey and Ram, as well as Owl and Rat.

"O Maheśvarī, the methods of killing according to the three classes of birth have been explained as they truly are; they bestow success without delay. Thus he will state in the twenty-first [chapter].
Let the results be as follows:
the relationship of the bound and the binder is considered to exist between humans and *rākṣasas*, while there is enmity between gods and *rākṣasas*.
There is affection between gods and humans, and there is also equality with one's own kind. Thus [ends verse 126].

*Śāradātilaka*: In the [twelve] zodiac signs (*rāśi*), the letters are divided in order as follows: *vā*, *laṃ*, *gau*, *raṃ*, *khu*, *raṃ*, *śo*, *ṇaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *mī*, *śo*, and *bhe*. In the sign of Virgo (*kanyā*), the letters from *śa* onwards are prescribed. (127) The twelve zodiac signs are: Ascendant (*lagna*), Wealth (*dhana*), Brother (*bhrātṛ*), Kinsman (*bandhu*), Son (*putra*), Enemy (*śatru*), Wife (*kalatra*), Death (*maraṇa*), Dharma (*dharma*), Fortune (*bhāgya*), Income (*āya*), and Expenditure (*vyaya*). (128) One should write the letters from *a* to *kṣa* within a square consisting of four compartments, starting from the first letter of one's own name. (129) Now, he explains the division of the zodiac signs among the letters, beginning with the verse "vālaṃ".

Vā 4, Laṃ 3, Gau 3, Naṃ 2, Khu 2, Naṃ 2, Śo 5, Ṇaṃ 5, Śa 5, Mo 5, Śo 5, Bhā 4—thus the letters are distributed among the zodiac signs (rāśis) as stated by way of division. In Virgo (Kanyā), the last of the vowels (the letter *au*) occurs, and the letters beginning with *śa* are situated there;
here, by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, and *la* are included.
The letter *kṣa* enters into the sign of Pisces (*mīna*).
As the teachers have said: "A daughter born from the letters *ma*, *śa*, and the *varga* of *la* is considered [to belong to Pisces]";
likewise: "The letter *cc* (representing *kṣa*), together with the four letters beginning with *y*, resides in Pisces."
By this, [the correspondences] such as "a, ā, i, ī" with "ram" (meṣa), and so forth, are to be understood. || 127 ||

"The twelve zodiac signs" [is stated] because of the metaphorical identification of the fruit and the bearer of the fruit. Herein is the method: starting from whichever sign the first letter of the practitioner's name resides, one should count up to whichever sign the first syllable of the mantra resides.

The sixth, eighth, and twelfth positions are censurable. As it has been said: "One should count from the first letter of the practitioner's name up to the letter designated as the *sādhya*; those letters which fall under death (*naidhana*), enemies (*ari*), and expenditure (*vyaya*) are not auspicious.
Furthermore: "The first, fifth, and ninth are known as kinsmen; the second, sixth, and tenth are servants."

"Those who nourish [the mantra] are equal to the three, the sages (seven), and Rudra (eleven); those who destroy it are twelve, eight, and four. If this statement is read within the section on the results of the zodiac signs (*rāśiphala*), then it must be calculated starting from one's own birth sign up to the sign of the mantra; thus, it is indeed a different method. As it has been said: "Having examined the signs, vowels, and so forth of the mantras along with the [mantra's] own sign, starting from the birth sign and ending at the sign of the mantra, one should recite the mantra when it is devoid of enemies.
If this is not read in the section on the zodiac signs, then it should be explained as the result of the *akaḍama-cakra* which is about to be described; such is the secret. 128.

He describes the method for purifying the *siddha* and other classes of mantras with the words "caturastra" (square). The practitioner (*mantrī*) is one who is not distinct from the tradition of the science of mantras (*mantraśāstra*). Since it will be stated later, "the practitioner should again [purify] the *siddha* and others by means of the *siddha* and others," the extraction of the sixteen squares is indicated. The second chapter: "The practitioner should arrange the *siddha* and others; he should again [purify] the *siddha* and others by means of the *siddha* and others. A *siddha* mantra grants success through recitation (*japa*); a *sādhya* through burnt offerings (*huta*) and so forth; a *susiddha* by mere attainment; and an *ari* (enemy) mantra devours the practitioner. 130. This has been indicated.
Therein, one should draw five lines extending east-west, north-south, and south-north;
thus sixteen squares are formed.
Therein, one should write the syllables.
The remainder is that they are separated by one [position] each.
As for the method of writing: the first [syllable] is placed in the first of the first group of four;
the second is placed in the first of the second group, proceeding clockwise.
By way of circumambulation, the third [verse] is recited at the first [turn], and the third [verse] again at the third [turn].
The fourth [verse] is recited at the first [turn] of the fourth [round].
Thus, by way of circumambulation, the fifth [verse] is recited at the second [turn] of the first [round].
In the second of the second [syllables], the sixth;
in the second of the third, the seventh;
in the second of the fourth, the eighth.
Thus, by moving clockwise, the ninth [verse] is in the first and third;
the tenth is in the second and third;
and the eleventh is in the third and third.
The twelfth [is applied] to the fourth of the third;
likewise, the thirteenth to the fourth of the first;
and the fourteenth to the fourth of the second.

One should place the fifteenth vowel in the third and fourth squares; one should place the sixteenth vowel in the fourth and fourth square. Having thus completed the writing of the vowels, one should write the consonants beginning with 'ka' according to that same sequence.

As it is stated in the Kādimata: "In the first of the first [cells], one writes the first [syllable]; likewise in the first of the second, the second; in another place, another; and one should likewise arrange the others. In each respective cell, one should write the fifth syllable of that respective [group]."

And thus it is said in another Tantra: "One should write four [syllables] within each of the four sets of four squares, starting from the northeast (Īśa) and ending with the southeast (Agni), and likewise in those belonging to the southwest (Nairṛti), and similarly again in those belonging to the northwest (Anila)."
The wise person should likewise write the letters beginning with *ka* in those same compartments; the intelligent one should complete it by the fourth enclosure in the southwest and northeast.

And whichever name begins with the first group of four syllables, that very [name] is the beginning of its own [set]. Therefore, one should understand the four groups of four as Siddha and so forth, in their proper sequence.
And in this same manner, among the four classes beginning with the Siddhas, their status as Siddhas and so forth is to be understood.

Thus he states its purpose: "beginning with the square of the first letter of one's own name" (*svanāmādi*); the remainder is that it continues up until the square of the first letter of the mantra (*mantrādi*).
He himself will clarify the phrase "one should imagine" and so forth on the occasion of explaining the words, their meanings, and their results, beginning with "the Siddhas and others."

Thus, in whichever tetrad one's own name appears first, that is the *siddha*-tetrad; from there, the practitioner should proceed clockwise with the three tetrads beginning with the *sādhya*, and then again with the *siddha* and so forth.

In whichever four-square grid one's own initial letter is located, that is the "Siddha-Siddha" square. Then, in the three squares following that same four-square grid in a clockwise direction, one should assign "Siddha-Sādhya," "Siddha-Susiddha," and "Siddha-Ari.
If the first letter of the mantra is also in this very four-square grid, then according to this same calculation:
"The Siddha letters are said to be kinsmen; the Sādhya letters are remembered as servants; the Susiddha letters should be known as nourishers; and the Ari letters are considered killers. (131)
Siddham.

If, in this first tetrad, the initial letter of one's own name [is placed] and then the initial letter of the mantra in the second tetrad in a clockwise direction, then—starting from whichever square in the first tetrad contains the initial letter of the name—one should likewise assign the squares in the second tetrad in a clockwise direction as: Sādhya, Siddha, Sādhyasādhya, Sādhyasusiddha, and Sādhyāri.

If, however, the first syllable of the mantra is located in the third group of four starting from the first four syllables of one’s own name and proceeding clockwise, then as before, one should determine from that very square and proceeding clockwise: *susiddha*, *siddha*, *susiddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.

If, however, the first syllable of the mantra is located in the fourth group of four starting from the first four syllables of one’s own name and proceeding clockwise, then as before, one should determine from that very square and proceeding clockwise: *ari-siddha*, *ari-sādhya*, *ari-susiddha*, and *aryari*.
If it is asked, "What is the restrictive rule here for counting from that very same square in the second group of four and so forth? it is said in reply:
the sequence of the original subject matter (*prakṛti*) itself is the restrictive rule, and that is found in the first quarter of the fifth chapter.

"For when the constituent elements (padārthas) have been obtained, there is consideration regarding their sequence; and they are obtained here with a sequence already established by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), not otherwise. Because they are devoid of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), no further sequence for them is devised. When the question arises as to what exactly should be accepted from such statements, the *Piṅgalāmata* states: "Whether it be the name that is well-known [to the person], or his birth-name, or that which has been given by the Guru through the falling of flowers for ascetics (*yatis*), one should cause the syllables of that very name to be divided [into groups]."
Thus, in other instances as well— whether it be a name well-known in the world, or one given by the mother or the father—

and in other cases too: "He who sleeps yet remains awake, who speaks even while standing at a distance, and who utters words even when his mind is elsewhere"— in such cases, that very name should be taken here.
Thus it is stated elsewhere: "The name given by the mother or father must be corrected with effort.
Others, however, have said that in this case, only the birth-name (janmanāma) should be taken.

As it has been said: "Having observed the letter corresponding to the birth asterism, one should look for the first letter of the mantra there. Within four squares, there is one [central square]; thus there are four squares. Furthermore, within those squares, starting from the letter of the birth asterism and moving to the right, the wise should know that they are, in order: Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari."

Thus, regarding the asterisms such as Aśvinī and the rest at the time of birth, their syllables are *cu*, *ce*, *co*, and *lā*; Aśvinī is declared [as the first], the second [is Bharaṇī], and so forth. Therefore, "starting from that" means starting from the syllable of the birth-name;
this should be understood to apply here as well in the phrase "starting from the syllable of birth."
Furthermore, this alternative should be understood as referring to those whose names are well-known by birth and those whose names are not;

for when it is asked, "What is this?", the results such as *siddha-siddha* and so forth are stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* as follows: "From that which is [already] stated, the *siddha-siddha* is achieved through double the recitation (*japa*). From the *siddha-sādhya*, however, one's enemy is destroyed. From the *siddha-siddha* [of the second type], one's kinsmen are destroyed. From the *sādhya-siddha* [of the first type], food is obtained. But the *sādhya-sādhya* is useless."

A *siddha* [mantra] that is *siddha* for you destroys enemies through half the required number of recitations (*japa*); one that is *susiddha* for you destroys those born in the same lineage (*gotra*) through half the recitation. A *sādhya* that is *siddha* for you [destroys enemies] through double the recitation; a *susiddha* that is *siddha* for you destroys planets and the like, as well as those born in the same lineage. A *siddha* that is an *ari* (enemy) for you kills a son; a *sādhya* that is an *ari* for you kills a daughter. A *susiddha* that is an *ari* for you kills the wife; an *ari* that is an *ari* for you destroys the practitioner himself.
Thus,
in the Piṅgalāmata, the calculation of the groups beginning with Siddha for each syllable has been stated.

That which is called the "matr-pitr-kṛta" (the syllables derived from the mother and father) is that which has been formed by one's ancestors; having separated its phonemes according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, one should then begin the purification of the mantra-seeds (*mantra-bīja*). One should exclude those arising from the *bindu*, the double-*bindu*, the *upadhmanīya*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the feet [of the alphabet], as well as those resulting from combined pronunciation, redundant syllables, corrupt letters (*apabhraṃśa*), and the four neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) letters. One should purify each of the name-syllables together with the mantra-syllables: consonants with consonants, and likewise vowels with vowels. Having purified the first [syllable] with the first, and the second with the second—if the syllables in the mantra or the name should be uneven—then one should begin with the mantra and apply them until they become equal. O fair-faced one, in whichever mantra the perfected syllables (*siddha-varṇa*) are at the beginning and end, it will, in a very short time, be the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). That which is joined by the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) at the end and beginning is accomplished only with great difficulty. But that which is well-perfected (*susiddha*) at the beginning and end bestows the power of all desires. If there is an enemy (*ripu*) at the beginning and end, that mantra should be abandoned. *Śāradātilaka* 1.37–45.

That which is *siddha* at the beginning and *sādhya* at the end is accomplished by means of a twofold recitation (*japa*). That which is *siddha* at the beginning and *susiddha* at the end is accomplished through the recitation as previously described. That which is *siddha* at the beginning and has an *ari* (enemy) at the end must be abandoned by those most skilled in mantras. Furthermore, that which is *sādhya* at the beginning and *siddha* at the end is accomplished through a threefold recitation. That which is *sādhya* at the beginning and has an *ari* at the end should be avoided with great effort. However, that which is *susiddha* at the beginning and *siddha* at the end is accomplished precisely according to what was stated.

A *susiddha* [name] and so forth require the four groups beginning with *sādhya* at the end; a *susiddha* and so forth that has an enemy at the end is proclaimed as mediocre (*madhyama*). One that has an enemy at the beginning and a *siddha* and so forth at the end must also be abandoned in this rite. A *siddha* at the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end bestows auspicious results; it is declared in the *Tantra* by Svayambhū that one which is *udāsīna* (neutral) throughout is entirely *sādhya*. One that is *susiddha* in all three positions certainly accomplishes all goals.

A mantra with an enemy [seed-syllable] at all three positions is death; of this there is no doubt. That which begins with *siddha* and ends with a pair of *sādhya*s is called "useless" by the wise. That which begins with *siddha* and ends with *dviḥ-siddha* (twice-successful) accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. That which begins with *siddha* and ends with a pair of enemies is proclaimed as destructive. When the enemy is at the beginning, the *siddha* is in the middle, and the *sādhya* is at the end, the accomplishment of the task occurs with great difficulty, and its fruit will be very small indeed.

If at the beginning there is an enemy [sign] and in the first and middle [positions] there is a pair of *sādhya* signs, the undertaking will be delayed; however, it will perish very quickly at the end. When the *sādhya* sign is at the beginning and the end and the *siddha* sign occurs in the middle, [success is achieved].
When that which is already accomplished at the beginning and end becomes the object of practice in the middle,
both of them— being both the object of practice and the accomplished— are indeed perfected through an abundance of recitation.
A Siddha [mantra] encircled by an Ari becomes a Susiddha as well;
it should be known as causing the destruction of everything for the practitioner—of this there is no doubt.
Whether the object of proof is established by one's own tenets or even by another's tenets, this mantra will shine forth;
thus the Lord himself has declared.
But if one whose enemy has been neutralized by the final doctrine should act even with great effort, that mantra does not become an enemy; rather, it accomplishes its purpose with difficulty.

The second chapter. If the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished), the *antarita-siddha* (the one whose success is obstructed), and likewise the *susiddha* (the well-accomplished) [mantras] are present,
they will be mastered by the practitioner with extreme difficulty, and not otherwise.
If a perfected one (siddha) is obstructed by an enemy, or even one who is well-perfected (susiddha) is likewise so obstructed—
having observed such characteristics, one should avoid him from afar.
A mantra corrupted by an enemy or interrupted by one should never be given at any time.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, it is stated: "A mantra that abounds in harsh syllables is censured."

Having written down the name and the mantra, one should purify the first syllable by means of the first [letter], then purify the second syllable by means of the second [letter]. Upon the completion of the name, having written the name again, one should continue purifying until the completion of the mantra. The meaning is that one should avoid that mantra in which corrupt syllables, syllables of the victim (*sādhya*), or syllables of enemies (*vairin*) are more numerous than others. Regarding this, some say that there is no purification for certain syllables, such as those joined with the *praṇava* (the syllable *Oṃ*), the word *namaḥ*, and corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*) syllables.
O Goddess of the gods, one must perform the counting while strictly avoiding [the forbidden].
Thus it is said.
In that very context, the proponent of the *Tattvasāgara* has stated another method for the conceptualization of the *siddha*s and others:
"Alternatively, on the twelve-spoked wheel, [one should place] those [letters] excluding the *kūṭas* and *ṣaṇḍhas*."
One should write the letters starting from the beginning (A) and ending with Ha, proceeding from the east up to the northeast.
One should write the numbers from one to twelve starting from the east in sequence;
thus, the four states—Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari—will become clearly manifest.
In the first, ninth, and fifth houses, [the planet] is Siddha (accomplished); in the sixth, tenth, and second, it is Sādhya (to be accomplished);
in the third, seventh, and eleventh, it is Mitra (a friend); and in the fourth, eighth, and twelfth, it is Ripu (an enemy).
Alternatively, I shall briefly state another portion of the mantra:
the collection of letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Ha'.
Having assigned each syllable in sequence into the four squares,
the knower of mantras should count them in order as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *vairin*.
Wherever there are phonemes arising from the name-mantra,
one should prescribe the mantra by means of those phonemes, according to the distinctions of *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth.
Alternatively, having added the numerical values of the mantra and the name together, and dividing that sum by four,
the mantra will be classified as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari* starting from the remainder of one.
Thus it is said.
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra, however, it is stated: "Mantra is proclaimed to be of three kinds: Siddha, Sādhya, and Susiddhaka.
— Śāradātilaka.

One with few syllables is "accomplished" (siddha); one with a garland or half-garland is "to be accomplished" (sādhya). Beyond that, it is "well-accomplished" (susiddha), but it is highly censured for the purpose of poetic composition.
Thus it is said.
There is yet another distinction: one who is pure should worship the mantra that bestows both visible and invisible fruits—the *sakala*, the *niṣkala*, the *sūkṣma*, and likewise the *sakalaniṣkala*.
Śiva spoke of the sixfold mantra:
the one with parts (sakala), which resides in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and the partless (niṣkala) one situated below that.

The mind is named *sūkṣma*, residing in the heart, both with parts and without parts; it is situated in the *bindu*, undivided from the *kalās*, yet transcending the *kalās* above that. That *kalā* is indeed Kuṇḍalinī, the power of *nāda*, as declared by Śiva.
Thus it is said: "A mantra contemplated upon these six locations is 'situated in its place' (sthānastha) and bestows fruit; otherwise, it does not.

As it is stated in the *Mālinīvijaya*: 'Mantras situated in their place grant boons, and those situated in meditation bestow fruit; but those devoid of both meditation and place are enemies, even if they are well-perfected (*susiddha*)."
Thus it is said.
Now, the ritual for the complete renunciation of the enemy-mantra (arimantra) is clearly explained.
Having become pure and composed, one should begin on an auspicious day.
For the destruction of all suffering without exception, the Teacher [prescribed] the supreme rite;
therein, first, in a beautiful pavilion, he [performed] the pot-rite according to the sequence of the initiation ritual.
The wise one should place [the vessel] within the maṇḍala and fill it with auspicious water; having invoked the deity therein by reciting the mantra in reverse order.

Having visualized [the deity] in its entirety and performed worship, one should worship the enclosures (āvaraṇas). Thus, having worshipped the deity of the mantra along with the enclosures, the practitioner (mantrī) [proceeds].

Having offered oblations with clarified butter while reciting the mantra in reverse order, the wise twice-born man should likewise offer either one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight oblations even for a cow.
Likewise, at the end, one should satisfy the Lord with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam";
thereafter, one should duly offer the bali-oblation to the deities upon the milk-rice.
Likewise, in the intermediate and main directions, with the following supreme mantras:
"Come, O Indra, Lord of the gods, Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī!"
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and the like.
Come, O Lord of Splendors, O Bearer of Oblations, O Bestower of Boons!
The Second Chapter.
Accept these well-offered flowers, incense, and other offerings, as well as this bali;
O King of the Pretas, come hither, you whose splendor is like that of crushed collyrium!
Having accepted this offered oblation, be well-pleased and grant us boons.
Homage to you, O Lord of the Rakshasas; you, Nirṛti, have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and so forth, presented by me with devotion.
Come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, Lord of the Water-world; homage be unto you!
Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you find delight;
O Prāṇapate, the Wind-god, come hither along with your retinue.
"Accept with respect this offering duly presented by me;
O Kuvera and Tārakādhīśa, you two best of gods, please come!"
May you two, being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, become the bestowers of boons upon me.
O Lord, O Blessed One, O Master who is the refuge of all knowledge, you alone are the Sovereign.
Honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be pleased for the sake of our prosperity;
O Brahman, Lord of all worlds, come to this worship.
Take hold of all my obstacles and turn them back; salutations be unto you!
Come, O bestower of boons, O Unmanifest One, O Viṣṇu, Leader of the universe!
"Worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the bestower of happiness upon me.
Then, one should worship the deity of the mantra along with his retinue.
Then, with the mantra recited correctly and with offerings of flowers and lamps,
the wise one should pray to the deity of the mantra who has been worshipped.
O Lord, without considering what was appropriate, I, with a fickle mind,
have received and honored the true form of the mantra.
Therefore, dispel entirely this agitation of my mind;
may my evil be warded off, and may there be eternal well-being.
"May devotion to you alone, which is purifying, extend my welfare"—
having thus prayed, one should recite the mantra *manveśoṃ* in reverse order.
Having written it, one should worship it with *amalaka*, camphor, and sandalwood;
having placed it upon the water-pot (*kalaśa*), one should do so endowed with supreme devotion.
Then, having tied that leaf upon his own head, the wise man should bathe with the auspicious waters contained within the consecrated jar, which are imbued with mantras.
*Śāradātilaka*:
Again, having filled the jar with another water while remaining self-controlled,
one should then cast the *mantra-patra* into its midst and worship it.
One should cast that jar onto the bank of a river or into another pure body of water,
and then one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability.
For one who has performed the ritual in this manner, the ailments arising from the mantras of enemies are destroyed without a doubt; gradually, clarity of mind arises,
and his family becomes exceedingly prosperous and flourishes in due course.
Thus.
Now, the method for the calculation of debts and assets as stated in the *Mantramuktāvatī* is written here:
Multiply the things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by three, four, eight, and nine.
Then, multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten, one, seven, eleven, eight, three, four, twenty-four, six, and fire (three).
Having subtracted the name-number from the fruit-number and the ascendant-number from the Jupiter-number, the remainder of both shall be either a debt or a wealth.
When the mantra is a debtor it yields auspicious results, while when it is a creditor it is inauspicious; however, when they are equal, it is declared by the lords of sages to yield neutral results.
Thus it is said.

Regarding that, the method is as follows: one should set aside the syllables of the name of the mantra to be accomplished, the practitioner, and the disciple, having separated them according to their vowels and consonants.

Then, having formed four groups of eleven syllables each from the *mātṛkā* consisting of the letters *a*, *ka*, *ṭha*, and *ba*, one should multiply the mantra-syllables—distinguished by their nature as vowels and consonants—by the [deities] beginning with Indra and their respective limbs (*aṅga*).

One should multiply the syllables of the practitioner’s name—distinguished by their nature as vowels and consonants—by the [deities] beginning with the Directions and their respective limbs. In this regard, the method of multiplication is as follows:
In whichever place a particular digit (varṇa) occurs, one should multiply that digit by the value of that place;
the meaning is that one should multiply it by the measure of that position.
For example:
The letter *a*, situated in the first square, should be multiplied by fourteen; there, one multiplied by fourteen is simply fourteen.
Likewise, the letter *i*, situated in the second square, should be multiplied by twenty-seven;
thus, twenty-seven multiplied by two is fifty-four.
Thus, the letter *u*, situated in the third position, becomes six when doubled.
In the same way, one should multiply the letters of the practitioner’s name by ten and so forth.

Among the letters of the practitioner’s name and the mantra—namely *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *e*—the numerical values (aṅka) are to be understood as those of the light-moving (*laghucara*) vowels alone.
Then, the entire sum is unified and divided by eight;
whichever quantity is greater is the debtor (the one in debt),
and the lesser quantity is the creditor (the one to whom the debt is owed).
In that case, if the mantra is the debtor, then it should be accepted;
if not, it should not be accepted.
Now, the method for the clearing of debts and assets as taught in the *Kādimatatantra* is as follows—this is the second chapter.

Starting from the first letter of the name up to the final letter of the mantra and so forth, one should divide it into three parts and pierce them with the vowels; the other [method] is the reverse of that.
Thus [ends the citation].
Its meaning is as follows:
