having counted from the first letter of the practitioner’s name up to the first letter of the mantra according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā* (alphabet), one should multiply that number by three and divide it by the seven vowels.
This is the heap of the practitioner (*sādhaka-rāśi*).

Thus, having counted from the first letter of the mantra up to the first letter of the practitioner’s name according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā*, one should multiply that by three as its limb and divide it by seven; this is the heap of the mantra (*mantra-rāśi*).
The rest is as before.

Or, the method for clearing debts and assets mentioned in another *tantra* is as follows: "The name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), doubled and combined with that of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), should be divided by eight; the remainder is one [type], while the other is the reverse."
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows:
one should double the syllables of the mantra, having separated them according to their nature as vowels and consonants.
One should also separate the letters of the practitioner’s name into vowels and consonants and combine them with those;
then, one should divide by eight.
This is the numerical total of the mantra.

In this way, having separated the letters of the practitioner's name according to their vowels and consonants and doubled them, one should join them with the mantra-syllables—likewise separated by vowels and consonants—and divide the total by eight. Thus is the practitioner’s heap (*sādhakarāśi*).
The rest is as before.

When these [cases] have been stated, the clearing of debts and assets regarding mantras must necessarily be performed by whichever one [is applicable]. In that regard, how do mantras possess the state of being a debt? It is stated in the *Kādimata*: "Due to the practice cultivated in previous births, there is a lack of attainment of results for this [mantra] because of sin.
When the sin is destroyed, the attainment of results occurs in due time through the dissolution of the body; thus it is a debt."
By the mere attainment of the mantra, the previous one becomes effective for success;
that man who has received the mantra from a guru who possesses a perfected mantra becomes a partaker of accomplishment.

"He who, disregarding [the mantra] out of pride in his wealth, has always been worthy of worship and has obtained the enjoyment of the mantra—that mantra must be treated as a creditor by him; its service is the prerequisite. Therefore, the purification of that debt must be performed by everyone, in every way.
Thus it is said.

In another treatise, a different method for the purification of mantras is stated: "Having drawn a six-petaled wheel, one should write the letters beginning with 'A'—one by one—in the petals starting from the east, excluding the neuter (*niṣpaṇḍha*) and compound (*kūṭa*) vowels."
One should investigate starting from whatever letter is the first of one's own name:
in the first [case], prosperity is declared; in the second, the destruction of prosperity.
In the third, however, one should know there is wealth; in the fourth, conflict with kinsmen;
in the fifth, one becomes full of doubt; and the sixth is the destroyer of everything.
Thus [it is said].
In all these cases, the exceptions regarding the purification of the *siddha* and other categories are stated in another work,
the *Śāradātilaka*.

There is no fault in the Piṇḍa, Tāra, Svapnalabdha, the six-syllable mantra, Prāsāda, Ārka, Vaipura, Nārasiṃha, Mālā, Māyā, Mātṛkā, Vārāha, Kāmāstra, Svagraha, Veda, or Ratna mantras, provided they have been obtained through one's own [legitimate] lineage.

Thus, the nature of the *mālā-mantra* is described in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "Those mantras which consist of many syllables are known as *mālā-mantras*. A *mālā* consists of more than ten syllables, while an *ardhamālikā* consists of more than five."
A rosary of five beads is not for the elderly, the aged, or children; a rosary grants success in old age, while a half-rosary does so in youth.
In childhood, the five-syllable mantra situated below [the heart] bestows accomplishment.

Thus it is said. However, in the *Prayogasāra*: "Those mantras which end with nine syllables are proclaimed as seed-mantras (*bījamantra*); furthermore, those mantras ending with twenty syllables are likewise declared to be [seed-mantras]."
Mantras with more syllables than that are proclaimed as *mālā-mantras*; they grant success in subjugation (*vāśya*), while *bīja-mantras* are effective in youth.

"And *mālāmantras* are especially renowned for bestowing success (*prasiddhi*) in Vāikha. Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are known as *mālāmantras*; mantras consisting of more than ten syllables are designated as *bījas*."
Mālā-mantras grant success in old age, while ordinary mantras grant success in youth;
those consisting of more than five syllables grant success in childhood, and all others grant success at all times.
Thus it is said.

In the *Apekṣitārthadyotinī*, it is stated: "In states other than those already mentioned, one should recite the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), and the mantra for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhārtha*) twice as many times.
Likewise: "So too for the eight-syllable *haṃsa* and the five-syllable [mantra]."
One should not purify the perfected ones (siddhas) and so forth for a seed-mantra consisting of one, two, three, or more syllables.
Likewise, in mantras consisting of one, three, five, seven, nine,
eleven, six, or thirty-two syllables, no division into *aṃśakas* is reckoned.
In the Gāruḍa and other solar mantras, in those of Viṣṇu, and in the Buddhist and Jain mantras,
as well as in the Mahākūṭa mantras, there is no purification of the Siddhas and so forth.
Starting from a mantra of forty syllables,
increasing by one syllable at a time up to sixty-two seed-syllables, such a mantra bestows manifold fruits.
Thus it is said:
"Furthermore, those mantras which are not established through formal initiation, but are obtained by the grace of the Yoginīs—
whatever such mantras may be— they bestow the fruits of all desires."
Thus ends the second chapter.
Rites performed by resorting to the location of the lamp yield their fruit.
For those other than these [three], purification is indispensable.
As it has been said: "Whether it be a mantra, a vidyā, a hymn (stava), or even a sūkta, it becomes a destroyer of the body of the meaning and its kin in an instant."

Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the wicked everywhere—not only in the case of mantras, but especially among embodied beings. A relationship should be established after mutual examination; it should not be otherwise. Thus it is said.
Regarding a mantra that does not accord with the Siddhas and others, another method has been stated therein.
As they say: "In all these defects, one should first insert either *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) or *kāma* (*klīṃ*), and then bestow *śrī* (*śrīṃ*), for the sake of liberation from those flaws.
Likewise: "Or even a corrupted mantra becomes effective when encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*)."
"Whichever mantra one has devotion for, that very mantra will be accomplished for him.
Likewise, in the *Bhuvaneśopārijāta*: "A *piṇḍa* mantra, when joined with the seed-syllable of *māyā*, becomes a bestower of swift accomplishment;
even a solitary *piṇḍa* mantra, when illuminated by the seed-syllable of *māyā*, [achieves the same]."

"If the vital breath (prāṇa) is the seed-syllable of Māyā, then the seed-syllable possesses the power of consciousness. Thus, by means of an arranged garland of letters situated in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, if the mantras are recited while uniting each individual letter with the mind, even hostile mantras will grant swift success to men; how much more so other mantras? Thus it is said.
At the outset, for the sake of practical application, he states other designations for the *siddha* and other classes of phonemes, beginning with "the *siddha*-phonemes.
Since the fruit [of the practice] has already been mentioned previously, he now states the location for the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra: "at the lamp," etc.
The meaning of the word *dīpa* (lamp) is stated elsewhere: "That place where a person shines is called a *dīpasthāna* (lamp-location)."

Likewise, I shall explain the "Lamps" (dīpa) as they are taught in the Brahmayāmala, by which temples, villages, houses, and so forth are to be known as auspicious or inauspicious. The letters from *ka* to *ca* are designated as "Lamps" (dīpa), while the sixteen vowels are to be known as the "Seats" (pīṭha) by the best of mantra-practitioners. Thus it is said: "The vowels are called the Seats, and the consonants are indeed the Lamps."
"One should know that the square in which the planet remains is its place; this is the planetary station (dopasthāna) in the Kūrmacakra, without doubt. Thus says the Śāradātilaka.
Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a group of nine squares.

One should write the seven groups [of consonants] in order, beginning with the eastern square. In the central square, which is the seat of Lakṣmī, one should write the vowels in pairs. In the directions starting from the east, wherever the first letter of the name [of the practitioner] is situated, that is the "place of the lamp" for that [name]; for this very reason, he will later state: "the means for accomplishing the success of mantras."
To explain the knowledge of the placement of defects, he states "four" regarding the tortoise-diagram (*kūrma-cakra*):
therein, one should draw two lines extending east-west and two extending north-south within a square;
thus, nine compartments are produced.

In those nine compartments, the nine guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) are to be worshipped, as it is said: "These nine guardians of the fields are in the nine compartments of the lord of the lamp [mandala]: Amṛta, Ṛṣabha, Śailarāja, Vāsuki, Arthaka, Śaktikṛt, Padmayoni, and Mahāśakya. These are to be worshipped starting from the eastern compartment; that is to say, beginning from the compartment in the eastern direction.

"The seven groups" refers to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*. One should write them in sequence ending with the northern [corner], starting from the center as far as possible in each square.
As it has been stated: "In the eastern square, the five-fold *ka*-group [is placed] from the center in order; likewise, the *ca*-group is in the southeast, starting from the center and elsewhere."

Regarding the instruction that "one should write the vowels in pairs in the central square," the method of writing therein is stated elsewhere: "One should write two *a*s in the front part of the central square. One should know the pair *i* in the southeast (Āgneyī), and one should write the pair *u* in the south (Yāmyā). One should know the pair *ṛ* in the southwest (Nairṛtī), and likewise the pair *ṣṭa* in the west (Dāruṇā). One should know the pair *e* in the northwest (Vāyavī), and the pair *o* is desired in the north (Saumyā). One should know the final pair [ai-au] in the northeast (Īśāna); having thus placed them, one should deliberate.
This sequence of writing is indeed indicated by the phrase "one should divide according to this sequence" which will be mentioned below.
Regarding the term "known as fields" (*kṣetrākhyā*):

here, the word "field" (*kṣetra*) is indicative of villages and so forth, as it has been said: "The pedestal (*poṭha*), the field (*kṣetra*), the city (*pura*), the town (*nagara*), and the village (*grāma*)."
The characteristics of the *talla* are described elsewhere: "From *ka* to *na* there is the field (*kṣetra*); from *pa* to *ma* there is the village (*grāma*).

One should know that the second [set] is its face; the two legs are situated on both sides. The two breasts are in the square (*koṣṭha*), the two feet are the remaining [parts], and the tail is said to be the rest."

By this sequence, one should divide even that which is situated in the middle into parts: that which is in the mouth attains success; that which is in the hands has a short life; that which is in the belly is indifferent; and that which is at the feet shall experience suffering. The practitioner situated at the tail is tormented by imprisonment, eradication, and the like. This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, the means for achieving the perfection of mantras. The city beginning with *ya* and ending with *ṣa* has been correctly explained by the best of teachers.
"Sahānta" is said to be the city; this is the characteristic of the field (*kṣetra*).
Thus, the characteristic of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) was previously stated: "The sixteen vowels are called the pedestals.
However, in some places it is also said: "In forests, mountains, cities, villages, temples, and so forth."

"In both places" (ubhayataḥ sthitau) refers respectively to the hands, the flanks, and the feet; thus, on each side of the first [limb], there is the next one, and the tail is what remains. He states the result of this: "situated in the mouth," where "the practitioner" (mantrī) is implied.
The meaning is that he has taken up a mantra according to the method of initiation (*dīkṣā*) taught in the Tantra.
This same meaning is to be understood for the two occurrences of the word "mantrins" (*mantriṇām*) that follow.
"Life" (*jīvana*) is that by which one lives; it means enjoyment (*bhoga*). One whose life is short is "short-lived" (*svalpajīvana*).
As it has been said: "When this [Kūrma] is situated in the mouth and conjoined with two benefics, it is 'hand-held' (karastha) and possesses very little movement," and so forth;

likewise: "In the mouth, there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; in the two hands, it brings about only slight success," and so forth; and likewise: "Therefore, one should undertake all rites by resorting to the mouth; in its absence, one may resort to the hand, but one should not resort to any other part of the Kūrma."

In this regard, a specific detail mentioned in another text is as follows: "Wherever there exists enmity between the names of the deity and the practitioner, one should understand that from the scriptures and properly avoid each such instance. Enmity is said to exist between the pair of *ṛ* sounds and the letter *ga*; between the letter *ṭha* and the pair of *ṛ* sounds, and also between the letter *ṭha* and that same [pair]. Between the pair of *la* sounds and the letter *pa*, and also between the letter *pa* and the pair of *la* sounds;

between the pair of *o* sounds and the letter *ṣa*, and between the letter *ṣa* and the pair of *o* sounds; between the letter *ja* and the letter *ṭa*, and between the letter *kha* and the letter *ka*."

The letter *u* is an enemy of *ta*, *pha* is an enemy of *dha*, *śāradātilaka* [is formed] from *bha* and *ra*, and *ya* is an enemy of *sa*. These letters are enemies; for others, there is a state of friendship. In the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*), the practitioner should diligently avoid the positions of the enemies. Thus it is said.

And an illustration for that very point is shown right there: "Just as Garga’s [place] is Vairi and Aṭṭahāsa is the great city of Amareśvara, so one should apply [the names] beginning with the letter 'A'. For Ṛṣabha it is the one called Cakra; for Lṛtaka it is Padmaka;
Oḍḍiyāna is for Ṣaṇmukha, and Or̤ra is for Ṣaḍguṇaka. Jayantī is for Ṭaṅkaṅgana, Ariḥ for Khaṇdhāra, and [the place] from Saṃjhabhaṭṭa."
The *taraṇi* belongs to Ḍakadeva, the one called *dhūma* to Phaṇjaka, the *ramyaka* to Bhaṭṭa, and the lake (*saraḥ*) to Vairi Yajñamitra.
Having thus purified them in sequence, the wise man should abandon the location of Vairi.
Thus it is said; furthermore, one should apply the initial letter of each of these to the previous paths.

If that same circle of letters is devoid of the first [letter] and the *poṭha*, one should exclude all the names' syllables when they are joined with the *poṭhas*. Having taken those beginning with the first [syllable] according to the path, one should discard the vowel. Furthermore, among the syllables of the village name, having omitted the initial, middle, and final letters, the second syllable—wherever it may reside in the square—is the "face" (*mukha*). Thus it is said.
Elsewhere it is also said: "That face is where the second syllable of each respective name resides.

This, however, concerns names beginning with vowels; regarding the case where there is a conjunct consonant at the beginning of a name, he states the specific rule: "Wherever there is a triad of syllables in village names and the like," and so forth.
Wherever the tone, mounted upon the middle syllable, abides—that is the "mouth."
If two syllables of your name appear clearly among the names of villages and so forth, and the first vowel therein is the letter *a*, that is desired as the face.
And likewise: "If the first syllable of the mantras that accomplish the field (*kṣetrasādhaka*) is indeed one and the same, that mantra will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments."
Thus another [author] declares the specific results: "For the sake of liberation, one should perform [the rite] in the east; for malevolent magic, in the south;
desiring prosperity, having stayed in the west; it shall be a bestower of peace in the north."
In the northeast there shall be the destruction of enemies; in the southeast, [the fire] bestows enemies.
Chapter Two:
A sacred field, a riverbank, a cave, or a mountain peak.
The regions of sacred fords, the confluences of rivers, and the purifying forest.
Secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, a mountain slope, a temple, the shore of the ocean, and one's own home—
these places are praised for the practitioners of mantras.
In the southwest there shall be fear of enemies, but in the northwest there shall be flight.
He who performs the recitation of mantras without knowing the *kūrmacakra* gains no fruit from that recitation; rather, it leads to his own misfortune.
Thus is the specific rule in the Kādimata: having divided the length and breadth by eight and understood the remainder, one should designate one of those [remainders] as the first letter of the name.
When the forms of the *vāstu* (sacred sites) are unknown, they shall be known by name;
the consonants belong to the *deśakūrma*, while the vowels likewise belong to the *gṛhakūrma*.
Thus,
while stating the locations for the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa-japa*), he speaks regarding the subject of the *kūrma-cakra*: "sacred" refers to the bank of a sacred river.
Since a common riverbank is prohibited,
the relationship of qualifier and qualified is expressed as "the purifying forest";
this same logic applies here to the phrase "secluded and pure gardens."
The lexicon states: "Vivikta means pure and solitary.
By the phrase "these are the locations," it is also indicated that which is taught in other systems, as they say:
"In the place of Śiva facing west, devoid of bulls and the like..."

In the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā* it is also stated: "Japa is recommended in the vicinity of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), the *vilva*, and the *tulasī* grove; or amidst other flowers; and in the presence of the sun, fire, the guru, the moon, a lamp, water, brāhmaṇas, and cows."
Or rather, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Thus,
in that very context, the specific fruit resulting from a specific location has also been stated:
"Recitation performed at home is said to be ordinary, but in a cow-pen it is a hundredfold."
And likewise in a grove or a forest, it is said to be a thousandfold.
Alms-food,
sacrificial offerings, vegetables, prescribed fruits, milk, roots, and barley-based products— these are the edible foods for practitioners of mantra.
Ten thousandfold on a holy mountain, a hundred thousandfold by a river,
ten millionfold in a temple of the gods, and infinite in the presence of Śiva.
Thus, in this way, the eight groups of eight sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth should also be understood within the mantras of specific powers (*śaktiviśeṣa*);
elsewhere it is said: "in a place free from barbarians, the wicked, wild beasts, serpents, lions, elephants, and other such dangers."
Or in a secluded forest, free from censure and filled with devotion.

One should dwell in a beautiful region, in a righteous kingdom, where food is abundant, free from calamity, and delightful— a place inhabited by devoted people— rather than depending on the shelter of another.
The path by which kings, ministers, royal officials, and powerful men travel— that path the knower of reality should not dwell upon.
One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, houses, or the grounds of ruined trees; nor on riverbanks, mountain peaks, or in cavities in the earth and the like.
Thus he has stated the rules for the conduct of one performing the *puraścaraṇa*; regarding the phrase "alms-food," this refers specifically to the student (*brahmacārin*) and the ascetic (*yati*).

The nature of alms-gathering has been described elsewhere: "Alms should be received by the twice-born from the houses of those who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and born of noble lineage."
"Thus, 'fit for oblation' (haviṣya) refers to that which is fit for the sacrificial vow-food (vrata-haviṣya), but not to the *śrāddha*-oblation and so forth;
and that is stated in another Smṛti: 'Winter rice, white [rice], unswollen grain, barley, wheat, and sesame.'"
Kalāya, kaṅgu, and novāra grains; vāstuka and hilamocikā.
Sixty-day rice, black pot-herbs, radish, and other tubers such as kemuka; rock salt and sea salt; and the curd and clarified butter of a cow.
Milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, myrobalan, tamarind, cumin, and orange.
Sages declare that plantains, lavalī fruits, emblic myrobalan, and honeyed products— provided they are not fried in oil— constitute *haviṣya* food.
Thus, the fruit, milk, and root are prescribed; the word "is ordained" is to be supplied [to each].

The second chapter:
For the attainment of the goals of human existence, a worthy disciple should take refuge in a guru— one who is pure by birth and lineage, pure in disposition, and has conquered his senses.
He was one who knew the essence of all scriptures, understood the true meaning of all treatises,
was devoted to helping others, and was intent upon recitation, worship, and other such practices.
His speech was unfailing, he was tranquil, and he had mastered the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas; he followed the path of yoga and had reached the heart of the deities.
It has been stated that "one who possesses true discipleship should take refuge in a guru";

therefore, he describes the characteristics of a guru with the words beginning "from his mother," meaning one who is pure on both the maternal and paternal sides, i.e., born of parents who are themselves pure.

And that purity is to be understood through worldly renown and through an investigation of one's conduct, as it has been said: "The sons, devoid of propriety, cast aside their own duty and reveal those secret deeds which were committed by their mothers when they were blinded by the intoxication of youth."
Thus,
"pure disposition" means a pure state of mental activity;
otherwise, due to wickedness, he would not even be worthy of service.
One who has conquered the senses [overcomes] one whose senses are unconquered, because of being devoted to the deities.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context function as a punctuation mark indicating the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]
He knows the essence of all scriptures;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between the various traditions such as Śaivism and others,
for he understands the true meaning of all treatises.
Otherwise, the investigation of the scriptures and the treatises would be untenable;
one who is devoted to the welfare of others would otherwise lack compassion for the learned.
Without that compassion, even a mantra becomes averse,
despite one being intent upon recitation, worship, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth," meditation and fire-offerings are included.
Otherwise, for one whose observance of the rules has been abandoned, there is an absence of the deity’s presence;

as it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "A mantra, even if well-perfected, does not become gracious if it is not meditated upon or worshipped; it does not desire to grant success if it is not recited, nor does it yield fruit if it is not offered oblations."
Therefore, if the practitioner desires his own success, he should perform these four rites— worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering— every day.
Thus it is said.
His speech is unfailing, he is capable of bestowing grace,
and he is peaceful; otherwise, he would be avoided by the world as one who is censurable.
"Having mastered the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas"—
by this, his steadfastness in his own proper conduct is expressed,
as it has been said: "By a person who possesses the conduct appropriate for their caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person [is attained]."
Viṣṇu is propitiated by the Path; there is nothing else that causes him satisfaction.

Thus it is elsewhere as well: whatever [practice] such as the propitiation of deities one performs apart from one's own duty (svadharma) shall perish in that very moment, like a structure made of sand.
Thus,
the guru, endowed with such qualities as those described in the *Śāradātilaka* and other texts, is approved by the Āgamas.
Following the path of yoga,
otherwise there would be an incapacity even for the bestowal of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth;
"heart-pleasing to the deity" means heart-pleasing to the deity— that is, captivating and having a serene appearance.
Just as there is satisfaction in the mind through the vision of a deity, so too does satisfaction arise in the mind through seeing that [the preceptor],
for it has been said: "The conduct of men follows their actions, and the mind follows their conduct."
"Form generally follows the mind, and qualities follow form.
Thus, wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, there the attainment of the fruit is certain.
As it has been said: "In that which the mind and the eyes delight, there lies prosperity."
Likewise, there is the recollection of the learned Kālidāsa: "For the mind [remembers] associations from previous births," and so forth.

Furthermore, as stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "Neither too young nor too old, neither lame nor humpbacked, neither with extra limbs nor deficient in limbs, neither bald nor having protruding teeth."

"One who is of noble family, eloquent, brave, well-established, and has mastered the scriptures; one who has practiced the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), is discerning in extracting splinters (*śalya*), knows the sequence of ritual procedures, and is a discerning master of the *mudrā* tantras. Thus it is said.

"One who is pure, well-attired, young, whose intellect is equal toward all beings, wise, of a humble mind, grateful, affectionate toward disciples, full of faith, and free from malice— such a householder is called a guru. This and other such passages from other texts should also be consulted.

Since it is stated elsewhere that "the teacher, the maternal uncle, the officiating priest, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law, and the king— these six are also gurus," the qualification "approved by tradition" (āgamasammata) is used here [to distinguish them from those].

"He who rescues embodied beings submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra* by providing them with the boat [of instruction]—he alone is remembered here as the Guru. Regarding this statement, there is a specific rule for the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasvata*: "Whether he be a native of Āryāvarta or otherwise, provided he is devoid of the eight *ka*-letters."
"One who is proficient in the Śaiva Siddhānta and has mastered the mantras for consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
And in the Vīrāgama it is said: "A learned man born in the region between Kumārī and Himavat, which is naturally inhabited by black deer, is worthy of the office of an Ācārya."
Also in the Yogaśivapaddhati: "The most excellent gurus are those born in Madhyadeśa, Kurukṣetra, Nābhī, Ujjayinī, Antargiri, Pratiṣṭhāna, and Āvantī."
The Caulas born in the Gauḍa country, the Māgadhas, the Keralas,
as well as the Kauśalas and the Daśārṇas, are considered to be the middling teachers.

"The Karṇāṭakas, Koṅgaṇakas, Ākīras, as well as the Kacchātas, Oroṅgas, Kāliṅgas, Kāmarūpas, and Kāmbojas are considered the lowest. Thus it is stated in the Devīmata. And in the Śaiva scriptures: "The preceptor (ācārya) is one who knows the Śaiva teachings and is born in the land of Śiva."
"Whether a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) or a householder (*gṛhastha*), one who is devoted to devotion to Śiva and whose birth is favorable to the patron (*yajamāna*) is called a *deśika*.
Thus it is also stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "A householder or one established in celibacy, who is free from the eight defects beginning with the letter 'ka'..."
"One should always revere a teacher who is devoted to the vow of fasting.
Likewise: "That twice-born man who perceives the Self as distinct from everything else—he is a teacher, even if devoid of all [other] characteristics; of this there is no doubt."
But one who has awakened after five nights and knows the reality of the meaning of the Siddhānta is declared to be an Ācārya, even if he is devoid of all [other] characteristics.

"He who possesses supreme devotion for Viṣṇu as he does for his guru—he alone is to be recognized as a true teacher; I tell you this truth. Thus, in the *Atītāgama*, there is this specific instruction regarding Śaiva initiation: "Whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a top-knot, he should be born in a praiseworthy region."
A twice-born man who has mastered the true meaning of the Śiva scriptures and is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.

"He who constantly takes refuge in Śiva alone through the actions of speech, mind, and body is designated as the true Ācārya in the rites of Śiva-initiation and the like. Thus it is said regarding pacificatory rites: "One who is well-versed in the Vedas, whose soul is serene, and who has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva..."
The wise one who has entered the Śiva-āgama is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
"One who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, whose body is marked with the trident,
who is born of a pure region and lineage, who is endowed with good character and conduct,
and who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras— such a person is called a Guru possessed of knowledge. Thus it is said.

Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*: "The officiant (*liṅgin*) is one who possesses knowledge of the characteristics [of the ritual], is skillful in the sequence of rites, knows the reality of the pervasion of the deities, and is proficient in the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvan*)."
Whether it be the signs of the auspicious and inauspicious— what need is there for further detail?
A disciple who is of noble birth, pure in soul, and devoted to the goals of human endeavor [should study] the Śāradātilaka.
Having studied the Vedas, he was proficient and had long since cast away the god of love.
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, a believer who has abandoned atheism, devoted to his own duty, and striving with devotion for the benefit of his father and mother.
"Perfect knowledge of birth, conduct, and so forth—these three qualities belong to him who is the most excellent Guru, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.

Thus, even for a renunciant (yati), the status of being a Guru is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "The mantra-practitioner who has observed the vows of right conduct, who possesses knowledge, and is well-composed..."
"A renunciant who is eternally established [in the Self] shall be known as a Guru, even if he is a householder.
Thus it is said in the *Bātulottara*: "Having obtained such a Guru—one who bestows fearlessness through knowledge and is free from greed and fickleness—who would not be liberated from bondage?"
In the Pauṣkara, however, it is said: "Even one who is devoid of all [other] characteristics is called a guru if he possesses knowledge;
and that knowledge is the realization of reality (tattva-vijñāna), which rests upon the knowledge of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva). Thus [it is stated].
He states the characteristics of a disciple: "A disciple" refers to one who is *kulīna*, born of pure mother and father;
otherwise, because of the impurity of the *golā* and so forth, there would never be any fitness for touch.
He was pure in soul and of non-cruel mind because he did not impart knowledge to a cruel person;
as the Śruti says: "Knowledge, indeed, came to the Brāhmaṇa."
"Guard me as your treasure;
do not speak of me to one who is envious, dishonest, or unrestrained, so that I may be possessed of wisdom"— thus [should one pray],
being devoted to the goals of human life.
By this, his freedom from calamities is stated,
for otherwise instruction would be purposeless;
by the phrase "one who has studied the Veda," his purity is stated.
As it has been said: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra in this very life, along with his lineage.
Thus [he is] skilled and not deluded.
Because one who is deluded is unfit for the awakening through mantras,

and because a lustful person— due to being possessed by passion and having an impure mind— is devoid of the power of the mind of love, they lack the qualification for the propitiation of mantras; thus, [the teacher] is always a well-wisher of living beings.
Otherwise, the sin of one who delights in activities such as *abhiṣeka* and so forth [performed] with a mantra taught otherwise would touch even the Guru;
for an *āstika*— one whose intellect holds that "the next world exists"—
otherwise, in the state of being an atheist (*nāstika*), there would be no propitiation of the deity of the mantra, and thus the deity would become angry with the Guru.
Having abandoned nihilism and renouncing association with nihilists—
otherwise there would be the defect born of such association—
he should be devoted to his own duty and possessed of proper conduct.

Since one who does not practice [the rules] lacks the qualification, he should be devoted to the welfare of his mother and father with sincerity, and not through hypocrisy or the like; this alone is declared to be his supreme duty. Thus ends the second chapter.
Devoted to serving his gurus with his speech, mind, body, and wealth,
he has abandoned pride toward his teachers on account of birth, learning, wealth, and so forth.
Indeed, for the sake of observing the commands of his preceptor, he is ever intent on even sacrificing his life;
having set aside his own affairs, he is constantly devoted to the service of his guru.
The disciple who always dwells with his guru like a servant,
performing his commands day and night, remains devoted solely to the service of the guru; by Vyāsa and others,
through such passages as "with speech and mind," non-deceitfulness has been declared.
By the phrase "of such a kind," one should understand what is stated in other texts, such as "the youth who has subdued all his faculties and is an abode of compassion.
As it says in the *Prayogasāra*: "There too, [it is taught] for a son endowed with devotion and for a giver of wealth."
In the Nārāyaṇīya as well, one who serves the teacher through the actions of mind, speech, and body,
being pure in disposition and possessed of great enthusiasm, is known as a disciple (boḍā).
"But Upadeśya, Puca, Vyatyaya, and Vasuda—there is no other [worthy recipient]," by this statement the exclusion of others is declared.
Likewise, elsewhere, after describing the faults of a disciple, it is said: "One should not accept as a disciple one who is endowed with such qualities [as these]."
If one should accept it, that fault will likely touch even the teacher.
Just as the fault of a minister reaches the king, or that of a wife reaches her husband, so too does the fault committed by a disciple undoubtedly reach the teacher.

If one accepts [a disciple] for initiation out of affection or even out of greed, then a curse from the deity shall fall upon that guru along with his disciples; therefore, a guru should always accept a disciple only after having thoroughly examined him. Thus it is said.

In the *Bhuvaneśopārijāta* it is also said: "He who would speak [the teachings] to one who is not a disciple becomes a perpetrator of a great sin. However, in another text there is this specific distinction: "When the Guru is speaking words, one should then speak these words:"
"Be gracious, O Lord, O God," he said with reverence, "and likewise, 'So be it.'"
Having prostrated, he should sit at the side; likewise, he should move about with permission.

He should attend upon [the teacher] while looking toward his face and perform whatever is commanded with reverence. The disciple, obeying the command of the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body, [should act thus]. — *Śāradātilaka* —
Whoever may be such [a person] at that time should be accepted, and no other, by one desiring auspiciousness.
He who always conceals the secrets of the worship of Manu,
and he who, knowing the truth of the conduct prescribed by the Agamas, pays homage at the three times of day;
Only such a person should be made a disciple, and no other who leads a meager life;
endowed with such qualities as these, one becomes a disciple, and no other.

One should not speak untruth in his presence, nor should one indulge in excessive chatter; likewise, one should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, derisive laughter, flattery, fickle behaviors, crookedness, and lamentation.
"A disciple desiring prosperity should never engage in lending money, receiving loans, or the buying and selling of goods with his teacher.
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The teacher, mother, father, master, kinsmen, friends, and Śiva [are all to be honored]."
Having thus fixed the mind, one should constantly worship the guru with one's whole being.
One should not speak untruth to the guru, nor cause him to be censured;
one should dissuade others from beginning [harmful acts] against him, and if unable to do so, one should abandon that place.
One should behave toward the wives of one's teachers exactly as one does toward the teacher himself;
one should regard elder brothers like teachers and younger brothers like oneself.
Whatever has been commanded by the guru, whether it be desirable or even undesirable,
that he should immediately carry out with a mind free from deceit.
"One should always worship the future guru through thought, word, and deed.
Thus it is stated in the *Devī-āgama* as the word of Śiva: "One should avoid separate worship and offerings in the presence of the guru;
one should avoid [conferring] initiation, exposition, authority, and so forth, in the presence of the guru."
In that very same [text]: "One should worship the seat, the bed, the garment, the ornament, the sandals, as well as the shadow, the wife, and whatever else has been touched by him.
Also elsewhere: "As it is with the deity, so it is with the mantra; as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru."
"As it is with the Guru, so it is with one's own self; such is the traditional sequence of devotion. Thus ends the second chapter. In one year a Brāhmaṇa becomes qualified, and in two years a king.

"A Vaiśya [should wait] three years, and a Śūdra four years, before being accepted by the Guru as a servant for initiation, sacrifice, vows, and so forth. Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, which states the duration of time for the examination of the disciple. "Eka... [etc. *Note: The final fragment "eketi" appears to be the beginning of the next section or verse.*
The phrase "he would be fit for the Guru" is connected everywhere;
as for the statement "the Śūdra [is fit] with four," if it is asked, "How then can a Śūdra have the right [to initiation and so forth]? [the answer follows].
It is not so;
for it is established that the Smṛti prescribes a lack of entitlement only with respect to the study of the Veda and the rituals enjoined therein, while elsewhere there is indeed entitlement.
For this very reason, the Smṛti states in the section concerning Śūdras: "One should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation."

Thus, these mantras were proclaimed by Īśvara; therein, the Lord himself has demonstrated the respective eligibility [of practitioners] as stated in the section on the Prāsāda-mantra: "For women and Śūdras, this mantra ending in 'namaḥ' brings auspiciousness."
"Having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should initiate even the Cāṇḍālas.
Thus it is also stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "The knower of mantra should perform initiation for the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas."

Elsewhere it is also stated: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, possessing pure intellects, shall be eligible for worship [of the image] when they are devoted to the worship of the Guru, the Deity, and the twice-born.
By this, he has no eligibility for the direct Vedic mantras, such as the Rāma-ṣaḍakṣara, the Saura-aṣṭākṣara, the Mantrarāja, and others beginning with the Praṇava.

And so, in the *Praṇavavyākhyāna* by the teacher Padmapāda, it is stated: "By the phrase 'consisting of the letters A, U, and M,' it is indicated that within the three divisions [of the Veda], only those of the three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*) are qualified for the *praṇava* and other mantras, and not women or *śūdras*.
Likewise, in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*: "They do not desire the *Sāvitrī*, the *praṇava*, the *Yajus*, or *Lakṣmī* for a woman or a *śūdra*;
if a woman or a *śūdra* should know the *Sāvitrī*, *Lakṣmī*, the *Yajus*, or the *praṇava*, he is said to go downward [to hell]."
Thus it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra regarding the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa: "No mantra is exalted by the Veda if it abandons the *praṇava*;
therefore, the mantra is considered supreme to the Veda, and the *āgama* is remembered as a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda."

All rites for specific desires, such as subjugation and attraction, which bestow both visible and invisible fruits, are accomplished through the Veda by means of sacrifices to the planets and the like; indeed, there are no sacrifices without the Veda, nor are there sacrifices devoid of the Veda. (Śāradātilaka)
Therefore, the Veda is the supreme mantra; there is no mantra for one who abandons the Veda.
"There is no entitlement for Śūdras regarding mantras; this is a supreme restriction.
Indeed, because of the absence of mantras, every ritual is performed without a mantra.
Thus it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*, in the section concerning the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa: "The Pañcarātra system is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas."

"It does not even reach the path of the ears of Śūdras and others. Likewise, regarding the Veda, his Smṛtis prescribe punishments: "If he hears it, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac; if he recites it, his tongue is to be cut off; if he retains it, his body is to be split asunder. Enough said on this point. Elsewhere, it is stated generally for a period of one year: "The status of teacher or student [is established] by living together for one year."
Thus it is also stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "The true guru shall observe the disciple who has sought refuge for one year."
Some have said that this refers to the domain of Brahmins;
however, in the *Daśapaṭalī*, it is stated: "Having examined [the candidate] for a year, or else for a matter [of duration], one should never act otherwise."
In the *Prayāgasāra*, however, it is stated: "The examination of a Brahmin is recommended after three years, that of a Kṣatriya after six years, and that of a Vaiśya after nine years."
Regarding all twelve [classes], those who are *vṛṣala*s and so forth—
this is the specific detail in the *Siddhāntasārasaṃgraha*: "A Brāhmaṇa and likewise a Kṣatriya should give the aforementioned sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
The best of Vaiśyas [should give] double that, and the most excellent of Śūdras triple that.

"One should bestow the fruits of one's own virtues according to the desire for the rules of mantra-siddhi. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, the commentary on the *Śrīśāradātilaka* composed according to the true tradition. Oṃ. The Third Chapter:
Thereafter, I shall describe the ritual of the Vāstu-yāga, which is a limb of initiation (*dīkṣā*), preceded by which the knower of mantras attains the fruit of initiation.

Thus, the *dohā* (verse) concerning the means of receiving the mantra—which grants all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) and whose nature has been elaborated according to the method previously described—is presented. To state that [means], he pledges to elaborate upon the *vāstuyāga* (sacrifice to the site) and other such rites which constitute its ancillaries (*aṅga*), beginning with the word "tataḥ" (thereafter).

Relying on the principle of Bhaṭṭa—that the transcendental potency (*apūrva*) of the principal rite, when assisted by the transcendental potencies of the ancillaries, becomes capable of producing the fruit—he says "kṛtena" (by having performed).

In this context, by way of a digression, something else stated in another tantra regarding the auxiliary elements of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga*) is mentioned: "Failure, the attainment of the [initiatory] ground, death, the destruction of kinsmen, the increase of lifespan,
the destruction of progeny, prosperity, and the accumulation of jewels."
The attainment of auspiciousness, loss of position, intelligence, wealth, and subjugation—
these are to be known as the results for the months beginning with Caitra; however, one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
However, elsewhere the Āṣāḍha month is also said to yield perfect results: "The commencement of a mantra in the month preceding Vaiśākha is very difficult to endure;
in Vaiśākha it bestows wealth, and in Jyeṣṭha it would bring about death."
In Āṣāḍha, it is for the attainment of a son; in Śrāvaṇa, it is considered to bestow auspiciousness;
and in Bhādrapada, the loss of knowledge is proclaimed by the wise.
In Āśvina there is complete success; in Kārttika, it bestows the perfection of knowledge;
Mārgaśīrṣa will be auspicious for those on the path; and Pauṣa brings about suffering.
In Māgha there is an increase of intelligence, and in Phālguna there is mastery over all.
Thus it is said.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, however, there is a specific distinction: initiation during the autumn season or the month of Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit.
Although the month of Caitra is censured, as are Pauṣa and Bhādrapada, it is stated that initiation is auspicious even during these censured months if it occurs during an eclipse.
Thus,
in that case, there is a prohibition because the month of Āṣāḍha is included within the *uttamāna* [period], and there is an inclusion because it is included within the *kaṣṭāna* [period].
In this way, it should be understood that the prohibition regarding the month of Jyeṣṭha also arises precisely from the fear of the supreme *ananta* [obstacle].
And so says the *Śāradātilaka*:
"In the *Kālottara*, the conjunction of autumn and winter is prescribed for the performance of the rite of initiation."
"In the absence of those two, it is praised elsewhere [to perform it] even without the *varṣī*.
Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*: "Initiation (dīkṣā) shall not take place without [the proper] lunar day (*parvan*), nor during the rainy season, nor in the months of Vaiśākha or Pauṣa.
The prohibition of Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa is due to their being [respectively] the highest and intermediate [degrees of] Ananta.
In the month of Āṣāḍha-pūrva and in the months of Āṣāḍha and Mārgaśīrṣaka,
a wise person should not perform the initiation (dīkṣā); however, one may perform it in other months.
Thus it is said.
It should be understood that the prohibition regarding the month of Mārgaśīrṣa follows from the fact that it is included within the "Uttama" (excellent) period.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā: "Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, initiation brings all auspiciousness."

In the Kālottara, however, there is this distinction: "Those desiring prosperity [should perform it] during the bright fortnight, while those desiring liberation [should do so] during the dark fortnight."
Thus it is said in the *Saṃhitā*: "The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh,
as well as the thirteenth and the tenth— these are praised and grant all desires."
But elsewhere it is said: "On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth, or on one of the five festival days (parvan).
In the *Mantrasārasaṃgraha* as well: "The second, the fifth, or especially the sixth [lunar day]."
It should be performed on the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth day.
Thus it is said.
In the *Mantraratnāvalī*, however, it is stated: "The fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth [lunar days],
with the exception of the full moon day, are said to be beneficial for those seeking liberation."
Thus it is said.
However, in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*: "Having carefully observed each respective lunar day (*tithi*), one should initiate those who are devoted to that [deity] therein.
Indra.
"Whose specific lunar day (tithi) is prescribed for whom? Tell me in detail, O Nārada.
Nārada replied:
"The full moon (paurṇamāsī) is prescribed for Brahmā, and the twelfth day (dvādaśī) for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu)."
The fourteenth day is said to belong to Śiva; the thirteenth is said to belong to Vāc;
the second is said to belong to Śrī, and the third to Pārvatī.
The fourth is said to belong to Gaṇanātha, while the seventh belongs to Bhānu;
the eighth and fourteenth are the daily [observances] of Pārvatī on the paths.
Thus [it is said].
However, there is a specific rule regarding the Viṣṇu-initiation in the *Paśvarātra*: "On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, as well as during the sun's transit.
This is the third chapter.

The *saṃkrama*s other than Viṣṇupadī are as follows; and the *Kālottara* states: "Those which are the gaps of the day (*dinacchidra*), those that are liberated (*mukta*), and those that touch three days."
Thus it is said.
However, in the *Ratnāvatī*, it is stated: "For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya (Sunday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), and Sauri (Saturday)."
In the *Saṃhitā*: "It should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Saturday, Monday, and on the days of Mercury and Venus"—
the meaning is "in the bright fortnight" (*site pakṣe*).
Elsewhere: except for the three [asterisms] following Uttarā, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Puṣya, Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā), Dhaniṣṭhā, Vāyu (Svāti), Mitra (Anurādhā), Āditya (Punarvasu), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Nairṛta (Mūla),
Aiśa (Abhijit), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and Hasta— these are auspicious for initiation (dīkṣā).
Thus:
Vāsava is Jyeṣṭhā.
Vāyu is Svātī; Mitra is Anurādhā;
Aśvin is Aśvinī.
Maghā belongs to Pitta; Citrā belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ;
Mūlā belongs to Nirṛti.
Ārdrā belongs to Īśa;
Śravaṇa belongs to Viṣṇu.
Also in the Saṃhitā: "And in the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Hasta..."
In this manner, the consecration with mantras should be performed during the three constellations beginning with Jyeṣṭhā and Uttarā.
Thus it is said.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "The three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Maghā, Mūla, and Revatī."
Abhijit and Śravaṇa.
Thus.
And for the purpose [of the rite], the asterisms are Pauṣṇa, Rohiṇī, Āditya, Śravaṇa, Aśvinī,
Sāvitra, Tvāṣṭra, Vāyavya, Aindra, and Nairṛta.
O observer of excellent vows, the constellations Tiṣya (Puṣya), Viśākhā, Uttarāphalgunī, Ārdrā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and the birth-star of the disciple are praised for the rite of initiation.
Thus:
Revatī belongs to Pūṣan; Punarvasu belongs to Āditya.
The Hasta constellation belongs to Savitṛ; Mṛgaśiras belongs to Soma. Furthermore, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras [are auspicious].
Puṣya and Śatabhiṣā are said to be the lunar mansions for initiation (dīkṣā).
Thus it is stated.
In the *Ratnāvalī*, however, it is stated: "The first lunar day with the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the fifth with Kṛttikā,
the sixth with Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise the tenth with Rohiṇī."
The twelfth [tithi] with the asterism Āśleṣā and the thirteenth with Mṛgaśiras—
these are known as *nakṣatraluptā* (asterism-deficient), and they bring destruction even to the gods.
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, the defectiveness of lunar days (*tithi*) and asterisms (*nakṣatra*) due to their conjunction with Monday and other such factors is to be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
Likewise: "In all auspicious yogas, initiation (*dīkṣā*) bestows all that is auspicious."
In the *Ratnāvalī*: Yoga, Prautirāyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Śubha, Sukarmā, Dhṛtivṛddhi, Bhuva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
The Śāradātilaka:
Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Aindra are the sixteen.
Thus it is said:
"They declare that auspicious actions depend especially on dexterity;
one should avoid the *śakuni* and other [karana-s], and particularly the *viṣṭi*."
Thus,
in the *Saṃhitā*: "On the day of the purification of the five limbs, at its own rising, [one should consider] the lunar day and the weekday."
When Jupiter and Venus are rising, in a pure ascendant cleared of the twelfth house,
and when Venus and Jupiter are strengthened and endowed with power;
When there is an auspicious conjunction with the moon, in an auspicious division (*varga*), and at an auspicious rising (*udaya*),
there is the collection of all mantras and the source of all happiness, and so forth.
Thus it is said;

and likewise in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "When Jupiter is in its sign of debilitation, or in retrograde motion, or moving with excessive speed, or eclipsed, or set, the wise should diligently avoid—regardless of whether Jupiter is in the sign of Leo—the commencement of a solar eclipse, religious processions, the performance of vows and observances, ear-piercing, initiation (*dīkṣā*), the tying of the sacred thread (*mauñjībandha*), the marriage rites of the *gaṇas*, and the consecration of temples."
Thus it is said.

One who moves in such a manner should be entirely avoided. In fixed signs, malefics situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses grant happiness, while benefics [saumyas] situated in angles (kendras) and trines are auspicious for initiation (dīkṣā).
However, those situated in the eighth house are said to cause total destruction. Thus it is said.
By the term "āya," the eleventh house is indicated; by the term "kendra," the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses;
and by the term "trikoṇa," the fifth and ninth houses.

Likewise, the eighth position is a "hole" (randhra) on the following occasions: on the birth day of the three types of disciples, at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), at the solstices (ayana),
on other meritorious conjunctions (puṇyayoga), and during lunar and solar eclipses.

"Or, at a time favorable to the disciple, purification of the body brings auspiciousness. Thus it is said in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "When these asterisms, lunar days, and so forth are present, on a yoga-day, the instruction of mantras by the Guru and the practice [of sādhana] bring auspiciousness."
In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara* as well, everything regarding the lunar days and so forth has been stated: "Having carefully observed [the time] by such means, the preceptor should perform the initiation;
for one seeking liberation, no restriction of time or other factors is prescribed.
And from the *Ratnāvalī*: "All those [restrictions] are censurable, whereas [initiation] is praised for the sake of liberation."
And having observed the fire-wheel (agnicakra) that is about to be described, the day for initiation should be determined;

furthermore, there is this exception: "During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, at the birth of the disciple, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn (makarasaṃkrānti), and at the time of the Guru’s passing, [the influence of] constellations and so forth is not required for initiation. Thus it is said.
The third chapter:

Likewise, on the days of a disciple’s birth, during a transit, at the seizing [of a planet], or even on the day of the Moon or the Sun, or when joined with an auspicious conjunction (*puṇyayoga*), the supreme accomplishment of mantra for men is declared. Thus.

In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* it is also stated: "Even at the equinoxes, at the solstices, on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, at the time of a solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*), during the festivals of Dama and Mada, and at the proper times for the rite of the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) should indeed be performed.
And in the *Kālottara*: "During initiation, during consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and likewise during the formal reception of the mantra..."
At the time of undertaking a vow or its conclusion, at the commencement of a rite involving materials, on the full moon days of Kārttika and Vaiśākha,

during an eclipse of the sun, during an eclipse of the moon, at the six and eight auspicious moments (ṣaḍaśītimukha), during planetary and lunar conjunctions, at the equinoxes, at festivals, and at all solstices— on these occasions, every astrological yoga bestows the fulfillment of all goals. Thus it is said.

In the Rudrayāmala it is also stated: "At a sacred pilgrimage site, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, on the Damanaka festival, or when performing the initiation of a Mantra (manvadīkṣā), one need not purify the month, the asterism (nakṣatra), and so forth.
And from the Agastyasaṃhitā: "At the time of a solar eclipse, nothing else need be sought."

There is nothing else equal to the time of a solar eclipse. Whatever is performed there becomes the giver of infinite fruit; on the occasion of a solar parvan, there is no need for the calculation of months, lunar days, or weekdays. At that time, whatever is offered or received from a preceptor among men, the mantra attains accomplishment effortlessly and swiftly. Those desiring the accomplishment of a mantra should perform [the rites] with every effort. Thus it is said.

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "At a meritorious pilgrimage site, at Kurukṣetra, at the four seats of the Goddess (Devīpīṭha), at Prayāga, with one's own Guru, or in Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the proper time and the improper time.
Thus, in the *Tattvasāgara-saṃhitā*: "Listen now to the special occasion for initiation even without regard for the lunar day (*tithi*)."
When the company of holy men, so difficult to find, has occurred even once, and when their permission is obtained—that is the great occasion for initiation.
Whether in a village or a forest, in a sacred field by day or by night, whenever the Guru arrives by providence, then the initiation shall take place. Thus it is said.
Likewise: "Whenever there is the desire [to be initiated], then initiation occurs in accordance with the command of the Guru.
There is no need for a specific lunar day, no vow, no fire-oblation, no ritual bathing, and no recitation of mantras;
rather, the cause of initiation is simply the attainment of a true Guru according to one's own wish. Thus it is said.

Having slain the Rākṣasa named Vāstu and having occupied his body, the fifty-three deities remained; one should first offer the bali-oblation to them. The origin of the Vāstu-sacrifice is stated [in the verse] beginning with "rākṣasam."

Regarding what was said, "having slain"— it is stated that Siṃhikā, the wife of Kaśyapa and mother of Rāhu and Vātāpi, gave birth to two sons; the elder had his neck severed by Hari, while the younger was struck down by the gods.

In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as well: "Formerly there was a great being, a source of terror to all creatures, who was slain by the gods; he is known on earth as Vāstupuruṣa. As long as the earth remains stable in the world, so long does the demon Vāstu remain;
but at the time of dissolution, he goes to absorption along with the gods, all the planetary deities, and the rest. His extent is a hundred crores of *yojanas* all around."

He stands pervading the earth, lying on his back, black in color; with his knees and elbows touching the ground, his forearms reaching toward the northeast and northwest, his feet toward the southwest, his head toward the northeast, and his hands joined at the heart; with hair standing erect, very stout, with round eyes and the form of an asura—thus it is described elsewhere that he is face-downward.

Indeed, the asura named Vāstuśana, who possessed a massive body and had been granted boons by the gods in the past, remains worshipped even now, lying upon the earth with his feet and hands stretched out and his face forever turned downward. O Lord of Dvārakā, his head is situated in the northeast (Īśāna), his two arms in the northwest (Vāyu), and his pair of feet in the southwest (Nairṛta). His two hands are in the west (Varuṇa) and his pair of feet are established in the direction of the night-stalkers (the south, Nairṛta).

The true nature of the *vāstu* is stated elsewhere: "In ancient times, during the battle with the demon Andhaka, the terrifying sweat-water fell from the forehead of the enraged Trident-bearer onto the earth," and so forth.
However, Somaśambhu has set forth the established rule: "The *vāstu* [diagram] has its hands contracted, is face-up, and has the form of a demon."

One should remember [the deity] with the face turned downward when established on a wall or similar surface during worship. When the knees are joined to the elbows, he is situated in the directions of wind and fire; in the southeast (paittryāṃ), his feet are joined; in the northwest (rauyāṃ), his head is in his heart, and his hands are in *añjali*.
Thus he remains, yet out of fear of rising again...
Thus it is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra, Chapter Three:
"The bali-maṇḍala for these [deities] is now described correctly.

One should lay down a thread extending from east to west according to the prescribed measurement. Furthermore, one should worship all the deities residing in the site (vāstu) in all ritual activities."
"Therefore, he subsists on that; otherwise, he would rise from the Mādhava [oblation].
Thus it was said: "One should first offer the bali to them. Consequently, those acts performed by those who are averse to their worship—

They would take up what is auspicious and perform evil deeds. Therefore, for those virtuous ones who perform the worship of these [deities] every year, only auspicious things quickly arise, and not even a mention of the inauspicious.
Thus it was also said by Maya: "In the construction of houses and such, if the deity Vāstu is not worshipped with effort..."
In that case, everything would be empty, destroyed by demons, obstacles, and the like; therefore, those who desire perfect success should perform the Vāstu-worship properly.

And likewise: "In auspicious rites, in initiation, in the construction of pavilions, and in the rules for houses and so forth, the Vāstu-oblation should be performed as prescribed for the sake of pacifying demons and obstacles and for the attainment of success."

In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* it is also stated: "When first acquiring land, as well as when laying the foundation stones and for the sake of constructing water reservoirs and houses, one should especially worship Vāstu. In other matters as well, such as sacrifices and fire-offerings (*yāga-homa*), the Guru, having laid out the lines, should construct the Vāstu-maṇḍala. A very level site is conducive to happiness; an uneven one does not bring happiness."

From Brahmā down to Aditi, fifty-three deities are proclaimed as the presiding lords of all sacred sites (vāstu). Indeed, one should not construct temples or other edifices without first worshipping them all.
"Non-origination would be destruction for both the property and the substratum.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "pūrvakhe" and so forth, he speaks of the production of sixty-four squares for the complete meaning of the mandala as it truly is.
The word "vinyaset" (one should place) is the usage of the root *as*, which belongs to the Bhuvādi class, meaning "to go," "to shine," or "to take."
It has been stated according to measurement;
that is to say, by whatever measurement is prescribed in the *Vāstuśāstra*, by that measurement [it should be made].
However, there is a specific rule in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Of houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water [reservoirs]..."
The site-plan (vāstumaṇḍalaka) should be made eight cubits in size, but not larger than that.
Thus [it is said].
*Śāradātilaka*: Having fixed a point slightly within that center, one should draw two fish-like marks on both sides;
then, one should place a thread between them, extending from south to north.
One should draw crocodiles in the corners using two [lines] each from the two outermost points;
then, one should drop the threads so that their tips rest in the middle of the fish.
That [area] should be square, provided with four compartments;
the mantra-practitioner should then divide that again so as to form sixty-four squares.
"Into its middle":
the meaning is that, having supported oneself slightly on its middle, one should support oneself slightly more than that in the center.
When the question "Why? arises, the remainder of the sentence is "from the tip of the cord."
In this manner, on both sides— that is, to the north and south of the eastward line (*prācīsūtra*)—
one should produce two "fish" figures as marks. The method for doing so is as follows:
Having placed the beginning of the thread at the eastern tip of the eastern thread, one should rotate the thread from the central mark to the eastern tip;
likewise from the western tip as well.
From this, one *matsya* (fish-shaped intersection) is formed.
The same applies elsewhere; thus is the second fish.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Then, for the purpose of establishing the *somasūtra*, one should rotate the tip of the cord;
having placed the hand on the eastern limb and the western limb, one should perform [the measurement]."
As the fish moves successively to the north and south along the line, it is born;
when the middle is cut, the tail and mouth of the fish are extended.
The moon-line (somasūtra) should be all around.
Thus.
Regarding the phrase "by two":
there, by means of two [measures] at each of the two tips, one fish [mark] is made as before;
that is to say, with a cord measured by half of the eastward cord and fixed at the tip of the eastward cord, one should draw a half-moon in the northeast and the southeast.
Then, with that same thread fixed at the tip of the northern thread, one should draw a half-moon in the northeast and the northwest;
thus a fish is produced in the northeast.
Likewise, as before, with that same thread fixed at the western tip, one should draw a half-moon in the northwest and the southwest; thus a fish is produced in the northwest.
With that thread placed with its tip pointing south, one should draw a half-moon in the southwest (nairṛtya) and the southeast (āgneya). From that, two fish-diagrams (matsya) arise in both places.

As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "With a thread measuring half the field, one should mark signs in the cardinal directions. Taking those signs in the directions as a basis, one should mark the limbs in the corners.
With a thread measuring half the field, [one proceeds] in reverse and direct order."

Thus, when the four fish-marks have been produced, one should lay down four lines from their centers to their tips; this is what he states in the verse beginning with "matsya" (the fish), and so forth.
It is "quadrangular" because the body of the site (vāstu) is quadrangular.
As it has been said: "A certain asura of quadrangular form is the destroyer of all."
The third chapter: With a concentrated mind, one should apply two threads in this manner— from Īśāna to Rakṣas, and from Agni to Prabhañjana— to form the ear-thread (karṇasūtra).
Also in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "That Vāstupuruṣa was established by the gods as being square. The teachers also say: "He is situated in a square."
Thus it is said;
and in the *Prayogasāra* as well: "That Vāstupuruṣa should be known as being situated in a square."

"Endowed with four compartments" means that within the square and at the four corners below, another set of four outer compartments is mentioned for the purpose of worshipping Guru, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Cetreśa. "That" refers to the construction;
the syntactical connection is that one should divide it in such a way that it becomes sixty-four squares.
Regarding the phrase "from Īśāna":
*prabhañjana* is Vāyu; the corner having him as its presiding deity is denoted by that word, [meaning] as far as that point.
In this manner, one should lay down two threads known as the *karṇasūtra*.
In the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*), the diagonal cord is designated as the *karṇasūtra*.
The term "concentrated" (*samāhita*) is connected to both [the practitioner and the cord] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākācigolakanyāya*).

Therein, the practitioner (*mantrī*)—who is attentive (*sāvadhāna*) and, by way of tradition, inseparable from the science of mantras (*mantraśāstra*)—should lay down the cord extending from east to west; thus he is construed as the agent in seven ritual actions, beginning with this.
Because it has been prepared beforehand.
In that regard, the method for producing sixty-four squares is as follows: one should lay down four diagonal lines across four squares;
then, upon the fish-figures produced in their centers, one should drop two threads extending from east to west and two threads extending from south to north.
In this way, sixteen squares are produced.

Then, one should again draw four diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) within the four corner squares. Upon the fish-figures thus formed, one should drop two threads extending east-west and two extending north-south.
When this has been done, fish-shaped figures are formed in the two central squares; within those fish, one should draw two threads running east-west and two running north-south.
In this way, sixty-four squares are produced.
Therein, one should erase the diagonal threads other than the two diagonal threads mentioned in other texts.
In this regard, the specific rule stated by Īśānaśiva is: "The sixty-four squares are to be worshipped by Brahmins; the eighty-one squares by kings and others.
However, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, it is said: "An architectural site (*vāstu*) consisting of eighty-one squares is recommended for domestic construction;
an architectural site consisting of sixty-four squares is recommended for temples."
Thus [says] Somaśambhu: "One should construct the Vāstu-maṇḍala for a temple with sixty-four squares;
however, even for a house, one should perform the Vāstu ritual with eighty-one squares."
Thus it is said in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "For a temple, sixty-four [parts]; likewise for a house, eighty-nine."

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "Having divided [the ground] into eighty-one squares, one should perform the rite for the site (vāstu) in houses and the like; however, for a palace, a sixty-four-square site was prescribed by Brahmā."
"Thus it has been said; now I shall describe the excellent pavilions (maṇḍapas) in accordance with the proportions of the temple (prāsāda).
Thus ends the *Śāradātilaka*.
One should first worship Brahmā in the center of the four central squares.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Ārya in the four cardinal directions, beginning with the East.
"By that" means: this Vāstu-maṇḍala [is drawn] in the maṇḍapa of the preceptor.
Regarding the phrase "Brahmāṇam":

the connection is that one should worship Brahmā in the four central squares at the beginning and in the middle; "samāhita" means that [the area] has been cleared into a single form within those four squares.
In that [mandala], one should draw a lotus.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "One should worship Brahmā upon a lotus in the center of the twenty-five squares."
In the Kādimata as well: "In the very center, one should properly worship Brahmā, seated upon a lotus, golden-hued, four-faced, and distinguished by the study of the Vedas."
Thus;
by the word "in the beginning," the association with Sarasvatī is expressed.
By the word "composed" (samāhita), this is what is meant:
Having first worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should afterwards worship Brahmā therein.

Having worshipped there [the deities] beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), and having worshipped the nine pedestal-powers (*pīṭhaśakti*) beginning with Aṇimā and all the Siddhis, the pedestal-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) is:
*oṃ sarvajñānakriyāvyaktakamalāsanāya yogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
"Oṃ, salutation to Brahman"—this is the root mantra.
Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi);
Paṅkti is the meter (chandas).
Brahmā is the presiding deity.
His limbs are formed by the syllables.
Brahmā should be meditated upon as holding a rosary of beads, a sacrificial ladle, a staff, and a water-pot.
The meditation on Aṇimā and the others is described in the Kulaprakāśatantra: "Aṇimā, seated upon a bull, is to be worshipped; she is yellowish-white in color and has four arms.
She holds a boon-granting gesture (varada) and a lotus (vajra? in her right hands, and she bears the gestures of fearlessness (abhaya) and a treasure-vessel (nidhāna) in her left."
One should worship Mahimā, who is mounted upon a buffalo, possessing the luster of a blue garment,
holding a staff and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a spear and a rosary of beads in her right hands.
Stationed on a lotus stalk, she is light-bodied, dark-complexioned, worthy of worship, and four-armed;
she holds a serpent-noose in her right hand, while in her left she displays the gestures of fearlessness and the lotus.
Resembling a mountain of gold, she is to be worshipped; she stands upon a tortoise and likewise possesses great weight.
O Dakṣa, she holds a mace and the gesture of granting boons, while in her left hands she bears the gestures of fearlessness and bestowing treasure.
The goddess to be worshipped, who has gone to the realm of the pretas, resembles a mass of blue lightning;
she holds an excellent sword in her right hand and a chopper with the gesture of fearlessness in her left.

The worshipful Vaśitā is smoky-colored, seated upon a deer, and possesses four arms; she holds a lotus and a banner in her right hands, while in her left hands she displays the gesture of boon-granting and a lotus.
Chāgalā has extremely red limbs; she is intensely devoted to worship.
She holds a rosary of beads in her right hand and a water-pot in her left.
The third chapter. Then [one should place] Vivasvat, then Mitra, and after that Mahīdhara;
again, in the pairs of half-cells at the corners, surrounding [the center] starting with Vahni (Agni).
The learned one [should worship] Sāvitra and Savitṛ, Śakra and Indrajaya,
Rudra and Rudrajaya, as well as Āpa and Āpavatsaka.
The worshipful Prāpti, who is seated upon a bull and possesses a brilliance like that of snow,
holds a trident and a supreme spear in her right hands, while in her left she displays the gesture of fearlessness and a lotus.
Sarvasiddhi, possessing the luster of a ruby, is to be worshipped; she has four arms and holds a rosary, a lotus, a citron, and a lotus stalk.
Thus.
Regarding "the directions": one should worship in the four directions, beginning with the east.
The word "in a clockwise direction" (*prādakṣiṇyena*) is to be understood as a supplement.

This also applies to the four squares (*koṣṭha*); therefore, Bhārya is to be worshipped in the eastern direction, Vivasvān in the southern direction, Mittra in the western direction, and Mahīdhara in the northern direction. As it has been stated by the Teachers: "One should worship in the four squares of the directions—east, south, west, and north."
