In the corner of the Brahma-square—that is, in the lower corner-cell of the southeast (Agni) section, which is demarcated by the diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*)—one should worship Sāvitra in the upper cell of that square and Savitṛ in the lower cell. "Around" means in the four directions. As stated by Somaśambhu: "Brahmā occupies nine squares in the center; the remaining [deities] are said to occupy one square each. Marīci and the others occupy six squares each, positioned in order in the directions starting from the east. There, the eight lords of the corners are situated within the eight half-squares of the corners."

Thus, although the phrase "above or below" (*upary-adho vā*) is not present here, nevertheless, by means of the description of the abiding of the deities within the body as stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, the upward sequence is obtained as follows: Rudra is situated on the head; Parjanya and Āditi are situated in his two ears; the Waters (*Āpaḥ*) are well-situated in the mouth; Āpavatsa is situated in the throat; Jayanta and Diti are in the two shoulders; Pañcārgalā and others, as well as Mahendra and others, are in the two arms; Rudra and Sāvitrī are on the chest; likewise, Savitṛ is the servant [of Sāvitrī]; Brahmā is established in his heart; Pṛthvīdhara and Marīci are in the two breasts; furthermore, Vivasvat and he named Mitra are in the two sides of the belly; and the Pitṛs (Ancestors) are situated in the feet. From the *Śāradātilaka*: On both sides of the thread of his ears, in the pairs of squares, the Preceptor [should place] Śava, Guha, Aryaman, Jṛmbhaka, and Pilapicchaka.
Pāpa and the others, as well as Pūṣan and the others—these seven are located in the seven long shanks; Indra resides in the penis, and Jaya is situated in the testicles.

Thus, it should be known that Rudra, Īśāna, Dāsa, Rudrajaya, Pṛthvīdhara, Mahodhara, Marīci, Āryya, Pitṛ, Nirṛti, Pāpa, Roga, Indra, and Śakra are the names [of the lords]. As it has been said: "He is Īśa and Īśāna-Rudra; his conqueror is Rudradāsaka; he is known as Marīci-Āryyaka; and Pitṛ shall be the lord of the Rākṣasas."

"Evil is known as disease"—thus it is said elsewhere: Having taken recourse to *Dhāṭavanī* and having placed three squares below, one should worship *Sāvitra* there in the square named *Vāsava*. Between *Vidhi* and *Sāvitra*, having taken recourse to *Savitṛ* in three squares and having placed *Pitṛ* and *Dhātṛ* below, one should worship the highly fortunate *Indra* in the square well-known as *Loka*. Likewise, *Indrajaya* is to be worshipped situated between *Brahmā* and *Śakra*, having taken recourse to *Vāyu* and *Dhātṛ* and having placed two squares below; there, one should worship the god *Rudra* in the square named *Bhuvana*. Similarly, between *Īśa* and *Vedhas*, *Tajjaya* is in three squares in the northeast (*aiśānī*), well-situated in the three squares of *Kāma*; then, O child, one should worship [the deity] between *Āpa* and *Vedhas* in three squares.

Thus, Somaśambhu also states: one should offer red flowers to Savitṛ in the southeast corner cell; in the cell below that, one should offer water with *kuśa* grass to Savitṛ. To Indra, one should offer rice cooked with turmeric in the southwest corner cell; to Indrajaya, one should present sweet food below Indra. To Rudra, one should offer ghee-cooked rice in the square below the northwest corner; below that, one should present moist meat to Rudrajaya. Then, to Āpaḥ in the northeast corner, and likewise to Tattva below that.

Thus, because it is on both sides of that diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*) at the beginning, and because the diagonal line serves as the purpose here, it is called a "corner-half-square" (*koṇārḍakoṣṭha*).

"Tad" (that) he points out and instructs to his disciples; "Manu" refers to the teacher who is a master of mantras—this is the third chapter. One should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in sequence; one should worship these in the directions starting from the east, in the positions beginning with the syllable *sa* and ending with *ḍī*.
The best of teachers [should worship] eight gods each, according to their divisions, in sequence: Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara; [and likewise the others].
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are situated in the eastern direction; as are Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, and Yama the guardian of the house.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern direction; then come Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa.

Puṣpadanta and Śeṣa stand at the two thighs; in the western direction are situated Vāyu, Mukhya, Nāga, Soma, and Bhallāṭa; and in the direction of Kubera (the north) are those named Argala, Diti, and Aditi.
Having filled the places of the aforementioned deities with five kinds of unprecedented powders, one should then offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) to them.

"In all cases, according to the sequence" means that the sequence surrounding the fire-altar (vahni) and so forth should be followed; "ending with *sājī*" means those words which exist together with the beginning and the end—that is, with the initial augment *aṭ* and the final suffix—these are obtained from the square marked by a diagonal line (karṇasūtra) forming a half-angle.

He describes the performance of the *bali* offering with the words "of those mentioned": with the five colored powders (*rajas*) to be described for the *sarvatobhadra* mandala, one should fill in the lotuses there in the manner that will be described. Among them, the central lotus is white and the others are red; as it is said in the *Divyasārasvata*: "Having cleared away the nine squares in the center, one should fill them with white powder, and likewise in the four directions surrounding them."
Having wiped away the six [squares], one should fill them with red powder; as for the remaining squares here, one should arrange them in their proper places.
Then, in the midst of those various [offerings], one should thoroughly worship Brahmā.

Thus, the boundary lines of the squares are white, and the squares are variegated. Now, the meditation on the deities of the Vāstu, as described in another Tantra, is written down: the form of all the aforementioned deities is now declared—[he holds] a rosary and a sacrificial ladle in his right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in his left.
One should worship him who bears the *Śāradātilaka* and possesses eight eyes, seated upon a lotus in the center; all the gods stationed within the body of Vāstu have four arms.
With palms joined in reverence, all of them—swords and shields in hand—gazed intently at Brahmā, facing toward him.
When they are situated in their own respective places, it is declared to be "common" (sādhāraṇa). Marīci is white in color, and Vivasvān is red in color.
Mitra is like refined gold, Bhūdhara is black in color, Savitṛ has the luster of blue, and Sāvitra has a smoky form.
Indra has the luster of the color of dawn, and Indrajaya is white; Rudra resembles coral, and likewise Rudrajaya is green.
Āpa is white like cow's milk; Āpavatsa has the luster of a japā flower; Īśāna is white like bark-garment; Parjanya resembles collyrium.
Jayanta is like the color of collyrium, Mahendra has stainless luster, Āditya is red in color, and Satyaka is variegated in hue.
Vṛṣa has the luster of the vanbūka flower; Antarikṣaka has the luster of a kunda flower; Agni has the luster of the rising sun; and Pūṣan resembles red lotuses.
Bhṛṅgarāja is the color of a bumblebee, Mṛga resembles a cloud, Nirṛti has the luster of fire, and Pota is known as Dauvārika.

Sugrīva has the luster of a peacock’s neck, Candrābha is like the moon, Puṣpadantaka is like a flower, Varuṇa has limbs with the brilliance of crystal, and the Asura is considered to have the luster of a bumblebee.
The Moon is like a blue lotus; the Earth is like a sapphire; Vāyu is black in color; and Nāga is like a pale moon.
Mukhya resembles a pearl, Bhallāṭa a white lotus, Soma crystal, and Agni a red lotus in luster.
Diti is remembered as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, while Aditi is tawny; Caraka is like a conch shell, and Vidārī has the brilliance of fire.
Pūtanā is like snow, Pilapicchikā has the luster of a cloud; [they hold] a sword, a drinking vessel, a small dagger, and likewise a pair of scissors.
The third chapter:
Those who assume terrifying forms are proclaimed to be the Rākṣasīs;
white, red, yellow, and black are the Grahas beginning with Skanda.
Vaṣva, Śakti, Khaḍga, and Pāśa—these, with distorted faces, are declared to be the terrifying Grahas beginning with Skanda.
The eighteen lines are to be meditated upon as both the channels (nāḍīs) and the respective deities.
As it has been said: "Lakṣmī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Sukalā, Śivā, Subhagā, Sumukhī, and Nandā—these are the [channels] emerging from the eastern direction."
Dhanyā, Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Niśā, Virajā, and Vibhavā—these channels are known to have gentle faces.

The plural form in the word *pāyasānnaiḥ* (with milk-rice offerings) is intended to include other items; by this, the substances such as parched grain (*lāja*) and others to be mentioned are included. Regarding that, the specific materials for the offerings and the mantras for each deity are stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "With milk-rice, cooked rice, and parched grain, combined with incense and flowers, along with unbroken rice (*akṣata*) mixed with sesame seeds, and adorned with black gram (*māṣa*) and boiled rice, etc."
Accept this offering, O Brahman, and destroy the defects of the site.
O you named Āryaka, accept this cake with sugar and fragrant substances placed upon milk-rice; destroy all defects.
O Lord, accept this [offering] honored with sandalwood and other substances, adorned with camphor and agallochum;
O Vivasvat, destroy all defects.
O Lord, accept this pleasing oblation of milk-rice with jaggery, accompanied by flowers and other offerings; O Mitra, grant me peace.
O Lord of the Earth, accept this rice mixed with black gram and meat, combined with perfumes and milk; destroy all my faults.

Having thus offered the internal oblation (*antarbali*), although the worship (*arcā*) of all other [deities] begins from the southeast (*āgneya*) and so forth, one should nevertheless offer the oblation (*bali*) starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and so forth, in accordance with the scriptural injunction. As the scripture states: "The oblation for all things is generally declared to proceed clockwise from the northeast; this is the specific rule for determining the positions."
Elsewhere, worship even of Īśa and the others is prescribed:
"One should worship the deities in the northeast corner and the other directions according to the rule.
Also elsewhere, in the *Śāradātilaka*: "The wise one should worship those situated in the four corners beginning with Īśāna."
Likewise: "O Water, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk mixed with sugar and adorned with flowers and other ornaments; grant me peace."
O child, accept this offering of curd mixed with jaggery and adorned with fragrant substances and other items; dispel all obstacles here.
O Sāvitrī, accept these flowers, kuśa grass, and water scented with camphor and agallochum; grant me peace in this matter.
O Lord Sūrya, accept this sacrificial offering of flour-cake mixed with jaggery and adorned with red perfumes and other offerings; destroy all obstacles here.
O Śakra-deva, accept this cool, fragrant offering of flowers combined with saffron and other ingredients; take this bali, O Heart, homage be to you!
O Indrajaya, accept this pleasing offering of rice mixed with clarified butter and adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments; salutations be unto you!
This meat, both cooked and raw, combined with cloth, flowers, and other offerings—accept this bali; O Lord Rudra, I bow to you, my heart.
O Rudrajaya, accept this offering of heart-flesh cooked with ghee and combined with perfumes, flowers, and other ingredients; grant me well-being.
O Vidārī, you who possess red flowers and red flesh, and are endowed with red garments and the like, accept this; destroy the poison of the Rākṣasas.
O sinful one, take this offering joined with bile, blood, and bone, adorned with the scent of blood and other things; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
Accept this offering of cooked beans with clarified butter, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments; O Śarva, destroy these obstacles caused by Rākṣasas.
O Skanda, accept this offering (bali) consisting of meat combined with flowers and other items, and adorned with black gram cakes; destroy the obstacles caused by the Rākṣasas.
"Take this meat of a donkey mixed with flour-cakes and accompanied by cooked meat and water;
accept this wealth and destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa."
O Jṛmbhaka, accept this offering of blood, meat, rice, fish, along with perfumes and incense; pacify the obstacles caused by Rākṣasas.
O Pilipiccha, take this meat provided with goat's ears, accompanied by garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasas.
The third chapter:
"O Carakī, take this meat prepared with ghee and endowed with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa!"
O Lord, accept this oblation— consisting of cooked rice with clarified butter, adorned with garments, perfumes, and the like—
which removes the defects of the dwelling.
O King of Gods, accept this pleasing offering consisting of blue lotuses, milk-rice, and garments; salutations be unto you.
O son of Jiṣṇu, accept this five-cubit, well-fashioned banner adorned with flowers and other offerings; take this pleasing oblation; salutations be unto you!
O King of the Gods, accept this pleasing bali offering consisting of rice porridge filled with clarified butter and adorned with the five precious gems and other ornaments; homage be to you!
O Bhāskara, accept this heart-pleasing offering consisting of cooked food mixed with red flowers and prepared with red perfumes and other ingredients; homage be to you!

O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored [clouds], beautifully adorned with perfumes and other offerings, and provided with cloth; accept this bali offering; salutations be unto you.
"Indeed, this meat-offering, honored with garments, perfumes, and other gifts—
accept this bull-oblation and destroy the defects of the site."
But this śāhala meat, well-prepared with offerings and the like—
accept this pleasing oblation, O Vyoman, and grant me peace.
O Seven-tongued One, accept this gold, flour-cake, and [offering] prepared with garments, perfumes, and the like, accompanied by clarified butter; salutations be unto you!
O Lord Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering consisting of parched grain mixed with rice and adorned with red flowers and other ornaments; salutations be unto you.
O Vitatha, accept this offering endowed with the fragrance of curd and other such things, and accompanied by red flowers; destroy the obstacles here.
O Lord Yama, accept this pleasing offering consisting of cooked rice, honey, and venison, adorned with red garments and other ornaments; salutations be unto you!
O Guardian of the House, accept this cooked rice with meat, fresh butter, and adorned with garments and other ornaments—this which brings delight; homage be to you!
O Gandharva, accept this offering combined with various fragrances and joined with red flowers and the like; destroy all defects.
*Śāradātilaka*: "O Śākunī, O Jina, you who stand upon a meal of black gram—accept this *bali* offering and grant me peace, O Bhṛṅgarāja!"
O Mṛgadeva, accept this pleasing offering of barley mixed with ghee and sesame seeds, combined with perfumes, flowers, and other articles; homage be to you!
O King of Rākṣasas, accept this oblation consisting of sugar-candy mixed with sugar, adorned with cloth, perfumes, and other offerings; homage be unto you!
O Gatekeeper, accept this pleasing offering consisting of sandalwood, agalloch wood, and various fragrant flowers; homage be to you!
O Lord Sugrīva, please accept this milk-rice offering adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; grant me peace.
O King of Waters, accept this pleasing offering of barley, grains, cow’s milk, and wine that has been steeped over cooked rice; homage be to you!
O Puṣpadanta, accept this bundle of kuśa grass bound with black gram and infused with the scent of clarified butter and other fragrances; destroy all defects.
O Lord of Asuras, accept this offering prepared with honey, ground flour, and adorned with perfumes and other fragrances; destroy all defects.
O Śeṣa, accept this oblation consisting of ghee mixed with food and well-scented with camphor and other fragrances; grant me complete peace from all afflictions.
O Lord, accept this offering of barley and rice, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and the like; O Disease, destroy all defects!
O Lord who rides upon a deer, accept this pleasing offering consisting of fried cakes and sweetmeats adorned with various foods; homage be to you!
O Lord of Pātāla, accept this food, including meat and fish, adorned with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings; may every obstacle here be destroyed.
O Chief One, accept this offering consisting of coconut water, cooked rice, and garments for the boat, and utterly destroy the defects of the site.
O Soma, accept this *bali* offering—milk-rice mixed with honey, adorned with various flowers such as the *nāgapuṣpa* and *pota-puṣpa*—and destroy every fault.
O Bhallāṭa, accept this oblation of cooked rice mixed with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant flowers; you are our heart—salutations be unto you!
This third chapter is declared to be the Vāstubali offering, which bestows the abundance of all prosperity.
O you named Argala, accept this pleasing offering of eighteen māṣas, anointed with ghee and adorned with flowers, perfumes, and the like; homage be to you!
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this liquor mixed with sugar-candy and adorned with various flowers; destroy all defects!
O Mother of the Gods, accept this palanquin joined with honey and provided with perfumes, garments, and other offerings; accept this pleasing oblation; salutations be unto you!
May those deities residing in the dwellings who exist throughout the heavens and the netherworld accept this pleasing oblation; being satisfied, may they return to their own abodes.
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and others who desire offerings, as well as those who belong to the retinue of Viṣṇu, accept this bali-offering.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the Piṭhas and the Kṣetrapālas according to one's desire, one should worship with kuśa grass, flowers, and so forth, in the absence of the prescribed path.

Thus, by the phrase "all prosperity" (*sarvasampat*), the offering to the quarters (*digbali*) is also indicated. As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The offering to the quarters is proclaimed here as that which follows the remaining rites of the site (*vāstuśeṣa*), which bestows all protection and splendor, and grants satisfaction to the spirits (*bhūta*)."

That offering to the quarters which is intended for all beings, including the assembly of the guardians of the directions, and which consists of worship performed by their names ending with the ritual dismissal (visarjana), is to be understood as the *diśāṃ bali*.
One should offer the bali-oblation with curd, water, blue lotuses, flowers, parched grain, flour, sesame seeds, and fat, using the appropriate substances according to the sequence of the directions.
Furthermore, that which belongs to the splendor of the gods, as well as to the pretas, the progeny, the rākṣasas, the waters, the vital breaths, and the constellations;

One should offer the aforementioned oblations to the lords of the sciences (vidyādhipas); for the retinue and the Śakti, it is said that one should include the words "together with their vehicles" (savāhana).
Then, having joined [the palms] with "to all his attendants," he should again offer the *añjali* in due order to the *bhūtas*, proceeding clockwise.
It removes the fear and distress caused by enemies, piśācas, vetālas, rākṣasas, and rathas; it is especially an offering to the quarters that bestows the abundance of all prosperity.

In the case of building a site or a house, during an outbreak of disease, when there is injury to living beings, at the entry into a new home, and during an extensive peace-offering (śāntihoma), the bali offering to the directions should be performed for the sake of success.

Thus [ends] the *Śāradātilaka*. Therein, the ritual application is written according to the oral instruction. Now, the patron (*yajamāna*) should cause the preceptor (*ācārya*) to be honored. Then the preceptor, having selected a site with the characteristics to be described, and having performed its purification according to the method to be described, should sprinkle the ground with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the five Brahmans. In the center of that [site], with a golden needle or a gem—or in their absence, with any one of silver, fruit, flower, or grain—he should draw [the lines]: "The [nine lines] are known as Śāntā, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Viśālā, Prāṇavāhinī, Satī, Sumanā, Nandā, and Subhadrā as the ninth."

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from east to west, beginning from the south and ending in the north—[the rivers] Hiraṇyā, Suvratā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Priyā, Jayā, Kalā, and the ninth is remembered by the wise as Viśokā.

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from south to north, beginning from the west and ending at the east, and having then perfectly smoothed them with a woollen thread (*śukta-doraka*) or similar means, one should construct a beautiful mandala adorned with five colored powders (*rajas*) according to the previously described method, provided with the four corner-squares mentioned before. To the west of that, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit and having three enclosures (*mekhalā*). Then, outside [the mandala], one should invoke and worship all fifty-three deities residing in their respective positions according to the sequence of the ritual objects (*padārtha-anusamaya*), starting from the teachers (*guru*), Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Ceta-pāla located in the outer corner-squares; Brahmā occupying the four squares in the center (*nābhi*); Āryaka occupying the four squares to the east of him; and so on, ending with Aditi occupying half a square and [the deity] occupying the corners. One should invoke them all with the words "O Brahman, come here! Stay here! and worship them with offerings such as water for the feet (*pādya*) using their respective names in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*, preceded by the *praṇava* (Om). Next, in the northeast corner of the mandala, one should place a firm water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon unbroken grains (*akṣata*). The pot should be free of cracks, not black at its base, decorated externally with curd and rice, its mouth covered with sprouts of mango, *avattha*, *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and *plakṣa* trees, wrapped in a pair of cloths, containing within it the five gems and various fruits, and filled with pure water. Then, one should install Varuṇa in the pot with the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa" (RV 1.25.19), which is the *gāyatrī* of Varuṇa: "May the Ganges, all rivers, oceans, and lakes come here, bringing about the destruction of the misfortunes of the sacrificer."

Having thus invoked the sacred fords (*tīrthas*), one should bring seven types of earth from a settlement, a place where an elephant stands, an anthill, the confluence of rivers, a mountain, a cow-pen, and a street, and cast them into the pitcher. Then, with the mantra "Vaṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa," one should worship Varuṇa in that pitcher with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Thereafter, one should add the "all-healing herbs" (*sarvoṣadhī*): *murā*, *māṃsī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śaileya*, the two types of *rajanī*, *śaṭī*, *campaka*, and *musta*. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and performed the rites beginning with the consecrations up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), one should offer oblations to each of the fifty-three deities beginning with Brahmā—either one thousand and eight, one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight times—with barley or black sesame seeds, using fuel sticks (*samidh*) of *udumbara*, or other trees such as *kṣīravṛkṣa*, *aśvattha*, *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, and so forth. [End of] the Third Paṭala.
One should offer oblations with any one of the blades of *kuśa* grass or with fire-sticks (*samidh*). Some say there should be one hundred oblations for Brahmā and ten oblations each for the others;
then, with the mantra "Oṃ vāstoṣpataye namaḥ" or with five Vedic mantras containing his indicative marks, one should offer five *vilva* fruits or *vilva* seeds.

Then, having completed the *Uttaratantra*, the preceptor should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with either the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* or the Varuṇa-mantra. Having offered the ritual bali-offerings (*bali*) to the fifty-three deities using the substances prescribed in the Tantra along with their respective mantras, and having performed the bali-offerings to the cardinal directions, the preceptor, facing west, should perform an auspicious consecration (*maṅgalābhiṣeka*) upon the candidate facing east with the water from the Peace-pitcher (*śāntikalasa*) using the mantras taught in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā* beginning with "Oṃ, may Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you," as well as Vedic mantras; thereafter, he should bathe him with waters containing all medicinal herbs (*sarvoṣadhi*).

Then the preceptor, having again worshipped the gods beginning with Brahmā with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), [should recite]: "May all the hosts of gods depart, taking with them this earthly worship, for the sake of fulfilling desired wishes and for the purpose of returning once more."
Having recited this, the disciple should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher.

Then the preceptor, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the western part of the pavilion and having seated the person to be initiated (*sādhya*) upon it, should empower him with the *Sudarśana* or *Aghora* mantra. Having himself assumed the form of that deity and adorned himself with a red turban, garments, an upper cloth, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, he should stand facing north on the right side of the initiate. Taking a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or another such metal, he should place the ritual balls (*piṇḍas*) offered to the deities beginning with Brahmā therein according to their respective positions. Having established those various deities together with the *Vāstupuruṣa* in that very spot, and having placed a lamp of clarified butter upon each ball and adorned them with red flowers, he should sprinkle the initiate with water. Then, taking that vessel with both hands, [he should recite]: "Whatever beings dwell here, may they accept this offering (*bali*) duly presented."
May they arrange their residence elsewhere; let them forgive us here—homage be to them!

Having consecrated the subject with this mantra, one should prepare a mixture of blood-water measuring one *āḍhaka* and *bhūtakrūra* in another vessel; having placed nine lamps therein as well, and having consecrated [the subject] with that [mixture], one should—sword in hand, surrounded by many others with swords in their hands, surrounded by hundreds of torches, with the quarters of the sky resounding with the five kinds of musical instruments and the chanting of *svasti* hymns—go to a crossroads, the root of a great tree, or one of the sites such as a pond, a river, or a temple. There, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with cow dung and facing east, one should install the respective deities, place the ritual balls (*piṇḍas*) here and there, and offer oblations (*bali*) in the four directions with *bhūtakrūra* using the previously mentioned mantra. Having poured the blood-water there and circumambulated [the site] clockwise, and having washed his hands, feet, and eyes, while repeatedly looking back at all that [ritual apparatus] without seeing it [clearly], he should send his attendants on ahead and, remaining himself absorbed in meditation, approach the subject and perform protection for him.
This is the primary method;
as they say: "One should perform the pacification of the site with sacrificial fuel (samidh) and the offering of oblations (balikarman);
the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, provided with three enclosures."
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
Then, on an auspicious day favorable to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), and the day of the week (*vāra*), upon a pure patch of ground free from husks and charcoal...
With barley, black sesame seeds, and likewise with samiṅgī, those produced from milk and sugar-cane, and with wood from the palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, and udumbara trees.
Or it may be performed with five *kuśa* or *dūrvā* grasses combined with honey and clarified butter, or even with five *bilva* fruits or *bilva* seeds.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) in the site of the dwelling (*vāstu*) with various kinds of food, both solid and soft; one should present these specific offerings in their proper sequence.
By such statements as these, it is declared elsewhere that this [rite] must be performed at a specific time every year;
as they say: "Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day, every year..."
In one's own home, during the worship of Vāstu, according to the sequence of the ritual with oblations within the maṇḍala.
For one who acts thus in the home, no misfortune ever occurs.
There shall be no untimely death, nor afflictions from diseases, spirits, ghosts, and the like; no harm from serpents, no mutual quarrels, and no inauspicious events.
In that house, one enjoys the prosperity of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female servants;
being free from disease, victorious, and renowned, he lives for a long time.
In all royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens, in the residences of ministers, counselors, and generals, and likewise throughout the city.
The preceptor should perform [the rite] every year according to the prescribed method;
otherwise, there will be constant suffering resulting from fruits contrary to what was taught.
Thus [it is said].

Regarding the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the text says "under a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*); the connection is that one should construct the pavilion on an auspicious day under a lunar mansion, zodiac sign, and weekday favorable to the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), according to the methods prescribed in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, and on an auspicious lunar date (*tithi*) as specified in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.

Thus, it is stated in the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*: "Under the Sun (Sunday), the two [Mūla] (Saturday and Tuesday), Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā), Puṣya, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Maghā, Anurādhā, and Pavana (Svātī)—provided these are pure and conjoined with auspicious stars..."

On days of the benefic planets, in a yoga free from malefic influences, on a lunar day that is "virikta" (cleansed), and on a day devoid of the Viṣṭi karana, the sages declare that undertakings such as building a house are auspicious.
Thus,
regarding the pure surface of the earth,
the examination of the ground has been described there in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*; this is the third chapter.
In that regard, one who is skilled in the knowledge of sites should examine the ground for cracks, for embedded thorns, for anthills, and likewise for red soil.
Ground that is cracked should be avoided from afar, for it steals away longevity and wealth;
saline soil brings about death and causes the destruction of riches.

Accompanied by friends, it constantly bestows freedom from afflictions; though there is danger from enemies due to its unevenness, that [house] situated in the northeast corner certainly grants prosperity to the builder.
The eastern wind brings increase and bestows boons; the northern wind bestows strength;
the southern wind causes enmity, death, and disease; and the western wind is the earth itself.

That ground which flows toward the south—the flow of the King of Dharma—is constantly a source of fear of death and causes the destruction of the household; and that ground flows toward the direction of Nirṛti.
Pṛthvī is said to cause the loss of wealth, Varuṇapnavā likewise causes wind-related ailments, and Bhūmi constantly causes agitation.
The white [cow] is known as Brāhmaṇī, the red indeed as Kṣatriyā;
the Vaiśyā should be understood as the yellowish-white, and the black is proclaimed as Śūdrā.
The Brahmin woman should have the scent of clarified butter; the Kṣatriya woman should have the scent of blood;
the Vaiśya woman should have the scent of milk; and the Śūdra woman should be like the earth, smelling of raw flesh.
The earth is known as sweet when it is Brahminic, astringent when Kṣatriya,
bitter when Vaiśya, and pungent when it is Śūdra.

The ground for a Brāhmaṇa should be covered with Kuśa grass; that for a Kṣatriya should be filled with Śara reeds; that for a Vaiśya with Kuśa and Kāśa grass; and that for a Śūdra with all kinds of grass.
White, yellow, red, or endowed with a black color; possessing stable water, firm, and smooth—such ground brings all happiness.
Cold touch during the hot season, the touch of fire at the onset of winter, and both touches during the rainy season— this is proclaimed to be auspicious.
Thus it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "O best of beings, there [in that place] is the delight of cows together with their calves,
and there is the delight of beautiful women together with men."
It possesses the fragrance of Kāśmīra sandalwood, the scent of camphor and agallochum, and the aroma of lotuses and water lilies, as well as the fragrance of jasmine and campaka flowers.
She has the fragrance of the *pāṭala* and *mallikā* flowers, the scent of *nāgakeśara*,
the aroma of fragrant rice, and she is endowed with auspicious scents.
The earth is considered common to all social classes alike.
Having understood this thus, one should examine the ground: it should be auspicious, flooded by water from the east, free from narrowness, covered with grass, and saturated with moisture.
When the pit is being filled with auspicious soil that remains even more than before, and upon which a heap of flowers does not wither, it is a favorable sign.
Just as a lamp does not sink into water, nor does the ear become wet, so too white, reddish, yellow, and black [complexions] are praised for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
That which has a scent equal to clarified butter, blood, perfume, or wine,
and which is sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent;
"That which is gathered from *kuśa*, *śara*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā* grasses.

Thus it is also stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having fashioned a cavity in the ground with an extent of one *vitasti*, one should deposit that earth within it; when those [materials] remain, it is auspicious."
One should know that [ground] level with the surrounding area is middling, while that which is uneven is said to be inferior.
Having thus diligently examined the site and abandoned an inferior plot,
one should then prepare the ground, removing charcoal, husks, hair, and bones.
"Tuṣa" refers to the husks of grain; "aṅgāra" refers to extinguished embers;
and "keśapāṣāṇabhasmādi" refers to hair, stones, ashes, and so forth—[the field] is free from these.

Otherwise, because defects are observed, it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "When a stone is encountered in the earth while digging a pit, then there is danger of untimely death; [furthermore], wealth is accumulated by means of bones, hair, and charcoal."
It is said that ashes indicate fear of fire and husks indicate poverty; in this regard,
the *Ādiyāmala* states that the *ahibalacakra* should be understood as the primary means for extracting the thorns [of planetary afflictions].
It is as follows: I shall now describe the snake-wheel (ahicakra), just as it was spoken by the All-Knowing One.
The substance is like a thorn, yet it is empty; by means of this, practitioners come to know it.
Eight lines should be drawn upward, and likewise five across.
In the snake-circle (ahicakra), there are twenty-eight squares;
therein, the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī,
and Uttarāphalgunī are to be written as the fixed seven in the head.
Having drawn Ahibudhnya, Ajapāda, Gatabha, Brāhma, Sarpa, Puṣya, and Hasta situated in the second row—
this is the third chapter.
Abhijit, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Dhaniṣṭhā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Raudra (Ārdrā), Punarvasu, and Citrā— these seven constellations belong to the third line of the Dhiṣṇya;
likewise, Viśvadeva (Uttarāṣāḍhā), the Water-constellation (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Maitra (Anurādhā), and Viśākhā.
Having placed Svātī at the fourth position in the row, one should observe the wheel:
Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī belong to the first lord;
Pūrvabhādrapadā, Śatabhiṣā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Puṣyā, and Hastā belong to the second row.
Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Citrā belong to the third lord;
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Viśākhā, and Svātī belong to the fourth lord.
Thus is the arrangement produced in the wheel in the form of a lotus.
The door-posts belong to Maghā, the southern part of the door is considered to be Kṛttikā;
the triad beginning with Abhijit, the pentad beginning with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Revatī, and the three stars beginning with Pūrvabhādrapada belong to the Moon; the remaining [stars] belong to the Sun.
The nadīs situated at sunrise and so forth are subtracted from the remainder obtained by dividing by sixty;
when added to the moon’s motion for the day, that becomes the moon at that specific time.
One should calculate the sun in the same manner as the moon, determining its position in the asterism at the desired time.
Thereafter, one should observe those two; if they are situated in one's own asterism (nakṣatra) or in another, and the Sun and Moon are in the Moon’s asterism, then the treasure is certain.
If those two are situated in the Sun’s asterism, then it is possible [to find it], and not otherwise.
The second [measure] should be known as being in its own respective sign; there is nothing contrary to this.
The magnitude is determined by the number of fingers multiplied by twelve, according to the portion of the zodiacal sign traversed.
And thus: "The treasure-store (nidhi) is to be known in the place of the Moon, while the thorn (śalyaka) is in the place of the Sun.
Having learned this wheel from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform the extraction of the thorn.
One should make it exactly one *nivartana* in size; a staff (*daṇḍa*) shall be ten cubits long, and thirty such staves constitute a *nivartana*.
Within that [space], another wheel should be drawn twice;
"not above that," say those who know the tradition. Alternatively, the extraction of the *śalya* (the core pin) should be performed according to the method taught in the *Mahākapila-paśupatārātra*.
It is as follows: especially at the time of commencing the construction of a temple, and particularly for houses and the like.
One who desires his own welfare must perform the extraction of the *śalya* (the structural core).
At the time of commencing the construction of a temple, the wise man should know that whatever part of the body of the *vāstu* a person touches, there is a *śalya* located in that very spot.
In the *Śāradātilaka*,
it is stated that if a man scratches his head, one should extract a splinter from the head;
there, a bone is to be understood as the "splinter" when digging three hand-breadths deep.

Fire, feverish disease, and loss of wealth arise; if one desires one's own welfare, one should diligently uproot the *śalya* (thorn). When there is itching in the arm, however, one should predict an iron chain.
If it remains with two hands, the characteristic described for you is that one should know the death of one's master, or likewise his departure to a foreign land; therefore,
if one desires one's own success, one should diligently uproot the Śatya.
If one scratches the thighs, one should indicate a splinter of bell-metal (*kāṃsya-śalya*);
it will remain with only one hand. Thus has the characteristic been described to you; moreover, one's wife will become unchaste and loss of reputation occurs.

If one desires one's own welfare, one should carefully uproot the *śalya* (thorn/obstacle); however, if the hand merely scratches it, one should indicate a *kaṅkāla* (skeleton/bone). One should remain with a steady hand while digging, and not otherwise.
There will be fire, burning, disease, and the death of one's crops;
one should diligently uproot the plant if one desires the welfare of oneself. However, if it scratches its back, one should predict a hundredfold strength of arms.

If it remains with only one hand, no deliberation need be made on this point; there will be the destruction of the master, or the wife becomes unchaste. But when scratching the feet, one should predict the loss of a hand.
It should be established at a distance of one cubit; this is the characteristic described to you.
The destruction of cattle, royal punishment, and loss of crops will arise;
therefore, one who desires his own success should carefully extract the thorn.
When the belly is being scratched, one should indicate a stone there;
the characteristic mark is said by you to be at a distance of two cubits,
and since a snake-bite may occur there, one should dig out [the earth] to the depth of a cubit.
If one scratches the knee, ashes should be indicated there; it will remain for two months. The characteristic has been told to you:
there will be burns from fire, mental anguish, and afflictions, suffering, and fears.
One performs such a rite; therefore, one should indeed rescue that person.
Having had the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited, one should construct a beautiful pavilion. This is the third chapter.
Gośṛṅga, pota, maṇḍūka, śaṅkha, śukti, kacchapa, and śambuka are praised as auspicious when their intervals are measured by five, seven, or nine finger-breadths; as are other varieties of gems.
One should remove charcoal, husks, hair, bone,
and thorns while digging for water, until the defect of the site is eliminated; otherwise, if the water is situated too far or too high, it cannot be reached by digging at all.
It should be dug five cubits deep for the sake of pacifying the defects of hidden shafts; then, having extracted any shafts, one should fill it back up so that it is perfectly level.
Also in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "A defect-causing stake (śalya) in a temple site may extend as far as the water's edge;
therefore, the ground for a temple must be purified down to the water's edge, or until it reaches a stone, or gravel, or until it attains complete purity."
Having thus caused the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) to be recited— this recitation of the auspicious day is most well-known among the Bahvṛcas.

Alternatively, [the officiants] should say three times, "May the worthy ones declare this to be an auspicious day for this sacrificer; may the worthy ones pronounce 'Svasti' (well-being); may the worthy ones pronounce 'Ṛddhi' (prosperity).

Regarding this, Bodhāyana has stated: "Having caused [the officiants] to recite the formula for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), beginning with *svasti* and *uḍi*, preceded by *oṃ*, and having caused them to pronounce each blessing (*āśis*) three times.
In that regard, one should construct the pavilion and other structures only after first determining the knowledge of the directions, such as the east and so forth.
Otherwise, because faults are seen,
it has been said: "If one were to act exactly as [the world] perceives, one would fall into ruin and go to hell."
"Having determined the directions by the movement of the sun, the preceptor should perform the rites.

Thus it is said elsewhere: "Where the direction is not correctly known due to irregularities in the site, one should establish a gnomon there and thereby ascertain the position of the pure cardinal points."
The means for knowing that [time] is stated in that very same work: "In that regard, listen as I describe the determination of the directions according to the rule:

having drawn a circle on a perfectly level surface by means of rotating a board, one should place a twelve-finger-long gnomon at its center. By means of the two shadows at the tip [of the gnomon] upon the eastern and western parts of the circle, having marked the points for the forenoon and afternoon, one should likewise mark them around those [points]."

Having again formed two circles by rotating [the compass] together, one should place a thread in the middle of those two, situated between the east and north, at the two junctions produced by their union.
Then, one should lay down a thread from east to west through the middle; subsequently, one should determine the directions starting from the east using the tips of those threads. Thus it is said.

In the *Kriyāsāra* as well: "Having made the ground level there, one should place a circular gnomon (*śaṅku*) made of *khadira* wood, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height and one cubit in diameter; or, if that is unavailable, a fresh bamboo staff. Wherever the shadow of that touches [the circle], the wise man should know that the center of that [shadow] is the middle point."
One should extend the thread from the Tīrtha; the middle [thread] is remembered as being between the south and north.

From the extension of four threads, the other four corners are formed. Thus, the thorough knowledge of the directions has been clearly explained. Having understood this, the wise man should properly construct the pavilions and other structures. Thus it is said.
In that regard, there is a specific rule in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "When the sun has reached the equinox, one should perform the rite of the sacrificial post (*śaṅku*).

One should set up a post made of *khadira* wood, twelve finger-breadths in width. Having made it steady, one should take an iron mallet and strike it oneself eight times; it is recommended that the blows be applied gradually and lightly."
When the horned mallet falls from the hand while being struck,
then a great and insurmountable grief arises for the striker,
regardless of whether it was made of muñja grass, silk, cotton, or even animal hair.

One should wrap a thread four *yava*s in girth around the two pegs (*śaṅku*). When the thread being wrapped suddenly releases the peg, one should know that at that moment there will be the death of a son; if it breaks, there is indeed self-destruction. Even in that case, the destruction of the inauspicious occurs through a *nārasiṃha* oblation. Thus it was also said by Maya: "The peg is prescribed to be made of heartwood trees; this [diagram] of his is a variegated circle."

Having prepared it correctly at the beginning of the day, one should place it on level ground. With a measurement double that of a conch-shell, one should draw a circle in its center. When the shadows of the eastern and western sides enter the interior of that mandala, a thread passing through those two points is considered to be the east-west direction. A line drawn between the two points, revolving around them like the tail of a fish, [marks the north-south axis].

In this manner, one should lay down two threads, one running south to north and the other likewise; then, the wise architect should cast out the threads from their tips to the opposite ends, facing east and north. Thus ends the third chapter.

Also in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Having made the ground level with water, resembling the surface of a mirror, one should draw a circle there with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Having fixed an immovable gnomon (*śaṅku*) in the center, one should observe its shadow.
One should determine the entry and exit of the gnomon's shadow upon that outer circular line which has been delineated."

One should determine the east and west by means of the shadow of a conch-shell and the light of a flame; when the sun has moved to the east or west, one should determine the north and south. On the equinox, in a cloudless sky, one should determine the direction with a gnomon. Likewise, during autumn and late summer, one should determine the directions from the sun, or the eastern direction by the piercing of the Puṣya asterism, or by the interval between Citrā and Svāti. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere also—as the specific knowledge of the distinctions between the eastern and western directions has been taught here in brief—one should discern that subject matter and perform the rites exactly as instructed.
Thus, for example, the method for determining the east at night: "The interval between Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Citrā, and Svātī..."

"This is the form of the eastern direction when the city has risen for a yoke-measure"—thus it is stated in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* as well: "The East is [defined] by the rising of Śravaṇa, and likewise by the rising of Kṛttikā;
between Citrā and Svātī is the East, but for the Moon and the Sun, there is no fixed East."
The calculation of the subtle eastern direction should be performed by means of the rule of three (trairāśika),
as follows:
on the second day as well, having prepared the flour in the same manner, one should perform the measurement at both the forenoon and the afternoon.

In that regard, one should divide the middle ground between the two days—the preceding and the following—by means of sesame seeds and so forth. Then, the application of the rule of three (trairāśika) is as follows: "If this interval is obtained by sixty ghaṭikās, then what [interval] is obtained by the ghaṭikās lying between the preceding day and the preceding and following points? This is the rule of three. Regarding that, the aphorism for the rule of three is: "The first and last terms of the three quantities are of the same kind; they are the measure (pramāṇa) and the desired quantity (icchā)."
"Divide the product of the other [measure] by the first, using the last quality as the divisor.

By this method, one should avoid the intermediate space—which has been determined as the measure for the sesame seeds and so forth—to the north during the northern solstice (udagayana) and to the south during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), right at the eastern mark;
there, one should draw a line.
By the statement, "This subtle [line] is the eastern [direction];
one should construct the pavilion," the threefold pavilion—distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior—is indicated.
Regarding that threefold nature of the pavilion, it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: [as quoted in the *Śāradātilaka*].

Now we shall describe the construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) as declared by Brahmā; that is considered to be of three kinds—excellent, middling, and inferior—according to their respective measurements.
By this [statement], the avoidance of defects such as those mentioned in the *Kriyāsāra*, namely "whether it is excessive in measurement or deficient," and so forth, is indicated.

He states the measurement for all three types of pavilions with the words "by five," etc. Regarding that, the literal explanation is as follows: the smallest pavilion has a width and length of five cubits, resulting in a ground area of twenty-five cubits;
the middle-sized one, however, has a width and length of seven cubits, resulting in a ground area of forty-nine cubits.
The best [mandapa], however, is nine cubits in width and has a ground area of eighty-one cubits;
the discussion regarding that best mandapa will be carried out first,
and the author will later describe the position of the nine sacrificial pits (navakuṇḍīya) in this very mandapa before the deity.

And in those pits (*kuṇḍas*), one, three, or five girdles (*mekhalās*) should be made, leaving a space equal to the width of the altar’s foot (*vedyāḥ pādāntaraṃ*) according to the method to be described;
as it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "O Dear One, there should be one girdle, or three, or [five], which is the number of the elements."
In another Tantra it is said: "O Goddess of the Gods, there may be five, three, or even one girdle.
And in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "For all fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*), there may be either one or three [girdles]."
"Or there should be five girdles," as it is also stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "The girdles should be made five."
In that regard, in the system of five girdles (*mekhalā*), there is no inclusion of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) at all; however,
the system of three girdles is what has been stated by the author of the treatise,
and in that case, the sacrificial pits are included in some manner or other.
There is no place for the performance of the *homakartṛ* (the performer of the fire-oblation) and others due to extreme overcrowding;

furthermore, there is no room even for the altar (*vedi*) intended for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, which is to be described later, nor for the bed that is to be described as "one should sleep on the altar.
Even if there were additional sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) for other rites or for an abundance of oblation materials, even then there would be no space for the inclusion of those pits.
What need is there to mention the mediocre and inferior [sites], since even for the five-pit [site] at Pañcakuṇḍī, an entry [into the ritual] is impossible; therefore,
the author has proposed the nine-pit [site] even in that case.
That [explanation] would be utterly inconsistent;
therefore, the literal interpretation is not correct.
However, some say that the meaning of the intermediate term "antara" is what will be described as the "object of knowledge" (vedya).
According to that view, the smallest pavilion (maṇḍapa) has a length and width of fifteen cubits and an area of two hundred and twenty-five square cubits;
the medium one has a length and width of twenty-one cubits and an area of four hundred and forty-one square cubits;
while the largest has a length and width of twenty-seven cubits.
The area is seven hundred and twenty-nine square karas;
yet even that is not accepted by the virtuous,
because such a measurement is not mentioned in other texts.
In the Manvamuktāvalī and other texts, there is also a further authority: "Either twenty-four cubits or likewise twenty cubits.
In another place as well: "The pavilion and the peak-hall [kūṭa] should be measured at twenty cubits."
Thus it is said;
twenty cubits and twenty-four cubits have also been mentioned.
Therefore, this is the third chapter concerning the meaning of this autumnal *pavitra*.
It is to be explained as follows:
"by five and seven" is a collective expression.
Therefore, the smallest pavilion (maṇḍapa) has a length and width of twelve cubits, and its area is one hundred and forty-four square cubits.
Then, it follows "by five and by nine";
thus, the middle pavilion has a length and width of fourteen cubits and an area of one hundred and ninety-six cubits.
Furthermore, it follows "by seven and by nine."
Therefore, the best pavilion (maṇḍapa) has a length and width of sixteen cubits and an area of one hundred and fifty-six square cubits.
Thus, the three types of pavilions have been described.
As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "This [smallest] is twelve cubits; then, for the sake of increasing prosperity, [the others follow] in sequence."
Thus, by this, the fourteen-cubit [dimension] is stated to be the medium size, and the sixteen-cubit [dimension] is the superior size.
Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The pavilion may even be twelve cubits."
Other pavilions should also be constructed, increasing by two cubits at each stage.
Thus it is said.
Somaśambhu also states:
"The pavilion may be twelve cubits, or ten cubits; the remaining auspicious pavilions should increase by two cubits each."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Starting from twelve, one should increase by two at each step."
Elsewhere also: "A wise man should have a pavilion constructed in the northeast portion of the house, measuring twelve, eight, six, or sixteen cubits on all sides."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Now, a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with a width of twelve [units] is known as the smallest."
Likewise, in the *Pañcarātra*: "In this case, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be sixteen cubits [in size] for it to be excellent.
Also, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "They say that sixteen cubits is likewise the measurement for the excellent [pavilion]."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, this sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be made quadrangular.
As stated by Kātyāyana in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "The measurement is quadrangular, unless otherwise specified."
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well, it says: "It has four sides and four doors.
Its perfect squareness, however, should be established according to the procedure prescribed for the *vāstumaṇḍala*.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The height of the site of the pavilion is said to be twelve digits (aṅgulas)."
Thus it is said.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, concerning the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), it is stated: "The height should be one cubit, perfectly level and very beautiful."

Elsewhere it is also stated: "The pavilion (maṇḍapa) of the earth-weapon is lofty. Now, one might object: "In this case, since the desired result is achieved by the smallest pavilion alone, there would be no performance of the medium or large sizes at all. This is not so; for according to the principle that "since the fruit arises from the completion of the ritual action, there shall be a distinction in the fruit based on size, as is seen in the world," a gradation of results is postulated, and thus there is no fault.

For instance, heaven is heard of as the fruit of both the Agnihotra and the Jyotiṣṭoma; since that [heaven] is accomplished by the first alone, no one would engage in the second, which is more extensive. With this concern, the author of the *Ākara* (the *Tantravārttika*) has refuted the assumption of a gradation in the fruit. *Śāradātilaka*:
"It is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the middle."
Twelve [images], eight cubits in height, should be installed on all sides.

21. This is because, by the statement "or because it is a part of the conceptualization" (*arthād vā kalpanaikadeśatvāt*), conceptualization itself is also stated to be a part of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*). Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* has stated that this is established even by the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*):
"Regarding actions, whether small or great, and their respective fruits within their own domain..."
Although there is no distinction because of the commonality of the place of division, it has been enjoined.
Thus [it is said].
The systematic exposition of this has been set forth on the basis of the commonality of the locations of the karmas;
for example—just as that [sequence] applies to the fruits within their own respective group in the middle, so too does it apply to the others.
Because of the commonality of measurement, even when not stated specifically, [it is understood].
Thus it is said.

As for the statement made by someone that "the two middle [measures] are considered to be ten *śara* (fingers) in length and one *karā* (span) in breadth, while the other two are eleven *karā* in length," asserting thus that the twelve-cubit [measure] has both forms— that is incorrect.
Because this would result in a contradiction with the measurements for the sacrificial posts (*stambha*) and other elements.

[The literal interpretation of the text should also be applied according to the circumstances in the case of a single pit (*kuṇḍa*) or five pits, but not in the case of the nine pits mentioned by the author of the treatise.]
He describes the method for installing the pillars in the pavilion with the words "sixteen" and so forth.
Regarding the four [pillars]: among those pillars, four situated in the middle are to be placed at the corners of the altar (*vedī*).
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "There should be a set of four pillars in the middle; in their midst, the altar is prescribed."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "One should place pillars that embody the Vedas in the corners of the altar, following the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya)."
Thus, it should be understood that the installation of the twelve external pillars also follows the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth.
As it has been said: "In the raising of the pillars, the laying of the stone slabs, the application of the measuring lines, and the setting of the stakes..."
In the preparation of a pit for digging, the commencement should take place when the fire is in its proper domain.
Thus it is said.
And those [pillars] are eight cubits in height.
By the author of the treatise stating the height of the pillars, he has indicated that sixteen cubits alone constitute the maximum [height].
As it is stated in the *Pañcavarātra*: "Elevated for the purpose of the pavilion, numbering four according to the Vedas, and likewise provided with crests.
Regarding the word "abhitaḥ" (on all sides):
The meaning is "near the central pillars.
As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having leveled the ground and demarcated it with a cord, one should install the pillars in a straight line."
Furthermore, there are twelve pillars on the exterior as well, according to the stated measurements and their respective divisions.
Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Pañcarātra*, in the third chapter:
"Those [stakes] should be five cubits in measure, free from cracks, straight, and auspicious;
the best knower of the Tantras should bury one-fifth of them in the earth."
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves and other foliage;
at the doors, there should be arches made from trees that produce milky sap, arranged in due order.
23. Of what nature are the sixteen pillars?
They are *niśchidrāḥ*, meaning free from holes;
by this, their solidity is expressed.
"Upright" means straight, not crooked. "In no way thick nor thin" means that they are therefore auspicious;
and such a state of theirs is not possible without their being endowed with essential strength (*sāra*).
This is also stated by implication [that the pillars should be made from heartwood],
as it says in the *Pañcarātra*: "One should make the pillars firm, straight, and even, produced from heartwood."
Others may be pure-hearted, but they are not trees of another kind.
A pillar that is dry, crooked, ancient, or produced from inauspicious ground is like a thorn in the house; it must be abandoned in the work of erecting pillars.
Thus:
for the medium and inferior [altars], the measurement of the twelve pillars is to be calculated by the rule of three;
"the fifth part of that" means that having divided the height of the pillar into five parts, one should bury a fifth part in the ground.
Regarding the phrase "all around that":
on all sides of that pavilion, one should cover it everywhere except for the doors with bamboo and coconut leaves;
in the absence of coconut leaves, one should enclose it with mats.
As it is stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*: "The pavilions (maṇḍapas) such as Saṅka and Vijaya, along with Kaṭa and others, should be constructed by the virtuous.
And in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should adorn the pavilion on all sides with fresh branches."
As for what is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*— "having constructed a wall all around"— that should be understood as referring to pavilions for permanent images and the like,
because it is stated in that very same work: "This rule is fully declared for rites involving permanent liṅgas."
He speaks of the installation of the arches (*toraṇa*) with the words "at the doors" (*dvāreṣu*).
Now, one might ask: since the doors themselves have not yet been mentioned, how can there be this mention of "at the doors"?
True.

By the phrase "at the doors" (dvāreṣu), the doors themselves are implied. Their measurement and location are stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions at one-fifth [of the width].
Thus, the doors are in the directions from the center.
In the Kriyāsāra as well: "The wise one should also place archways at those very same doors."
Thus it is said.

Regarding the measurement for the five-night rite, it has been stated: "In the shortest [case], the opening should be two cubits; from that point, it increases by four finger-breadths for the medium and the best [sizes]."

"One should deposit" means one should bury it by a fifth part; this is from the *Śāradātilaka*. Furthermore, the *Vāstuśāstra* states: "One should deposit a fifth part in the ground; this is the rule common to all."
Thus it is said.

In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, concerning the pillars of the archway (*toraṇastambha*), it is stated: "The excavation for all [pillars] shall be one-fifth [of their height], as declared by Śiva. This is according to the sequence.
In the east, south, west, and north directions [are] "milk-trees," namely the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*,
according to the technical definition: “*Nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* are the milk-trees.”

Thus it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "A gateway made of *nyagrodha* wood is prescribed for the east; in the south, one made of *uḍumbara* is considered appropriate; in the west, one produced from *aśvattha*; and in the north, a gateway made of *plakṣa*."

"In the east, one born from a *plakṣa* tree is prescribed, and a *nyagrodha* (banyan) in the north. Thus it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *bodhidruma* (pipal), and *vaṭa* [trees] are for the four archways (*toraṇa*) in order starting from the east. Somaśambhu also says: "The archways made of *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* should be constructed in order starting from the east; or else, there may be a reversal of the beginning and end. In the absence of these, one should install even a single one of them in all directions."
Furthermore, in the *Mamvamuktāvalī*: "Then, one should install the eastern archway with the mantra 'Agnimīle';
with the mantra 'Iṣetvoje tvā', one should install the southern archway; with the mantra 'Agnā āyāhi', the placement of the western [archway];
and with the mantra 'Śanno devī', one should offer the northern archway. Thus it is said.

In the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra* as well: "The gods are stationed in the form of archways (toraṇas) within the sacrificial pavilion for the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice. One should place a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*) in the eastern direction, likewise an udumbara tree in the southern, a pippala tree in the western, and a plakṣa tree in the northern; these should be most beautiful and consecrated with the excellent mantras of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas."
One should place [the image] named Subhadra in the south with the mantra "iṣe tvā ūrje tvā"; [the one] named Sukarman in the west with the Sāmaveda and other [mantras];
and one should install Suhotra in the north with the mantra "śanno devīḥ.
As for the statement made by someone that the placement of these—Aśvattha, Udumbara, Jaṭī, and Vaṭa—is in the east and so forth, that is irrelevant.

Because it contradicts various written statements, this placement of the archway pillars (toraṇastambha) should be understood as being at a distance of one cubit outside the pavilion (maṇḍapa); for it has been said: "Outside the door of the pavilion, according to the measurement of the altar (vedi), in the sequence of the directions."
One should install an archway (toraṇa) made from the wood of the *punnāga*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees. Thus ends the third chapter;
the height of their pillars is recorded as being seven cubits each.
Its circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure. The measurement of the horizontal cross-beams (tiryaṅ-phalaka) should be half the measure of the pillars.
One should fashion spikes (śūla) in the middle of the archway (toraṇa), measuring one cubit (hasta).

In the *Vāstuśāstra*, however, it is stated: "One should cause these gates of the pavilion to be made from branches of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees, positioned in each direction.
Since this refers to the gates being constructed at the entrances, the term "gates" (*dvāra*) here indicates the archways (*toraṇa*).
However, regarding the west, south, north, and east, it should be understood that one may proceed either counter-clockwise or from the western door; there is no distinction here.

In this regard, the *Siddhāntaśekhara* states: "In the absence of these [materials], there should be one; in their absence, the *śamī* tree is prescribed for the archway (*toraṇa*), as are *jambū*, the heartwood of *khadira*, or the *tāla*."
But in the Kriyāsāra it is said: "The pillars on the archway should be straight, with their bark intact, and fresh; such are auspicious. || 23 ||
Regarding the phrase "stambhaiḥ sapta-hastaiḥ" (with pillars seven cubits [in height]), the author of the treatise has stated all the measurements for the *uttama* (superior) pavilion;
the phrase "pṛthak pṛthak" (separately) means that the measurements for the *madhyama* (middling) and *adhama* (inferior) types are distinct from one another.

Accordingly, for the middle [grade], they are six cubits; for the lowest, five cubits. Regarding the pillars of the archway, the *Vāstuśāstra* states: "They shall measure five cubits in height and two cubits in width."

"The six limbs increase [by one angula each], and likewise the best [type] is seven cubits [in height]. Here, by the word "breadth" (vistāreṇa), the measurement of the horizontal plank is intended; thus, although the six-cubit height for the medium type is not explicitly stated, it is understood through logical necessity.
This has been stated by Kātyāyana: "The measurement [of the circumference] is derived from the object's suitability.

Thus, the circumference—the width—of those arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*) is to be known through the calculation of the perimeter (*paridhi*). The method for calculating the rough perimeter was stated by Bhāskarācārya: "When multiplied by twenty-two and divided by seven, it shall be the rough [perimeter], or rather, suitable for practical use."

Thus Vyāsa [states]: when [the circumference] is multiplied by twenty-two and divided by seven, the quotient is the circumference of that wooden [ring]; its diameter is ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 24 ||

Regarding the horizontal beam situated above in the form of a lintel between the two vertical pillars: its measurement is stated to be one and a half cubits, being half the measure of the pillars, which are five cubits in height.
These are the toraṇa pillars.

The plural number in "of the pillars" (stambhānām) is to be understood as referring to the plurality of the archways (toraṇa) due to the multiplicity of doors; by this, it is also indicated that in the smallest pavilion, there are five cubit pillars for the archways. This measurement of the horizontal beam (tiryak-phalaka) applies only to the largest [pavilion].
It should be understood that for the other two [sides], there is a reduction of six-six finger-breadths each, according to what is stated in the Vāstuśāstra; furthermore,
the plural number in the word "śūlāni" (stakes) refers to the number four.
The singular number in the word *toraṇa* is used in the sense of a class;
therefore, according to the *Śāradātilaka*,
one trident (*śūla*) should be made for each archway (*toraṇa*).
And that [measurement] is one cubit; therein, the insertion is three finger-breadths and the circumference is six parts;
and this is the same for all three pavilions.

In that regard, the nature of the tridents (*śūla*) is as follows: there is a straight central shaft with a sharp tip; on either side of it are two curved [shafts] with sharp tips, whose curved portions are situated at the level of the middle shaft. This is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus constructed the archway, one should place three tridents above."
"A trident one cubit long should be placed upon them," as it is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The door-frames should be marked with a trident at their own tops."

The central spike (madhyaśūla) should indeed be straight, while those on the two sides should be slightly curved. Both of these are thus described; one should then plant them at a distance of one finger-breadth (aṅgula). When the word "toraṇe" (on the archway) is intended as a singular, then the plural "śūlāni" (spikes) is determined to refer to three according to the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* rule;
thus, "measured by a cubit" refers to the measurement of the three taken together.
This is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus constructed the archway (*toraṇa*), one should place three tridents (*śūla*) at the top.
For the central trident, the length is nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and the width is one-fourth of that;
for the remaining [tridents], the increase is by two finger-breadths, and the entrance [width] increases by one finger-breadth."
And on the middle portion of the two front [panels], there are tridents on the frieze;
these must indeed be made of that same wood and belong specifically to Śiva— this is the rule.
Regarding the Vaiṣṇava [temple], however, there is this distinction from the *Vāstuśāstra*:
"On the summit, one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, made of its own wood, using a twelfth part [of the height] according to the sequence starting from the east. Thus it is said.

Since it is stated that these [architraves] are made of the same wood as the pillar, it follows by logical necessity that the tridents (*śūla*) occupying these positions in the Śiva temple are likewise made of the same wood.

In that context, the "twelfth part" refers specifically to the *toraṇa* pillars, because in the preceding supplementary statement—“likewise, seven cubits are prescribed for them”—it is those very pillars that are the subject under discussion. Therefore, the measurements for the branches (*śākhā*) and so forth in the superior and other types [of temples] are, respectively, fourteen and twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
As for the width, it should indeed be one-fourth of itself;
as for that which has been stated by someone else— that the measurement is four finger-breadths and so forth based on one-twelfth of the plank—
that is incorrect.
Since that [measurement] was not the subject under discussion and because a measurement of nine finger-breadths for the trident has been stated,
their placement should also be understood as being the same as before.
Then, one water-pot (kalaśa) should be placed at each archway (toraṇa), two on each side of every door, and one in each corner.

As it is said: "One should place pots provided with perfumes, flowers, and cloths, and worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vākpati, and Vighneśa within them. These [deities] are to be worshipped in sequence in the pots situated in the corners of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).

Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala— these, along with Śakra and the others, should be worshipped in the pitchers stationed at the doors by those most excellent among his devotees. Thus ends the third chapter.

One should fasten banners in the various directions that possess a radiance equal to that of the world-protectors (Lokapālas), and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments. As it is stated elsewhere: "In the pavilion, one should place two jars at each door, filled with filtered water and beautified with raw rice grains and sprouts."

Regarding the banners in the directions, the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha* describes their essential form as follows: "The banners are known to be five cubits in length and colored yellow, red, and so forth;
they are considered to be joined with staffs made of bamboo, measuring two or three cubits."
The banners should be made five cubits or ten cubits long;
elsewhere it is also said: "The banners should be made five cubits, but in case of deficiency, two cubits;
the staff should be ten cubits long, and they should be placed in the eight directions. Thus it is said.
In the *Kriyāsāra*, however, there is this specific detail: "The characteristics of the banners are now correctly described as they truly are.
Outside the pavilion, together with poles ten cubits in length, one should duly install eight banners in the eight directions, beginning with the east."
Their width at the two hands is two vyāmas; the middle part is measured by one's own hand; half of the width is the crest (śikhara), and the tail (puccha) measures three cubits.
The crest has the appearance of a fish, while the tail-crest is triangular.
Between those two, one should likewise fashion a quadrangular area for the banners;
one should draw an elephant, a goat, a buffalo, a lion, a fish, a deer, a horse,
and a bull in the middle of the banner in due order and according to rule.
Alternatively, one should depict the eight elephants of the quarters, headed by Airāvata,
upon the banners using the aforementioned minerals;
thus has the auspicious characteristic of the banners been described.
Thus the necessity of the banners has been stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme installation of the banner (*dhvajāropaṇa*),
by performing which properly a person shall obtain the fruit of all [merits]."
The Yātudhānas, Guhyakas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, and those who move through the sky— these foremost of Asuras— contemplate the abode of the gods as being devoid of its banner;
for, O Brahmin, in a pavilion lacking a banner, all becomes in vain.
In the Śāradātilaka it is said: "All worship, fire-offerings (homa), and recitations (japa) performed by the wise,
as well as whatever is given without protection, perishes for the owner of the field."
Without a banner, a temple of the gods would likewise perish in every way;
for the cruel attendants of Viṣṇu, such as those known as the Kuṣmāṇḍas and others,
seize the offerings and the like if they see the deity unprotected.
But having seen the banners of the god in the pavilion, blazing with the luster of fire,
they all perish like darkness dispelled by the rays of the sun.

"Having a radiance equal to the world-protectors" refers to those possessing the colors of the world-protectors, which will be described in the fourth [chapter]. The installation of the banners is also stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Banners for each pit have been prescribed by those learned in the meaning of the scriptures."
The banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide;
they are described according to the colors of the world-protectors, and the ninth is like the luster of snow.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara as well: "It should be joined with flags and banners. Somaśambhu also states: "The flags should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide."
