The staffs of the banners shall be ten cubits long, wrapped at their five parts;
the banners and the components of the weapons shall be provided with flowers and perfumes.
He describes the decoration of the pavilion: "The canopy" refers to the moonlight-like awning;
"the garland of darbha grass" refers to darbha blades strung together with cord.
By the word "etcetera," one should understand such things as the wrapping of pillars with *dukūla* cloth and the binding of garlands of mango sprouts;
this has been stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Adorned with canopies featuring garlands of mango sprouts, covered with variegated cloths, and decorated with pillars of the *tulā*."
One should construct a pavilion adorned with fruitful plantain trunks, betel nuts, coconuts, various kinds of edible fruits, stakes, and chowries, and made radiant with jewel-like flowers.
Thus it is also stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should decorate the pillars with mirrors, chowries, and bells, as well as with cloths,
water-pots, small jars, and likewise with supporting stones."
Thus,

the defect resulting from the improper construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is stated in the Kriyāsāra: "A pavilion constructed with unmentioned materials, or one that is crooked in shape, or one that exceeds or falls short of the prescribed measurements, brings about the destruction of the patron."
This pavilion, which is well-constructed with the means prescribed by verbal roots, is beautiful, symmetrical, pleasing to the mind, and brings auspiciousness to the performer of the rite.
The third chapter:
Then, on a field measured according to the true proportions, one should prepare a square altar (vedi) measuring one cubit (aratni) for the sake of the mandala.
He speaks of the vital point (marmāṇa) of the altar as "that":
in a field measured by that third part—the third portion—of the thread in the middle of the pavilion;
otherwise, if one were to take merely a third of the area of the field, it would be anything at all.
As it has been said: "Then one should prepare the line for the pavilion as threefold;
by means of its middle portion, the altar (vedikā) is established in due order starting from the east."
And as a result, the altar (vedikā) is formed by the ninth part;
as it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Having divided the pavilion (maṇḍapa) into nine parts, the altar is considered to be in the central part."

One should prepare a square altar (*vedi*) in the middle of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), raised to the height of one *aratni* or one *hasta*, for the sake of the mandala—the *Sarvatobhadra* mandala to be described later.

Regarding this, it is stated in the description of the pavilion: "Then, in the center of that [pavilion], a wise person should construct an altar three parts wide, raised to the measure of one *aratni*, resembling the interior of a mirror, and captivating to the mind."

Thus, the term *aratni* has been employed by many authors even for the hand; as stated in the *Kādimata* regarding the definition of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*): "From four of those [finger-breadths] there is a fist (*muṣṭi*), and from three times that [fist] there is a span (*vitasti*)."
"O Śivā,
by two *aratnis* there would be one *hasta*, and by two of those [there would be one *vyāma*]," thus Kātyāyana also employed the word *aratni* for a *hasta* in many places in the *Śulba-sūtra*.

In the *Mantramuktāvalī* and regarding the *lakṣahoma*, it is stated that "four cubits (*caturhasta*) is an *aratni* increased by twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Thus, even here, the word *aratni* is explained as being equivalent in measure to a *hasta*.
This is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "It should be elevated by one *hasta* and wide on all sides by four *hastas*."

Thus it is said even in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "A wise person desiring success should joyfully construct an altar out of bricks, resembling a mirror in shape and one *hasta* high according to the royal measure."
Thus,
the king’s hand, ending with the middle finger,
is also stated in the *Pañcarātra*: "The altar [should be] one-third of the pavilion."
"Her height is one-fourth [of its width]"—
thus it is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the pavilion into three parts, the middle portion shall be the altar (*vedikā*)."

Its height should be one cubit, and it should be made square and level; the altar should be constructed as firmly as possible with either baked or unbaked bricks— this is the best method— or, in their absence, even with clay.
"Her thighs are straight and very smooth, resembling the surface of a mirror"—
thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
Seven days prior to the day of initiation, one should perform the offering of the *aṅgura* according to the rules for the attainment of all auspiciousness.
(28) *Utsedha* means height or elevation.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara, however, there is a specific distinction: "The altar (vedī) therein is of four kinds—the square (caturasrā), the lotus-shaped (padminī), the Śrīdharī, and the Sarvatobhadrā. For the installation and other rites during initiations, the square, four-cornered altar bestows all fruits."
In the consecration of tanks and similar works, the altar should be like a lotus-pond;
for the royal bath, it should be the *sarvatobhadra* or *caturbhadrā*;
and for marriage, the *środdharī* altar, provided with twenty sacrificial weapons (*astras*).

In the *Kriyāsāra*, the defect resulting from a different configuration of the altar (*vedikā*) is stated as follows: "It should resemble the surface of a mirror, being devoid of depressions and elevations; [an altar] that is crooked at the sides, damp in the middle, or rough is unseemly to the eye."
"That which is deficient or excessive in measure destroys the work of the performer"—
thus it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā regarding the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*): "Having performed everything previously mentioned, or even without the pavilion and so forth."
Having prepared the mandala as before, and especially the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), thus [it is said].

Regarding the ritual for the offering of the seed-syllables (*aṅkurārpaṇakarma*), the phrase "even before" means that it should be performed seven days prior to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*). By this, it is stated that it must be done in such a way that the day of initiation becomes the eighth [day].
By the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is indicated that it may be performed with nine, five, three, or even immediately.

As it has been stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "In the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), bathing (*sthāpana* or *snāpana*), and likewise in festivals (*utsava*), as well as for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*) during sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*), marriage (*vivāha*), and the tying of the sacred grass girdle (*mauñjibandhana*)."
"In all auspicious rites,
one should perform the offering of the finger-ring (aṅgurārpaṇa) on the ninth, seventh, fifth, third, or even the first day prior to the day of the consecration. Thus it is said.

Also in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made by the Brāhmaṇas, the preceptor, performing auspicious rites, should carry out [the ritual] on that very same day."

"Even before the seventh or the ninth [day], let alone the day of the ritual action. Elsewhere it is also said: "In various festivals, such as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the installation [of deities], and during the rite of the *pavitra*, the performer of the ritual first plants auspicious sprouts; from that, the rite becomes auspicious."
The third chapter:
On the northern side of the pavilion, one should construct a secret chamber extending from east to west; then, within it, the wise practitioner should fashion the mandala.
One should lay down five threads measuring five cubits each,
extending from east to west, with an interval of twelve finger-breadths between them.
In the same manner, one should apply eleven threads from south to north.
Forty steps arise for you; one should wipe them clean.

On the seventh day prior to the auspicious day of the prescribed yoga, or on the ninth, or on the fifth—a favorable day and an auspicious moment—one should perform the rite of anointing the body with auspicious substances. Thus it is said.
In that regard, having observed a fast on the preceding day and performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to the procedure prescribed in one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should commence the *aṅkurārpaṇa*.

As it has been said: "The preceptor, being pure, should perform the auspicious *aṅkurārpaṇa* on the seventh day prior to the day of purification, after making the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and observing a fast."
"One should perform the Nāndīmukha-śrāddha on the preceding day and the Svastivācana;
one should indeed carry out this according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
Also, in the Saṃhitā: "In all cases of the Abhyudaya-śrāddha, there is likewise the production of sprouts."
"One should perform [the preliminary rites] at the very beginning of an action whose nature is prosperity. || 28 ||
Regarding the hall (*śālā*):
therein, the measurement of twenty *karas* in length and ten in width is the superior measurement for a hall.

Since there is no purpose for a hall exceeding two *advaitas* in length, this hall should be constructed with half of that measure as its middle dimension. Therefore, it should be made ten cubits long and five cubits wide.
He states that very same thing: "extending from east to west."
One should construct a hut that is long and square in shape, concealed, surrounded on all sides by mats and the like, provided with a single door on the south side, and free from drafts.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having made that firm hut situated toward the southwest and free from drafts.
Within that, one should arrange the mandala to be described. (28)
He describes the mandala itself with the words "five cubits" and so forth.

Having laid a single thread five cubits in length, extending from east to west, in the middle of the hall's width, one should lay two threads each at intervals of twelve finger-breadths on the southern and northern sides of that central thread. Then, by intersecting those [with others], one should apply eleven threads in total.
The phrase "taddat" means at intervals of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In this way, five cubits (*hasta*) are fully accounted for.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having stretched out the cord, one should snap it so that it extends from south to north."
One should cause each of those two sides to be laid out with a measurement of five cubits.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"In the row, there are four paths (*vīthī*) at the ends on both sides of the four squares;
thus, two paths and three sets of four squares remain below. (32)
One should color those squares with white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black powders;
then, the wise one should fill the pathways with dark (green) powder.
They say there are various types of powders for the work of applying the lines.
The *pālikās*, the five-faced [liṅgas],
and the *śarāvas* are declared by all the Tantras to be, respectively, of the nature of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva.
Their heights should be inferred as sixteen, twelve, and eight [units].
"In the same manner, according to the previously mentioned measurement, one should successively lay down eleven threads from east to west, each twelve finger-breadths apart;
then, within those lines, [one should mark] the interval between the eastern threads."
The word "should sweep" (*pramārjayet*) connects with what follows. One should sweep four paths (*vīthī*) in a row;
that is, on the outside.
Because it is stated that [the word] "inside" (*antar*) is to be supplied:

one should clear away (mārjayet) one row of four squares on the east, a row of eight squares for the southern path, again a row of four squares for the western path, and a row of eight squares for the northern path.

Then, there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) to be supplied here: "one should clear away two paths, consisting of two squares each, on both sides—on the two flanks—of the inner four-square [area], that is, the central four-square [area]."
Thus, the greatness of the fruit has been declared.
Here, in this mandala, three sets of four squares remain;
those twelve squares situated in the three sets of four are the "sweet" ones.
One should color each individual square with powders such as white and so forth;
therein, white is for the quarter of Vāyu,
and yellow is for the quarter of Agni.
The *aruṇa* [color] is at the station of Rakṣas;
the *asita* [color] is at the station of Īśa—this was stated by the term "the wise one" (*sudhī*).
As it has been said by the Teachers: "One should carry [the colors] beginning with yellow, red, white, and black at each step, ending with Śarva."
Immediately thereafter, one should fill the path with dark green. || 30-33 ||
Regarding the vessels for offering the finger-sprinklings (*aṅgurārpaṇa*), he says "vessels.
Large, high shallow bowls (*śarāva*) are referred to by the term *pālikā*.
Those same *pālikās* that are slightly lower and provided with five openings are called *pañcamukhī*.
The *śarāva* vessels are well known.
By the phrase "in all tantras," it is stated that there is no distinction of vessels in the rites such as the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the five deities.
The first [vessels] have the form of Hari.
The second [vessels] have the form of Brahmā; the third have the form of Śiva. By this, it is stated that Hari, Brahmā, and Īśa are to be worshipped in these vessels.
Thus it is stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "In those aforementioned vessels, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
This concludes the third chapter.
Having wrapped those auspicious [vessels] with thread in successive finger-breadths (aṅgula),...
Having washed those vessels and placed rice within them,
the preceptor should set them down, beginning from the west, upon bunches of fragrant *darbha* grass;
he should then fill those vessels with dried cow-dung, sand, and clay.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara as well, it is said: "One should worship Rudra with sandalwood and flowers in shallow bowls (śarāva), Viṣṇu in earthen mounds (pālikā), and Brahmā in small jars (ghaṭikā). [34-35]
"Gradually by finger-breadths" is connected with what precedes.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "The width of the mouth of the *pālikā* is said to be sixteen finger-breadths;
the neck-opening should be eight finger-breadths wide."
The width of the footstool is declared to be six finger-breadths;
its height is four finger-breadths, and the joint between them shall be one finger-breadth.
At its junction, there should be neither "I" (A) nor the foot-stool (Ā);
thus, the five-faced Ghaṭikā shall be the granter of all desires.
They say the openings are indeed five, four, and one, with a width of four finger-breadths each, according to the rule, in the four directions and upwards.
The width of the *ghaṭikā* is said to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
some teachers, however, state it should be sixteen finger-breadths.
"The mouth of the *śarāva* is said to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width;
its base at the bottom is said to be four finger-breadths in width.
Also elsewhere: "In this [practice], there should be a five-faced vessel (*ghaṭikā*) measuring one palm (*tāla*) in both width and height."
One set of four faces is directed toward the cardinal directions, while another set is turned toward the center.

The mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) should be as wide as a palm tree; its handle should measure half the diameter and height; its neck should have a circumference of four finger-breadths, and it should be raised except for the opening.
"They may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, or else they may be new.
However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* it says: "Or one should prepare the *pālikā* vessels and so forth according to what is available.
The word "those" (*tāni*) refers to the vessels (*pātra*).
"Pure" means free from black discoloration, wounds, and the like.
"With thread" means with a triple-stranded cord.
In this regard, it should be understood that the washing comes first, followed by the wrapping with the thread.
The *darbhakūrca* is as will be described below.
Regarding the phrase "starting from the west":
one should place four *pālikās* in the western group of four, four five-mouthed vessels (*pañcamukhī*) in the central group of four, and four *śarāvas* in the eastern group of four.
It should be understood that the installation of the [deities] starting from Āgneya (southeast) and so forth occurs in the center of that.
As it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The knower of the Tantra, having washed the seed-syllables with milk using the Sudhā-bīja, [should proceed]."
Having consecrated them with the root mantra preceded by the five sounds,
the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should offer [the oblations] into those vessels, following the auspicious customs and the benedictory words of the twice-born. || 38-39 ||

In the *Prayogasāra*: "One should place the vessels within them, individually in each of the four squares, starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast. Regarding the word "karīṣa": [it refers to dried cow dung].
*Karoṣa* is the powder of dried cow dung.
With these, one should fill all the vessels in successive order.
And it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should fill them in successive order."
In the *Prayogasāra* as well: "One should fill the vessels from above with clay, sand, and dried cow-dung.

Regarding that, there is a specific detail in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings on another day, [the rite should be performed] accompanied by song and dance, and attended by elephants and horses."
The preceptor and the others, some mounted on chariots and others on elephants,
went to the bank of a lake, a river, or a flower garden.
There, having swept a pure portion of the ground with *darbha* grass while reciting the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*),
and having sprinkled it with consecrated water while recollecting the respective mantras;
Having invoked the Earth with the heart-mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, having dug the ground with a spade while reciting the weapon-mantra, [one takes] the earth.
Having taken it with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should fill a bronze vessel;
having cleansed the clay with the Hṛdaya mantra and covered it with a cloth, one should hold it.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the city or the residence with the sounding of all auspicious instruments, the preceptor should lead [the image] to the pavilion.
A wise person should perform this rite during the daytime and not at night. Thus [ends verses 36 and 37].
Regarding the sowing of seeds in them, he says "with sudhā": with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, which is *sudhā*. "With milks" means with cow's milk; "having washed" [is the meaning].
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Having stirred [the seeds] with water by means of the twelve-syllable mantra.
In the *Sārasvatamata* as well: "Those seeds, having been washed in turn with water and a cloth.
This is indicated by the phrase "one who knows the tantra" (*tantravit*).
Regarding "with the root": it should be given after being consecrated one hundred and eight times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
This is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, Chapter Three:
"A measure (*āḍhaka*) of rice, mung beans, sesame, *niṣpāva* beans, and mustard seeds..."
The seeds of *kulattha*, *kaṅgu*, and *māṣa* are used for the rite of germination (*aṅkurakarma*).
Having sprinkled them with water mixed with turmeric and covered them with cloths,
the preceptor should offer oblations (*bali*) from various vessels in the directions, beginning with the east.
"When no specific number is mentioned for recitations (*japa*) and the like, it shall be one hundred and eight or one thousand.
The five sounds (*pañcaghoṣa*), however, consist of the *paṭaha*, *ḍhakkā*, *mṛdaṅga*, wind instruments, and the conch shell.
"Auspicious conduct" (*maṅgalācāra*) refers to that which is well-known in the respective region, preceded by the sound of *ulūlu* and so forth.

By the phrase "the preceptor with a restrained mind," it is stated that having gathered those seeds together, one should sow them at night in the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, facing either east or north, while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

This is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Facing either east or north, one should sow all the seeds in the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, in due order, using the root mantra as the primary [mantra]."
"Soma is the lord of seeds; therefore, one should offer them at night. Thus it is said.
In the Sārasvata-mata as well: "Since he [Soma] is radiant toward the seeds and the deities at night, the Guru should sow the seeds only during the night. (38) (38)
He mentions the seeds, beginning with "śāli":
*śālis* are winter rice;
*śyāma* is *śyāmāka*, which is well known as *sāvā* in the Kānyakubja dialect.
The *ār̤haka* is the *tūvarī*;
the *niṣpāva* is the *rājamāṣa*,
as explained in that manner in the *Śrīdharyā*, a commentary on the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.

"One should avoid *niṣpāva* and *rājamāṣa* seeds while the deity is asleep"—since this is stated separately, it does not sublate [the general rule]. In the *Sārasvata-mata*, the worship of deities for each individual seed is prescribed:
"Skanda for *priyaṅgu*, Vāyu for *niṣpāva*, and Agni for *kulatthaka*."
One should offer Nirṛti in the Āḍhakī plant, Soma in the Mūlaka, and Vaivasvata in the sesame seed.

"One should worship Prajāpati with rice-grains (*śāli*), Ananta with mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), Indra with dark grains (*śyāma*), Varuṇa with black beans (*māṣa*), and [Brahmā] with *nīvāra* grains, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, the daily worship of Soma is also prescribed:
"One should worship Soma daily, up until the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*)."
"When the day of the formal acceptance (adhivāsa) has arrived, the preceptor should dismiss the Soma," so it is said. || 40 ||
Regarding *haridrā* (turmeric):

the mantra for that is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Salutations again and again to Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, to Śiva, to the foremost of all worlds, and to the one who possesses the [sacred] staff."
"Having scattered [the seeds] with this mantra, one should rain down water mixed with turmeric powder; one should sprinkle them with water every day. Thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
With names beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*,
[one should worship] the spirits, ancestors, yakṣas, nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and Hari,
night after night; these are declared to be the deities of the seven nights.
For the *bhūtas*, flour mixed with sesame, *tila* seeds, turmeric, curd, and parched grain; for the *pitṛs*, rice mixed with sesame and rice grains are prescribed;
and for the *yakṣas*, *karambha* and parched grain accompanied by coconut water.
One should offer flour of *saknu* to the Nāgas, a lotus to Brahmā,
food with cakes to Śarva, and rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍaudana*) to Viṣṇu. Then, one should duly present the *bali* offering to the Lords of the World (*lokeśvara*).
One should perform the offering of the finger (aṅgurārpaṇa) when initiation, consecrations, the entry into a new house, and festivals have been successfully accomplished;
it culminates in the state of threefoldness.
"Having covered" means with one [cloth] for each of the four vessels. The syntactical connection is that one should offer the *bali* at night.
In the morning, having again performed the cleaning of the ground and so forth, the offering of the *bali* is to be made at the beginning of the second night.
Regarding the phrase "beginning with the *praṇava*":
the mantra for that occasion is: *Oṃ bhūtebhyo namaḥ [may they accept this bali-offering, together with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel-leaves; svāhā]*.
The mantra is to be understood in the same way in other instances as well.

In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, there is this distinction: "Then one should sprinkle [the seeds] with pure water mixed with fragrance for three nights according to the rule, or even for five nights.
In the *Sārasvaramata*, however, it is said: "One should never speak of the sprouts once they have fully emerged."
"Only the teacher or his disciple, by his command, should enter. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Having carefully covered them with cloths, one should cause them to be well-guarded. (43)
Regarding the sacrificial offerings for the *bali* on each of the seven nights, he says, "To the *bhūtas*," ending with "sānā";
these six [offerings] are for the first night.
This very [rite] has the name *bhūtakrūra*.
As it has been said: "Parched grain, sesame, red powder, water, rice-mash, and cooked grain are known as *bhūtakrūra*.
*Karambha* is curd mixed with parched grain;
*akṣata* refers to unbroken rice grains.

When the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) takes place over nine nights, then the materials for the oblation and the deities have been stated by the teachers: "If the oblation is prescribed to be offered sequentially during the nine nights, it is for Viṣṇu [on the first], milk-rice (*dogdhānna*) for the Dogdhras, and *kṛsara* for the Vaiṣṇeyas. (43–45)
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):
having performed the bali offering with milk-rice and other substances in each respective direction,
therein— in the third section between the southwest and the west— [the ritual proceeds].
In the pavilion previously described, the wise man, having divided the area outside the altar into three parts,
should designate the central portion for the east and other directions,
and then sequentially fashion fire-pits of beautiful form in the eight cardinal points.
"Of Ananta, between the east and the northeast, [is the offering] to Brahmā.
By the phrase "according to rule," it is indicated that the previously mentioned bali-offering to the directions must also be performed.
The application of these vessels will be stated later.
The examination of the fingers is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "For the sake of accomplishing the desired object of the patron, one should examine the fingers;
they should be properly grown upward, tender, and white."
One should avoid families that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or similarly situated horizontally, as well as those that are dark-green, for such families are inauspicious.
O Kṛṣ� smoke-colored Aṣṭaṣṭi causes strife as well as the destruction of people who have not yet reached full maturity, along with famine and dark-bodied portents.
If Mars is situated in the eighth house, there will be disease as well as fear of enemies;
when such an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).

The Guru, together with those who bear the [divine] forms, should perform the oblation with the root mantra, or with the Aghora-weapon mantra or the Astra-mantra, one hundred or even a thousand times. Thus it is stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the performer by means of the syllables of the limbs (aṅgas) according to their growth."

With dark and black sprouts there is loss of wealth; with those that have grown crooked, disease; with those that are swaying, sorrow; with those that are difficult to grow, death; with those that are bent, diseases; and in the place of their growth, the loss of desired objects. Thus [it is said]. || 46 ||
Regarding the location of the *kuṇḍas*, he says "in front" (*prāk*) and so forth:

outside the altar (*vedikā*), on all sides of the field, one should divide the line through the middle of the field into three parts; then, in the middle of each of those sections, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise through the eight directions, the wise man—meaning one who also knows the five girdles (*mekhalā*) and so forth—should sequentially fashion the *kuṇḍas* of beautiful form. This is the connection [of the verse].
The meaning is "in the quarters and intermediate directions ending with Īśāna.

Because of the technical rule stating, "Since the limits have been specified starting from the East, the sequence itself is intended," it follows that the meaning is fulfilled as follows: having set aside a space equal to one foot from the altar (vedī), and having further set aside the space there suitable for the girdle (mekhalā) to be described later, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are to be constructed.
This was stated by Somaśambhu; and it is also said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Having abandoned the other [portion] up to the edge of the Veda," and "the fourth part of the Veda has been abandoned."
Thus it is also stated in the Nāradīya: "The space between the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (vedī) should measure one and a quarter cubits."
In this context, the word "pāda" (quarter) indicates something slightly more than that;
therefore, according to the *Śāradātilaka*, this applies to the medium and superior pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).
Quadrangular, semi-circular, triangular,
perfectly circular, hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal— these are their names.
The preceptor’s sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be in the center, [and those for] the Lord of Gaurī and Mahendra [in their respective directions].
One should fashion the ground measuring one cubit as described before.
This sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square on all sides and auspicious;
those who know the subtle [proportions] recognize it as being one cubit plus twenty-four finger-breadths.
The measurement of a finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be the length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of the artisan.
Also, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The distance between the altar and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be two cubits."
Thus, this concerns the twenty-four-cubit pavilion;
however, in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* it is stated: "Having set aside thirteen finger-breadths from the four sides of the altar..."
"One should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as prescribed in one's own scripture, according to the various rites.
Here, "pits" refers to those provided with girdles (mekhalās).
He states that very sequence as "quadrangular" (caturasra);
this has been stated in the Āmnāyarahasya: "In the procedure for the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), when the eight pits are situated in the cardinal directions... (48).
Regarding the "preceptor's pit" (ācāryakuṇḍa):
between Gaurīpati and Mahendra, in the intermediate direction between the northeast and the east, there should be the preceptor’s pit.
As it is stated in that very same [text]: "One should cause the ninth pit to be made in the interval between the eastern and northeastern directions."
It may be circular or square;
as it has been stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Between Indra and Īśa (the northeast), it should be either circular or square."
Since that has been prescribed by the Teacher,
some scholars maintain that even elsewhere, in the middle [of the figure], there should be a circle between the directions of Gaurīpati (the North-East) and Surapati (the East).
Thus,
it is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The central area for the two lords of Taurus and Leo may be either circular or square."
In that regard, because it serves as the archetype for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), he first describes the characteristics of the square pit, beginning with the word "one cubit" (*hasta*).
The connection is that one should fashion it on all four sides according to the method previously described for constructing the square of the *vāstu*-mandala.

Regarding the characteristics of the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *hasta* has been mentioned; now, for the sake of establishing those characteristics, he also states the definition of the *aṅgula*. The word "four" refers to the measure of the *kartṛ*—that is, the disciple who is to be consecrated—and not the preceptor (*ācārya*). This is because the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is applied to the disciple as well, since he is the actual performer of the action.
Now, one might ask: why is the preceptor alone, who is denoted by the primary term "agent," not understood here?
To this it is replied:
"In the acts of giving, reciting, touching, choosing a bridegroom, choosing a boon, and in the observance of vows and measurements, one should understand the sacrificer. Thus ends the third chapter.
A finger-measure (*mānāṅgula*) is said to be constructed from eight barley grains.
"A wise person should divide a square field into five parts"—this is from the words of Kātyāyana.
If it is asked: "Is this not Śrauta (Vedic), while the present context is Tāntrika? How, then, can there be consistency between them? [the answer follows].
Therefore,

because of the statement, "That which is spoken by another and is not contradictory [is authoritative]," as in the case of the Vedic Soma sacrifice and so forth: "One should always perform [the rites] wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and with the topknot tied."
Just as the Smṛti rule that "the ritual must be performed by one who is pure" and so forth is accepted because it is not contradictory, so too is it here;
for this very reason it has been said: "The single action is understood through all the Śākhās."
By the phrase "one who knows the tantras," it is stated that there are various definitions of finger-measures (aṅgula) taught in their respective tantras.
By the word "parvan" in the expression "of the joint of the middle finger," the middle joint is meant.

The connection is as follows: that which is the measure of the length of the middle [of the hand] is an *aṅgula*, or alternatively, that which is the measure of the middle joint of the middle finger is an *aṅgula*. (50–52)

"In the beginning, the author of the treatise will employ the conventional usage of the *yava* according to its sequence," and so forth; for the sake of establishing that, he says "of the *yavas*" [in the verse], meaning that one-eighth of a *māṣaka* is a *yava*.

This is another name for that very same *māna-aṅgula*, and not a separate definition of the *aṅgula*, because there is no use of the word "or" (*vā*) or similar particles [to indicate an alternative].
The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the first among the measures of weight.
A *trasareṇu* should be understood as consisting of eight *paramāṇus*; these *trasareṇus*, when multiplied by eight, are traditionally known as a *reṇu*.
Eight of those particles of dust are known by the wise as a "tip of a hair" (bālāgra);
eight tips of a hair are a "nit" (likhyā), and eight nits are known as a "louse-egg" (yūkā).
Eight *yūkās* are said to make one barleycorn (*yava*), and eight barleycorns make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). A span (*ratni*) is to be understood as twenty-one finger-joints (*parvan*).
"Twenty-four [finger-breadths] shall indeed be one *hasta*.
Thus, two finger-breadths are stated as a single unit.
In the *Trailokyasāra* as well: "The measure of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) is from the middle joint of the middle finger of the maker..."

Eight barley-corns lying on their side [make] one *yava*; three *brīhi* grains [make] one *ūrdhvāgra*. Thus, according to the measurement of the *mātrāṅgula*, a *hasta* is prescribed by Śiva for the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*.
Furthermore, the best [measurement] is by the width of the middle joint of the middle finger.
According to this measurement in finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*), the girdle, the neck,
the navel, and the womb (*yoni*) of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be constructed.
Thus,
by Maya also, in the passage beginning with "increased by the sequence of atoms, it is declared as the measure of a finger," it is stated that eight barley grains [in length] constitute one finger.
"An *aṅgula* shall be one *mātrā*, and a *vitasti* is twelve *aṅgulas*," ending thus; "An *aṅgula* consists of eight *yavas*, and a *kara* is twenty-four *aṅgulas*;
another [measure] of twenty-four *aṅgulas* is measured by one's own thumb (*svāṅguṣṭha*).
Thus, in that context, there is indeed equality between the middle joint of the thumb and the [standard] *aṅgula*.

If it is argued that even though there is no use of the word "or" (*vā*) and so forth, a choice will nevertheless occur through the two terms *mātrāṅgula* and *mānāṅgula* themselves— that is not so, because even later on, there is no usage of them as distinct [categories].

However, whereas in the *Pañcarātra* the definition of the five finger-breadths (*pañcāṅgula*) is stated and their specific application (*vyavasthā*) is also explained, here no such application is mentioned; therefore, it is merely a synonym. As it is said in the *Pañcarātra*: "Those rays of the sun which reach the path of the window..."
Within them, subtle particles called *trasareṇus* move about.
Eight of those atoms (paramāṇus) make one minute particle (reṇu); eight of those make one "hair-tip" (bālāgraka); eight of those make one nit (likṣā); and eight of those make one louse (yūkā).
Eight of those *yavas* are declared to be one *aṅgula*; that same [unit] with seven *yavas* is the best finger-breadth (*uttamāṅguli*), while that with eight is the middle.
Six barley grains are declared to be a *sādhamā*, which is defined as a measure of one *mānāṅgula*;
when eight barley grains are laid side-by-side, that constitutes a *mānāntarāṅgula*.
The length of the *mātrāṅgula* is declared to be the distance between the two joints of the middle finger of the disciple’s right hand.
A fist formed by the remaining fingers without the thumb is said to consist of four parts; one part is known as the "thumb-fist."
Having divided the height of any man into ten parts,
and having further divided one of those parts into twelve, one such part constitutes one *māṅgalya*.

One should know that which is called the "finger-measure obtained from the body" (dehalabdha-aṅgula); furthermore, the height of the image shall be based on the "great measure finger" (mahāmāna-aṅgula).

That which is the finger-measure of the great standard (mahāmāna) is declared to be the measure-finger (mātrāṅgula); one should fashion the limbs of the image using precisely that other standard finger-measure. Thus ends the third chapter.
One should construct palaces and other such structures using that very same measurement or by another measurement;

furthermore, the rules for the altar (vedikā), the pedestal (pīṭha), the palanquin (śivikā), the chariot (ratha), and so forth, must be according to the measurement of the finger-breadth (aṅgula) alone, and not by any other.
One should prepare the implements for the sacrifice here according to the *mānāṅgula* measure;
the components of the *homa*, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, as well as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), should be based on the *mudrāṅgula*.
One may also fashion the sacrificial pits and other items using the *dehalabdha-aṅgula* measure.

Thus, in many manuscripts, the reading at both places is simply "mānāṅgulam"; in one case, the term *mānāṅgula* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*), while in the other, it should be explained etymologically (*yaugika*) as "a finger-measure by means of a standard" (*mānena pramāṇena aṅgulam*).
The area of a quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) has been described according to its characteristics;
however, since that area is measured in *aṅgulas*, it cannot be stated if those [characteristics] are unknown.

Therefore, it is now stated as follows by Bhāskarācārya in the *Līlāvatī*: "In the case of an equilateral triangle, a square with equal sides, and likewise a rectangle, the area is the product of the base and the perpendicular."

Thus, in the *Triśatikā*, Śrīdharācārya also states: "In a quadrangle with equal sines and in a triangular field, the calculation arises; one should multiply half the sum of the base and the face by the middle sine."
In this manner, twenty-four multiplied by twenty-four results in five hundred and seventy-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) as the area;
this very same area is to be applied to all eight types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*),
and therefore this alone constitutes the fundamental form for all of them.
In another tantra as well, this very [square] is declared to be the archetype, stating: "Within that, I shall describe other fire-pits (kuṇḍas) to you by name.
Elsewhere too it is said: "The field (kṣetra) should be square; from this, one may generate other fire-pits as well."
Thus,
all fire-pits (kuṇḍas), such as the womb-shaped (yoni) and others, indeed arise from the square;
therefore, I shall first describe the characteristics of the square.

In the *Kriyāsāra* as well, from the passage beginning with "Thus... and ending with "...this is declared to be the cause for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*s)": "This four-footed, four-cornered [figure] shall be called the field (*kṣetra*)."
Since all types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), such as the square and others, are possible here,
he describes the *yoni* pit as being of the nature of the square, stating "that which has been described for the square."
One should divide a square field into five parts;
since there is no purpose for dividing the entire area of the field, it is stated by the term "the wise one" that the division should be made only of the central line.
Therein, this fifth part consists of four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), six and a half barley-corns (yavas), and slightly less than that.
The knower of mantras should place one part in front according to the measurement of half the diagonal,
and likewise rotate another part by the measure of the diagonal.
Then one should lay down two threads; the pit (kuṇḍa) should be shaped like a womb (yoni).

Having thus established the portion, one who knows the mantras should place it on the northern part of the thread extending from east to south and increase it—this is what is stated by the phrase "one who knows the mantras.
Then, with a measurement equal to the distance from the corner to the sun (the center), one should rotate [the compass] according to the measure of the corner.

Here, by the word "corner" (koṇa), the corner-line is understood; its "half" is the point of intersection in the middle of the two diagonal lines (karṇasūtra); the "half of that" is the point of junction of the second diagonal lines in the other pair of squares.
By that measurement: from that measure, one should rotate [the thread] by means of the diagonal measurement, adhering to the corner.

As for the method: having fixed the beginning of the thread at the point where the two diagonal threads of another single square intersect, one should rotate the thread from the tip of the middle horizontal thread until it reaches the southern end of the thread situated to the south of the north-south line; the knower of mantras should rotate the other [thread] in the same manner—this is the meaning.
Therein, too, is the method.

Having fixed the starting point of the cord at the location where the two corner-cords of the second side-compartment intersect, one should rotate the tip of the cord from the second end of the central horizontal cord— keeping it attached to that corner— down to the southern end of the north-south cord; then, one should lay down a pair of cords,
dropping two cords from the two ends of the circles located on both sides up to the front-end of the previously laid cord.
Thus, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be shaped like a womb and face north.
As it is stated in the Kādimata: "Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-fifth of its middle portion, from the central point between the eastern and western lines..."

O Dear One, one should rotate [the cord] according to the measurement of that corner, reaching from the western tip to the northern tip, and likewise to the southern tip; then, by supporting it upon the horizontal line in the middle of that, one should proceed accordingly.
"One should cast two lines up to the limit of the Brahma-thread that has been opened;
this is the Yoni-kunda, O auspicious one.
Thus it is also stated in the Kāmika: "Having placed the fifth part in front, [one measures] in the middle by the measure of four parts."
"The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is said to have the appearance of an ashvattha leaf due to its curvature";
thus,
having divided the site into five parts, one part is [set aside] in the east.
Having fixed [the cord] there, one should then fix it on the two sides up to the middle;
then, from each respective corner, one should rotate the western line separately so that it reaches correctly to the three corners.
When it has been done in this way, the pit becomes stable like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
thus ends the third chapter.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara it is also said: "The pit called Yoni is described as being in the southeast, facing north; it is recommended for the rites of Prajāgara and Prātapa. There too, as before, one should make four equal squares, and the fifth part of the field [is the Yoni]."
One should join [the thread] at the outer tip of the *somasūtra* on the northern side;
one should place a thread at the portion of the two tips of the *garbhasūtra*.
By this, the tip of the petal for the two right compartments is established.
And at the end of the middle square, one should rotate [the cord]; from that rotation, the back of the petal becomes perfectly formed, like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
thus this shall be the *yonikuṇḍa*.
Thus,
here the derivation of the field is stated;
therein, on one side, it is a semicircle.
On the second side is the syllable *aiṃ* and a circle;
thus there is one circular field,
and situated between two circles is one downward-facing triangle.

Above that is one triangle facing upward; thus there are three fields. Having separately calculated the area of each of these three and combined them, one obtains the area of the *yonikuṇḍa* (womb-shaped sacrificial pit).
Among those, the area of the circular field is first stated:

Regarding the calculation of the area of a circle according to the method stated by Bhāskarācārya— namely, "the square of the diameter multiplied by ten and fire (three), and divided by five thousand, yields the fine result"— the statement of Śrīdharācārya, that "in twenty [units], it is coarse," has been disregarded. In that case,
the diameter is seventeen *aṅgulas* less one thirty-fourth part of an *aṅgula*.

The derivation of that is as follows: by the rule "the simultaneous application of those two operations," the measure of the ear (karṇa) is brought forth, and half of that becomes the diameter (vyāsa).
This will be clarified later in the section concerning the method for constructing a pit (kuṇḍa) measuring two cubits.

Therein, the placement of the diameter is as follows when reduced to a common denominator; by the aforementioned calculation, the area of the field is known to be one barley-corn (yava), four barley-germs (yūkā), and three barley-dusts (likhyā).

The methods for reduction, fractions, and so forth have not been stated here for fear of making the book too voluminous; they should be consulted in the *Līlāvatī* and other works on arithmetic (*pāṭīgaṇita*).
Below that is the result of the square root.
"Half the base multiplied by the perpendicular becomes the area in a triangle"— according to this path stated by Bhāskarācārya,
there the base is *aṅgula*s and the perpendicular is *aṅgula*s; therefore, half the base multiplied by the perpendicular [is the area].

This is the result for the *madhyatīkṣṇa* [instrument]; from that, the result for the *ūrjātara* [instrument] is its ground (*bhū*) in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). According to the method stated in the text, the perpendicular (*lamba*) is in finger-breadths; there, from the middle line (*madhyasūtra*), it is minus one-fifth part. Then, as stated, the placement (*nyāsa*) is for the purpose of equalizing the two denominators; the equalization is the summation (*yoga*).
If the field-area produced by the calculation is slightly more than five *yavas*,
then within that field-area, two *yavas* and four *aṅgulas* are deficient;
this same result is to be understood even in the definitions of the *Kādimata* and other such systems as cited.
In this regard, someone, having cited such a result from the *Kāmika*, has refuted [the text]; however, the *Śāradātilaka* is indeed greatly mistaken.

For even though there is uniformity among all [authorities], defects arise—such as the statement "poverty results from a lack of measurement," or "whatever measurement is deficient or excessive causes the destruction of the patron"—therefore, equality of the area of the site (*kṣetraphala*) must necessarily be required here.
Since the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) must necessarily be described by means of calculating their area according to the mathematical methods taught by Bhāskarācārya and Śrīdharācārya—
as stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Whatever the measurement is for the eastern pit, that is the measure of the area for the others."
The author [of this work] has also established that the square is the fundamental form (prakṛti) solely for the purpose of calculating equal areas;

likewise, even the venerable Kātyāyana—who composed the Kalpasūtra based on fifteen branches—is seen to proceed, in his *Pariśiṣṭa* and *Śulba-sūtra*, when desiring to describe the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), by means of calculating area according to the methods taught by Śrīdhara Ācārya and Bhāskara Ācārya.
Therefore, the equality of area must necessarily be stated.
Thinking that the student’s intellect might be strained by such extremely subtle calculation, the Teacher overlooked it;

however, for that purpose, the traditionalists prescribe the addition of three barley-corns (*yava*). To ensure equality with the area of the field, I shall now describe a method applicable to all cases:
having divided the middle line into twenty-four parts, one should lay them out toward the front.
And from each corner-foot, one should [draw] five parts and three-twentieths for each.
From the two corners, one should then extend the middle horizontal line to its end; from there, the two lines should reach the ends of the front-omitted lines, forming the shape of a vulva (bhaga).
In this manner, it should be understood that the area of the field is unerring.

Here, one should extend the middle line by five *aṅgulas* along with barley-corns (*yava*), nits (*yūkā*), and four particles of dust (*likhyā*). Then, the perpendicular (*lamba*) is reduced to a common denominator; the resulting area of the field, according to the stated sequence, is six barley-corns, three nits, and five particles of dust.
Thus, all this field-area combined is to be understood as subtle. However, according to the *Kādima-tantra*: "The ground that lies around the square, having been set aside, is obtained elsewhere;
therefore, in all fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), everything is [to be calculated] from every side."
Those very same [beings] are born again in the form of six-fingered creatures upon the grassy land.
Thus,

it is also stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should apply a cord equal in length to the side of a square field, multiplied by four, along the perimeters of all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), such as the yoni-shaped and others."
If that quadrangular pit is level, it is auspicious; such is the case for the yoni-pit and other types of pits.
Thus,
this accords with what we have stated here;
for Vyāsa says, "When the product of nine and three is divided by zero, five, and twelve, that is the subtle circumference," according to which method the circumference of the circle is subtle.
The gross [measurement] consists of finger-breadths. Having divided the field made square by the ear-line into ten parts once more,
the knower of the tantra should discard one part each at the bottom and at the top.

This [measurement] in finger-breadths (aṅgula), produced by summing the results according to the method stated as "the point of conjunction of those two," amounts to sixty-six finger-breadths; however,
because this measurement is excessively coarse, it deviates in many instances, and for that reason, it has been disregarded.
From that [measurement], the semicircle has a circumference of four and three-eighths finger-breadths;
for the triangle, it is four and one-eighth finger-breadths; and for the circle, it is slightly more than four finger-breadths.
Six *aṅgulas* [are] *yavas* and *yūkas*;
eight *aṅgulas* [are] *yavas*.
Since this does not coincide anywhere, it is merely something arbitrary.
Some have explained this verse of Śāradā differently:
one should extend the eastern thread by a fifth part;

then, at the two corners—namely the southwest and northwest produced by the western and northern threads—one should increase it by half of that fifth part at one corner and likewise by half of the fifth part at the other corner, according to the measure of half and half.

From the northwest corner (vāyavya), excluding the diagonal line, one should draw an arc reaching as far as the western end of the eastward line; likewise, from the southwest corner (nairṛtya), excluding the diagonal line, one should draw an arc reaching as far as the western end of the eastward line.
Then, from the two excluded corners—the northwest and the southwest—one should lay down two lines reaching as far as the ends of the excluded eastward line.

Because it lacks traditional authority (*asāṃpradāyikatva*), because there are no words that establish this meaning, and because it contradicts written authorities such as the *Kādimata* and others, this is a mere fabrication of one's own imagination (*svakapolakalpita*).

Since even the area (*kṣetraphala*) is excessive when calculated precisely, this is merely something trivial— the characteristic mark of those who pride themselves on being experts in mathematics and those who pride themselves on their scriptural tradition (*āgamana*).
Having given four corner-lines with one hundred and ninety-eight parts, the Lord [Śiva] then increased these portions by thirty-eight at the two hips;

from the front, on the pair of lines, there is a triangle, and then from the middle of the two hips, one should draw a semicircle outside—that shall be the excellent *kuṇḍa* shaped like a womb (*yonivat*).
Thus,
one should exclude thirty-eight parts from both sides of the western horizontal line across the two square hips—
nineteen to the south and nineteen to the north— because this contradicts the *Svakapola*, *Kriyāsāra*, *Kādimata*, *Kāmika*, *Siddhāntaśekhara*, and other authoritative texts.
And having understood that the area of the field is slightly greater than the calculated area, the great ones should be satisfied;

here, due to a scribe’s error, there is a faulty reading of *bhrāmayet* (one should cause to revolve), for by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (the short vowel replaces the long in roots ending in *m*), it becomes *bhramayet*, thus the correct reading is indeed *bhramayet*. || 54 ||
Because its nature is square, he describes the half-moon-shaped sacrificial pit (*ardhacandrakuṇḍa*) with the words "made square.
By the word "field" (*kṣetra*), as before, the central line is understood; one should divide that into ten parts.

Then, from one part [of the square] at the bottom and northwards, one should drop a cord for the bowstring; then, by revolving it with that measurement, this beautiful pit, resembling a half-moon, shall come into being. || 56 ||

Having left [the center] to the right of the top, one should drop a chord-measure of an arbitrary length from the front point on the northern side; this is indicated by the phrase "stretching that out. Then, from that measurement at the center, one should rotate [the compass] according to the diameter-measure; the method for this is as follows.

Having fixed the beginning of the cord at the junction of the chord-line and the middle line, one should rotate it from that point where it is held in the northern part up to the end of the chord-line;
thus there arises a pit resembling a half-moon facing north.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Now the half-moon [pit] is described."
In the south, that [rite] for killing is always recommended when facing north.
Thus,
here is the derivation of the field;
from that, by discarding one-tenth from both sides, there results the discarding of one-fifth of the whole.

And these [units] are: finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), barley-corns (*yava*), nit-mites (*yūka*), lice-eggs (*likhyā*), hair-tips (*bālāgra*), dust-particles (*reṇu*), *trasareṇu*, and atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Thus, this remaining diameter (*vyāsa*)—consisting of finger-breadths, barley-corns, nit-mites, lice-eggs, hair-tips, dust-particles, *trasareṇus*, and atoms—is nineteen finger-breadths plus one-fifth for the purpose of calculating the area; when the area is calculated using this diameter, the resulting area is three finger-breadths plus half a barley-corn greater.
Since that was overlooked by the Teacher due to its insignificance, the method applicable to all [mandalas] without exception— which does not deviate from the area of the field— is now stated:
when the cord is divided into twenty-four parts, the width in the half-moon [mandala] is [one part].
Three twentieths of one part make nineteen sub-divisions; by this measurement, using a circular arc, [the petals] are formed at the tips of the petals with the aid of a cord.
Then this Vyāsa [states]: "Fingers, barley-corns, nits, lice-eggs, hair-tips, dust-particles, water-drops, and atoms.

Then, regarding the finger-breadth: barley-corns, nits, lice-eggs, hair-tips, dust-particles, water-drops, and atoms—one should discard this portion from above, and likewise discard such a portion from below.

Therein, for the purpose of calculating the area of the field, the diameter is set down as nineteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and three parts of one finger-breadth divided into twenty. This is converted into a common denominator; then, for the sake of finding the area of the circle, it is doubled.
Since the divisor is halved, the numerator consequently becomes double; thus, this is the complete diameter of the circle.

Then, the area of the half-moon should be understood as subtle by taking the area obtained from the verse beginning with "The square of the diameter is nine times the fire" (*bhanavāgni*) and so forth—just as in all other cases—and halving that.
Alternatively, in a pit measuring two cubits, one should double the square of this [diameter] and take its square root;
that itself is the diameter there.
This same [method] should be inferred for what follows as well;
this is the definition of a certain person who possesses pride in his knowledge of mathematics,
from the third chapter.
If a square field is divided into twenty-four parts,
one should divide it by nineteen parts plus twelve-twentieths (one and three-fifths) of a part.

One should divide the circumference of the circle from the eastern limit; the arc situated toward the west should be pierced at that point with a horizontal thread from the east, and from that [piercing], the [perpendicular] line shall arise.
Resembling the moon in the midst of a lunar mansion, it is enchanting to those with right vision.
Thus, even by this subtle calculation, there is a deficiency of three finger-breadths;
therefore, the area of the field is obtained according to the method stated by Śrīdharācārya: "The square root of ten times the area derived from the square of the diameter [minus the correction]."
And that [calculation] is coarse because this is the method of the mathematical treatises (*gaṇitagraṃtha*), wherein even the derivation of results is stated to be coarse; however,
since both methods were taught by the venerable Śrīdhara Ācārya in his *Bṛhatpaddhati*, only the coarse methods have been written down in their summary, the *Triśatī* treatise.
However, Bhāskarācārya has stated in the *Līlāvatī* that even the subtle methods are indeed coarse;
having examined that extensive recension, I have derived this subtle result.
If one considers that alone to be the subtle [result], then there would be an excessive abundance of the result in the original root.
Furthermore, because it faces north, the statement that one should extend the thread from the eastern limit to the western limit of the bow-shape is indeed inconsistent;

for while describing the characteristic of the *yoni* himself in his own work, he said: "In the fire-pits situated in the directions of Indra (East), Agni (Southeast), and Yama (South), this [yoni] is exactly at the middle part, above the girdle."

The claim that “having placed the moon-faced [line] in the direction of Yama” indicates that Kātyāyana failed to notice even the contradiction between the earlier and later parts of his own work is trivial;

as for the statement of Kātyāyana in the *Śulba-sūtra*: “One desiring to make a circle into a square, having divided the diameter into fifteen parts, should discard two; the remainder is the *karaṇī* (the side of the resulting square).”
That too is intended as a rough estimate and not as an exact calculation;
nevertheless, if doubt should arise in the mind of any great person,
he should perform a direct examination.

Having caused a square vessel one cubit in measure to be made from metal, wood, or clay, and having likewise caused a circular vessel one cubit in measure to be made according to the dimensions mentioned by him or by me, one should fill the square vessel completely with water and fill the circular vessel with that very same water.
That circular vessel which reaches perfect fullness should be considered pure.

Regarding its further characteristic: in a four-cornered field where the quality is situated at the center of the Jina-fraction (one-twelfth), the wise person should leave out one and a half [units] below and the same amount above.
Subtract a sixteenth part from that portion; above it, draw a chord equal to half the circumference. From that measurement as well, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is shaped like a half-moon.
Thus,
here the width is nineteen finger-breadths and one and a half barley-corns;
however, by precise calculation, it is five finger-breadths less.
Even by the method of gross calculation performed therein, it becomes deficient by half a finger-breadth; as for that which is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"In a field divided into four parts, one should place [the lines] on both sides..."
One should mark each part according to that measurement from the front;

then one should draw two lines, and thus the quadrangular *kuṇḍa* is described. That [claim] which was stated—that it should be corroborated by the statement of Kātyāyana, "the mandala is quadrangular"—is also unproven, because there is no corroboration.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara, however, it is said: "When a square field has been divided into nine equal parts, one should then discard one part each on the south and the north; by drawing a circle with a thread from the middle of the seven parts, an *ardhacandra* (half-moon) is formed."

Thus, in the Kāmika as well: "When the square [area] is divided by the planets (nine), one should discard the first and last [results]; then, by the measure of seven middle parts, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a crescent moon through rotation."
Thus, in both these cases, the diameter is eighteen finger-breadths plus two-thirds; therefore, the area is extremely small. || 55 || 56 ||
Regarding the square sacrificial pit (*vāstu-kuṇḍa*) by virtue of its square nature, he says "by four":
when the field has been divided into four parts along the central line of the square,
one should increase each part on both sides— namely, on the sides of the horizontal westward line— by one portion.
From that measurement, one should mark a point in front at the measure of a fourth part; then one should lay down three threads. The procedure for this is as follows:
One [method] is that one should extend the western line as far as the two marks on the sides of the horizontal and western lines.
A second [method] is that one should drop a cord from the avoided southwest corner to the mark placed at the tip of the middle line.
A third [method] is that one should drop a cord from the avoided northwest corner to the mark placed at the tip of the middle line.
Thus, the triangular *kuṇḍa* has its apex pointing upward and its base facing east;
as it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The triangular *kuṇḍa* is prescribed for the southwest; the *kuṇḍa* shown for the purpose of inciting hatred follows the same procedure as before."
Thus, here the derivation of the area is as follows:

by the rule "the earth [side] is the base, the perpendicular from it is the height; the area of the figure is the product of half the base and the height," etc., the resulting area is thirty-six *aṅgulas* less than a triangle.
Since the two sides are thirty-six units and the square root of their sum is the hypotenuse— calculated according to that method— the two [sides] consist of twenty-five units; however,
in the case of a triangular pit (*trāstra-kuṇḍa*), equality among the three sides is required,
and for that purpose, some explain it otherwise.
When the field has been divided into four parts, one should increase each part by one unit on both sides.
Then, at the distance from that [increase] which is thirty-six units, one should mark the front;
this is the method for marking there.
Having placed the beginning of a thread measuring thirty-six *aṅgulas* at the two sides that have been excluded, one should mark the tip of the eastern thread;
then, as before, one should lay down three threads.
When this is done, equality of the three sides is achieved.

They say that by meeting on both sides and adding four *yava*s, the equality of the area of the hand-measure (*hasta-kṣetra-phala*) is achieved; this is what is indicated by the word "wise" (*budha*). However, I shall now state a method that applies universally so that the figure becomes an equilateral triangle and its area is neither less nor more than the original.
When the cord is divided into twenty-four parts,
one should discard nine parts from one side and nineteen parts from both sides combined— discarding them alternately— and from these three equal cords, a triangle shall arise.
The meaning of this is as follows:
one should omit six finger-breadths, plus two barley-corns less a yava, on one side; likewise on the second side.

Then, excluding the eastern thread, it measures seven fingers, four barley-corns, and six yūkas; from there, the ground measures [seven] fingers, [four] barley-corns, and [six] yūkas, while this perpendicular (lamba) measures one and a half likhyās and so forth, [namely] seven fingers, four barley-corns, and six yūkas.

In that regard, for the purpose of calculating the area of the figure according to the method "the segment of the sum of the base and the face multiplied by the perpendicular," the placement of the perpendicular (*lamba*) is as follows: the base is reduced to a common denominator, the face is zero, and thus their sum is this very [base]; then, because the divisor is doubled, one applies the rule "the segment of the sum of the base and the face multiplied by the perpendicular. When divided by the divisor, the resulting quotient is the area of the figure.
Here, the three sides are indeed equal; the equality of the sides has also been stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the field into eight parts, one part on each side is placed outside."
Having fixed that, one should lay down three lines equally using that mental thread.
Thus,
even here, the area of the field certainly deviates [from the expected value],
because the perpendicular is the area of the field.
Because it is excessively deficient, others explain it thus:
"two degrees on each side" means two degrees on one side and two degrees on the second side; consequently, fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) become less within the area of the result.
Furthermore, there is a correspondence with the meaning of the verse from the *Śāradā-tantra* as explained in the second [chapter],
and in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra* as well, the equality of the arms is stated:
"One should certainly lay down the thread, thirty-two finger-breadths in length, in three parts."
Having first prepared the pit, one should then delineate a triangle.
Thus,
even here the area of the field certainly deviates,
because [the calculation] is in finger-breadths (aṅgula) and barley-corns (yava), while the height is the area of the field.

Elsewhere also: "Having set aside two parts from the sides of that field which was divided into six parts during the night, the wise man should lay down two lines using that measurement; this shall be the *kuṇḍa* known as Rudranetrāstra."
Thus,
these two characteristics are stated with reference to the sixfold enclosure lines; furthermore, equal-sidedness is also mentioned in the Kādima system described below.
Regarding this, I have replied to those unskilled in calculation:
according to the *Śāradātilaka*, however, for those who know calculation, the square root of the difference between the squares of the perpendicular and the side is produced as the perpendicular.
Thus, having derived the perpendicular and computed the area of the figure, one should be satisfied;

or else, even without the perpendicular, half the sum of all the sides placed in four positions and diminished by the [opposite] sides, and the square root of their product, is the approximate result;
this is declared to be the exact result for a quadrilateral, but not for a triangle.
In this manner, one should bring [the calculation] to completion and be satisfied;
now, the method for bringing about the non-obstruction of the remainder of the root and so forth is stated:
"The remainder of the root, multiplied by the number of parts, should then be divided."
The square root of twice the [number] multiplied by one is considered to be the parts of the result.

Alternatively, according to the method stated by Bhāskarācārya: "The square root of the difference between the square of the multiplier and the product of the divisor and the numerator, multiplied by the multiplier and divided by the divisor, will be close [to the true value]."
Thus, this [treatise] is near its root;
for there exists in someone who is both excessively proud of his mathematical knowledge and devoid of pride in the scriptures a dual characteristic:
the state of being a field (*kṣetratva*) and the desire for the fourfold [arrangement] in front, below, and on both sides.
Excluding the [central] line, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be formed by three lines drawn with the *trāstra* mantra.
Thus,

when the middle quality of the field is divided into shares for the Jina, the wise one should increase the arrows by one-sixteenth part separately at the two shoulders; then, excluding the eighth part, ten lines are applied here, and by using three of those, the *kuṇḍa* is formed.
Thus,
here the previously mentioned characteristic is that one *trāstra* is slightly hanging down, while the second is greatly hanging down;
and in the measurement of the field, there is a deficiency of one *yava*.

If it is argued that this [shape] is called a triangular *kuṇḍa* because its area is equal to that [of the square] and because it has a triangular form, then the essential nature of the *kuṇḍa* would be inconsistent; for in that case,
the measurements would be such that the perpendicular (*lamba*) is [measured in] finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and barley-corns (*yava*).
The area in *bhūs* is finger-breadths;
here too, the field-area is exactly the same.
In this way, the triangular pit (*kuṇḍa*) may be [calculated] in a thousandfold manner.
Therefore, in the case of a triangular pit (*trikuṇḍa*), the mere calculation of the area is not the sole authority;
rather, equilateral triangularity is also necessarily required. Enough of this.

Now, Kātyāyana states in the *Śulba-sūtra*: "Having made a square twice the size of the fire-altar (*agni*) in the *prauga* (fore-part), including its wings and tail—[the altar] which has its front-measuring-line in the middle and its two hips at the [two corners]—that is the fire-altar."
The meaning of this is stated concisely:
one should lay out the field that one intends to make triangular by doubling it.
Then, from both sides of the western corner-line toward the tip of the central line, one should apply two lines.
The area of this [altar] exceeds by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) and so forth;
however, the commentator on that [text] has explained that the seer (*ṛṣi*) overlooked this so that there might not be mental distress for the student.
This hanging [portion], moreover, is for the purpose of constructing the brick-pile (*iṣṭakā-citi*) therein.
But it is not for the purpose of producing the shape of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
This is the third chapter.
If it is argued: "Let this very statement from the *Kalpakalpa* be the authoritative proof for producing the shape of a sacrificial pit," [the response follows].

In that case, a contradiction is observed among the views of the authors of the *Śāradātilaka* and others, as well as in many other works composed by sages, such as the *Kādimata*, *Pañcarātra*, *Kāmika*, *Kriyāsāra*, *Siddhāntaśekhara*, *Āmnāyarahasya*, and *Mahākapilapañcarātra*.
Consequently, there would indeed be doubt as to which [view] should be accepted.
Nor can it be argued that the *Kalpasūtras*, having their roots in directly perceived Śruti, possess greater authority than the *Smṛtis*, whose roots in Śruti are merely inferential.

This is because the nature of a *kalpa* consists in the compilation of the meanings of Vedic texts (*śruti*) as imagined through indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other means found in various recensions (*śākhā*); for the author of the *Bhāṣya* has established the authority of the *kalpas* in the section beginning with the sūtra "If it be said that [the Kalpas] are a manual of performance" (*prayogaśāstram iti cet*).
However, the author of the *Vārttika* has constructed this section differently;
for he does not undertake here an investigation into the authority or lack of authority of the *kalpas*.
Rather, having cited the Kalpasūtras, this is considered:

do they possess authority as independent works like the Vedas, or are they dependent on Śruti like the Smṛtis? In that regard, their authority has been established as being precisely like the Smṛtis, due to their dependence on Śruti. Furthermore, in the section concerning contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), the authors of the Bhāṣya concluded that the statement of the Kalpa-author, "The *audumbarī* post should be entirely covered," is rooted in greed because it contradicts the direct Śruti text, "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the *audumbarī*."

Therefore, because all the *smṛtis* are contradictory, there is no scope for the statement, "Where there is a conflict between two *śrutis*, both are considered *dharma*," and since it is tainted by manifest defects, there is no optionality; thus, doubt alone remains.
Consequently, there would be a total non-performance of the rite prescribed therein.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only that which possesses equilateral sides and equal area is the triangular sacrificial pit (*tri-kona-kuṇḍa*).
Among all the descriptions of characteristics [for a sacrificial ground], some deviate regarding the area and yield, while others deviate regarding the equality of the sides.
Therefore, it should be understood that those [descriptions] have as their result merely the production of a square shape.
However, in another text it is said: "When the field has been divided into five parts, one should discard two parts from the exterior."
Having left [space] on neither side and having grasped the middle, one should draw two ear-threads; thus a triangle clearly comes into being.
Thus,
in this case, there is equality of the three sides when ninety-two finger-breadths are subtracted.
When the field has been made square, one-eighth of the field is outside.
One should place three threads at the tip of the central line (garbhasūtra) on both sides of the western thread;
this is said to be the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus it is said.
And here, there are one hundred and seventy angulas less [than required], and the sides are unequal. One should, however, expand the sixth part of that very [measurement] on both sides.
Then, each of the two [side] threads should be marked with that measurement from the last thread.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The wise man should place one [part] outside on a field divided into eighteen parts; by that measurement he should rotate [the cord] to form an excellent circular *kuṇḍa*."
By means of its placement from the end of the Brahma-sūtra down to its tip as a support.
Thus, according to the Kādima system, there are one hundred and thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) less than the required for equal sides;
this definition refers to the sixty-sixth line of the circumference.
As it is stated in the Kāmika: "Divided by eight, with three fish-marks [at the joints], it becomes the night-stalker (the lunar month)."

In this regard, the authors of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* have explained that there is an increase of one part at each of the three locations; according to their view, sixty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) are added. Others, however, have explained that there is an increase of the bamboo beam at the front, and on both sides, an increase of one part by half the value of the wealth.
In that opinion, sixty-four finger-breadths are deficient;
in both opinions, however, the arms remain unequal—enough said.
Regarding the circular pit (*kuṇḍa*) due to its square nature, he says "eighteen" and so forth.

In the field, as before, when the middle line of the square is divided into eighteen parts—that is, partitioned eighteenfold—one should exclude one part on any line on the outside. By that measure, one should rotate [the cord] from the center using that excluded measure; then there is a circular pit facing the east.

Because there is nothing superior to it, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*). Here, the field (*kṣetra*) is the basis of calculation; therein, eighteen parts constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), which consists of [eighteen] barley grains (*yava*) and [eighteen] louse-eggs (*yūkā*).

In that case, when the square (vṛtta) has been made and the diameter (vyāsa) established, if it is doubled, there are finger-breadths (aṅgula), barley-corns (yava), and louse-eggs (yūkā); so much is reduced. Then, for one finger-breadth, there are two thirds. This diameter is thus reduced to a common denominator (savarṇita). Alternatively, the arrangement (nyāsa) is exactly according to the method stated by the author of the treatise.

In that case, eighteen parts (aṃśīs) constitute one ninth part (navamāṃśa). To achieve a common denominator, the arrangement is as follows: [the fractions] are reduced by three, and that same [resulting] value is then squared according to the method beginning with "the square of the diameter," and so forth. Thus, the area obtained is five hundred and fifty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
