Consequently, a field of eighteen finger-breadths remains deficient. Therefore, a method applicable to all cases that does not deviate from the true area is stated: "In a circular kuṇḍa, one should divide the central cord into twenty-four parts."
A circle drawn outside from the center by means of a rotation, measuring one and a half parts plus a twenty-fifth part of a single part, is declared to be the *kuṇḍa*.

In this context, one *aṅgula* consisting of the *saṅghāṃśa* (the aggregate portion) comprises four *yavas*, twenty-five parts of one [unit], along with two *yūkas* and one *likhyā*. When the circle is made, these values are doubled: [two] *aṅgulas*, [eight] *yavas*, [two] *yūkas*, and [two] *likhyās*. By means of that, the calculation for the diameter of everything is thus rendered homogeneous: "The square of the diameter [is divided] by sixty-three. This is the third chapter.
The area obtained by the above method is the area according to precise calculation.

However, in the *Śulba-sūtra*, Kātyāyana states: "One desiring to transform a square into a circle should drop a cord from the center to a corner and draw a circle around it from that side; whatever remains in excess, one should draw the circle together with a third of that [excess]. This is the solution.
Here, the word *aṃśa* refers to a corner (*koṇa*).
That half of the ear-line (*karṇasūtra*) is [four] finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) minus two *yūkās*. And that [half] is five finger-breadths minus two *yūkās* from the middle line (*madhyasūtra*).
Its excess is one-third of it: one finger-breadth and two-thirds of a finger-breadth; by that, the radius (*vyāsārdha*) is four finger-breadths and two-thirds of a finger-breadth.
This diameter, when doubled and reduced to a common denominator, results in an increase of ten finger-breadths in the area of this field.

As for the definition of those who pride themselves on their knowledge of calculation: it is that which, having divided the middle cord of the field sixteenfold, excludes the portion situated at the front.
Then, by revolving here within each individual circle, there arises the appearance of the inner consciousness within the mandala-pit;
in this case, the diameter is twenty-seven finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and its area is [calculated as follows] finger-breadths.
In this regard, the claim that "four *aṅgula*s are deficient" is also not correct.
For it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The circular *kuṇḍa* here is said to be [formed] by the subtraction of one-eighth of the distance between the ears (*karṇa*).
'Subtraction' (*saṃnyāsa*) is the proper reduction [of measurement] from the front."

In this regard, there is a great discrepancy, as [the measurement] is fourteen finger-breadths plus one-eighth for half the width. However, in another text it is said: "Having first made a square according to the measurement of the sacrificial pit's field, and having divided that into nine parts, one should set aside one part on the outside."
Therefore, having grasped the center in this manner, it becomes a circle through that rotation.
Thus,
here the diameter consists of twenty-nine finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus one-third of one;
by that, the interval is larger.

Some say that one part should be placed outside, with the remainder [to be divided] by halves; thus they maintain that there is syntactic unity [with the preceding]. However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* it is said: "When the square has been well established, one should place an eighth part of the field in the cardinal directions from the center, along its measuring-line."
Thus, by means of wandering and causing to wander, the Kuṇḍa is described.
Thus it is said.
Here, the diameter is thirty finger-breadths; therefore, there is a very great difference. Consequently, the statement from the Siddhāntaśekhara is interpreted differently by some.

One should place one-eighth part of the field in the external directions; the remainder is to be divided into half-and-half portions. Thus, by combining both sides, it becomes one-eighth of the whole.
At that time, the width and the area of the field are each reduced by four *aṅgulas*.
This should be understood according to precise calculation.
If a rough calculation were to be accepted, there would indeed be a great discrepancy with the written statement of Kātyāyana; therefore, enough of this.
From the *Śāradātilaka*:
One should divide the field eightfold on both sides of the central line;
one should place a single part on each side, and with this same part, [mark] from the center.
The most excellent of embodied beings should draw four fish-designs on both sides;
then he should lay down six lines to form the most excellent hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Regarding the hexagonal *kuṇḍa* due to its four-cornered nature, he says: "In eight parts. Here, the phrase "the middle line" (*madhyasūtra*) refers to the line extending from south to north; in this context, by the term "middle line," the south-north oriented line is understood.
Because of the statement "on the two sides," otherwise one would have simply said "below and above";
on its two sides— the southern and northern tips— one should place one part each and exclude the exterior.

Then, by this measurement—free from pride, free from marks, and from the middle and the two sides—one should form four fish-marks on the southern and northern sides of the center of the thread extending south and north, in the eastern and western sections;
this meaning is to be understood through this very tradition, as stated by the "best of those who know the Tantras.
In that regard, the method for producing the fish-marks is as follows:

Having placed the beginning of a cord, measured by the mark made to the north from the center of the field, at the center of the field, one should draw a semicircle in the interval between the east and the northeast. Then, having placed the beginning of that same cord at the mark made to the north, one should draw another semicircle intersecting the first; thus is the "fish" figure (matsya) accomplished in the interval between the directions of the east and the northeast. In the same manner, from the center of the field and from the mark made to the south, one should likewise form a "fish" in the interval between the directions of the east and the southeast.
In this very manner, one should successively draw two fish-marks between the west and the northwest, and between the west and the southwest.

Then, from the northern mark, one should lay down a first thread reaching as far as the fish-mark between the east and the northeast, and a second thread reaching as far as the fish-mark between the west and the northwest.

Next, from the southern mark, one should lay down a first thread reaching as far as the fish-mark between the east and the southeast, and a second thread reaching as far as the fish-mark between the west and the southwest.
In this manner, having laid down four threads,
one thread should then be given from the two eastern fish to each other, and likewise one thread from the two western fish to each other.
Thus, by the intersection of six threads, there arises a six-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) facing the east.

This has been stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the field into eight parts, having placed one part on each of the two outer sides, one should lay out [the lines] from the center according to this measurement so that they are equal. One should lay down six lines—four for the corners and two for the sides; by means of these, there shall be a six-cornered (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Thus it is said.

In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "When a square has been established as equal, one should add an eighth part of the field on the outside from that location at the two tips of the central thread (*garbhasūtra*). Having placed the measuring instrument—a cord of the same length as the measurement of the center of the womb—on the outer portion at the center of the womb, [one should mark] with the cord. [End of] the Third Chapter.

"Then, on the north and south, outside the two [central] lines; then in the outer portion of the north, in the pair of norths; thereupon, one should lay down six lines in sequence—this is declared to be the hexagonal *kuṇḍa*.

Here, "of the central line" refers to the line running from south to north. "On the north and south" means on the northern side and the southern side of the center of that south-to-north line, excluding the line itself.
Here, for the derivation of the area, one should imagine two unequal quadrilaterals;
then, for one of them, let the base be *aṅgula*s, the face [the top side] be *b*, and the perpendicular height be *h*.
Then, by the method stated as "the area of the sum of the sides multiplied by the length," the resulting area for the first quadrilateral is four *yavas* more [than expected];
likewise, for the second quadrilateral as well, it is four *yavas* more; when these are combined together—
Thus, there are nine additional finger-breadths, and the equality of the six sides is indeed established;

here, the calculation of the perpendicular height is to be understood by means of the rule: "The square root of the difference between the square of the side and the square of half the base is produced as the perpendicular."
Alternatively, one may conceive of three fields:
a long quadrangle in the center and two triangles on the sides;
therein, the area of the long quadrangle is as follows.
The yield of one *āsra* is exactly four *yava*s more [than the standard];
likewise for the second, and thus the total area of the field is the sum of these two.
Thus, having calculated four unequal squares, one should be satisfied when the result for each comes out to be two *yavas*.
When six triangles are calculated, the result for each should be verified as being four *yavas* more;
in this way, the verification of results through other methods should also be inferred.
Others, however, describe it differently:
one should divide the central line of the square field into eight parts;
one part each should be placed below and above, on both sides of the central line and the eastern line.
On both sides, below and above the central line that runs from south to north, one should set aside one part;
then, from the center and by this measurement, one should form four fish-marks on the two sides. The method for forming those fish-marks is as follows:
From the two marks made by the east-west thread, one should draw two fish-shapes to the south and north using that same measurement.

There, where the south-north line intersects the east-west boundary line of the square, one should mark that boundary line one finger-breadth above and below. Then, having drawn a semicircle in the southern portion of the previously made mark on the east, one should draw a semicircle from the southern mark on the boundary line such that it intersects the previous mark;
thus is the formation of the "fish" (matsya) accomplished in the southern portion.

In the same way, in the northern part as well, having made two marks on the western perimeter line of the square according to the aforementioned method, one should draw two fish in the southern and northern portions of the mark made in the western direction.

Then, from the mark on the southern side excluding [the center], one should lay a thread extending to the fish in the southeastern portion, and a second thread extending to the fish in the southwestern portion.

Thus, from the northern mark [of the eastern direction] to the northern part of the western fish is the first thread; from the northern mark of the western direction to the northern part of the eastern fish is the second thread. In this way, four threads are laid out. Then, one thread is drawn between the two eastern fish marks, and another between the two western fish marks—thus it is described in the *Śāradātilaka*.
Thus, from the intersection of six lines according to the sūtra, there is a hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
herein, having constructed two unequal quadrilaterals, [one calculates] the area of one of them.
In this way, when combined with the second [statement] as well,
according to that view, there occurs eight occurrences of the phrase "on both sides of the middle line."

Furthermore, that in some places the term "middle line" (madhyasūtra) refers to the eastward line, while in others it refers to the north-south line, is inconsistent; for there is no authoritative evidence [to support this], and the word "in the middle" (madhyataḥ) would thus be rendered meaningless.
The courtyard formed between the lines of the square perimeter for the purpose of producing a fish-figure (*matsya*) is likewise a fabrication of one's own fancy;
it is thirty-six finger-breadths less than the area of the field, and its possession of unequal sides is a manifestation of ignorance.

As for their desire, in the commentary on this very [work], that the corners should fall upon the eastern and western parts of the original line—that results in nothing but fish-figures. Now, many methods may be conceived there for the purpose of restoring equality of area.

In this regard, someone might divide the field into eight parts; one part each should be placed above and below the central line, while from the cardinal directions, [parts] are on the two sides. If the field is to be increased, then from the eighth part of the field, one should make the upper and lower lines extend as far as the cardinal lines from the eighth part of the field. Having intersected the sixth part of the field by means of the [third] quality (guṇa), thus [is formed] the northern fish-tail.
"One should cast six threads upon them; therein, the six-cornered *kuṇḍa* is supreme.

Here, having excluded eight *aṅgulas* from the central thread running from south to north, the area of the field is indeed neither less nor more [than the prescribed measure], yet there is no equality of the six sides.

And so it is said: "In a field of one hundred and eight parts, having multiplied the internal [side] by two, one should mark points on both sides of the internal thread at the increase of the *bha* (side) by the number of limbs (24);

at the remaining parts (84), there are increases of the *aṅga* (12) parts by the 'fishes' (24) in front and below; from the pair of 'fishes' (24), doubled twice (96), by the multiplication of the two sides, the hexagon is declared for those two. Even here, the area of the field is neither less nor more, yet there is no equality with the six-sided [figure].

Furthermore, this is the Vāyavya (north-western) pit, and it is oriented with its front toward the east; however, because the corners would fall exactly between the east and west, there is no space for the placement of the *yoni* [vulva-shaped altar], as it is said:
"The one most skilled in the Tantras should not place the *yoni* within the corners of the pit."
Because the placement of the *yoni* in a corner is prohibited, the rule that the *kuṇḍa* should have its front facing east is contradicted;

furthermore, this very characteristic has been stated by [the author] himself in his own work regarding the *kuṇḍas*: "The three *kuṇḍas* starting from the east have their fronts facing north, while the five *kuṇḍas* situated in the south have their *yoni*s facing north."

By stating the characteristic of the *yoni* as "the *yoni* here has its tip pointing eastward and its opening facing west," it is also said: "In the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) situated in the directions of Maghavan (East), Śikhin (South-East), Tānta (West), and [the North], this [yoni] should be placed with its girdle (*mekhalā*) in the middle part; in the southern direction, facing north; and in the western pit, facing east. Thus ends the third chapter. Therefore, the claim that there is no contradiction between earlier and later parts of his own work is merely a trifle.
And likewise,
one should increase the eastern middle sūtra by three finger-breadths;

then, from the excluded *cihna* (mark), one should produce two fish-diagrams (*matsya*) by means of the lines of the eastern perimeter of the square, measuring four finger-breadths to the south and north.
In the same way, in the western direction as well, one should increase the thread extending southward and northward by three fingers plus a sixth part of a finger;
even so, the area of the field remains no less than required.
Furthermore, many other methods may be conceived.
This is for the sake of achieving equality of area, and not merely for the sake of achieving equality of the six sides; otherwise, the irregularity of the *kuṇḍa* would result.
Therefore, in a hexagonal *kuṇḍa*, the equality of all six sides must necessarily be accompanied by the equality of the area.

Since the equality of the six arms is taught here in the *Kriyāsāra*, the *Kādima*, the *Kāmika*, and also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, the method common to all of them is stated as follows: One should divide the central line of the hexagram into twenty-four parts;
from the center, [the lines] are reduced by twenty-three parts minus one-ninthth of each.
"One should rotate it; by means of that, one should mark the circle of the desired circumference with a radius equal to half its diameter.
By drawing six lines at six points, that becomes a hexagon.
This is the meaning of this [verse].
Three parts are three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). What is that? It is diminished by one-ninth of one [finger-breadth].
Therefore, this diameter is [calculated as] fingers, barley-corns, and slightly less than *yūkās*.

For the purpose of reducing it to a common denomination (*savarṇana*), the mathematical operation (*nyāsa*) is performed; the square root of that is the radius, which is one-fourth of the diameter, and this very value is the offset (*abādhā*).
Then, the perpendicular (*lamba*) is derived by means of the rule: "The square roots of the squares of the respective offsets and the sides... and so forth.

In the section for the sum of the hypotenuses, the result obtained by multiplying by the sagitta and dividing by the divisor is the area of the first irregular quadrilateral; likewise for the second. The total area is the sum of these two areas.

Alternatively, one may construct a long quadrilateral in the middle and two triangles on the two sides. Therein, the arrow (*śara*) is one-fourth of the diameter; this very value is the perpendicular (*lamba*) of the triangle on both sides. Then, the square root of the product of the diameter minus the arrow and the arrow itself, doubled, becomes the chord (*jīvā*) here. Thus, the chord calculated by this method is slightly less [than the true value].

Then, by the rule "the product of the base and the height of a figure that is both intermediate and rectangular, as well as of a rectangle," one should calculate the area for the two triangles as before; the total area of the field is obtained by summing all these.
In this manner, having conceived either four unequal quadrilaterals or six triangles, the consistency of the results should be inferred.
Here, there is equality among all six sides.

That [should be understood] by calculating the radii according to the method stated by Bhāskarācārya: "When the circumference of the circle is multiplied by the digits 0, 0, 0, 15, 6, and 9, and divided by the digits 0, 0, 0, 15, 12, and 12, the radii are obtained in sequence.
As for what is said in the *Kādimata*: "Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-twelfth of its middle [measurement],"...
Having made the circumference clear by that same measurement in such a manner—this is from the *Śāradātilaka*—if one has made it square, one should divide it into eighteen parts;
having excluded one part from the outside, one should rotate [the cord] with that to form a circle. One should arrange three circles for the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and so forth on the outside.
"This lotus-pit (padmakuṇḍa) is said to be pleasing to the eyes. Having drawn a circle within that [larger] circle, one should perform the marking;
there, by the laying down of six lines, the pit becomes hexagonal.
In this case, out of the total area of five hundred and sixty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas), seventy-two finger-breadths are deficient.
The equality of the arms indeed exists [in that case].
According to the rule, "By adding six and eight parts, with four fish-tails, there shall be a hexagon," however, there is a great discrepancy in the *Kāmika* [Tantra];
yet, the equality of the arms indeed exists [there as well].
This definition is intended with reference to the sixty-sixth perimeter line.

As for the explanation given by the author of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, who states that one should place four marks on the eastern and western perimeter lines of the square in accordance with the four [lines] extending from that pillar—that should be disregarded, as it is merely devised according to the area of the field; for there is an absence of such words [in the source texts] and an absence of equality in the sides. He describes the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) as having the square as its basis, using the phrase "made into a square" (*caturastrīkṛtam*).
This has been explained regarding the circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*).

In that case, one should fashion three circles for the pericarp and so forth on the outside. If three circles are made there on the exterior of the circle already constructed, then: "The excavation is said to be as wide as the extent of the pit."
Because of this statement, it is not known how large the *kuṇḍa* should be; thus, this has not been explained.

What then? The repetition [of the word] "outside" (*bahiḥ*) implies "from the middle" (*madhyāt*). Therefore, the meaning is that once the circle is made, one should make three circles outside the middle—that is, outside the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus drawn [the circle] as before, one should rotate three circles within that;
having rotated them in this manner, one should fashion the shape of a lotus with the pericarp and so forth.
Then, the very circle that was drawn on the outermost edge shall become the circle at the tips of the petals.
In that case, if the tip of the petal is omitted when constructing the petals, there would be an extreme deficiency in the area of the field.
Previously, in the circular *kuṇḍa*, a deficiency of eighteen *aṅgulas* was shown;
here, there would be a deficiency even greater than that.
Therefore, it is explained by some as follows:

"That which was stated by the author of the treatise as a *vṛtta* (circle) refers merely to the inclusion of the field; the meaning is that it is the circle of the field's boundary (*kṣetrasīmāvṛtta*).
[This is] in the context of the forthcoming construction of the lotus: 'Having abandoned a twelfth part of the lotus-field on the outside, O wise one...'"

One should divide that middle portion into three equal parts by means of three circles. As it is stated [in the third chapter]: "Thus it has been said. Here, one-twelfth of the diameter is two and a quarter *aṅgulas*. There, below that which is the circle of Soma (*somāvṛtta*), one should draw a circle at a distance of one *aṅgula* and one *yava*.
Above that as well, one should construct a circle using that same measurement.
By that means, a lunar (Soma) circle is formed in the center.
Therein, the diameter of the inner circle is twenty-four finger-breadths and three barley-corns.
Therein, one should draw three circles with equal divisions.
Then, by means of a radius diminished by one-twelfth part, one should form the tips of the petals.
In that regard, the diameter of the outer circle is twenty-eight finger-breadths and seven barley-corns.
In that case, having combined the areas of both the lower and upper sectors and taking half of this sum as the area of the sector,
there is still an error here;
for when the area of the lower sector and the area of the uppermost sector are added together and halved, it results in being thirteen *aṅgulas* less than the actual value.
In reality, however, that method for constructing the lotus which produces the *padmakṣetra* should be understood as applying only to the *sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala* and similar diagrams.
In the construction of the nine sacrificial pits (*navakuṇḍa*), there would be an excess of area in that [method].

As for what the author states in the *Kriyāsāra*, namely, "three circles outside the pericarp and so forth," or "three circles," that should be understood as referring specifically to the circles for the petals and the ground.
To indicate that one should make the circle at the tip of the petal larger, its area is also slightly greater.
Therefore, it should be understood that in the construction of a lotus-shaped reservoir (padmakuṇḍa), there are exactly five circles;
consequently, the method for constructing the moon [circle] as described here does not apply in this case.
Here, the method that is universally applicable and never deviates from the area of the field is stated:
one should divide the central cord of the lotus-pool into twenty-four parts.

One should rotate [the compass] from the center of the pericarp (karṇikā) with a radius equal to half the diameter of the bamboo-staff (vaṃśa). On a circle with a radius equal to one-sixth of that diameter, the filaments (keśara) are placed. On a circle with a radius equal to one-ninth of that diameter, there shall be the space between the petals (pattramadhyabhūḥ). From half a circle of twelve parts, the base of the petal (pattroṅghabhūḥ) is prescribed. Having made half a circle of fifteen parts—diminished by five parts, leaving one part, which is divided into sixty-four sub-parts—one should fashion the tips of the petals from the ends of the lines to the edge of the petals, bending them accordingly. Here, in the center, the pericarp has a diameter of six finger-breadths (aṅgula); for it will be stated later: "Whatever is the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the excavation is said to be of that same measure."
By that [proportion], the excavation for the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is also obtained.
Therein, the pericarp should be made somewhat elevated;

although its height is not explicitly stated here, nevertheless, in the description of the navel (*nābhi*), he will say: "the navel of one cubit [should be] provided with two and four finger-breadths."
Therefore, that [base] is four *aṅgulas* in width and one *aṅgula* in height.

In this regard, if the height of a base four *aṅgulas* wide is one *aṅgula*, then what would be the height of one six *aṅgulas* wide? Thus, the height should be calculated by means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*). Regarding this, the formula for the rule of three is: "The standard measure (*pramāṇa*) and the desired quantity (*icchā*) are of the same kind and occupy the first and last positions; the result (*phala*) is of a different kind."

"In the middle, [the value] multiplied by that [last term] and divided by the first shall be the result of the proportion; the reverse rule applies in the case of inverse calculation. Thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.

Regarding this, the arrangement for the rule of three (*trairāśika*) is as follows: the middle value is multiplied by the last and divided by the first; the quotient is the height. This is stated in the *Kāmika*: "Then one should fashion the elevation according to the measurement of one-eighth of the pericarp."
Therefore, the author will state later in the text: "One should avoid the yoni in a yoni-shaped pit, and the navel in an alakūṇḍa.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should not place a yoni within a yoni; one should not fashion a lotus within a lotus."
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "O Four-faced One, one should not fashion a yoni or a navel within the lotus-pit; rather, they should be made in sequence [outside].
Therefore, having established the height of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) at three finger-breadths, the remainder should be excavated.

Having also excavated the location for the filaments (*keśara*), one should place the filaments in the lower portion. The entire middle of each petal should be excavated so as to take the form of the tip of a petal.
There, one should skillfully fashion the tips of the petals with the outer hand, ensuring that only half of the circle—which lies outside the circle having a diameter of twenty-four—is taken up.
The curvature of the petals from the very hand [of the artisan] is the "petal-soma-line" (*pattra-somarekhā*).
From the intersection of the circle drawn on the ground for the petal-base up to the center of the petal, by drawing lines on both sides, this is the lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*).
Herein follows the proof of the area.

In the case of the twenty-four-fold circle, the area as before is [calculated in] finger-breadths (aṅgula), barley-corns (yava), and louse-eggs (yūkā). For the outer circle of one finger-breadth, with a diameter of nineteen finger-breadths reduced by sixty-four sixtieths of ten, the area is [calculated in] finger-breadths, barley-corns, and louse-eggs. This is the total combined.
For this purpose, the area of the field [is calculated].
This result is extremely subtle.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The pericarp should be formed by dividing the square into eight parts."
One should fashion the filaments with one part outside of that.

In the third [layer], one should carefully fashion the centers of the petals; in the fourth, the tips of the petals; and outside the square, one should likewise diligently fashion the points of the petals.
Thus [it is said].

Here, the area of the field is four *aṅgulas* greater. As for that which is stated in the manual (*lakṣaṇa*) by those who pride themselves on being experts in calculation: "In a square field, a circle is made with one-thirtieth of the length; it is further reduced by one-sixtieth of the field's diameter, diminished by its fifths."
One should fashion the tips of the petals by leaving out half the field; this [mandala] would be thirty parts in width, and by twice that amount it becomes a circle on the outside.
Here, one should dig a pit with a height equal to half its own diameter, having omitted the inner pericarp, and making it marked with filaments as an eight-petaled lotus, or else with four petals.
Thus ends the third chapter.
One should likewise divide the previously mentioned [area] into twenty-four parts.
One should fashion a square outside of it, occupying one part.
In this case, the area of the field is deficient by eleven *aṅgulas*.
Thus: "One should increase the circumference of the circle by one-eighth of its own diameter on the outside;
having increased it there from the center, one should draw a second outer circle."
Then, one should draw another [square] of that same size;
thereafter, one should divide that field sixteenfold by means of eight lines.
Just as the outer hand [line] is from the end of the thread situated in the middle of the petal,
one should draw a circle from the point of intersection, using the end of the thread situated at its side.
Just as much ground as is left out from the inner path for the sake of the tips of the petals in half the circumference, that much is taken up by the outer path.
By means of the cord-measure, there should be a pericarp in the center, and the petals should be reduced by their own [respective] proportions;
one should then excavate the entire interior according to that same form.
In this way, an excellent fire-pit arises, resembling eight petals at its navel.
Thus [it is said].
Herein there is a great inconsistency;
for even in the *Kāmika*, the state of having four petals is also mentioned.
Elsewhere it is also said: "The remaining petals may be four, eight, or even sixteen.
Having laid out the tenth part, one should rotate a single measure on the outside by that same [measure] to form the circle of the petals.
A wise man should also make a pericarp in the middle of the exterior, and the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padmakuṇḍa) should have eight petals.
Thus [it is said].
Here, there is only a slight difference.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "When the square is divided into eight parts, one should draw four circles."
The pericarp and filaments are circular, and the third [layer] is a collection of petals.
The tips of the petals should be in the fourth [square]; one should thus fashion the circles. Having placed a compass at the center of the pair of squares, one should rotate it.
Starting from the junction and revolving outward for the sake of the petals,
a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) resembling a lotus with four petals in the four directions is thus described.
Alternatively, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Thus;
however, in this case, the area of the field is extremely small.
He describes the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as being of a square nature, stating "as previously mentioned.
This refers to the area previously mentioned in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"By means of a measurement equal to half of half the corner of the inner square."
One should mark the two corners of the outer square.
One should cast eight lines toward each direction according to the rule;
this is indeed declared by those who know the ritual manual to be the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should divide the central sūtra of the square into twenty-four parts.
The meaning is that one should place one part outside in the four directions, thereby creating an outer square with a length and width of twenty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Here, the word "corner" (koṇa) refers to the corner-sūtra.
The diagonal line of the inner square is thirty-four finger-breadths minus four *yūkas*. Half of that is seventeen finger-breadths minus two *yūkas*.
Half of that is eight and a half finger-breadths minus one *yūka*.
One should mark from the two corners of that external square;
the meaning is "located on the perimeter line of the external square.
"From the two corners" refers to the north-east and south-east corners.
Thus [it is said] "by means of the Āgneya and Nairṛta [lines]," and so forth.
Then, by the intersection of eight lines toward the directions, there is an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In that regard, the method for laying down the lines is as follows.
Of the two marks at the two corner sides, one [mark] is common to both; likewise, there are four lines in the cardinal directions.
The lines of the outer square are indeed the lines connecting the centers of the pairs of marks.
Thus, there are eight lines consisting of the lines in the four directions.
In that context, because eight lines can be produced, there is the statement "one should drop eight lines.
This very point is expressed by the phrase "according to the rule.
Herein lies the derivation of the field.
In that regard, there are three fields: one in the middle is a long quadrilateral, and those on the two sides are irregular quadrilaterals.
Regarding that long [quadrilateral], one side is the first arm and the second side is the other; "in a long [quadrilateral], the product of its arms and perpendiculars" [is the rule].
By this, the resulting area is obtained in finger-breadths (aṅgula), barley-corns (yava), and louse-eggs (yūkā).

Then, for the irregular quadrilateral and so forth, the base is *mukha* (face) and the height (*lamba*) is equalized for those two; the area obtained by the rule "the product of the height and half the sum of the face and the base" is [calculated as] *aṅgulas*, *yavas*, and *yūkas*.
The same applies to the second [figure]. All combined amounts to [the total] *aṅgulas*, *yavas*, and [so on].
Therefore, it is deficient by up to forty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus one-quarter.
Furthermore, there is no equality of the eight arms.
If it is argued that the accomplishment of the *kuṇḍa* occurs simply by calculating the area as neither less nor more, then there would be many different types of eight-sided *kuṇḍas*.

For instance, when a square measuring twenty-six [units] in width and length has its two corners marked on both sides by seven *aṅgula*s plus half a *yava*, one side of the central elongated square is [x] *aṅgula*s and [y] *yava*s, and the other side is [z] *aṅgula*s and [w] *yava*s.
The area of this [central figure] is [a] *aṅgula*s and [b] *yava*s. For the pair of unequal squares, the base is [c] *aṅgula*s and [d] *yava*s, and the top is [e] *aṅgula*s and [f] *yava*s.
The length is seven and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Its area is calculated in the third chapter: [it is] finger-breadths and barley-corns (yavas).
The same applies to others as well.

The total area [of the field] is the sum of all parts. Likewise, in an outer square measuring twenty-seven units in width and length, when marked on the sides of the corners by six barley-corns and eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), the side of the resulting oblong rectangle is nine and a half finger-breadths; its area is as follows:

for each of the two unequal quadrilaterals, the base and the top are nine and a half finger-breadths, and the perpendicular height is eight finger-breadths plus six barley-corns. This is the area of one of them.
This much is also for the other [section]. The total area, when combined, is as follows:

In an outer square measuring twenty-eight units in length and breadth, marks are made on the sides of the corners at ten *aṅgula*s and one and a half *yava*s. One side of the central elongated square is thus determined; the other side is seven *aṅgula*s and five *yava*s. The area of these two unequal squares has a base of seven *aṅgula*s and five *yava*s, and a face of ten *aṅgula*s and one and a half *yava*s. The perpendicular height is ten *aṅgula*s and one and a half *yava*s.
Its area is [measured in] finger-breadths and barley-corns;
the same applies to the other [side]. The total area of the field is the sum of these.
Thousands of such varieties may be conceived;
yet not even all of those would constitute eight-sided sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*),
for it would follow that the pit lacks uniformity.
Therefore, those who know the tradition maintain that an eight-sided *kuṇḍa* is precisely that which possesses both equal eight sides and equal area.
Its universal method is now described:
one should divide the central cord of the eight-sided *kuṇḍa* into twenty-four parts.
One should place one part outside, consisting of one and a half-eighths of a part.
In the four directions, according to that measurement,
there shall be a square interior consisting of forty-six parts combined with sixty-four parts.
One should mark the exterior of the square on its three sides with seven parts;
from the intersection of the eight lines in the directions, there arises an eight-cornered figure with equal arms.

Here, the outer square has a width and length of twenty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) and three barley-corns (yava); that [inner square] is seven finger-breadths, five barley-corns, and six minute particles (yūkā). Marked at the sides of the corners by this measurement, one side of the central elongated square here is calculated, and the other side is calculated; the area of the field obtained is as before.
Thereafter, the area of the pair of unequal quadrilaterals above and below is expressed in algebraic symbols (savarṇita).
The face (mukha), the perpendicular (lamba), and [the base] are expressed in algebraic symbols; here, this is the result for one, and the same amount for the other as well.
Having thus combined the results of the diagrams, it is established here that there is equality among the eight sides;
this very [figure] should be understood as the eight-sided sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The equality of the four sides is established through direct perception.

For the other four [types of altars], however, it should be understood by the method stated as: "The conjunction of their two sides is the ear (diagonal), O Karṇa. By the word *tat* (their), the two sides (*koṭi*) and the base (*bhuja*) situated outside the square are meant, as well as those standing above that diagonal. Alternatively, another easy method is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"In an eight-sided altar (*kuṇḍa*), one should divide the central cord into twenty-four parts."

Having divided [the circle] into one-third and thirty parts, and proceeding with an increase of one part, a circle is formed; in its center, by drawing eight lines in the cardinal directions, an equal octagon is produced,
wherein all eight sides are equal.

But that [radius] is to be calculated according to the method stated by Bhāskarācārya: "The sine [of the arc] is obtained by multiplying the sine of the desired degrees by the radius and dividing by the radius; when the circumference is multiplied by the radius and divided by the product of zero, zero, sky, and sun (1200), the sines are obtained in sequence."
Regarding the characteristics of the *gaṇitajñāna*: one should remove the middle line of the square by one-sixth part, increased by one-eighteenth part;
having thus created an inner square of that same measurement extending outward, one should mark it at every half-point of the corners.
Then, from each of the eight points, the wise man should draw a thread toward each mark; having smoothed the space between those intersections,
he likewise forms both squares.
One should show the eight-sided [altar] and the pit, which have equal area;
thus,
having increased four parts out of twenty-four parts of the field's diameter by one part and likewise by a thirty-sixth part, one should proceed according to this sequence.

Likewise: "In the middle of the directions and intermediate points, having established [the lines] endowed with the noble qualities of the Vedas (four), and with the eight limbs joined with the third set of eight qualities, there shall be an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsri*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
These [rules] as well are not traditional.

Since the area of the field is consistent in some way [with other authorities] up to the third mark from the first mark, the laying down of the cord (sūtrapāta) has not been mentioned anywhere; therefore, this is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination.
Furthermore, when such an eight-cornered (aṣṭāsra) sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) exists, there is no place at all for the installation of the yoni.
Because the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has a cornered form in every case,
the author will state in a certain passage: "The one most skilled in mantras should not place the womb (yoni) within the corners of the pit."
In the *Kāmika*, however: having laid out twelve parts from the center in the four directions within that interval, one should lead another [line] of equal measure as a fourth part;
then, by means of the measurement of its diagonal (*karṇa*), one should mark it upon the arms (*bhuja*) as well.
In that regard, it is said that "a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with eight corners arises from the intersection of eight threads," but here there is a great inconsistency.
In this regard, the author of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* explains that the word *karṇa* refers to eight marks according to the favorability or unfavorability of the ears and shoulders;
however, that is incorrect,
because there is no authoritative statement to support it, and because it results in an unequal distribution of the arms and a discrepancy in the area of the figure.
Thus ends the third chapter. Here, in all cases, the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) regarding the generation of the field have not been elaborated upon for fear of making the book too voluminous;
they are to be found in my own commentary on the *Līlāvatī*, the *Subodhinī*.

Although there is no utility here for one who knows only the traditional scriptures (Āgama) in the labor performed by me, may that rare person of virtuous character— who understands even the *Gaṇita-āgama*— be satisfied; this is the excellent system of the *Navakuṇḍikā-gaṇita*.
One who is unable to construct these specific types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should make all the pits either square or circular;
as it has been said: "The sacrificial pits for the Āgneya [rite] may be square or shaped like a circle."
Somaśambhu also says: "Those [mandalas] are always praised as being either circular or square"; and elsewhere it is said: "They may indeed be four-cornered, or perhaps circular in some cases."
Thus, the middling [type] consists of five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
As it is said in the *Āmnāyarahasya*: "Nine, five, or even one [pit] should be made, endowed with the proper characteristics."
Somaśambhu also says: "Having abandoned the interior of the altar (vedi), there are nine or five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas)";
and in the Siddhāntaśekhara as well: "Having abandoned a fourth part of the altar, there are nine or five sacrificial pits."
Thus,
even its placement is stated in the secret tradition of the Āgama: "In the arrangement of five sacrificial pits, the fifth should be in the northeast."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī* as well, it is stated: "In the directions, there are [mandalas] shaped like the Vedas, arrows, wheels, and within the range of the five mantras.
Here, by the word *vṛtta*, the circles, half-moons, and lotuses are understood.

Or, with the intention of referring to the fourfold and eightfold varieties of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) already mentioned, Somaśambhu also says: "One should fashion the fifth [pit] in the northeast in due order."

In the Nāradīya [Tantra] as well, it is taught that in rites where a set of four *kuṇḍas* (sacrificial pits) is prescribed, the wise man should construct four *kuṇḍas* resembling a triangle, a bow, a crescent moon, and a lotus,
located in the east and other directions; furthermore, O twice-born one, he should cause a fifth *kuṇḍa* to be made facing the direction of Ishana (the northeast).

As for the statement of a certain person, "If there are five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), they should be arranged in the cardinal directions, with Īśa [the northeast] and Pūrva [the east] at the ends," that is incoherent.
Because it contradicts written texts,
the teachers have stated that the placement of the smallest [fire-pit] is one cooked in a single pit: "Alternatively, one should construct a single square pit in the northern direction."
Thus, in some places, its installation is also described for the western direction,
specifically for the purposes of enjoyment, liberation, nourishment, and especially for the restoration of the dilapidated.

Regarding the *docā-homa*, as well as for pacification (*śānti*), Somaśambhu also states: "The wise man should cause [the fire-pit] to be made facing the direction of Varuṇa (the west), or else in the direction of Śiva (the north)."
Thus, according to the *Śāradātilaka*,
in the case of a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), it should be made either square or circular.
As it has been said in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) may be square or even circular, for the worship of the immobile, the worship of the mobile, and for the daily fire-oblation."
In the Piṅgalāmata also: "The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in size and circular, with a girdle, a neck, and a navel;
for daily rites, initiation, pacification, and nourishment, it should be even and auspicious."
Thus, the pit measuring one cubit has been described, as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "In all initiations (*dīkṣā*), installations (*sthāpana*), and so forth,
as well as in the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*) involving a thousand oblations, one should always construct pits measuring one cubit."
Thus, the method for two cubits and so forth is stated:
the area of one cubit is doubled for two cubits, tripled for three cubits, and quadrupled for four cubits; this should be extended up to ten cubits.
In that context, the square root and its respective length-measuring line (āyāma-sūtra) are synonyms for the *karaṇī* and the *madhyasūtra*.
Therein, the calculation of the square root should be understood according to the rule stated by Bhāskara Ācārya as follows:
"Subtract the last odd term from the number; double the quotient to obtain the root when the [number] is even. Having subtracted that quotient from the first odd term, place the result doubled."

"In a row that is equal and reduced by its own row, having subtracted from the last odd position, one should place the square of the quotient and twice that [quotient] in the row; thus, repeatedly, the half of the row shall be the square root. The meaning of this has not been stated here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
That [measurement], however, should be seen with examples in my own commentary on the *Lolāvatī*, the *Subodhinī*.
Alternatively, the diagonal line (*koṇasūtra*) of a one-cubit [square] is itself the length-measure (*āyāmasūtra*) for a two-cubit pit;
likewise, the diagonal of a two-cubit [square] is the length-measure for a four-cubit pit, and the diagonal of a three-cubit pit is that of a six-cubit [pit].

For a [square] of eight cubits, the diagonal cord is four cubits; for one of ten cubits, it is five cubits—this is to be understood accordingly. Now, for the sake of those unskilled in calculation, the Karanis (square roots) up to ten cubits are written down.
In a two-cubit [measure], thirty-four [parts] minus one-seventeenth part [are used];
by this, the finger-breadths (aṅgulas), barley-corns (yavas), and louse-eggs (yūkas) are written. This much is the construction of the two-cubit [measure]:
from one hundred twenty-eight, added by seventy-three.
In the case of a three-cubit [square], there should be forty-one finger-breadths;

by this [measure], one determines the finger-breadths, barley-corns, nit-seeds, and louse-eggs. The diagonal (karaṇī) for a two-cubit [square] is forty-eight [finger-breadths]. Now, for a four-cubit [square]:
In a five-cubit [measure], there are forty-four and three-quarters [aṅgulas];

by this [calculation], there are finger-breadths (aṅgulas), barley-corns (yavas), and nit-segments (likhyās). In the construction of the five-cubit [measure], nineteen is subtracted from four; thus, sixty minus one is the remainder, and beyond that...
The third chapter:
The depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit (kuṇḍa).
By this [measurement], there are finger-breadths (aṅgula), barley-corns (yava), louse-eggs (yūkā), and nit-dusts (likhyā); thus is the construction of the six-cubit [pit] performed.
In a seven-cubit [scale], sixty-three ten-thousandths (ayuta) are considered the *karaṇa*;
in an eight-cubit [scale], sixty-eight [ten-thousandths] minus seventeen pairs is the *karaṇa*.

By this [calculation], one determines the number of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), barley-corns (*yava*), nit-eggs (*yūka*), and lice-eggs (*likhyā*) contained within these eight cubits; such is the eight-cubit *karaṇa*.
In the nine-cubit construction, the [central] line should be seventy-two finger-breadths;
in each direction, it is reduced by two and nineteen [finger-breadths], making seventy-six.
By this [proportion], one calculates the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), barley-corns (*yava*), and nit-segments (*yūkā*). This is the method for the ten-cubit construction.

Having thus established the desired square, one should proceed according to the path described for the yoni and other parts; in this manner, I have clearly explained the construction of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) up to ten cubits in size.

Now, regarding the excavation of the pit (kuṇḍa), he says "yāvān" and so forth; the meaning is that the excavation should be made with a measurement equal to the width of the pit, which is its central cord (madhyasūtra). It is stated in the Kādima-tantra that all pits are one cubit (hasta) in measure: "For all the pits mentioned, the measure of the excavation is one aratni."

Thus, the proportional relationship between the *aratni* and the *hasta* has been stated by him; as it was, so it was shown previously elsewhere: "Whatever measurement is stated for the width of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), that same measurement is prescribed for its depth."
Thus say the teachers:
one should mark out the area of ground with a cord measuring twenty-four finger-breadths, and one should dig it to that same depth.
Thus it is also stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be as deep as it is wide."

In the *Divyasārasvata* as well: "Having first fashioned a square of four compartments with threads according to the previous measurement of one cubit, one should dig a trench of equal depth and length in its center."
Thus it is also stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "It should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length, provided with a corresponding excavation."
Others, however, say that the pit [should be dug] together with the girdle;
as it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "One should dig a pit one cubit deep, both horizontally and vertically, together with the girdle."
Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "Having ascertained the height of the three-fold girdle consisting of five parts, one should dig the remainder below."
Thus Viśvakarman also said: "The width of the moat is declared to be one-eighth [of the circumference], while its depth is nine digits, and it is elevated by nine digits."

Thus he himself will state even in the first [chapter]: "The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is [measured] across and upwards by the twenty-four finger-breadths (jināṅgula) together with the girdle (mekhalā)."
Thus [it is stated] in the *Śāradātilaka*; in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "The measurement of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) shall be together with the girdle (*mekhalā*)."
Thus,
among these three positions, only the first position appears to be logically sound,
because: "One should know the true nature of the *kuṇḍa* as the supreme body of Prakṛti."

Since the girdle (*mekhalā*) is designated as a constituent part (*aṅga*) by such statements as these, and since it is of the nature of an ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), its inclusion in the bath (*snāna*) along with those [other parts] is not tenable;
if it is argued that, being an ornament, there might even be occasions when it should not be performed—[the answer is: no.
Since it has been stated that "that which is devoid of *śṛṅgāra* leads to the destruction of the sacrificer," ornaments are also necessary; furthermore, [it is said]:
"Death occurs when the girdle is broken."

If it is argued that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because defects are stated in cases of its deficiency— such as, "likewise, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a worn-out girdle," and "in a pit with an excessive girdle, diseases increase"—
then let it indeed be an auxiliary; nevertheless, the act of digging together with that [girdle] remains logically untenable.
Because it is logical that the understanding of the effect pertains to the primary element;

furthermore, since the essential nature of the *kuṇḍa* cannot be achieved without the excavation (*khāta*), it is also improper to establish the accomplishment of the excavation—which is a directly contributing auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka-aṅga*)—along with the girdle (*mekhalā*), which is a remotely contributing auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka-aṅga*).
And it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "The excavation is equal to the purpose of the *kuṇḍa*; its status as an auxiliary has been proclaimed."
It is distinguished from the girdle and other items by way of its direct, cooperative assistance.
Thus.

It should not be argued that, because the wife has not been seen [in this context], the girdles (*mekhalā*) do not constitute a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the pit (*khāta*), as is the case with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of rice grains;
for they are prescribed as subordinate parts of the pit itself by such injunctions as, "There are three girdles for the pits.

Furthermore, if the application of the ritual effect is not accepted as belonging to the primary act, then the doubling of the area would not apply even to pits of two cubits and so forth; for in those cases as well, the doubling or other increase of the result—which is the cubic volume of the excavation of one cubit—would have to be produced from the measurement of its root (the side length).

And that is undesirable; moreover, in your view, it follows that the excavated space would not be uniform, as one excavation would be different in the case of three tiers and another in the case of five tiers.

Regarding the alternative view that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is twelve *aṅgulas* high, there is another [authority]: "The depression is fifteen *aṅgulas*, while the height from the base is nine *aṅgulas*," according to the words of Viśvakarman.
Furthermore, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "Having determined the height of the five triple-girdles, one should dig the remainder below."
Thus,

by means of the syntactic unity of these two specific statements, other general injunctions— such as "together with the girdle worn upward"— must necessarily be interpreted in relation to the scope of specific rules like "he divides the portion for Agni into four parts."

Just as there is the general injunction, "One divides the sacrificial cake into four parts," and according to the statement in the Vārttika that "a general rule which is unclear is to be completed by means of a specific one," even against your will,
you must accept that a single girdle-ring may be excavated without a girdle.

Since there is no prescriptive authority for performing [the rite] together with the girdle (*mekhalā*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the pit should be dug even without the girdle; however,
the scriptural injunctions regarding digging together with the girdle apply to sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring four *aratnis*, one *hasta*, and so forth.

Since there is no purpose for exceeding the prescribed dimensions of the pit when performing the fire-offering (homa) starting from fifty [finger-breadths] and so on, the third chapter [concludes that] the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is such that the girdles (mekhalās) are likewise. There are three girdles for the sacrificial pits; however, in the case of a pit measuring only one fist, they follow in sequence as follows: [67] The sacrificial pits have three girdles, and in the case of a pit of the measure of a single fist, they are [arranged] in order.
They should be known as being equal in height and length, measuring half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula) from the letter *na*.
It should be understood that these are their respective domains;
however, where there may be a conflict between two scriptural authorities (*śruti*), both are remembered as Dharma.
But when there is a conflict between two Smṛti texts, their respective subject matters must be distinguished.
Because of this statement, and with this very intention, it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should cause three girdles to be made, measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively;
or else, one may make a single girdle in abbreviated rites."
As for what was stated by that same [author]—namely, that in this case, where the plural number is intended, it is logical to favor the many—that too is not correct;

for since our own position involves the mention of many [authorities], that very position should be accepted. And it has been said by Jaimini: "In a conflict of contradictory dharmas, there should be the dharma of the majority."
Thus, in that case, the result for the first position is the product of the cubit; in the other position, it is [the same]. (66)
Then Mekhalā said: "Of the *kuṇḍas*...

This means that whatever is the form of the *kuṇḍas*—such as the squareness of the square, the womb-shape (*yoni*), and so forth—the girdles (*mekhalā*) should have that same form; that is to say, in a square [pit], the girdle should be square in form, and in a womb-shaped [pit], the girdle should be womb-shaped.
By this it is stated that the girdles (mekhalā) should be made in the shape of a bowl (kuṇḍa); furthermore, there is no loss of their squareness in terms of their essential form.
"Three" refers to the middle position.
The position of five girdles is the best,
while the position of one girdle is the least;
however, according to the author of the treatise, the position of three girdles alone is the superior position.
Then, the position of three girdles is the middling one, and the position of a single girdle is the inferior one;
as it is said in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "There may be three girdles, or two, or even one."

Thus, it is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) provided with a navel and a yoni, and possessing three girdles (*mekhalā*), is excellent; a pit with two girdles is middling; one with a single girdle is inferior."
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "When there are three girdles on the sacrificial pit, or two girdles on the girdle, or when the wise man uses a single girdle..."
In the *Somaśambhu*, however, it is stated: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for a Brahmin has three girdles (*mekhalā*), one for a Kṣatriya has two girdles, and for a Vaiśya there is but one girdle.

Since this is said there with reference to the one-cubit pit which serves as the archetype for all pits—according to the rule "the [girdles] are four, three, two, and one finger-breadths [in height]"—it is understood that in every case the girdles should be made respectively by the sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts of the [pit's] circumference.
"According to the Bhaṭṭa principle that 'the modification should be performed according to the original model,' it was stated by Somaśambhu in the Śāradātilaka:
'In a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit (aratni), those [lines] shall consist of three finger-breadths (aṅgula) each.'"
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, the measurements are four, three, and two finger-breadths (aṅgula).
That which is the twenty-fourth part of the pits is designated as a finger-breadth; by means of this unit, the girdles (mekhalā), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the navel (nābhi) are to be fashioned.
Thus,
it is clearly stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "The first [line] is said to be one-sixth of the pit (kuṇḍa), the second is remembered as one-eighth,
and the third shall be one-twelfth."
Thus it is said.

Also in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Listen to me, O Goddess, regarding the girdles, especially those on the hands and other limbs; six auspicious nāgas, measured by the portions of space, should be kept secret."

As for what has been stated by the author regarding the *muthyādi* (muṣṭi) and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) being two cubits (*dvihasta*) and so forth, that should be understood as being according to gross measurement; whereas [the measurement] when it is merely a handful (*muṣṭimātra*) is as follows.
Regarding the phrase "utsedhāyāmataḥ" (in height and breadth),

it applies everywhere up to the limit of one cubit (*hasta*). According to the measurement of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) mentioned here, a pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring twenty-one *aṅgulas* is equivalent to the measure of a fist (*muṣṭi*), since "fist" and "jewel" (*ratna*) are synonyms.
In that *muṣṭikuṇḍa*, the first [measurement] is one and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and so on;
the middle is one and five barley-corns (*yava*) and a finger-breadth;
the third is one and three-quarters finger-breadths.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be one *aratni* in measure; according to the measurement of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), this is twenty-two and a half finger-breadths.

This is because it is stated: "An *aratni* is a hand together with the little finger, [which is] a hand minus its sixteenth part. In that case, the first [measurement] is three and three-quarter finger-breadths.
The middle [girdle] is six and a half finger-breadths wide,
and the third is one finger-breadth less; herein is the method for constructing the girdles (mekhalā).
In a one-cubit [stūpa], the first girdle (mekhalā) starting from the neck should be made two finger-breadths high and nine finger-breadths wide;
above that, the second should be two finger-breadths high and seven finger-breadths wide;
and above that, [the third] should be four finger-breadths high and four finger-breadths wide.
Thus, by way of their results, they indeed possess the nature of being the earth, fire, the eye, and the limbs;
and it has been said: "Whichever was the previous girdle, that is declared to be the earth."
By that [measure], the first [layer] is nine finger-breadths high internally and four finger-breadths wide; externally, it is four finger-breadths high.

The second is five finger-breadths high internally and three finger-breadths wide; externally, it is three finger-breadths high. But the third is six finger-breadths high and six finger-breadths wide on both sides.
This has been stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "With four corners [and] three, three, and two finger-breadths. Here, "four corners" means four;
elsewhere it is also said: "Whether with four, three, or two finger-breadths, all three are beautiful everywhere."
Viśvakarman also said: "The height [of the girdle] and so forth is nine aṅgulas.
In the Kriyāsāra as well, it is stated that the height of the principal girdle here is nine aṅgulas.
The height of that outer girdle is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths.
This concludes the third chapter.
The height of the girdle outside of that is, in sequence, two finger-breadths.
"Four, three, or two finger-breadths in width, provided with three girdles"—
thus it is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*: "The first [girdle] is nine finger-breadths in height and elevated by nine finger-breadths."
"The middle [line] is one *vāḍgu* finger-width, while the outer third is by *yamāṅgula*s.
Thus it is also stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The twenty-fourth part of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) is traditionally known as a *aṅgula*."
Thus,

having again defined the measurement in finger-breadths (aṅgula), it is said that three lines— measuring four, three, and two [finger-breadths] respectively— are positioned above, in the middle, and directed downwards; this is the case both in terms of width and height.

Thus, by this [explanation], two alternative interpretations are refuted: namely, that the first [line] is four finger-breadths [in width], the one above it three finger-breadths, and the one above that two finger-breadths; and that externally it is four finger-breadths, while internally the middle [line] is two finger-breadths and the one touching the neck is three finger-breadths.

As for the definition given by someone: "When the width [of the altar] is divided into twenty-four parts, three parts each of four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent are considered to be the girdles (mekhalā) outside the neck (kaṇṭha), with a height of nine, eight, and seven parts respectively."
In this regard, the assertion that the second and third [houses] possess an altitude based on a six-part division is irrelevant,
because it contradicts many written texts and because there is no statement establishing this.

As for what was stated by that same person— namely, "Some have said that these [altars] are equal in width and height"— that too is a manifestation of ignorance, due to a failure to understand the meaning of the specific scriptural passages that establish those points. Furthermore, his reduction of statements such as "by the digits, the Vedas, the Rudras, and the limbs" to mean only the width is likewise a sign of lack of understanding.

And as for what the Teachers [have said]: "The girdles (mekhalās), preceded by the [element] *sattva* and endowed with the qualities (*guṇas*), rising sequentially twelve, eight, and four finger-breadths high, and four finger-breadths wide on all sides, are considered to bestow all accomplishments (*siddhis*)."
Other followers of that same school have also stated that the measurement for all the girdles is "by eight vitastis and half of that" (i.e., nine vitastis);
however, because it is explicitly stated there that [the girdles] are "considered to bestow all perfections," one should understand that there is a distinction in the results.

In that case as well, the first girdle outside the neck is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width and four finger-breadths in height; above that, the second is eight finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height; and above that, [the third] is four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width—this is how it should be understood.
Thus, in the portion of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the height is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
This is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "Therein, the first girdle (*mekhalā*) is twelve finger-breadths in width, and its height is four finger-breadths all around."
And above that, there should be a parapet (*vapra*) four finger-breadths high and properly eight finger-breadths wide on all sides.
— *Śāradātilaka*
The edge of the girdles (*mekhalā*) should be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) all around;
for a pit (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit (*hasta*), the wise man should increase that gradually up to ten cubits, according to the measure of half a finger-breadth for each subsequent size.
Furthermore, above that, a third embankment should be constructed;
it should be four finger-breadths wide and likewise elevated to the same height.
Thus.

Regarding the view that there should be five girdles (*mekhalā*), their measurement is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*: "The girdles should be made as five, or [measured] by six, five, four, three, and two [units].
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "Or the five girdles should be measured by six, five, four, three, and two [units]."
Thus,

regarding the view that there are two girdles (*mekhalā*), their characteristic is stated in another tantra: "The pair of girdles is considered to be [in proportion] to one-sixth and one-eighth [of the width]."

Even in the case of having only one girdle, the author of the text has already indicated the measurement by stating that the characteristic of the *yoni* is that it possesses a length and width of six and four *aṅgulas*, and a height [of two].
This measurement is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The single girdle is considered to have a height and width of six *aṅgulas*."
Thus it is also stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "Or else, the girdle (mekhalā) is prescribed; its width is one-fourth [of the width of the linga]."
In the *Prathama* as well: "One girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) outside the neck (*kaṇṭha*)";
and in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* also: "One should make the girdle of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) six finger-breadths [in height] if there is only one."
Thus Somaśambhu also says: "The letter 'A' [is formed] by six finger-breadths."
Elsewhere it is said: "The girdle may be six parts in width and height, or even a single part.
However, there is a specific rule in the *Kāmika*: "In that case, it should be one-third of the [total] height."
The width and height of the girdle should be equal to that of the [central] mound, and the girdle should be shaped like a bowl (kuṇḍa).
However, for the sake of brevity, only a single girdle should be constructed here for all of these. (Verses 67–68) He states the measurement for the necks of the girdles as follows:

The connection is that the rim (*nemi*) of a one-cubit (*hasta*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be [one] finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) from every part of the interior of the girdles (*mekhalā*) on all sides; that is to say, it extends finger-breadth by finger-breadth. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here with the elision of the preposition *vyat*.
If the reading is *aṅguli*,
then it should be construed as being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
by this, it is stated that the rim (*nemi*) is one twenty-fourth part of the diameter of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Even for [mandalas] of two cubits and so forth, the rim (*nemi*) is precisely one twenty-fourth part of that *karaṇī*;
as for the statement that others should increase it sequentially up to ten cubits by virtue of half-finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*),
that is intended with reference to the increase in the number of cubits.
In a two-cubit [square], there is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), three barley-corns (*yava*), four louse-eggs (*likhyā*), five particles of dust (*reṇu*), and four atoms (*trasareṇu*).
This is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, Chapter Three:
"In a two-cubit sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), those [measures] should be known as six, four, and three finger-breadths."
In sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring four cubits (*hasta*), the necks are eight, six, and four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively.

By that [proportion], in a pit of one *ratni*, the neck is seven barley-corns (*yava*); in a pit of one *aratni*, it is seven and a half barley-corns; and in a pit of one *ratni*, it is seven barley-corns.

As it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "The neck is eight barley-corns in pits measured by a cubit, seven and a half barley-corns in those measured by an *aratni*, and seven barley-corns in those measured by a *ratni*."
But in the *Kāmika*, it is stated otherwise: "His lips [are formed] by the space of the field.
Somaśambhu also says: "In some scripture, the throat is said to be one finger-breadth externally and two finger-breadths [in thickness]."

The traditionalists, however, maintain that there is only one *paṭṭa* (band), as it is accepted in the *Bahu-tantra*; thus it is said, beginning with the single hand: "Outside the pit is the neck (*kaṇṭha*) measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and outside that, the girdles (*mekhalā*) in sequence."
Thus it is also stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "One should leave a space of one aṅgula from the edge; such shall be the position of the girdles."
Elsewhere as well—in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*—it is stated: "The neck should be made one finger-breadth outside [the mouth];
in a pit measuring one cubit, one should then make the neck one finger-breadth [in height]."
Thus, in the Kālottara: "The neck [of the pit] shall be one finger-breadth outside the excavation; this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
One should calculate one twenty-fourth part as one finger-breadth."

Thus it has been explained by the commentators of that [work]: "A barley-corn multiplied eightfold is a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*)," and so forth. While the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) was previously described according to the well-known conventional usage of *hasta*s and *aṅgula*s for the sake of performing the fire-oblation (*homa*), this present technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is formulated for the purpose of stating the measurements for the excavation and other dimensions.

Having divided the area of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) intended to be constructed into twenty-four parts, one should determine the measure of a *māṅgalya* (finger-breadth) to be equal to the twenty-fourth part;

for this very reason, it is said that this rule applies to all sacrificial pits. As stated elsewhere: "In a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit (*kara*), the neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be eight barley-corns (*yava*) in measure."
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "The rim of a single-hand-sized sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) all around on the outside.
Indicating the width and length of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring two cubits and so forth, he speaks of the girdles (mekhalā).
Here, in all cases, the girdles should be constructed according to the sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts as previously described.
The statement "to be known by their width and height" connects with everything that follows, just as before.
"Six, six, and five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

The teachers have disregarded this slight discrepancy for the purpose of testing the intellect of the disciples, so that the students may develop the faculty of reasoning and critical discernment (*ūhāpoha*).
In that regard, five finger-breadths consist of five barley-corns (*yava*) and two louse-eggs (*yūkā*); this is the first [measurement].
The middle [circumference] is four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) and two barley-corns (yava);
the last [circumference] is two finger-breadths, six barley-corns, and five louse-eggs (yūka).

Although the girdles (mekhalā) for altars measuring three, five, seven, and nine cubits (hasta) are not mentioned here, nevertheless, ahead [in the text], an altar measuring one cubit is prescribed for a single-lakh [sacrifice].
One should increase [the height] by a cubit for every ten lakhs [of oblations].
*Śāradātilaka*:
In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of six cubits, those [lines] should be provided with eight fingers [in width].
In a pit measuring eight cubits, [the lines] are twelve, twelve, and eight finger-breadths;
in a pit measuring ten cubits, they are fourteen, twelve, and ten finger-breadths.
The wise should know that the girdles (mekhalā) are equal in width and height on all sides.
In front of the Hotṛ priest is their opening (yoni), which is shaped like an aśvattha leaf.
Thus, the application of the *vihasta* and other measures has been stated.
Therefore, its girdle measurement (*mekhalā-māna*) should also be understood as being, as before, the sixth, eighth, or twelfth part.
In that regard, the *vihasta* [measure] has a length of six *aṅgulas*, seven *yavas*, three *yūkas*, and three *likhyās*.
The *madhyamā* [finger] is five *aṅgulas*, one *yava*, four *yūkas*, and four *likhyās* together with half [a *likhyā*].
The *antyā* [finger] is three *aṅgulas*, three *yavas*, five *yūkas*, and six *likhyās* less one-third.
Regarding "four hands":
there are eight Vasus, six Tarkas, and four Yugas.
Here, the fact that these represent the sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts has been made explicit by the author himself.
In this same way, it should be understood for five cubits and so forth as well.
Regarding the phrase "the *yoni* of the Hotṛ":
upon these girdles (*mekhalā*), in their middle portion at the front of the Hotṛ, a *yoni* should be fashioned like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
This was stated by Somaśambhu: "Upon them, in the middle, there should be a *yoni* like a leaf of the *aśvattha*."
Thus [it is said].
And this aforementioned womb (yoni) should be made in the shape of a pit (kuṇḍa). By the phrase "in front of the Hotṛ," the following is meant:

Just as the altar does not fall toward the back, and so that the Hotṛ priest faces either east or north, the *yoni* should be placed by some on top of the western girdle (*mekhalā*) and by others on top of the southern girdle.
This is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*: "For the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) facing east, southeast, and south, the *yoni* is said to face north."
"The remaining [goddesses] are traditionally held to face east, positioned according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Also, in the *Trailokyasāra*: "The one situated in the south faces southeast; the one situated in the water [northwest] faces northwest."
"Even for the ninth pit, the *yoni* is situated in the south-west.
Thus it is said;
and in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "The *yoni* of the pits in the directions of Indra (East), Agni (South-East), and Yama (South) is traditionally held to face the North."
"The womb [of the fire] is remembered as facing east in other [rites], while in [the Śrāddha] it is recorded as facing east, northeast, or north.
Also, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The [fire] should be placed in front of the performer of the oblation, or to the south, or even to the west."
Thus [says] Somaśambhu as well: "The *yoni* of the fire-pits (kuṇḍa) situated in the east, southeast, and south should face north;
