however, for the remaining ones, it should face east, while for those two [the northeast and northwest], either one [of the two orientations] may be used."
Thus:
by the term "not facing northeast" (avaiśānya), the ninth pit is taken as being oriented by a single direction.
By this, it is established that while the eastern, southeastern, and southern pits, as well as the ninth pit, have their openings facing north, the other five pits have their openings facing east.
The third chapter: The womb (yoni) of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas), which measure one fist, one ratni, or one hasta,
is said to be characterized by a length, width, and height of six, four, and [four] aṅgulas respectively.
Regarding its measurement, he says "muṣṭi" (a fist).
Since all fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) are one cubit in measure, the *yoni* should everywhere be made with a length, width, and height consisting of four, six, and twelve parts respectively.
As it has been stated in another treatise: "The yoni of the pit's length should consist of the fourth, sixth, and twelfth parts;
it is elongated, wide, and high, while its tip is one-fourteenth part."
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "Its length is six finger-breadths and its width is four finger-breadths.
This, however, refers to the case of a single girdle (*ekamekhalā*).
Others, however, describe it differently:
"six and four finger-breadths in length" means six finger-breadths in width, twelve finger-breadths in length, and six finger-breadths in breadth;

[and] eight finger-breadths in width and two finger-breadths in height. This is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*: "From the middle of the girdle, the *yoni* is half the size of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in width."
Thus; and also in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "The yoni [pedestal] is eight finger-breadths in width with long solar joints;
its height is one finger-breadth."
Thus it is said.

Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should fashion the womb (*yoni*) in the middle of the division, twelve finger-breadths in length and one-twelfth of that in height, slightly recessed for the placement of the jar."
Thus it is said.
In some places, even a height of one *aṅgula* is mentioned; as stated in the *Nāradīya*: "The width of the *yoni* is equal to its height, according to the rule of the *kuṇḍa*."
"It should be long by half of the *kuṇḍa*.
Also, in the *Trailokyasāra*: "The *yoni* is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, and less than that in width according to the *tantra*."
"However, it is one finger-breadth high.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The width of the yoni is eight fingers, and its height is measured at one finger."
Thus it is said;
elsewhere also: "The height is one finger-breadth.
Therefore, there is an option between a height of two finger-breadths and a height of one finger-breadth.
The width at the base is eight finger-breadths;
because it is said that the tip is contracted like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, a slight depression should be made in the middle of the *yoni*.
This is stated in the *Trailokyasāra*: "In the middle, however, there is the support for the clarified butter (*ājya*)."
The traditional authorities also consider the womb (yoni) to be of this very kind.

Others, however, state that it is connected to the height and length as "six and four fingers" (ṣaṭcatuṅgula); therefore, they say the womb should be made twelve fingers wide, twelve fingers long, and twelve fingers high.
As it is said in the Pañcarātra: "One should fashion the womb with a height of twelve fingers and an extent of the same."
Thus,
because it consists of the twelve vowels, the *yoni* should be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length; its height and breadth are equal.
Thus [ends] the Śāradātilaka:
"One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth in size, slightly facing downwards."
One should increase the width of the *yoni* by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) for each subsequent fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In the *Prayogasāra*: "The first girdle (*mekhalā*) is of the *sāttvika* type, twelve fingers wide;
thereafter, the second girdle is declared to be of the *rājasa* type, [eight fingers wide]."
The third belt is known as *tāmasī*, measuring four finger-breadths [in width];
the width of each of these is separately four finger-breadths according to measurement.
It is situated in the west, extending correctly fifteen finger-breadths in length.

"One should construct the *yoni* of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a width of two and five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), a depth of six and four finger-breadths respectively, having the distinct shape of an *aśvattha* leaf, recessed, placed within the pit, and thirteen finger-breadths in height. Thus it is said.
"In the western [direction]"—this is to be understood according to the view that there is only a single pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Regarding "one finger":
by this twenty-fourth part, it is stated that everywhere the tip of the vulva (*yoni*) should also be made slightly downward-facing and enter into the pit.
This has been stated in the *Nāradīya*: "The rim of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) is like the leaf of the Bodhi tree.
The meaning is that the "rim" (*oṣṭha*) is the tip of the womb (*yoni*), having entered the front of the pit;
likewise, it enters within.
"Endowed with the proportions of a water-pot and resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Trailokyasāra*, and in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "One should fashion the girdle in the middle, or on the west, or even on the south."
"Beautiful at its front, slightly sloping, gradually uprooting [the earth],
facing the pit with its tip, and having its girdle slightly cast aside."

Here, for fear of excessive length, the measurements for the *yoni* and its tip and so forth have been stated up to the ten-cubit *kuṇḍa*. Nevertheless, something is said: the length is equal to the width; then the width is one-sixth of that [length];
the height should be half the width; and the tip should be half the height.
"In blind [square] sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), one should avoid the *yoni* by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) at each side;
likewise, one should avoid the tip of the *yoni* by a sequence of two barley-corns (*yava*).
This, however, is stated according to measurement by area for those who are unskilled in calculation."
But this is not intended to mean an exact calculation.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Beginning from the base, the stalk should extend to the center of the womb and be provided with a hole.
One who is most skilled in the science of the body should not place the *yoni* in the corners of the *kuṇḍas*;
rather, one should fashion a navel within the *kuṇḍas*, resembling a lotus.
Alternatively, its measurement is declared to be in proportion to each respective *kuṇḍa*.
For those [fire-pits] with fists, jewels, or axes as their hand-measures,

the navel should be provided with two, three, or four finger-breadths in height and width; in other pits, one of noble intellect should increase the navel by a sequence of two barley-grains at a time.
One should avoid drawing the vulva in the vulva-pit and the navel in the navel-water pit.
Having divided the navel-circle into three parts, one should fashion the pericarp in the center;
with two outer segments, one should arrange eight petals.
Regarding the statement "the stalk from the ground," it means that the stalk should extend from the ground to the womb;
by the phrase "from the ground," it is stated that the stalk must be made so as to be attached to the outer girdle.

The meaning is that one should construct an altar (*vedi*) four finger-breadths in height and width, joined with the outer girdle (*bāhyamekhalā*), and place the stalk (*nāla*) upon it. How so? It means that it should have a hole in the middle; thus, having fashioned a cavity in the center above the middle girdle for the purpose of laying the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and spreading the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*), the central portion—the "hole"—is to be filled. This is stated in the *Pañcarātra*: "Starting from the ground, the womb (*yoni*) should be level with the outer girdle."
Thus,
he who stated that "with a hole in the middle" (*sarandhuka*) is a qualification of the stalk (*nāla*) is indeed mistaken, because only the *sarambhra* plant is denoted by the word "stalk."

It should not be argued that because of his speaking of the perforated [reed] and because of the presumption (*arthāpatti*) of an unseen purpose, the placement of the fuel, the enclosure, and so forth must be done from the stalk;
for there can be no sublation of the seen by the unseen.
Furthermore, due to the absence of a space for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*),
the *Prayogasāra* states: "To the west of the yoni, a stalk (*nāla*) one cubit in length, three or four finger-breadths in width, and with its tip gradually tapering, is prescribed."
Regarding the phrase "the navel of the fire-pits" (*kuṇḍānāṃ nābhi*):
one should fashion a navel within the fire-pits;
having made the navel either circular like the pit itself or shaped like a lotus, one should place it in the center of the excavation—this is the meaning.

Regarding the word *nābhi*, as stated in the rule "The word *nābhi* [is used] for the sun, for a Kṣatriya, for a part of a living being, and in two genders," the word *nābhi* exists even in the masculine gender.
Here, by "height" (*utsedha*) is meant both elevation and breadth;
as before, since a single cubit constitutes the standard form for all fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), it is said that the [navel] is broad by one-sixth of the width of the pit and its height is half of that.
He states the very resemblance to a lotus in the words "the navel" (*nābhiḥ*) and "one should make" (*kuryāt*); the word "with a portion" (*aṃśena*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
And it has been stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "On the side of the sacrificial ground, in a pit, there is a vessel with a navel and a girdle."
Thus [it is said]:
"A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one fist is declared to be for a hundred [oblations]. *Śāradātilaka*.
At a hundred oblations, the pit is one *aratni* in measure; at a thousand, it is one cubit (*hasta*). At ten thousand, it is two cubits; at a hundred thousand, it is declared to be four cubits.
At one million, it is six cubits; and for ten million, it is traditionally remembered as eight cubits.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for ten hundred thousand oblations; one should increase it by one cubit for each subsequent ten-fold increment,
until a pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a crore of oblations.

The quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is declared to bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*); the *yonikuṇḍa*, which has the appearance of a half-moon, bestows auspiciousness. He states the application of the sacrificial pits beginning with the *muṣṭi* and ending with the eight-cubit [pit] for the sake of [attaining] a crore [of results].
In the case of a hundredfold oblation (*śatahoma*), the word "aratnimātram" is to be analyzed [as a compound].
As it has been said: "For a hundred [oblations], the measure is a fist; for a hundred [oblations], the measure is an *aratni*."
In the *Saṃhitā*, however, it is said: "Even for ten million oblations (*koṭihoma*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be eight cubits.
He states another alternative view with the word "eka" (one).

This [measurement], however, refers to objects consisting of small materials such as flowers and clarified butter, or to a *homa* performed by a single agent; it extends up to five cubits (*karas*). Beyond that, it should be understood to refer to large materials or to rites involving multiple agents. By the phrase "eight cubits for ten million [offerings]," there is an option regarding the [standard] "ten cubits."

In the Siddhāntaśekhara, however, there is a specific distinction: for a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is three cubits; for ten lakhs of oblations, it is said to be four cubits;
for twenty lakhs, six cubits; and for one crore, seven cubits, respectively.

Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "Some say that for a *lakṣa* homa, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be two cubits; for ten *lakṣas*, four cubits; for a hundred thousand (*vilakṣa*), three cubits; for four hundred thousand (*vedalakṣa*), four cubits; and for five hundred thousand (*pañcalakṣa*), five cubits."

In a rite of one hundred thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be seven cubits and seven hands; at one million oblations, it should be eight cubits and eight hands; at ten million oblations, it should be nine cubits and nine hands;
and at one hundred million oblations, it should be ten cubits and ten hands.
"For indeed, on this earth, there is no pit greater than ten cubits.
Thus [it is said].
Now, he states the specific fruits of the pits with the words "all," etc.
"Cutting" (chedaḥ), "annihilation" (ucchedaḥ), and "expulsion" (uccāṭanam)— that is to say—
this specific result is to be understood as occurring only when the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is constructed in the respective directions previously mentioned.
Thus it has been said in the third chapter.
For the rite of pacification (śāntika), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be circular;
for subjugation (vaśya) and killing (māraṇa), it should be hexagonal and resemble a lotus;
and the eight-cornered pit is said to bestow vision and alleviate disease.
For Brahmins, it should be square; for kings (Kṣatriyas), it is desired to be circular.
For Vaiśyas, it has the appearance of a half-moon; for Śūdras, it is said to be triangular.
However, some Tantrikas desire it to be square for all castes.
One should know that the *kuṇḍa* is the supreme body of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Its head is said to be in the east, its arms in the south and north,
its belly is called the *kuṇḍa*, and its womb and feet are in the west.

In the *Kāmika*: for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), it is square in the eastern direction; in the southeastern quarter, it is shaped like a vulva; for killing (*māraṇa*), it is half-moon-shaped in the southern direction; in the southwestern corner, it is triangular;
for pacification (*śāntika*), it is circular in the western direction; and for driving away (*uccāṭana*), it is six-cornered in the northwest.
"In the north, for nourishing rites, a lotus-shaped [pit]; in the northeast, an eight-angled one, which grants liberation.
Thus it is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "In the north, for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is shaped like a lotus."

In the northeast, for subduing the six enemies, the shape is that of a boar; in the south, for killing, it is the shape of Yama; in the east, for paralyzing, it is the shape of a thunderbolt; for attracting, in the southeast, it is the shape of the vulva;
in the west, for pacification, it is circular; and in the northeast, the triangle of Tvaṣṭṛ bestows liberation.

Thus, it is also stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) called yoni is said to be in the southeast, facing north; it is used for the increase of progeny and in the rite of tāpa. Now, the half-moon (ardhacandra) is described."
In the south, it is recommended for that [rite of] killing; one should always face north.
In the southwest, there should be a triangular fire-pit (kuṇḍa) for the rite of inciting hatred, facing east.
Hereafter, I shall describe the circular pit, which is beneficial for the rite of pacification in the west.
The hexagonal pit is said to be effective for the rite of eradication in the northwest.
Next, I shall describe the lotus-shaped pit; it increases prosperity when situated in the north.
Furthermore, I shall describe the eight-sided pit in the northeast, which grants all desires.
Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, should be one *tāla* in measure."
And it has been said: "O Four-faced One, [this applies] to mobile and immobile [objects], but not to a fixed [image].
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the path described here with its proper characteristics, even a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra should have it bound with copper."
If that is unavailable, however, one should make it very firm by joining it with bricks and smear it with clay according to the manner previously described;
one may also fashion it from clay alone, provided it possesses the required characteristics.
This pit (kuṇḍa) is for the mobile worship (carārcā), not for the fixed worship (sthirārcana).
O bull among the immortals, one should properly purify a copper pit with acid, an earthen one with cow-dung water, and a stone one with lime.
"For earthen pits, one should decorate them along with their joints on all sides with red clay and rice flour, making them as pleasing to the sight as possible.
Thus it is said.

Regarding this, Viśvakarman states the defect that arises when the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) are deficient, excessive, or otherwise deformed: "If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken rim (*mekhalā*), death. In a pit lacking a rim, there is grief; if the rim is excessive, there is an accumulation of wealth."
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is made without a vulva (yoni) is said to cause the destruction of one's wife;
a pit that is devoid of a neck is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring. Thus it is stated.
In another scripture as well: "If [the measure] is excessive, death occurs; if deficient in measure, poverty. And so forth.

Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that is either less or more than the prescribed measure, one with a cracked girdle (*mekhalā*), or one devoid of beauty, leads to the destruction of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)."
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* it is also said: "If the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) here is deficient or excessive, it bestows many defects;
therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should examine it thoroughly before constructing it.
And in the *Siddhānta-śekhara*: "When there is a deficiency in measurement, there is a great disease; when there is an excess, there is an increase of enemies."

"Seizure (apasmāra) occurs when the *yoni* is deficient; verbal punishment (*vāgdaṇḍa*) when the throat is deficient. Thus it is also stated in the *Jayadrathayāmala*: "When the *sūtra* is deficient, there is hatred toward friends; when pride (*māna*) is deficient, there is poverty; when the throat is deficient, there is suppression of speech (*vāgrodha*); and when the *asiñci* is deficient, there is loss of teeth."
If there is an excess, there will be demonic enjoyment; if the girdle is excessive due to pride, diseases increase greatly; and if there is a division [of the girdle], epilepsy shall occur.
The third chapter:
One should perform the daily, occasional, and optional rites either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or by means of sand; one should make that [mound] very beautiful, measuring one cubit.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) thus described are square on all sides with a height equal to the breadth of a finger; following this, the large and small ladles (sruk and sruva) are now explained.
If [the fire] bursts forth or has a crack or a fissure, there will be censure.
Thus, its necessity is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "That fire which is devoid of direction, place, and sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is indeed worldly;
therefore, the directions, places, and pits should be adopted according to the prescribed characteristics."

"Such a *kuṇḍa* may not exist, or one should resort to a *sthaṇḍila*"—this statement by the author of the text refers to the *nitya* (daily) rite and to the intention of using a single *kuṇḍa*, wherein the *kuṇḍa* is of the nature of a hollow pit and the *yoni* is at the western side. He states the alternative for the *kuṇḍa*: "the daily [rite]...
endowed with a height of one finger."
"A finger" (*aṅgula*) has the characteristics previously described;
or rather, it is that which possesses the height of the four fingers, which are the branches of the hand.

As they say: "The sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is one cubit (*ratni*) in length, raised by the joint of the thumb, well-proportioned, constructed with sand, and four-cornered; some wise ones say it is two fingers high and one cubit in width."
This has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "In a concise fire-rite (*homakarma*), the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) should be the measure of an arrow.

However, in the *Kriyāsāra*, a specific location for the sacrificial ground is also mentioned: "The oblation is performed in the eight directions; it should face east, or else be inclined toward the northeast."
"A region sloping toward the north, or the tail [of the diagram], is remembered as the *sthala* of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

However, there is a specific distinction in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "For the fire-oblation (*homa*), a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or a small hearth (*hasantikā*) is recommended."

In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā as well: "Now I shall describe the fire-ritual (agnikārya), whether it be performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), or on an altar (vedi), or in a new, auspicious vessel made of iron or clay."

Alternatively, the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) may be made with sand or even with the dust of red clay; furthermore, during the fire-oblation (*homa*), the wheel of fire (*agnicakra*) should also be visualized. This specific detail is stated elsewhere in the *Trikayasāra*.
Having drawn a grid of nine squares, one should then place [the syllables] in order in the northeast and southwest, in the west, north, east, and southeast, and in the south and north.
In the sacrifice, the Guru should fashion the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles from one of the following— *śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or *khadira*— according to the method that will be described hereafter.
Having taken that [measurement] and divided it by thirty-six,
the staff (daṇḍa) shall consist of twenty parts, and the altar (vedī) shall consist of eight of those parts.
The neck is measured by one part, the mouth by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be like that of the pedestal (vedī).

The opening at the top of the throat should be equal to the size of the little finger; one should fashion the mouth-path for the exit of the clarified butter according to the measurement of the little finger.

Having placed the Sun and the others in the central square and Ketu [in its own], one should declare the result: there will be grief during the period of the Sun, and the acquisition of wealth during that of Mercury.
In the house of Venus, there shall be gain of wealth; Saturn would cause loss;
one should know that the Moon brings profit; and Mars brings death or imprisonment.
The Guru (Jupiter) leads to the attainment of wealth, while Rāhu is considered to cause loss;
indeed, by Ketu, one always meets death in the circle of fire.

"One should count three and then another three, starting from the solar day (sūryarca) up to the day of the lunar mansion (dinabhāva); however, one need not deliberate on this in the case of daily (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites, such as the fire-oblation (homa) to Durgā. Thus [ends the section on] "the foremost" (agram).
This mouth is equal to the throat in height and has a width of one-third of the *veda*;

since the length of all [parts] has been stated and it is said "for the exit of the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*)," it is called the "path" (*mārga*), which pierces through the boundary above the throat and the *veda*.

Thus it is said in the *Mantramuktāvatī*: "The wise one should create a passage below the throat for the exit of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and he should perform the piercing at the mouth with a heated iron rod.
This is also stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*. [End of] the third chapter.
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part; outside of that, one should fashion a pit (avaṭa) on all sides with one part.
66. Its pit should be circular with three parts and one part [of the total] for the rim;
one should fashion petals all around with a single part.
The molding (mekhalā) for both the mouth and the altar-base (vedi) should be made all around according to the measurement of one-quarter part.
At the base and the tip of the staff, there should be two *kumbhas* measuring respectively three and four *aṅgulas*;
the pair of *gaṇḍīs* should consist of four parts (*yamāṃśa*), and this is declared to be the circumference of the staff.
The back portion of the altar should be shaped like a tortoise with six parts;
one should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a boar.
This is declared to be the characteristic of the *sruk* ladle at the rear of its face.
Outside that pericarp, on all sides,
two parts of that [measurement] are taken together as the depression or pit (avaṭa).
The meaning is "by three parts," that is, by two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

"Outside" means all around the pit (*avaṭa*); "around the circle" implies that two parts are included. The syntactical connection is: "the girdle (*mekhalā*) should be [formed] around the mouth and the altar (*vedi*) according to the measurement of one part."
By that same one part, a girdle (*mekhalā*) should also be made for the face; it is circular in shape.

Therein, by one part a pericarp (*karṇikā*) is formed, by two parts a hollow (*avaṭa*), by one part a circle, and by two parts the petals. By one part—that is, by the half-portion—the construction of a square border (*sīmā*) should be made all around.
This has been stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "The *śobhā* should be half a finger-breadth, or equal [in size], or even painted"; here, the word "finger-breadth" (*aṅgula*) denotes a part.

Thus, all eight parts of the *soma* (the square) are utilized; according to the instruction, a variegated design consisting of folds and so forth should be made in the corners. [86–87] Regarding the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*), since this is a section concerning parts (*aṃśa*), the word "finger" (*aṅgula*) here denotes a part.

By that [measurement], at the base it should be made with one part facing the mouth of the *tantra*, while at the top it should be made with four parts facing the mouth attached to the altar (*vedī*), according to the sequence; this applies also to what follows.

There, the corners (*danta*) joined to the base-pitcher (*kumbha*) are one part, while elsewhere the corners joined [to the body] are four parts. The *gaṇḍī* should be fashioned in the shape of a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*).

Since the lexicon states that the word *yuga* means "pair" (*yugma*) as well as "plow" (*kṛtādi*), and since there is no evidence for accepting a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the literal meaning of duality is already possible,
it was said by Somaśambhu: "If the two knobs (*gaṇḍau*) at the base and the tip of the staff were like bracelets (*kaṅkaṇavat*)."
Thus,
by this, eleven parts have been produced;
in the middle, a staff measuring nine parts remains for the purpose of support.
One should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
its handle is declared to be measured by twenty-two parts.
The circumference of its head is one hundred and four parts; it should hold one *karṣa* of clarified butter.
One should bury two parts in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint.
At the base and the tip of the staff, there should be a *gaṇḍī* adorned with a bracelet;
thus the procedure for the excellent [staff] has been declared. Now, following the recitation, the mandalas are described.
This has been stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "The staff (*daṇḍa*) shall be six *rasa* finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long.
In this context, if the word *aṅgula* were taken to mean [six] finger-breadths, then three and a half parts would remain for the staff.
Then, for the sake of support, there would be no space at all; therefore, the width of the handle (daṇḍa) should be made with six parts.
The back portion of the *vedī* is of the shape of a tortoise; this is indeed a separate [instruction].

However, those who connect the statement "the circumference (*ānāha*) of the staff is said to be its length" as a separate [rule], and then further connect it with "the back portion of the *vedī* is of the shape of a tortoise" by means of six parts, are truly deluded.
This is because the word *ānāha* does not denote length, and length has already been mentioned previously.
This has been stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "The circumference of the middle of the handle is declared to be six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the form of a tortoise," because the mention of "six parts" would otherwise be redundant, the connection is that one should draw the face of a swan or similar creature on the back part of the mouth of this *sruk* ladle.
Of the boar with a large belly. || 88 ||
He states the characteristics of the *sruva* with the words "the *sruc*": the circumference (*ānāha*) is the width, consisting of four parts;
this is the connection to the word "of this" (*etasya*).
In the *Mantramuktāvalī*, it is stated: "The staff (*daṇḍa*) shall consist of four fingers' breadth.
Regarding the *karṣa*: as for the definition of a *karṣa*—ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* are declared to be one *karṣa*.
Thus,
with two parts one should fashion its head.
The connection is that one should dig a depression in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint so that it may hold the ghee when drawn out.
Because of the statement "adorned with bracelets," the word *gaṇḍa* here is a synonym for *ghaṭa* (pot).
As it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "One should fashion two very beautiful pots at the base and the tip."
And those two [the *kaṅkaṇa* and the *pavitra*] are to be prepared as before, since no specific details have been stated.
The *kaṅkaṇa* also is to be prepared as before.
There is a distinction elsewhere: "In the absence of that, the oblation is offered with two leaves of the *palāśa* tree."
In this context, the phrase "by means of two leaves" should be understood as referring to the two middle leaves, because of the Vedic injunction: "He offers with the middle leaf.
Furthermore, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* it is stated: "The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of metal; those of bell-metal or iron are not to be used."
Or they may be made of wood or even of cloth by the practitioners, according to the approval of the artisans.
The Third Chapter: In a square divided into four compartments and provided with diagonal lines, one should likewise draw four diagonal lines within each of the four compartments. 103.
In such a way that fish-like marks appear at regular intervals,
the mantra-practitioner should drop [the cord] extending east-west and north-south;
upon those fish-marks, one should drop four cords equally.
As before, one should drop the diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) into the corner squares.
When the fish-figures (matsya) have arisen from those, one should apply four threads.
Then, there will be fish-figures within the squares; one should drop threads upon them.
The mantra practitioner should cast the lines there according to that same procedure, extending for two hundred and fifty-six steps.
Or, [he may use] a leaf from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree or another such tree, which is unblemished and grown in the center.
Thus it is said.
But elsewhere: "In the absence of Palāśa leaves, however, one may use leaves from the Pippala or Udumbara trees."
In the *Saṃhitā* as well: "O Sage, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles [should be placed] on a beautiful, flawless leaf of the *palāśa* tree.
Now, regarding the construction of the *sarvatobhadra* and other mandalas upon the altar, it says "quadrangular" (*caturasra*).

The meaning is that one should construct a quadrangle provided with two diagonal lines and consisting of four squares, according to the method described for the *vāstu*-mandala. With two verses, he describes the method for producing sixteen squares, beginning with "in the four... (*caturṣu*).

In the four squares, one should likewise draw four diagonal lines (koṇasūtra) in such a way that fish-figures (matsya) are formed in each center. The connection is as follows: the mantra-practitioner should cast this set of four equal lines upon those fish-figures—one pair extending east-west and another pair extending north-south.
In this manner, it becomes composed of sixteen squares. He describes the method for producing sixty-four squares in a verse and a half, beginning with "as before" (pūrvavat).
This applies to three locations. The method for that is as follows:

having drawn four diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*) in the four corner squares as before, one should apply this set of four lines—two with their tips pointing east and two with their tips pointing north—upon the four fish-figures produced by those lines, just as previously described.
Furthermore, one should lay two threads—one with its tip toward the east and one with its tip toward the north—across the four fish-shaped spaces produced by the intersection of these four lines.
In this way, sixty-four squares are accomplished. || 103–106 ||
The meaning of the phrase "by that very same procedure" is as follows:

having drawn four diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*) in the four corner squares as before, one should place two threads on the four resulting fish-marks (*matsya*), one directed eastward and one directed northward.
Then, from these threads—[this is the *Śāradātilaka*].

In the center, one should draw a lotus with its characteristics using thirty-six squares; the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of one row outside that, and the pathway (vīthikā) of two rows. One should arrange the doors, the ornaments, and the secondary ornaments with the remaining two [rows].
Then the wise mantra-practitioner, according to the procedure taught in the scriptures, should draw a lotus.
Having set aside one-twelfth part of the area of the lotus field on the outside,
he should divide its center into three circles with equal proportions.
The first [circle] should be the location for the pericarp; the second, for the filaments;

and the third, for the tips of the lotus petals, which are like pearls. A wise person, according to the prescribed rule, should determine the measurement of the space between the outer and inner circles.
Having placed half-moons around the tips of the filaments,
in this way, one hundred and fifty-six squares are produced.
He states the application of the compartments with the words "thirty-six.
He will describe the method of drawing the lotus immediately thereafter. The word "outside" (bahih) connects with all three locations.

Outside [that], one should construct a pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of twenty-eight squares on all sides by means of the outer row, according to the method to be described. Outside that, one should construct a pathway (vīthikā) consisting of eighty squares on all sides by means of a pair of rows, according to the method to be described. Outside that, one should construct the doors, the beauties (śobhā), the sub-beauties (upaśobhā), the weapons (astra), and the corners (koṇa) by means of the remaining two rows consisting of one hundred and twelve squares on all sides, according to the method to be described. || 108 ||
He describes the method for constructing the lotus with the word "padma" and so forth.
Therein, the lotus-field, consisting of thirty-six squares, is divided eightfold by two lines for the cardinal directions and two diagonal lines (karṇasūtra).
Those very same lines serve as the central lines for the petals.
Regarding the method therein: having divided the length of the lotus-field into twelve parts, one should discard one part on all sides.

Then, having divided those ten parts into six, one should place the beginning of the thread in the center and construct three circles—one with two parts, another above that with two parts, and yet another above that with two parts.

It should be understood that the statement beginning with "the first" (ādya) and so forth is intended to indicate the locations of the limbs, coverings, and other elements that will be described later.
Regarding the phrase "by a portion of pearls," this refers to a twelfth part, as he will state in the verse immediately following.
Regarding the word "bāhya" (external):

the wise one, having fixed [the measuring line] at the tips of the filaments—that is, at the edge of the circle of the filaments—by means of the measurement of the space between that which is external to the petals; [the phrase] "with a thread and so forth" is to be supplied;
according to the rule, on both sides all around, [this is done] within the center of the lotus. This is the third chapter.
Having written [the measurements] located at the joints, one should drop the threads there. One should draw the circle with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals.
Within that space, on both sides of the central thread, the wise one [should proceed].
One should draw the tips of the petals all around with the outer hand; "of the threads" is the ellipsis.
Having drawn the half-moons situated at the joints—that is, the half-moons situated at the junctions—one should drop four threads there; such is the connection.
Regarding the reading *mānaṃ yadudvidhineti*, the meaning is: "by that measurement which is the measure of the interval between the circles.
The procedure there is as follows:

having fixed a measuring cord at the intersection of the filament-circle and the cardinal-direction cord, one should draw a half-moon on both sides of that cardinal-direction cord, with its two ends touching the filaments and the circle of the petals.
Thus, when the four lines for the cardinal directions and the four lines for the corners have been drawn, eight half-moons are produced.
And this is understood from the plural number in the phrase "at the tips of the filaments" (*keśarāgreṣu*);
because there are eight locations for the filaments in the middle of the eight-petaled [lotus], the eight petals are thereby established.
Then, at the eight junctions formed by the mutual intersections of the two half-moons, one should draw a single line between each pair of facing halves.
In this way, eight boundary lines for the eight petals are produced.
The crescent moon-shapes situated below the junctions, located on both sides of the boundary lines, are to be erased.

As it has been said: "Having placed a thread at the junction in the middle of a petal already established, one should establish the petal by means of crescent-moon segments arising from the meeting of both sides of the space between the petals."
Thus it is said.

Also elsewhere: "Having fixed another [line] upon the directional thread of the aforementioned field and having straightened the other direction, one should extend the two diagonal threads from the measurement of the fish-figures at the cardinal points of the circle."
"Having placed the junctions of the petals upon the tips of the filaments, one should mark them;
then, having dropped the threads, one should draw the eight petals there. (112–113)
He states the fourth circle with the words "dalāgra" and so forth.
One should construct the fourth circle at a distance from the tips of the petals equal to that measure which was left outside in the form of a twelfth part.
He describes the method for forming the tips of the petals with the word "tat" (that).

The connection [of the text] is as follows: within that interval—namely, within the interval of the circle of the tips of the petals—one should skillfully draw the tips of the petals in all directions and intermediate directions (vidiś) using the outer hand on both sides of the central axis of the petals (patramadhyasūtra), which is the same as the middle line. The method for this is as follows: having placed the beginning of the thread at the tip of the junction-line on both sides of the petal-center-line within the interval of the fourth circle, one should apply two threads from the middle circle up to the point of intersection with the petal-center-line at the circle of the petal-tips.

In that regard, concerning the edge of the thread: one [finger] touches the leaf, while the second touches the intersection of the thread at the middle of the tip of the petal; and so that the two tips of the threads may face each other, it is said "with the outer hand."

Then, having removed the circle drawn upon the pericarp, one should properly erase the three outer circles and all the lines within the middle of the lotus petals, so that an eight-petaled lotus appears beautiful to the eye.
One should arrange the filaments in pairs at the bases of the petals;
this lotus is declared by those who know the Tantras to be the common [type].
One should sweep away three squares at each corner of the pedestal for the sake of the feet;
with the remaining squares, the wise man should fashion the limbs.
One should sweep away the squares situated along the pathways according to the undivided rows.

Then, one should construct doors in the cardinal directions using two by four squares; next, the *śobhās* (ornamental projections) on both sides of the doors should consist of three squares and one square respectively;
immediately thereafter, the *upaśobhās* (subsidiary projections) should consist of one and three squares.
With the remaining six words, there should be a set of four corners.

118. He describes the manner of the filaments (*kesara*): "With the *dala*" [means] on both sides of the central axis of the petal, within the interval between the lines marking the edges of the petals located at the joints, one should fashion two filaments on each petal. Their bases should be attached to the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), their tips should touch the circle of the filaments, they should be slightly thick at the tips, and they should face one another.
He concludes with the word "this" (*etad*).
Wherever it shall be stated that one should make a lotus, this method is to be understood as applicable there.

Regarding what was stated, "one should construct the pedestal," he explains the method: "of the squares. One should erase three squares for the purpose of the pedestal—namely, each corner square and the two squares situated on either side of it; with the remaining four squares, one should fashion the limbs of the pedestal.
One should perform the cleansing of the two rows established for the sake of the pathways (*vīthī*) in a single form.
Regarding the doors, he says "in the directions" (*dikṣu*):

for the sake of the four doors, one should cleanse the two squares situated on both sides of the central thread within the inner row—which was established all around for the purpose of the doors—and likewise the four squares situated on the sides of the central thread within the outer row, for the sake of the doors.
In this way, there would be four doors.
Regarding the statement "the *śobhās* [are made] with words":
one should erase the three squares located at each side of the door within the inner row, and one square located at each side of the door in the outer row;
in this way, there will be eight *śobhās*.
Regarding the *upaśobhās*:
one should erase three outer-line squares on each side of every single square situated within the row that is attached to both sides of the *śobhā*;
in this way, there will be eight *upaśobhās*.
With the remaining [lines],
one should erase the three cells located within the rows that are attached to the ornaments on both sides, as well as the three cells located in the outer rows;
in this way, there will be four corners.
The third chapter:
One should color that enchanting maṇḍala with five colors;
yellow should be made from turmeric powder, and white from rice.
116. Red is the powder of safflower; black is produced from burnt husks of grain;
and dark is that produced from the leaves of the bilva tree and others—thus the five colors have been described.
The auspicious boundary lines are white, measuring one hundred and twenty finger-breadths in height and width;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are reddish.
The practitioner of mantra should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with dark pigment; alternatively, the pericarp may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be black and white in color, or alternatively, yellow and black.
One should color the interior of the pedestals; the feet [of the lotus] should have a reddish luster,
its stalks should be white, and so too the four walkways.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits, variegated with various colors and enchanting to the sight of all.
The twelve gates are white in color; the primary ornaments (śobhā) are red and well-proportioned;
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color; and the corners are black.
One should draw three lines on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence;
this is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all.
Having divided the square ground into twelve parts from the cardinal directions, the wise one should drop threads therein; thus, one hundred squares are seen.

However, there is a distinction in another tantra: "If one who is capable desires fierce accomplishment, he should adorn the mandalas here with gems of those colors—namely, with pearls, topaz, rubies, sapphires, and green gems."
Thus [is described] the boundary line; thus all [the lines] were previously marked with white lotuses, and he speaks of the red lotus when [he says] "yadā" (when).

However, regarding the initiations (*dīkṣā*) of the Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, and Śaiva traditions, it should be understood that there is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*), namely that one must be initiated by a *pota*.
Having concluded this second position, he states the primary subject at hand with the words "by the *pota*."
This conceptualization is according to one's own will:

"the wombs of the seats" (*pīṭhagarbhāṇi*). Here, that which has a womb (*garbha*) is a corner (*koṇa*); thus, "womb-corner" refers to the location of the corners. *Kamalacetrakoṇān* means the corners of the lotus-field.
Because it is not neuter, its neuter gender [is established]; thus, the depiction of the *poṭha* as a *kalpalatikā* (wish-fulfilling creeper) is to be understood through instruction.
"Outside" means outside the boundary line established on all sides;
however, there is a specific rule in the *Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"A boat should be provided in the east, white [in color], and likewise in the west and the north."
The red [lotus] is on the right, the black is situated in the southeast, and the pale-red is in the southwest.
In the southwest it is blue in color, in the northwest it is smoky-colored, and in the northeast it is designated as fair (gaura); this is the sequence for the eight petals.
Thus [it is said].
[Please provide the text to be translated.]
He states another mandala with the words "caturasrām" (the square one).
Since the method for producing the fish-shape is impossible here, the expression "twelvefold from the directions" is used;
therein, having divided the ground twelvefold in the four directions, one should drop the lines upon it.

Regarding that, the method is as before: having made sixteen squares, one should divide one square into equal parts; [thus] the third layer consists of forty-four [squares], after which one should fashion the lotus with twenty-six squares.
One should arrange the pedestal (pīṭha) in a row; there are no pathways (vīthikā) here at all.

Just as before, no secondary ornamentation (upaśobhā) is seen at the door-decorations; the knower of the tantra should form the corners with the remaining six squares and complete the rest as previously described— thus is the auspicious mandala.
The wise one should arrange sixty-four squares in a square formation;
with four of those squares, there shall be a lotus in the center, and again around that.
One should draw four paths ending at the edge of the mandala, and within the squares situated in the cardinal directions, one should paint lotuses.
The wise one, having divided the four intermediate squares into sixteen parts,
should erase them in the form of a svastika using white, yellow, red, and black [colors].

Having divided that [square] into three parts, one should first lay down two threads from east to west. Then, upon the tails of the fish formed by the intersection of these two threads at each corner, one should lay down two threads each from north to south; thus one should cast eight north-pointing threads.
Thereafter, upon the pairs of fish formed by the intersections of those threads, one should lay down two threads each from east to west; thus one should apply six east-pointing threads.
In this way, one hundred and forty-four squares are produced;
the word "by means of squares" connects back to the previous context, and it is precisely according to the method previously described for the lotus.
In the row, the pedestal is as before;
as for the remaining [elements],
there is one square situated within the row and five squares situated in the outer row.
The meaning is "thus by six";
as for the word "the rest," he refers to the nine-naveled mandala.
Regarding the phrase "square-shaped," one should there, as before, create sixty-four squares, and within that central group of four, draw a lotus as before.
Then, one should construct four paths consisting of eight squares each in the four cardinal directions;
thus, eight groups of four squares remain in the eight directions.
Having marked those, one should erase them as sixteen [units] in the same manner as before.

As for the method of cleansing, it is sixteenfold: having cleansed one square from each of the four central squares in directions mutually opposite to one another, one should then cleanse three squares—beginning with the corner square—of the adjacent outer path in that same direction.
In this way, by cleansing four squares each in the form of an *upaśobhā*, they result in the shape of a *svastika*.
Some, however, describe the cleansing differently.

Having cleared away two squares from the eastern direction of the central four-square group toward the east, one should then clear away two squares situated in the outer path connected to that [group] extending as far as the southern direction.

Likewise, having cleared away two squares from the southern direction toward the south, one should fill those [remaining squares] with colored powders (*rajas*) starting from the northeast (*śiva*) in the form of *svastikas*.
One should fill those *svastikas* with powders starting from the northeast.
One should complete the remainder by the very path previously described;
this mandala, called the Nine-Centered, is said to bestow all accomplishments.
This fivefold maṇḍala, excluding the svastika, has been taught.
For the purpose of worshipping the deity during initiation, these four types of maṇḍalas have been taught according to all tantras, bestowing all prosperity.
Thus ends the third chapter in the venerable Śāradātilaka.
One should erase the two squares situated in the outer path (vīthī) extending to the western direction.

Likewise, having erased the two squares in the western direction, one should erase the two squares situated in the outer path connected to them and extending to the northern end. Then, having erased the two squares situated in the north in the northern direction, one should erase the two squares situated in the outer path connected to them and extending to the eastern direction.
Even the subsequent [portion] is indeed traditional:
from Śiva onwards, or from Īśāna to Vāyu, the remainder consists of the coloring of the lotuses and so forth, the writing of the *kalpalatikā* on the paths, and the three lines.
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars (||) and does not contain any content to translate.]
"Excluding the svastikas" means that one should erase the four svastikas;
this refers to the group of four. Their application has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*, where the "nine-naved" [mandala] is described: "This supreme state is declared for nine jars."
Likewise, at the previously mentioned location, one should visualize a lotus as before.
Having joined the four sets of four from both ends,
one should draw svastikas in the cardinal directions and erase the corner squares.
This should be the supreme position for the five jars;
likewise, one should draw a lotus in the square place as described.
It is said that for the single deity of the jar, the common position is prescribed.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, the commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*).
Oṃ. The Fourth Chapter.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of those who seek mantras, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), without which the fruit of all mantras cannot be obtained.
The mantra practitioner who accomplishes one [mantra] through numerous rites such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, finds that the others become perfected for him with only slight effort.
For a person who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished;
what then need be said of one who possesses many mantras—he is indeed Hari himself.
Thus, according to the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*, and elsewhere as well:
"O beautiful one, he by whom a mantra written from a book is recited does not achieve success; rather, there is only loss at every step."
Thus it is said;

likewise elsewhere: "Just as those twice-born who have not been initiated have no entitlement here to their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like, so too [they have none] until after the initiation ceremony."
Likewise, those who have not been initiated have no authority over the worship of mantras and deities and so forth; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva.
Thus [it is said].
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Whether heard by chance, or even through deception or non-deception, or if it is written down like a verse, one should recite that which causes no harm."
Thus it is said.

In that very context: "Having entered according to the rules and having heard the *dīkṣā* ending with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should accomplish the desired mantra obtained from the Guru after learning the *tantra*."
Thus it is said elsewhere: "All rituals performed under the guidance of the preceptor bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, those who are intent on liberation should always serve the preceptor with great composure."
Since all actions not performed under the guidance of a guru will certainly be fruitless.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "The rite of recitation and the worship of the deity must be performed by men endowed with initiation;
for there is no sin nor any impurity of birth (sūtaka) for those who are self-restrained."

Since the fruit of the mantra received through initiation has been stated by such passages as these, and because no fruit is accomplished from those [mantras] obtained without the ritual procedure in its absence, he makes a formal promise to explain the necessary initiation, beginning with the word "Now" (atha).

"Now," that is, immediately after the description of the mandala, I shall proclaim the initiation of mantras out of a desire for the welfare [of others]; the remainder of the sense is "for the disciples previously mentioned."
Alternatively, "of the Vedic people" is the ellipsis;
this indeed is the traditional reading,
by which [it refers to] the Śāradātilaka.

It has been stated that the "defect of the mantra" (*mantradoṣa*) is said to be of a universal nature; as it was said by Īśānaśiva: "That [initiation], being common to all, is indeed fourfold according to the divisions of Mantra, Śiva, Śakti, and Viṣṇu;
it is known as the 'Mantric Initiation' (*māntrikī dīkṣā*), and it applies likewise to the groups of mantras."
And among the castes, O twice-born one, it likewise exists among the ancient Śākta and Vaiṣṇava lineages.
Thus it is said.

Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "According to the path of Mantra, the Guru awakens the disciple and initiates him into the mantra by means of the direct [realization] of his chosen deity; that is called initiation."
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*: "That initiation is threefold; the first is the āṇavī, the next is the śākteyī, and the other is the śāmbhavī, which bestows immediate liberation."
Initiation performed through means such as mantras, worship, postures, locations, meditation, and other methods,
according to the form prescribed in the scriptures, is declared to be the individual (āṇavī) initiation.
Having observed his own power, the Siddha performed initiation for the child by means of that power alone, without any external means; this is proclaimed as the Śākteyī initiation.
And even without any ulterior intention, for both the teacher and the noble disciple,
it brings about the manifestation of Śiva-nature solely through the grace of the instructor.
Let this initiation of Śambhu be received, which brings about the immersion into Śiva.
Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, the author will state in the Bhairavī-paṭala: "having received initiation"; there, the meaning is "having received initiation through Śakti."
Likewise, regarding the phrase "one initiated into the twelve-syllable [mantra] with senses conquered," the meaning is that he is initiated there according to the Vaiṣṇava path;
similarly, he is also initiated into the five-syllable [mantra] of Śiva by way of the Śaiva path.

Regarding that, it is said: "In this context, the initiations (dīkṣā) for Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are to be understood according to their respective Tantras; [this applies] to the practitioners of mantra (mantriṇām). In the reading "for the benefit of the practitioners of mantra," they explain that because the word *mantra* is uttered in the latter half [of the verse], the term "of the mantras" (*mantrāṇām*) is connected here, as the fruit of all mantras is being taught.

However, because there is no connection with the principal word *manu* itself, even that which is a mantra-word is [merely] embedded within the grammatical formation (*vṛtti*); thus, the reading is not correct. The Teacher also says: "Now, for the welfare of the world, I shall duly proclaim the rule for the initiation of the Manus."
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: "In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: that of Śambhu, that of Śakti, and that of Mantra."
By the mere sight of the Guru, by touch, or even by conversation, consciousness arises immediately in the person; that initiation is considered Śāmbhavī.
The fourth chapter:
Since it bestows divine knowledge yet causes the accumulation of sin,
it is therefore called *daucca* by the teachers who know the reality.

The initiation by means of power (*śāktī-dīkṣā*) is that which, being possessed of knowledge, is performed by the Guru through the path of yoga and with the eye of wisdom after having entered the body of the disciple.
Initiation consists of the mantra-based and the ritual-based, preceded by the sacrificial pit, the water jar, and the mandala;
for this reason, because of that cause.
Without that initiation (dīkṣā), none of those mantras nor their fruit can be obtained or attained;
by this, the following is stated.

Any mantra whatsoever must be received from the gurus by the disciple through initiation alone, because there is no rule that it would otherwise yield its fruit; furthermore, while by the initiation of Śiva and others only those respective mantras yield their fruit, by this [initiation], all mantras do so.
And "this and all" should also be explained as qualifying the fruit— that is, the fruit of that mantra—
meaning that by mere instruction and so forth, the entire fruit is not obtained, but by this [practice], everything is indeed attained.
Since instruction is also prescribed in other tantras,

the etymology of the word *mantra* is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Because one who has attained perfection effects the contemplation (*manana*) of universal knowledge and protection (*trāṇa*) from the bonds of saṃsāra, he is therefore called a *mantra*."
Thus [it is said].

And in the Rudrayāmala: "O Dear One, because of protecting through contemplation and because of awakening to my own form, it is rightly called 'mantra' (protection through contemplation) due to my presiding presence."
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "Mantra is so called because it is secret instruction, because it involves reflection (manana), and because it provides protection (trāṇa)."
He states the etymological derivation of the word *dīkṣā* as follows: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "destruction" (*kṣaya*)—taking the first letter of these two, this is the etymology.
This is according to the statement of Yāska: "One may explain [a word] even by means of similarity of syllables."
As it has been said: "Because she bestows here a divine state, because she exhausts the impurities of *māyā* and *karman*,
and because she yields the fruit consisting of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), she is therefore designated as *dīkṣā*."

In the *Prayogasāra* it is also said: "Knowledge is bestowed and the accumulation of sin is destroyed; therefore, that rite which is called the severing of bonds (*pāśaccheda*) is to be known as *dīkṣā*."
Thus,

since the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is also to be described here within the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself, something regarding the obligatory duty (*nityakṛtya*) prior to bathing is stated as indicated by the word "by the teachers" (*deśikaiḥ*).

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed purification (*śauca*) and other rites for bodily cleanliness according to the rules prescribed in the *Smṛtis*, one should discard the night garment, put on another cloth, and perform the ritual bath with mantras (*mantra-snāna*). Then, having gone to the temple and performed sweeping, smearing [with cow dung], and other such tasks, one should remove the deity’s remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) and worship with leaves and other materials left over from the previous day, offering salutations; for otherwise, faults are observed—thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
As they say: "A beast overcome by thirst, a bound animal, a maiden in her menses, and a deity with its floral offerings removed—these destroy previously accumulated merit."

Thus it has been stated in the *Mantratattvaprakāśa*: "Having performed the ritual purification (*śauca*) correctly according to the procedure prescribed in the Smṛtis, having washed his feet and sipped water (*ācamana*), and having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) with a restrained mind; having entered the abode of the deity and removed the previous offerings (*nirmālya*), the wise devotee should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), as well as the water for honor (*arghya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*). He should provide water for washing the face and indeed provide a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*);
he should also provide water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and a pure, auspicious garment."

Thus, having sat down in the aforementioned posture, one should meditate on the gurus at the crown of the head; in the morning, one should remember the guru— who has two arms, three eyes, a white complexion, a serene face, and is peaceful— while reciting his name first.
I am the Divine and not another; I am Brahman, not subject to sorrow. I am the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, possessing a nature that is eternally liberated.

Having thus meditated upon the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and one's own self, one should pray: "O Primordial God, O Śrīnātha Viṣṇu, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, by your very command, having risen in the morning, I shall follow the journey through saṃsāra for the sake of your pleasure."

I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. Whatever I am appointed to do by whichever deity residing in my heart, that I perform.
Thus, here [in the mantra],
one should perform the appropriate substitutions (*ūha*) for Śrīnātha Viṣṇu,
Śiva, and so forth— such as "O Caṇḍośa, O Śambhu," and so on— and then, proclaiming the qualities and names of the deity, one should go to a river or other location for the purpose of bathing.
The instruction beginning with "having bathed" (*snātvā*) is for the purpose of stating the sequence [of preliminary rites],
because it is said: "Deities do not preside over a person who wears unclean clothes, has not bathed, and is without ornaments."

By this it is stated that one who is unable to perform the ritual bath with immersion (majjana-snāna) should perform another type of bath; as they say: "In times of distress, [the bath] may be performed with ashes or with the dust of cows, or even with mantras alone."

Furthermore, having bathed according to the rules and performed the morning rites, it is indicated that the mantra-bath (*mantra-snāna*), the mantra-sandhyā, and the mantra-libation (*mantra-tarpaṇa*) must be performed.
Now, I shall proclaim the auspicious bath which removes all sins;
by performing this correctly, the practitioner becomes capable of accomplishing all rites.
Thus, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, the fourth chapter [begins]:
"That [Śakti] is declared to be fourfold, according to the divisions of Kriyāvatī and the others:
Kriyāvatī, Varṇamayī, Kalātmā, and Vedhamayī. (3)

In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* as well, the procedure for the mantra-bath and other rites is stated in such passages as: "Having first performed the Vedic bath, one should thereafter perform the Tantric [bath].
Therein, the mantra-bath is of two kinds: internal and external.

Regarding that, the Vaiṣṇava bath is described in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who resembles infinite suns, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with a crown and a garland of forest flowers. One should contemplate the stream of water arising from His feet falling upon one's own head, entering one's body through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and thereby washing away all impurity residing within the entire body.

At that very moment, the mantra arises, resembling a crystal. This bath is considered superior to [reciting] a thousand mantras. Thus is described the internal Śākta bath in the *Śrīpañcamīmata*: "The method of bathing is twofold, distinguished as external and internal."
I shall respectfully describe this internal bath, though it is an absolute secret, for the destruction of worldly existence and for the attainment of the four aims of life.

Having recollected the threefold consciousness from within the midst of the three feet [of the Guru], one should contemplate oneself as being bathed by that stream of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) which flows forth, which is the object of meditative realization, and which is the means for the liberation of yogis through mere remembrance. One should thus contemplate oneself as purified by that for the sake of the cessation of worldly existence.
Thus, regarding "internal bathing," the Śaiva Āgama describes internal bathing as being performed mentally with the root mantra, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform a mental bath; for that is prescribed in all circumstances.
Thus the external method is described:

having bathed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body—[one recites]: "O Sun, the holy waters within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays."
"By that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford (tīrtha). O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters!"
Those [mudrās], which bring about prosperity, are described in their proper sequence in this *Śāradātilaka* tantra:
"O beautiful goddess, I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing."
Come, O Gaṅgā; salutations to you, who are endowed with all sacred fords.

Thus, having drawn the *tīrtha* from the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*) with the mantras and the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), having invoked it and joined it to the water with the syllable *vaṃ*, having visualized there the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, having consecrated it twelve times with the nectar-seed-syllable (*amṛtabīja*) *vaṃ*, having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and consecrated it eleven times with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should worship it with: "Oṃ! I bow to those waters which are the support of Viṣṇu, who possesses all forms and incomparable splendor, and from whom those [waters] were born, sharing His very nature. Having thus worshipped, one should immerse oneself; having worshipped with this, one should immerse in the *tīrtha* while meditating upon Hari.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, having meditated there upon the root mantra and the form of the deity, and having emerged, one should consecrate oneself seven or twelve times with the root mantra using either the conch mudrā or the flask mudrā, [reciting]: "The entire universe of all beings is repeatedly born as pure semen; may the divine Waters, the mothers of all creatures, purify me. One should utter this, encased by the *tāra* (Oṃ) and the *vāruṇabīja* (Vaṃ).
May the waters, which by their very touch dispel misfortune in the form of impurity residing within all beings, purify me eternally.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with these two mantras: "Whatever misfortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or on my head, forehead, ears, or eyes—may the Waters destroy that; homage to you! Longevity, health, sovereignty, the destruction of the enemy faction, happiness, contentment, forbearance, faith, and knowledge—may these be yours; homage to you! Thus one should consecrate [him].
Thus, one should consecrate oneself with the external mantra-bath using the Vāruṇa mantras and the root-vidyā,
as stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.

As it has been said: Having performed the necessary obligatory rites, such as purification, sipping water (ācamana), cleaning the teeth, and washing the face, one should perform the bath. Having drawn the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the mandala by means of the *ham-mudrā* and *kuśa-mudrā*, and having invoked the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, one should unite them with the water.
The Fourth Chapter:
Having reflected deeply, the mantra-practitioner, being well-composed, should immerse himself in the center of that;
having repeated the root-mantra, he should mentally delineate the multitude of rays.

Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should thereafter perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon himself with the root mantra, using the mudrā known as the "vase" (kalaśamudrā).
"Then, having consecrated [the disciple] with water over which the seven mantras have been recited," so it is said.
Also, in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "Having performed the six-limbed placement upon the limbs, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma)..."
Having drawn forth the sacred water (tīrtha) from the glorious solar disc with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, [one should proceed].
Having bathed [the object] with the syllable *vaṃ* and veiled it with the *kavaca* mantra,
one should protect it with the *astra* mantra and consecrate it with the *mūla* mantra eleven times, O Rudra.
Having immersed oneself therein, one should meditate on Śrīdevī while reciting the mantra according to one's ability;
then, having emerged and formed the water-pot mudrā (kumbhamudrā), one should bathe twelve times thereafter.
Having placed the water from a Śālagrāma stone mixed with the fragrance of Tulasī into a conch shell and having whirled it three times, one should sprinkle it upon one's own head.
He who, without drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, merely pours it upon his head,
is declared to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should first drink the water from the feet of a Brahmin before drinking the water from the feet of Viṣṇu;
practicing what is contrary [to this] out of delusion, he is called a destroyer of his own self.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, they are all present in the ocean;
and all those sacred fords together with the oceans are contained within the right foot of a Brahmin.
Then, having briefly satiated the gods, humans, and ancestors,
and having carefully washed his hands and feet while pressing against his garment, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should wear two pure garments, an undergarment and an upper robe, that are uncut, well-appearing, and white; then, seated upon a stool, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having applied either the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) or the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra), one should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).

Thus. The characteristics of the *aṅkuśa*, *kumbha*, and *śaṅkha* mudrās are as follows: having grasped the left fist with the right fist, one should extend the middle finger and bend it slightly downward; this is the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.
Having placed the right thumb over the left thumb with both hands, one should form a fist with some space remaining; this is the *kumbha* mudrā.
*Śāradātilaka*:
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist,
one should turn the fist upward and then extend the thumb.
The remaining fingers of the left hand, joined and well-extended,
touched by the right thumb— this is declared to be the conch mudrā.
In that regard, there is a specific rule for the Vaiṣṇava tilaka: "A mace should be made on the forehead, and likewise a bow and arrow on the head;
if a Brahmin marked with the conch and discus dies even in a cremation ground, O Nārada, he attains that same destination which is proclaimed for one who dies at Prayāga."
Thus [it is said].
However, according to the Śaivas, immediately after applying the *puṇḍra*, one must also apply the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes;
for the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is mandatory for the twice-born (*dvija*). As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "He upon whose forehead a straight and beautiful *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is seen..."
Even that outcaste, if pure in soul, is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
Even a man who is impure, lacking in proper conduct, and committing evil with his mind,
shall always remain pure if he is marked with the upright *puṇḍra*.

O Four-faced One, for the sake of what is dear to him, for the sake of auspiciousness, or for the sake of protection, my devotee should always wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) without negligence.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the procedure for wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) therein: a wise person should bring ash produced from the Agnihotra fire after it has been purified; or else, having brought cow-dung that has not touched the ground, [he should purify it] with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Having dried it in the vessel with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should burn it away with the Aghora mantra;
having lifted it up with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, one should purify it with the Īśāna mantra.
Having thus consecrated the ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agniriti," and having wiped his limbs and touched them, he should take them up again with the mantra.

One should recite the mantra "tad rudrāya" with the number of Rudras, using the names of the limbs preceded by the *praṇava*, ending in the dative case, and concluding with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, and abdomen with the five-colored powders and other substances, and on the head with the five-syllabled mantra.
Wearing the triple mark while reciting the mantra, he is like another Śiva himself.
Thus [it is said]. The mantra, however, is:
"Fire is ash, wind is ash, water is ash, earth is ash, and space is the fourth ash. This is the fourth chapter.

"Everything here is indeed ashes; the mind and these senses are ashes. Therefore, this is the Pāśupata [practice]: that one should smear the limbs with ashes. Thus, that is Brahman; this is the Pāśupata for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
By means of the five-syllabled Yajus—this is the meaning.
Or in another way: Brahmā is to be worshipped on the forehead, Havyavāhana (Agni) in the heart, Skanda at the navel, Pūṣan in the throat, and Rudra in the right arm.
Āditya is in the middle of the right arm, and Śaśin is at the wrist;
Vāmadeva is in the left arm, and Prabhañjana is in the middle of the left arm.
The Vasus are at the wrist, and Hara is said to be in the region of the back;
Śambhu is proclaimed to be at the hump of the neck, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is said to be in the head.
Thus it is said.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) without mantras is also mentioned:
"Furthermore, with hands separated, the practitioner of mantra should draw the triple mark with ashes."
Thus it is said.
The collection of ash is also mentioned in that very same place:
"The ash from the fire of Śiva should be collected, or else that which is a byproduct of the Agnihotra."
Or even food cooked for a wedding or for a guest, which is pure and fragrant.
The white excrement of a tawny cow, caught as it falls from the sky,
is neither wet nor too hard, neither foul-smelling nor putrid.
If [the offering] has fallen, one should discard it from above and below;
having gathered it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire with the root mantra.
Having discarded both the uncooked and the over-cooked white ash,
one should take it with a cloth, knead it, and cast it into the receptacle for ashes.
One should collect the ashes while the deity has not yet been dismissed;
for once the dismissal has been performed, the ashes become *caṇḍabhasma* (impure ashes).
Thus.
Then, having performed the twilight rite (saṃdhyā) as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā), one should perform the mantra-saṃdhyā. It is as follows:

Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should take water from the sacred site (*tīrtha*) in the right hand, recite the root mantra over it three times, and perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) three times with that same root mantra. Then, placing the sacred water from the right hand into the left hand, one should consecrate it threefold with the root mantra. Sprinkling oneself seven times with the drops of water falling from it while reciting the root mantra, one should take the remaining water in the right hand, bring it near the nose, and—imagining the accumulation of sins as being drawn out of the body through the *iḍā* channel—visualize that water as black in color as it is expelled through the *piṅgalā* (right) channel. One should then cast it upon the previously visualized diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) while reciting the mantra.
This is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
