Again, taking water with both hands joined as an *añjali*, the preceptor, having bathed according to the rules and performed his morning rites, should offer the *arghya* to the Deity residing in the solar orb, using either the respective *gāyatrīs* or the root mantra, according to the *Śāradātilaka*: "I offer this *arghya* to the Deity situated in the solar orb."
Adorned and observing silence, he should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice.

Having offered water for the feet (*arghya*) three times while meditating on the Deity residing within the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*), and having performed worship (*upasthāna*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should recite the *Gāyatrī* of the respective mantra or the root mantra twenty-eight times.

Then, having uttered the root mantra and performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) twenty-eight times with the words "I satiate the Deity," and having visualized the Deity within the solar disc and offered *arghya* to the Sun, one should dismiss the sacred water (*tīrtha*) with the *saṃhāramudrā*. After bowing to the Sun and others, and reciting a hymn of praise (*stuti*) to the Deity, one should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
Thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having performed the twilight worship (*sandhyā*) and recited the hymns (*stotra*), one should go to the temple of the deity.

Likewise: "Having performed the Tantric bath according to the prescribed rule, having performed both the Vedic and Tantric twilight worship, and likewise the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should go to the abode of the God while reciting hymns and [the Lord's] names."
By this [term] *mauna*, the prohibition of conversing with blind persons is intended.

As for the characteristic of the *saṃhāramudrā*: having placed the right hand, which is facing upward, upon the left hand, which is facing downward, one should join the fingers of the two hands together and rotate them. This is called the *saṃhāramudrā*; it is highly recommended for the act of offering (*arpaṇa*). Thus [it is said].

This has been stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Having sat down in a pure place and performed three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) in succession by means of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), one should indeed perform the purification (*mārjana*) of the body with water. Then, touching the nose with that water, the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite is prescribed using the entire [mantra]; this auspicious *arghya* offering removes sin. Thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform the worshipful salutation (*upasthāna*) by means of the Reality."

Having remembered Viṣṇu, who consists of light and is the great soul residing within the maṇḍala, the practitioner should thereafter perform the recitation (japa) with the root mantra, or with the Gāyatrī or a Vaiṣṇava mantra, preceded and followed by the two instances of the syllable Om (praṇava). Having sat down in a pure place, he should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa);
there, he should diligently offer libations to the deities known as Viṣṇu, as well as to the ancestors and human beings. After that, he should ask for forgiveness from the sacred ford (tīrtha).

One should proceed while reciting the root mantra until one reaches the house. Having reached it, having diligently washed both hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should approach the sacrificial pavilion and enter after performing a circumambulation.
Thus [it is said] elsewhere as well. This concludes the fourth chapter.

Having sipped water again and performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) as before, the wise one should take water in the left hand and perform a sevenfold sprinkling with the dripping drops of water while uttering the root mantra at the head. Then, taking the remaining water in the right hand, he should draw it in through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] into the interior of the body, thereby washing away the accumulation of sins.
That black-colored water, having been expelled through the *dakṣanāḍī*, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate it as the form of sin in his right hand;
then, facing a diamond-stone (*vajrapāṣāṇa*), he should cast it away with the *astra-mantra*. Standing, he should offer three handfuls of water to the Sun;
then the wise one should recite the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Having prostrated before the Lord residing within the solar disc, he should ask for forgiveness.

Having purified the sacred water (*tīrtha*) with the *saṃhāramudrā* and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should remain silent. Having thus completed the twilight worship (*sandhyā*), one should then begin the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Then, having made the sacred water consist of the nature of Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva, one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with that water using the *saṃhitā-mantras*. [The method is: joining the water fallen from the left hand with the right hand.

The cleansing of the head with the Krama-mantras is thus described. Having brought that white water, which is the very form of consciousness, into the hollow of the right hand and led it up to the tip of the nose, one should draw it in through the left nostril and retain it by means of *kumbhaka*. Then, visualizing that sin as having the appearance of soot, one should expel it through the right nostril (*piṅgala*) and cast it upon a stone slab; this constitutes the *aghamarṣaṇa*. [This is performed] with the *Śiva-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, accompanied by *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water.

Having offered a handful of water (*añjali*) for Śiva, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra according to one's ability. Having sipped water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, one should offer the *arghya* with a handful of water containing red flowers and other substances, using the root mantra, to the Sun. Thus, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods and others, one should carry out the rites up to the end of the Brahma-yajña.

Having meditated upon Mahādeva as situated within the maṇḍala and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rule, one should then offer food (arghya) to that Śiva who is in the form of the Sun. Thus,

having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rule and having performed the general offering (sāmānyārghya) there, and having sprinkled the door with water containing unhusked rice (masūra), one should perform the worship of the door.
The mantra "Vyomavyāpin," those which are the five Brahmans,
the mantras of the Śiva-Gāyatrī, and Rudra— in this sequence— this Vidyā known as the Śivasaṃhitā is declared to be the destroyer of all sins. Thus [it is said].
One should proclaim "Āmoṃ Mūṃ Ādya" and then "Vyomavyāpine";
this [mantra], enclosed by the Praṇava at the beginning and end, is proclaimed as Vyomavyāpin.
Thus is the general rule.
The specific mantras for the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other rites should be understood as those prescribed in their respective *kalpas*.

Furthermore, this twilight devotion (*sandhyā*) should be performed at the three times of day, as stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*: "Having meditated upon Rāma as one's own self and as the Guru, one should then perform the Rāma-sandhyā."
"In the evening, in the morning, and at midday"— thus,
the knower of mantras should perform the *saṃdhyā* at dawn, noon, and sunset. Regarding the term "having sipped water" (*ācamya*),
it refers to that location outside the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
Because it is stated thus in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:

"According to the rule" means by the rule prescribed in the Smṛtis and by the Vaiṣṇava rules and so forth, as they say: "Facing east or north, with the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder, having tied the topknot, and with the arms placed between the knees."

Then, having sat down comfortably and being composed, one who intends to eat should look at the water. For the sake of purification, one should sip water that is not hot, which is free from insects, foam, and bubbles, and is untainted by foul tastes or odors; it may even be water that has been merely looked upon. Water reaching the heart, the throat, and the mouth respectively purifies the wise, the twice-born, and even Śūdras and women; however, for those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) such as the Kuṇḍa, it purifies them only if drunk once.

Having sipped water three times, one gratifies the three Vedic Persons (the Vedapurushas); by wiping [the mouth] twice, the Atharvanas are pleased; and by touching with the thumbs, the six-limbed Sacrificial Person (Yajñapurusha) becomes gratified. By touching the eyes with the ring finger joined with the thumb, one gratifies the Sun; likewise, by touching the two nostrils with the index finger joined with the thumb, one gratifies the Wind; by touching the ears with the little finger and the thumb, one gratifies the Quarters; by touching from the navel to the heart, one gratifies the Vasus; by touching the shoulders, one gratifies the Self (Atman); by touching the head, one gratifies the Speech and the Sages (Rishis); and by touching with all the fingers together, one gratifies the entire body. Thus it is said.

Alternatively, the Vaiṣṇava method of *ācamana* (sipping water) is as follows: having sipped with three [mantras] beginning with Keśava, one should wash the hands with two, wipe the lips with two, and likewise cleanse the mouth with two. The Fourth Chapter:
[Salutations to] Umā, Gaṇeśa, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.

Then, on the right branch [of the hand], one should worship Vighna and Īśa elsewhere. Having washed one hand with one [water] and likewise the feet with another, one should sprinkle the head with one more; then, with [the mantras of] Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, one should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, navel, chest, neck, and arms. Having performed the *ācamana* (ritual sipping) in this manner, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself. Keśava and the others were mentioned previously; I shall now describe those beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, Acyuta,
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Viṣṇu— these indeed are the twelve.

Having thus performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), [one should worship] with the principles of the Self (ātmatattva) and so forth, preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with Svadhā.

Then, one should touch the mouth, the three [eyes], the nose, the two eyes, the ears, the navel, the heart, the head, and the shoulders. It is taught that the salutation is performed with the heart-mantra and the ears.

Having contemplated the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, as well as the Praṇava and the Vāgbhava [mantras], one should drink water three times using the Brahma-tīrtha, accompanied by the Śambara mantras.

One should know the three principles (tattvas) consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, respectively, by means of [the syllables] beginning with *ātmatattva* ending in *svadhā*; likewise, *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *hūṃ* are the *śambaras* in sequence. Having thus performed the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should do so outside.
The general *argha* is described in the *Mantramuktāvatī*: "Having purified the vessel with the *astra* mantra, one should fill it with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having invoked the *tīrtha*, one should cast in the perfumes and other substances with the *praṇava*.
One should then display the *dhenu-mudrā*; this is declared to be the general *argha*. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that by the word *praṇava*, the five *praṇavas* are to be grasped according to their respective contexts.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having placed a common vessel facing the door and recited "Oṃ hraḥ, I prepare the water for the door (*dvārārghya*)," [one proceeds].
The sequence stated in the verse beginning with "by the mere vessel" (pātramātreṇa) should be followed:
having recited the Astra mantra, one should sprinkle the door with the water from the general arghya vessel.
The general weapon-mantra (*sāmānyāstra*) will be explained further on;

here, at the beginning of every section, even before the weapon-mantra and others that are about to be presented, one should apply the general weapon-mantra at the end of the secondary weapons (*anvāstra*) with the formula: *astrāya phaṭ*.
This applies likewise to all limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*).
Some say that in the case of unpalatable [substances], sounds such as "phaṭ" arise from the mere genus alone.
He describes the worship of the door itself:

one should worship with flowers and water the *ūrdhvāḍumbaraka*—the horizontal beam above the two door-posts—and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā situated at their sides; furthermore, one should worship the *astra* (weapon-mantra) on the threshold at each door in due order.

The term "udumbara" refers to a branch of the *udumbara* tree; however, because of the similarity between that and the lintel (*dehalī*) situated above, the word "udumbara" is used there figuratively.
In the center of that [lintel] is Mahālakṣmī, the Goddess of the Door.

The connection is that one should worship with "flower-waters," meaning with water and flowers for the *arghya* offering; as it has been said: "Having worshipped the Goddess of the Door (*Dvāraśrī*) above [the door]," and elsewhere: "Above the door, 'Salutation to Dvāraśrī'; on its right and left..."
"Vighnaṃ Sarasvatīṣva.
Then, in the two corners situated at the base of the [central] pillar, one should worship Vighna and Sarasvatī starting from the south;
"on the southern branch" means below the southern branch.
In this regard, some maintain that the worship of Durgā is performed elsewhere; the connection is that Kṣetreśa is located below the Vāma-śākhā.
As it has been said: "In the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kṣetreśa";
by the words "of those two," [it refers to] Vighna and Kṣetreśa.

By the phrase "the Gaṅgā and Yamunā are on the sides," the worship of the doors and so forth is indicated as before; that same [worship] is stated further on by the phrase "in due order. *Vāri* refers to the water for general ablution (*sāmānyārghyajala*).
The mantras for these [deities] are preceded by the first syllable consisting of the *tāra* (oṃ), the *sabindu* (the nasalized vowel), and the name, ending with *namaḥ* and *diṅ* (the directions).
The practical application is as follows: *oṃ hrāṃ dvāraśriyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Ḍāmara*: "The first syllable of the name is situated between the *oṃkāra* and the *bindu*."

"That is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the deities; it bestows supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and accomplishment (*siddhi*) in worship. This will also be stated later in the text: "Beginning with the first letter of their own names," and this [rule] should be understood as applying to those cases where the seed-syllable has not been explicitly mentioned.
"At the threshold" means: "Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ namaḥ"—thus is the worship of the weapon (astra) performed with flowers and water.
As it has been stated: "The letters *ha* and *ra*, accompanied by the *visarga*, followed by the utterance 'astrāya phaṭ' at the end."
"In the interval between [the recitation], the wise man should here release mustard seeds, unbroken grains, or flowers.
Others, however, desire the worship of the Vāstu-puruṣa in this very place;
as it is said: "The Vāstu-man is to be worshipped there, at the center of the door-sill."
Thus,
their meditations are to be understood according to their respective contexts;
for this very reason, the term "Mahālakṣmī" is employed here.
By the term "at each door," this is what is meant:
as they have said— "To Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and to Gaṅgā and Yamunā, [one should offer] first at the beautiful door on its right and left branches."
Oṃ! To Bhadra and Subhadra, a cow and a black [animal] are offered as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the south;
and to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, the Revā and Tāpī rivers are offered in the west.
Oṃ, to the treasure of the conch and the lotus, [bestow] Vāṇī and Veṇī likewise in the north. Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Immediately thereafter, the preeminent teacher, by means of his divine vision, [beheld].
One should dispel divine obstacles with water from a celestial source, and those that move through the atmosphere with water from the sky.

Somaśambhu also says: "One should [place] two rivers with their own names ending in the dative case. Elsewhere, however, it is said: "Bhadra and Subhadra, and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, on the two door-panels."
One should worship [the mantra] ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ" at the eastern gate.
One should worship at the southern gate the mantra "Balaprabala-cic-chakti-māyā-śakti," ending with "namaḥ" as the fourth component.
One should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, as well as Gaurī and Uccaiḥśrī, at the two doorposts with [mantras] ending in the dative case and ending in "namaḥ," in the western direction.
One should worship Jaya and Vijayā, as well as the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures,
ending with the fourth [treasure] and followed by "namas," in the north;
thus some say that the worship of the door-keepers mentioned below is also obligatory.
All of this should be understood as being the same for the daily worship as well;
as they say: "This is to be performed everywhere, especially in the case of consecrated [images]."
Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), however, there is a specific distinction mentioned in another tantra:
one should worship the door-keepers according to the various divisions such as Vaiṣṇava and so forth,
with two on each side of every door, making eight in total in due order.
Nanda, Sunanda, the one named Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, the one named Bala, Prabala, the one named Bhadra, and Subhadra are considered Vaiṣṇavas.
Then Nandi and Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa and the Bull, and then Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Skanda, and Pāḷatośa as the seventh.
Caṇḍeśvara is the eighth; these are the Śaiva door-keepers in order:
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana, the one named Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and Vighnarāja as the seventh.
Dhūmrarāja is to be known as the eighth; these are the Gāṇapatyas in their proper order.

"The Mothers are said to begin with Brāhmī, and the Śākteyas are the door-keepers. However, others state that Gopāla and Rāmacandra are the door-keepers: "Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are in the east; Dhāta and Vidhāta in the south; Jaya and Vijaya in the west; and Bala and Prabala in the north."
And that which was indicated by the words "immediately thereafter" is [further clarified]:
by the phrase "O Lord of Teachers," one should ward off the formidable obstacles with three blows of the heel upon Sadāśiva, who is one's own self, according to the *Śāradātilaka*.
Touching slightly with his left hand the branch of the threshold, the Guru should leap over it; contracting his body within, he should enter with his right foot.
In the south-western direction, one should worship Vāstoṣpati and Brahmā,
and sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and water for the arghya offering.
Having reflected thus, it was said that the very beholding of one's own visible form as Sadāśiva is indeed the beholding of the divine vision;
"with waters" means with ordinary sacrificial water.
Regarding the blows with the heels, the mantra for that occasion is as follows: "May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva."
"May the spirits and piśācas depart in all directions; without causing offense to anyone, I shall commence this rite of Brahman.
Thus it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* after reciting the verse beginning with "apasarpan... and so forth.
Having struck the ground three times with the palm of his hand while reciting this mantra, the wise knower of mantras, having driven away the hosts of spirits, should sit upon his seat.
Thus says Somaśambhu: "With three strikes of the right hand, [he should dispel] the three kinds of beings residing in the earth."
Thus,
in this manner, [one should overcome] the three kinds of obstacles.
"A limb" refers to the left limb; "contracting" means doing so in order to provide space for the emerging obstacles.
As it has been said: "While granting *darbha* grass to the left for those obstacles that have been driven away."
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "For those who are departing and creating obstacles, one should grant them passage by means of the gesture of contracting the left side of the body."
Thus,
it is likewise stated elsewhere: "and having expelled the host of obstacles from the left."
The triad beginning with *antaḥspṛśan* has a perceptible purpose, because even the body is worshipped as the deity;
*vāsvośam* refers to the *kṣetrapāla* (field-guardian) of each respective field,
and these shall be described by me in the *Kṣetrapālamantra*.
The section beginning with "divyadṛṣṭi" and ending with "brahmārcana" is the same for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) as well;
the method for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) will be explained in the twenty-first [chapter].
"One should sprinkle the water for the *arghya*—the general *arghya* water"—thus it is stated that [the water] should be offered consecutively;
as it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should sprinkle the site of initiation with cow-products, purified by the mantra."
Thus [it is said].
The Fourth Chapter:
One should perform the purification up to the crossroads by means of inspection and so forth;
inspection is performed with the root mantra, while sprinkling is considered to be done with the weapon-mantra (śara).
Striking with *darbha* grasses is prescribed by that very [mantra], and sprinkling with armor [mantras] is considered [the rule];
the wise one should fumigate the interior with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
and scatter *vikirāḥ* there, consecrated seven times with the *īśvara-mantra*.
Parched grain, sandalwood, *siṅghārtha*, ashes, a raised finger, a goad, and unbroken rice—
these are designated as the *vikira* offerings, which destroy the entire multitude of obstacles;
one should sweep them away with a handful of *darbha* grass over which the mantra has been recited.
In the direction of the Lord (the East), one should prepare a seat for the *vardhanī* vessel;
having caused the Brahmins to pronounce the *puṇyāha* blessing and having satisfied them,
[one should place] the scattered offerings (*vikira*), which are either pure parched grains (*lāja*) or grains consecrated seven times with the weapons-mantra.
These [darbha blades], sprinkled with water from the Astra-mantra, veiled with the Kavaca-mantra, having the forms of various weapons, warding off the multitude of obstacles,
and fashioned from darbha grass thirty-six finger-breadths long according to the measure of a palm; [one should contemplate them as such].
Having recited the Śivāstra mantra seven times, one should wipe the fist with it; thus, with the mantra "the supreme sword of awakening," one should perform the scattering and wiping.
Having drawn one of the mandalas mentioned in the *Śāradātilaka* upon the altar,
he should enter and sit upon a seat of earth, facing either east or north, while reciting the mantras.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, observing silence, composed and having conquered his senses,
the preceptor should place the articles of worship on the right side and enter.
"A soft seat" means for the sake of avoiding agitation; this is for a visible purpose,
because when there is agitation, the mind goes toward that very thing and not toward recitation, worship, or the like—
this is what is expressed by the word "mantra."
Having recited "Homage to Anantāsana, homage to Vimalāsana,
homage to Padmāsana" and placed the consecrated kuśa grass upon the seat, one should worship the seat.
For the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*): Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chanda*), Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for sitting upon the seat.
Oṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Therefore, support me always, O Goddess, and make this seat pure.
Thus, one should sit with the seat-mantra (āsana-mantra).

As it has been said: "For that seat, they declare the sage to be Kūrma, and the metre should be Sutala; the wise one has declared Pṛthivī to be its deity. Its utility is stated for rites such as recitation (japa) and so forth."
Thus,
the seats for that [practice] as stated in other tantras are: a seat made of silk, or iron, or cloth, or skin, or wool,
or cane, or palm leaf, or blanket, or darbha grass.
The practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, wood, earth, grass, or shoots, as it bestows poverty, disease, and suffering; however,
the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation occurs upon a seat of cloth, antelope skin, and kuśa grass.

Thus, a specific distinction regarding the *dāḷīsana* is stated elsewhere: "One should have the seat for ascetics made in the shape of a tortoise; however, for others, one should have it made four-legged and square."
A wise person should always avoid a seat made of cow-dung, clay, or split bamboo, as well as one made of Palāśa or Pippala wood, or one pierced by metal; likewise,
one should avoid performing giving, sipping water for purification, fire-offerings, eating, or the worship of deities upon such a seat.
One should not perform Vedic study or the libation of water (tarpaṇa) with the feet placed upon a seat,
nor with the feet resting on the knees or the shanks; he who has formed a cross-legged posture in this manner is said to be one with "propped-up feet" (prauḍhapāda).
"Thus,
with the lotus posture bound"—
he will explain the lotus posture later on.

One should bind the two thumbs; this is the fourth chapter. One should place a beautiful vessel, filled with well-scented water, on the left for the washing of the hands, and afterwards, one should set down the foot [pedestal].
The preceptor should place auspicious lamps fed with ghee all around,
as well as a mirror, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, and a beautiful palm-leaf fan;
he should also place vessels containing auspicious sprouts in the various directions.
Having joined the palms in *añjali*, and having bowed to the gurus and Gaṇeśa at the left and right sides, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Having accomplished the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), one should thereafter perform three claps (*tāla*).

The portion "with the two desired [feet]" is applicable only to the *yoga* posture; it does not apply here because in other systems (*tantrāntara*) the definition of the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) is stated exactly as follows:
"Having taken the left foot, one should place it upon the right."
In the same manner, one should place the right foot upon the left;
having firmly pressed the heels against the thighs, with the eyes fixed on the tip of the nose—
this is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is honored by all.
The term "lotus posture" (padmāsana) is illustrative;
as they say: "Seated in a single posture such as the lotus, the svastika, or the heroic (vīra), one should perform recitation, worship, and so forth; otherwise, it shall be fruitless."
By the phrase "thus [observing] silence," there is a prohibition of conversation prompted by worldly attachment;
as it has been said: "One should not converse even with those present in the assembly during the performance of japa, homa, worship, and so forth."
Thus,

"samāhitaḥ" means concentrated, "sāvadhānaḥ" means attentive, and "jitendriyaḥ" is a descriptive compound meaning one who has conquered the senses; "pūjādravyāṇi" refers to the materials for worship, such as flowers and so forth.
The term "deśika" (preceptor) is connected with what follows;
by this, it is stated that one should also place the vessels for *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *madhuparka-ācamana* on the left.
"Suvāsita" means [perfumed] with camphor and so forth.
"Manoharam" (charming) is an adjective qualifying all four items beginning with the mirror; the syntactical connection is "one should place the mirror," and so forth,
ending with "one should enter," etc.
This much is the same even for the daily worship (*nitya-pūjā*);
by the statement "the preceptor should place in the directions those auspicious vessels containing sprouts which have had seeds sown according to the aforementioned method," this is what is meant.

According to the stated sequence, having thus performed [the rite] three times in the eastern direction and so forth, this alone is their ritual of realization (*pratipatti-karma*). This occurs precisely during the initiation (*dīkṣā*);
having joined one's palms in reverence, one should bow to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna on the left and right sides—thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
The preceptor should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) by means of the Arkoḍamastra;
he should provide protection on all sides with the splendor generated by that [mantra].
This is the connection.
Therein, the ritual application is: Oṃ Gaṃ, homage to the Gurus;
Oṃ Gaṃ, homage to Gaṇapati.

The mantras for the limbs of the sacrifice, beginning with Guvvā and Tārā and ending with Lokeśa, should end in the dative case followed by "namaḥ" during worship; however, for the purpose of casting spells (vaśīkaraṇa), they should end in "ṭhaḥ."

Since it is stated here that "examples are for the sake of understanding," this includes the tongues of fire and so forth that will be described later, because the performance of the *homa* sacrifice with the mantras of the Lokapālas follows immediately thereafter. By the use of the plural form "gurus," the Guru, Paramaguru, Parāparaguru, and Parameṣṭhiguru are all included.
As they say: "Then, beginning from the very start, one should bow to the lineage of gurus";
therefore, one should recite this verse.
"Oṃ, salutations to the great ones, salutations to the children, salutations to the young, salutations to the aged;
let us worship the gods if we are able; may we not fall into the reproach of our elders, O gods.
Thus is the purification of the hands.

In this context, [the phrase] "with the *astra* mantra" is connected to the three [rites] beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). Among these, that which is called the purification of the hands consists of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *astra* mantra by way of pervasion upon the fingers beginning with the thumbs, both on the interior and exterior of both hands, and on both sides of both hands. As it has been said: "The mantra is on the interior and exterior of the two hands, which are the pervaded and the pervader, and on their sides."
"Digbandha" (the binding of the directions) refers to the placement of the weapon-mantra (*astramantranyāsa*) in the ten directions using the *nārāca-muṣṭi* (the arrow-fist) with the index finger;
this is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having covered the directions with the index finger, whose tip is pressed against the tip of the middle finger."
Elsewhere it is also stated: "If the tip of the thumb touches the middle of the middle finger while the other fingers remain unattached,
then that shall be the mudrā of the supreme weapon named Nārāca, the destroyer of elemental beings."

There is a distinction elsewhere: at the conclusion of the *praṇava* and the heart-mantra, one should likewise utter the word "Sudarśana" with the dative case, and then, with the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, one should fashion the ten directions.

By the word "deśika" (the guide), it is indicated that one should construct the fire-rampart (*agniprākāra*) both with the *sudarśana* mantra and with the fire-rampart mantra to be described hereafter.

Regarding the mudrā for the fire-rampart, it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Placing the two hands at the tips of the trident and moving them crossed over on both sides—this is declared to be the *astra-mudrā*, characterized by the fire-rampart."
"It pacifies the malice of others and removes the fear of serpents and thunderbolts.

Thus it was said; then, having purified [the site] with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one performs the hand-clapping (*pāṇi*), the triple-sound (*tritāla*), the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), and the fire-hall (*hutāśaśālā*).

He states their fruit with the words "by that": "One who is composed should unite the self with the Supreme Self by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, according to the method joined with yoga, using the *cin-mantra*. This concludes the fourth chapter.
One should also contemplate the principles (tattvas) of all beings within the Cause (kāraṇa),
merged in the state of seeds (bīja-bhāva) in reverse order within the Supreme Self (paramātman).

The connection is as follows: being composed, one should—by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā* and through the method joined with yoga—unite the self (*ātman*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by means of the "consciousness-mantra" (*cinmantra*).
In this context, "the self" refers to the individual self (*jīvātman*) residing within the heart-lotus.

Regarding what they have said— "The soul, which is the size of the tip of a needle, should be contemplated by the wise within the heart-lotus born from the bulb of Brahman and possessing the stalk of knowledge"—
this is the meaning of the phrase "by the method joined with yoga."

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī by means of the syllable *haiṃ* according to the path taught by the Guru, and having visualized her as residing in the heart-lotus, one should then grasp the individual soul (*jīva*) at its opening and visualize it as having reached the thousand-petaled lotus;
for this very reason, there is the expression "composed" (*samāhita*). This is done with the *citt-mantra*, that is, the *ātman-mantra* which will be described hereafter.
As they say: "The supreme white [principle] is to be led by means of the *haṃsa* to the *dvādaśānta*";
and elsewhere as well: "Having drawn up that *jīva* from its own abode in the sky by means of the *haṃsa* through its own path."
Elsewhere also: "Then, having joined the *jīva* with the *haṃsa* by way of the difficult-to-traverse central channel (*nār̤ī*) into the extremely subtle *Śiva* seated in the *puṣkara*"—
the meaning is that [this occurs] within the Supreme Self, which has reached the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: one should contemplate the principles (*tattva*), beginning with earth, as dissolved by way of reversal into their causal state within the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the cause of all beings, in the form of a seed (*bījabhāvena*).
In this context, "reversal" (*vyutkrama*) refers to the order of dissolution in relation to the process of creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
In all cases, the dissolution of the effect into its cause is observed;
for this very reason, the description of emanation was given in the first chapter,
because without emanation, there can be no knowledge of cause and effect.

Therefore, the qualifying expression "the cause of all beings" is used; furthermore, by the word "also," it is implied that he should likewise withdraw the phonemes from their positions of placement, as it has been said: "Having thus meditated, one should then withdraw the phonemes from those points of placement."
And its sequence is according to the Tantra: by way of reversal, the movement is from the letter *la* to this *ha*; from *ha* to *sa*, and then from *sa* to *ṣa*.

Having diligently brought about the dissolution [of the elements] in sequence up to the letter *a*, one should place that *a* in the *sahasrāra* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). The word "iti" (thus) serves to include the preceding [elements] in conjunction.
Then, one should dry the body with the wind-seed (Ya) and the wind-element;
by that same fire-seed (Ra), one should consume the entire physical form.
Then, having sprinkled the impurities with the nectar-like water of immortality, one should flood the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
The word "tataḥ" means by the wind, that is, by the seed-syllable *ya* (yakāra), or by the wind arising from it.

By this, the inhalation (pūraka) is described; with that very *repha*, the seed-syllable of fire, he should burn his entire body— along with the personification of sin in the form of his own impurities— by means of the fire arising from the seed-syllable of fire.

The meditation on the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) is as follows: he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head, the theft of gold for his two arms, the drinking of liquor for his heart, and the violation of the Guru’s bed for his two hips.
The pair of feet joined with it was the falling of limbs and minor members;
its hairs were the minor offenses (upapātaka), and its beard and eyes were red.
"One should visualize [the sin] as holding a sword and shield, the size of a thumb, facing downwards, black in color, within the right side of the abdomen.
By this, the *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) is described.

Then, when the burning has occurred, by the statement "one should separate the impurities—the ash of the personified sin (pāpapuruṣa) which is the very nature of the defects"—the exhalation (*recaka*) is described. In that context, it should be understood that the separation of the ash also occurs through the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*).
As the teachers have said: "One should release [the breath] according to the previous rule."

Thus says Nāgabhaṭṭa as well: "By means of the wind [emanating] from the Lord of Sāsyā, he removed that entire heap of ashes. And likewise in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "That whole mass of ashes, by means of the wind arising from the seed-syllable of Vāyu..."
"Having scattered [it]," and elsewhere: "The body, consumed by the fire of the rising city of the ten directions, having its ashes cast away by the wind.
Regarding these three locations, some say they follow the sequence of the numbers sixteen, sixty-four, and thirty-two.
Others say that the number is fifty-two or twenty-five;
as it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "By means of the seeds of Marut, Agni, and Sudhā, there are fifty measures (mātrās).
And the Teachers [say]: "Alternatively, when the body has been purified through the process of drying, burning, and flooding..."
One should duly restrain the vital breaths through fifty distinct measures of duration.
"Furthermore, although consisting of fifty [syllables], the *tāra* is taught to be divided by its constituent parts (*kalā*);
for one who knows the reality, the *kalās* become established through that very measure.
Thus, some maintain that there is a threefold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) for each of the three locations.

The connection is as follows: with the nectar, that is, by means of the seed-syllable of nectar "vaṃ," one should cause the body—from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head—to be pervaded by the ambrosial water arising from that [syllable]. Fourth Paṭala:
At that time, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved in the Self to return to their own respective locations.
One should bring one's own self into the heart-lotus of the Supreme Self.

"His own place" (svasthānam) means that, according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) and the method described in the first chapter, by the word "then" (*tadā*), it is stated that one should also cause the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* to reach their own places in the order of emanation.
As it has been said: "Having brought down [the mantra] consisting of all the phonemes from this [state] through the recitation of the letter *la*, one should fashion [it] with that."

"Having fashioned the entire body as being sprinkled by a flood of nectar"—this is the connection: having thus fashioned the body with half of a hundred syllables, one should bring the self from the Supreme Self to the lotus of the heart by means of the mantra of Haṃsadeva.
The "Lord of Haṃsa" (Haṃsadeva) is the Supreme Self, because He is the object of worship for the individual soul (jīva).

By that mantra, "so'ham" (I am He), or alternatively, it is connected with the word "manunā" (by the mantra) referring to the Supreme Self; thus it was previously stated that one should first unite [it] with the Supreme Self, from which the meaning "thereafter" is obtained. This is then connected with the subsequent phrase "of the divine Haṃsa."

This has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "Having thus sounded that primordial [Maṅkhī] at the end of the *nāda* by means of the *so'ham* mantra, which is meditated upon as perfected (*siddha*), one should place the digit of the individual soul (*jīvakaḷā*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) into the heart.
This is also stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Having brought the consciousness of the Self from the sky of consciousness (*cidambara*) by means of the thought 'I am That' (*so'ham*)."

In this regard, the procedure is written down according to the teacher’s instruction for the sake of attaining the qualification for the worship of the deity and other rites: having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), "I shall perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth," one should visualize the *kuṇḍalinī*—arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, radiant with the brilliance of a thousand flashes of lightning, and in the form of a lotus fiber—having reached the heart-lotus by way of the *suṣumṇā*. Then, taking the individual soul (*jīva*) from the heart-lotus in the form of a lamp-flame, and visualizing it as having gone to the thousand-petaled lotus at the *dvādaśānta*, one should unite that individual soul with the Supreme Self there by means of the *haṃsa* mantra.

Then, one should contemplate the square earth-maṇḍala, extending from the feet to the knees, as a yellow color. Therein, having recollected the foot, the act of moving, the destination, smell, the sense of smell, the earth, Brahmā, the Nivṛtti-kalā, and the Samāna-vāyu, one should utter this mantra: "Oṃ hrāṃ, to Brahmā, lord of the earth, whose nature is the Nivṛtti-kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this, one should dissolve all of them into the waters through the gateway of Kuṇḍalinī; thus one should withdraw them into the locus of water.

From the knees up to the navel is the white water-maṇḍala in the shape of a half-moon; there, having recollected the hand, the act of taking, the object to be taken, the sense of taste, the water, Viṣṇu, the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], and the *udāna* [breath], one should utter this mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ! To Viṣṇu, the lord of waters, the essence of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! and, thinking "I dissolve all these into the fire through the door of Kuṇḍalinī," one should withdraw them into the locus of the fire.

From the navel up to the heart is a triangle, the fire-maṇḍala, red in color. Therein, having meditated upon the four—Pāyu, Visarga, Visarjanīya, and Rūpa—as well as Tejas, Rudra, Vidyā, and Vyāna, one should utter this mantra: "Oṃ Hūṃ! To Rudra, the Lord of Fire, whose self is the Kalā of Vidyā, Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Thinking, "I dissolve all these into the wind through the door of Kuṇḍalinī," one should withdraw them into the locus of the wind. Then, from the heart up to the eyebrows is a black circle marked with six dots, as described in the Śāradātilaka.

There, having recollected the wind-maṇḍala, its attendant bliss, its object—touch—the tangible wind, its lord, its tranquility, and the apāna breath, one should utter this mantra: *oṃ haiṃ īśānāya vāyudhipataye śāntikalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, thinking "I dissolve all these into space through the door of Kuṇḍalinī," one should withdraw them into the locus of space.

Then, from the space between the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), one should contemplate the clear, circular sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*). Within that, having recollected speech, face, the inexpressible, sound, the sense of hearing, space, Sadāśiva, Śāntyatītā, and Prāṇa, one should utter this mantra: *oṃ hrauṃ sadāśivākāśādhipataye śāntyatītākalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having uttered it, one should dissolve all those [elements] into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) with the thought, "I dissolve them into the ego. Having dissolved that ego into the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), and having dissolved the Great Principle into Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*)—which is the essence of the *Hṛllekhā* and whose nature is the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) known as the *Mātṛkā*—one should dissolve it with the thought, "I dissolve it. Then, one should dissolve that very Nature into the Supreme Cause, the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by Truth, Knowledge, Infinity, and Bliss, which is self-luminous, and whose essential nature is eternally awakened and pure. One should thus dissolve it.
As it has been stated in the *Manvatantraprakāśa*: "One should dissolve the earth—consisting of smell and so forth and conjoined with the sense of smell—into water;
one should dissolve water—consisting of taste and so forth along with the tongue—into fire;
and one should dissolve fire—consisting of form and so forth together with the eye—into air."

The wise one should dissolve the ether, along with its quality of sound, into the ego; the ego, along with its qualities such as touch, into the skin; and that skin, along with all powers, into the Great Principle (Mahat); and the Great Principle into the Unmanifest, the supreme cause.
"One should contemplate that everything, from the earth onwards in sequence, is dissolved therein— that supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Thus [it is said].

Then, having stated: "The Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is the Seer (*ṛṣi*), Truth (*satyam*) is the Deity (*devatā*), Nature-and-Spirit (*prakṛti-puruṣa*) is the Metre (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purification of the person of sin together with the body"—one should contemplate the person of sin in a white form situated in the right side of the abdomen. Having stated: "The seed-syllable *Yam* is the Seer Kiṣkindha, Vāyu is the Deity, Jagatī is the Metre, and its application is for the purification of the person of sin together with the body"—one should contemplate *Yam* at the root of the navel within the circle of six dots (*ṣaḍbindu-maṇḍala*).
That seed-syllable of Vāyu is smoky in color and joined with a flickering banner.
"Oṃ dhū dhū, the purifier of all, whose deity is Oṃkāra.

Having meditated thus, by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should repeat the seed-syllable sixteen or twelve times; then, one should visualize the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) together with the body being dried up by the wind arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "Raṃ is the seed-syllable of fire; Kaśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for burning that [sin]," one should contemplate a red triangular mandala of fire in the heart.

Having meditated thus upon [the seed-syllable] as being conjoined with the *vidyā* and *kalā*, presided over by the deity Rudra, and uttered as "ram," one should repeat the seed-syllable sixty-four or fifty times by means of the practice of *kumbhaka*. This concludes the fourth chapter.
One should visualize that [the body] being reduced to ashes by the fire arising from that seed-syllable (*doj*).

Then, with the exhaling breath (*recaka*), for thirty-two or twenty-five *mātrās*, one should bring forth the previously mentioned form of the wind-seed (*vāyubīja*) and exhale the ashes of the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*).

Then, having stated: "Vam is the Varuṇa-seed; Hiraṇyagarbha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Haṃsa is the deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*); its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of flooding (*plāvana*)," one should contemplate a white Varuṇa-maṇḍala at the crown of the head, resembling the half-moon.
"Situated upon a pair of white lotuses, there is the syllable *vaṃ*, whose deity is Varuṇa.
Having meditated thus, one should visualize that the ashes of the corpse have become a solid mass through the nectar produced from its seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "For the seed-syllable *laṃ* of Earth, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Indra is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is for the purpose of solidification," one visualizes the Earth-maṇḍala marked with a thunderbolt within the Foundation-maṇḍala.
One should meditate in the mind, as before, upon a square, firm [mandala] of yellow color, whose presiding deity is Indra, and which is joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*.
Having thus meditated, one should conceive of the body as being made firm by the solidity arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, having recited: "The seer is Brahmā, the deity is Ākāśa, the metre is Paṅkti, and the application is for the purpose of expansion (*vyūhana*)"—one should meditate upon the sphere of space as circular at the end of the twelve [fingers], brilliant with the syllable *haṃ*, joined with the *śāntyatītā* kalā, and presided over by the deity of space.
Having thus meditated, one should conceive of space through that very space which has arisen from it.
As it has been said: "With *glauṃ*, the seed-syllable of earth, one should bring about stability;
with the seed-syllable *oṃ haṃ vaṃ*, the formation of the limbs occurs."
Having thus contemplated one's own body, one should cause the principles (*tattvas*) to return to their respective places through the process of emanation from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Thereafter, one should bring the individual soul (*jīva*) from the Supreme Self into the heart-lotus by means of the mantra "So 'ham" (I am He); this is the summary.
Furthermore, this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is essential.
A worship performed without the purity of the five elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*)—as well as recitation (*japa*) and so forth—is like black magic (*abhicāra*);
it yields a contrary result. Likewise, worship performed without devotion brings the same.
Indeed, Nirṛti destroys the fruit of those who lack the prescribed rites and are devoid of compassion.
"And by the command of Śaṅkara, he also exercises lordship over the night-stalkers.
Thus it is stated in the Śaivāgama;
and elsewhere as well: "The purification of the elements that constitute the form of the body..."
This purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is considered to arise from contact with the immutable Brahman;
without this purification of the elements, rites such as recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and worship (arcana) are ineffective.
— *Śāradātilaka*
Then, according to Manu, the knower of mantras should perform the nyāsa of Haṃsadeva and subsequently assign the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity (daivata) of the mantra;
otherwise, everything performed in any manner whatsoever will be fruitless.
Thus,

immediately following this, the consecration of one's own vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) must necessarily be performed with the mantra for the consecration of the vital breath that is about to be recited,
according to tradition and the instruction of the Guru.
Regarding this, there is a specific instruction in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "Having placed the hand upon the heart, one should perform the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*).

Then, for the sake of accomplishing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as birth and so forth, one should perform sixteen repetitions of the *praṇava* and contemplate the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*)."
Thus [it is said].
He states what is to be done immediately thereafter: "of Haṃsadeva.

The connection is as follows: then, having performed the three-fold breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to rule with the root mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth of Haṃsadeva.

In this context, the meaning of the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathā-vidhi*) is as follows: when it is the *ajapā* placement, it is performed with the *ajapā*; when it is the *praṇava* placement, it is performed with the *praṇava*; when it is the external *mātṛkā* placement, it is performed with the *mātṛkā*; likewise, when it is the placement of Bhuvaneśī, it is performed with her; and when it is the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), it is performed with the mantra being recited.
In this regard, there is a specific rule for the *mātṛkā-prāṇāyāma*,
as they say: "One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* with the vowels (*svara*), retain it with the consonants (*sparśa*),
and then exhale through the *piṅgalā* with the letters beginning with *ya*."
In the same manner, there should be filling (*pūraṇa*), retention (*kumbhana*), and again exhalation (*recana*) through the *iḍā* [nāḍī];
then, filling and the other two [retention and exhalation] should be performed again through both [nāḍīs].
Having performed these three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*), one should afterwards practice the pervasive [breath-control] (*vyāpaka*).
"From the letter 'A' up to the letter 'Cha', [one should contemplate] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
While this mantra is being recited, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) using a single principal seed-syllable of the mantra.
Or, if [the mantra] consists of a single syllable, there should be sixty-four repetitions during one *kumbhaka*; if it consists of eight syllables, thirty-two times, and so on, as they say:

"One should restrain the well-praised vital air by reciting the ten-syllable mantra twenty-eight times for the sake of desired results. This should be understood accordingly if the mantra consists of eighteen syllables.

Practicing the meditations taught by the sages and reciting the mantra according to its syllables, a man skilled in the application of breath (*prāṇaprayoga*) should perform the practice preceded by exhalation (*recaka*);
thus is the placement (*nyāsa*).
The first [syllable] of Ajapā is at the root, the next at the head, and likewise on the right and left sides;
therein, this is the application.
"Haṃ, obeisance to the Self as Puruṣa; Saḥ, obeisance to the Self as Prakṛti;
Haṃsaḥ, obeisance to the Self as both Prakṛti and Puruṣa"—this is the pervasive mantra.
In that same manner, the internal nyāsa of the Mātṛkās is also performed;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), [it includes] worship, the recitation on the day prior [to the rite], and the fourth chapter:
[the placement] upon one's own head, face, and heart in due order.
Having performed the *prāṇāyāma* according to the rules with the root mantra,
one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, and immediately thereafter the *mantra-nyāsa*.
One should place [the mantras] on the fingers beginning with the thumb, together with their respective *aṅga-mantras*.
Following this, there is the offering (*nivedana*) and the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the recitation of that day.
Subsequently, because the *praṇava* originates from the *haṃsa*-mantra, its ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed;
one should place it in the locations of the *mātṛkā* as follows: *oṃ aṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ āṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, and so forth.

The names, however, I shall explain in the final chapter during the discourse on the origin of the *praṇava*; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the ninety-four digits (*kalā*) produced from that has also been indicated.
The locations for their placement are as follows: one should place the fire-born digits within the three triangles of the *mūlādhāra*;
and the twelve solar digits upon the petals of the heart-lotus.
In the midst of the sixteen petals of the Mūlādhāra, there are the digits (kalās) born of the Moon;
those born of the Nāda reside in the place of the vowels, while those born of the Bindu reside in the five faces.
In the east, south, and north; facing west and upward;
and upon the heart, throat, shoulders, navel, belly, back, and chest.
One should also place the syllables born from the letter *m* upon the two breasts;
those born from the letter *u* are placed on the feet, the private parts, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the buttocks.
One should place the five secret kalās born from the syllable *A* upon the soles of the feet, the palms of the hands, the nose, the two arms, and the two feet.
"In the heart, the secret place, and the feet of Kāśyapa"—
this is a general designation.

Since the deity is also obtained here, the mention of "of the self" (ātmanaḥ) is made. By this, [it is meant]: of the *ajapā* in the *ajapā*-placement; of the *praṇava* in the *praṇava*-placement; of the *mātṛkā* in the external *mātṛkā*-placement; of that [deity] in the *bhuvaneśī*-placement; and of her in the placement of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*); [and] of the mantra being recited [in the case of other mantras].
By the phrase "by the knower of mantras, in due order," the placement of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*) is also stated.
Some say it is on the right and left sides of the abdomen;
others say it is on the secret parts and the feet;
still others say it is on the breasts.

The necessity of performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity (devatā) is stated elsewhere: "When [a mantra] is recited without the placement of the seer, the meter, and the deity, even if it has been mastered, its fruit will be meager."

The connection is that immediately thereafter, one should perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and the placement of Bhuvaneśī (*bhuvaneśīnyāsa*).
As they say in the *Śāradātilaka*:
Having cast the weapon-mantra upon those two palms, one should perform the *tālavaya* and other gestures;
with a concentrated mind, one should bind the directions by means of that very [mantra] using snapping sounds (*choṭikā*).
The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and Hṛllekhā—these are the triad of nectars;
Lord Śiva has declared them to be the illuminators of all mantras.
Thus it is said in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "In that regard, first is the Haṃsanyāsa, and indeed the Praṇavanyāsa;
third is the Mātṛkānyāsa, and after that, the Brahmanyāsa."
The fifth is said by the virtuous to be Vyāsa, consisting of five syllables;
among these, one or several may be employed in rites such as worship.
Thus [it is said].

Immediately following this, he describes the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) for those mantras already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, beginning with the word "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*).
By the word "immediately following," it is stated that the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) must be performed by means of the root mantra.
Therefore, it will be stated in the *Lakṣmīpaṭala*: "Having purified the two hands with the mantra.
As it has been said: "The wise one [should place] the mantra between the two hands—the pervasive and the pervaded—on the inner and outer sides, along with the *Tāra* and *Rudra*.
By the *aṅgas*, meaning by the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantras*) prescribed for each respective ritual procedure (*kalpa*).
In that regard, having recited the *han-mantra*, the application is as follows: "Salutation to the two thumbs," and so forth.
As the Teachers have stated: "One should place [the mantras] upon the fingers in sequence, beginning with the thumb."

The phrase "with those of the same kind" (sajātibhiḥ) is connected with what follows. Regarding the expression "of the *tattala*s," the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the fingers because they are the subject under discussion; by them, the hand is indicated.
By the word *tala*, both the inner and outer palms are included.

Therefore, having uttered the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one says "namaḥ" with the palms and backs of the hands; this is the application of the weapon-mantra. As it has been said: "Namaḥ to the two thumbs, *hrāṃ hrīṃ* to the two index fingers, then *namo hūṃ oṃ* to the two middle fingers, and then *namaḥ* to the two ring fingers."

"Oṃ hrauṃ, [with] both little fingers, and namo on the backs of the hands. Thus one should perform the clapping of the palms and so forth; this is the application of the limbs and the weapon-mantra (*aṅgāstraviniyoga*).
Its essential nature has been stated elsewhere: "One should utter three *tālas* with the palms spread out.
He clarifies what is indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "three *tālas* and so forth" with the word "directions" (*diśaḥ*).

"By that very [mantra]" refers to the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). A "snap" (*choṭikā*) takes the form of the *nārāca-mudrā*. The *nārāca-mudrā* is a snapping sound produced by the tips of the thumb and forefinger.
This is because of its definition as such.
The term "composed" (samāhita) is connected with what follows.
The connection therein is as follows:
Then, being composed, one should place the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) upon the heart and other [limbs] with the syllables of the *Sudhā* lineage.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the previously mentioned [limbs], such as the head and so forth. This concludes the fourth chapter.
The word "tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the placement (*nyāsa*) of the respective mantras as prescribed in the various *kalpas* that are about to be described.
As they say: "First is the placement of the *ādhāra-śakti* and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*);
then the two pervasive placements of the fingers (*aṅgulivyāpaka-nyāsa*) and the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdādinyāsa*)."
"The binding of the directions (digbandha) is performed with the *tālavaya* [mudrā].
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should thereafter perform the ritual placement on the body (*dehanyāsa*)."
Afterwards, one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa); this is the general procedure.
Thus it is said.

The teachers also have stated that this general procedure for mantras applies up to the end of the six-limbed nyāsa at the commencement of recitation: "For this is the common method for mantras at the start of japa."
By the phrase "composed and wise," the six-limbed mudrās are indicated.
As it is stated in another Āgama: "The heart [mudrā] is formed by the palm of the hand spread out;
the head [mudrā] likewise; the crest [mudrā] is properly formed with the fist below, using the thumb."
With such hands placed upon the shoulder of the armor and so forth,
the index, middle, and ring fingers are said to correspond respectively to the three eyes.
When the two eyes are indicated, then the index and middle fingers [are used].
Thus it is said.
Here, the phrase "with the palm spread out" means with the four fingers excluding the thumb. As it has been stated: "The four fingers, excluding the thumb, [are placed] at the heart and the head;
at the crest-lock (śikhā), there should be a fist, with the stalk [of the hand] joined by the thumb."
The integration of all limbs up to the navel, and the binding of armor upon the two hands.
Thus, regarding the six-limbed mudrās of Śakti in another tantra: the heart is said to be formed by the middle, ring, and index fingers;
the head is formed by the middle and index fingers; and the topknot (śikhā) is said to be formed by the thumb.

The armor (kavaca) is said to consist of ten [syllables], the bow (nātra) of three; the weapon (astra) is said to consist of two fingers' breadth. This is considered the arrangement of the limbs (aṅga-klṛpti).

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the six ancillary mudrās of Śiva in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having formed fists with both hands and placing the thumbs at the heart, this is declared to be the Heart Mudrā (hṛnmudrā). Now the Head Mudrā (śiromudrā) is proclaimed."
Placing the hands with palms hollowed and fists formed against the forehead,
one should extend the two index fingers upward, positioned outward from the thumbs.
Having joined the two hands at the crest-lock (śikhā) in the form of hollowed fists,
the wise one should then place the limb-mantras upon the heart and other locations, according to the *Śāradātilaka*.
First, "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" for the heart; then "Śirase vadbhivallabhā" for the head.
"Vaṣaṭ" is said for the crest-lock (śikhā), "Hum" is uttered for the armor (kavaca),
"Vauṣaṭ" is for the three eyes, and "Phaṭ" is for the weapon (astra) in due order.
One should apply the six limbs, as previously described, to the six parts [of the body];
however, for a mantra that has only five limbs, one should omit the eye-limb.
One should provide the missing limbs for a mantra deficient in its parts by means of one's own [mantra];
one should perform the various ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the procedure prescribed in the respective ritual manual (kalpa).
The tips of the index fingers are directed downward, and likewise those of the little fingers are directed upward.
This is the Śikhāmudrā, which destroys all calamities; it is formed by joining the two thumbs and the two index fingers together in the shape of a triangle.
Having turned the face backward at the base, one should lead [the hands] along both sides;
with the two hands reaching as far as the heart, this is the mudrā of the armor (kavaca) that bestows fearlessness.
Having formed the hand with the fingers directed toward the eyes, with the thumb and little finger joined,
one should extend the middle finger slightly and bend the other fingers.
This is declared to be the Netra-mudrā, which destroys the afflictions caused by Rākṣasas and Bhūtas;
one should then forcefully snap the tips of the hands against each other.
Thus [it is said].
