The Fourth Chapter. The wise preceptor should fashion a seat within his own body, beginning with the channels (dhama) and so forth in due order, moving clockwise through the two shoulders and the pair of thighs.
Thereafter, one should perform the act of total devotion by means of the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
The wise one, by means of the Śiromantra, performs the intake of sense-objects into the Supreme Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
With devotion, one should respectfully perform the firm visualization of one's own deity as consisting of the heart, head, crest, armor, and eye, using the *śikhā-mantra*.
The accumulation of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed for the deity whose essence is mantra, by means of the splendor expressed by the mantra on all sides, using the *vaṃ* mantra.
That which bestows supreme knowledge within the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, is the light consisting of the heart and other centers; this is known as the "eye."
That which destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner,
born of ignorance and partless— that is proclaimed as the supreme abode.
Thus, the wise say that recitation (japa) performed without the ritual placement (nyāsa) is demonic and fruitless;
having become identical with that [deity] through nyāsa, and having become the deity itself, one should worship it.
Thus: "He who constantly performs the ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the path taught in the scriptures attains the state of the deity, and the accomplishment of mantra arises."
That foolish-souled person who, having deposited a collection [of wealth], should squander the principal,
will be afflicted by all kinds of obstacles, just as a young deer is by tigers.
O Dear One, when one recites the mantra while covered by the armor of the nyāsa,
the obstacles flee upon seeing him, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion.
Thus: One who is not Śiva should not practice Śiva; one who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva;
one who is not Śiva should not meditate upon Śiva; and one who is not Śiva shall not attain Śiva.
Thus [it is said].
The author of the treatise also states: "One should place the syllables of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing the state of being the deity."
Regarding the construction of the *poṭha* (pedestal) within the body for the sake of the sacrifice of the self (*ātmayāga*), he says "one should construct":
"One should install Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in sequence upon the body of the self by means of the [mantras] beginning with *Dharmā*," as stated in the *Śāradātilaka*.
One should install Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in their proper order.
One should fashion the lower [sections] at the sides of the mouth and the sides of the navel.
Dhama and the others are remembered as the feet, while others are the pedestal and the limbs;
within the heart is the infinite lotus, in which are the sun, moon, and fire.
The meaning is that one should prepare a seat.
By the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*) here, the following is intended:
[one should worship] with "Oṃ Maṇḍakāya namaḥ" on the base (*ādhāra*).
"Salutation to Kālāgnirudra"—thus at the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
"Salutation to Kūrma"—thus at the navel.
Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Ādhāraśakti and the others in the heart, one subsequently performs the placement of Dharma and the rest.

As they say: "One should place in the region of the heart the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), primordial nature (prakṛti), the tortoise (kūrma), Śeṣa, the earth, the oceans, Śvetadvīpa, the great pavilion (mahāmaṇḍapa) honored and radiant with jewels, and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa)."

Regarding the word "shoulder" (*aṃse*): by the term "the wise preceptor" (*vidvān deśikaḥ*), it is stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins from the right shoulder and extends up to the right thigh in a clockwise direction, following the sequence of circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇyena*).
This is the traditional view (*sāmpradāyikaḥ*).
Thus it has been said by Īśānaśiva: "One should worship the power called Ādhāra in the heart, on the right shoulder, on the left shoulder, and also on the two thighs."
"Sovereignty is attained through detachment.
Thus, the word "gradually" (kramāt) is connected with what follows.
Regarding the word "mukha" (mouth):
here too, the phrase "in a clockwise direction" (*prādakṣiṇyena*) is to be supplied.
By the word "kramāt" (in sequence), this is what is stated.
Then the face, then the left side, then the navel, then the right side.

As it has been said: "In the face, on the left side, at the navel, and on the right side—therein lies knowledge regarding unrighteousness, as well as the absence of dispassion and the absence of lordship."
Thus it has been stated by Īśānaśiva as well:
"Then, ignorance is in the lowest face; and on the left side and the right side of the navel."
"Lack of dispassion and lack of sovereignty.

As for the statement of the Teacher— “by the face, the navel-base, and the two sides”— that too has been explained by the commentators of that [text] precisely as "by the face, the sides, the navel-base, and the flanks."
The meaning is that those very [factors] such as non-dharma (adharma) and so forth, and not others previously [mentioned].
"Apara" refers to those beginning with the lowest (adhamā).
"In this" means in the infinite (ananta).
"Padma" refers to that which will have its characteristics described later.
By this [statement], it is stated that each preceding [element] serves as the support for each subsequent one.
In this lotus, the sun, moon, and fire are to be joined [as the supports].
The Fourth Chapter: In these [locations], one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the forty zeros (khakhakalā), preceded by the first letter of each name;
likewise, the most excellent Guru should place the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with Sattva, along with the three syllables Oṃ.
One should protect the self, the inner self, and the supreme self;
having properly established the self whose nature is knowledge, one should then place the mantra of the pedestal.
Thus, one should meditate upon the chosen deity on the pedestal consisting of the body;
having duly presented the mudrās, one should perform the ritual installation of the arghya water.
"In these" refers to the three mandalas. Regarding the first letter of the name, those [mantras] preceded by the letters beginning with *ka*, *bha*, and *ya* are used there; this is the sequence.

Having placed the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) there, one should place its digits (*kalā*); then the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*) there, with its digits; then the fiery disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*) there, with its digits—thus one should place them.
The phrase "in that very manner" means upon each preceding one.
The word "preceded by the first letter of the name" (*nāmādya-kṣarapūrvakān*) is drawn over here from the previous context.
"Therefore, one should place those [syllables] preceding that which is the first of the name.
Here, the term "the most excellent Guru" is connected with what follows.
Consequently, the practical application begins with: *oṃ saṃ sattvāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
As it has been said: "By the initial syllables, [one denotes] sattva, rajas, and tamas.
And this is merely an illustration;
for it has been stated in that same manner everywhere previously.
In this context, the word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction with respect to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
even among the triad beginning with the individual self (*ātman*), the seed is indeed the *āgya* alone.
However, regarding the nature of consciousness (*jñānātman*), it is stated by the term "the highest Guru" that there is the seed-syllable of *māyā*.
By the phrase "then one should deposit the seat-mantra," the following is intended:

*māṃ* [is] *namaḥ* to the principle of *māyā*; *kaṃ* [is] *namaḥ* to the principle of *kalā*; *viṃ* [is] *namaḥ* to the principle of *vidyā*; *paṃ* [is] *namaḥ* to the supreme principle (*paratattva*).

One should install the nine pedestal-energies (*pīṭhaśakti*) at the tips of the eight petals of the heart-lotus, at their bases, and in the center. As it has been said: "Having installed the Māyā-tattva, the Kalā-tattva, the Vidyā-tattva, and likewise the supreme [Śiva-tattva], one should then install the mantra of the pedestal."
Thus [it is said].

Then, having placed the nine Śaktis in the eight directions around the periphery and in the center, as well as the great mantra of the pedestal (pīṭha-mantra) according to rule within the middle of its pericarp—
Regarding "mudrā":
the specific mudrās for each [deity] shall be described by me in their respective chapters (*paṭala*) as taught in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
By the word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is stated that immediately following this, one should perform mental worship (*mānasī pūjā*) and then entreat the deity.
Therein, the mantra of invitation is: *Oṃ, welcome, O Lord of the gods of gods; be present, O Keśava!
Accept this mental worship, contemplated according to its true meaning.*
Thus [it is said].
Here, in the phrase "O Keśava," one should perform the modification (*ūha*) by substituting the names of the respective deities.

As it has been stated: "Having thus meditated upon himself as the son of Nanda with a sharp and clear intellect, he should worship him before him with blameless offerings, beginning with water for the feet (*arghya*)."
Thus [ends] the Śāradātilaka:
having sprinkled the conch with water from the *amṛta* [vessel], [one places it] to the left in the fire-mandala.
The wise one should establish the common base with the nectar-like substances produced from the Bindu.
One should fill that [vessel] according to the prescribed rite with water, fragrant flowers, and so forth;
[one should contemplate] the support as fire, the conch as the sun, and its water as consisting of nectar.
Elsewhere it is also stated: "Having meditated upon the deity and displayed the mudrās according to the injunctions, one should perform the placement of the *arghya*.
He states the procedure for that [placement] with the words "the conch," etc.
It should be understood that "to the left" means on the left side, in front of oneself.
"Before oneself, a conch"—
the grammatical connection is that on the fire-mandala, at the tip of the *ūrja* [line], there is a triangle together with its support, which is the conch.
By the word "the wise one," it is stated that here "fire-mandala" is used as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that this refers to [the deity] being worshipped with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), held within the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā) consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square.
As it has been said: "Having first drawn a triangle and then a hexagon outside of that, and having drawn a circle and a square, one should write the Māyā [syllable] in the center."
Then, having displayed the conch mudrā, one should perform the worship of the limbs in the corners and so forth.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "One should fashion a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square;
then, supporting the conch-mudrā, one should worship the six limbs. Thus it is said.
Some say that the *bindu* is the center of the eyebrows, while others say it is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
because of the presence of the lunar orb there.
"By means of [streams] consisting of nectar flowing from the *bindu*"—this refers to the visualization of the ocean in the case of Somaśambhu.

Having filled [the vessel] with water in the form of nectar produced from the *bindu*, and having worshipped it with the heart-mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should consecrate it with mantras. Thus [it is said].
By the phrase "one should fill it according to the rule," this is stated: one should recite the *mātṛkā* ending with the *bindu* in reverse order, as well as the root mantra in reverse order.
As it has been said: "The wise man should fill [the vessel] with pure water using the syllables in reverse order, ending with the *śiras*."
Thus,
regarding the support:
the conch is the support as the circle of fire, water as the circle of the sun, and [the lotus] as the circle of the moon.
Within those mandalas, one should also remember the respective kalās;
some even perform worship there according to this practice.

Having drawn a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle mandala in front of oneself to the left, and having stabilized it with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) according to the sequence of worship using flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Then, having washed the base (*ādhāra*) with the *astra-mantra*, one should install the base with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the support for the seat of the *arghya* vessel, which consists of ten kalās and belongs to the fire-mandala. Thereafter, one should worship the ten *kalās* starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. Then, with the *śaṅkha-mantra* (the *śaṅkha-mantra* as stated in the *Puruṣottama-paṭala*), [one should worship the conch]. This is the fourth chapter.
One should remember the digits of fire, the sun, and the moon in their respective order;
having touched [the body], the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra and perform the placement (nyāsa) of its limbs.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra, one should cover [the disciple] with water from both hands.
The preceptor, regarding the deity with the mindset of the divinity itself, should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
having protected it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and veiled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra),
and having performed the cow-seal (dhenumudrā), he should seal it with the space-seal (khamudrā).

Having washed [the vessel] with "Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve digits, for the *arghya* vessel named so-and-so," one should place the vessel upon its base. Then, having worshipped the twelve digits of the Sun in the twelve locations in a clockwise direction, and while reciting the reverse *aṣṭākṣara* mantra and the reverse root mantra, one should fill the conch with pure water. Having worshipped it with "Uṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen digits, for the nectar of the *arghya* named so-and-so," one should worship the sixteen digits of the Moon there in a clockwise direction.
Then, having invoked the *tīrtha* from the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) by means of the mantra "Gaṅge ca" and the *aṅgaśamudrā*, the preceptor should also invoke the Deity from his own heart-lotus;

for it will be stated that the Deity is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātrī*). As it has been said: "There, one should invoke the *tīrtha* from the orb of the hot-rayed sun by means of the *tīrtha-mantra*."
"Thus, like a bee from a lotus, [one seeks] Hari"—
this definition of the *aṅga-mudrās* was stated in the context of bathing.

Regarding that which is to be given, it is said: "The *aṅkuśa-mudrā* is to be understood as having the middle finger straight, its middle joint bent, and the index finger pointing downward; it is curved at the middle joint. Thus.
"Having touched" is connected with "water," and "one should place" is connected with "in water."

Regarding the phrase "of that," it is stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra is performed precisely through the worship according to the sequence of directions to be described by the words "knowing the limb-mantras.
The connection is with the word "having fully worshipped" (*abhisampūjya*), which refers to the water (*apaḥ*).
By the phrase "covering with both hands" and the word "the teacher," it is stated that this refers to the *matsyamudrā*.

Its definition is as follows: "The two hands placed face down and positioned upon one's own [lap], with the thumbs extending toward the sides—this is called the *matsyamudrā*. Here, regarding such procedures, it is stated that by the use of the terms *mūlamantra* and *vidyā*, the distinction between male and female deities (*puṃstrī-devatātva*) is not intended.
Otherwise, if one were grasped, the other would not be grasped;
therefore, according to the rule, this number— seven times or eight times— should be understood as established even previously.
As it has been said: "Touching [the object], he should mutter the mantra eight times. (Verses 44–47). The connection is: "having protected that [object]."
And that protection is to be understood as being performed with finger-snaps;
here too, the word "that" connects back to it, and that [protection] is performed with the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā.
Having performed the *samāpatti*, one should place the sprinkling vessel (*prokṣaṇīpātra*) on the right and fill it with water;
having taken a small amount of water for the *arghya*, one should join it with the water in the sprinkling vessel by means of the seed-syllable of Mṛta (the letter *sa*). || 46 ||
"With one's own mudrā" refers to the Sannirodhinī;
the Avaguṇṭhana, Dhenu, Sannirodhana, and Mudrā are described in the twenty-third [chapter].
Thereafter, one should display the Śaṅkha, Muṣala, Cakra, Mahāmudrā, and Yonimudrās over the conch.

As it is said: "One should contemplate the sacred site as consisting of consciousness; having brought [the water] by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* and having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā* from the sacred sites within the belly of the universe, one should display the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, the *cakra-mudrā*, and that called the *muṣala*.
Having performed the supreme consecration with effort, one should indeed display that called the *guhya*. Thus.
The specific details should be investigated accordingly: for instance, the display of the Gālinī mudrā when following Kṛṣṇa, and the display of the Garuḍa mudrā when following Rāma.
The definition of the Śaṅkha mudrā has been stated previously; however, the definitions of the others are as follows: having formed fists with both hands, placing the right hand over the left...

This is the *muṣala-mudrā*, which destroys all obstacles. Having joined the two little fingers together, [place] the ring fingers with the two index fingers; the ring fingers should be embraced by the long middle fingers, and one should place the tips of the two thumbs below them. This is declared to be the *yoni-mudrā*. Thus it is said.
Having inverted the palms of the left and right hands, one should interlace the two thumbs between the little fingers and the ring fingers;
this is declared to be the auspicious Wheel Mudrā (cakramudrā), which bestows all accomplishments. Thus it is said.
The twenty-third [chapter], concerning the characteristics of Mahāmudrā, will be explained:
the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are held together, straight, and firmly joined.
"This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, moved over the conch. Thus,
having brought the two hands face-to-face and formed them, one should join the two little fingers together,
likewise the two thumbs, and then bend the middle and ring fingers like the two wings of a crane.
"This is the Garuḍa-mudrā, which destroys all poisons. [Thus it is said. 48. "The right" refers to the vessel made of copper or other such materials.
As they say: "Gold, silver, copper, earth, wood, and bell-metal—these are the vessels for the worship of Acyuta; those made of lotus and Palāśa leaves are excellent even without mantras.
Among all, copper and conch are the most excellent, and the copper vessel is highly praised for the worship of Varṣāyāṇa. (48)
The fourth chapter:
To the north of the *arghya* water, the teacher should perform the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* rites; he should then sprinkle himself, the sacrificial materials, and the mandala. (50)

Then, with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should worship Dharma and the other [deities] upon one's own body in due order, using the mantra according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
"Of the *arghya*" refers to the *arghya* vessel.
If one has the capacity, these [offerings] should be prepared separately;

if one lacks the capacity, everything may be done with a single vessel—as it is said: "Alternatively, one may prepare the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth, in a single bowl."
The connection is that one should sprinkle [the materials] with the root mantra "iti manunā";
and this is a general injunction.

However, in another specific mantra, a *prokṣaṇa*-mantra is mentioned; in that case, the sprinkling should be performed with that very mantra. By this [rule], it is stated that this *prokṣaṇa* is to be done three times.
As it has been said: "Then, with this mantra, one should sprinkle one's own body three times with the hand, and likewise all the ritual materials such as flowers, sandalwood,
and so forth."
The connection is that one should sprinkle other sacrificial materials and articles of worship in sequence.
He describes the internal sacrifice with the word "should place" (*nyaset*);
as it has been said: "The worship of the *manu* who has attained [realization] is twofold: external and internal."
"The distinction between renunciants (nyāsins) has been declared; for others, both [types of sacrifice] apply likewise.
Thus, having first performed the internal sacrifice beginning with the preliminary rites and ending with the fire-oblation, a person should subsequently perform the external sacrifice.

O moon-faced one, a householder does not attain auspiciousness in this world or the next through mere knowledge alone, without [the performance of] gifts, fire-offerings, and so forth. If a householder were neither to offer oblations nor to give gifts, nor even to worship according to the prescribed rule, who would perform this daily? O beautiful lady, a student (brahmacārī) has no authority to give gifts.

Who indeed will provide what is required even for all the gurus? In the Kali age, forest-dwellers have no power, nor do they exist; a wandering mendicant [lives] by knowledge alone, without giving, fire-offerings, and the like.
One becomes liberated from all the demons of suffering; it is not otherwise.
Thus says the Śāradātilaka regarding the wandering mendicant who is unattached, as well as the householder who is detached.

With flowers and other offerings, up to the end of the *pīṭha-mantra*, one who is single-minded should again perform the offering of handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) five times over that supreme deity,
sequentially upon the head, the heart, the navel, the feet, and all the limbs.

One should worship [the deity] with offerings such as perfumes and so forth, even without the food offering (naivedya), according to the procedure taught by the Guru; one should complete all the remaining rites,
employing this [procedure] with water from the sprinkling vessel (prokṣaṇī).
O lotus-faced one, both types of women— those who are meritorious and those who are householders— and those seeking auspiciousness, should immerse themselves in the Kumbhapāka rite;
they should perform worship with auspicious materials and offer gifts and honors.
If forest-dwellers and ascetics were to act in this manner every day,

they would not turn back from the cycle of worldly existence due to the fault of transgressing the injunctions; for these men, having already ascended to the state of asceticism, would become vessels of suffering.
Thus, by the phrase "by means of the sequence of nyāsa," the following is intended:

one should worship Maṇḍūka, Kālāgnirudra, and Kūrma in the regions of the *ādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and the navel; then, having worshipped Ādhāraśakti and the others in the heart, and subsequently the eight [deities] beginning with Dharma in their respective places, one performs again in the heart the worship starting from Śeṣa up to Paratattva.
This has been stated in the *Rāmapūrvatāpanīya*: "One should worship Māyā and Vidyā, which are the two principles (tattva) beyond Kalā, as well as the powers (śakti) beginning with Dvimālā.
Here, "beginning" (*ādya*) refers to fragrance (*gandha*); the plural number is used in the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*), meaning "with fragrance and the rest."

Such a construction serves the purpose of including "flowers" by means of the word "ādi" (and so forth); alternatively, it refers to "flowers and the first [item], namely fragrance," because among the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), flowers are specified immediately after fragrance.
"Up to the seat-mantra" (pīṭhamantrāntam) means up to the mantra of the seat (pīṭhaśakti).
"In that" (tasmin) refers to the connection with what follows: one should worship the Supreme Deity with offerings such as perfumes upon such a seat consisting of the body.
By the first [verse], he states the distinction regarding the flower there;
by the words "with mind fixed on no other," it is stated that it is "the twentieth."
As it has been said by the Teachers: "One should offer even a handful of flowers upon one's own body five or twenty times,
provided there is no food offering (naivedya)."
The intention here is as follows:
having demonstrated the ritual procedures beginning with the seat and ending with the removal of defects, one should not offer the external food offering (naivedya).

Then, having raised Kuṇḍalinī according to the method taught by the Guru and led her to the *dvādaśānta*, one should unite her there with Śiva and satisfy the Deity with the stream of nectar arising from that union.

"Taught by the Guru" refers to the remaining [elements]: mental incense and lamps, the recitation of the mantra, the offering of the recitation, the dedication to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpanā*), and so forth, excluding the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). As they say: The Fourth Chapter.
Having poured out the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should refill it as before;
then, one should properly worship that mandala with mantras and perfumes and other offerings,
having filled the center of the pericarp with *śāli* rice and then with *taṇḍula* grains on top.
Having adorned them and spread darbha grass upon them, the knower of the body, having meditated, should worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings, as well as mental incense and lamps;
at the time of eating, having performed some recitation, he should present the offering.
Thus it is the same;
however, this is the distinction regarding the daily worship.
One should pour this very water from the conch into the *vardhanī* vessel;
then, having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should perform the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) one thousand and eight times, and again perform three *prāṇāyāmas*.

Furthermore, as it is stated: "One should cast [the water] into the *vardhanī* water" before the recitation, and it is also prescribed after it, according to the saying: "Then the wise should perform the three realities (*tattvatraya*)."

As it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) with devotion one thousand and eight times, that which is recited daily is known as the obligatory recitation (*nityajapa*). [This applies] at the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun."
On the twelfth lunar day and on the full moon, the occasional (naimittika) recitation performed on those occasions is twelve times the daily (nitya) recitation; likewise applies the worship of Hari.
Having described the internal sacrifice, he speaks of the external sacrifice with the word "tataḥ" (then).

"Then," meaning immediately after that, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should worship that *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala—which was previously described as being "excellent" (*sādhu*) because of its auspiciousness on all sides and which is drawn in the center of the altar—with perfumes and other offerings; such is the connection [of the words].
By the word "etc. (ādi), it should be understood that the worship mantra, "Oṃ sarvatobhadramaṇḍalāya namaḥ," is indicated by the phrase "with flowers and mantras";
[this refers to] "with rice grains" (śālibhiḥ).
The meaning is that having decorated the top with rice grains over the *śāli* [grain], one should place rice grains there;
furthermore, immediately thereafter,
upon those rice grains.

That measurement has been stated elsewhere: "Having placed śālī rice, measured by one āḍhaka, together with its filaments (karṇikā), and having added one-eighth part of that in unhusked grains (taṇḍula), one should place a tuft of grass (kūrca) on top."
The definition of an *ār̤haka* is as follows: “A *kur̤ava* consists of four *palas*;
a *prastha* consists of four *kur̤avas*; and an *ār̤haka* consists of four *prasthas*.”
Then, "eight parts" refers to two *kuḍavas*, which is eight *tolakas* as stated in the scriptures; this is called a *pala*.
A *kūrcam*—also known by the synonym *viṣṭara*—is made of twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, woven together in the shape of a braid.

Thus it is stated in the *Ḍāmara*: "A seat (*viṣṭara*) made of twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, adorned with a knot at its tip, is proclaimed as the characteristic for all sacrificial rites (*sarvayajñeṣu*). — *Śāradātilaka*.
One should place a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca) together with unbroken grains (akṣata) upon them;
then, beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should worship the pedestal consisting of mantras.
Below that, [one should worship] her who stands upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), possessing a luster like the autumnal moon.
One should worship the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), who holds two lotuses; upon her head,
one should worship the tortoise of a blue hue,
and above that, Ananta, seated upon the Brahma-stone, resembling a kunda flower in color.

Regarding the phrase "the foundational power" (ādhāraśakti), one should first perform the worship of the Guru and Gaṇapati; as it has been said: "First, to the north of the pedestal for worship, there is a row of venerable [deities] starting from the northwest and ending at the northeast."
"Elsewhere also, Ambikeya (Gaṇeśa) is to be worshipped, holding a noose, a staff, and a goad in his hands.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "The knower of mantras should worship the lineage of gurus on the northern part of the pedestal."
Starting from the northeast corner (Girīśa) up to the northwest corner (Vāyu),
one should then worship the Guru, the Paramaguru, and likewise the Parameṣṭhiguru; thereafter, one should worship the Paramācāryaguru and the Ādisiddhiguru, as well as one's own Guru.
Thus,
joined with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*) or meditating upon their own Hari,
they should be visualized at the beginning of worship; through such meditation, one becomes possessed of knowledge.

Thus, regarding the Śākta and other systems, there is this distinction in another Tantra: "They are adorned with red garlands, garments, perfumes, and ornaments; they possess matted locks, sit upon lotus seats, are all established in yoga with a support (sālambana-yoga), and have attained the goal of the eight qualities of universal sovereignty."
Thus, in that context, the formula "Salutation to the venerable gurus" and so forth is employed for the deity,
the guru, the place of the guru, the sacred field (kṣetra), and the presiding deities of the field.
Because it is stated, "One should utter the Siddha-mantra, the offices of the Siddhas, and the Śrīpūrva," it is said that one should perform worship. 56
He says that very thing with the word "below" (adhaḥ);
by this, the following is meant:

In the pericarp, one should worship the large-bodied Rāṃ Maṇḍūka with the mantra "Obeisance to Maṇḍūkāya. Above that, one should worship the ten-armed, five-faced Kālāgnirudra, whose right and left sides are red and black, with the mantra "Obeisance to Kālāgnirudrāya. Above him is the large-bodied tortoise. This is the fourth chapter.
One should worship the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), who bears the earth upon his head;
having touched that stainless one who wears blue lotuses,
one should then honor this Earth, whose girdle is the shimmering ocean.
Upon that [altar], one should worship a lamp made of jewels, and within that, a pavilion of gems (maṇimaṇḍapa).
Therein, one should worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpataru) which grant the desired accomplishments to the practitioner;
beneath them, one should worship the altar-platform, radiant with the pavilion.

62. Afterwards, one should again worship the pedestal (pīṭha) upon that [seat] with Dharma and the other [principles]. [One should worship] those whose forms are the feet, possessing the luster of red, yellow, green, and sapphire-blue. 63. "Obeisance to Kūrma."
This is stated in the *Śaunakakalpa*: "One should worship Maṇḍūka, Pṛthivī, and the others in sequence within the pericarp.
And in the *Nārasiṃhakalpa* as well: "On the eight-petaled lotus, one should worship Maṇḍūka, ending with Paratattva."
Thus:
"kūmmeśilā" means a stone in the shape of a tortoise; she is mounted upon that.
It should be understood that the one previously worshipped is indeed Kūrma himself, known as Kūmeśila;
however, the Kūrma to be described hereafter is distinct from him.
As it is stated in the *Tāpanīya*: "And [he worships] Śakti, called the Support, with Kūrma in the navel."
The meaning of the phrase "of the autumn moon" is to be understood as before.
*Brahmaśilā* is the designation for the stone situated beneath the primary image (*mūlapratimā*).
As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "One should cast the purified *brahmaśilā*, smeared with sandalwood paste, into the pit."
Then, having performed the deposition of the jewels (ratna-tattva) by means of the nine names of the Śaktis.
One should cast minerals such as yellow orpiment, as well as seeds and fragrant herbs,
upon the Brahma-stone according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva scriptures.
By the passage beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "prāgudakplavanaṃ kiñcit," [it is established that] the *liṅga* is upon the *brahmaśilā*. Regarding the term "anantam":

“Neither human-shaped above nor serpent-shaped below, without earrings and possessing a thousand hoods”—this is His essential form. Elsewhere, His vehicle is described: “The splendor of Viṣṇu, honored by its own thirty-two principles beginning with Earth and ending with Vidya, is indeed called Infinity (Anantya); that is the seat, and that serpent Ananta is in the form of a pedestal.”
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, elsewhere: "In this [system], by means of the thirty-two principles beginning with Earth (dhara) and ending with Knowledge (vidyā), Ananta indeed takes the form of the pedestal (pīṭha); he is proclaimed as the seat of Ananta."
Thus.

The compound is "one who wears blue lotuses" (*nolendovare dhārayatīti*). It will be stated later: "O blue lotus (*indīvare he*). By the phrase "the earth girdled by the shimmering ocean," the meaning is that after the earth, the ocean is to be worshipped with the mantra "Salutation to the Ocean" (*sāgarāya namaḥ*).
One should worship the deities beginning with Dharma, who have the forms of a bull, a lion,
and a ghost; one should worship them in the directions according to the previously stated characteristics, preceded by the syllable *na*.
Then, one should worship the lotus in the corners beginning with the southeast and in the cardinal directions;
first the bulb of bliss (ānandakanda), and immediately after that the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla).

65. In that regard, in the mantra of Sarasvatī, there is an ocean of knowledge; in the mantra of Lakṣmī-Viṣṇu, an ocean of wine; and in the mantra of Gaṇeśa, an ocean of sugarcane juice. Elsewhere, it should be understood as an ocean of nectar, and so forth.
In that distinguished [tongue]...
Regarding "vṛṣa": *keśarī* means a lion;
*bhūta* refers to a divine being (*devayoni*).

The true nature [of these beings] is stated elsewhere: "Clad in red garments, black, with claws and fangs, possessing formidable tusks, holding drums and skull-topped staffs in their hands—these are the Rākṣasas of terrifying form."
Likewise,
those who are distressed have downcast faces.
"Ibha" means an elephant.
[The deities] preceded by the negative particle (nañ) are Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya;
they possess the characteristics already described, namely, the colors red and so forth, and the forms of a bull and so forth.
And it is said: "Dharma is red and has the form of a bull; Jñāna is a dark lion; Vairāgya is yellow and has the form of a boar."
Dispassion is the elephant-faced one with a white body, and sovereignty is Poṭhapāda; these follow in sequence.
The four beginning with Adharma are the lords of the pedestal; they are indeed delightful in their described forms.
Thus.
Regarding the phrase "in the Āgneya and others":
by the word "others," the corners of Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa are included.
"In the directions" refers to the east, south, west, and north.
The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).
This is because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "By the word *dik* (direction), the directions beginning with the East and ending with the North are obtained.
Also, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "And [the qualities] beginning with *adharma* and ending with *anuttara*, starting from the East in successive order..."

Thus, the teachers maintain that the eastern direction is that which faces the deity. Accordingly, it is stated in the Āgama: "The direction situated between the deity and the practitioner is here called the east."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "In the presence of the deity and in one's own presence as well, the eastern direction has been declared by the teachers;
indeed, that which is truly east is designated as the 'east' when the worship of the deity is performed."
Thus it is said.
Also in another Tantra: "Wherever the sun rises in the sky, those who know the Vedas call that the East;
likewise, those well-versed in the sacred traditions always proclaim that [direction] which lies between the worshiper and the object of worship."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, on the occasion of the worship of the doors, it is stated elsewhere: "Beginning from the face of the deity, one should designate the eastern direction;
the arrangement of the limbs and other enclosures for the retinue begins with that [direction]."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, there is also a logical justification:
at the occasion of the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities of the seats (pīṭha-devatā) upon the body, the placement of the syllable *adhī* is prescribed for the mouth.
And that is the foremost portion.
Chapter Four.
Immediately after worshipping the lotus which consists of the essence of all principles (tattva), [one should proceed].
The minister [should visualize] the petals as the primary elements and the filaments as consisting of the transformations.
Then, one should worship the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables;
within that, one should worship the Sun, Moon, and Fire along with their limbs and digits.

In the context of the worship of Mahāgaṇapati, after stating that one should worship [the deities] outside the triangle in the four directions starting from the east, he says, "in front, beneath a bilva tree.
Similarly, in the second enclosure of the Rāma-pūjā, after stating, "Hanumān together with Sugrīva," he further says, "Hanumān in front, holding a book in his hand.
Moreover, worship facing north has also been prescribed.
Furthermore, regarding the intermediate directions and facing west and so forth,
the worship of Adharmā and the others, as well as the worship of the limbs and so forth, might sometimes occur according to an alternative sequence;
at other times it would occur according to the [standard] sequence, and so on— this is contradictory.
And in another tantra: "The eastern portion is prescribed for the Hotṛ priest; the southern portion is for those with mantras;
one should know the northern portion as belonging to the Dakṣa; and this western portion is declared by the wise."
Thus it is said.
And in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*: "Now, in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), one should designate the east as being in front;
the worship of the attendants beginning with that [deity] is performed in a clockwise direction."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The goddesses beginning with Lakṣmī, holding chowries, [are seated] upon the petals beginning with the eastern one."

For this very reason, it will be explained that in the worship of the *poṭha* (pedestal), the *śakti*, and so forth, one begins from the foremost petal (*agradala*) and so on. Therefore, even in the case of worship facing east and the like, one should understand that the eastern direction is defined by one's own front part; thus, the worship of *dharma* and the other [qualities], as well as the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*), proceeds accordingly. By this, it should also be understood that when inscribing syllables upon the petals of a *yantra* and the like, the inscription must begin from the foremost petal.
This is the general direction regarding the worship of the mobile [deities].
Now, as for the instruction "one should worship the lotus," it refers to the sequence that will be described.
Here, by the word "now" (atha), it is indicated that one should first worship Ananta with the mantra "Obeisance to Ananta" before the lotus.

As it has been said: "Then the remaining lotus is in the heart. And at the time of performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body, the author of the work also stated: "In this [body], there is an infinite lotus in the heart."
65 || 66 || Regarding the phrase "to the Maṇḍala consisting of ten digits" (*maṇḍalāya daśakalātmakavadbhimaṇḍalāya*), some explain the meaning of this as "together with the digits.
Others, however, describe it differently:
that the state of possessing twelve digits and so forth is obtained even though it was not explicitly stated.

Having worshipped the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) therein with its twelve digits (*kalā*), then the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*) with its sixteen digits, and then the fiery disc (*agnimaṇḍala*) with its ten digits—one should worship them. This is the traditional position. Regarding the phrase "in that" (*tasyām*), [it refers to] the *Śāradātilaka*: "Then, by means of the three syllables of the *praṇava*, one should [worship] the qualities such as *sattva*."

*Indravallī* is a specific type of creeper, namely *indravāruṇī*;
*caṣaka* refers to a vessel of the *kalaśa* type, such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) and so forth;
by the word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), the recitation of the root mantra is indicated.
Silk cloth is what is available from that [goat's hair]; in its absence, silk cloth (*paṭṭavastra*) and so forth;
elsewhere, even wrapping with a single garment is mentioned.
"One should wrap the jar with a thread that is extremely subtle, pure, and new, having the nature of the *māyātattva*. (85–86)

Regarding "the deity of the mantra," it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka* that in the case of initiation into a single mantra, if one follows the procedure for initiation into the sixfold abode (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one should establish five pitchers and invoke the respective deities into each pitcher; this is what is meant by the term "mantrin" (one who possesses the mantra).
Thus it has been said by the Teachers: "By this very procedure for the jar, whether with a single one or with many jars.

Furthermore, the sequence for the installation of the deities in the *pañcāyatana-dīkṣā* is stated in the *Jñānamālā*: "But when one should worship Śaṅkara in the center and Śrīpati in the northeast..."
Likewise, one should place Haṃsa in the southeast and the Son of Pārvatī in the southwest.
And Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, should always be worshipped in the northwest;
however, when Govinda is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast.
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should worship Gaṇanātha in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Ambikā in the northwest.

When [the sun] is at the meridian, one should worship the Thousand-rayed [Sun] in the center, the Lord of Mountains (Śiva) in the northeast, the One-tusked [Ganesha] in the southeast, and Acyuta (Viṣṇu) in the southwest.
One should worship the goddess Bhavānī—the sole ground for liberation through enjoyment—in the northwest;
however, when she is in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast.
The teacher should worship Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest, and Pradyotana in the northwest.
When Heramba is in the center, one should worship Acyuta in the northeast,
Pañcavaktra in the southeast, and Jagadambikā in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should worship the Sun with a mantra while remaining unwearied;

for deities who have been removed from their proper places bestow sorrow, suffering, and fear, and the king as well as the practitioner perishes if they remain within that [disordered] mandala. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere it is also stated: "When Śambhu is in the center, Hari, Naha, Hara, Bhū, Devī, Hari, and Śaṅkara are established; Āsyena, Agasutā, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Aja, and Ambikā are established. When Devī is in the center, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravi, Lambodara, Aja, Ekhara, and Āyyaina are established. These [deities] are exceedingly auspicious when placed starting from the portion of Śaṅkara; if they are reversed, however, they bring about loss. Thus it is also taught: "Śaṃ, Nā, Ra, Ga, De, Madhyāt, Nā, Śaṃ, Garabheśataḥ, Sū, Śaṃ, Ga, Nā, De, Denā, Śaṃ, Gara, Ga, Nā, Śaṃ, Bha, Sū—these are to be worshipped in the intermediate directions."
Elsewhere, installation is said to follow the sequence beginning with Agni:
Sūrya, Ekadanta, Acyuta, Śakti, Rudra, Vighneśvara, Īśa, Adrisūta, Arka, Kṛṣṇa, Śrīnātha, Vighneśa, Bhaga, Ambikeśa, Śvaṇḍeśa, Heramba, Pataṅga, and Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Śambhu, Sūrya, Khuratha, Ambaka, and Kṛṣṇa are to be worshipped in the center and the intermediate directions, remaining in their respective places;
by doing so, all desires are attained here, and they destroy misfortunes in the hereafter.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.

In another place as well: "Having worshipped Hari in the center, [one places] Gaṇeśa, Pārvatī, and Indra; in the center [of those], Śiva, Umā, the Sun, and Viṣṇu; then the Sun, Vighneśa, Śakti, and Īśvara;
Śakti in the center, then Īśa, Vighna, and the Sun, and Viṣṇu; and Hara in the center, with Sūrya, Ambikā, Śiva, and Acyuta placed starting from the southeast corner.
Thus, although the order of installation differs in both cases, they are identical in their result.
As for the worship, it should be understood that it begins with Gaṇapati where Gaṇapati holds primacy, but where he does not, it begins with Sūrya;
as they say: "Having offered a handful of flowers to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place."
"If Gaṇeśa alone is the principal [deity], then the sequence of the Sun [is performed] as an ancillary to that.
Regarding this explanation, they perform it in two ways:

first, having offered merely a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the principal deity, and afterwards, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others, [it is called] the "principal worship" (mukhyapūjā).
Others, however,
maintain that by the term "handful of flowers" (puṣpāñjali) is included the handful of flowers offered at the conclusion of the worship;
thus, the worship of Gaṇeśa and others occurs immediately after the primary worship of the deity.
This should be understood according to the specific tradition of one's own guru;
this very sequence for the installation of the deity is the same for daily worship (*nityapūjā*) as well.
In that regard, daily worship should be performed upon a *śālagrāma*, a gem, a yantra, or an image made of stone and so forth.
Thus it is said in the Jñānamālā: "The gods became intent on obstacles for the sake of the pleasure of Girijā’s lover;
having heard that conduct of the Goddess, a most terrible curse was pronounced."
Afflicted by the curse of Pārśvatī, the gods—
including Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and other foremost deities— attained the state of stone.
O gods, she has become a bestower of boons even while in the state of a stone;
they shall worship her in her own place for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
"He alone is granted as the boon who is capable of giving [the fruit] according to my word;
therefore, worship must be performed even toward stone images. Thus it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Made of clay, fashioned from wood, born of metal, and likewise born of jewels..."
It is known to be of seven kinds: that born of stone, that born of fragrance, and that born of flowers.
An image made of flowers, one of incense, or one made of clay is beneficial;
when worshipped at that very time, these grant the fruit of all desires. Thus it is also stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "Whether made of stone, or of metal, or of gems, or even of wood..."
And that made of clay—these five types of images are thus proclaimed.
For all these deities, an image made of mahānīla stone bestows fame;
according to the Śāradātilaka,
one made of wood is said to grant desires, while one made of gold bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A vessel made of silver bestows the fruit of heaven; one of copper increases longevity; one of bell-metal wards off many calamities; and one of tin destroys enemies.
A stone [liṅga] bestows all enjoyments; one made of crystal brings forth radiance; one known as being made of clay indeed bestows great enjoyments and is truly auspicious.
"A statue in the home should be worshipped measuring fifteen finger-breadths according to the measurement of one's own hand; indeed, one larger than that is not recommended.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "Beginning from the size of a thumb-joint up to a span (vitasti)."

Regarding the statement: "In the home, however, an image should be made; one that is larger than that is not recommended by the wise," as for the [contrary] saying: "A gentle image one cubit in height bestows wealth; one two cubits high leads to forgiveness and abundance; and one three or four cubits in height [brings great prosperity]."
That should be understood as referring to an installed image.
Regarding an earthen image, a specific detail is stated therein: "I shall describe the earthen image; learn it from me exactly as it is.
Earthen images are said to be of two kinds, according to the sequence: baked and unbaked."
Everyone praises an image made of burnt clay; an unbaked image is highly esteemed, and that alone should be fashioned by the wise.
It should never be made with lime nor ever with stone powder; one should fashion it from clay alone, according to the rules and in the proper sequence.
"For a Brāhmaṇa, white clay is prescribed; for a Kṣatriya, red is recorded; for Vaiśyas, it should be yellowish-white clay; and for a Śūdra, black is proclaimed. Thus it is said.
There is another distinction elsewhere: "If the clay comes from an excessive limb, there is fear of the king; if from a deficient limb, there is incapacity for the performer."
In Cāmodarī there is hunger and thirst; in Kaśāṅgā there is the destruction of wealth.
One should indicate death by the falling of a weapon upon the truth-teller;
if Vinatā is on the left, she destroys the wife, while Vinatā on the right destroys the life-span.
A gaze directed upward causes blindness, and a downward gaze causes anxiety.
"In this manner, one should understand the auspicious and inauspicious [aspects] in all images as stated by Bhāskara.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "A deity should never be fashioned with either extra limbs or missing limbs."
An over-large belly brings destruction to the artisan; a whip-like belly destroys wealth; a thin-waisted belly portends famine; a fleshless belly destroys riches;
a crooked nose leads to misery; and one with well-rounded limbs inspires fear.
The fourth chapter: One with flattened features leads to suffering and grief; one without eyes destroys the eyes;
one with a deficient mouth causes misery; likewise, one with emaciated hands and feet does the same.
O King, one who lacks shoulders or whose birth is defective causes delusion and madness;
one with a parched mouth brings misfortune to the king, and one lacking hips kills him.
If a woman is devoid of hands and feet, a great hell arises for her.
That image which is deficient in the jaw is said to cause the destruction of enemies;
that which is deficient in the chest leads to the ruin of sons and friends;
but that which possesses all its limbs complete always bestows longevity and prosperity.
"Having thus attained the [proper] characteristics, the supreme image should be fashioned.
Regarding this, there is a specific rule elsewhere: "In the case of one that is broken, cracked, fallen, burnt, or devoid of the [proper] measurements..."
In these ten cases— the sacrifice being concluded, or the remains having fallen on impure ground,
or when another [deity] has been worshipped, or when it is defiled by the touch of a fallen person—
the denizens of heaven did not grant their presence.
Thus Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, made this declaration;
elsewhere it is said: [an image that is] broken, cracked, worn out, or scorched by fire...
"One should carefully avoid an image that is broken or has lost its proper characteristics; one should cast an image made of wood into fire, and likewise cast any other [metallic image] into water."
Likewise: "If the daily worship is interrupted for one day, one should perform double the worship;

if for three nights, however, a great worship (mahāpūjā) is required; beyond that, a sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) is prescribed. If the daily worship is interrupted for even one day after the lapse of a month..."
Some will perform the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), while others follow the procedure for *saṃprokṣaṇa* (sprinkling).

Regarding the characteristics of *saṃprokṣaṇa*, it is as stated in that very same source: "As for the *saṃprokṣaṇa* of the deity, having first dismissed the deity as before, one should bathe him with clay and water in successive order."
Having bathed [the deity] with the products of the cow and purified it with water from *darbha* grass,
one should sprinkle it with consecrated water while reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times; then, placing the hand— adorned with flowers and *kuśa* grass— upon the head of the deity.
One should recite the root mantra five times, followed by one hundred and eight repetitions; then, with the root mantra, one should touch the head and so forth, ending at the pedestal (pīṭha),
according to the *Śāradātilaka*.
One should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the placement of the syllables (lipinyāsa), and the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa);
one should carry out the consecration with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra and perform a great worship according to the rules as taught in the Svatantra-tantra.
"In cases such as those where a sacrifice has been omitted, the rite of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) is generally prescribed.
Thus it is said.
Elsewhere it is also stated: "The daily worship of Hari should be performed upon a śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, a mandala, or an image, but never on bare ground alone."
Also in the *Rāmapūrvatāpanīya*: "The form of this twofold deity is the arrangement of the yantra;
without the yantra, if there is worship, the deity is not pleased."
In the *Saṃhitā* as well: "The gods declare that the yantra consists of mantra, and the deity has the form of the mantra;
the Lord, if not worshipped with the yantra, does not quickly become pleased.
Likewise, for all mantras, worship in the yantra is praised."
Thus it has been stated by Īśānaśiva: "One should worship Śakti in a circle, on a painting, or on a cloth through identification with one's own self, but never on the ground;
if, out of delusion, he should worship her as situated upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), he shall fall from the three aims of life—so say the masters of mantra."
Thus,

the worship of Śiva should be performed upon a form of Śiva, whether it be a fixed or a mobile Śivaliṅga; regarding the mobile [liṅga] made of stone or other materials, the characteristics such as the five lines (pañcasūtra) that have been described must necessarily be observed.
However, there is no fault even in the case of a *liṅga* made of jewels and the like if they lack those specific characteristics;
as it is stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should not perform the extraction of marks for those made of jewels that are mobile by nature;
O twice-born, their own natural luster is indeed their mark, and this applies even to those made of gold."

Therefore, one should not perform the extraction of characteristics (lakṣaṇoddhāra) here, as in the case of a stone liṅga; for immovable and metallic [liṅgas], characteristics may optionally be desired in some cases,
but the characteristics should be fashioned according to rule upon a liṅga intended for installation.
On a movable linga, the Guru should fashion the marks with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
or he may even mentally contemplate the marks situated upon the linga.

Somaśambhu also states: "The extraction of characteristics is not [found] in lingas made of iron, nor in those born of stone, nor in those born of metal, nor has it been seen anywhere in the scriptures;
their essential form and characteristic is that their luster is stainless in gems."
Thus ends the fourth chapter:
having recited the root mantra, the wise one [should proceed] by way of the suṣumṇā path.
Having brought the radiance from its own place, it emerges through the nostrils;
the consciousness is then placed within the hand upon the lotus of the Mātṛkā and amidst the collection of flowers.
The wise one should join [the thread] through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and invoke [the deity] with the thread.
However, there is a specific rule elsewhere: in the home, there should not be two *liṅgas*, nor even two Gaṇeśas.
A wise man should not worship a stone that possesses the three powers (*śaktitraya*), nor one marked with a corpse, nor one marked with the ten [signs] beginning with the fish;
likewise, he should not worship two conch shells, nor a *śālagrāma* stone that has two discs, nor one belonging to Dvārakā, nor one with two suns.
By constantly worshipping these, one's household shall attain freedom from distress.
It was stated that "one should worship after invoking"; regarding that, he describes the method of invocation with the words beginning with "mūla":
[from] its own place, namely, from the heart-lotus.
Others say [the deity comes] from the solar disc;
as it is stated in the *Vaihāyasa-mantrakośa*: "Then, from the sun or from the heart-lotus, one should invoke the son of Nanda, who is well-attired."
Elsewhere it is also said: "One should invoke the Great Goddess from the lotus of the heart,
or from the orb of the sun, or from one's own [subtle] center at the dvādaśānta."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the wise one, having uttered the root mantra, brings the radiance from its own place through the path of the *suṣumṇā* by means of the door of the *brahmarandhra*; having brought that consciousness—which has exited through the nostrils via the door of the *brahmarandhra*—and having joined it with the collection of flowers in the lotus of the *mātṛkā* located in the hand, he should invoke it into the form. Here, "in the door of the *brahmarandhra*" and "in the collection of flowers in the lotus of the *mātṛkā* located in the hand" are two locative cases in apposition (though distinct in their referents).
As it has been said: Having brought the deity through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
and having visualized [the deity] emerging from the left nostril and resting within one's own joined palms,
one should place that flower upon the image or other representation.
Thus,
the invocation (āvāhana) is the act of summoning by means of the verse used for summoning.

And that [invocation] is performed at the end of the root mantra in the manner "āvāhito bhava namaḥ," or else at the end of the verse from the Āgama; or alternatively, as stated by the word *sudhīḥ*, it is done by reciting the verse from the Āgama at the end of the root mantra— this indeed is the primary method.
In the *Saṃhitā* as well, the incense mantra is stated: "Thus, with 'evam' at the end of the seed-syllable, the incense mantra is proclaimed," and so forth;
likewise, this should be applied to the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and others that follow.

The verse is as follows: "O Supreme Lord, I invoke you—the unborn, pure, and abiding within the self—into this form, just as one brings the consumer of oblations (the fire) into the sacrificial wood. — *Śāradātilaka*
One should perform the stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), the placement (*sannidhāna*), and the immediate cessation (*sannirodha*);
thereafter, one should perform the totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*).
Having performed the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should effect the supreme transformation (*paramīkṛti*).
One should perform these [rites] in sequence with the appropriate mudrās while remaining composed in meditation.
(61) These acts, beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), are not to be performed for the Śālagrāma stone and similar objects;
as it is said: "In the case of the Śālagrāma or a stationary image, there is no invocation nor dismissal."
"Lord Hari is eternally present in the Śālagrāma stone and other such objects. Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: "In the worship of a permanent image, there is neither dismissal nor invocation;

for a non-permanent image, there may be an option; however, in the case of a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), both should be performed. But in the worship of the Śālagrāma, there is indeed no invocation or dismissal."

Thus, regarding this matter, there arises a doubt: in the ritual procedure for the five deities (*pañcāyatana*), should one perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of each deity individually and then the installation (*sthāpana*) of each deity individually—this being *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance by item)—or should one complete the entire sequence from invocation up to the food offering (*naivedya*) for one deity first, and then do the same for the others—this being *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by section)? In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is *kāṇḍānusamaya*, because:
"Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place."
Thus it has been stated;
therein, the word *arcana* denotes worship (*pūjā*), and that [worship] extends from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of food (*naivedya*).

Furthermore, this was established as the final conclusion in the section titled "But by the scriptural statement, it ends with the binding of the cord" (*vacanāt tu parivyāṇāntam*) in the second quarter of the fifth chapter. 88. 88.
The connection is that "the wise one should perform the installation";
"installation" means establishing, and that [is performed] by means of the Sthāpinī [mudrā].
The verse, however, states: "O Lord (Vibhu), this form of yours is your majesty; within it, I establish you, who are all-pervading, like a lamp drawn forth by the force of devotion and affection.
By the words "thus the wise one," it is meant that the act of sitting upon the seat should be performed.

Thus, at the end of the root mantra: "O God, inner controller of all, consisting of all seeds, auspicious, abiding in my own self, supremely pure—I prepare this seat for you. Accept the seat; *namaḥ*.
Then, at the end of the root mantra: "O God, seated comfortably upon this excellent seat, whose nature is the Imperishable (*akṣara*)."

"May you be firmly established; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Be seated!"—this is the prayer for the presence [of the deity] and for its remaining in a state of constant proximity, through the mantra that effects such presence.
The verse, however, says: "O Lord of Gods, O Master, this power of your form is not other than you;
you who are intent on favoring your devotees, please manifest your presence within it.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.

It involves cessation and the act of ceasing, with no longing for any other state of mind. Regarding that cessation, there is this verse: "O Lord of Gods, O ocean of compassion, O ocean of virtues, by this [prayer] of yours..."
"O Father, O Guru, I restrain you who are solely satisfied with the bliss of the Self.
Thus, in the *Siddhāntasāgara*, another definition of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites is stated:
"Of the Reality (*tattva*), which is by its very nature completely full, in these acts such as worship..."

The manifestation [of the deity] before one with reverence is called *āvāhana* (invocation). The continuous stabilization of this invoked Śiva within the *vidyā-deha* (body of knowledge) during worship with devotion is designated as *sthāpana* (establishment). When he has accepted the worship being performed and possesses the capacity here to bestow grace and so forth, that is declared to be *sānnidhya* (proximity). Indeed, the proximity of Śiva consists in the manifestation of the worship.
"Along with its cessation, it has been taught by the power of this Lord.
By these words, and by the phrase "immediately thereafter," the manifestation [of the deity] and the prayer have been described through the pair of mudrās.
As for the two verses: "Due to lack of food, due to mental distress, or due to a deficiency in the means of accomplishment..."

"Even when the task remains incomplete, remain present before me. O Maheśvara, do not remain fixed in your form as one who has reached ultimate perfection, thereby filling my seat in vain with a shower of nectar.
Thus is the description of the mudrās: "The two thumbs, held in the fists, should face each other."

One should join them closely and raise them upward; this is the *sammukha-mudrā*. With hands facing each other, one should join the fingers of both hands and extend them together at the heart; this is the *prārthanā-mudrā*. Thus ends the *sakalīkaraṇa*, which is the prayer for remaining in a state of complete perfection.

And that veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) upon the limbs of the deity, through the performance of the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), is the rendering [of the deity] as an object invisible to unworthy eyes; that is the function of the veiling-mantra (*avaguṇṭhanī*).

The verse is as follows: "O You of immeasurable luster, who are far beyond the reach of the speech, mind, eyes, and ears of the non-devotees—be swiftly enveloped on all sides by Your own fivefold splendor.
Thus is the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), which is the state of being established in the fullness of bliss.
The supreme transformation by means of the Dhenu-mudrā is the capacity to endure all transgressions;
that [transformation] is performed by means of the Mahāmudrā.

"By means of their own mudrās" refers to those that will be described in the twenty-third [chapter]. By the phrase "being composed," it is stated that one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, encased within the root mantra, upon the body of the deity; for this will be explained in the section on worship. — *Śāradātilaka*

Then, one who knows the Mantras should perform the ritual services beginning with the welcome; the Guru should first utter the words of welcome and inquiries regarding his well-being. Regarding the word "atha" (then), its meaning as a ritual service (*upacāra*) has been stated in the *Jñānamālā*: [The text continues: "The term 'service' (*upacāra*) refers to that which brings about the attainment of the desired goal through the performance of various acts. [The text continues: "The sequence of services is said to begin with the welcome, followed by the inquiry into well-being, the offering of a seat, water for washing the feet, water for sipping, the guest-water (*arghya*), bathing, clothing, ornaments, incense, flowers, unguents, food, betel, and finally, prostration. [The text continues: "Among these, the welcome consists of a greeting accompanied by a smile and a pleasant countenance. The inquiry into well-being is the question: 'Are you free from illness? Are you at ease? Is your family well? The offering of a seat is the act of presenting a seat while saying, 'Please be seated. [The text continues: "Water for washing the feet is that which removes fatigue and impurity. Water for sipping (*ācamana*) is for the purpose of purifying the mouth. The guest-water (*arghya*) is offered according to the prescribed rules. Bathing is performed with fragrant substances and water. Clothing is for the sake of beauty and modesty. Ornaments are for the sake of splendor. Incense is for the purpose of removing odors. Flowers are for the purpose of adorning the deity. Unguents are for the purpose of beautifying the body. Food is for the purpose of nourishment. Betel is for the purpose of refreshing the mouth. Prostration is the act of bowing down with devotion. [The text continues: "One should perform these services in due order, without omitting any, and with a mind focused on the deity. By performing these services, the practitioner becomes worthy of receiving the grace of the mantra."

Because these are offered with devotion to the God and cause the attainment of the desired goal through divine proximity, they are called *upacārakas* (services). They are also so designated because they circulate [the practitioner] near the fruits [of their practice].
Thus, sixteen are mentioned in the root text, while others are also stated in the *Jñānamālā*.
They are as follows: the thirty-eight, the sixteen, the twelve, the ten, and the five modes of worship (*upacāra*).

Having categorized them, I shall explain what they are and what is accomplished by each. First among these is the seat (*āsana*); then the invocation (*āvāhana*), the attendance (*upasthiti*), the presence (*sānnidhya*), the orientation (*ābhimukhya*), the stabilization (*sthirīkṛti*), and the adornment (*prasādhana*). Then the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the water for rinsing the mouth (*upaspṛśa*).

Bathing, the lustration rite (nīrājana), clothing, sipping water (ācamana), and the sacred thread; again sipping water and ornaments, then the beholding of the mirror; thereafter, in sequence: fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and the food offering (naivedya); then drinking water, water for rinsing the mouth, and hand-perfume;
following that, betel leaf, unguents, and the offering of flowers again and again; as well as song, instrumental music, dance, hymns of praise, and circumambulation.
"The offering of a handful of flowers and prostration are declared to be thirty-eight.
Thus it is also stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Among those [rituals], the seat is considered first, then the invocation, followed by the salutation and the presence."

By the passage beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "puṣpāñjalinamaskārī viṣṇuprītyai bhavantyamī triṃśaccāṣṭau samākhyātā upacārā manīṣibhiḥ," the sixteen [services] are clearly explained in the root text.

Likewise: having set aside the twelve [services] beginning with the seat (*āsana*), welcome (*svāgata*), clothing (*vastra*), and ornaments (*bhūṣā*), there are the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for washing the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and also the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) with its subsequent sipping. The ten services (*upacāra*) from fragrance (*gandha*) to food offering (*naivedya*) are performed in sequence;

however, fragrance and flowers, incense (*dhūpa*), lamp (*dīpa*), and food offering—these five are traditionally remembered [as the core]. These are said to be of five kinds including the *pathyā* [formula]; one should perform at least one of them.
The Fourth Chapter:

One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the lotus-feet of the Deity with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; this is declared [to be done] with *yava*, *kāśmari* seeds, and *viṣṇukrāntā*. One should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) in the mouth with the *sudhā-mantra*.
This has been stated by those who know the Tantras using nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola. Furthermore, in the *Prayogasāra*, the sixth [item] is mentioned:

"Then there is the guest-offering (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), incense, and the lamp; others have declared that the food offering (*naivedya*) constitutes the seventh limb, making it sevenfold."
"Welcome" refers to an inquiry after one's welfare; this is the explanation of the meaning of "welcome.
The verse, however, states: "The gods desire the sight of him for the sake of accomplishing their own desired goals."
"Welcome, welcome to You, the Supreme Lord; and may there be a welcome for me as well.
Following this, at the end of the root mantra, the verse for a very warm welcome is: "I am fulfilled, I am graced; my life has become fruitful."
The Lord of the Gods of gods has arrived; once again, a very warm welcome to you!
The water for the feet (*pādya*) is offered with the *hṛdayāṇu* (heart-mantra) and the *namaḥ* mantra;
the verse is as follows: "From contact with even a minute particle of whose power, the arising of supreme bliss occurs..."

"To you, the pure one worthy of being served, I offer water for the feet. Having recited this verse here and uttered the *namaḥ* mantra, he should say, "Accept the water for the feet; *namaḥ*," and pour out the water held in his joined palms. The same applies hereafter.
Where a specific mantra is not mentioned, it should be understood that the root mantra itself is intended;
"this" refers to *śyāmāka*, commonly known as *śyāmā*.

Also in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "Dūrvā grass, the consort of Viṣṇu (lotus), śyāmāka grain, and the lotus itself—these four are briefly declared to be the components of the water for the feet (*pādya*)."

With the *sudhā* mantra, namely "vaṃ," the verse is as follows: "O Lord, for the sake of the Veda of even the Vedas, for the divine self of the gods, we prepare this rinsing water (*ācāma*) for the purification of those who are already pure. Thus.
Jātī, jātīphala, kakkola, kośaphala, and kavāva—these are the names in the Kānyakubja dialect.
As it is stated in the Agastisaṃhitā: "O Sage, one should likewise offer jātīphala during the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and when drinking."
"Even clove and kakkola are recommended as substances for the *ācamana* rite.
Thus, in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, the materials for the *ācamana* rite are stated differently than in the *Śāradā-tilaka*.

Then the preceptor should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *Śiras-mantra*, using sandalwood paste (*gandha*), flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* grass; this is declared to be the *arghya* for all the gods.
Then, with the *sudhāṇu* mantra, he should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth; this mixture of clarified butter, curd, and honey is so described by the wise.

With that same mantra, one should perform the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka). "Camphor, agallochum, and flowers are the substances for the water for sipping"—this is the specific detail elsewhere: he offers the water for honoring (arghya), he offers the water for the feet (pādya), and he offers the water for sipping (ācamanīya) six times.
Thus,

this wise one should offer [the oblation] to the deity who has arrived and is seated upon the throne for worship, as well as to one desiring to depart after the rite; likewise, when the time for bathing has arrived and at the commencement of the food offering (naivedya).
The wise have likewise declared that there are three types of rules regarding the water for washing the feet.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, regarding the fruit [obtained] at the tip of the *kuśa* grass with the head-mantra ending in *svāhā*, it is said:
"White mustard seeds, unhusked rice, *dūrvā* grass, and sesame seeds."
"Barley, fragrance, fruit, and flower—this is called the eightfold [offering] for the ancestors.
The phrase "of all the gods" is to be connected everywhere;
the meaning is that the substances mentioned, such as the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, are common to all deities.

The verse is as follows: "I prepare for you this divine madhuparka, which removes the threefold suffering, is characterized by supreme bliss, and is itself liberated from the threefold suffering. Thus [ends the section on] the madhuparka.
The verse is as follows: "O Lord, for you who are free from all impurity and whose nature is perfect bliss, I prepare this madhuparka; be gracious unto me.
Having thus recited it, in the absence of the substances prescribed by Atri and others, one should offer only rice grains.
Thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "In the absence of [other] substances, auspicious moving rice grains (*cālitataṇḍula*) should be offered.
Also elsewhere: "One should throw rice grains into them; but in the case of not obtaining those substances, [ones equal to them]."
Thus, by that very Manu [it is meant] "by the particle of nectar" (sudhāṇu);
the verse, however, is as follows: "Even if one is impure or even unclean, by the mere remembrance of whom..."
"He attains purity; therefore, this water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is offered to you. Thus, the sipping at the conclusion of the *madhuparka* is illustrative;

by this, one should also provide the sipping whenever the occasions prescribed in the Smṛtis arise—namely, at the end of the bath, at the end of the gift of clothing, at the end of the gift of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and at the end of the food offering (*naivedya*).
The Fourth Chapter:
One should cause a bath with fragrant water to be performed, have two garments put on,
and give a divine sacred thread along with necklaces and other ornaments.
As it is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcaśāstra: "One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) during bathing, while wearing clothes, and likewise when eating";
thus, there are six occasions for ācamanīya.

Thus it is said in the Jñānamālā: "Ācamana should be offered during the washing of the feet, at the honey-mixture (madhuparka), at the ritual bath, when putting on the garment and the sacred thread, and during the meal."
Prior to the bath, there is a specific detail in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "Then one should offer incomparable perfume and oil to the God.
Regarding this verse: "O Great-souled Lord of the World, accept this oil with affection."
"O pure-souled one, I bestow supreme affection upon all worlds.
Thus [ends the section on] massage in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Rajanī, Sahadevī, Śirīṣa, and Lakṣmaṇā as well..."
"Sadābhadra and kuśa tips are what is called 'udvartana' here.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well: "One should also perform the great bath (mahāsnāna) along with oil massage and udvartana."
Regarding "with scented water," it is stated in the *Manvatantraprakāśa*: "Scented water is a hundred times superior to pure water;
