the fruit [obtained from] the waters of sacred sites such as the Gaṅgā, as proclaimed by the scriptures, is to be understood in each respective case. One should understand that [fruit] in those various instances.

Thus, one should not fetch water that is dirty, defiled by hair, insects, and the like, nor with a vessel that is dirty, cracked, or impure. Regarding the specific details: unbroken grains, perfumes, and flowers—these three likewise [should be placed] in the bathing vessel.
The verse is as follows: "To him whose own form is immersed in the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss."
"O Lord, I perform for you this bath along with its primary and secondary limbs.
Following this, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the deity with water from a conch shell, as it is said:
"One should consecrate [the deity] a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times, according to one's capacity."
"Having filled the conch with that very [water] along with flowers, [one should bathe] the deity.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "Having bathed the Lord of the World with fragrant water according to one's capacity."
In this regard, there is a distinction: one should always perform the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) with a conch alone;
indeed, this [conch] is praised everywhere except for the worship of Śiva and the Sun. Thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.

Having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings using the Mātṛkā syllables encased by the mantra according to the sequence of Nyāsa, one should then worship the limbs (Aṅgas) and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a specific rule in another Tantra: "One should not perform a daily ritual bath for images, cloth-paintings, or yantras."
"One should likewise perform the removal of impurity on a festival day.
By the dual number used for "clothes" (*vāsasī*) here, the upper garment (*uttarīya*) is understood;
for the verse states: "To him whose own secret splendor is covered by a cloth of illusion and variegated patterns..."

"O consciousness free from obscuration, I offer you a garment; to that Supreme Lord, relying upon whom the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) constantly deludes the world, I offer an upper cloth. Thus, the specific detail regarding this is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "A yellow garment of silk is proclaimed for the propitiation of Viṣṇu."

Red cloth is dear to Śakti, Arka, and Vighna; for Īśvara, white cloth that is free from impurities, without holes, and made of either silk (cauma) or cotton (kārpāsa) is preferred. From cloth defiled by oil and such, disease arises; from cloth with holes, one incurs censure; from worn-out cloth, poverty comes to the wearer; and from dirty cloth, a lack of reputation. Thus it is said.
The verse beginning with "hārābdhyābharaṇaiḥ" refers to Him by whom this entire universe is pervaded through His three powers, and who is the sacred thread (*upavīta*).
The verse says:

"O you who are praised by the gods, I fashion various ornaments for you, whose limbs are naturally beautiful and who are the locus of manifold powers—for you to whom I offer this garland of praise. Thus [he speaks].

The meaning is that, by way of metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the deity, the practitioner (*mantrī*) should worship each individual syllable, encased within the root mantra,
sequentially according to the order of the hundred-fold placement (*nyāsakrama*) using the syllables encased within the mantra.

First, with perfumes and other offerings, there is the practice renowned as "the Deluder of the Three Worlds" (*trailokyamohana*) directed toward the deities of the human realm; this was taught by the Ācārya.
Regarding the phrase "having worshipped the Goddess" (*devīm abhyarcya*), the mention of "the Goddess" is an elliptical expression meaning "one's own chosen deity."
In some places, the characteristics of the *devapuṭita* meter will be explained in the twenty-third [chapter].
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, the fourth chapter follows;
perfume is said to consist of sandalwood, camphor, and black agallochum.
The two types of *kamala*, the two types of *karavīra*, the two types of *kumuda*, the two types of *tulasī*, the two types of *jātī*, the two types of *bītaka*, *he*, *kavāra*, *campaka*,
*utpala*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *punnāga*, *pāṭalā*, and *nāgacampaka*. (100–101)
One should worship the Āragvadha, Karṇikāra, Pārantī, Navamallikā,
Saugandhika, Koraṇṭa, Palāśa, Aśoka, and Mallikā; furthermore,
one should worship the intermediate directions and the protective enclosures of the limbs and so forth.
Thus, this prescribes the sequence;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "with perfumes and so forth," flowers are included,
and by "limbs and so forth" (*aṅgādīni*), the specific limb-offerings and the like mentioned in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*) are intended.

The intention here is this: having offered fragrance and flowers to the principal deity and having worshipped the guardians of the world (lokapālas) such as Aṅga and the others, one should offer incense and so forth. || 88 ||

Having stated "with perfumes and so forth," he explains their essential nature with the verse beginning with "perfume" (gandha), which runs as follows: "O Supreme Lord, out of compassion, please accept this supreme perfume, which fills the quarters of space with the fragrance of ultimate bliss."
This offering of fragrance should be understood as being performed with the little finger,
as it is said: "One should offer the fragrance contained in a conch vessel with the mantras using the little finger."
Then one should display the fragrance mudrā;
its characteristic is as follows: "The fragrance mudrā is proclaimed to be formed by joining the little finger and the thumb."
Regarding "kamale" and "de," [the reference is to] the yellow and red [colors]; the verse, however, states: "Born from the fourth forest, it is enchanting with its manifold qualities."
"Let this supreme flower of unyielding fragrance be accepted.
Then, one should display the flower mudrā; for the white and yellow *ketakī*, [one says] "O *ketake*! and "O *he*! respectively.
*Mandāra* is *arka*;
*punnāga* is *nāgakeśara*;
*āragvadha* is *rājavṛtta*; and *ghanavadarī* is so called in the Kānyakubja dialect.
*Pārantī* is a species of creeper and *saugandhika* is a species of *kalāra*.

By the statement "these have been taught by the teachers for worship," it is indicated that those [flowers] prescribed in other chapters on flowers are to be accepted, while those prohibited for the respective deities are to be rejected.
In the *Jñānamālā*: "One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains (*akṣata*), nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*, nor Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, nor the Sun with *bilva* leaves.
The *unmatta* flower and the *arka* flower should always be avoided by the wise when [worshipping] Viṣṇu."
One should offer mācca, vārkamandāra, āditya, and likewise tagara to the Goddess.
Red flowers are most dear to Gaṇeśa and Sūrya;
[the flowers] śāradātilaka, dhūstūra, sarjaka, bilva, arjuna, and munipuṣpaka [are likewise favored].
A wise person should also take other fragrant leaves and flowers prescribed by the teachers for worship; however,
one should avoid those that are soiled, touched by the ground, or defiled by worms, hair, and the like.

O Śivā, one should avoid the kunda flower at dawn; the bandhūka and ketaka at midday; the red javā at twilight; and one should likewise abandon sindūra, kūṭaja, mālatī, saffron (ghusṛṇa), the red aśoka (hayāri), and barbara.

One should not offer to Śambhu that which is foul-smelling or odorless, defiled by worms, hair, and the like, or brought by those with impure vessels, hands, limbs, or clothing, and who are contemptible in nature; even through negligence, such an offering is considered a fault.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with buds, nor without campaka and lotuses; nor with dry leaves, flowers, or fruits,
nor with those brought after bathing, nor with stale offerings, nor with those obtained by begging, nor with black-colored ones.
One should avoid the *ṛṣhatodana*, *kāñcanāra*, and *kuruṇṭaka* flowers that bloom in the evening and have fallen to the ground of their own accord; however,
worship may always be performed with all other prescribed flowers.

Devotion must be practiced toward all the gods; this is the essential cause here. A flower, a leaf, or a fruit should not be offered with its face turned downward; that is declared to be a giver of sorrow. An offering should be presented exactly as it was produced.
In all types of variegated worship (*citrapūjā*), there is no fault even if [the flowers] are not pierced;
however, offering them face-down is not desired in the rite of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
In all *lakṣapūjās*, one should offer each flower individually.
"If worship is performed by means of a collection [of flowers], that is the offering of one hundred thousand flowers.
Thus it is also stated in the *Mantratantvaprakāśa*: "Flowers are said by the sages, such as Nārada and others, to be of five kinds:
supreme, near-supreme, excellent, middling, and likewise inferior."
The superior [image] is said to be made of gold; the inferior is made of variegated cloth.
Flowers from trees, shrubs, and creepers are proclaimed as the best;
leaves, water, and so forth are the lowest; and those consisting of fruits are the middling.
The fourth chapter:
The Guru should discard that which has been touched by a limb, smelled, or left overnight;
he should always place flowers upon the head of the Deity. 105
At the time of worship, one should not wave the hand over the deity;
rather, with aguru, uśīra, guggulu, sugar, honey, and sandalwood—[these are] always suitable for the supreme and the non-supreme, provided they have not been discarded as unfit for ritual use. (106)
Among leaves, *tulasī* is the most excellent; the *bilva* and *āmalaka* are auspicious, as are *maruka*, *devakavārī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *apāmārga*, *gāndhārī*, *patrī*, and that known as *surabhi*.
Betel leaf, dūrvā grass, and likewise the kuśa leaf are considered suitable;
so too the leaf of the agastya tree and the dhātrī leaf are meritorious.
Among fruits, the āmalaka is best, as are those produced from the jujube and the tamarind.
One should always worship Viṣṇu with these: pomegranate, citron, rose-apple, jackfruit, plantain, mango, and the excellent jambū fruit—with leaves, flowers, and fruits as well. Thus it is said.

Likewise, on that day, one should perform worship with flowers that bloom during the day; in the absence of all such flowers, one may worship with young shoots (*pravāla*), but not with buds (*koraka*). Flowers gathered for another purpose are defective, as are those already enjoyed by another.

As stated in the *Jñānamālā*: "There is no fault in stale [flowers] regarding the water-born lotus, the *utpala*, the *campaka*, as well as the *tulasī*, *agastya*, *vakula*, *bilva*, and the water of the Gaṅgā.

Thus, the *bilva*, *apāmārga*, *jātī*, *tulasī*, *śamī*, *śataketakī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *dūrvā*, *mandāraka*, *ambuja*, *ahi* (lotus), *darbha*, *muni*, *tila*, *tagara*, *brahmakāṣṭha*, and *manī* [are likewise acceptable].

Campaka, khārātika, kumbha, maruvaka, damanaka, and vikhata; these [plants] should be used for twenty, three, ten, eight, four, eight, and one day respectively. Thus ends the "Hundred" [chapter], the Hundred-petalled [Lotus].
Bhṛṅgaṅga is Bhṛṅgarāja; Manda is Mandāra; Āhi is Droṇakalaśa.
The *brahmā*, *palāśa*, *aśvārāti*, and *karavīra*—
the leaves and flowers of these should be taken as appropriate.
Six enemies and Yama make seven;
thus, the number of days for those brought [together] by a single eightfold [arrangement].

Furthermore, the preceptor should incense the deity with the *Śāradātilaka* incense mixed with clarified butter, using either excellent incense containing camphor, or ghee, or oil made from sesame seeds. (107)
Having placed [the offerings], one should show lamps that are fragrant and elevated,
along with pure *khāṭu* side-dishes and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with sugar.
Such is its meaning.

According to the second interpretation regarding the number of days for *darbha* and other materials, it is stated in another Smṛti: "The *paṅkaja* [lotus] should be used for five nights, the *bilvaka* for ten nights;
however, after eleven days, one should wash the *tulasī* and worship it again."
There is not even the fault of being "nirmālya" (remnants of an offering) regarding Tulasī, as they say: "Whether fresh or even stale, the *nirmālya* of Tulasī is never defiled;
nor is Hari pleased by other things in the way that He is satisfied by Tulasī. (100–106)
Having finished what was indicated, he speaks of the subject at hand: "he should offer incense.
This means that while ringing the bell—which has been worshipped with the bell-mantra—with his left hand, the preceptor (deśika) should offer incense;
by the word "preceptor," the worship of the bell with its mantra is also implied.
As they say: "Then, having uttered the mantra *jayadhvani tato mantramātaḥ svāhā* and having worshipped while ringing the bell.
However, in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having consecrated the incense vessel with the Astra-mantra and worshipped it with the Hṛdaya-mantra..."
One should burn guggulu while ringing a bell that has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
As for the verse: "Endowed with the essence of the lord of forests, fragrant and most enchanting—O son of Atri, may this incense be accepted by all the gods. Thus it is said.
As it has been said: "Sounding the bell, which has been worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers...
and elsewhere: "Then one should offer the incense while sounding the bell with cries of victory.
This is the ritual application here.

Having consecrated the incense burner with the Astra-mantra and offered flowers with the *namaḥ*-mantra, while touching it with the left index finger, one should recite the root mantra and the verse, saying: "I offer incense to the deity together with his limbs and retinue; *namaḥ*. Then, having poured out the water from the conch and displayed the incense mudrā, one should fumigate the deity while ringing the bell—which has been worshipped with the bell-mantra—with the left hand, proclaiming the qualities, names, fame, and praises of the deity.
As it is said: "Having thoroughly worshipped the place of the incense, one should touch it with the left index finger."

Having thus offered a handful of flowers with the *saṅgalya* mantra, one should recite the *Yaśas* hymn. Also, in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*: "While fanning the incense with a fan, while waving incense before the limbs [of the deity], and during all acts of royal lustration (*nīrājana*), one should proclaim the name of the deity and so forth. The Fourth Chapter:
The practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should offer [the oblation] accompanied by plantain fruit and clarified butter (*ājya*).
In each of those instances, one should offer water at intervals between the ritual services;
one should raise shouts of victory, recite the *Kāruṇya-stotra*, as well as sounds of auspiciousness and hymns of praise to the Seed of the World. Thus it is said.
"One should not burn tainted incense [made] from cotton seeds or hair.
Thus, in the offering of lamps as well, one should perform everything such as ringing the bell and so forth, just as before.
The distinction here is that, during the general offering (*utsarga*), one touches the lamp vessel with the left middle finger and displays the lamp mudrā;
the verse is as follows: "This great lamp is brilliantly radiant, dispelling darkness in every direction."
"May this lamp, which is light both external and internal, be accepted.

And it is said in the *Jñānamālā*: "The gods are fond of all-sounds (*sarvanāda*); no single person is capable of creating them. The bell consists of all-sounds; its essence is resonance, and it is produced by all-sounds."
The teachers maintain that "not high" refers to the region of the deity's navel and "high" refers to the region of the eyes; for it is said:
"One of clear intellect should [recite] from the eyes up to the feet in a high tone.
In the case of many wicks, an odd number of wicks should be taken.
As they say: "The *ārātrika* lamp, however, is provided with many wicks of various sizes.
But in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should display a high lamp joined with a wick, using either sesame oil, the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilājya*), beeswax, or some other oily substance. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that if it is with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), then [the offering] is on the right; if it is with oil (*taila*), then on the left.

Likewise, if the wick is white, the offering is on the right; if it is red, it is on the left. However, in the Śaiva Āgama it is said: "Then, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with drops of water from a conch containing *darbha* grass, which has been consecrated seven times with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*."

Then, having consecrated [the offering] with the *cakra-mudrā*, one should sprinkle the oblation (*havis*) with water over which the seed-syllable of air (*vāyu-bīja*) has been recited twelve times. Having dried away its defects with the air arising therefrom, one should contemplate the fire-seed syllable (*agni-bīja*) on the palm of the right hand; placing the palm of the left hand against it and showing it toward the food offering (*naivedya*), one should burn away its defects with the fire arising therefrom. Then, contemplating the nectar-seed syllable (*amṛta-bīja*) on the palm of the left hand, one should place the palm of the right hand against it and show it toward the food offering; visualizing it as being flooded by the stream of nectar arising therefrom, one should sprinkle it with water over which the root mantra has been recited. Having meditated upon all of that as being of the nature of nectar, one should touch it, recite the root mantra eight times, display the *dhenu-mudrā*, worship it with water, fragrance, and flowers, and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the deity. Meditating that the radiance has emerged from the mouth of the deity, one should touch the principal vessel of the food offering with the thumb of the left hand. (From the *Śāradātilaka*)

Taking water with the right hand, one should recite the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and the following verse: "O Lord, together with Your attendants, I offer this excellent vessel containing consecrated food, consisting of various kinds of delicious edibles; please accept it. Having recited this verse, one should say: "I offer this *naivedya* (food offering) to the Lord, along with His limbs (*sāṅga*) and retinue (*saparivāra*); obeisance! Then, casting the water away, one should display the *naivedya-mudrā*.
Next, having sprinkled the *naivedya* vessel three times with both hands holding flowers, one should recite: "I offer this to You; O Hari, may You graciously enjoy this oblation (*juṣāṇedaṃ haviḥ*)."
In place of the word *hare* therein, the name of each respective deity should be substituted, as they have said:

"Having consecrated it with the *ari-mudrā* appropriate for the [mantra], dried it with water from the northwest (vāyavya), burned it with the fire of the right hand, and then filled it with the nectar of the left hand, one should consecrate it with the mantra-nectar and recite the mantra while touching it. Having recited the mantra eight times, one should worship it, made complete by the *surabhi-mudrā*, with perfumes and other offerings."

Then one should worship Hari with palms joined in *añjali* as he approaches; as he departs, one should radiate light. Reciting the root mantra ending with "svāhā" (as in *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃphaṭ*, or *namas*), one should then pour water and offer that oblation (*havis*) which is of the nature of nectar, lifting it up with both arms along with flowers. This is the mantra for the offering of the oblation (*nivedya-arpaṇa-mantra*), used by one’s own name in all forms of worship. Thereafter, showing the *grāsa-mudrā* with the left hand and the *prāṇa*-mudrās and so forth with the right hand, one should mutter the mantras beginning with "To Prāṇa, svāhā," and so on.

As they say: "Displaying with the left hand the *grāsamudrā*, which resembles a blooming lotus, one should display the *prāṇa* and other [vital winds] with the right hand. One should touch the two fingers, the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*) and the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*), with the tips of one's own thumbs; this is the first *mudrā*. Likewise, another is formed by the index finger (*tarjanī*) and middle finger (*madhyamā*). Then, the middle finger and ring finger together form the next. The fourth consists of the ring finger, index finger, and middle finger, along with the little finger."

Likewise, the five mudrās taught here—Prāṇa and the rest—are joined with their own respective mantras. When joined with the fourth vowel [I] in sequence, these mantras of the path of Kṛṣṇa are Tārā, Dhārā, Vadhvā, and Cedā.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the mudrās for the offerings such as flowers are as follows: the thumb is joined for the flower, and the index finger for the incense.
The middle finger is proclaimed for the lamp, and the ring finger for the food offering (*naivedya*). Through the joining of the other fingers, the five *mudrās* are proclaimed.

These same *mudrās* should be displayed even when the perfumes and other offerings are presented. Whatever is performed with a *mudrā*, that yields inexhaustible fruit for whomsoever [it is done]. Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Regarding the phrase "therein":
the Supreme Gurus maintain that one should wash one's own hands after offering handfuls of flowers and water at intervals between the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Now, the specific detail mentioned in another Tantra is being written down.

Worship is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is without remains (anirmālya) and that which is with remains (sanirmālya). Worship without remains consists of divine substances born of the mind, such as perfumes, flowers, garlands, and the like; it bestows both celestial enjoyments and liberation. Worship with remains is that which is properly performed by devotees using delightful sacrificial materials produced from villages, forests, and other sources.

In that regard, the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā* states the nature of *nirmālya*: "Flowers as soon as they are born are by their very nature already 'smelled' (used) by the five great elements, by the sun, by the moon, and likewise by living beings such as bees and other insects; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, they are called *nirmālya*."

If it is argued that [the sacrifice] is devoid of flesh, one might wonder how the fruit [of the rite] could be obtained by this means; anticipating this doubt, it is stated in that very same [text]: "Just as fruit is produced from a cluster of flowers, but not so [directly] from the mind, therefore—because it is unavoidable, because otherwise there would be no means, and because of the limited intellect of men—the ritual action must be performed with external flowers."

Furthermore, worship is considered to be threefold—superior, inferior, and middling—and it is divided again into a hundred ways according to the qualifications and the specific circumstances. Worship performed with all the ritual implements for sacrifice is considered superior; worship accomplished with whatever materials are available and perceived [at hand] is middling; and worship accomplished with leaves, flowers, and water is designated as inferior.
The worship performed by stainless Brahman-sages who have understood the entire meaning of the Vedas is Sāttvic; it bestows liberation.
The worship that is properly performed by royal sages established in austerity and knowers of the Lord’s true nature is Rājasic; it bestows happiness.
The worship that is performed constantly by devotees such as women, children, the elderly, and the ignorant, whose minds are limited, is proclaimed as Tāmasic.

Furthermore, it is divided into five types: the afflicted, the postpartum (sautakī), the terrified, the ignorant (daurbodhikī), and the one lacking the means for practice. If a disease extending even to fasting is observed in oneself, then, according to the Śāradātilaka, worship should not be performed on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or upon images.

One should not perform bathing, nor the use of a tooth-stick, nor even the fire-oblation (homa). Having gazed upon the solar disc or a [divine] image, and having repeatedly recited the root mantra, one should cast forth a flower along with unbroken grains of rice. Whether exhausted by extremely fierce diseases or worn out by fasts, or even by one's own ritual commitments, one should complete what is to be done by oneself. Then, having bathed and worshipped the deity, the fires, the gurus, and the Brahmins.

"By your grace, let there be no fault in me for this worship having been interrupted for so long"—having prayed thus, one should perform the rite again as before. Now, I shall describe the worship for one in a state of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), as enjoined by the scriptures: having bathed and performed the daily obligatory rites (*nitya*) through mental action, one should worship according to the procedure for external worship, employing the appropriate placement (*sthāna-yoga*). Whether there is a specific desire or no desire, one should always perform it as previously described.

The worship for those who are fearful is now described, exactly as enjoined by the Āgamas. Whether obtained or unobtained, the implements such as the vessel for the *arghya* offering should be used with water for the worship; however, if even water is not available, one may worship the Deity with flowers of meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*). I shall now describe the "worship for the dull-witted" (*daurbodhikī*) as enjoined by the Āgamas. Those who are considered dull-witted include fools, women, children, the elderly, and others.
For them, the worship of the Jewel-Pavilion, the four [inner] elements beginning with Dharma, the serpent, and the lotus, as well as the primary forms and their limbs, is prescribed.

It has been stated that for all others as well, [the rite] is prescribed in brief form during the performance of the ritual. Indeed, Nārada said: "In the absence of all the materials for the services, purity through mental visualization alone is sufficient; it is not by means of water," thus he spoke.
Regarding one who is unable to perform worship: "If one is unable to propitiate [the deity], one should give the means for worship;
if one is not able to give at all, one should at least look upon the worship. He who does not possess even a single [article] goes downward indeed, and not otherwise.
But the wise person who, with devotion and effort, having personally procured everything, performs the worship with the requisite means, shall obtain the complete fruit."
The fourth chapter:
One should also worship the enclosures, beginning with the limbs (aṅga) and ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla).
On the filaments, starting from the southeast corner, one should worship the heart-mantra and the others. || 110 ||
In this manner, the deities of the limbs should be meditated upon in the front and the various directions,
possessing rays that are white as frost, crystal-like, dark, blue, black, and reddish.
He who worships according to the rules with devotion and with materials brought from others shall obtain only a portion of the fruit of worship, but not the complete fruit.
Thus [ends verse 108]. It was stated that one should worship the limbs and so forth again;

therein, since the two [phases] at the beginning and the end are general, he summarizes once more in order to explain the visualization, the location, and the application for those two, as well as to clarify the meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "the limbs and so forth," since the occasion for worship has already been mentioned previously, he will therefore say: "Having thus worshipped according to the rule, ending with the food offering.
That [worship] in which the limbs, the eight limbs, and so forth come first.
"At the end, that which consists of the eight world-protectors" (*lokapālāṣṭatiḥ ante*) is an adverbial modifier meaning "from the limbs (*aṅga*) up to the world-protectors.
It should be understood that by the word "world-protector" (*lokapāla*), the inclusion of their weapons and retinues is intended.
And this [instruction] is intended as a possibility, since it is seen to be so in many instances; it is not a strict rule.
Because of the word "api" (also), the phrase "one should offer water at intervals" is to be supplied here as well.
He states the worship-place common to all for the worship of the limbs: "In the filaments," etc.
By the word "beginning with the southeast" (*agnikoṇādi*), the southwest, northwest, and northeast corners are intended.

As it has been said: "One should worship the limbs, beginning with the heart and ending with the armor, starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast; one should worship the eye-mantra in front, and again the [other] mantras in the directions on the outside."

Elsewhere it is also stated: "In the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Śiva, [the mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Varma [are placed]," while others explain them as being in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Nirṛti, and Vāyu.
As they say: "Having visualized [the deity], one should worship the heart in the southeast (āgneyī), the head in the northeast (aiśānī);

the crest-lock (śikhā) is to be worshipped in the southwest (nairṛtī), and one should worship the armor (kavaca) in the northwest (vāyavī). Having worshipped the eye in front, one should then worship the weapon in the [remaining] direction."
Elsewhere it is also stated: "The worship of the limbs beginning with the center, such as Āgneya, Āsura, Vāyavya, and Madhya;
and the determination [of this] is according to the teacher's instruction."

Here, the directions beginning with Āgneya (southeast) are in reference to the previously established front direction, and not according to their conventional [cosmological] sense. || 110 || Regarding "the eye at the tip," this refers to the front of the deity within the pericarp; in the worship of the mantras beginning with the head, it should be understood that they end with *namaḥ*, whereas in the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the heart-mantras and others, they end with *svāhā*.
In the first and second [sections], there is no application of that [term] precisely because they are already endowed with that genus;
this point is established by the very nature of the subject matter (*adhikaraṇasiddha*).

For instance, in the section beginning with "In a mantra, the status of being a supplement to its own sentence may arise from the instruction of a quality," regarding the *svāhākāra* and *vaṣaṭkāra*, the *Śāradātilaka* states:
The eight principal female deities, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as described in the ritual manuals, should be worshipped in succession thereafter;
finally, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their primary retinues.
[One offers] to the deities in the directions starting from the east in sequence, endowed with their respective weapons, classes, and lords.

Regarding the rule that one gives oblation to the gods ending with the word *svāhā*, which is prescribed as a general rule, there is no subsequent sublation (*bādha*) in mantras such as "To the Earth, svāhā! or "To the Atmosphere, svāhā!"—unlike the case of the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses where there is a specific restatement (*upasaṃhāra*)—and thus it remains established that there is no sublation in other mantras. Padmapādācārya states: "Women are the bodies of the principal [deities]; [the mantra] consists of fifteen words."
And it has been said: "The deities of the limbs, who bear the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness and have the forms of women, are to be worshipped.
Regarding the positions of those mentioned as the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), he says: "behind," and so forth.
"Subsequently" means immediately after the ritual circumambulation of the limbs (*aṅgāvṛti*);

this too is a general rule (*prāyika*), because there are cases where it occurs even prior to that, according to the established tradition (*satsampradāya*). || 112 || And from the authoritative tradition.

The term "end" (*anta*) refers to the outer square, because it was previously stated that the enclosure ends there; and this interpretation is supported by the fact that it is seen thus in the *Vaihāyasa-mantrakośa* and the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*.
The connection is that one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Indra and Agni, in the directions starting from the east and proceeding in order until the end;
in this regard, since the general formula "Obeisance to Indra" (*indrāya namaḥ*) and so forth would otherwise apply, he states the specific rule beginning with the word "root" (*mūla*).
The word "ante" (at the end) is also connected here;
therefore, the meaning is that this word must indeed be placed at the very end of everything,
and this will become clear in the written formulation of the practice.
The meaning of the phrase "accompanied by their primary retinues" (*mūlapāriṣadānvitān*) is as follows:

when there is worship of Indra and the others during the enclosure of the Śaktis, then it should be understood that "to each of the Śakti-retinues" is an epithet for both the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) such as Indra and the others, as well as [the attendants] such as Vañca.
Likewise, in the worship of Śiva, [the phrase applies] as "to each of the Śiva-retinues."
Thus, in the worship of Gaṇeśa, for each [offering], one says "to the attendants of Gaṇeśa" (gaṇeśapāriṣadāya);

likewise, in the worship of Sūrya, for each, one says "to the attendants of Sūrya" (sūryapāriṣadāya); and likewise, in the worship of Viṣṇu, for each, one says "to the attendants of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇupāriṣadāya).
The transposition of the feet was made for the purpose of concealment;
here too, the word "end" (anta) is connected with "because" (hetoḥ),
meaning that [the transposition occurs] at the end of the verse beginning with "indrāya."
In this case as well, in the formal application (*prayoga*), the birth-giving lords (*jātyadhipānām*) are uttered first and the weapons (*hetīnām*) afterwards;
however, in the root text (*mūla*), the word *heti* is placed first because it consists of fewer syllables. *Hetayaḥ* means weapons (*āyudhāni*).

It should also be understood that the classes [of beings] consist of the worlds of gods, radiant beings (*suratejas*), pretas, rakshasas, water-beings, living beings, stars, spirits (*bhūta*), and nagas, together with their vehicles and retinues.
As for the vehicles, they are: Airāvata, elephant, goat, buffalo, man, crocodile, deer, horse, bull, chariot, and swan.

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "The [deities], beginning with the caste (jāti), the presiding lord (adhipa), the weapon (heti), the vehicle (vāhana), and ending with the retinue (parivāra), should be worshipped in sequence.
And he himself will say in the Nityā-mantra: "At the end, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapāla) together with their vehicles and weapons."
Thus ends the fourth chapter:
[Salutation to] Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Vidhu.
[He meditates on] Īśāna, the lord of serpents, below, and Pitāmaha above;
[the colors are] yellow, red, white, smoke-colored, white, smoke-colored, and both white.
These are proclaimed in order by color as fair (gaura) and ruddy (aruṇa);
it should be understood that they are accompanied by their Śaktis.

Thus it is said in the *Vaihāyasa-mantrakośa*: "One should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) upon the terrestrial mandala, together with their weapons, powers, vehicles, and attendants, using sandalwood, flowers, and incense; that mantra [is for] one's own desired aim."
It should also be understood that [the mantras] arise from their respective seed-syllables (bījas), which are:
Laṃ, Raṃ, Maṃ, Caṃ, Baṃ, Yaṃ, Śaṃ, Haṃ, Naṃ, Kaṃ.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "The third [syllable] follows the direct order (anuloma), while the second is in reverse order (viloma)."

The fourth [syllable] is by the forward order of *pha*, and the eighth by the forward order of *ra*. The third is by the reverse order of *pa*, and the third from the reverse order of *la* is the third. The fourth and seventh syllables are established by the forward order of *ra*.
The fourth [syllable] is in direct order (anuloma), and the third is in reverse order (viloma);
all of that is indeed differentiated by the vowel preceding the penultimate letter and by its own name.
This seed-syllable (bīja) is stated in regular sequence, beginning with Vāsava (the letter *ka*) and ending with Brahmā (the letter *ha*).
Thus, some say these are the long vowels,
while others say they are the seed-syllables of the noose of Māyā belonging to Ananta and Brahmā.
As it has been said: "The [deities] beginning with Earth, Fire, Wind, and ending with Varuṇa, Anila, and Īśvara,
joined with Ananta and Bindu, are to be worshipped with the noose of Māyā."

In that regard, [the sequence] beginning with "Raca" refers to Nirṛti, Pavana (Vāyu), Vidhu (Soma), Pannagādhīśa (Ananta), and Pitāmaha (Brahmā); these are to be placed in the directions starting from the east in order,
where the well-known directions beginning with the east are to be understood.
As it has been said: "One of pure intellect should worship [the deities] in their respective directions, together with their retinues consisting of their own classes, Adhokṣaja, and their weapons.
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "And Indra and the others in their own directions..."
Thus, the author of the text also states: "One should worship the world-protectors, such as Indra and the others, in their respective directions."
There, in the eight directions, eight [deities] are to be worshipped:
Ananta between Nirṛti and Varuṇa,
and Brahmā between Indra and Īśāna.

As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "One should worship Viṣṇu in the southwest (Nairṛti) and Brahmā in the northeast (Īśvara), outside the lotus; one should also worship the weapons, beginning with the discus and ending with the goad, in their well-known forms in the directions of the world-protectors in due order."
Thus [ends] the Śāradātilaka; [he should visualize] the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, and the mace.
One should know that their weapons, in order, are the trident, the discus, and the lotus.

They are proclaimed to have the colors of yellow, white, bright, sky-blue, lightning-red, white, black, and the luster of a *karavinda* flower and pale pink (*pāṭala*), beginning with the thunderbolt and the others.

Having thus performed the worship according to the rules up to the offering of food (naivedya), the wise preceptor should then prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south, kindle the fire there,
perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) according to the rules, and carry out the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
There, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings the deity whose form has been described, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows:
*Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to Indra, lord of the gods, together with his weapons, his vehicle, his retinue, and his power, the attendant of Viṣṇu.*

Thus, in the worship of these [deities]—beginning with "Oṃ Raṃ, to Agni, Lord of Radiance" (tejo'dhipati)—the mudrās of the World-Protectors (lokapāla) should be displayed. As they say: "With the bases of the hands well-joined and all the fingers extended, this is the mudrā of the World-Protectors; one should display it during their worship."
"Thus [is] the thunderbolt," thus [is] the sword, the blade.
The sky is not blue in color;
"karavinda" refers to a tree consisting mostly of blue flowers,
meaning it has the color of those flowers.
As it has been stated by the teachers: "Having the color of a red lotus," the application therein is as follows:
*Oṃ, salutation to the retinue of Viṣṇu, who is adorned with a crown of *vacā* flowers, who possesses weapons, vehicles, attendants, and powers*—and so forth, which should be inferred accordingly.

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "The images [should be visualized] externally, adorned with their own beautiful crowns, their lotus-hands raised holding their respective weapons and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Thus, from the preparation of the form with the root mantra up to the offering of food (nivedya), the procedure is the same even for the daily worship (nityapūjā).

By the phrase "the wise one, having consecrated according to rule," it is stated that the four purificatory rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*, the purifications of the clarified butter (*ghṛta-saṃskāra*), and the purificatory rites for the fire beginning with *garbhādhāna*—performed in the sequence of offerings of clarified butter—must be performed.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Having offered oblations with the *Tāra* (Oṃ), the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the root mantra, the knower of mantras [proceeds].
Having offered twenty-five oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should worship her again with perfumes and other offerings; then,
having joined her to the mercury situated upon the pedestal, one should dismiss the Vajrī.

One should scatter the remaining oblation as a *bali* offering all around for the attendants (*pārṣada*) of the deity, accompanied by fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Then, having set aside the food offering (*nivedya*) and purified it, one should offer water once again.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should present the fly-whisk and the chowrie,
and offer betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor;
then, with undistracted mind, one should recite the root mantra one thousand times.
Having recited that [mantra] for the sake of all prosperity, one should offer it to the deity;
by the word "tataḥ" (then), this is what is meant:
one should give water for the sake of the *pādma* [rite].
At the end of the root mantra, the verse is as follows: "O Lord of all gods, supreme bringer of satisfaction to all, filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water. Thus.
Then, having offered the remnants of the food and water and withdrawn the splendor (*tejas*) from the mouth of the deity, one should give a portion of the *naivedya* to Viśvakarman and others;

as it has been said: "From the primary vessel, one should take out a portion of the *naivedya* from the northeast for the Supreme Being, the highest *parameṣṭhin*, who is the embodiment of all the gods."
One should offer salutations to Śrīrāma, to Viśvasena who is joined with an army,
and to Gaṇeśa Vakratuṇḍa; one should offer [oblations] to Sūrya Caṇḍāṃśu,
to Ucchiṣṭicāṇḍā among the Śaktis, and to Caṇḍeśvara in the case of Śiva.
Thus, in the phrase "to the attendants of the deity" (*devatāyāḥ pārṣadebhyaḥ*), these very [attendants] are also understood by the word *pāriṣada*; furthermore,
in the expression "for the sake of the complete perfection of the deity" (*sarvasampattyai devatāyai*), there are two fourth-case endings in a non-co-referential construction (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Regarding the instruction "one should offer":
here, in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), having offered betel, an umbrella, a mirror, and chowries— according to the *Śāradātilaka*—
"the intellect together with its latent impressions is fashioned as the mirror, and [the auspicious signs] are the auspicious objects."

Your manifold mental fluctuations have been fashioned by me into the form of a dance; the sounds have become songs, and the various types of vocal and instrumental music have taken shape. O Lord, the nine umbrellas have been fashioned by me as lotuses.
The *suṣumṇā* nerve is in the form of the banner, while the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others are in the form of chowries;
the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the elephant, and speed is fashioned as the chariot.
The senses are in the form of horses; sound and the other objects are the path of the chariot;
the mind is in the form of the reins; the intellect is in the form of the charioteer;
and everything else is likewise fashioned as your various implements.

Having recited these verses and having chanted the root mantra according to one's ability, [one should say]: "O You who protect that which is most secret among secrets, accept this recitation from us!
O Lord, may success be mine through Your grace, for You abide within me."
By this [verse], one should offer that recitation (*japa*) to the deity.

As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having recited the mantra-verse, one should offer it to Śambhu with water for the *arghya* offering from the root mantra, poured into the hand with the right hand."
Thus it is said.
Then, having offered the center facing away [from oneself], one should worship Śaṣva.
As it is stated in the *Manvatantraprakāśa*: "The wise one, being capable, should indeed worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, just like a god."
Thus it is said elsewhere: "O best of Brahmins, whatever holy places exist in the three worlds abide within Vāsudeva; therefore, one should always worship Śeṣa."

Thereafter, one should perform circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). Regarding this, there is a specific rule in another Tantra: "One should offer one circumambulation to Caṇḍī; seven to the Sun; three to Vināyaka; four to Keśava; and five circumambulations to Śiva."
Thus.
Then, having offered praise and performed prostration, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).

In this regard, there is a specific rule in another Tantra: "Whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done by the mind, by speech, by the two hands, by the feet, by the belly, and by the organ—may all that become an offering to Brahman, *svāhā*."

"I offer myself and everything belonging to me to Hari; Om Tat Sat"—with this mantra of *brahmārpaṇa*, having offered oneself, one should dissolve the Deity into the lotus of one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*; this is the specific procedure.
The definition of the *saṃhāramudrā* has already been stated.
Upon accepting the grace (*prasāda*), the devotee of each respective deity must indeed accept the grace of that particular deity.
In the worship of the secondary deities (*paccadevatā*), however, [the purification] occurs through the touch of a *śālagrāma* stone of Viṣṇu himself and by other means as well.
This is the fourth chapter.
Then, in the direction of Śambhu (the North-East), the preceptor should scatter the previously collected offerings.
Having placed a water-filled jar adorned with gold, cloth, and other ornaments,
one should [visualize] her seated upon it, mounted on a lion, and holding a sword and a shield.
One should worship the weapon-deity (astradevatā) of the western face, who has a terrible form;
having worshipped her with the moving seat (calāsana), the Guru should take her up once again.
Saying "Protect! to the world-protectors with water released from the mouth of the vessel, he should circumambulate the interior while making the command of the gods heard.
Having recited the Astra-mantra, one should install it as before;
then, having worshipped the Astra once more with perfumes and other offerings, it should be placed upon its firm seat.
126. Then, having purified the two curved vessels with cow's urine, one should cook the *caru* in a new vessel made of copper or another material, which has been cleansed with the *astra-mantra*.
And likewise, the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa* states: "The offering made to Viṣṇu is remembered as *pavitra* (purifying) by the gods, Siddhas, and sages.
Having eaten the food offering of another deity, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Leaves, flowers, fruits, and water that are unfit to be taken—
by the touch of a Śālagrāma stone, all of them attain purity.
Thus it is said:
"If, due to distraction or perhaps through ignorance, an interruption occurs during the recitation, fire-offering, or worship, then one should again perform the six-limbed ritual placement (nyāsa)."
Thus [it is said].
"In the direction of Śambhu" means in the northeast (aiśānī).
A *karkarī* is a water-vessel with a spout.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that one should worship the weapon-deity (*astradevatā*) who is of such a nature.
"With a moving seat" means with a raised seat.
Regarding the word "that":

the Guru, taking that water-jar (*karkarī*), while proclaiming the divine command—"Protect the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with the water released from its mouth"—should circumambulate the inner altar within the pavilion clockwise and place it there as before; this is the connection. There, in that jar...
The meaning is that he is seated upon a firm seat, that is, an immovable seat.

Regarding "tataḥ" (then): "when the fire has been consecrated by the teacher in his own *kuṇḍa*" means that since the rite for generating the fire (*agnijanana*) which is to be described in the subsequent chapter has already been performed by the teacher at this very time, there is a reference back to it with the words "when the fire has been consecrated."
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra* and the *Śāradātilaka*:

"Having consecrated fifteen handfuls (*prasṛti*) of rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety with the root mantra, one should cast them [into the fire] and perform the recitation for the propitiation of the horse."
Having washed his face and covered it with the *kavaca* mantra,
the preeminent teacher, facing east, should cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the root mantra.
When [the deity] has been thoroughly cleansed with clarified butter and *suṣeṇa*, one should offer the "hot aspersion" (*taptābhighāraṇa*);
afterwards, one should cause [the deity] to descend with the *mūla-mantra* and bring it down with the *kavaca-mantra*.
In a mandala that has not been consecrated with mantras and is strewn with kusha grass, the Guru, according to the ritual procedure,
should divide it into three parts and assign one part to the deity.
134. The preceptor himself should then offer oblations into the blind fire;
he should then eat together with the disciple, having performed the prescribed sipping of water (ācamana).
Having sprinkled water over the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and established the fire therein,
one should then duly worship the deity, beginning with the rite of placing the fuel sticks (anvādhāna).
Having added a handful of rice grains to that milk, one should cook the caru oblation.
Thus [it is said].

Nārāyaṇa also states: "There, having accumulated the necessary materials and having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the scattering of rice and other acts with the root-mantra, the head-mantra, the limb-mantras, and the vidyā-mantras."
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru), one should cook it in milk and then divide it into three parts.
After offering the supreme portion as an oblation, the Guru, together with his disciples, should consume the other portion.
Thus [it is said].
130 || "Rice grains" (taṇḍulān): the ellipsis is "measured by fifteen handfuls.
The connection is that the rice grains were thrown while reciting the Astra-mantra.

The characteristic of the *prasṛti* (ladleful) will be stated [later]. Regarding the phrase "with the *sruva*": the connection is that once the *caru* has been prepared, one should offer the sprinkling of heated clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the root mantra.
By the expression "the Guru according to rule," it is stated that an equal division [of the materials] should be performed using *kuśa* grass together with the root mantra.
133 || 134 || Regarding the word "andha" (oblation):
by the statement "in the fire," meaning the teacher should offer oblations into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), this is what is meant.

Furthermore, the oblation mentioned as being performed twenty-five times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) in the subsequent chapter—according to the rule "with *sāttvika* [food] and likewise with *caru*"—should be understood here as well.

"One should eat. In this regard, there is a specific rule stated by Somaśambhu: "The third part of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be measured as three morsels, or it may be eight morsels in size; [it should be consumed] while avoiding looking at or touching it."
The Fourth Chapter.

Having brought the disciple who has sipped water and performed the ritual identification (*sakalīkṛta*), the Preceptor [should provide] a staff (*daṇḍa*) made from trees such as *kṣaura* and others, measuring the height of a palm tree (*tāla*), over which [the mantra] has been recited one hundred times.
Then he should give a tooth-stick to the disciple who is self-restrained;
having cleansed his teeth, the disciple should then rinse it and discard it.
For liberation, [one should eat] from a vessel made of *pālāśa* leaves; for enjoyment, [one should eat] from a leaf of the *pippala* tree.
One should cause [the guest] to eat with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and cause them to sip pure water with the mantra.
Thus [it is said].
135 || Regarding "sakalīkṛtya," it means having applied the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to its limbs.
Regarding "tāla": *tāla* is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the middle finger of an outstretched hand.
As it has been said: "The wise declare that the distance between the tips of the thumb and the middle finger when the hand is extended is one *tāla*."
Thus it is said.
By the phrase "the preceptor should give," the mantra for the gift is stated.
As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "One should offer [the gift] with the syllables *māyā*, *daṇḍin*, and *ṭhahaṃ*, and with that [mantra]."
Thus [it is said].
After the dismissal (*visarjana*), that which is beyond perception (*parokṣā*) should be performed; this is what is expressed by the word "one should dismiss" (*visarjayet*).
Having washed it, one should cast it upon the ground with the left hand from the left side.

Thus [it is said]. There is a specific rule in the *Prayogasāra*, as follows in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra* a tooth-stick made of *ūrīṣṭa*, *kṣāra*, or other such materials, one should clean the teeth, cut [the stick], rinse it, and then cast it into water."
In the directions starting from the east and ending with the nadir, its falling on the head results, respectively, in: increase, penance, death, wealth, loss, peace, illness, and money.
"It proclaims these fruits: happiness, prosperity, supreme suffering, and so forth;

likewise elsewhere—in separation from a beloved, untimely death, misfortune, ill health, or the onset of calamity—if the toothbrush falls with its tip facing downward, it indicates an inauspicious result through an oblation of sesame seeds at the root.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "Now, in this case, a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths in length should be given to the mango tree; its tip should be chewed by the teeth."

One should cast the face of the *ūṅgha* there into the mandala and determine the pedestal (*poṭha*). A fall toward the west, north, Rudra (north-east), or Indra (east) is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious.
"One should offer a hundred oblations into the fire to destroy ill omens.

Furthermore, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* it is said: "If that wind which has been exhaled is seen by the Guru, then the Guru, having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) according to rule and protected by the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*), should place him together with [the disciple] upon a bed of *darbha* grass on the altar. From the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The Guru, having performed the ritual rinsing according to rule and protected by the binding of the topknot, should place him together with [the disciple] upon a bed of *darbha* grass on the altar."
One should sleep upon that [seat] for that night; this is declared to be the consecration (adhivāsa). Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Śrī-Śāradātilaka.
[The thread should be laid] with its tip pointing east, north, west, or northeast; the auspicious [thread] is white, while the other is otherwise.

When that face of an inauspicious quarter appears, the Guru, for the sake of pacifying its defect, should recite the root mantra one hundred times, or half of that, or a quarter of that. Thus [it is said]. (136–137)

The connection is as follows: "having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule and having protected [the head] by binding the topknot (śikhābandha) according to rule. Regarding that, the procedure for the sipping of water has already been stated by me previously;
however, regarding the binding of the topknot, by the phrase "according to rule," this is what is meant:

The Guru should bind the topknot with the root mantra together with the crest-mantra (*śikhā-mantra*) of the same class, or with the Aghora-mantra and so forth; "he should lie down" means that on that altar, he should lie for that night upon a bed of *darbha* grass together with this disciple— such is the connection.
The term "on the altar" (*vedyām*) signifies proximity as the sense of the locative case;

this has been stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Then, having caused that disciple—who has sipped water and is protected by the tying of the topknot—to sit upon the altar, the Guru should sleep together with him on a bed of darbha grass."
By the word "guru," it is stated that the teacher should cause the disciple to lie down on his right side with his head toward the east;
for it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Relying upon the *māṇava* sleep, one should cause him to lie down with his head to the east."

In the *Somaśambhu*, however, it is said: "Householders, protected by the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), should be placed with their heads toward the east upon beds of *darbha* grass; ascetics (*yatis*) should be placed with their heads toward the south upon beds of *saṅgasma*.
Furthermore, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "On the right side of the deity, the pure disciple should be made to dwell [overnight] on a bed of *darbha* grass spread over a new, unwashed cloth."

Having consecrated it with mantras and meditating upon Śiva, the Guru should sleep at night with his head toward the east; then, using the tip of a thread tied to his topknot, he should [bind] the disciple's topknot.

Having caused [the deity] to enter and having covered him with a new cloth, one should surround him with three lines of ashes, sesame, and mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra; then, one should offer oblations to the lords of the directions outside of that. Thus it is said.

Regarding the *svapnamāṇava* mantra among the Vaiṣṇava mantras, as revealed in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: *oṃ haṃt sakalalokāya viṣṇave prabhaviṣṇave viśvāya viśvarūpāya svapnādhipataye namaḥ*. This is the fourth chapter.

"This is the Svapnamāṇava mantra as taught by Nārada and others. Thus it is stated in the Śaiva and Śākta traditions; however, in the Piṅgalāmata, it says: "The Tāra (Om), followed by 'hili' twice, then 'to the Trident-bearer,' and ending with the Dviṭha (Svāhā)—this is proclaimed by Śambhu as the Svapnamāṇava mantra. Thus [it is said].
The specific detail mentioned in another *Tantra* is as follows: "Homage to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;

homage to the Left-handed One (*Vāma*), who has the form of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Dreams! O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dream regarding all matters without exception; through your grace, O Great Lord, I shall accomplish the success of my undertakings. Having thus propitiated the God at the time of sleep with this mantra, one should go to sleep.
And in the morning, an examination of the dream must be performed;
as it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "In the morning, the Guru should ask the disciple about what was seen, whether auspicious or inauspicious, in the dream;
if it was auspicious, he should declare it to be auspicious for him, but if inauspicious, he should perform a hundred oblations."

"By means of the Astra-mantra," thus is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple taught in due order. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "If the moon is in a cruel sign, it is inferior; if it is invisible, it is middling; but if it is visible, it is most excellent.
And in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as well: "Having performed the worship of the Guru's feet, fasting and with senses subdued..."
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, one should report whatever dream is seen.
A maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, a river, an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a serpent, and a tree.
Having seen a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, liquor, spirits, and all such things as these, one shall attain success.
A Cāṇḍāla, a young camel, an artisan, an empty vessel, an inauspicious thing, a man smeared with oil, a naked man, parched grain, thorns, and a eunuch.
Having seen a palace or a *matala* tree, a person may fall ill;

likewise, having seen a bad dream, one may attain success through the performance of a *homa*. Thus, the "fasting" (*anopavāsa*) here refers to the prohibition of obtaining food out of passion, but it does not prohibit the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) prescribed by the scriptural injunctions.

Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Then, having risen in the morning and reflected upon a dream one has seen, one should recognize it as auspicious if it is auspicious, and suppress it if it is inauspicious," and so forth— thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
In the Nārāyaṇīya, however, it is said: "At dawn, the disciple should report the dreams he has observed to the guru; through auspicious ones there is success, and through others, devotion."
"Adhivāsa is declared to be performed on the day preceding the taking up of the mantra";
however, in the Piṅgalāmata, it is also stated that the adhivāsa may be performed immediately:
"Or else, one should perform the adhivāsa immediately according to the prescribed rule."
Thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "A wise man should not perform the rite of initiation on two days;
he should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) immediately if it is to take place on a single day."

The meaning of the word *adhivāsa* is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "When the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the verbal root *vas* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, this usage *adhivāsa* attains its established form."

"Or, staying together with the Guru and others at night according to the prescribed rules—this is indeed considered the meaning of the word *artha*, since it is held that particles (*nipāta*) possess multiple meanings. (138) Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, the commentary on the *Śrī Śāradātilaka* composed according to the authentic tradition. Om.
The Fifth Chapter: Thereafter, I shall describe the generation of the fire according to all the tantras,
duly performed in the preceptor’s sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) which has been consecrated according to the path of the scriptures.
There are eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as enjoined in the Tantras:
sprinkling with the root mantra, sprinkling with the [five] arrows is prescribed;
striking with those same [arrows], and sprinkling with the armor mantra is recorded.

The digging up and extraction [of the earth] is performed with the *astra-mantra*; the filling is done with the *hanman-mantra*. Leveling is performed with the *astra-mantra*, and the sprinkling is considered to be for the sake of the armor (*varma*). The pounding is done with the *hetiman-mantra*, and the cleansing of the armors is performed with the *varma-mantra*.
The application of ointment, the fashioning of the artistic forms, immediately thereafter the drawing of the three lines, and finally worship with the heart-mantra— this is considered the procedure.

(Verse 5) Regarding the rites such as the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be performed by the preceptor on the very day of the consecration (*adhivāsa*), following the worship of the weapon-deity (*astradevatā*), he says "then" (*tataḥ*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "In the consecrated *ācāryakuṇḍa*, according to the path of the scriptures and in accordance with all tantras, the generation of fire shall be described in the prescribed manner. || 1 ||
He states that very procedure [with the words] "eighteen," etc.
"With the arrow" means with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Here, in all instances, the weapon-mantra and others are to be understood as being placed before the mantra to be given.

Since it is stated at the outset that "sprinkling [is done] with the root mantra," some say it refers only to the *jāti-mantra*; and that is the traditional practice. Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed with the palm of the hand turned upward.
"One should sprinkle with the palm turned upwards," according to the sūtra. || 2 ||
*Abhyukṣaṇa* means sprinkling everywhere with water by means of a clenched fist.
*Uddhāra* is the filling of a dug-out pit with other earth. Sprinkling (*secanam*) is indeed the same as *abhyukṣaṇa*.
This is because, since the root meaning of the verb *abhī* follows its primary sense, it is stated that something may follow that [meaning]. ||3||
One seeks the cause by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
The phrase "by means of the *vam* mantra" is connected to each of the four [actions] that follow.
As it was stated by Somaśambhu: "The sweeping, the smearing, and the visualization of the form of the digits (*kalā*)."
The threefold encircling.
*Śāradātilakam*:

One should perform the purification of the site with the Astra-mantra; the clearing of the crossroads with auspicious *kuśa* grass using the Hana-mantra; and the breaking of the beads with the Tanutra-mantra.
In the sacrifice, one should consecrate the sacrificial pits with these aforementioned consecrations; or else, one should consecrate them with the four [rites] beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
One should draw three lines each, directed eastward and northward, with the heart mantra; the deities residing in the lines directed eastward are remembered as Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara.
For lines extending toward the north, [the proportions] are Brahma, Vaivasvata, and Indu; or else, one should draw there a triangle surrounded by a hexagon and an octagon.
Having sprinkled all [the items] with the *tāra* [mantra], one should then worship the Yoga-pīṭha,
as well as Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus.
"Vaccīkaraṇam" means the firm contemplation [of the self] as being like a goat.
"Catuṣpatham" means the making of four paths in the four directions from the center using *kuśa* grass.
"Tanutreṇa" means by means of the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).
Some say that *akṣapāṭana* means "the warding off of the senses. Others, however, maintain that *capāṭanāḥ* refers to *rākṣasa*s; thus, it is that in which no *kṣapāṭanā* (night-stalkers) exist.
The meaning is that one should effect the warding off of *rākṣasa*s by means of the sound *huṃ*.
But other traditionalists [explain] that *aṭa-paṭa* means "going," where "going" is knowledge; it is the piercing (*pāṭana*) or pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
He says "or else" with reference to those who are incapable [of this].
"Three":
one should draw three lines;
by this word "cows," the following is meant.
The lines with their tips pointing east are arranged facing north, and those with their tips pointing north are arranged facing east;
furthermore, according to tradition, all of them should measure one *prādeśa*.
This is stated in the *Sautrāmaṇitantra*: "One should draw [the lines] starting from the south, with the east in front and the north as the end."
"One should draw [the diagram] with its tip pointing upward, situated in the east, and beginning from the west;
having thus drawn three lines each, one should raise them up with the Vāgbhava [syllable].
Alternatively, one may draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon.

In this regard, some have not read the reading as "a hexagon, an octagon, and a triangle. That is a manifestation of ignorance. And so the teachers [state]: "Alternatively, by the instruction of the gurus, [one should draw] a hexagon, an octagon, and a triangle."

And likewise in the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, one should draw an eight-petaled [lotus] within a hexagon, and here [within that], a triangle. Also elsewhere: "Having drawn lines from the center, [one forms] a hexagon and a triangle."
Thus [it is said]. || || ||
Regarding "all [these]":
having consecrated these with the *praṇava*, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha— consisting of Vāgīśa, the Yoga-pīṭha, Maṇḍūka, and so forth, up to the fifth layer—
together with Vāgīśvarī, using the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
Whether it be produced from sun-crystals and the like, or obtained from the house of a Vedic scholar who is a physician.
Having brought the fire in a vessel, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters;
then the preceptor should consecrate it according to the rule by means of inspection and other rites.

Having worshipped up to the ultimate reality (*paratattva*), and having worshipped the nine pot-shaktis as previously mentioned, one should worship the yoga-seat (*yogapīṭha*) with the mantra: *kroṃ vāgīśvarayoryogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Here, it should be understood that by the word "Tāra," the inclusion of the five *praṇavas* within their respective mantras is intended according to the context.
[The instruction] is "one should fully worship."
On the seat [of the disciple], one should worship Vāgīśī with the seed-syllable *Śakti*, and Vāgīśa with the mantra of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
This has been stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Vāgīśī with the *Śakti*-seed, and Vāgīśa by means of the *sādhya*-mantra.
It is also stated elsewhere: "That deity with the *sādhya*-mantra," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sūryakānta, etc.," fire produced from a fire-drill (*araṇi*) is included.
As it has been said: "Whether born from the sun-gem, from fire-sticks, or from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*). This refers to that which is born from the house of a Vedic scholar.
*Śrotriyatva* consists in being a student of the Vedas and performing their prescribed rites;
by this, the intended meaning is the possession of the sacred fires (*sāgnitva*).
As it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "Having forcibly brought fire from the house of one who has maintained the fires according to the rules, one should establish it here."
"By means of a vessel" refers to a vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) or similar materials;
"covered by another vessel," so say the teachers.
However, elsewhere it is said: "Either produced in the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), or even that which arises from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*)."

"Or even that produced from fire-drills (araṇi), cast into a vessel of gold or the like"—thus [it is said]. Also: "In another auspicious vessel, such as one of copper, covered by another vessel"—thus [it is said]. "One should perform the bringing of the fire in a shallow bowl (śarāva) or even in such [a vessel]"—thus [it is said]. Furthermore: "Having placed it in a vessel made of excellent gold, or in a copper vessel, or even in an earthen vessel, and having covered it, the one of pure and vast intellect"—thus [it is said].

As for the statement in the *Smṛtisāra*: "One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), a broken vessel, a potsherd (*kapāla*), or even on a firebrand (*ulmuka*); [to do so] brings about the danger of loss of health," the intent of this is that when a primary vessel is available, a shallow dish (*śarāva*) should not be accepted.
[Furthermore, one should] discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*).

It should be understood that [the offering] to Nairṛti is performed with the Astra mantra. As it has been said: "O Dear One, having taken up the fire with the Astra mantra and covered it with the Kavaca mantra, one should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) toward the southwest (nairṛtya) with the Astra mantra."
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Meditating on the unification of Mars with the gastric fire and the fire of the bindu,
one should then unite consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire within the sacrificial fire."

The practitioner, having consecrated it with the *tāra* mantra, rendered it nectar-like by means of the bow-mudrā; thereafter, he protected it with the weapon-mantra and enveloped it with the armor-mantra.
Then the preceptor, having circumambulated it three times while honoring it above the sacrificial pit,
should perform a circumambulation preceded by the loud recitation of the *tāra-mantra*.

Except for the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*), there is the abandonment of the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyādāṃśa*). As it has been said: "Having brought [the portion] with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should discard the flesh-eater’s portion in the southwest (Nairṛti).
One should abandon that flesh-eater’s portion, and thereafter purify it with the mantra and the weapon-mantra.
And: "The wise one should establish the divine portion (*devāṃśa*) in front with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*)."
By the phrase "according to rule," it is stated that sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and moistening (abhyukṣaṇa) should likewise be performed so that the fire remains as it was brought;
by the word "etc. in the phrase "by sprinkling etc.," the triad of purificatory rites (saṃskāra) is intended.
Regarding the word *audayya*:
the *bindu* is well-known as being the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*),
because it possesses the nature of both fire (*agni*) and the moon (*soma*).
The fire arising from that consists of the bindus;
others say it is the bindu at the center of the eyebrows. This belongs to Bhauma, the earthly one.
Of the wealthy Agni.
Regarding the word "by Tāra": the meaning of the term *tāra* is as previously explained.
The teachers maintain that "rendered into nectar" means by means of the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛta*).
As it has been said: "Then one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the seed-syllable of water accompanied by the bindu of fire.
[The word] "protected" refers to the binding of the directions (digbandha).
[The word] "clockwise" is connected with what precedes.
"Recitation of the Tāra mantra" means the recitation of the Tāra, which is the Praṇava mantra, the root mantra.
As it has been said: "The practitioner of mantra should first place him [the disciple] upon the Yoni, and afterwards the fire facing himself with the root mantra.
Here too, the meaning of the word *tāra* is as explained previously.
"Raṃ, obeisance to Vahnicaitanya"—thus say Padmapādācārya and others.
However, others maintain that by the word *tāra* (the syllable Om) one should utter *Hrīṃ*, and by the word *mantra* one should utter "Obeisance to Vahnicaitanya.
As it has been said: "Hūṃ, preceded by Vahni (Ra), Caitanya, ending with the fourth case (dative), followed by 'obeisance' (*namaḥ*)."

Having recited the mantra and subsequently raised that fire, the preceptor, kneeling with his knees on the ground, should circumambulate the upper part of the sacrificial pit three times in a clockwise direction, while remaining within the range of the womb of Vāgīśī.
"Having meditated upon it as the seed-syllable of Śiva (śivabīja), one should quickly cast the fire. Thus, according to the *Śivabījadhīti*,
this [is taught] in the Śaiva tradition.

Because it is stated thus in the Śaivatantra, he himself will say: "Having uttered 'cit piṅgalam hana daha paca yugmāni', [followed by] 'sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā', this is the mantra previously mentioned. (18)
I worship Agni, the blazing one, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations— pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in all directions.
One should conceive of him by the name Śivāgni as well.
Thus it is also stated in the Nārāyaṇīya: "Having generated the fire of Śiva."
Therefore, in the *Saṃhitā* it is said: "One should contemplate there the fire produced by the village-rite (*grāmyadharma*) between Lakṣmī, who is in her menses, and the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
For this very reason, the author of the present work will also state in general terms: "of the fire, the father."
And further on: "one should offer oblations in a Vaiṣṇava forest"— the analysis of this compound is "by him who has touched the surface of the earth with both knees."

In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, however, it is said: "Having uttered the seed-syllable of Fire (Raṃ), the reciter should place the fire upon his seat, either by way of the *yoni* [the perineum] or facing toward himself. (Verses 14, 15, 16).
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "ācamanādikam," the inclusion of the subsequent rites following the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is intended.
Because of this statement, [the phrase] "one should kindle" refers to that which is about to be described.

In this regard, there is a specific rule: one who is about to offer oblations or has already offered into the fire should not blow upon the fire with the hands, a winnowing basket, a *sruva* ladle, or similar implements, nor should one use a fan or the like. One should blow upon the fire only with the mouth, for it was born from the mouth.
As for the injunction "one should not [blow] on the fire with the mouth," that should be applied only to the case of ordinary, worldly fires. Thus [it is said]. 17.
In the mantra "citpiṅgalam," the accusative case is used because it functions as an object of sound; however, in the ritual application (*śabdakarmaṇi*), it is connected with the following words.

The meaning is that the mantra previously mentioned and indicated—the one consisting of the three pairs beginning with *hana*—is the mantra to be recited with this [following] mantra for the purpose of kindling.
In some places, however, the reading is *samudīrita* (uttered).
Here, one should display the *Jvālinī-mudrā* for the kindling of fire;
its characteristic definition is as follows—according to the *Śāradātilaka*:
One should worship the fire according to the rule with this mantra;
one should place the tongues of the fire-eater within one's own body,
[namely] in the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, everywhere.
The letters from *sa* to *ya*, joined with the lords of the half-moons (*va*, *bha*, *ra*, *ṛ*, *u*) and accompanied by the bindu,
are declared by the teachers to be the mantras of the seven tongues. Among them,
those tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities in their ritual applications.
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā are considered to be the Sāttvika [lines] in sacrificial rites.
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā, [are likewise].
Immediately after Lohitā are Śvetā, Dhūminī, Karālikā,
