Rājasyā, Rasanā, Viśvamūrtti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, and Manojavā; these tongues of fire have been ordained for rites performed for desired ends.

Having made the two wrists level and the hands with fingers extended, having joined the two middle fingers and placed the two thumbs between them— this is that supreme mudrā of Jvālinī for the rites of homa. || 18 || 18
One should place those [energies], which are exceedingly red and multiformed, in sequence upon the penis, anus, head, mouth, and eyes, and then upon all the limbs; thus it is said.

The letter *va* is *repha* (the letter *r*), and the half-portion *i* is the letter *u*; joined with these, the letters beginning with *sa* and ending with *ya*, and those beginning with *sa* and ending with *ya* in reverse order—these syllables, together with the *bindu*, constitute the mantras. ||20||21||
The term "of the Jinas" applies to all three types [of lingas];
therein, the application is as follows: "Obeisance to Hiraṇyāya" in the case of the *sūtra*, and so forth for the *liṅga* and others, [referring] to Agni, whose seed is auspicious (*kalyāṇaretas*).
The presiding deity said: "Amātye.

Here, the mention of the presiding deities of the Victors is for the purpose of their placement (*nyāsa*) in their respective locations; therefore, [the mantra begins with] "Homage to the gods" (*surebhyo namaḥ*) and so forth.
Others, however, say that the fifth is Lohitā, the sixth is named Karālā, and Kālī is said to belong to Tamas;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
The tongues of Kalyāṇaretas are equal in luster to the color of smokeless fire;
non-humans, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities of these seven tongues. || 27 ||
One should assign the limbs of Vānta to the body by the method already stated,
followed by Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa,
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara in sequence.
The six-limbed mantras have been declared, joined with their respective seed-syllables (jātis).
[The sequence begins] with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Gods, to Hiraṇyā," and so forth.

Furthermore, this is for the purpose of demonstrating that by visualizing each respective deity situated within the center of the tongue, the attainment of the fruit occurs when the specific rite is performed with the appropriate materials for each respective deity.

And likewise, the Teachers [state]: "One should offer oblations of *jihvās*, *vidaśas*, and so forth, for the completion of their respective tasks; those deities, consisting of the essence of the gods, shall grant the desired accomplishment.

Thus, in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*, specific substances are also mentioned: fuel-sticks (*edhāṃsi*), honey (*hiraṇyā*), sky-plant (*gaganā*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

The practitioner should offer barley into the Bahurūpā fire when it is red; into the Kṛṣṇā fire, he should offer parched grain (lāja); into the Suprabhā fire, he should offer groats (saktu); and into the Atiraktā fire, he should offer sesame seeds. Furthermore, into the Kanakā fire, the practitioner should always offer all substances in all rites. Thus it is said.

Regarding their ritual applications (*karmāṇi*) as well, it is stated in another tantra: "The fruits of these [goddesses] are proclaimed in sequence according to the distinction of the desired results:

the first is for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); Gaganā is considered for paralyzing (*stambhana*). Raktā is for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*); Kṛṣṇā is for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
Suprabhā is for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*); Suraktā is considered for eradication (*uccāṭana*)."
"Though she is one, she is indeed multiformed, bestowing the fruits of all desires"—thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "in the body," it refers to one's own body; the word "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is to be supplied as a complement.

Likewise, in what follows as well, the fact that the names beginning with Sahasrārcis end in the fourth case is established by tradition, according to what was stated previously in the preceding chapter.
"Salutation to the heart, Sahasrārcis," and so forth. 28.
The teacher, observing the vow of the stomach-fire, should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Śābdālika [mantra] above the urine and [other elements].
Even when voiding urine, one should face downward; however, the pelvic region should be directed upward,
and one should place the limbs in a clockwise direction, for if they move otherwise, there will be torment.
Jātavedas, having embraced this which is known as the seat (āsana),
there is another called Adhorajra, also known as Punarāvartana.
The various types of *tārā* (lunar mansions), as well as the two *dhruvas* and *devamukha*, are recorded [as follows]:
the first are the *rāma* (three), *muni* (seven), and so forth; the *khalu* (nine) are joined with the *yantṛ* (seven) and the *vaṅga* (six).
Having prepared the seat, one should contemplate the form of that seat as being liberated from the Khastika-bond, with two legs bent and two extended, glowing like the hibiscus flower.
He should lead [the deity] onto the lotus-seat with two verses;
he should carry the garland of matted locks with four verses;
and he should cause it to shine upon the girdle with the verses beginning "bhame bhame bhame."
The movement of the form occurs within fifty million *japā* flowers; among the five left [hands], it is pure.
Afterwards, [one should place] the waist and the sides on the right.
Thus, Tāra, Prabhava, at the end: *dhṛtiṃ padaṃ dhṛtiṃ padaṃ dhṛtiṃ padaṃ*; one should deposit that *dhṛti* of the watches (*yāmān*), which is universal in form (*viśvarūpā*).

One should perform the *homa* with the mantra "Hyāhlādam," and one should worship the steadfastness (*dhṛti*) of the *Nalnanā* during the *homa*; indeed, with this "Hyāhlādam" [mantra], one should offer salutations to that which is praised by the weapons of yoga.
In the ritual applications, having fashioned the seat with the mudrās and so forth for Vamadeva Jātavedas,

one should contemplate the reality of the vowels beginning with *a* (Manu) ending in *ra*, which is subtle above the six cakras; this is the support (*dhṛti*) of the Āmnāya, residing in the nose within the body.
Conceptual construction. || 33 ||
He speaks of meditation (dhyāna) with the words "radantā" and so forth.
The boon has been seen;
one should bestow it upon those to be meditated upon by means of the darkness of the laughter of Karāhā.
In this [practice], there is a compendium of compounds (*samāsaraḥ*) arising from the middle term, characterized by a throbbing joy joined with what is emitted from oneself.
In that [state] where the girdle of the union of the throbbing [energies] is marked by the *ājā* [syllable], one should worship the Fire within one's own heart.
The king is marked by the *ājā*. 34.
One should perform that through constant application; for instance, having gathered the fivefold group together in one place, if the object of meditation manifests clearly while remaining seated.
"It should shine forth as undivided by directions— east, west, above,
and below. Thus,
within this body, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is the wheel of the navel, clearly manifest with the cardinal directions and so forth.
Thus [ends the section]. 35.
The Fifth Chapter:
The most excellent Guru should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the directions, excluding the east;
having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, he should install the forms beginning with Brahmā within them.
One should meditate upon [the fire] and worship it in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, bring [the deities] here;
at the end of the word 'Lohitākṣa,' say 'accomplish all rites'."
The mantra beloved by the Fire-god is said to have the wife of Vahni as its limit.
One should worship the tongues, radiant with flames, in the middle and in all six corners;
one should worship the deities of the limbs upon the filaments according to the stated method.

By the phrase "O most excellent Guru," it is stated that the ritual strewing (paristaraṇa) and other rites must be performed even in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with only a single rim (*mekhalā*). As they say: "In a pit with one rim, O sharp-witted one, one should strew [the grass] below the rim; in a pit with two rims, above the second rim; and in a pit with three rims, one should place it upon the rim situated between them."
The syntactical connection is that one should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the directions starting from the east.
As for the enclosing sticks, they are described by Kātyāyana:
"He places the enclosing sticks—those used in the *āgnīdhra* [fire-altar], measuring one cubit (*bāhumātra*), made of *pālāśa*, *vaikaṅkata*, *kāśmarya*, or *vailva* wood."

Even on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the placing of the enclosures (*paridhi*) must necessarily be performed, because it has been stated that these are to be done "on the middle girdle" (*mekhalā*).
One should not think that because there is no girdle on a leveled mound, the spreading of grass and so forth should also not be performed;
for those [elements] are auxiliary to the installation of the fire (*agni-sthāpanāṅga*), not auxiliary to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍāṅga*).

However, when there is an expectation as to where the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth should be performed in the *kuṇḍa* with three girdles described by the author himself, it is stated that it should be done "in the middle girdle.
As they say: "Outside this, the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is provided with three enclosures, with *darbha* grass [spread] pointing eastward and northward."
Elsewhere also it is said: "Then, one should place three boundary-sticks (paridhi) outside the sand on the sacrificial mound. || 36 ||
"In the middle" means in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), which has been worshipped with the mantras beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Poṭha.

As it is stated in the *Sautrāmaṇitantra*: "The knower of the ritual procedure, having worshipped in sequence within the center of the pit with the mantras beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Padmāsana, [should worship] the powers of the seat (*āsana-śaktis*) one above the other."
"They are to be worshipped in sequence at the bases of the petals starting from the east, and in the center.
Thus [it is said]. He states the mantra for Agni as "vaiśvānara"; the wife of Vahni is Svāhā. || 37 || 38 ||
He describes the worship of the enclosure of the fire with the words "in the center.
By this, the fire-altar (*agnipīṭha*) consisting of a six-cornered pericarp and eight petals is indicated.
"Radiant with flames" refers to the visualization of the tongues of fire.
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "All tongues should be fully known as having the appearance of flames by their very nature.
— *Śāradātilaka*.
The particle *api* is displaced [in the verse].
The connection there is that one should worship the tongues both in the six corners and in the center.

Regarding this, those who know the tradition maintain that after worshipping the six tongues in the six corners—starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending at the northwest (Vāyu) corner according to the prescribed order—one should worship Bahurūpā in the center, exactly as she was installed.

This has been stated by Somaśambhu: "In the directions of Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, and Anila, Hiraṇyā and the others reside in the forest as the six tongues in due order; Bahurūpā, however, is in the center."
Also, in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Then one should worship the tongues in the center and in the six corners.
Hiraṇyā, having the luster of molten gold, is situated in the direction of Śūlapāṇi (the North-East). Gaganā, the color of cat's-eye (vaidūrya), is established in the eastern direction.
Raktā, resembling the rising sun, is situated in the direction of Agni (the South-East). Kṛṣṇā, resembling a dark blue cloud, is stationed in the direction of Nairṛti (the South-West)."
Suprabhā, with the luster of a ruby, is situated in the western direction; Atiraktā, with the brilliance of the Java flower, is situated in the northwestern direction;
and Bahurūpā, whose appearance corresponds to her name, is situated in the south and north. These flames are yellow in radiance and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus it is said.
Elsewhere it is also said: "In the six corners and in the center are the tongues; the limbs are on the filaments.
And in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "Hiraṇyā is in the northeast, and Kanakā is situated in the east."

The tongue in the southeast is red; that in the southwest is black; another is considered to be of excellent luster (*suprabhā*); that in the northwest is exceedingly red; and the one in the north is of a luster corresponding to its own name. The middle tongue is called *triśikhā* (three-crested), while the others are named *bahurūpā* (multiform). One crest of that [middle tongue] blazes toward the right, and the other toward the left. These are to be recited immediately after their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus it is said.

Some, who do not respect the order of recitation as it was heard, say that one should worship the six tongues as they were installed: first the central one, then [the others] in clockwise order starting from the northeast (īśāna) corner up to the northwest (vāyu) corner. Their intention is this: having worshipped whichever tongue is situated in the center for each respective rite, one should worship the others in the [other] directions starting from the northeast.
As it has been said: "Now, in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), that tongue named Hiraṇyā is praised; on earth, at the beginning of the ritual sequence..."

The one named Kanaka is intended for rites such as immobilization (stambhana); the Red one is indeed intended for rites such as inciting hatred (dveṣaṇa). The Black one is declared on earth for the rite of killing (māraṇa), while Suprabhā is [intended] for pacification (śānti) by the best of the wise.
Fifth Chapter.
One should worship the forms upon the petals, bearing the power (śakti) and the svastika.

Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the directions according to their prescribed characteristics. Afterwards, taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands, facing them downwards, the preceptor (*deśika*), having taken darbha grass, should heat them thoroughly in the fire.
"She is exceedingly red in the rite of eradication (uccāṭana).
Thus it is said;
however, according to those who know the tradition, this applies specifically to initiation (dīkṣā), because Bahurūpā bestows the fruits of all desires.
And it is said: "She always spreads auspicious things in the middle.

But in another tantra, other wise ones who have reached the further shore of the scriptures and possess pure intellects have declared: "The one of great splendor stands in the direction of Indra; the dark one in that of Yama, the Lord of Ancestors; and again, the golden one in that of Varuṇa."

"One should [place] Bahurūpikā in the west, the red [form] of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) in the north, Atiraktikā in the southeast, and Kanakā situated in the center of the sacrificial pit. Following this, the worship of the presiding deities (adhidevatās) should also be understood as taking place in these same locations,
according to the stated method— that is, as described in the previous chapter.
In that regard, the manner of worship is as follows:
"Homage to the heart, Sahasrārcis; Svāhā to the head, Svastipūrṇa; homage," and so forth. || 38 ||
"One should worship the forms" means according to how they were previously assigned.
Within this interval, the teachers beginning with Padmapādācārya also desire the eight Mothers and Bhairavas.

In some places there is an addition: "The Mothers are to be worshipped on the tips of the petals, along with the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga. These possess the characteristics mentioned [previously], their essential nature being as described in the preceding chapter. || 40 ||

Having spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward, one should place upon them the *praṇītā* vessel and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *ājya-sthālī* (clarified butter pot) and the *caru-sthālī* (porridge pot), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, two *kuśa* blades with their roots intact, five fuel sticks of *palāśa*, and other vessels mentioned previously. Having placed these pairs of vessels face down, they should be sprinkled with water using the root-mantra and the *pavitra* strainer, then turned face up. The *praṇītā* vessel is filled with water, into which the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are invoked; having added the *pavitra*, unhusked rice, and so forth, it is purified and established in the northern direction. A small amount of that water is placed in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and with that water—reciting either the *namaḥ* mantra or the root-mantra—all the materials intended for the oblation are sprinkled. Then, having invoked the *brahmā* priest with the words, "In this rite, you shall be the *brahmā*, overseeing what has been done and what remains to be done," and having honored him, he should be seated upon the *āsana*.
This is stated in the *Śāradātilaka-saṃhitā*:
"One should purify those [three]—the top, the middle, and the root—with them in due order;
having grasped them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the right. (42)

Having arranged the vessels according to the rules, even in sets of two, the knower of mantras should gaze upon them, cover them with a purifier, and turn them face upwards; then he should wash the vessel again, fill it with pure water,
place unhusked rice and a purifier within it, and having strained that [water], he should set it down.
In the northern direction, that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise;
then, having taken a little of the *praṇītā* water,
one should sprinkle the collection of materials for the sacrificial fire with those waters while reciting the root mantra.
Then, having invoked Brahmā, one should worship him with the root mantra;
in that context, sprinkling (avokṣaṇa) is performed by pouring water with the hand turned downwards.

Because of the injunction, "One should sprinkle [the offerings] with the hand turned downwards," it is stated elsewhere as well: Having spread *darbha* grass with tips facing north on the left, and having placed the vessels two by two above them—first with their faces downward and then turning them face upward—one should consecrate one of them with the *ham* mantra. Then, having sprinkled all the sacrificial materials (*havyajāta*) located on the left with water purified by mantras while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the sprinkling with the *kūrcaka* [grass-bundle].
Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward on his own left side,
he should place upon it vessels made of gold or other materials according to his means, turned face down, in the form of the moon.
Having turned the vessels upward, one should fill them with water and other substances;
then,
having strewn darbha grass on the left side with their tips pointing toward the direction of the beloved of Pulomā’s son (Indra).

Then the wise one should place all the vessels with their openings facing downward in the form of Indra; thereafter, the learned one, having filled one of those upturned vessels with water and having well-visualized the sacred waters (tīrthas) therein,
should sprinkle the collection of materials situated on the left side with kūrca-grass using the Hṛdaya mantra.
Thus he describes the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
"taking them" (*ādāya*) should be understood as taking them specifically at the two openings [of the mouth].
Since it is stated that "one should heat them while facing downwards," one should purify [them] with each of the right and left hands respectively.
The meaning of "in due order" (*yathākramāt*) is as follows:

with the roots of the *darbha* grasses one [cleans] its root, with the middle parts of the *darbha* grasses its middle, and with the tips of the *darbha* grasses its tip; this is done with the right hand.
"One should sprinkle" means with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
In the fifth chapter:
having again heated those two mantras, one should cast the darbha grasses into the fire and place them upon a bed of kuśa grass on one's right side.
Then, taking the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra);
having poured the clarified butter into it, one should purify it through the rites of inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth.
By the phrase "again thus," it is stated that the two hands, with palms facing downward, [should be placed] three times;
in this manner, one should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire— this constitutes the concluding rite (*pratipatti-karma*).

By means of the *mantra* [of the root syllable], one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) respectively at the base, middle, and tip;
it should be understood that by means of the *namas*-mantra, one should place *Śakti* in the *sruk* and *Śambhu* in the *sruva*.
In the Śaiva system, however, there is the triad of principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*).

As they say: "Having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, with their faces upward and downward respectively, one should heat them three times in the fire in succession and touch them with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass.
Having heated them again three times, one should cast the *kuśa* blades into the fire with their faces downward."

One should place the powers, beginning with Icchā, in sequence at the base, middle, and tip of the śakti; one should place Śakti in the sruk-ladle and Śambhu in the sruva-ladle, using the Heart-mantra.

In the Śaiva Āgama, however: Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, with their mouths facing upwards and downwards respectively, one should heat them three times over the fire in sequence and touch them with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass. Upon the sections of the *kuśa* grass, one should contemplate the nature of the Self (*ātman*), Knowledge (*vidyā*), and Śiva.

Having sequentially assigned the three principles (tattvas) with the mantras *hāṃ*, *hīṃ*, and *hūṃ* in order, one should assign Śakti to the *sruca* ladle and Śambhu to the *sruva* spoon. Having wrapped their necks with three threads, they are worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
Having placed those two [the *sruc* and *sruva*] upon the *kuśa* grasses to their own right— thus the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the *sruc* and *sruva* have been described.
The word "tāu" (those two) refers to the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; in all instances, the masculine gender should be understood according to the sequence of the recitation.
He describes the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*):

"With the water of the *astra*" means with the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*) over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited; the connection is that one should pour the clarified butter—which has been purified by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth—into that vessel known as the *ājyasthālī*.
In this context, other substances such as cow-products should be understood;
as it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Cow-butter is to be known as the best, buffalo-butter as middling, and goat-milk-derived [butter] as inferior; therefore, cow-product is praised."
For this very reason, the author of the work will state in various places: "with cow's ghee," "mixed with buffalo butter," and "anointed with sheep's ghee. || 44 ||
Having removed [the fire] from the Śāradātilaka [mandala], one should place the embers in the northwest with the heart-mantra;
this is designated as *tāpana* by the teachers who know the Tantras.

Having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter (*ājya*), the Guru should throw them into the fire while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*; this is the rite of purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
With a pair of blazing *darbha* blades and the armor-mantra,
he should offer clarified butter into the fire; this is declared to be the *darbha-abhidyotana* (illumination with *darbha*).
Having displayed blazing darbha grass with the Astra-mantra,
the Guru should cast them into the fire; this is considered the "illumination" (udyotana).
In the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāra) are to be known from the Śiva scriptures;
eight [are performed] with the vessel (sruk), the ladle (sruva), and the pure [fire].
Thus [ends the section].
Fifth Chapter:
Having taken the clarified butter and pushed back the embers, one should touch water in the fire with the thumb and ring finger, holding two blades of *darbha* grass a span (*prādeśa*) long.
One should purify the ghee with the Astra mantra while performing this purification;

The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti and the rest, are proclaimed as the path of kalās (kalādhvā). The path of principles (tattvādhvā) is divided in many ways according to the different Śaiva Āgamas.
There are thirty-six Śiva-tattvas, twenty-two Vaiṣṇava-tattvas,
and twenty-four Maitra-tattvas; furthermore, ten and seven tattvas are said to belong to Prakṛti and the soul in distress, respectively.
The Śaiva principles are said to be: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā; these five are indeed the pure (śuddha) principles.

Passion is the Puruṣa; these seven—pure and impure—are Nature (prakṛti):

the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), the mind (manas), the organs of knowledge, the organs of action, the five subtle elements (tanmātra), and the five gross elements (bhūta). These are the teachers.
These twenty-four are said to be impure in the Āgama;
furthermore, elsewhere it is stated: "The path of mantras (mantrādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) are according to the word;

From Śiva comes Śakti, from that Nāda, from that Indu, and Sadāśiva; from him Maheśvara arises, and from Maheśvara comes Śuddhavidyā.

The fifth chapter:
thus has the classification of the principles (tattvas) of the Śaivas been demonstrated here— the individual soul,
the vital breath, the intellect, the mind, and then the organs of knowledge and action.

The five subtle elements (tanmātras), the gross elements (bhūtas), the heart-lotus, the luminous energies (tejas), and Vāsudeva and the others— these are the principles (tattvas) of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The five elements, the subtle elements, the sense organs, and likewise the mind [constitute these principles].
The wise know that the womb-born intellect (*garbhī buddhiḥ*) and *pradhāna* are the *maitrāṇī*;
from that come the five digits (*kalāḥ*) beginning with *nivṛtti*, and then again the digit (*bindu*),
the resonance (*nāda*), the power (*śakti*), and Śiva preceded by *sadā*, as they know them to be beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Self-knowledge is Śiva, and subsequently Śiva is knowledge itself; furthermore,
all principles (tattvas) and the principles of the individual soul have been proclaimed as the path of principles (tattvādhvā) by those who know the various Āgamas.

The wise declare that the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) consists of the worlds; the sages say that the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*. The path of words (*padādhvan*) is the combination of phonemes, while the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) consists of the multitudes of mantras.
She is the sovereign power of speech (*vācāmīśvarī śaktiḥ*) belonging to the Trident-bearer known as Vīreśa.
She who unfolds as the Mother (Mātṛkā) in the form of phonemes (varṇa),

then, through her union with the Infinite (Ananta), brought forth Time (Kāla), Necessity (Niyati), and Limited Agency (Kalā); from Kalā [arose] Knowledge (Vidyā), and from Kalā [arose] Attachment (Rāga) and the Individual Soul (Puruṣa).
Thus, according to the *Śāradātilaka*,
the most excellent of gurus should purify these six paths in their proper sequence.
Then, the Guru should remember the child’s feet, navel, head, and crest-lock;

The path of words (*padādhvan*) consists of a collection of words that is undivided and inseparable from the non-dual;
it exists as the constituent parts of great mantras and secondary mantras. As the primary constituent, that path consists of five words.

the collections of mantras: the seven mantras consisting of *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*.

This is the method of purification at the crown aperture (*brahmarandhra*) of the head:

having recollected the path of *kalās* in the feet, and having placed the *kalās* beginning with one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*) upon the feet, the secret place, the heart, the right side, and the head, one subsequently performs the purification of the path of *kalās*.

Thus, having recollected the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) in reverse order and having projected those [principles] into the preceding locations, one subsequently performs the purification of the path of the principles.

Likewise, having recollected the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) at the navel and having projected the [mantras] beginning with their own seed-syllables (*svabīja*) into the immediately following locations, one subsequently performs its purification.

Some [teachers] say it is "by the sequence of the sacrifice of the self" (ātmayāgakramāt), meaning by the sequence of the sacrifice of the manifest expansion (prapañcayāga) which is not yet being described; however, the traditionalists (sāmpradāyika) maintain that "ātmayāga" refers to the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), and thus it means "by its sequence," namely by the sequence of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as taught therein.
In that regard, the fifth chapter concerns the withdrawal of the elements.

Then, having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the five-fold offerings, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the body of the child as prescribed by the respective mantra.

once the mandala is adorned, one should seat the disciple upon another [seat].
Since the creation of the elements has already been described, the syntactical connection is: "having withdrawn the body, [he] should produce it again immediately thereafter.

This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should cause the dissolution of the elements, beginning with earth, into their constituent qualities (*guṇāṃśa*), according to the proper method of withdrawal, so that they remain within the subtle body (*piṇḍa*)."
"Then, one should contemplate the *piṇḍa* (the body) precisely according to the reverse order.

"One should personally consecrate the disciple, who follows the path of the *ātmatattva*, seated upon a pedestal on a square altar with the tips of *darbha* grass held in hand. Thus says the *Śāradātilaka*.
While the five musical instruments resounded, the Guru, having duly lifted the water-pot with the blessings of the Brahmins, [placed] the celestial trees at its mouth.

Regarding the instruction "one should seat [the disciple]," it should be understood that for a meal one faces east, while for initiation one faces north; as stated by Somaśambhu: "For bathing one faces north, for initiation one faces east for the sake of a meal, having raised the upper body."

In that regard, "according to rule" means reciting the root mantra in reverse order and likewise in its original form.

As it has been stated by the Teacher: "Just as previously the jar was filled with nectar-like syllables, so too the excellent preceptor, filling the body of the disciple with those very same [syllables], should perform the consecration for the swift attainment of all desired perfections."
Elsewhere it is also said: "A person of good intellect, reciting the mantra, should perform the consecration";
and elsewhere: "One should perform the consecration correctly."
With the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *m*, filling the entire body, and recited three times along with the *anuvānas*.

Directly, according to reality.

in this interval, the bull among sages, with a serene countenance, should address that disciple, saying: "May it be so that it yields equal fruit for both of us."
The Guru should contemplate the knowledge, consisting of light by its own nature, as it departs;
the disciple should contemplate it as it arrives.

In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, however, it is said: "Then, by the command of the guru, the disciple, in the presence of Śiva, the fire, and the guru, should utter the words of initiation while forming this intention with devotion."
Better is the abandonment of life, or even the piercing of my head, than that I should eat without having first worshipped the Blessed Three-eyed One.
Thus, following the gift of knowledge, the guru should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;

One should place the lotus-feet of that [Guru] upon one's own head;
one should offer one's body, wealth, and all of one's vital breaths to him.
Reciting this mantra, one should perform either the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) or five-limbed (pañcāṅga) prostration; this is the meaning.

With both arms, the knees, the head, the speech, and the mind—

"Having given to the guru a sacrificial fee consisting of either his entire property or half of it, excluding whatever has already been spent, the reception of the mantra is then considered complete."

Thus,

If one does not have abundant cattle, land, gold, houses, fields, and so forth, or even a portion thereof; or if one lacks these things for that purpose.

the duties of the preceptor as stated in other tantras are now written down:

One should utter the names preceded by "Śrī" for the deity, the Guru, those in the position of the Guru, the conscious principle (cetana), the presiding deities of the field (kṣetrādhidevatāḥ), the Siddhas, and those who hold the office of the Siddhas.

One should not revile a woman who is intoxicated, one born of an unknown lineage, one who is menstruating, one whose breasts have fallen away, one who is deformed, one with disheveled hair, or one who is overcome by passion.
One should not look at a woman with exposed breasts who is naked, has hair on her body, and is covered in dust; one should avoid the property of others and the wives of others.
One should not stretch out one's feet toward grain, cows, teachers, deities, fire, knowledge, a treasury, or kings; nor should one even look at them in such a manner.
One should avoid laziness, intoxication, delusion, deceit, backbiting, and strife, as well as envy, self-conceit, and the disparagement of others.
One should not find fault with a Brahmin who bears the marks of his order and observes his vows, nor with the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Saṃhitās, the Purāṇas, the Āgama scriptures, or the Kalpas.
A pair of wooden plow-shafts, a pestle, a stone, a rope, a winnowing-basket,
a broom, a staff, a banner, and a vaidūrya gem as a weapon.
The water-pot, the fly-whisk, the parasol, the mirror, as well as ornaments, and whatever other sacrificial materials are suitable for enjoyment.
Whatever objects are in great sacred places, or whatever divine things are spoken of in temples, or indeed those things possessed by spirits;
One should never step over these, nor touch them with one's feet: a cow-pen, those who are despised by the world, and those who wander about according to their own whims.
One should never engage in that which consists of harming others,
nor should one accept gifts out of a desire for personal enjoyment.
One should diligently acquire wealth for the sake of honoring the deities and guests,
and one should maintain straightforwardness, truthfulness, gentleness, equanimity, and fortitude.

"One who always performs the oblations prescribed here in the *Śāradātilaka*, and practices the conduct appropriate for this world and the next, that initiated sacrificer attains peace, compassion, detachment, and divine power at all times. Thus [it is said].

Likewise, one should not take shelter under the Vibhītaka, Arka, Kāraskara, or Nūhoca trees; nor should one rely upon pillars, the excrement of humans or other living beings, nor upon the tips of nails, hair, spittle, bathing water, or water from a cloth or a jar.

"One should cast far away these [impurities]: donkey, dog, old goat, and dust"—thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*. However, in the *Somaśambhu*, it says: "One should not revile the Lord who is the Cause, nor the scripture composed by Him."
Neither the Guru nor the practitioner should step over the shadow of the Liṅga;
one should not eat the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor should one give them to one initiated by Śiva.
Also, in the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*: "One should not transgress the command of the guru, nor should one speak back to him;
by day and by night, one should carry out his instructions like a servant, and one should abandon untruth, that which is inauspicious, and excessive speech."
One should never speak unpleasantly, nor display laziness, nor especially lust and anger; one should never speak with an uncovered face in the presence of the guru,
nor should one harbor pride on account of wealth, caste, stage of life, or other such factors.
One must never consume the teacher’s property if it has not been given by him;
if it is given, it should be accepted as a gracious gift and never out of greed. Furthermore, one should renounce non-duality before the deity and before the teacher.
One must not step over the sandals, the meditation belt, or other personal effects of the Guru;
one should never touch them with one's feet, but always bow down before them. Likewise, one should never stretch out one's legs upon the bed or seat provided by him.
One should not engage in restless movements or fidgeting in the presence of the Guru.
One should go to and come from [the Guru] after bowing to the Guru’s sandals. Having reflected upon it, one should perform the Guru’s work with a gracious mind.

One should not step over the teacher's shadow, nor walk ahead of him; one should exit behind the teacher's feet and, having bowed, leave the teacher's house. One should not display power or attempt to gather disciples in the presence of the teacher.
One should not harbor egoism, nor should one maintain an arrogant physical bearing; from that time forward, with undivided focus, one should do what is pleasing to the Guru.
Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in its entirety to the officiating priests with a delighted mind,
he should afterwards gratify the Brahmins with various kinds of food and drink along with further gifts.
This is declared to be the ritualistic initiation (*kriyāvatī dīkṣā*), which bestows all prosperity.
Now I shall describe the initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), as known from the Āgamas.
The phonemes consist of the nature of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and the body is likewise of that same nature.
One should not, out of hunger [for gain], bow to one's own guru in the presence of the Great Guru.
"Having seen one intent on performing prostrations, the Guru should restrain him.
Likewise: "One should not give an assignment from the Guru, nor should one speak [in such a manner] at all."
By the statement "thus one should do what is pleasing to the guru," the primacy of the guru’s satisfaction is expressed;
as it has been said in the *Daśapaṭalī*: "The disciple must also always perform service to the guru."
Without service, knowledge cannot bear fruit for us;
when the guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased, and when Śiva is pleased, the three worlds are pleased.
But when the guru is angry, O Maheśānī, neither I nor you can protect him.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not cause anger in the Guru;
thus [it is said] from the *Ṛtvigbhā* regarding Brahmā and the others.

In this regard, it should be understood that after performing the purification of the *praṇītā* water, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahman priest, and having dismissed the Brahman, one should consume the remainder of the cooked oblation (*caru*).
This is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Having performed the purification of the *praṇītā*, one should give the fee to the Brahman according to one's own means, free from greed and delusion."
Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should feed the Brahmins;
then, being gladdened by the words of blessing from the learned, one should become happy.
Thereafter, one should consume the remnant of the oblation in a quantity the size of a hen’s egg.
Having consecrated it with the Gāyatrī mantra of the Veda,
one should apply the ashes while reciting the other mantra: "O Agni, that which is life-giving."
One should sprinkle oneself with a full vessel filled with water consecrated seven times, using all those tulasī leaves; now,
he describes the initiation consisting of the letters which follows in due order, beginning with "atha."

"Thus, thus," said the supreme teacher; having united that consciousness (taccaitanya) with the consciousness of the disciple within the Supreme Self (paramātman), because of his state as the deity (devatābhāvāt)—that is, because he himself is the deity—and for that very reason, because of the perfection of his command (ājñāsiddhatvāt), by his own command according to the prescribed rite in reverse order—that is, by reversing both the phonemes (varṇa) and the positions (sthāna)—[he performed the rite]. Therefore, the preceptor should project the phonemes onto the body of the disciple;

then, by the command of the deity and through the state of being the deity, the best of preceptors should withdraw those phonemes, joined with their respective locations, in reverse order according to the ritual rule.
Then, with his constituent principles dissolved, this disciple shall possess a divine body.
Having united that consciousness within the Supreme Self, the supreme Guru should then produce those phonemes from it and install them once more upon the body of the disciple.
One should duly apply consciousness according to the sequence of emanation;
thus, the state of the deity, consisting of supreme bliss, arises in the disciple.
One should then withdraw the phonemes together with their respective locations.
The meaning is "he should withdraw";
this connects with the subsequent phrase "the supreme teacher" (guruttama), [referring] from that Supreme Self.

The word "vada" [indicates] that from the preceding position and phoneme, one should proceed to the subsequent position and phoneme, and by the word "ca" (and), the phrase "in the body of the disciple" (*śiṣyatanau*) is to be supplied along with consciousness (*caitanya*).
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Indeed, the scripts were created as transformations of the union of Fire and Moon; by these [scripts], when recited in reverse order, this body [is purified]."
Having thoroughly pervaded the entire body composed of the elements and joined with skin, blood, and so forth, according to the prescribed method,
[the yogi] should place those respective letters of the four classes in the vowels beginning with *u*, *ṛ*, *s*, and *m*, and likewise those others in the consonants; then,

having combined them in sequence with the points of articulation (*sthāna*), and with his physical body entirely dissolved, with the inner end situated at the forehead, having reached and pervaded the fourteen worlds, let him go to my very state of being.

From the *mūlādhāra*, she whose radiance is like a flash of lightning, subtle in form, and the root-source of all splendors, becomes exceedingly minute at the crown of the head for the seeker; she, skilled in traversing the path of the *suṣumṇā* and permeated by the Sun, when meditated upon, immediately causes the nectar of the Sun to flow from the *soma*-accompanied [Moon].
That stream of drops of ambrosia which falls upon the head becomes composed of letters; with those [letters], O dear one, [one should worship] the face and other limbs.
Having cast down all obstacles, he should kindle his own splendor like fire in clarified butter;
then, having withdrawn and extracted that very body which consists of light and pervades the entire world,
he should, by means of the power of his resolve, place that self-form consisting of will-power back into his own self.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, verses 116–120.
This initiation consisting of the [five] colors has been described as bestowing consciousness;
thereafter, the initiation of the Kalās is duly explained.
Since the five Kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are the powers (śaktis) of the elements, [they constitute this initiation]. 121.
Therefore, having visualized them within the body composed of the elements, one should pierce [the channels] of the disciple:
Nivṛtti is situated starting from the soles up to the knees;
Pratiṣṭhā stands pervading the space from the knees up to the navel.

123. The Vidyā-kalā pervades from the navel up to the throat; beyond that, the Śānti-kalā pervades from the throat up to the forehead, and from there up to the crown of the head (śikhā). 124. This should be known as the Śāntyatītā-kalā; thus is described the pervasion of the kalās.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, the Guru [transfers the consciousness] from one location to another location.
Having united them, the wise one should pierce them by command up to the level of Śiva.
This is declared to be the initiation of the *kalā*, which bestows a divine state.
126. Next, I shall describe the piercing-initiation (vedha-dīkṣā), which liberates one from saṃsāra.
One should meditate upon [the deity] within the center of the disciple’s body, at the four-petalled mūlādhāra.
In the center of the triangle, O Pure One, where the threefold radiance unfolds,
[I worship her] who is endowed with a multitude of enclosures and possesses a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Having pierced the six lotus-chakras, one reaches the Goddess who consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose form is pure consciousness, the subtle and most subtle Power.
Proceeding by the middle path toward the divine state up to Paraśiva,
one should withdraw the phonemes situated in the petals from Va to Sa into the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā).

Having joined that [energy] within the six-petaled lotus at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which is endowed with the letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*, the Guru should pierce it by means of the *ājñā*.
The Guru should dissolve those letters into Viṣṇu, and him again into the navel-lotus;
he should then join him to the ten-petaled lotus, which consists of the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*.
The Guru should withdraw those channels into Rudra, and him again into the lotus of the heart;
having joined [the soul] with Īśvara, enriched by the twelve solar syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*.
One should withdraw those phonemes into this [heart] and then again into the lotus of the throat;
having joined the vowels once more to the sixteen-petaled [lotus] of the palate.
Having withdrawn them into Sadāśiva, the Guru then joins him once more within the lotus of the earth (the womb), specifically in the leaf of the heart that has been cleansed.
Then, the Guru should withdraw that [consciousness] into the point (bindu) and join it to the digit (kalā);
thereafter, he should join that to the sound (nāda), and finally join the sound to the end of sound (nādānta).
136. Moving; known as Kamalāsana, in Brahmā, the presiding deity of the Ādhāra [cakra].

In this manner, Viṣṇu and the others are to be understood as the presiding deities of their respective seats, beginning with Svādhiṣṭhāna. "Him" refers to Brahmā; "those letters" refers to the consonants from ba to la.
One should join that Viṣṇu in the lotus of the navel, which is the Maṇipūraka;
"then one should pierce" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Those letters [are] from Ḍa to Pha.
Having joined that Rudra within the heart-lotus— anāhata— consisting of twelve petals and known as the "arkapattrā," one should pierce him; this is the syntactical connection.
The grammatical connection is that the Guru should dissolve those letters from *ka* to *ṭha* into Īśvara.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, having joined them into this lotus of the throat (*kaṇṭhapaṅkaja*) in the Viśuddhi [cakra], he should pierce it—this is the syntactical supplement.
Having dissolved those vowels into Sadāśiva—this is the connection.
Having joined that Sadāśiva to the lotus of the brow in the Ājñā [cakra], one should pierce him—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
The meaning of "one should join" and so forth in the subsequent passage is "one should pierce. Its purpose is for the sake of *ha* and *pau*.
In the *bindu*, which is Śiva; for it is said that "the *bindu* has Śiva as its essence. [He worships] that Śiva.

Having united that [energy] with *unmanī*, and having placed it within the mouth of the Moon and the Sun,

137. Together with his own self, he should thus pierce the power within the Supreme Lord;
then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple—his bonds severed—shall fall [into grace].
Having attained divine awakening, he perceives everything at that very moment;
he becomes Śiva manifest—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
136. This initiation consisting of piercing bestows all consciousness;
the fourfold initiation has been correctly explained in this treatise in due order.
These six wheels are situated one above the other;
for this very reason, the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*) constitutes the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).

Thus, according to the sequence previously mentioned, the connection is that one should pierce the power (*śakti*), Kuṇḍalinī, into the Supreme Lord Śiva by means of the self—that is, the individual soul of the disciple.
Because it is impossible for the Piercer (vedhas) to act without Śakti,
it is said that one should first meditate on Śakti in the Mūlādhāra.
Consequently, it should be understood that the piercing also occurs through Śakti alone in the Svādhiṣṭhāna and the other centers.
"Severed bond" means liberated from the three bonds.
As stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The bond is said to be the attachment to actions, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous;
that bond, which is the instrument of bondage, should be known to be threefold."
The first is the innate bond (pāśa), and the next is the adventitious;
the third is the incidental (or associative) bond—thus is the triad of bonds traditionally taught.
Thus,

by means of the piercing (*vedha*) performed by the author’s supreme guru, Somānanda Ācārya, the author’s gurus, Utpalācārya and others, became one with Śiva. The lineage of the author’s gurus has been shown in the commentary on the third verse.
Likewise, through the piercing (*vedha*) performed by the teacher Caṇḍeśvara, Śivasvāmin became one whose self is Śiva.

Similarly, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhācāryas said: "The knowledge of time, as well as the deception of time in another body, entry [into another body], piercing (*vedha*), and so forth, are obtained when Śiva is pleased."
Thus he concludes with the word "gradually.
In the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*, it is stated that this individual initiation (*āṇavī dīkṣā*) is of ten kinds.
Namely: the individual (āṇava) initiation is manifold, while the empowered (śākteya) and the blissful (śāmbhavī) are each single; thus it is recited by the learned who are experts in the scriptures.
It has been stated that the *āṇavī* [power] is manifold; that is now explained here:
it is the *smārttā*, the *mānasikī*, the *yogī*, the *cākṣuṣī*, and likewise the *spārśanī*.
The *Abhiṣecikī* [initiation] consists of the oral, the mantra-based, the *hautra*, and the scriptural [rites]. According to the *Śāradātilaka*:
"A guru residing in a foreign land, having remembered his disciple, [should sever] the three bonds in succession."

Having separated [the soul] through the procedure for the limbs of absorption and enjoyment, its perfect union with the supreme Śiva— this is called the "Smārta initiation," which consists of the form of such conjunction.
Having perceived with the mind one who is seated near oneself and pure,
that which liberates from the three impurities by means of specific methods is indeed the mental [initiation].
Having entered the body of the disciple according to the sequence taught in Yoga, the yogin takes hold of that disciple's self and performs the union with his own self.
That is declared to be the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā), which destroys the three impurities;
it consists of gazing while firmly resolving "I am Śiva," with eyes moistened by compassion.
That initiation by sight is the Cākṣuṣa dīkṣā, which destroys all sins;
having himself become Paraśiva, the Guru possesses a mind free from doubt.
With the hand of Śiva, one should touch the disciple’s head;
that is declared to be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
Regarding the characteristics of the Hand of Śiva (Śivahasta): one should place the *gandharvamaṇḍalaka* upon the right hand in the sky;
having worshipped the Lord there according to the prescribed rite, it becomes the Hand of Śiva.
Thus,
having visualized his own mouth as the mouth of the Guru, the Guru, with reverence,
[should place] the divine mantras and so forth into the disciple by means of the application of the Guru’s mouth.
Together with the placement of mudrās and so forth, one should bestow this which is indeed the vocal initiation (vācikī dīkṣā);
likewise, the supreme [initiation] is that in which the body is conjoined with the placement of mantras.
Having himself assumed the form of Manu, he should reverently bestow the mantra along with its ritual sequence upon the disciple; that is the Mantra-initiation which destroys impurities.
Having deposited the fire according to the prescribed rule, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila),
one should proceed through each path (adhvan) in due order, following the sequence of dissolution (laya) and enjoyment (bhoga).
This initiation consisting of the Hota’s duties, which takes the form of fire-oblations, is said to have as its pure object the very worlds of the mantra, phoneme, kalā, tattva, and pada.
The initiation (dīkṣā) of a worthy disciple who is devoted and intent upon service and worship,
together with the threefold words of the scriptures, is called *śāstrī*.
Having respectfully worshipped both Śiva and the consort of Śiva in the ritual jar (kumbha),
that initiation which follows from the consecration with the water from the Śiva-jar shall be known as the *ābhiṣecikī* (consecratory) initiation.
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, the measurement of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) is declared:
one karṣa of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and one śukti of milk is likewise recorded.
The five products of the cow have been described by the wise as equal [in merit]; honey, milk-rice, and food not exceeding the size of a mouthful are declared to be equal to them.

The curd should be the measure of a handful; the parched rice grains should be the measure of a fist; the flattened rice (pṛthuka) should be of that same measure, and the roasted flour (śaktava) is likewise declared to be so.

Jaggery should be half a pala in measure, and sugar is considered to be the same; the portion of sacrificial porridge (caru) should be the size of a mouthful, and sugarcane is considered to be measured by a single joint;
one should likewise prepare each leaf, flower, and cake as a single unit.
The wise know that plantains and oranges are each cut into one piece; a citron is divided into four sections; a jackfruit is made into ten pieces;
and coconuts are cut into eight pieces.
Those that are shattered, split in two, short, crooked, thick, thin, split at both ends, infested with worms, long, or skinless should be rejected;
for a shattered one causes the destruction of life, while a split-in-two one gives rise to disease.
If it is straight, one meets death; if it is crooked, it likewise causes obstacles. According to the *Śāradātilaka*, the fruit of the *bilva* and the *kapittha* should be cut into three pieces.
The fruit of the *urvāruka* is prescribed for the *homa*, but it should be cut into three pieces;
other fruits should likewise be cut into pieces. The fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be ten finger-breadths long. *Dūrvā* grass is specified as being four finger-breadths in length.
Brohi rice should be one handful; likewise for mung beans, black gram, barley, and rice.
Kodrava grain should be measured at ten handfuls, while wheat and red kalama rice are prescribed at the measure of one handful.
Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful; mustard seeds are of that same measure. Salt is the size of a *śukti* (a small shell), and long peppers are twenty-one in number.
*Pura* is the size of a jujube fruit (*vadara*), and asafoetida is remembered as being equal to that.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron—
each the size of a tamarind seed— are prescribed by the masters;
for if they are large, they take away prosperity, while if they are small, there is a loss for the sacrificer.
If the fuel-sticks are split in two, diseases of the eyes will arise; if they are bitten by insects, there will be loss of wealth.
Long sticks are known to cause harm, while those without bark are said to be fatal to life.
Fuel-sticks that are neither too long nor too short grant all desires.
A wise person should offer as oblation fuel-sticks that have moist bark, are cut evenly, and are as thick as the middle finger; by doing so, one attains vast prosperity.
These types of fuel-sticks are proclaimed for use in rites according to the Śruti, the Smṛti, and the Tantras.
Thus,
another distinction is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should collect sacrificial fuel-sticks from trees other than the *śleṣmātaka* and the *piśāca*."
Those [measures] the size of a fist are equal to a *pala*; those the size of a palm-cup are equal to two *karṣas*;
and those the size of a handful are equal to one *karṣa*.
By the word *pāṇitala*, a handful is meant;
*śukti* is two *karṣas*;
*pura* is *guggulu*.
One *rāmaṭha* (asafoetida) is measured at eighty *guñjās* of *vadarāmaṇa*.
Furthermore, according to the *Śaiva Āgama*: "One should offer into the fire three pieces of the roots and five fine [portions]."
The eighth part for bulbs and two finger-breadths for creepers;
thus ends the fifth chapter.
In all rites, the wise preceptor should meditate upon Vaiśvānara as standing during oblations of fuel-sticks;
as reclining during oblations of clarified butter; and as seated during the remaining materials;
and he should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire.
Fire with smoke should be known as the head; fire without smoke is indeed the eyes. The blazing black fire is the ears, and the wood of the fire is likewise the nose.
The intensely flaming fire is the tongue; this indeed is the characteristic of fire.

If [the smoke] reaches the ears during the fire-oblation (homa), disease occurs; if it reaches the eyes, blindness is declared; if it reaches the nose, mental affliction results; and if it reaches the head, there is an accumulation of wealth.
It resembles gold, vermilion, the rising sun, saffron, and honey.
The color of Suvarṇaretas is proclaimed to be beautiful,
situated within the mouth, both stationary and rising.
The characteristics of the mouth and other parts have been described elsewhere: "Fire with smoke should be known as the head, and fire without smoke as the eyes;
the ear becomes a flame of straw, and the nose is the wood of the fire. Where the fire flows as saliva, it has the luster of pure crystal."

"In that [rite], its opening should be understood as measuring four finger-breadths," so it was proclaimed by the Guru. Furthermore, in the *Vanadurgākalya*, for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) there upon the tongue.
Having understood the four ears and so forth, the best of preceptors should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
If that which is offered with sparks of fire occurs, it will cause fear through disease;
there will be great suffering in the nose and the destruction of the eyes.

It is declared that where there is smoke on the hair, it brings poverty; therefore, one should perform the oblation (homa) upon the tongue. Where there is wood, that is the ear; where there is smoke, that is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there is ash, that is the head.
By the words "wherever the fire blazes, there your tongue is proclaimed," this is what has been stated by the term *vipaścit*.
In the homa for the destruction of an enemy, by offering oblations into the specific limbs [of the fire], the destruction of those respective limbs occurs;
as they say: "If one should offer into the head of the fire, the nose, the ear, or likewise the eye, then it will quickly destroy those very limbs."
Thus ends the Śāradātilaka,
which brings auspiciousness through sounds like those of a kettledrum, a rain-cloud, or a lordly elephant.

The experts in the Tantras have declared that the auspicious fragrance of fire resembles the scent of the nāga, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, and yūthikā flowers, and is like that of lotus, blue lotus, kāvāra, ghee, and guggulu resin.
The crests of the peacocks, moving clockwise and free from trembling,
bring auspiciousness to the sacrificer, especially to his kingdom; likewise, smoke as white as a kunda flower or the moon is declared to be a harbinger of good fortune from the sacrificial fire.
A black complexion resulting from a black lineage would destroy the sacrificer;
as it is said in the venerable *Matanga-paramekhara*: "Whether among the divine or the non-divine, that which is always described as resembling shining gold or like yellow orpiment [is auspicious]."
It is taught that [the complexion] resembling turmeric, realgar, or yellow pigment (rocanā),
as well as vermilion and the rising sun, is auspicious for the sake of victory. This is how it should be understood.
For it is stated therein: "The fire that possesses the brilliance of a ruby, or even one resembling lac-dye, and which shines like the rising sun, is praised by the wise for the sake of victory."
Regarding other rites, it is stated in that same source: "A fire resembling an *indragopaka* insect, blood-red, or like fire;
one resembling Indra’s bow (a rainbow), or like saffron water;
a color equal to various kinds of red flowers—such a hue is praised."
Thus,
"the sound of the bherī drum" and so forth is an illustration;
it is like the resonance of the jīmūta, vallakī, śaṅkha, and mṛdaṅga.
"The sound of the fire is for the sake of success; therefore, any other is said to grant no success"—
this refers by implication to the *nāga* [breath] and so forth.

As it is said: "The scent of fragrant substances, the fire, and the beautiful scent of ghee [are auspicious]," the lotus-scent leads to long life, while the scent of the blue water-lily (*indīvara*) and others leads to good fortune;
as it has been stated: "A fragrance equal to that of the blue water-lily is immediately commended for good fortune."
"For long life, one should have the scent of a lotus, and for one of good vows, the scent of *bilva*;
this is the distinction. Furthermore, a pungent scent is recommended here for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), while the scent of fire is always auspicious."
Thus,
"having the appearance of a parasol" is an elliptical expression,
because it is stated: "An arm shaped like a parasol is excellent, resembling a banner or a fly-whisk."
The fifth chapter:
A white [sound] quickly destroys a kingdom; one resembling the cry of a crow brings misfortune;
and a sound like the braying of a donkey causes total destruction in the forest.

If the fire emits a foul odor, it will bring about suffering; if its flame has broken curls, it will cause death and the depletion of wealth. Smoke resembling the color of a parrot’s wing or the luster of a pigeon [is likewise inauspicious].
A black horse causes the loss of horses and cattle before long;
a white horse destroys the kingdom of the sacrificer.
This should be understood to apply to those rituals where colors such as red or yellow are prescribed.
But not in a general sense,
as they say: "Having understood that [result] which corresponds to each respective action according to its nature,
one should always adopt the action that is favorable to it, or abandon it if it is the opposite."
Thus it is said.

A specific detail regarding that very point is as follows: "In this [mantra], for the rites of killing (*māraṇa*), driving away (*uccāṭana*), and causing depression (*avasādana*), a shower of black flowers is desired here in Vaṅga."
"The fire that is white and auspicious, even whiter than a conch shell, crystal, jasmine, or the moon,
is prescribed for all times, whether for rites of pacification (śāntika) or prosperity (pauṣṭika).
Thus it is said.
The blackness [of the hair] is also to be abandoned, as stated by that same authority: "A year resembling a bee, collyrium, or a sword does not bestow success.
Furthermore, there is a specific distinction regarding blindness: that which resembles the eyes of a cat or the plumage of a parrot is unacceptable.
"Resembling the neck of a peacock, with the luster of a variegated pigeon.
Thus [it is said].
"Putrid odor" means a foul smell.
"Death," and so forth, is according to the sequence.
By the phrase "of such a kind," this is what is meant:
fire that is equal to a bull or an elephant as a vehicle always bestows nourishment.
That which has the form of celestial chariots (*vimāna*), canopies (*vitāna*), or palaces (*prāsāda*),
as well as the forms of swans and peacocks, is praised;
the lion-shaped [structure] is always considered by the wise to grant immediate success.

The form of other fanged creatures is not recommended for the rite of fire-offering (homa). The forms of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and the like do not lead to success here. However, that which is glossy, turning clockwise, and possesses a pleasant sound is auspicious.
"He is to be known for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose; otherwise, he is a creator of obstacles.
— *Śāradātilaka*.
Regarding such defects, the preceptor [should prescribe] an expiation.
One should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Śrī Śāradātilaka.
[A person who is] harsh, making "caṭa-caṭa" sounds, and always moving in a counter-clockwise direction...
"O best of sages, whoever digs into the earth and whoever has his crest-point downward— none of these shall be admitted into this scripture of the Supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "twenty-five":

according to the principle that whenever two or three defects are observed, the remedial rite (*naimittika*) must be repeated for each respective cause, twenty-five oblations (*āhuti*) should be offered that many times.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śrī Śāradātilaka* composed according to the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*).
Oṃ.
The Sixth Chapter. Now I shall describe the exposition of the phonemes (varṇatantra), which brings about the awakening of the universe;
without the realization of which this entire world is inert.
The Seer is declared to be Brahmā; Gāyatrī is said to be the metre;
and Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity by the best of teachers.
[This is done] by means of the six groups of consonants, in order, excluding the sibilants (ha) and those situated between the short and long vowels.

The teachers should perform the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) conjoined with the [appropriate] caste-mantras. Since the mantras must be taught immediately after the description of initiation, he begins [the next section] in order to state the Mātṛkā, which serves as their source: "Now," etc., regarding the arrangement of the letters, the Mātṛkā.

The meaning is: "that power" refers to the power that unfolds (*unmolinī*) and ordains (*vidhāyinī*) all cognitions (*bodha*)—which consist of the expansion of the capacity for knowledge (*jñānaśakti-prasara*) and produce them—in their forms as *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and *parā*.
By the word "designated" (*samuddiṣṭa*), there is a connection with the term "rule" (*vidhi*);
by the word "uttered" (*īrita*), there is a connection with the term "deity" (*deva*).
By the phrase "thus declared," the application of the *mātṛkā* and the *paṭala* is indicated;
this is the consensus of the teacher Padmapāda.
By the phrase "by the best of instructors," it is suggested that the *bījas* and *śaktis* are also to be mentioned.
In this regard, some maintain that the consonants are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the vowels are the powers (*śakti*).
As it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "O Supreme Goddess, the consonants are the seed-syllables and the vowels are the powers."
It should be understood that these very *bīja* and *śakti* belong to all mantras of the *mātṛkā*, including those ending with the *lipi* on the ground, excluding the *prapañca-yāga*.
Elsewhere, other *bīja* and *śakti* are mentioned;
as they say: "The *bīja* of this [mantra] is known as the sound (*ghoṣa*), and the *śakti* is proclaimed to be the life-force (*jīva*)."
Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere, others say: "The seed-syllable of this is proclaimed to be the letter 'A' together with a bindu."
"The letter *a* accompanied by two dots is designated as Śakti.
As for its application (*viniyoga*), it is stated: "Its application is in the recitation [of the mantra] during the time of reciting the Mātṛkā-mantra."

It should be understood that, apart from its role as a constituent of a mantra, when it is being employed in the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*), its application (*viniyoga*) is as a constituent of that specific mantra. Regarding the term "non-neuter" (*aklība*): "neuters" (*klība*) are the neuter vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*; those devoid of these are the "non-neuters. These consist of the short vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, *o*, and *aṃ*, followed by the six long vowels; [the others] are included within or situated among these.

I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā), who possesses six groups of letters and the *Śāradātilaka* [script], whose face, arms, navel, and chest are adorned with the fifty phonemes; who bears upon her radiant crown a crescent moon; whose breasts are full and high; who holds in her lotus-hands the *mudrā*, the rosary, the three-stranded thread, and the jar overflowing with nectar; and who is of pure luster and modest mien.
And what are they? The plural number is used for the sake of including the first member.
They are the consonants beginning with *ka*—namely, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*. By these [the following is meant].
The heart-mantra and so forth, joined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti), are those conjoined with "to the heart, namaḥ" and so on.
The practical application (prayoga) is as follows: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ḍaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
By the word "by the teachers" (deśikaiḥ), this is what is meant:

Regarding this, it is stated: "Having performed the purification of the hands with the four neuter vowels, one should place [the letters] upon the fingers, beginning with the thumb, along with their respective *aṅga-mantras*. Accordingly, having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) from the palms to the backs of the hands—namely, *aṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, and so forth—one should then place the sixteen vowels upon the fingers of both the right and left palms and their backs, starting from the right little finger up to the left thumb. Then, starting from the left index finger up to the right index finger, one should place four letters on each joint and at the tip of each finger in sequence, namely the consonants from *ka* to *sa*. Finally, one should place the *hal* (consonants) on the two thumbs and the letter *ca* on all the limbs. This is to be understood as the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of the hands.

In this manner, it should be understood everywhere. As stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Then, one should place the six [syllables] beginning with 'Ta'—namely, *ta*, *ta*, *ta*, *pa*, *ṛṣṭha*, and *tadvyāpta*—starting from the little finger on the right hand and extending to the fingers."
Having placed [the mantras] ending with the left thumb, one should then place the consonants as well,
starting from the left index finger, four by four,
following the sequence of the fingers up to the right index finger.
"One should place [the letters] on the two thumbs; this is declared to be the remaining karanyāsa.
Thus [ends verse 3]. "Fifty" [refers to the fifty letters].
The state of being divided will become clear simply by the description of the locations for the placement (*nyāsa*) that is about to be stated.

The *mudrā* is the *jñānamudrā*, consisting of the union of the thumb and forefinger with their tips facing each other. As they say: "With the tips of the thumb and forefinger joined, one should extend the others."
"Facing the side, this is proclaimed as the *jñānamudrā*";
the meaning is that the *vidyā* (scripture) and the book constitute its mudrā.
The left fist is clenched facing oneself; this is the book-seal (*pustakamudrā*).
[She is] of brilliant luster and auspicious complexion.
This is an illustration for garments, body-unguents, and garlands;
likewise, it should be understood everywhere hereafter regarding those terms that denote colors.
The visualization of the weapons is as follows: "above," "in front," "to the right," "behind," and "on the left."

Here, immediately after the meditation, one should display the weapon-mudrās (*āyudhamudrā*). In the same manner, it should be understood that this applies up to the end of the mantra of Sarasvatī. The meditation on each individual syllable as taught in another tantra is as follows: Chapter Six.
Resembling gold, with eight arms holding a trident, mace, and sword, he has four faces and a massive body; his seed-syllable is the letter *A*, and his vehicle is a tortoise.
She is white, holding a noose and a goad, seated upon a lotus, and her vehicle is an elephant.
She should be sixty-four yojanas in measure and adorned with pearls.
She holds in her hands a boat, a thunderbolt, and an axe that destroys enemies.
She is one krośa in size and stands upon a tortoise.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context functions as a punctuation mark indicating the end of a section or chapter. [End of Section]
Ten yojanas long and five yojanas wide, she has a swan for her vehicle;
she is the syllable *Ī*, the bestower of nourishment, white in color, adorned with pearls, and possessing a white face.
Holding a mace and a goad in his hands, riding upon a crow, and adorned with black ornaments,
his height and extent measured two thousand yojanas.
The [deity] Kālaghna shall have four arms holding nooses and śaktis, be red in color, and have a camel standing upon a solar disc as his mount;
he shall possess the previously mentioned proportions and consist of two ṛ-vowels.
Seated upon a swan on a square pedestal, possessing a luster like that of a topaz,
holding a noose and a goad, and having two pairs of arms, this fierce [deity] is Nirodhana.

One should meditate upon the syllable Eka, which is dark blue in color, seated upon a ruddy sheldrake, adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and whose hands hold a mace, a fruit, an enemy, and a lotus.
Resembling a fresh jasmine flower, holding a trident and a sword in her arms,
and standing upon a lamp, this image made of iron, measuring ten million yojanas, bestows the power of poetry.
Consisting of consciousness, all-pervading, peaceful, and blazing with a thousand rays,
it is the boat situated in the cow-pen, whose form is the syllable *oṃ* and whose essence is the syllable *śrī*.
Resembling molten gold, with noose and discus in her arms, she bestows fearlessness;
for a thousand yojanas, she appears golden with immeasurable splendor.
Resembling fresh saffron, seated upon a lotus, adorned with red ornaments,
four-armed, and golden-hued, he bestows prosperity and destroys enemies.
One should meditate upon [the deity] who brings about the destruction of enemies, who is minor yet yields the fruit of battle, whose vehicle is a donkey,
who measures one thousand yojanas, whose name ends in a vowel, and who has two arms.
Seated upon the form of the earth and an elephant, resembling fresh saffron in color,
he should be depicted with tridents and vajras in his hands, measuring one thousand two hundred yojanas.
Holding a noose and a mace in his hands, mounted upon a ram, and acting as a restrainer,
Kṛṣṇa is terrifying and measures a thousand yojanas.

The letter Ga is the Śāradātilaka; it holds a noose and a goad in its hands, is seated upon a lotus and a serpent, possesses a ruddy luster, is adorned with serpents, and extends for a hundred yojanas.
He stands upon a camel and a mortar, holding a mace and a thunderbolt in his hands; he is immeasurable, possesses two faces, and is dark-colored, extending for a thousand yojanas.
Ten million yojanas in length and breadth, black in color and blazing with radiance, it has two arms and is mounted upon a crow; this is the syllable *ṅā*, which bestows minor fruits.
He stands upon a lotus at the beginning of the eon, four-faced and white in luster;
he has matted hair, is fragrant, and extends for ten million yojanas.
The lotus was likewise white and measured four cubits;
it shone with a brilliance of ten million, and its two stalks were four cubits long and possessed a white luster.
The vehicle of the crow is measured at thousands of yojanas;
it is the cause of enmity, black in color, and possesses two arms.
The deity of Krauñca is two-armed, possesses a great sound, rides upon a nāga, a reed,
and a lordly elephant, and shines with two hands.
The all-pervading Lord, who destroys poison, measures one hundred thousand yojanas;
in the letter *ḍa*, He likewise has eight arms and four faces, beautifully adorned.
Measuring a thousand yojanas, he stands upon the earth's surface; his body is like a mass of fire, ten-armed, and possessed of shimmering radiance.
He would indeed be a thousand *yojanas* in measure, mounted upon a tiger;
he would stand sixty years of age, possessing four arms and well-adorned.
He is a thousand cubits in height, fragrant, with the luster of saffron, and twelve syllables (in name); he may be ten million yojanas in measure, possessing eight arms and four faces.
Having the color of a water-pot, mounted upon a bull, and terrifying even in his own form,
he has six faces, six arms, possesses a crore-fold measure, and stands upon a buffalo.
The four-armed Siṃhavāha measures four hundred thousand [units],
while the two-armed Kākavāha should be measured at one thousand.
The one with twenty arms and ten faces, Pa, is stationed at the mouth measuring ten *koṭis*;
the letter Pha measures ten *koṭis* of *yojanas* and has two arms.
