Some, however, say "Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha together with Pūrṇodara," while others say "Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha [united] with Pūrṇodayā.
In both of these views, they maintain that the Rudras hold primacy.
Some also desire [the mantra] as "pūrṇodarīśrīkaṇṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ";
however, all three of those positions are non-traditional (*asāmpradāyika*).
In the first case, there is the employment of the word *sahita*, which was not mentioned [in the original source], as an addition.
In the second alternative, the fourth [syllable] is untenable in both cases:
because in one case it is obtained through its connection with *namaḥ*, while in the other there is an absence of a means to obtain it.
Furthermore, since it is stated in all three alternatives that [the mantra] is "joined with Rudra," the Mātṛkā does not have a direct, uninterrupted conjunction with the Rudras.
Therefore, the traditional method alone is superior. However, the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* stated the formula: "Obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodayā.
That too is incorrect;
for in the context of meditation (*dhyāna*), it is understood that both [deities] together constitute the divinity, just as in the case of Agni and Soma.
And in this application, there is a conjunction (*samuccitatva*) of the two deities;
for by the separate mention of the fourth case (*caturthī*), they are understood precisely as being independent of one another. Furthermore:

In the case of the injunction, "One offers to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening," although there is no syntactic connection of the action with each [deity] individually due to their mutual dependence created by the two words, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the deities is nonetheless intended.
In this present context, however, because that [mutual dependence] is absent and *namaḥ* is connected with each [name] individually, the conjunction of them is even more clearly understood.
Consequently, even in the *homa* and other rites, there is only a single oblation (*āhuti*) with the formula: "Svāhā to Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodarī."
In this same manner, it should be understood that [the same applies] to the Nyāsas of Keśava and the others, as well as those of Kāma and Gaṇeśa.
As for the fact that in some places the extraction [of the mantra] reads "and to Keśava" and "to Kīrti," that should be known to be for the sake of conforming to the meter.
"Along with the elements (sadhātu)": O Rudras, within those ten pervasive [letters] beginning with *ya* and so forth,
the elements— skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, breath, power, and the self— are to be known as being joined with these [letters] respectively.

In this context, although the word *rudra* is embedded within a compound, it is nevertheless referred to by the pronoun, according to Vāmana’s sūtra: "The recurrence [of a word] occurs through a pronoun for that which is concealed by a compound. As for the usage:
*Hsauḥ yaṃ*, salutation to Vāleśa and Sumukhīśvarī, who are the essence of the skin, at the heart, and so forth.

Here, the word *ātman* (self/essence) is employed according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). In another text, having stated that the word *krodha* (wrath) is used in place of the word *ātman*, it is said that the word *ātman* should be employed everywhere.

The masters of the Tantras declare that the deity of the Śāradātilaka is Ardhanārīśvara; the preceptor should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) using the seed-syllable "ha" joined with the six long vowels. (40)
Likewise: "The vowels and so forth, the elements, the vital breaths, the powers, the wrathful deities, and so on—these he unites with the Self.
And elsewhere: "The individual soul, the power, and even the wrath—he [unites] these with the Self."
Thus say the teachers: "O Ambikā, those two elements as well— beginning with *ya* and the rest— and the seven winds, along with *kṣa* followed by *ra*, are Krodha."

In this context, because the letter *kṣa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Narasiṃha, the term "wrath" (*krodha*) was employed by the teacher Padmapāda in his commentary on the first verse, beginning with the words "composed," etc.; thus, the mention of the place of the Mātṛkā is explained by these [terms].
The seven elements (*dhātu*) are indicated by these [letters], while by the word "heart" (*hṛd*), both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the Power (*śakti*) are denoted.

It has been stated that the Supreme Self is denoted by the syllable *ka* in the sense of bliss; following that view, the author of the root-text has here employed the term "Self. Now, one might ask: since the deity-self, beginning with the skin and ending with the Supreme Self, is already present within the body of the practitioner through the *yādi*-nyāsa alone, what remains for which the nyāsa of the remaining syllables is required?
We say that it is the conceptualization of the arrangement of specific parts of a deity;

nor is there any rule that first there must be a conceptualization of a general form and then a conceptualization of its particulars, such that the arrangement of letters would necessarily consist of the letter *ca* and so forth.
For the body of the deity is everywhere and eternally of the nature of both the universal and the particular;
it is generated through the ritual placement (*sannidhi-nyāsa*) within the body of the practitioner.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in first recollecting the proximity of the specific limbs through the placement of the letters beginning with *A*.

Furthermore, in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* according to the sequence of reabsorption, there is no violation of the proper order on the grounds that general reabsorption occurs first and specific reabsorption follows later;
for both types of reabsorption take place within the self alone.
Nor is the separate reabsorption of the particulars purposeless, since they are not already reabsorbed by the general reabsorption alone.
Since the contemplation of the sequence of the specific withdrawal (*viśeṣasaṃhāra*) must be performed,
it is stated that [the mantra] is joined with the six long vowels— ā, ī, ū, ai, au, aḥ— and with the *hasa*, namely the letters *ha* and *sa*, combined with the word *deśika*.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however,
is "OṂ HASĀṂ HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ" and so forth;
others, however, maintain that the limbs of the Mātṛkā begin with *ha*, *sa*, and *ā*.

The traditionalists, however, maintain the following practice: one should recite the Praṇava (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), and the five-syllabled mantras of Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāṇī, each preceded by its own seed-syllable and ending with a pair of *rakṣa* (protect). Then, for [the specific deity], one should recite "Amuka-vāhana" and so forth, ending with a pair of *rakṣa*; then "Amuka-haste" and so forth, ending with a pair of *māra-rakṣa*. Following this, one should recite the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Mātṛkās, which are encased by Māyā and pervaded by the three long vowels. Then, having uttered the words "Tātyacca," "Saṃjīvani," "Ūrdhvakeśini," "Jaṭilakeśini," "Viśvarūpiṇi," and "Tārākṣiṇi" twice, one should utter the heart-mantra and the other limbs. Such is the application.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ śivāya namaḥ | Haṃ Brahmāṇi, protect, protect! O you who ride the swan, protect, protect! O lotus-handed one, protect me, protect me! Hāṃ hoṃ hūṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hāṃ hāṃ hūṃ hsauḥ | To the heart of Sañjīvanī, namaḥ. Thus [are] the seed-syllables (bījāni). And the weapons (āyudhāni) are: the lotus, trident, spear, discus, mace, and thunderbolt.

May the pervasive one be present: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ śivāya hra cāmuṇḍe rakṣa rakṣa vetālavāhane rakṣa rakṣa pāśahaste mama sarvāṅga rakṣa rakṣa hā~ hoṃ hū~*. Having uttered the six short vowels and the long vowels from *a* to *kṣa*, [one recites] *hā~ ho ṣaṣṭhaḥ paṭalaḥ*.

We take constant refuge in the body of the Lord of Ambikā, who resembles a golden bandhuka flower, who holds a beautiful rosary, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with his own staff-like arms, who is adorned with the crescent moon, and who possesses three eyes. (41)
One should worship that [deity] according to the rule by the very same path previously described;
one should install the Mātṛkā beginning with Smara (Kāma), accompanied by "Oṃ Keśavāya namaḥ" and so forth.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with "Hūṃ Hsauḥ Sarvāṅgavyāpini Svāhā," one should install the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā.

In this regard, other pervasive mantras for the face and other parts should be known from the oral tradition, as stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The eight Mothers have arisen, and they are the leaders of the [consonant] groups;
they are Vyāpinī, Pālinī, Devī, Pāvanī, and again Kledinī."
Dhārin, Mālin, Haṃsin, and Śāntin— these eight leaders of the groups are proclaimed as the Bhairavas.

Thus ends the eighth [section], the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*). Having uttered [the phonemes] from *a* to *kṣa*, [one says]: "Salutation to Saṃhārabhairava and Śāntinī at the tip of the thumb (*savvīle*). [Then:
"O Bandhuka! (32180).
He holds the meditation on weapons in his right hands, starting from the upper one, while in the other left hands he holds a rosary and a water-pot. || 41 ||
By the phrase "according to the rule" (yathāvidhi), this is what is meant:
one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma, such as *smara* or *vālā*, along with its vessel (*āḍhakā*), using the formula:
"Kloṃ aṃ, obeisance to Kāma and Rati," at the hairline (*keśānta*) and so forth; such is the ritual application.

This meditation is as follows: one should meditate upon the form of Anaṅga, who has the luster of a fine pomegranate flower, whose body is adorned with red unguents, flowers, garments, and ornaments, whose limbs are beautifully decorated by a power (śakti) in his hand consisting of a blue lotus, who holds a flowery arrow and a sugarcane bow, and who possesses a beautiful form.
Thus, one should install the Gaṇapati-mātṛkā, either beginning with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati or with the six seed-syllables.
The procedure for this is as follows: "Gaṃ Aṃ, salutation to Vighneśa and Śrī at the hairline," and so forth.

In meditation, I shall contemplate the auspicious Gaṇeśa, who has the face of a lordly elephant, whose body is smeared with beautiful red unguents shimmering with the intoxication of youth, whose left side is embraced by a woman holding a red lotus in her hand, who holds in his hands the excellent elephant-goad and the noose, and who is adorned with three eyes.
Thus,
in this context, the connection with the skin and other [elements] should also be inferred for both pervasive [deities].
He describes the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with Keśava and others as "beginning with Smara" (*smarādyām*), meaning beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāmabīja*).
The traditionalists, however, [cite] the *Śāradātilaka*:
"In the case of the letters beginning with *ya*, the seer is declared to be Prajāpati and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; it is joined with the elements, the vital breath, power, and the self. (43)
Hari is the manifest Goddess Lakṣmī herself; one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel [Ā].
With his hands, he bears the lotus, mace, conch, and discus, as well as knowledge, the lotus-mirror, and a golden pitcher, shimmering like lightning amidst clouds.
May the body of Puṇḍarīka and Acyuta protect you—a body that has become one through the longing for embrace, with their left breasts high and their ornaments closely joined.

(45) Others desire the union of the three *tripuṭās* and the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa; others [desire] the union of the three *praṇavas*; and still others [desire] the state of being encased within the three *praṇavas*.
Some follow the conventional usage of "Śrobojayoga" according to their tradition;
however, the actual application is as follows: "Obeisance to Keśava and Kīrti," beginning with "O Keśānta," and so forth.
Some recite "Oṃ namaḥ keśavāya koṭyai" for Keśava and Koṭī;
others recite "Sadhātu" for Puruṣottama, the self of the skin, and "Vasudhāyai" (for Vasudhā); and so on, beginning with "Hṛdaya."

"Joined with the long [vowels]" means joined with the six long vowels previously mentioned; by that, [it refers to] the primary seed-syllable (ādi-bīja), which is the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja). Thus, *klāṃ*, *klīṃ*, and so forth are to be understood for the heart and the other limbs.
Others, however, maintain that the syllables beginning with *klām* are the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Mātṛkā.

The traditionalists, however, maintain that the limbs (aṅgas) such as the heart are formed by the consonants from *ka* onwards, encapsulated by the sounds of the Māyā-nārāyaṇa eight-syllable mantra (*om namo nārāyaṇāya*) and the Supreme Self mantra (*haṃsaḥ so'ham*), and joined with the goddesses Padminī, Viṣṇupatnī, Varadā, Kamalā, Rūpā, and Śūlinī.
The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows:
*oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'ham devyai hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth. [Verses 43–44]. Regarding "in the hand" (*haste*):
The attributes beginning with "cloud-like" (*megha*) are qualifiers of the body; "ornament" (*ākalpa*) refers to the decoration extending from the lower right hand up to the lower left hand.
Regarding the meditation on the weapons (*āyudhadhyāna*), it is established that human weapons are on the right and divine weapons are on the left;
this is the view agreed upon by the master Padmapāda.
And it has been said: "His hands are resplendent with the Vidyā-lotus, the mirror, the jar of nectar, the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, and the conch."
Thus,
in this context, the sequence should be understood as starting from the upper left and ending at the upper right;
furthermore, it should be understood that the meditation on the four-armed form in this ritual placement (nyāsa) pertains to Viṣṇu alone, and not to him when accompanied by Lakṣmī.
This too is indispensable, as they say: "Keśava and others grant the state of being Acyuta to embodied beings merely by means of nyāsa; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise. Chapter Six.
Having performed the worship and other rites truly as before, the best of mantra-knowers should perform the two mantras; preceded by the Śakti, he should then project the Mātṛkā onto his body.
The seer is remembered as Śakti, the metre as Gāyatrī,
and the deity is declared by the wise to be the one who brings forth the universe and bestows all prosperity.
The wise one should form the limbs with the *māyātman* mantra, joined with the long *arddhanḍu*.

May the Goddess of the World, seated comfortably upon a lotus with her face turned downward, grant you bliss— she whose lofty, full breasts rival the rising sun in brilliance, who is adorned with a crown, earrings, necklaces, a girdle, and anklets, and who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary, a noose, a goad, and a book.
46. One should worship the Goddess every day according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should install the Mātṛkā, endowed with the seed-syllable of Śaubha, upon the body according to the prescribed rite.
The sage is remembered as Bhṛgu, the metre as Gāyatrī, and she is remembered as the deity;
she is the source of all prosperity and the leader of the worlds, according to the wise.
The practitioner should form the limbs [of the mantra] using the seed-syllable previously introduced.

One should meditate upon the Mistress of the Universe, who possesses a luster equal to a garland of lightning; who is being sprinkled by four elephants resembling snow-white mountains with jars of nectar raised by their trunk-staffs; who holds in her lotus-hands a rosary, two lotuses, and a book; and who is radiant with brilliant jewels and has breasts that are slightly bent. (From the *Śāradātilaka*)
One should propitiate this [goddess] with flowers and other offerings according to the prescribed path;
one should place the Mātṛkā, beginning with Smara, which bestows auspiciousness, upon the body.
The sage is declared to be Sammohana; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is proclaimed by the practitioners of mantra to be the supreme Mother of all.
One should perform the arrangement of the limbs with the *smara* mantra joined with the long vowel.

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, who is radiant like ten million rising suns, who holds in her lotus-like hands a crystal rosary, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of Smara, and the Vidyā, and who is adorned with a necklace.
All rites, beginning with worship, have been declared according to the previously stated injunctions.
One should worship the Goddess, who begins with the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma, in the form of her letters.
The seer is as previously stated; the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is designated by the wise as Sammohanā, who brings all the worlds under her control.
One should fashion the six limbs by means of the three seed-syllables rotated [in the respective directions].

One should meditate on her who holds in her own hands a rosary, a sugarcane bow, and a noose; a lotus, a goad, and arrows; and a boon-granting book; who is ruddy, whose breasts are full, who intoxicates the mind, whose face is modest, and who is crowned with the crescent moon.
One should worship the most beautiful [deity] together with the enclosures and the ritual offerings.
I shall now describe the Prapañcayāga, which bestows the perfection of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
The beginning of the Vedas, Śakti, Ajapā, the great mantra of the Supreme Self,
and the wife of Vani— these five mantras are said to bring auspiciousness.
The knower of the ritual procedure should project the Mātṛkā, beginning with Tāra (Om) and Śakti (Hrīṃ), and ending with Ajapā (So’haṃ) and Dhiṭhā (Svāhā),
according to the prescribed path of emanation within the body.
The Śāradātilaka: Brahmā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas),
and its deity is the supreme splendor that pervades all phonemes.
One should fashion the five limbs with the five mantras beginning with *svāhā*;
the wise one should then direct the weapon-mantra toward the quarters with the syllables of *hari-hara*.

Worship that supreme light, which is being measured by the five mantras beginning with *Tāra*, which is inaccessible to the means of knowledge, the eternal root of the universe, the indestructible essence of existence and consciousness that pervades all, and a mass of dense nectar-moons.

The application is as follows: "So'haṃ svāhā" at the end of the hair (keśānta), and so forth. Since the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) will be described later, the term "creation" (sṛṣṭi) is used here. By the phrase "one who knows the procedure" (vidhānavit), this is what is meant: having meditated upon Mahāgaṇapati along with his retinue after first performing the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should mutter the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa forty-four times, and likewise the Mahāgaṇapati mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā" eight times. Then, having performed the placement of the pure Mātṛkā according to the prescribed method, one should also place the seven groups beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya* upon the face, arms, feet, belly, and private parts.
"With *svāhā* and so forth" means with the [mantras] reversed. The application is as follows: *svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *sohaṃ śirase svāhā*, and so on.
"In the directions" means with the *koṭikās*.
"Furthermore" means immediately after the sixth limb.
Regarding the phrase "Hari-Harācara," it is according to what is heard [in the scriptures].
As it has been stated: "The heart is from the fire of the wife (Jāyāgni), and the head is 'So'ham'; the self-nature of the Haṃsa is the tuft (Śikhā);
one's own sacrifice is the armor (Kavaca); the one called Tārā is the eye; and likewise, the void (Akha) is declared to be the Hari-Hara syllable as the very limb."
Thus [it is said].
Some say it is *kri*. Others say it is *tārādi*.
Worship that well-known supreme splendor, Brahman, incessantly and at all times.
Its supremacy is due to the fact that it is the source from which the splendors of others are obtained.
The phrase "a mass of thick nectar-moons" is a *vyasta-rūpaka* (an inverted metaphor).
Therefore, the fault of [the word] being in the masculine gender does not arise,
just as in the expression "the fingers were the sprouts.
By this, its nature as consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is implied.
Unfailing and changeless;
indestructible and imperishable;
all-pervading and omnipresent.

"Cit" is of the nature of self-luminous knowledge. "Sat" is that whose essence is existence. As the Śruti declares: "All this is Being, it is Being, it is Being," and "All this shines because of Cit."

It is the sole root of the world, because the world is of the nature of its transformation; it is inaccessible to the means of valid cognition, as the scripture declares: "from which words turn back."
Therefore he says: "The sixth chapter:
The letters consisting of the five elements were previously declared according to their groups;
therefore, those whose nature is the organs of knowledge know the phenomenal world (prapañca) to be composed of that."
The meaning is that these [mantras] are obtained through the recitation (*japa*) of these [components].

In this regard, because the five-limbed *Tāra* (the syllable Om) consists of the dissolution of all residual modifications (*vikalpa*), it culminates in the cognition of bliss through the non-difference of the limbs of the deity’s *Tāra* from its own limbs.

Furthermore, because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—which constitute the essence of the *Ajapā* mantra—are identical, and because the five limbs of *Dhiṭhā* (the syllable Hrīm) likewise have as their referent the consciousness (*cit*) that pervades everything.
In the Saṃhitā, however, it is said: "The Praṇava should be known as the Cit-kalā, whose nature is the pervasion of Māyā;
by the word 'Haṃsa,' O Goddess of Gods, she is directly the very nature of the Self."
From the three points (*bindu*) located there, this Vāmā, whose nature consists of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution,
was born from the first point as the embodiment of Brahman.
O beloved, by means of the second *bindu*, she protects the three worlds;
she is indeed Jyeṣṭhā, the Māyā of Viṣṇu, the primordial one, and endowed with the quality of *sattva*.
With the *bindu* at the end, everything is pervaded by the *rasa* and enveloped in darkness;
then, O Goddess, Ambikā gives birth to the three *bindus* of Rudra.
When this withdrawal, called the *haṃsa*, manifests the Self,
then it takes the form of a mirror and subsequently becomes composed of light.
O Dear One, by adding the two syllables "paraṃ jyotiḥ" after the wife of Vahni (the syllable Ra),
the mantra becomes Brahma itself when one contemplates it in this way.
Thus [it is said].

Here, the worship of the form of the Prapañcayāga is not mentioned; that which is taught in another tantra is as follows: "On a pedestal consecrated with the Mātṛkā-mantra, upon a lotus of well-formed letters, one should invoke the form of the Prapañcayāga and worship it."
The first enclosure is said to consist of the vowels; the second, of the forms beginning with 'ka';
and the third is designated as consisting of the eight powers of Bhāratī.
The fourth [wheel] is together with the Mothers, the Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga and others;
the fifth, however, is supreme, along with the lords of the directions beginning with Indra and their weapons.
Thus [it is said].
It was stated, "I shall describe the *prapañcayāga*. In this context, the *prapañcayāga* is so called because the *prapañca* (the manifest) is sacrificed (*ijyate*) and offered (*hūyate*) therein.
While explaining that very method of oblation (*homaprakāra*), he also indicates another form of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the phrase "of the five elements" (*pañcabhūta*).
"In the second [chapter], 'previously' etc.; 'having the nature of the organs of cognition' is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), by which [it is meant] they have the color of space."

Those whose nature consists of the organs of knowledge and action are the color of air (vāyu-varṇa); those whose form is their respective objects are the color of fire (agni-varṇa). It should be inferred that they take the form of the ten vital airs, such as prāṇa and the rest; thus, "consisting of that" means consisting of the five elements.
The body is also like that; the practitioner of mantra should project the letters in reverse order upon it,
joined with their respective locations, and offer them into the supreme radiance.
Having thus performed the fire-offering (homa) consisting of the [five] colors, one becomes possessed of a divine body,
after having deposited the two mantras according to the rule upon the body of the Mother of the Universe—
she who is "of such a nature," meaning composed of the five elements.
Regarding the instruction "one should assign the phonemes there," the procedure is as follows:

having articulated the ten phonemes of earth according to the *prapañcayāga*, one should assign them from the soles of the feet up to the knees; in this same manner, one should assign them up to the element of space.
Regarding "in reverse order":
one should again assign the phonemes beginning with space (*ākāśa*) to their respective locations down to earth (*bhūmi*);
this is the visualization for the reverse-order assignment (*viparītanyāsa*).
Having thus performed the meditation, one should place [the mantra] in reverse order.
The phrase "thus" (evam) extends by analogy what was previously stated regarding the *prapañcayāga*;
the procedure there is as follows: one should place [the mantra] ending with the letter Ā, namely: *oṃ hrīṃ caṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ svāhā*.

The essential meaning is that one should perform the *saṃhāranyāsa* while meditating: "I offer the letter *ca*, its presiding deity, and its respective location into the consciousness delimited by them.

This is the traditional view, as it has been said: "Of my beloved, who rises from the *ādhāra*, the *udyacchakti*, and the *bindu*, and who swallows the moon at the tip of the mouth [of the *liṅga*]..."
"The practitioner who casts down the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, permeated by fire and moon, is liberated from all kinds of diseases.
