He states the first letters of the nine groups with the words *āyambarārṇāḥ*. Therein, when the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) is applied to *a* and *e* by the rule *vṛddhir ecaḥ*, the result is *ai*. Then, by the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*, when *āya* is substituted [for *ai*], the form *āyambarārṇaḥ* is established.
Of the classes [of consonants], namely a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa.
He states that the classes of letters have the elements as their essence with the words "space" (*vyoma*), etc.
The meaning is that the letters have the nature of space and the other elements.
— *Śāradātilaka*.
Virinchi, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Agni, Prajāpati, and the Lords of the Directions,
accompanied by their respective powers of action (kriyā-śakti) and so forth, shall be the presiding deities of the classes [of letters] in due order.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre;
and the deity is said by the wise to be the supreme Parā herself, the Mistress of the Letters.
One should form the six limbs with the six groups of consonants together with their respective classes;
one should meditate upon the Goddess within that lotus at the root of the tree of letters.
The wise declare that the tree is eternally auspicious and composed of phonemes;
it has the great seed of supreme consciousness and the great root of *bindu* and *nāda*.
The earth has expanded throughout all directions with its branches of imperishable syllables;
the three worlds are completely covered by the openings of the water’s falling syllables.
Blazing with sprouts the color of fire like a celestial tree with its jewels,
they enhanced the beauty of their bodies with flowers radiant as the colors of the wind.
Bowing low under the fruits of the sky-ocean, he is the supreme refuge of all beings;
he sprinkles the Supreme Goddess with the nectars known as the supreme ambrosia.
The repetition [of the word] is to be understood. The construction is: "they know the nine phonemes to be distinct and individual, having the nature of ether, air, and so forth.

To the question, "Since the last and the penultimate [groups] consist of seven and eight syllables respectively, how can they be said to have nine phonemes?", he says: "In the first reading, it was stated that the phonemes of each group consist of the five elements; however, this does not apply to the second and ninth [groups], and therefore he says 'the second... [and so on].
The meaning is that the intention is to show the possibility of both [types of syllables] in both cases.
Since the second group consists of four syllables, there is no syllable consisting of the letter *bh*.
Since the ninth group consists of three syllables, there is an absence of both.
The deity of the ninth group says, "Viriñci. The lords of the directions are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma. What are they all like?
They are endowed with the powers of action and so forth, being possessed of the three powers of action, knowledge, and will, each repeated thrice.
However, some maintain that there are nine deities: one as the Lord of the Directions (Digeśvara), and the three beginning with the power of action (Kriyāśakti).

"Hādī" refers to the heart by means of the third group [of consonants]. In this manner, the other [limbs] are formed by the others [consonants], ending with the eighth and the final [letters of each group].
The application is as follows: *haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Regarding the instruction "one should meditate": one should meditate on the syllables within that [deity's] lotus.
Having stated "of the smeared tree," he describes its essential nature with the word "eternal" (*nityam*),
because according to the Vaiyākaraṇa school, phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal.
*Parasamvit* is Kuṇḍalinī.
Some say it is the supreme Brahman.
"Śiphā" means the root.
If it is said to be eternal, how can its production from a seed occur?
It is treated as being like a seed by virtue of its manifesting power.
Chapter Six.
[The temple] is fashioned according to the Vedas, Agamas, and other scriptures, and is beautiful in its lofty elevation.
It is manifestly composed of Śiva and Śakti, and it supports the three worlds like a shadow.
Relying upon this, sages may attain all their desires.

I take refuge in Vāgīśvarī, the primordial goddess, who is proud of her youth and whose breasts are high and full like ten million crescent moons; whose head is marked by half a moon; whose eyes roll from the intoxication of honeyed wine; and who holds in her hands a precious jewel, a *japavaṭī* rosary, a *vidyā*, and a skull-bowl, while her body is adorned with the letters of the alphabet.
The best of teachers [should contemplate] in the locus of the support, the substratum, at the navel, the heart, and again the throat;
then in the point (bindu), the resonance (nāda), then in power (śakti), and finally in Śiva.
Having duly placed the nine vowels upon the nine supports,
the wise one should place the consonants beginning with *ha* on the body, starting from the face and proceeding downwards.

The best of instructors, with a concentrated mind, should place the letters of the five groups upon the arms, feet, and [the rest of the body] in the directions of above, Mahendra (East), South, North, and West.
"Ādhāra" refers to the region between the anus and the genitals;
"adhiṣṭhāna" refers to the penis.
In the *bindu*, at the midpoint between the eyebrows;
in the *nāda*, at the limit of the hair;
in the *śakti*, in the region above that.
"In Śivā" means in the Dvādaśānta.

"In the nine supports" (navādhāreṣu) refers to the nine cakras beginning with the Ādhāra as previously described. By the phrase "according to the rule," it is implied that one should perform the meditative visualization (bhāvanā) of each respective support.
For this very reason, although it was already stated [in the verse] beginning with "ādhāra," the expression "in the nine supports" (navādhāreṣu) is repeated.
The meditation on the supports (ādhārabhāvanā) will be explained in the final chapter.
By the term "the best of teachers" (deśikasattama), the fact that the phonemes are accompanied by the bindu (sabinduka) is indicated.
He explains that very point—what was stated as "from the source of vitality" (*ūrjādita*)—by saying "he consumes" (*jaṅkṣati*).
By the words "the wise one," it is stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed through the conceptualization of his own five faces.
By the word "composed" (*samāhita*), the presence of the nasal bindu (*bindu*) in the phonemes is expressed.
Regarding "doḥ-padi":

the best of teachers should place the letters of the five groups (pañcavarga) upon the arms and feet—in the sequence of the tip, the root, the base of the root, the tip of the base, and the middle—extending from the abdomen to the back; this is the connection with what follows.
This is according to the *Śāradātilaka*.
But by way of the sequence of the tip, the root, the base, the tip,
the middle, the region, the belly, the pair of sides, the navel, and the back, one is fully concentrated.
One should place the three groups of letters beginning with *śa* in the secret place, the heart, and the earth-element respectively;
in the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), it ends with creation, while in maintenance (*sthiti*), it consists of fire, wind, and water.
One should place [the mantra] of another, ending with the emission of the *bindu* (*visarga*) in the forward order of the limbs;
for the withdrawal, one should place it in reverse order, adorned with the *bindu*.
The supreme practitioner, initiated by the path taught in the scriptures,
should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) one hundred thousand times, recite [the mantra] that many times, and offer oblations of sesame seeds ten thousand times.
The wise practitioner should worship the Goddess daily upon the pedestal described previously;
he should offer a seat made of the seed-syllables and fashion the form with the root-mantra.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *mūla* (root/base), *agra* (tip), *tayoḥ* (of those two), *samam* (equal), *upamūlāgram* (near the root and tip), *agram ca mūlam ca* (the tip and the root), and *upamūlāgram ca madhyadeśaś ca* (the near-root-tip and the middle region).
Here, *agra* refers to the ends of the fingers;
*mūla* refers to the base of the shoulders and thighs.
The region from the elbow to the root of the knee is the *upamūla*; the region from the tip of the hand or foot to the first joint of the fingers or toes is the *upāgra*;
and the middle region consists of the middle joints at the wrists and ankles.

By the term *samāhita*, it is stated that because he is intent on meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he perceives the absence of any reversal of his state. By the term *deśikasattama*, the presence of the nasal bindu (*bindu*) in the phonemes is indicated.
*Bhrūvile* means in the middle of the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*).
The word "gradually" (*kramāt*) is connected to all instances, beginning with one's own [deity]. Here, it means "according to the sequence stated in this mantra.
Regarding the phrase "in the creation" (*sṛṣṭau*):
The remainder is that the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) ends with *sarga* (the visarga).
The connection is that during the state of maintenance (*sthiti*), one should sequentially place that [script] which ends with *bindu* and *sarga*.
In response to the expectation of what that sequence is, he says: "He emits" (*vanoti*).
In that regard, having placed each individual phoneme of the vowels (vaha) and so forth, one should place them again in that very same order.
The sequence there is as follows:
uṃḥ, iṃḥ, ṛḥ, aṃḥ, luṃḥ, oṃḥ, aiṃḥ, auṃḥ, eṃḥ, and so on.
"By that which is stated in the *Āgama* and by that which is proclaimed in the *Kulaprakāśatantra*.
"The initiate (*dīkṣita*) first"—this is the definition.
In that regard, "one placement (*nyāsa*) and one repetition (*āvṛtti*)" is the sequence; this is what is meant by the phrase "the best of practitioners" (*sādhakottama*).
Regarding the instruction "one should worship":

here, someone has said that because of the statement "having first laid out the pedestal" (*pīṭha*), the worship must be performed on an eight-petaled lotus alone—namely, twenty-two [deities] by a twofold repetition of the sixteen powers, sixty-four [deities] by a fourfold repetition, and sixty-eight [deities] by an eightfold repetition; otherwise, the rule "having first laid out the pedestal" would be contradicted.
That is not according to tradition.
In their view, the state of having eight enclosures (aṣṭāvṛtitva) would be contradicted.
An enclosure (āvṛtti), by definition, consists of worship as a surrounding protection on all sides;
that [enclosure] is accomplished in one way simply through the worship of the eight powers (aṣṭaśakti).
If a second eightfold application distinct from that is worshipped, it constitutes a different cycle of worship;
it does not, however, have inclusion within that [first cycle].
Nor has this ever been observed in other mantras.

In the traditional interpretation, however, the meaning of "one should first worship the *pīṭha*" is as follows: one should also worship here the *pīṭha-śaktis* and *pīṭha-mantras* mentioned previously.
This concludes the seventh chapter.
One should worship the Goddess in that [mandala] together with the limbs (aṅga) and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇa).
It is taught that first comes the enclosure of the limbs, and afterwards the enclosure consisting of Ambikā and the others.
The second is proclaimed by the Mothers; the third by the sixty-two Śaktis;
and the fourth and fifth are further proclaimed by the thirty-two Śaktis.
The sixth enclosure is said by the leaders of the world to consist of sixty-four Śaktis;
furthermore, the seventh [enclosure] shall be with their weapons, and the eighth enclosure [is formed] by these.
Thus should the Śrībhūtalipidevatā, the sustainer of the world, be worshipped;
according to the prescribed rite, one should worship her in the aforementioned locations and worship her limbs.

Ambikā, Vāgbhavī, Durgā, and Śrīśakti are to be worshipped according to the previously stated characteristics; likewise, Brāhmī and the others, as well as Karālī, Vikarālī, and Umā, are to be worshipped as before.
If Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti,
and Dhṛti were to emerge at that time, then the worship described for the six corners and other parts would be untenable;
furthermore, the meditation on the pedestal (pīṭha) as consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, the Mātṛkā, and a lotus would also be inconsistent.

If it were argued that the phrase "on the previously mentioned pedestal" means "as stated in the visualization," then, because there is no statement prescribing the worship of the pedestal, its power, and the pedestal-mantra, their worship would simply not take place; so, enough of this.

Therefore, having drawn here an eight-petalled lotus, a sixteen-petalled lotus, and an outer enclosure (bhūpura) with four gates, one should worship the previously mentioned pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśaktis) therein. Having offered the seat of the "worship of the letters" (varṇārcanāsana), and having mentally projected the form (mūrti) by means of the root mantra, one should worship the Goddess there. One should worship the limbs (aṅgas) upon the filaments as before, and above that, one should worship the four [goddesses] beginning with Ambikā on the cardinal petals, the [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī in front of them, and the [goddesses] beginning with Karālī on the sixteen petals and so forth. Regarding the phrase "worship of the letters": the formula is *hsauḥ varṇānāya bhūtalipiyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Regarding that form,
he explains the word "beginning with the limbs" (*aṅgādi*) with the words "at the beginning," etc.
He states the place of worship for the limbs with the words "in the locations," etc.
"In those spoken" means in those spoken by the Fourth (Turya).
By the expression "according to rule," meditations are indicated.
He explains the word "beginning with Ambikā" with the phrase "one should worship."
The meditation (*dhyāna*) for these [goddesses] should be investigated in their respective sections.
Regarding the meditation for the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjā*), he says "as stated" (*uktā*):
those whose characteristics have been stated, namely, those whose meditations were described in the previous chapter (*prākpaṭala*).
"As before" means in the previously mentioned locations.
He explains the words "Dvāṣṭaśakti" and so forth with the word "Karālī. "To be worshipped" refers to [the goddesses] in the sixteen petals. — *Śāradātilaka*.
Holding swords and shields, dark-complexioned, well-adorned, and worthy of worship;
they are Vidyā, Jñā, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū.
The thirty Rudras are Vīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣā, Ṛddhidā, Śubhā,
Kālarātri, Mahārāvi, Bhadrakālī, and Kapardinī.
Vikkṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Śikhaṇḍinī who holds a crescent moon, the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī, she who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Viśūlinī, and Pālinī; these thirty-two.
Ambikā and Hlādinī are remembered as the twenty-second group of Śaktis;
they have discs in their hands, faces like Piśācas, and are to be worshipped with beautiful ornaments.
Piṅgalākṣī, Vir̤ālākṣī, Samṛddhi, Vṛddhi,
Śraddhā, Svāhā, she known as Svadhā, Māyā, and Vasundharā.
Vilokadhātrī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Vidyeśvarī,
Murūpā, Bahurūpā, Skandamātā, and Acyutapriyā.
Chapter Seven, Verse 36: Vimalā, Āmalā, followed by Aruṇī and Āruṇī;
then Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Sṛṣṭi, Sthiti, and Saṃhṛti.
She is Sandhyā, Mātā, Satī, Haṃsī, Mardikā, Rañjikā, and the Supreme;
she is Devamātā, Bhagavatī, Devakī, and Kamalāsanā.
Vimukhī, Saptamukhī, and the other Surāsuravimardinī;
Lamboṣṭhī, Ūrdhvakeśī, Bahuśīrṣā, and Vṛkodarī.
36. After that, the one named Ratharekhā, then another called Śaśirekhā, followed by Gaganavegā and Pavanavegā.
Then there shall be the one named Bhuvanapālā; after her, Madanāturā;
then Anaṅgā, Anaṅgamadanā, and likewise Anaṅgamekhalā.
Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, Asurabhayaṅkarī,
Akṣobhyā, Satyavādinī, Vajrarūpā, and Śucivratā.
Varadā and Vāgīśā are proclaimed as the sixty-four [deities];
all of them hold bows and arrows, possess flaming tongues, and are of great splendor.
Those fanged goddesses with hair standing erect, whose minds are intent on the commencement of battle,
and who are resplendent with all ornaments, should be worshipped with great effort.
The world-protectors are to be worshipped as before, and likewise the vajras and other implements;
the mantra-practitioner who thus worships the deity of the Śrī Bhūtalipi [script] shall attain success.
45. *Śāradātilaka*:
He becomes the ground for the two Śrīs (Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī) and is saluted even by the gods.
Having offered ten thousand lotuses into the fire, he shall bring a king under his control.
46. By offering oblations with blue lotuses (*utpala*), one attains great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*);
by offering oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one becomes a poet within a year.
By means of an oblation of *rājī* and salt, one may bring a woman under one's control;
the practitioner should also perform here the rites mentioned in the *Mātṛkā*.
The person who, having encapsulated the mantra with the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script),
recites it a hundred times in both direct and reverse order, for him the mantra becomes perfected.
Having brought the Kundalini, which has the form of a sleeping serpent, through the central path to the supreme station, the knower of breath [unites] it with the supreme nectars.
One should flood [the body] from the head to the base; this yoga bestows all perfections.
One whose body is thus consecrated by this [mantra] becomes like the sun in brilliance.
Having understood the specific applications of the yantras, one should accomplish the rites.

Having joined the *bindu* to that very sky (*gagana*), conjoined with Śiva, and joined with the fourth vowel [i] and ending with *namaḥ*, this mantra is prescribed for the middle [of the rite], along with the bonds and the movements of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Regarding the phrase "having joined the *bindu* to the sky": the sky is *ha*; having joined the *bindu* to it, it becomes *haṃ*.
That very *gagana* (the letter *ha*) is accompanied by the *bindu*.
*Śiva* is the letter *e*; joined with that, it becomes *haiṃ*.
Here, by the word "Śiva," the number eleven is indicated, as there are eleven Rudras; this is the seventh chapter.
The wise one should write the letters of the verses, each syllable enclosed by the letter *ha*, with the remaining letters written on the petals; then he should encircle it all with a circle.
This "sky-machine" (viyadyantra) is said to be fashioned from lac and sandalwood;
when Rāhu rises in the constellation Rohiṇī, it destroys poison and grants all peace.
54. *Lacitā*. By her [the letter *la*], there is the eleventh vowel, which is the letter *e*; this is denoted by the word *śiva*.
Joined with the dative case of the word *jñāna*, that is, joined with the fourth (dative) singular ending, it becomes *jñānine*.
This mantra, which ends with *namaḥ* and concludes with *namas*, is prescribed for the center; the meaning is that it should be written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

For the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—such as Devadatta who is seized by poison and the like—one should write the letters of the elements corresponding to those [syllables] on the petals, together with the letters from the "Siddha" square (since it is said, "The Siddhas are declared to be the kinsmen"). One should write these elemental letters mentioned in this chapter, letter by letter (*akṣaraśaḥ*), encased within the letter *ha*.
The "last" refers to the ninth; therefore, on the eighth petal, one should write two elemental letters of space (*vyoma*), each encased within the letter *ha*.
By the term "intelligent" (matimān), it is stated that all syllables are accompanied by the bindu.
"All syllables are accompanied by the bindu"—so say those who know the tradition.
The action "O Devadatta, remove the poison, O Hari! is to be written in the middle.
*Lāctā* means lac-dye.
Regarding the phrase "at the rising of Rāhu in Rohiṇī":
here, the asterism (nakṣatra) current at that specific time is given; for the rising of each respective planet, the corresponding day-count (*tithi*) should be recorded.
On that day, the ninth muhūrta is Rohiṇī, and during the night as well, the eighth muhūrta is Rohiṇī. At that time, there is the rising of Rāhu; at the rising of Vāyubhūta, the rising of Rāhu occurs.
Since, in each individual sign, the rising of the five elements is fixed, the rising of the nine planets also necessarily occurs.
As it has been said: "The vital breaths (prāṇa), fire (agni), earth (bhū), water (ambu), and ether (kha) are the winds (pavana) in their respective order;
[these correspond to] Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Mercury, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun."
"In due order, among the four elements, space becomes the soul of all.
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "And the Guru says that in the northwest [are] Mercury, Mars, and Venus."
Mercury and the Sun are to be inferred on the earth; the Moon and Saturn are in the water.
One should know that space, along with the planets, is thus present in all the zodiacal signs;
three hundred and sixty breaths of the void constitute one nār̤ikā.
One zodiac sign (rāśi) is proclaimed to consist of sixty nāḍikās;
a day [of the sun] consists of the twelve signs beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces.
Within these elemental signs, the risings of the planets are to be understood.
Wind, fire, earth, water, and space as the fifth—
indeed, within each of these, five subtle elements arise.

The Śāradātilaka states: One should fashion [the mantra] with *yo* and *ho*, each joined respectively with the crescent moon upon the head of the goddess Sācī; in the center, one should compose *kopeśa* (Kopeśa) joined with *namaḥ*. Having written the syllables of Vāyu (*ya*) enclosed by *ya* on the eight petals according to the rule, one should place the remaining syllable on the final petal. This [yantra], encircled by the abode of Vāyu (*ya*), when situated upon a palm leaf, becomes effective.
In all the zodiacal signs (rāśis), the first channel (nār̤ikā) is Vāyavya;
the second channel is Āgneya; and the third is considered to be Pārthivī.
The fourth is to be understood as belonging to Varuṇa, while the fifth is remembered as being named Vyoman.
In all cases, those rising in the east are auspicious, whereas those immediately following them are malefic.
Rāhu, Mars, the Sun, and Saturn—these are auspicious when situated to the south;
Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—these gentle planets bring auspiciousness when situated to the left.
Thus has the rising of the planets within the zodiacal signs and the elements been described.
The rising of the elements will be explained in another chapter.
The asterisms suitable for the muhūrta have been declared in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): Ārdrā, Aśleṣā, Anurādhā, Maghā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, and Rohiṇī.
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Śatabhiṣaj,
Uttarā-phalgunī, and Pūrvā-phalgunī are fifteen muhūrtas in duration during the day.
The eight beginning with Pūrvabhādrapadā, namely Gatra, Āva, and Drī;
Punarvasu, Kṣaṇa, Puṣya, Śruti, and the three beginning with Kara.
*Śruti* refers to the asterisms beginning with Śravaṇā and those beginning with Hasta;
*tisraḥ* refers to Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī. This same principle should be applied to what follows as well.
Others, however, say that it should be performed when Rāhu is in the Rohiṇī asterism.
He states the Vāyavya yantra with the words "the two which... Here, *akṣi* means the letter *i*.
This is because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that when no distinction is specified, [the term refers to] the left.

The vowel *e* is the lower lip (*adhara*). The crescent moon is the bindu. The analysis of the compound is as follows: *acyadharī* refers to those [vowels] together with the lower lip (*aci* and *adhara*); those two, along with the crescent moon upon their heads (*indukhaṇḍaśirasau*), are thus described.

Because it exists in sequence, [it is said] "yiṃ yaṃ. Joined with "kopa" and "īśa," it becomes "kopeśāya. Accompanied by "namaḥ," meaning joined with "namaḥ," one should fashion—that is, write—this mantra in the middle of the pericarp (karṇikā).

The *vāyavya* [syllables] are those with the colors of the wind-elements as stated in this chapter; the meaning is that they should be enclosed in *ya*-boxes according to the prescribed rule, letter by letter.
They should also end with a *bindu*.
One should encircle them with a circle marked by six *bindus*, because it is said: "The abode of the wind is a circle marked with six *bindus* for Mātariśvan."
In this case as well, the ritual action (kamma) should be written down as previously described.
The Seventh Chapter:
Under Svāti, when Mars rises, one should bury a yantra at the northwest gate of the enemy;
it will cause his expulsion, or his death will certainly occur.

The fifty-six letters, joined with the pair *vīja* (the seed-syllables) in sequence, along with *śravaṇa* (the letter *sa*), *sadya* (the letter *ha*), and the half-moon (*bindu*), followed by *kharau* (the letter *ra*), *rauḥ*, and *phaṭ*—this is the mantra consisting of forty-four syllables prescribed for the center.

One should write the letters obstructed by fire (*va*) on the petals, nourished by the letters of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Finally, the circle of fire should be drawn within the interior of the birch-bark leaf prepared for this purpose.
When conjoined with an auspicious weekday and a favorable planetary aspect, this yantra— composed of lac and saffron—
is declared to be the "Agniyantra," which provides protection against all malevolent beings.
If that [name], mixed with the blood of a killer, is written on a cloth during the rising of Mars in the asterism of Kṛttikā using charcoal from a funeral pyre, it shall destroy the enemy.
56. "The water [element] with half-moon and nose, joined with that [number] and half-moon and end; at the end of the moon, 'namo' is declared for earth, and in the middle, the *manu* of the Varuṇas.
Regarding "at the rising of Mandi in Svāti":
when there is the rising of Mandi—meaning Śanaiścara—in the constellation Svāti, it refers to the rising of water and earth.
The grammatical connection is that one should bury the Vāyavya yantra at the gate of the enemy.
He says that the fire [seed] consists of *va* and *dbha*.
In the *Śravaṇa* [nakṣatra], there is immediately the lunar drop (*indu-bindu*).
Joined with these in sequence, there is a pair of fire seeds consisting of two *repha*s; thus, they are *ru* and *roṃ*.
The other form is the word *hanamaḥ*.
This mantra is prescribed for the middle [of the wheel], situated within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
It should be understood that each syllable is enclosed by the letter *ra* (repha) and conjoined with the fire-syllable (*vaḍbhi*).

In this context, because it consists of a single syllable, the "enclosure" (rodha) results in a "box" (sampuṭa). According to the statement, "The nourishing [syllables] of the object to be accomplished (sādhya) are to be understood as the well-accomplished nourishing syllables," the meaning is "by means of the syllables from the box of the well-accomplished.
The meaning is that the place for the nourishing syllables is mixed with the syllable of the slayer (ghātaka), situated within a triangle marked with a svastika and surrounded by fire.
Because of the statement, "Those who dwell in the enemy's storehouse are considered slayers," the letters residing in the enemy's storehouse are the "slayer-letters.
In Kṛttikā— that is, during the muhūrta of the Kṛttikā nakṣatra, at the rising of Mars (Maṅgala), meaning at the rising of the element Fire—
on that day, on the funeral shroud (citāvastre).
"One should destroy" refers to [objects] buried in the house and so forth.
He describes the Vāruṇa Yantra with the words "nāsā" and so forth.
"Nāsā" is *ṛ*; "arjendu" is the crescent moon; "bindu" is the nasal dot (*anusvāra*). That [syllable] joined with these is *vaḥ* (the water element).
With that, *haiṃ*. That same "water" (*ambu*) is *vaḥ*, and the "manu" is *au*; joined with those and with the crescent moon and the nasal dot, it becomes *vauṃ*.
Here, by the word *manu*, the number fourteen—referring to the fourteen Manus—is indicated.
By that [number], the fourteen vowels [are meant]; thus, the vowel *au* is denoted by the word *manu*.
A widow is one whose husband is dead (*ḍento vidhurvidhavā*).
In the *Viṣvanta*, which ends with the word *vidhu*, for the sake of the earth (*bhuve*), [one writes] the *Śāradātilaka* for the sake of the *viṣubhu*.

Having written the letters of the *Sādhya* within leaf-caskets (*patrapuṭheṣu*) using the letters of the *Bandhuka* [mantra], and having surrounded this with the city of water (*apapura*), this becomes the *Vāruṇa* Yantra.
One should write this on birch bark with red sandalwood water at the rising of the constellation Kārttikeya; then, subjugation and other such results will be achieved.
The syllable *gaṇḍa* (ṅa) adorned with a *bindu* becomes *vasumatī* (ṅm); one should place two such *vasumatī*s between the two *gaṇḍa*s. One should write the mantra *jagī lu ke na ti* in the center.

One should write the letters ending in *la* (*lāntān*) enclosed within the letter *la* (*lārṇapuṭīkṛtān*) upon the petals, joined with the syllables of service (*sevāvarṇa*), according to the rule; one should encircle it with the house of the earth (*bhuvo geha*).
When the moon has risen in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, an earthen vessel fashioned from red ochre will,
when used as a yantra, immediately cause paralysis in all things.
Whoever worships the eternal deity of the Śrībhūtalipi, who is more secret than the secret,
shall be filled with auspicious sons, wealth, and grain.

"64. *Namaḥ*. This mantra, *namaḥ*, is said to be in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), meaning it is stated as that which is to be written. "Encased by the syllable *va*" means enclosed by the syllable *va*; [the letters] should be provided with the nasal bindu for each syllable.
Together with the water-city, the side-lotuses, and the victorious moon.
The *vāruṇa* [nakṣatra] is Śatabhiṣā; at that time, when the planet Venus (*śukra*) has risen—that is to say, during the rising of the fire-quarter (*vahnimūtodaya*).
From the word "subjugation" (*vaśyādi*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), enchantment (*mohana*), and the like.
He describes the *pārthiva* yantra with the word "gaṇḍa. *Gaṇḍa* adorned with a dot is the syllable *lṛ*; *vasumatī* is the letter *la*, and that same [letter] with a dot is *laṃ*.
The two *ga* syllables situated between the two *ṇḍa* syllables represent the *varṣa*. Regarding the phrase "between the two *gaṇḍa*s":
here, first there is the mere letter *ga*, and subsequently the letter *ṇḍa* joined with the *parasavarṇa*; thus, "gaja-gaṇḍa" is established.
The nature of the letter Lu is salutation (namas).
One should write this mantra in the middle of the pericarp.
It has been stated that [the letters] ending in *la* are not [to be written] because of their non-uniformity and deficiency;

therefore, the meaning is that on the eighth petal, the three *la*-sounds accompanied by the bindu (*ṃ*) should be written. This applies to each syllable when they are enclosed within the *la*-sounds.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with the letters of service" (*sevāvarṇayutān*), the meaning is "by means of the letters of the *sādhya*-box," as stated in the passage: "Those to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are known as servants (*sevakāḥ*).
"According to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*) means "accompanied by the nasal bindu."
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the asterism of Jyeṣṭhā, when the planet Mercury has risen— that is, at the rising of the earth—
in a vessel made of clay (mṛd); everywhere, "the pillar-maker" (stambhakṛt) should be understood as the immobilization of wind, fire, water, semen, the edge of a sword, armies, and so forth.
In this regard, the wise should understand according to the specific context that "eating semen" refers to retention, while "burying in an army" and so forth refer to interment.
The Sixth Chapter. The mountain (dr) conjoined with Varuṇa (va), followed by the two words "O Speaker" (vādini), and then the two syllables Ṭha (ṭha-ṭha)—
this ten-syllable mantra of Vāgīśvarī bestows the power of speech.

65. Having thus stated the *mātṛkā* mantras, desiring now to state the *Sarasvatī* mantras which are derived from them, he extracts the ten-syllable *Vāgvādinī* mantra, beginning with "adrir" (*adrir*):
"Adri" is the letter *da*; it is "enclosed" (*saṃruddha*) by "Varuṇa," which is the letter *va*. By that, "vadava" is produced.
"Da-vāg-vādini" is its essential form.
*Ṭha-dvayaṃ svāhā*. Because it bestows the excellence of the power of speech (*vāgvibhava*), it is called "the Bestower of the Power of Speech" (*vāgvibhavaprada*).
By indicating its application (*viniyoga*) through this [name], many varieties [of its usage] are suggested.
Thus it is stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "This [mantra], encapsulated by the *tāra* (om) and *māyā* (hrīṃ), bestows the great Sarasvatī.
The teachers have extracted this from the praise [of the goddess] beginning with the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) and *māyā*.

Having uttered the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) and the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśvarī*) as "vadavada," one should meditate upon the eternal Speech (*giram*) thus: "O Vāgvādinī, svāhā! [I meditate on her] who has scattered the burden of sins through her syllables.
Some say that the seed-syllable of speech should be encased within the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*).
Others say it is "māyādya" (the first of the māyā).
In another tantra, even the one beginning with the pure vāgbhava is mentioned.
In this very context, some say that the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs through the messenger (dūtī), while others desire the reverse; furthermore,
in the *Prayogasāra*, even a young girl (*bālā*) and so forth is prescribed.

One [mantra] is encased by five *praṇavas* at the beginning; another is joined with the seed-syllable of Vālā at the beginning and in the middle, as well as at the start of *khāhā*; the next has the vocative case encased by the *vāgbhava* syllable;
and yet another has the vocative case encased by the two *vālā* syllables.
The fifth [mantra] consists of the invocation enclosed by the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM);
the sixth is preceded by SVĀHĀ and joined with BĀLĀ.
Thus, there are many other variations of this [mantra] as well, which have not been mentioned here for fear of making the text too voluminous.
These [mantras] are to be known from the respective traditions of one’s own guru;

as it was said by the teachers in the *Stava*: "O Sovereign of Knowledge, distinguished by the five *praṇavas* at the beginning and end, with a blazing trident in hand, O *Pratyaṅgirā*, you conquer and destroy the magical spells (*kāma-yantra-vidyās*) of those who hate your devotees."
O Goddess, at the end of the repetition, [the mantra] is joined with the *Samaśāyaka* (the *Kūṭa*), and likewise at its beginning, it is joined with the *Vāgbhava*.
At the end of the invocation, one should worship the *Vidyottamā* together with the eight directions and the moon; O Goddess, I am bowed before you.
Alternatively, the *Sārasvata-sampuṭa*—consisting of your name—may be placed between the two *Vāgbhava* seed-syllables.

O Lord of Speech, I bow to that certain Deity whose name is yours, the Sovereign of Words, who—though born mute—by sheer force produces poetry; who is eternally embraced by Kāmeśvarī; and who brings about the delusion of both men and women. To him, I offer perpetual salutation.
I offer my salutation to him, by whose splendorous compositions of unrestrained poetry the tongue of the dull-witted shines forth, blossoming with the sprouts of immortality.
Others say that there is an additional vocative address, "O Vāgīśvarī";
the specific details of their meditations are to be learned from the mouth of the Guru, as stated in the Śāradātilaka.
The seer is Kaṇva, the metre is Virāj, and the deity is Speech as it is uttered.
Having assigned these syllables to the head, ears, nose, mouth, anus,
and genitals, one should arrange the limbs as previously described according to the Mātṛkā.
The sage (*ṛṣi*) is to be known as *dhiṣaṇa*;
this was stated by Īśānaśiva: "The sage is considered to be *dhiṣaṇa*, while others know him as Kaṇva."
Thus,
"Vāk" is the seed-syllable (bīja), and "Svāhā" is the power (śakti); "Brahman" is the seed-syllable, and "Māyā" is the power.
The individual soul (*jīva*) is the seed and the intellect (*buddhi*) is the power (*śakti*);
*udāna* is the seed and *kuṇḍalinī* is the power.

This triad of the subtle seed and so forth exists in all mantras. As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The Lord is the seed of the worlds, while the unborn Power consists of the qualities (*guṇa*)."
The Supreme Self, as well as the intellect, the vital air, and the Kuṇḍalinī—
these fourfold seed-powers constitute this triad of commonality.
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "One should contemplate the fourfold seed-powers (*bīja-śakti*) in all mantras;
among them, the triad is common, and that is now being defined.
Īśvara is the primordial seed of the worlds; He is called Brahman."

His Māyā is declared to be that power which consists of the Gaṇas; he himself is the Blessed Lord, the witness of the intellect (buddhi). This is declared here as the second seed-syllable; the intellect is said to be his power.
The *udāna* conjoined with consciousness (*cit*) is called the third seed-syllable;
therein lies the power (*śakti*), Kuṇḍalinī. This triad is to be understood as common to all mantras; therefore, one's own seed-syllables and powers [are to be known].
Thus,
"anviti" refers to the *liṅga* (sign),
and "prāgvat" means according to the manner described in the fourth [chapter].

Those who know the tradition hold that the limbs [of the mantra] are joined with the vowels *aṃ*, *kaṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *ḍaṃ*, *āṃ*— namely, "to the heart, *namaḥ*" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), and so forth— whereas others consider the limbs to be otherwise.
Oṃ hāṃ vada ṛgveda, heart;
oṃ hrīṃ vada yajurveda, head;
oṃ hūṃ vāk sāmaveda, crest-lock.
Oṃ haiṃ vādini atharvaveda vaṃ me oṃ hauṃ svāhā— this is the six-limbed eye-mantra (netra).
Oṃ kraḥ— having uttered all the mantras, including the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, Itihāsa, Kalpas, Gāthās, and Nārāśaṃsīs— this is the weapon-mantra (astra).

This has been stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "One should fashion the limbs of the mantra in sequence with the letters *ya*, *ma*, *na*, *e*, *tra*, *dha*, *ra*, the two *va*’s, *kri*, the pair of *ga*’s, *la*, *aṇ*, and *man*, as well as with *ḍrām* and so forth, and the four [syllables] beginning with *veda*."
The teacher Padmapāda, however, stated that the limbs [of the mantra] are the Mātṛkās, saying "Salutation to the Heart," and so forth.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
She, possessing a brilliant luster, bearing a crescent of the young moon, her body bent by the weight of her breasts, is seated upon a white lotus.
May the Goddess of Speech protect us—she whose splendor is the lotus rising from her own hand, and who holds a manuscript in her lap; she who is the source of all prosperity and fortune.
One should recite the mantra one million times, and thereafter perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that number using white lotuses smeared with milk, or sesame seeds soaked in honey.
On the pedestal described in the *Mātṛkā*, the wise one should worship Vāgīśa;
he should offer a seat made of the letters of the alphabet and fashion the form with the root mantra.
Having first worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*), he should afterwards worship these Śaktis.
Yogā, Satyā, Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, and Prajñā— these should be worshipped according to the ritual procedure on the petals, holding a seal (mudrā) and a book;
and on the tips of the petals, Brāhmī and the others should likewise be worshipped.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped on the outside, and their weapons are to be worshipped even further outside them.

In this manner, the practitioner (mantrī), intent upon recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and so forth, being pure, devoted to celibacy, and having cleansed his teeth, nails, and other parts of his body, should perform the worship.
Constantly recollecting all women with the thought that they are deities,
the wise man obtains poetic skill and the earth within twelve months by means of the Śāradātilaka.
Having drunk water consecrated by that mantra, one should recite it a thousand times every day;
within a year, there is no doubt, one becomes a great poet through this mantra.
Standing in water up to the chest, one should meditate upon the orb of the sun.
One should recite the mantra one thousand and two times daily while the Goddess is present;
through this, one obtains from the mandala a perfection of speech that is peerless on earth.
One should perform oblations with palāśa and bilva flowers consecrated with honey.
Through these *samidh* sticks or through those [mantras] beginning with "utthā," one attains the glory of the Lord of Speech (*Vākpati*).
This oblation bestows all forms of fortune and the Goddess of Prosperity (*Lakṣmī*).
With flowers gathered from royal gardens that have been treated with honey, [this rite is performed].
One should offer oblations with its fuel-sticks (samidhs) and shall obtain incomparable poetic skill;
thus has the ten-syllable mantra been declared for the success of those desiring speech.
Following the end of the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should then utter the word "bhagavati" followed by a pair of the word "vada."
One should extract the mantra beginning with Vāgbhava (Aiṃ) and ending with Vāgdevī and Vahnijāyā (Svāhā).
He extracts another mantra: "Hṛdaya" (Heart), ending with "Namaḥ" (Salutation).
The seventh chapter [describes] the essential nature of the Blessed One;
the mantra consisting of sixteen syllables bestows the fruit of mastery over speech.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the six parts of the *mantra* along with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*).

I salute the goddess of speech (*Vāgdevatā*), who is radiant white, adorned with clear unguents, garlands, and garments, shining with a crescent moon, seated upon a lotus, possessing beautiful breasts, smiling gently, bestowing the power of eloquence, three-eyed, and the granter of good fortune and prosperity.
(82) One who subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should properly recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
At the end, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*), numbering one-tenth [of the recitation].
One should worship the Goddess on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as described in the *Mātṛkā*, according to the previously stated sequence.
Day by day, at the time of dawn, one should drink water consecrated with that mantra.

A learned minister shall become [effective] after eighty-four years; there is no doubt about this. One should consecrate oneself with waters over which mantras have been recited during the ritual of bathing.
Here, it should be understood that when the *visarga* of the word *namaḥ* undergoes the change to *ru* and then *guṇa*, it becomes the vowel *o*.
"Speak, speak"— this pair of words [is addressed] to you; O Goddess of Speech, "speak" is the remainder [of the sense], meaning "speak of your own nature."

That mantra which begins with the Vāgbhava (vāgbīja) syllable at its end, preceded by "Koṭṭak manurvadbhijāyā svāhā," is the one; some maintain that there is also the application of *ha* and *sa* here.
Others say it is the reverse;
by stating the application (*viniyoga*) with the words "bestowing the fruit of mastery over speech," it is also indicated that it begins with the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Here, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the power (*śakti*) should be understood as previously described.
The ṛṣi and so forth are also exactly as previously stated; thus, with six words, the first word is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and "vadavadeti" is the fourth.
Others, however, say that one should join the seed-syllable of speech (*vāk-bīja*) to each word at the beginning of the two words *vadavada*.

The explanation of "the auspicious protector" (*śubhatrā*) is the *vyākhyāna-mudrā*. Its characteristic is as follows: with the tips of the thumb and index finger joined, one should extend the other fingers and display them.
This very mudrā, gathered for exposition, is to be employed facing the person being addressed.
[Thus ends the section on] the rosary, the string of beads, the vidyā, and the book.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the right thigh to the end of the left thigh; she is seated upon a lotus and stands upon a white lotus.
"Correctly" refers to the previously stated rule for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
reciting eight hundred thousand times while keeping the mind focused on the meaning of the mantra without distraction.

As it has been said: "Reciting the mantra according to the prescribed rule with undistracted mindfulness, one should offer libations to her with pure water; thus one shall obtain supreme intelligence."
The wise person should wear all flowers, perfumes, and other such items consecrated with that mantra;
he will be honored by the virtuous in assemblies and shall be victorious in debate.
Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Adhara (Ā), Bindu (M), Śakti (H), Tāra (Oṃ), and Sarasvatī (Aiṃ).
The eleven-syllable mantra is declared to be both proximate and ultimate.

One should sequentially place the syllables of the mantra upon the aperture of Brahmā, between the eyebrows, and the nine apertures; the assignment of the limbs is performed with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable.

[One should meditate on her] holding with her own hands, with devotion, the bow and the full moon—her face radiant as the full moon—and possessing the luster of camphor and jasmine, with her head marked by the crescent moon.
I worship her who holds a lute, a rosary, and a jar of nectar, who possesses lofty breasts, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments, and who is seated upon a swan.
(86) The best of practitioners should mutter [the mantra] twelve lakhs of times, or offer oblations with white lotuses, or with nāga-campaka flowers, [accompanied by] a thousand repetitions. (90)

The seventh chapter: One should worship her upon the pedestal (pīṭha) as spoken by the Mother, according to the sequence to be described; one should prepare a seat with a lotus of the [deity's] color and fashion the form with the root mantra. || 61 ||
To the right of the Goddess, the Saṃskṛta Vādyayā should be worshipped; then, to the left, the Prākṛta Vādyayā, who bestows all accomplishments, should be worshipped.
Having visualized the limbs as before, one should then worship Prajñā and the others.
Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Śakti, Smṛti, Vāgīśvarī, Mati, and Svasti— these are proclaimed as the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī; thereafter,
one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) and, outside of them, their weapons.
Thus one should worship the Goddess; one will become Vāgvallabha (the Beloved of Speech) in person.
One should also accomplish here the rites mentioned for the ten-syllable mantra.
The best of practitioners should perform the worship here as well, just as before. || 65 ||

One should recite "vācas-pate amṛte bhūyaḥ plavaḥ plu" [and so on]; this mantra, beginning with "vāk," was proclaimed by the sages and consists of eleven syllables. One should duly perform the limb-prostrations (aṅgas) using the five words beginning with "vāk."
One should first install the Mātṛkā according to the previous procedure and in accordance with the rules.

[The goddess] Śāradātilaka sits upon a lotus, holding a rosary, two lotuses, and a book in her hands; she wears a crown bound with the young moon and possesses the luster of pearls, moonlight, and jasmine.
May the Goddess of Speech, whose eyes are half-opened by her brow, who is burdened by the weight of her breasts, and who is constantly attended by hosts of sages, grant you prosperity.
(68) One should mutter the mantra one million times; one should offer oblations of clarified butter ten thousand times.
One should worship her upon a pedestal fashioned from the Mātṛkā letters, as previously described. (69)
By offering palāśa flowers, one attains supreme accomplishment; likewise with kadamba flowers or those produced from the śrauṣṭakṣa tree. By means of kunda flowers, one quickly attains eloquence.

Or, by offering oblations with *nandyāvarta* flowers, one shall become beloved of speech. Having cooked tawny-colored clarified butter with the juice of *brāhmī* and a paste of *vacā* while reciting [the mantra], one should drink it at the beginning of each day; by doing so constantly, one will become a knower of the meaning of all scriptures.
Now, some maintain that because it is stated, "one should perform the limbs with five words," there are only five limbs here;
however, this is not sound, for by the injunction "one should perform the limbs" (kuryād aṅgāni), six limbs are indeed obtained.
When there is a desire to know how that [attainment] is described, the statement "by five words" is made;
the phrase "by speech and so forth" is for the sake of indicating the sequence.
If only "by words" were said here, the doubt would surely arise as to what those six [words] might be.

In that regard, the expression "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) is used in order to indicate [the procedure] both individually and collectively through concealment (*gopana*); furthermore, because it is impossible for the primary [number] to be sublated by the word "by five" (*pañcabhiḥ*), and moreover, where it is intended to be exactly so, it will be prescribed accordingly by such statements as "one should conceive of the five limbs of the mantra" (*mantrasya pañcāṅgam iti kalpayet*). || 86 || 87 ||
Regarding "in the lotuses": this refers to the visualization of the weapons, starting from the white [lotus] in the south below and extending down to the base of the right [hand]. || 88 ||

The meaning is that by performing one hundred and eleven lakhs of Rudra-japa according to the method previously described as "eleven times [the standard]," one shall attain the perfection of speech (*vāk-siddhi*).
The connection is that one soon attains the splendor of speech, that is, excellence of speech. "Nandyāvarta" refers to *gandhatagara*;
the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an option with *kunda* and *samuṅgava*. || 88 || 100 || 101 ||
Regarding "the juice of *brāhmī*":

here too, following the method of cooking with the fresh juice (*svarasa-pāka*), one-eighth part of the ghee should consist of its own paste, and four times the amount of ghee should be the juice of *brāhmī*;
the rest is as previously described.
In some versions, the reading is "vacākalpaḥ"; the connection is that one should cook while reciting [the mantra].
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "recited with this vidyā for seven days."
"One should drink daily at the beginning of the day" means for one year or five years;
all such [instructions] beginning with "by this vidyā" should also be applied to the *Brāhmopatra*.
Both [the results] beginning with "all" and those beginning with "intelligent" are the fruits of both, according to the distinction in the duration of the practice (*samaya*).
Thus it is stated in the seventh chapter:
"By means of this vidyā, one who has performed japa may consume the state of Brahminhood;
the wise man does not again forget the Vedas and Āgamas he has heard."
What need is there for much? This Vidyā is a wish-fulfilling jewel for those who recite it.
[The mantra is: Viṣṇu’s bed situated in water, together with the absolute four-faced one (Brahmā);
the Bindu joined with the intellect (S), the Fire (R), the Bindu, immediately followed by Water (V), and Bhṛgu (M). 103–104.
The wise have declared three seed-syllables (bījas) for those seeking the grace of Sarasvatī.
One should fashion the limbs [of the mantra] using these seed-syllables, doubled and joined with their respective *jāti* syllables.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "He who drinks the juice of the *brāhmī* plant mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, having chanted [the mantra] over it at dawn for three years, becomes a scholar (*khaṇḍaka*) in three years."

He indeed retains what is recited once, and what is spoken three times he does not forget for five years, even though it has been held in his mouth; even the tasting of its sprouts is remembered in this way—
thus it is the wish-fulfilling jewel.
By this it is indicated that when this [mantra] is recited, it removes eye disease even from one born of a noble lineage.

One who subsists on urine, having recited the *tithilaka* mantra eight thousand times, should offer oblations with *yoṅgolla* ghee; he [will know] the past, the present, the future, and so forth. (102–103)
He extracts another mantra: "toyastham" (situated in water).
Viṣṇu’s resting place is Ananta, whose form is the letter *ā*; "situated in water" means situated in the letter *va*, or by that [letter].
The letter *ka* has four faces; it is "with its own" (*sakevala*), meaning devoid of vowel. Some say that speech (*vāk*) is this very portion of the mantra.

As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "That which is the portion of the sword, tall, ending with the letter *vedhā* (the letter *dh*), situated at the end of the ear, and possessing a staff, is the serpent."
"Sāmbha" (the letter *sa*) with the dental (*da*) and the nasal drop (*bindu*); "Bhṛgu" (the letter *b*)—these three are the seed-syllables of Vāgīśvarī. Thus [it is said].
The commentator has stated that "vāk" is a portion of the mantra;
others, however, say that "ka" is the four-faced one (Brahmā) together with the bindu, and thus "kāṃ" becomes the seed-syllable (*bīja*) when provided with the bindu.
However, those who know the tradition maintain that the word "vāk" previously extracted is what characterizes the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable;
thus, its status as a seed-syllable is established and it becomes associated with Sarasvatī.
Others, however, extract the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable by means of a different method.

Viṣṇu’s reclining posture is situated in water; the syllable *ka* denotes the head, and by that, the syllable *a*. The letter *i* is its essential nature (*svarūpa*). In the compound of *ka* and *i*, the word *ke* is formed. Of what kind is the reclining? It is "with hair" (*sake*), meaning accompanied by hair (*kesa*). *Vala* is the winding or joining; when that occurs, the four-faced one (*caturmukha*) is *ka*, and by that, the head [is formed].
Then, "Bindu" is the letter *ū*; "Ardhīśa" is the letter *va*; "Vana" is the letter *ra*; "Sadya" is the letter *o*; "Ambu" is the letter *va*; and "Bhṛgu" is the letter *sa*.
By the phrase "for those seeking Sarasvatī," the application (*viniyoga*) is stated.
The first is the seed-syllable (bīja), the last is the power (śakti), and the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth are as previously stated.

May Śāradā protect us—she who is as pure as a string of pearls, adorned with a crescent moon upon her head; who, with her eight arms, holds a commentary, a rosary of letters, a jeweled pitcher, and a book;
whose waist bows under the weight of her high, swelling breasts; the sovereign of speech, long worshipped by the three worlds, seated upon a white lotus. (106)

One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and perform oblations with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*) in the consecrated fire according to its tenth part. One should worship Vāgīśī upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) according to the rite prescribed for the Mothers.
Following the path previously set forth, the best of practitioners, by offering *vyāghāta* flowers every day, shall obtain incomparable mastery over speech;
likewise, by offering *jāti* flowers and white lotuses sprinkled with sandalwood water. || 108–109 ||

Having offered auspicious *nandyāvarta* and *kunda* flowers, one attains mastery over speech; by reciting the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the practitioner of mantra attains victory in the assembly.
Or, having consecrated white *vacā* or *brāhmī*, one should consume it day after day.
The practitioner attains the desire for wisdom; there is no doubt in this matter.

When these mantras have been thus spoken, he who is initiated and possesses a restrained mind, and who worships in this manner with devotion, shall become a partaker of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the ritual for Sarasvatī, worship is performed with fragrant flowers that have been well-washed;
the *dūrvā* grass, the seed-sprout, and the flower produced from the royal tree (*rājavṛkṣa*).
Chapter Seven.
One who constantly resorts to Sarasvatī should avoid these: blue lotuses, sindhuvāra flowers, and aṅgāra;
likewise, the āmrātaka, gṛñjana, bilva, karañja, and garlic. (114)

Oil, onion, oil-cake, and even garlic should be avoided in one's diet; everything that has turned stale must always be discarded by one who seeks the grace of Sarasvatī. One should not consume betel-leaf at night, nor should one approach a woman during the day.

One should never sleep during the two twilights, nor utter anything while impure; one should remain silent during the evening watches and must not gaze upon a woman clad only in a lower garment. One should not approach a woman who is menstruating, nor should one revile a beautiful-eyed woman.
A wise person should not speak false words, nor should they step over a book.
One should not neglect or tread upon the leaves that contain the sacred syllables,
especially on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, on festival days, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, and during eclipses.
A wise person should never recite the Vidyā during any transitions;
furthermore, during the exposition, one should abandon sleep,
laziness, yawning, anger, spitting, and likewise touching the lower parts of the body.

Humans, snakes, cats, frogs, mongooses, and so forth—these, which are about to be mentioned, one should avoid in food; this is the connection [of the verse]. *Āmrāta* is known as *avāra* in the Kānyakubja dialect.

*Gṛñjana* is commonly known as *gājara* (carrot). *Kalañja* is a specific fruit with black seeds; it is called *kaliṅgaḍa* in the Gujarati language, *kharbujā* in the Gauḍa language, and *roḍa* in the Kānyakubja language.
Oil that is visible and unmixed with condiments and the like;
*śāṅgaṣṭa* means "with the thumb" in the Kānyakubja dialect. *Sāṅguṣṭha* is a corruption, because eating with the thumb is prescribed [as a rule].
As they say: "Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the *bali* offering—these must always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, they belong to the *asuras*.
Thus, everything becomes stale, even that which has been cooked in ghee.
The meaning of the injunction "one should not use betel at night" is this: one should not go to sleep having placed betel in the mouth during the night.
The Smṛti also states: "One should discard the betel from the mouth."
One who is naked, wearing the directions as her garment—even one's own sister. || 113||114||115||116||117||118||118||120||
